en: Now, therefore, begins the inquiry into Dharma.

It should be understood that those words which are well-known in the world for certain meanings should, where possible, be taken as having those very same meanings in the Sūtras. Their meaning is not to be imagined through methods such as ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), nor is it to be defined by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*).
For in this way, the Vedic sentences themselves are being explained by them.
Otherwise, the Vedic sentences would have to be explained, and their own constituent word-meanings would also have to be explained; thus, an excessive burden of effort would result.
In that regard, this word *atha* is observed in common usage to signify the commencement of what follows immediately after what has preceded.
And yet, no such event is perceived here;
nevertheless, there must be one, in the presence of which the desire to know Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) becomes possible immediately thereafter.
For in this way, that [event] is postulated as having its meaning established by common usage.
But that [qualification] consists in the study of the Veda;
for it is only when that exists that [the capacity for ritual action] is possible.
This is not so.
The inquiry into dharma would be appropriate immediately after any other action, and even prior to the study of the Veda.
If this were so, then the study of the Veda would not precede the inquiry into dharma;
for thus they prescribe: "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath."

And here, one who, having studied the Veda, is about to perform the ceremonial bath (snāna) while desiring to know the Dharma, might transgress this traditional teaching (āmnāya). Yet, the traditional teaching is not something that should be transgressed.
To this it is said: "We shall indeed transgress this traditional teaching."
If we were not to transgress [the Veda], we would be rendering this Veda, which is meaningful, as meaningless;
for its purpose is seen to be the instruction regarding ritual action (*karman*).
And the venerable ritualists do not declare that there is any fruit from the mere recitation of it.

And even as for that which they seem to prescribe, there too—regarding substances, purificatory rites, and actions, "the mention of a fruit should be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) because they exist for the sake of another"—it will later state that it is indeed an eulogy.
Nor is this immediate succession after the study of the Veda being prescribed;
for there is no word here that expresses such immediate succession.
For the suffix -ktvā is traditionally taught to denote anteriority in time, not immediate succession;
moreover, the visible purpose of study would be frustrated if it were understood as immediate succession.
This meaning, however, could only be obtained through secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

And this bath is not enjoined for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Rather, they say that by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it marks the conclusion of the observances such as bathing at the same time as the study of the Veda—according to the injunctions, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe" and "One should not return from the teacher’s house"—precisely in order to avoid the consequence of [the observances] having an unseen purpose. The word *ataḥ* indicates what has already occurred (*vṛtta*) in the sense of a reason (*hetu*), just as in the expression: "This country is peaceful and well-supplied with food; therefore, I dwell in this country."

Thus, it is understood that the Veda, when studied, is the cause for the desire to know Dharma; therefore, immediately thereafter, Dharma is to be desired to be known—this is the force of the word *ataḥ* (therefore).
For indeed, one who has not studied the Veda would not be able to investigate the Vedic sentences regarding Dharma.
Hence, for this reason, one should desire to know Dharma immediately after [the study of the Veda]; such is the meaning of the word *ataḥ*.
The desire to know dharma is "dharma-jijñāsā";
for that is the wish to know it.
Furthermore, how is it to be investigated? What is dharma? What is its definition? What are its means of accomplishment? What are the fallacious means? And what is its ultimate purpose?

In this regard, what is *dharma* and what are its characteristics? This has been explained by a single sūtra: "Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). What are its means of accomplishment, what are the fallacious means of accomplishment, and what is its ultimate aim? These have been explained by the "remaining characteristics" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*). As for where the person is the primary goal and where the person is subordinate—this sūtra, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), serves as a summary of these propositions.
Dharma must be either well-known or unknown.
If it is well-known, it is not an object of inquiry;
if it is unknown, it is all the more so.
Thus, this section on the inquiry into Dharma is either purposeless,
or rather, it is purposeful;
for there are many learned people who hold conflicting views regarding Dharma.
Some say one thing is the Dharma, others say another;
thus, proceeding without investigation and adopting just some [view], one might be frustrated and pursue what is harmful.
Therefore, the Dharma ought to be investigated.
For we maintain that it indeed unites a person with the supreme good;
this is stated as follows:
Dharma is a beneficial purpose characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā).

[Objection: But might not an injunction (codanā) express even an object that is not as it is, just like any ordinary worldly statement such as "There are fruits on the riverbank," which may be true or it may be false? [Reply:
It is said: this is a contradiction to assert that it both "expresses" and is "false."
"It says" means it expresses; that is, it causes one to understand, serving as the instrumental cause for one who is understanding.
And when that which has become the instrumental cause exists, one understands; thus, it "causes understanding.
Now, if it is understood from the injunction (*codanā*) that heaven results from the *agnihotra*, how can it be said that it is not so?
Now, if it were not so, how could there be comprehension?
To say that one comprehends an object that does not exist is a contradiction.
Furthermore, from the statement "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," it is not understood with doubt such that one might think, "Heaven either comes to be or it does not."
Furthermore, this [cognition], being apprehended with certainty, cannot be false.
For that which, having arisen, subsequently perishes with the thought "this is not so," is a false cognition.
But this [cognition] does not undergo subversion at another time, in another person, in another state, or in another place.
Therefore it is not false;
therefore it is not false.
As for worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses, that too is indeed not false.

Furthermore, that which comes from an untrustworthy person, or that which concerns a matter beyond the reach of the senses, originates from human intellect and is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
For it is impossible for a person to know such a thing except through verbal testimony.
If it is argued that it was understood from another human statement, that too is equal to the former case.
In matters of this kind, the word of a human being does not attain the status of a valid authority, just as the word of those born blind has no authority regarding specific forms of color.
But surely, instruction is not possible for those who lack knowledge;
yet Manu and others have indeed provided instruction.
Therefore, wise persons who possess knowledge [understand this];
for instance, it is understood from direct perception itself that form is apprehended by the eye.
Now, one might object: "But surely this must be an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*)."
Having observed that human speech is false, one might infer that Vedic speech is likewise false because it shares the common nature of being "speech.
This is not so, because they are different.
For when one thing is false, it does not follow that another must be false, precisely because they are different.

For indeed, Devadatta’s dark complexion does not entail that Yajñadatta must also be dark. Moreover, the inference that the Vedic word is false because it shares the same nature as human speech is contradicted by the direct perceptual cognition produced by the Vedic word.
Furthermore, inference that contradicts perception cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the object characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*).
If this is so, then that which brings about the highest good must be investigated.
"What is the use of an inquiry into Dharma? It is replied: that alone which brings about the highest good (śreyas) is denoted by the word "Dharma.
How is this understood? For when someone performs a sacrifice, people call him "dhārmika" (righteous).
And whoever is the agent of something is designated by that term, just as one who cooks is called a "cook" (pācaka) or one who reaps is called a "reaper" (lāvaka).
Therefore, that which unites a person with the supreme good is alone denoted by the word *dharma*.
This is true not only in common worldly usage, but also in the Veda:
"By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to Sacrifice."
Those were the first teachings.

Thus, they teach that dharma is precisely what is denoted by the word "sacrifice" (yajati). Here, both are indicated by the injunction (codanā): the beneficial and the non-beneficial. What is the beneficial? That which leads to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites.
What is "non-benefit" (*anartha*)? It is that which leads to transgression, such as the *śyena* sacrifice, the *vajra* sacrifice, the *iṣu* sacrifice, and so forth.
In that context, the inclusion of the word "benefit" (*artha*) is intended to ensure that what is called "dharma" does not include such non-beneficial acts.
But how is this [the *śyena* sacrifice, etc. a non-benefit? For it is violence (*hiṃsā*), and that is prohibited.

But how is this harmful act taught as something to be performed? It is said: the Śyena and other such rites are not understood as things to be performed [as ends in themselves]. For their teaching is that "this is the means for one who wishes to strike down [an enemy]"; indeed, they prescribe, "One practicing malevolent magic (abhicaraṇa) should sacrifice with the Śyena," but not, "One should practice malevolent magic."
It is said: this applies only where the meaning is understood from the sentence itself;
that is the case with Vedic texts, but not with the *sūtras*.

When the meaning has been understood from another source, it is then understood that "the *sūtra* has such-and-such a meaning," and because a single portion [of that meaning] is indicated by it, it is called a *sūtra*.
In this regard, it should be understood that these two are merely parts of two distinct sentences;

or alternatively, since it is stated that "dharma" is the state of being characterized by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) of an existing object, they have indeed a single meaning. [Now follows: "The investigation of its cause."
We have already stated that the knowledge of dharma has its cause in *codanā* (Vedic injunction).
That was stated as a mere proposition;
now we shall examine its cause: whether it is *codanā* alone or something else as well.
Therefore, it is not yet determined that Dharma is an object characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā). To this it is replied:

when there is contact of a person’s sense organs with existing objects, the resulting cognition is perception; it is not the means [for knowing Dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is currently present.
This is now examined: perception, for its part, is not the cause [of knowing Dharma].
What is the reason? For it has such a definition: "Perception is the arising of cognition when there is contact of a person's sense organs with what exists.
That cognition which arises in a person when there is a connection between the sense organ and the object—that is perception.
Furthermore, this object that is to come into being does not exist at the time of its cognition;
and this perception is of what exists, not of what does not exist.
Therefore, direct perception is not a valid means [for knowing dharma].
This sūtra is not intended to establish a definitive restriction among these options—whether it be cognition (*buddhi*), birth (*janma*), or contact (*saṃnikarṣa*).
What is restricted here is merely this: that [perception occurs] when there is contact between the sense-faculties and their objects, and not when there is none.
If more than one [of these factors] were being restricted, the sentence would be split.
And because inference, comparison, and presumptive testimony are preceded by perception, they too lack the status of being independent causes [of knowledge].

Even non-existence (abhāva) does not exist [as a separate means of knowledge], since: "The relationship between a word and its meaning is innate; the knowledge thereof is instruction, which is non-deviant regarding an object not perceived [by other means]; that is the authority of Bādarāyaṇa, because it is independent."
By "autpattika" (inborn), we mean "eternal.
For "origination" (utpatti) is used figuratively to denote "existence" (bhāva).
The existence of word and meaning is inseparable from their relation; it is not a relation that occurs subsequently after both have already come into being.

The innate relationship between a word and its meaning is the means of knowing that dharma characterized by the agnihotra and other such rites, which is not apprehended through perception or other means of knowledge.
How so? Because there is instruction (upadeśa).
"Instruction" refers to the utterance of a specific word.
And that cognition is non-deviant;
for once that cognition has arisen, it does not turn out to be erroneous.

And as for a cognition that, having arisen, does not turn out to be erroneous, it cannot be said, "This is not so," or "It is not as it is understood, nor is it as it is not understood. Rather, it is exactly as it is cognized, and it is not otherwise.
One thing might be in his heart while another is in his speech;
thus, for one who speaks in this way, a contradiction is perceived, namely that something both exists and does not exist.
Therefore, that [scripture] is a means of valid cognition, because it is independent.
For this being so, no other means of knowledge or another person need be expected;
for this [knowledge] is self-evident.
This view of Bādarāyaṇa is set forth in order to honor Bādarāyaṇa, not to exclude his own view.

The author of the *Vṛtti*, however, has explained this passage beginning with "the investigation of its cause" (*tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ*) in a different manner: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) need not be investigated;
for perception and the others are well-known as the means of valid cognition, and the scripture (*śāstra*) is included within them.
Therefore, that too need not be investigated."
Surely, because of the possibility of error (*vyabhicāra*), the causal basis must be examined.
For since even mother-of-pearl appears as silver, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is fallible; and because inference and the other means of knowledge are rooted in it, they too are fallible.
One who acts without such examination may be thwarted in his purpose and may sometimes incur misfortune.
When there is contact with that [object], the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is true perception (*sat-pratyakṣa*).
When a cognition has a certain object, the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs occurs only upon contact with that very [object]; this is true perception.
A cognition that arises from contact with one thing while having another thing as its object is not perception.
But how, then, is this understood: that "this is associated with that" and "this is associated with another"?
That which is not associated with another is associated with that;
the opposite of this is association with another.

How is this known? For when one perceives even a mother-of-pearl shell as silver, one thinks, "My eye is in contact with silver. Indeed, where a subverting cognition arises—such as "this is not so; this is a false cognition"—it is because [the object] was in contact with something else, whereas [the initial perception] was a misconception due to contact with that [silver].

How is it understood prior to the arising of the sublating cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), given that at that time there is no distinction whatsoever between correct knowledge (*saṃyagjñāna*) and false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)? When the mind is afflicted by hunger and the like, or when the sense organ is affected by cataracts and so forth, or when the external object is characterized by subtlety and the like, then false knowledge arises; when these are unafflicted, there is correct knowledge.
For the conjunction of the sense organ, the mind, and the object is the cause of knowledge, since in its absence there is no cognition.
A defect inherent within that [conjunction] is the cause of false knowledge.
For knowledge regarding that which is defective becomes false.
How is this understood? Because we observe correct cognition when the defects have been removed.

If it is asked how one discerns what is defective and what is non-defective: if, while searching with effort, we do not perceive a defect, we shall consider it non-defective due to the absence of any evidence for its being so.
Therefore, that cognition alone is incorrect for which the instrument is defective and for which there is the conviction that it is false, and no other.
[Objection: But surely every cognition is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream;
for the nature of cognition is observed to be without an objective basis in dreams.
Even for one who is awake, there arises a cognition such as "a pillar" or "a wall";
therefore, that too is without an objective basis (nirālambana),
though it is empty (śūnya).
How so? We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition;
moreover, our cognition is directly perceived.
Therefore, we see that there is nothing whatsoever called the "form of the object" that is distinct from it.
This might be so, if cognition possessed the form of the object; however, for us, cognition is formless, whereas the external object possesses form,
for that [object] is perceived through direct perception as connected with external space.
For perceptual cognition has an external object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain;
for being momentary, it will not persist until the time of another cognition.
If it were argued that "this [cognition], while itself arising, is known and makes another object known, like a lamp," that is not so.
For no one perceives cognition when an object is unknown; rather, once it is known, one understands it through inference. In that case, simultaneity is untenable.
Moreover, even if cognition were of a single form, it would simply be non-existent, but not so the object which is directly perceived.
Nor is there a single form [for both]; for we infer cognition to be indeed formless, whereas we perceive the object as having a form through direct perception.
Therefore, cognition has the object as its objective support.
Moreover, the cognition of a cloth occurs only when threads, which are its specific causes, are being employed;
otherwise, even when threads are being employed, a person with unimpaired sense faculties might occasionally have the notion of a jar.
But such is not the case.

Therefore, cognition is not without an objective basis; thus, perception does not deviate from its object. Inference is the cognition of an object not present to the senses, arising from the observation of one part of a known relationship.

That [inference] is of two kinds: that based on a relationship perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*) and that based on a relationship perceived through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasaṃbandha*).
Among these, an example of that based on a relationship perceived through direct observation is the cognition of the form of fire from seeing the form of smoke.

An example of that based on a relationship perceived through generalization is the recollection of motion in the sun, having observed that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by motion.
Scripture (*śāstra*) is the cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of words.
Analogy (*upamāna*) also produces a cognition regarding an object not present through similarity, just as the sight of a *gavaya* [produces] the recollection of a cow.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of a fact because a seen or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for; for example, the postulation of Devadatta’s presence outside—though unseen—based on seeing his absence from home while he is alive.

Even non-existence (*abhāva*), which is the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), [serves] for the sake of this object—the fact that [something] does not exist—which is not in contact [with the senses].
Therefore, because it is already well-established, its defining characteristic (*nimitta*) need not be examined.
Now, let it be granted that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others are indeed other means of valid cognition; however, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition.
Why?
Because it is without cause, since it is the perception of what already exists;
"crushing" refers to the pleasure of crushing at that very moment.
If it is argued that it will yield its fruit at a later time, we say no; we understand that the sacrifice does not yield its fruit at a later time.
Why? Because when it existed, it did not give the fruit;
and when the fruit arises, it no longer exists.

And how can that which is non-existent bestow [a result]? Moreover, it is heard that the fruit occurs at the very time of the action; this is understood from the statement "the sacrifice is the instrument" (*karaṇa*), for if the instrument has arisen, there must be an effect. Furthermore, we perceive another visible cause for the fruit. And when a visible cause exists, it is not possible to postulate an invisible one, due to a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, we consider that for the Veda whose transgressions have been observed in this manner, even such results as heaven do not come to pass.
Furthermore, some Vedic statement contradicts what is perceived;

having prescribed the "piling of the sacrificial vessels" (pātracayana), it says: "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world," thereby referring to the perceptible body.
And that [fire] does not go to the heavenly world;
for it is seen directly to be consumed [there],
and thus the word "goes" is not an injunction.
And a statement of this kind, which contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is not authoritative, just as, for example, "gourds sink in water" or "stones float.
Because of its similarity to such cases, there would be no confidence even in the injunctions regarding the *agnihotra* and other rites.
Therefore, dharma is not an object characterized by injunction (*codanā*).
"But the relation of a word with its meaning is innate; from that [relation] comes the knowledge [of the meaning].
This might be so—but there is no relation at all between a word and its meaning; how then could it have a human origin?
Why? If there were a relation with the meaning, then upon the utterance of the words "razor" (*kṣura*) and "sweetmeat" (*modaka*), one's mouth would be cut open or filled [respectively].

If it is argued that [the relationship] is spoken of with reference to a connection characterized by physical contact (*saṃśleṣa*), then other types of connections—such as those of cause and effect, sign and signified, substratum and superstratum, or kinship—are simply untenable in the case of a word.

To this it is replied: You do not specify that single relationship which is to be designated here; namely, the relationship between the signifier and the signified, which is characterized as that of the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*).

He asks: "If a word is expressive, why does it not express its meaning when heard for the first time? It is replied: "In all cases, our observation (*darśana*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For we understand that a word is 'expressive' only after observing the cognition (*pratyaya*) [it produces]; we do not understand it as such upon the first hearing, because the cognition has not been observed at the time of that first hearing.
Only after a word has been heard a certain number of times is there an understanding of its meaning."

Just as the eye, though it is not a seer [in itself], does not fail to see because it does not illuminate without external light, so too, if this were the case, the cognition of meaning would not be possible. How so? For meaning is not perceived in the cognition of each individual syllable.
Furthermore, there exists no other entity called a "collection" distinct from the individual phonemes, by means of which the comprehension of meaning could occur;
for when the sound *ga* is present, the sounds *au* and the *visarga* are not;
and when the sounds *au* and the *visarga* are present, the sound *ga* is not.
Therefore, there exists another word "go" distinct from the phonemes *ga* and so forth, from which the comprehension of the meaning might arise.
If it is argued that the cognition of the meaning occurs through recollection even when the word has disappeared, we say no;
for since recollection is also momentary, it is equivalent to the phonemes themselves.
The final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the signifier; thus, there is no fault.
[Objection: But even so, the common worldly expression “we understand the meaning from the word” would be untenable.
[Reply: It is said: if it is untenable, let it be untenable!

For a worldly statement cannot be accepted as authoritative merely because it is illogical; an object that is not apprehended through perception and other means of valid cognition cannot be asserted on that basis alone.
Worldly statements are seen to have both logical and illogical meanings, such as "Devadatta, bring the cow" and so forth, and "ten pomegranates, six cakes" and so forth.
Moreover, this [statement in question] is not at all illogical in its meaning.
From the phonemes arises the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), and from the mental impression comes the comprehension of the meaning; thus, the phonemes are the cause for the comprehension of meaning.

If it is argued that this word [“cause”] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*), we reply: no, the status of being a cause in relation to the phonemes is not secondary, because [the comprehension of meaning] exists when they exist and does not exist when they are absent.
Even if it were secondary, one cannot postulate a meaning that is not apprehended through perception and the other means of knowledge merely on the grounds that a word should not be secondary.
For when it is said, "The boy is fire," one does not conclude that the boy is actually the flame itself just so that the word "fire" might not be considered figurative.
Nor is the word "cow" perceived as something distinct from the phonemes *ga*, etc., because there is no perception of difference and there is a perception of non-difference;
for the phonemes *ga*, etc., are indeed directly perceived.
Therefore, the word "cow" (*gauh*), which begins with the letter *ga* and ends with the visarga, consists of nothing but the phonemes themselves;
there is no other entity called a "word" distinct from them.
[Objection: But even in the hypothesis of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), there is the postulation of something unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*).
It is said: [in the case of] verbal conceptualization, there is both that [conceptualization] and the verbal conceptualization itself.
Therefore, the syllables alone constitute the word.
Now, what is the meaning of this word "cow" (*gauḥ*)? We say it is the form (*ākṛti*) characterized by the dewlap and so forth.
Now, is it the case that the configuration (*ākṛti*) is something to be established, or not? Being perceptible, it cannot be something to be established;
for indeed, "the *rucaka*," "the *svastika*," and "the *vardhamānaka*" are seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If you say this is a delusion, no.
It cannot be said that there is delusion regarding the reversal of conditions.
Therefore, Jaimini’s statement that "the word-meaning is the form" (ākṛti) is logically established.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate more precisely later on how it is that the form is the meaning of a word.
Now, what is this "relation" (saṃbandha)? It is that when a word is understood, its meaning is understood.
However, it has been previously established that this [relation] is artificial (kṛtaka).
Therefore, we consider that the Vedas were composed by some person who, having established a relation between words and their meanings, set them forth for the purpose of worldly communication.
This is now stated: "Because the relationship is not of human origin, it is established.

But how is it understood that this relationship is not of human origin? Because there is no person who could be its creator. How is it that there is no such creator? Because of the absence of perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because the other means of knowledge are preceded by it.
No;
for if a person were to establish a convention and then employ it in linguistic usage, he would necessarily have to remember it at the time of usage.
For an objective purpose is accomplished when there is agreement between the creator and the user of the convention, not when there is disagreement.

For indeed, by means of the term *vṛddhi*, those beginning with *ā*, *ai*, and *au* would not be understood by one who is not a follower of Pāṇini, nor by one who does not accept Pāṇini’s composition;

likewise, even by means of the letter *m*, a triad consisting entirely of long syllables (*sarvaguru*) would not be understood by one who is not a follower of Piṅgala, nor by one who does not accept Piṅgala’s composition.
Therefore, both the author and the user must reach a common understanding.
Therefore, those who employ the Vedas must necessarily remember the author of the relationship [between word and meaning] and of the linguistic usage itself.
For if the author of the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" were forgotten, one could not comprehend anything such as "that which has *vṛddhi* among its initial vowels is called *vṛddha*.

Thus, from the fact that [the author] is not remembered, we understand that the Vedas were not composed by anyone for the sake of linguistic usage after first establishing the relationship [between word and meaning].

Even if forgetfulness were possible, we could not establish a creator of the relationship without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as we do not accept the existence of a rabbit's horn merely because something that exists might be unperceived;
therefore, the relationship between a word and its meaning is authorless (*apauruṣeya*). [Objection: But surely we could establish the creator through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

For we do not observe anyone comprehending a meaning from a word for which no connection [to that meaning] has been established. If they were indeed to comprehend it, they would comprehend it even upon hearing it for the first time.
If you argue that because such comprehension is not observed, there must necessarily be a connection, we say: no.
It is like the case of one who possesses supernatural powers (*siddhavat*), because of the instruction:
"Just as in this region the word 'cow' refers to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, so it is in all inaccessible places as well.
How could many persons who establish the relationship [between word and meaning] ever come together?
Even a single one would not be capable [of producing it];
therefore, there is no connection.
Another says: "And there is no distinction."
Indeed, there is no time apart from the act of relationship in which not even a single word was ever connected with any meaning.
Why? Because the very act of establishing a relationship is impossible;
for one who establishes a relationship must necessarily do so by means of some word.

By whom was that [relation] which would effect [the understanding] itself created? If it were created by someone else, then by whom was that [second person] created? "By whom was that one?"—thus there is no end to the regress.
Therefore, this person who establishes the relation must necessarily admit that some words have their relations already established through the usage of elders (*vṛddha*).
If such establishment through usage exists, then there is no necessity for a creator of the relation; thus, even presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) does not apply.
It might be argued: "How can children, for whom the relationship [between word and meaning] is not yet established, understand it from the elders?
Indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is observed.
For we do observe children understanding from elders; however, they do not understand without having previously grasped the relationship, nor do they grasp the relationship of its creator.
Therefore, there is indeed a distinction:
when the object is not perceived,
that [cognition] is a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), because it is independent.
For this being the case, it does not depend upon another person or another means of cognition;
therefore, dharma is characterized solely by the Vedic injunction (codanā) and not by any other characteristic.
The mention of Bādarāyaṇa has already been explained.

Now, as for what was said—that sound is without a cause because its fruit is not seen at the time of the action, and because the action no longer exists at a later time, and thus there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it—it is replied: it would not be a means of valid cognition if there were only five means of valid cognition;
for whatever by which something is correctly cognized, that is a means of valid cognition.
An object is also cognized by means of verbal testimony; therefore, verbal testimony is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Nor does something become "not cognized" merely because it is not cognized by one means of knowledge after having been cognized by another. Furthermore, it is not heard [in scripture] that the fruit arises immediately upon the completion of the ritual act; rather, the fruit is attained *by means of* the ritual act.
As for the claim that there exists another perceptible cause for the fruit at a later time, this is not a fault;
for in that case, both that very [prior action] and the sound are the causes.

As for the statement that was put forward as being contradicted by perception—namely, "This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world," which points to the body as being perceptible—it is replied:
because of its connection with the body, he to whom that body belongs is also called "equipped with the sacrificial implements" by virtue of those implements.
He asks: "Who is this other [person]? We do not perceive him."
He asks: "On what basis is there this conviction that there exists a possessor of pleasure and so forth who is distinct from pleasure and the rest?
For we do not perceive its own nature apart from the rejection of pleasure and the rest;
therefore, it does not exist, like the horn of a hare."
Now it is said: "In the absence of that [self], whose are pleasure and so forth? We shall reply: "They belong to no one at all.
For it is not the case that whatever is perceived must necessarily have a possessor.
When both a relation and a related entity are perceived, it is understood that "this is the related entity of that.
For instance, having perceived the moon or the sun, one does not search for another related entity by asking, "To whom does this belong?
It is determined that it belongs to no one at all.
Therefore, there is no possessor of pleasure and so forth other than those very qualities themselves.

Now, if one must necessarily postulate a related entity for that which is perceived, then having perceived even the self in this manner, we would have to search for yet another related entity, asking "to whom does this belong?
Having postulated that one, and having postulated yet another, there would be an infinite regress.

Now, having postulated one thing, you will not postulate another related entity; you will stop at that much and be satisfied with that alone. Therefore, being satisfied with consciousness itself, you ought to stop right there. To this it is replied: if there is no knower other than consciousness, then who is said to "know"? The designation of an agent of cognition is logically established by this word [“knower”].
Thinking, “This word must be made meaningful,” we shall postulate a self distinct from consciousness.
It is said: we perceive the self through desire.
How so? For desire arises toward an intended object previously perceived, not toward one never before perceived.
Just as, for example, there is no desire in us regarding the sweet fruits of trees that exist to the north of Mount Meru and have never been perceived by those of our own kind.
Indeed, when an object has been perceived by one person, a desire does not arise in another who has not perceived it;
yet, when something was perceived on one day, a desire arises on the following day.
Therefore, we understand that this desire shares the same agent as that perception.
If this mere consciousness alone were the perceiver, then once it had perished, whose desire would there be on the following day?
On the other hand, if the knower were eternal and distinct from consciousness, then he who was the perceiver on one day would be the very same person desiring on the next day;
otherwise, desire would be impossible.
Here he says: "In what respect do we have the conviction that [something] is untenable? It is that which is not apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
We do not perceive anything other than consciousness (*vijñāna*);
and that which we do not perceive, we understand to be non-existent, just like the horn of a hare."

Nor is the existence of consciousness untenable in the absence of that [self], precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception. Its momentariness is likewise established by means of direct perception itself. Furthermore, even in the absence of a knower distinct from consciousness, and given that consciousness is impermanent, the desire [to know] on a subsequent day is not untenable, precisely because it is apprehended through direct perception.
Indeed, it has never been observed that the very same person who was perceived on one day is sought out on the next.
What is observed, however, is this: in some cases one person desires what was seen by another, while in other cases they do not;
within the same continuum one person desires it, whereas in a different continuum one does not.
Therefore, there is no other [self] distinct from pleasure and so forth.
To this, he replies: "Recollection, like desire, is also [explained thus]:
a cognition similar to a previous cognition, or a cognition having the object of a previous cognition, is called recollection."
And that [memory] is not impossible even when the perceiver has perished, because it is directly perceived as arising on a subsequent day.
The cognition of one aggregate-mass by means of another aggregate-mass is apprehended by another [person] born from that same continuum, but not by one not born from that continuum.
Therefore, the aggregate-masses are empty.
Now, regarding this matter, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "A mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death.
To this it is replied: This is not so.
For when something was seen on one day, there arises on another day the cognition: "I saw this."
And this occurs with respect to the inner self (pratyagātman), not with respect to another;
for that which was seen on another day is "another.
Therefore, there exists someone else distinct from that [body], upon whom this word "I" rests.
He said: "The word 'I' is also seen used figuratively for another, as in: 'I am indeed the son,' 'I am indeed Devadatta,' or 'I am indeed going.
He replied: "If there is a knower other than consciousness, let that be pointed out apart from consciousness—showing it to be 'this' or 'of such a nature.
But it cannot be pointed out."
Therefore, there is nothing other than that. To this it is replied: it is self-cognizable;
it cannot be seen by another.
How might this be demonstrated?

Just as a certain person with sight perceives form for himself but is unable to demonstrate it to another who is blind from birth—and yet, one does not conclude that it does not exist simply because it cannot be demonstrated—so too, this person perceives the self for himself but is unable to show it to another, because that other observer lacks the capacity for vision regarding that person.
That other person, too, perceives the self for himself, but not the self of another.
Therefore, all [beings] certainly exist, perceiving themselves by their own respective selves, even though they are not perceived by other persons.
Regarding this point, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "When speech has become silent, what light does this person have? 'The light of the Self,' O Saṃrāj," he said.
And regarding the fact that he is not perceived by another, there is also a Brāhmaṇa passage: "He is ungraspable, for he cannot be grasped."
This statement is intended to mean that [the self] is not perceived by another.
Why? Because of the declaration of its being self-luminous.
Regarding this, there is also a Brāhmaṇa passage: "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous."

That he who perceives for himself is not other than that person—this too is inferred from human activity; namely, when a person exerts effort on the following day toward the completion of tasks half-finished the previous day and toward the performance of remaining duties, it is understood from such activity that he certainly perceives the eternal within the non-eternal.

And it is taught by way of analogy: "Just as you yourself perceive your own self, understand through this analogy that I also perceive it in exactly the same way"—just as someone might describe their own sensation to another, saying, "It is as if I am being burned," "It is as if I am being struck," or "It is as if I am being obstructed.
Therefore, because it is perceived by oneself, there exists a person distinct from those [sensations].
As for what is said—"Setting aside consciousness, let that [object] be demonstrated"—if you are indeed negating the means itself, it is impossible to attain the goal without the means.
This is precisely the method regarding objects to be known: that by which something is known is the nature of that thing.
For example: what is called "white"? It is that in which whiteness exists.
What is this so-called whiteness? It is that wherein the word "white" is applied. Where is its application? It is that which is cognized when the word "white" is uttered.
Therefore, it is impossible to demonstrate the form of anything by setting aside consciousness.

Now, regarding what was said—that "this mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death"—to this it is replied: [Yājñavalkya] first raised an objection, saying, "In this very matter, the Blessed One has led me into utter confusion," and then, having denied that his statement intended such utter confusion, he explained its meaning: "Verily, I do not speak of confusion; for this Self, O Maitreyī, is indestructible and of a nature that does not perish; however, it comes into contact with the material elements (*mātrā*).
Therefore, it is not mere consciousness. Thus, there is a difference [between the two views].
As for what was said—that "he does not go" is not an injunctive word—let it not be an injunctive word;
it will be a restatement of what is already understood from another scriptural passage, namely, "one who desires heaven should sacrifice.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Some [maintain that it is] action, because it is seen there.
It has been stated that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal;
however, that is untenable because the word is non-eternal.
Once a word has perished, it is impossible for an uncreated relationship to arise again between this newly produced word and its meaning.
For no one understands a meaning from a word heard for the first time.
How, then, is sound impermanent? Because it is perceived at a time subsequent to effort.
Therefore, because it follows immediately upon effort, it is understood that the sound is produced by that [effort].
But could it not rather manifest it?
We say: no.
For there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for its existence prior to its manifestation;
and it is that which exists which is manifested, not that which does not exist, because [the latter] lacks a locus.
Because of the word "karoti" (he does).
Moreover, speakers employ such expressions as "make a sound" and "do not make a sound"; they certainly do not understand that "this very same sound" [is being referred to].
Furthermore, [the sound] occurs simultaneously in different beings.
Furthermore, we perceive sound simultaneously in various locations; this would be impossible for a single, eternal entity.

Since there is no distinction [in its nature], an eternal thing cannot possess multiplicity. However, in the case of many effects produced in various locations, their connection with multiple places is logically consistent.
For this reason also it is impermanent,
as is the case with both the primary cause and its transformation.
Moreover, they explain that in the case of "dadhy atra," the vowel *i* is the original form (*prakṛti*) and the letter *y* is the modification (*vikṛti*).
That which undergoes modification is impermanent;
furthermore, a similarity between the vowel *i* and the letter *y* is perceived, and by this also their relationship as original form and modification is indicated.
And its increase occurs through the abundance of performers.

Moreover, when it is uttered by many people, a great sound is heard. If that sound were merely manifested [rather than produced], it would be perceived as being of the same magnitude whether uttered by many or by few.
Therefore, we consider that surely some part of it is produced by each individual, such that through their accumulation this great sound is perceived.
But there, the vision is equal.
By the word "but" (tu), the position is reversed. As it was stated— that this [sound] is produced because it is perceived at a time subsequent to an effort—
if we are able to state the permanence of sound through a clear reason, then, by the force of the cognition of permanence, it will follow that it is manifested by effort.
If it is unmanifest prior to its utterance and is manifested through effort,
then this is the same for both positions;
[the reason for] the non-perception of that which exists is the non-arrival at the sense-object.
As for the further reason stated— that [the word] perishes as soon as it is uttered— even here,

if we are able to clearly demonstrate its permanence, then, by the force of that notion of permanence, we shall postulate some cause for its occasional perception and occasional non-perception upon seeing them.
And since that [perception] occurs when conjunction and disjunction exist, we shall maintain that conjunction and disjunction alone are the manifesters.
If it is argued that sound is heard when conjunction and disjunction have ceased,
this is not so;
for conjunctions and disjunctions do not truly cease, since sound is perceived [to arise from them].
"For they [the conjunctions and disjunctions] are not perceptible.

If sound is merely manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions and not produced by them, then—since sound has space (*ākāśa*) as its locus and space is unitary, such that this very auditory space here is the same as that in other locations—a sound manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions occurring in Śrughna would also be perceived in Pāṭaliputra.
But this is not the case.
For the air-molecules impelled by a blow, striking against other stationary air-molecules, produce conjunctions and disjunctions in all directions;
they persist as long as the momentum lasts.
And because air is imperceptible, those conjunctions and disjunctions are not perceived.
Sound is perceived only while those [causes] have not ceased, and not when they have ceased;
therefore, there is no fault.
For this very reason, sound is perceived from a distance when carried by a favorable wind.
The ultimate [result] of the application.
Furthermore, another reason has been stated: users of language employ such expressions as "Make a sound" and "Do not make [a sound].
If sound were undoubtedly eternal, the expression would have to be "Make the use of sound," just as one says "Make [a cake] from cow-dung" when referring to its production;
[the objection that] simultaneity [of sound] is like that of the sun [is also untenable].
Furthermore,
it is not unreasonable that the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air— which is itself imperceptible— are not perceived when they manifest in the region of the ear-cavity.
For this very reason, the delusion arises that sound exists in various locations.
And sound has space as its location;
furthermore, space is one.
For this reason also, [sound] does not exist in multiple locations.
Moreover, if there were a single form [of the word], then while it may be granted that the locations themselves are distinct due to the difference in place, the word is not.
Therefore, this too is not a fault;
the letter is not subject to modification.
And in the case of "na ca dadhyatra" (and not "dadhya atra"), there is no relationship of material cause and modification;
the letter *y* is a different sound from the letter *i*.

For those employing the letter *y* do not take up the letter *i* as their material cause, just as those wishing to weave a mat do not take up *vīraṇa* grass [as the material cause for a mat made of reeds].
Nor is something called a "prakṛti" (material cause) or a "vikṛti" (modification) merely by seeing a similarity;
for indeed, upon seeing a basket of curd and a basket of kunda flowers, one does not perceive a relationship of material cause and modification between them.
Therefore, this too is not a fault.
It is intent upon the increase of the sound (nāda).
But it must be eternal, because its manifestation is for the sake of another.
Sound ought to be eternal.
Why? Because its manifestation is for the sake of another.
"Manifestation" means utterance; it is for the sake of another, that is, to convey meaning to another.
For if a sound perishes as soon as it is uttered, one [sound] would not be able to convey the meaning to another;
therefore, it would not be uttered for the sake of another.
On the other hand, if it does not perish, then it is logical that the comprehension of the meaning occurs because it has been perceived many times.
If it is argued that meaning is understood through similarity to something meaningful, we say no;
for nothing is meaningful, since all [words] are new.
If it is argued that there will be an artificial connection for some prior word, [we reply: no.
It has been said that when something is understood to be "similar," the cognition might be diverted due to delusion, just as the cognition of a "garland" is diverted from the word "mālā.
If it is argued that—just as the cognition of "possessing a dewlap and so forth" does not cease upon hearing the word *gāvī*—the same will happen here; [we reply:
for there was no desire to utter the word *go* in that context.
In this case, there is no desire to utter another word,
nor is it possible to accomplish both linguistic usage and the connection with meaning through a single effort of utterance.
Therefore, because the act of perception is for the sake of another, the word is eternal.
Because [the cognition] occurs simultaneously everywhere.
Because of the non-existence of number.

People say, "The word 'cow' has been uttered eight times," not "eight words 'cow' [have been uttered]. What follows from this? If it is so, it is understood from this statement that they recognize [the same word].
We, for our part, recognize [the object]; it is not due to any deficiency in our sense organs.
Likewise, others also recognize it, thinking, "This is that very same thing."
Just as we do, others who recognize [the person] ought not to say that it is someone else.
Now, if it is thought that, despite there being difference, they will say "it is he" because they are deluded by similarity—
that is not so.
For they do not perceive [the object] as "this is similar to that," but rather as "this is that very same thing.
And since their distinctness is clearly known, it is understood that [the notion of identity] is a delusion;
for there exists neither perception nor any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to the effect that "this is not different [from that]."
Because of its independence.
Even among those substances whose origin is not perceived and whose mere existence is observed, the impermanence of some is understood when a cause of their destruction is apprehended.

For example, having seen a new cloth, and having neither perceived it being made nor [otherwise] understood its impermanence, one nevertheless realizes its impermanence upon seeing its form alone; one understands that "this [cloth], produced by the conjunction of threads, will perish through the destruction of the conjunction of threads or through the destruction of the threads."
No such cause for sound is apprehended by which it could be understood that it will perish upon its destruction;
furthermore, because there is no manifestation of a conjunction [of sound].
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
And there is indeed an indicative mark [for this], namely: "by speech, eternal and multiform.
For this sentence, being devoted to another purpose, restates the eternity of speech.
Therefore, sound is eternal.
Or rather, they would not be expressive at the time of origination, because the meaning does not have that as its cause.
Even if the word and its relation to the meaning are innate and eternal, nevertheless, Dharma is not characterized by *codanā*.
For *codanā* is a sentence;
indeed, from the sentence "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," it is not understood from any single word alone that heaven results from the Agnihotra.
But comprehension occurs when three words have been uttered;
and there is no fourth word here other than this collection of three words.
Nor does such a collection exist in the world, from whose usage the meaning could be understood.
These words have been employed [in common usage], and their meaning is eternal;
however, the aggregate [of sounds] has not been so employed.
Therefore, the meaning of the aggregate is either artificial or a mere delusion.
Nor is the meaning of the sentence merely the meanings of the individual words;
for a word functions with respect to the universal (sāmānya), whereas a sentence functions with respect to the particular (viśeṣa).
Furthermore, the universal is one thing, and the particular is another.
Nor can the meaning of a sentence be understood from the meanings of individual words, because there is no connection between them.
If one could understand another meaning when some word-meaning is understood despite the absence of a connection, then everything would be understood whenever a single thing is understood;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is something else:
"Today, in the groves of blue lotuses,
the kādamba birds, moving about with beautiful cries and clothed in blue silk, seem as if they are perishing."
Therefore, even the Vedic [texts] are composed by a person.
Therefore, the collection [of words] regarding beings is for the purpose of action, because the meaning [of the Veda] has that as its cause.
It is the utterance, for the sake of action, of words existing [as] those very word-meanings (*padārtha*) of beings;
a sentence is not established as having a distinct meaning independently of, or separately from, the word-meanings.
Why?
Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). There is no valid means of cognition by which we might measure [this];

for a word-final phoneme that does not depend on the word-meanings and is devoid of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes has no capacity to function toward a meaning distinct from the word-meanings.
In common usage, there would be a close proximity of application due to the restriction [of the term].

In the case of worldly matters, however, having perceived an object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), a restriction (*sanniyama*)—that is, a fixed connection (*sannibandhana*)—can be established there; such are sentences like "Today [there are] forests of blue lotuses.
Therefore, from the very words "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," those meanings which are understood, from them alone this is understood: that heaven results from the Agnihotra.
From words alone arises the cognition of word-meanings (*padārtha*), and from word-meanings arises the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
And some [hold] that the Vedas have a recent origin, because they are designated by personal names.

It has been stated: "Dharma is a purposeful matter characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā)," because the relationship between a word and its meaning is not created by a person. In that regard, the objection concerning words and sentences has been refuted;
now we shall raise another objection.

We maintain that the injunctions (*codanā*) are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). The Vedas, which exist in their present form, are of recent composition; and since they are collections of injunctions, if the Vedas are of human origin, then the injunctions are undoubtedly of human origin as well.
But how do some consider the Vedas to be of recent composition?
Because they are designated by the names of men—for the Vedas are named after persons, such as the *Kāṭhaka*, the *Kālāpaka*, the *Paippalādaka*, and the *Mauhula*.

For there can be no designation (*samākhyāna*) without a relationship (*saṃbandha*), and there is no relationship between a person and a word; otherwise, the person would be the agent and the word the product.
[Objection: But could the designation be characterized by the act of teaching (*pravacana*)?
[Reply: We say, no.
For a qualification must be unique; indeed, even many people could speak [of something] that has only one author.
Therefore, even if the author of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) were not remembered, he might still exist.
Consequently, it follows that Dharma is not an object characterized by the Vedic injunction, and thus [the Veda] is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And because of the perception of impermanence.
Furthermore, the contents of the Vedas are heard to possess birth and death,
such as "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired," "Kusuruvinda Auḍḍālaki desired," and so forth.
Since Auḍḍālaki is understood to be the offspring of Uddālaka, if this were the case, this text could not have existed prior to the birth of Auḍḍālaka.
Thus, impermanence [is established],
yet it has been stated that sound is preceded by [the act of] utterance.
We have already stated that for students, [the Veda] is preceded by verbal instruction;
only the refutation of the objection remains to be stated, and that is now being expressed:
"The name [of the Veda] arises from its teaching."
As for what was said—that the designation *Kāṭhaka* and so forth is based on the characteristic of an author—it is replied:

this is not a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), for they might use it even if there were no authors; that is, the teaching might have been performed by Kaṭha and others with excellence (in a manner unique to them), and yet they would still be the ones who provide the designation.
Moreover, it is recorded in tradition that Vaiśampāyana studied all the branches [of the Veda], whereas Kaṭha taught this particular branch alone.
In the presence of those who study many branches (śākhās), one who studies a single branch and has not studied other branches possesses a qualification that is unique because of its excellence;
however, there is merely a commonality of the word "branch" (śruti-sāmānya-mātra).

As for the claim that [the word] "prāvāhaṇiḥ" [is derived from *pravāhaṇa*], that is not so; because a person named Pravāhaṇa is unestablished, there can be no descendant of Pravāhaṇa called Prāvāhaṇi.
The prefix *pra-* is established in the sense of "excellence," and the root *vah-* in the sense of "carrying."

However, its collective form is not established anywhere. But the phoneme *ik* is established just as it is in the sense of "offspring" (*apatya*), so too in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) of an action.
Therefore, he who causes to flow is *prāvāhaṇiḥ*.
*Babara* is an imitation of sound.
Therefore, these two words will denote that very meaning which is eternal; hence it was said: "But there is merely a commonality of sound.
Or rather, there may be an application [of the word] once [the ritual] is performed, because of its connection with the action.
But surely this is seen to be untenable—such statements as "the trees performed a sacrificial session" and so forth.
It is not untenable;
otherwise, [statements] such as "one desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra" would also be untenable.

Moreover, even such statements as "the trees performed a sacrificial session" (*vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata*) are not untenable, for these are praises of the sacrificial session; the meaning is that even insentient things called "trees" have attended this sacrificial session, so how much more so learned Brāhmaṇas!
It is just as in common worldly usage: "Even the deer do not roam at twilight, so how much less so learned Brāhmaṇas!
Furthermore, since the instruction of a well-wisher is uncontradicted and well-established, how could one suspect it to be like the words of a madman or a child?
Therefore, it is established that Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (codanā).
Since the sacred tradition (āmnāya) has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless; therefore, they are said to be non-eternal.
And because it contradicts both scripture and what is observed.
The mind is a thief;
speech is a liar—statements of this kind lack authority regarding dharma because they are merely descriptive of existing facts.
Even if one were to interpret them through processes such as metaphorical transformation (*vipariṇāma*), it would follow that theft and lying must be performed.
And that [prohibition] cannot be practiced without violating the prohibitions against theft and false speech;
nor can there be an option (vikalpa), because of the inequality:
one [rule] would be a hypothetical injunction, while the other is directly perceived.
Likewise, because there is an absence of fruit.
With reference to the *Gargatrirātra-brāhmaṇa*, it is said: "The face of one who knows this shines. If this is a mere restatement of a fact (*bhūtānuvāda*), it is purposeless.
If it is a restatement of the fruit of study, then it is a false restatement. If it is argued that the fruit will occur at a later time, [the response follows].
For there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for this.
If it is argued that it must be an injunction (vidhi), we reply:

this is not intended as an injunction; for this matter—whether it is an injunction of a result or a mere explanatory passage (arthavāda)—will be considered later under the discussion of "substances, purificatory acts, and ritual actions."
But here, is it a restatement of an existing fact (*bhūtānuvāda*) or is it for the purpose of action (*kriyārtha*)?
The example is: "In the offspring of one who knows thus, a vigorous son is born," because otherwise [the statement] would be purposeless.
"If one could find honey on an Arka tree, why would he go to the mountain?
When a desired object is already accomplished, what wise person would exert effort?
Thus [it is said]. And because there is a prohibition against that which has no share [in the result].
"One should not pile the fire-altar on the earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in the sky"—this [injunction] prohibits an object that is not already subject to prohibition.
It is indeed understood from this that the fire-altar is not piled in the intermediate space or in the sky.
Furthermore, the statement intended for the purpose of prohibiting piling on the earth would, by implication, serve as a prohibition of piling altogether.
If, however, it is not authoritative, this contradiction does not arise.
How could that be authoritative which would disrupt another injunction while being itself confused?
[The injunctions] "one should pile the fire-altar" and "having placed gold, one should pile the fire-altar" [would be contradictory].
Because of association with the impermanent.

And the objection regarding connection with impermanent [persons], even if the Veda were authoritative, has been refuted on the grounds that there is merely a commonality of sound. Now, however, a further corroborative argument arises for those portions of the Veda that have been challenged, namely: "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired...
[The reply is: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they must serve the purpose of praising the injunctions."

If it is asked, "For what purpose is the praise? [the answer is: so that it might be pleasing and thus performed. But surely, prior to the statement of praise, the performance [of the rite] was already established by the words ending in "one desiring prosperity"; therefore, the statement of praise is useless.
Indeed, when there is no proximity to words of praise, then the injunction is by the former [word] alone;
when there is a connection with words of praise, then the taking up of the material for one desiring prosperity (*bhūtikāma*) is not enjoined.
Just as in the case of "the cloth comes into being" (*paṭo bhavati*), the meaning is that the cloth is produced.
And the two words [“red” and “cloth”] are mutually expectant.
When another word, “red,” is heard in reference to that very [cloth], then the meaning is that there is a connection with redness; and there indeed arises an expectancy toward the red.
Thus, when there are no words of praise, the incitement occurs through the injunctive word itself; when there is a statement of praise, then it occurs through the praising.

Now, if this is the case, what is the use of the words of praise? Let that which, being present, renders [the injunction] non-injunctive simply not exist. Even in its absence, one will be incited by the previous injunction alone.
True; even without it, the incitement would be accomplished.
But that [the purpose] does exist; while it exists, the meaning of the sentence which consists in the purpose of praise for those two is understood.
If that were not present, there would be no incitement by means of an injunction.
[Objection: But surely we shall understand the injunction even from that which is independent [of praise].
Let it be so; there is no contradiction in this case.
However, when there is a connection with words of praise (*stutipada*), the injunctive meaning (*vidhyartha*) cannot be intended [as the primary sense].

For a sentence (*vākya*) is the ordainer of a connection; if it were to ordain two connections—namely, "one desiring prosperity should sacrifice" and "by means of this sacrifice, this quality will come about"—then the sentence would indeed be split (*bhidyeta*).

Now, as for what was said—that neither action nor anything connected with it is understood—it may be that these words of praise serve the purpose of injunctions; for the words of praise, by praising and making the action attractive, will assist the performers of the action.
Thus, all these words together praise some matter and enjoin it.
Therefore, statements of this kind are indeed authoritative, such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity";
and the traditional transmission is equal [in authority].
Now, it might be argued: "Prior to the words of praise, the injunctive portions are independent and possess the nature of injunctions; the words of praise, however, are a mistaken reading.

This is not so, because the meaning is understood, and the traditional transmission is equal. Those properties which constitute the tradition—such as [observance of] days for study and non-study, learning from the mouth of the teacher, and the relationship between student and preceptor—are all equally applicable to both injunctive and explanatory (arthavāda) passages. For the sake of ensuring there is no obstacle to the tradition, people show equal respect for all such matters.
And the recollection is firm;

therefore, this is not a careless reading. Furthermore, the objection is untenable, for a contradiction would arise only in the case of actual application (*prayoga*); however, the meaning of the word is not something subject to application, and thus it remains consistent.
Moreover, this objection that was stated—namely, that there is a contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures and so forth—does not apply to such passages as "He wept" (so 'rodīt).

Why? Because a contradiction would indeed arise if theft and the like were being enjoined as actual practices; however, the meaning of the words here is not intended as a practical injunction. Therefore, it is logical: "the mind is a thief," and "speech is a liar. But this is merely figurative praise (guṇavāda).
As it has been stated—that praise is for the purpose of creating interest in that which is to be enjoined—how can this be applicable here, where one thing is enjoined and another is praised?

For example, in the injunction "one drags the fire with a branch of the *vetasa* tree and with *avakā* grass," the *vetasa* and the *avakā* are what are enjoined, yet the waters are praised: "The waters, indeed, are peaceful."
To this it is replied: "But it is figurative speech" (guṇavāda).
This is a figurative statement in which, while one related entity is to be praised, another related entity is praised instead;
for this is the ancestral lineage of the reed and the *avakā* grass.
Then, when they are born,
one who is of noble birth is praised by means of praise for his lineage;
just as Devadatta, being of the Aśmaka lineage, considers himself praised when the Aśmakas are being praised.

The same should be understood here as well. This is a supplementary portion of the injunction: "The *āditya* oblation is the *prāyaṇīya* porridge; the *āditya* oblation is the *udayanīya* porridge"—namely, "The gods, having settled upon the sacrificial ground, did not know the directions. Because this [injunction] is required [as a complement], it is a praise: the *āditya* porridge is the destroyer of all delusions, including even delusion regarding the directions.
How can there be the word "delusion" (*diṅmoha*) when delusion is absent? It is said:
because a vast collection of extraordinary rites is present, the word "delusion" is used figuratively; its figurative nature is indicated by such factors as the provision of scope for restriction.
This is based on "form" (*rūpa*) and "preponderance" (*prāya*).
"Gold is in his hand; then he takes it"—because this injunction is thus expectant of further detail, the supplementary statement "the mind is a thief, speech is a liar" follows.
This is a statement of censure intended for the purpose of praising gold, just as one might say, "What is the use of a *ṛṣi*? Devadatta alone should be fed.
But how can the mind, which is not a thief, be called a "thief," and speech, which does not speak untruth, be called a "liar," even for the sake of censure? [The answer is: it is so expressed.
But it is a figurative expression (guṇavāda) based on its form;
for example, just as "thieves" are those whose forms are concealed, so too the word "mind" (manas) is a figurative term [for the sun],
and speech is "mostly a speaker of untruth."
Because of its extreme distance.

An example of contradiction with perception (*dṛṣṭavirodha*) is as follows: "Therefore, from that [fire], only the smoke was seen by day, not the flame; therefore, from that [fire], only the flame was seen at night, not the smoke. Since there is a requirement for the injunction of two mantras containing mixed characteristics—namely, "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā" for the evening oblation, and "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā" for the morning oblation—the [statement regarding smoke and flame] is a supplementary portion (*śeṣa*). The justification for this is the praise that the oblation occurs when both deities are present together.
Because smoke and fire are not seen due to their extreme distance, the term [for them] is figurative;
and the sight of a son [is so called] because of the fault of the agent.

The contradiction with perceived reality (*dṛṣṭavirodha*) itself is the illustrative example: "And we do not know this. Since there is an expectancy for the injunction, "When the *pravara* is being invoked, one should say 'the gods, the ancestors'," this [statement] is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that injunction.
It is a praise (*stuti*) to the effect that even a non-Brāhmaṇa would become a Brāhmaṇa through the recitation of the *pravara*.

The statement regarding ignorance is figurative because of its difficulty to discern; this is difficult to discern from such [scriptural] passages as, "Because of the transgression of the woman, and because the father sees his son, protect this lineage with vigilance."
The desire for what is not immediately available.

An example of contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures: "Who indeed knows that? is a supplement to the injunction "He makes the quarters radiant," because the former is syntactically expectant of it;
it is a praise based on perceptible results.
The statement regarding the lack of arrangement is figurative, because its result occurs at a remote time.
Praise of Knowledge.
Universality pertains to those who hold office.

An example of a statement whose purpose is otherwise [redundant] is: "By the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one attains all desires. This is a supplement to the injunction "one offers the final oblation," because that injunction requires such a statement.
The phrase "and he who knows this thus" and "he overcomes death" are supplements because they do not require [an independent injunction];
the statement of the fruit is praise.
The statement regarding the attainment of all desires is figurative, being used with respect to the cause of all desired fruits.

The expression "all" when applied to things that are not all is intended with reference to those who are qualified [for the rite]. Since the fruit is produced from the ritual action, there would be a distinction in the fruit according to its magnitude, as is seen in the world.
Even if this statement is an injunction (*vidhi*), it nevertheless possesses purposefulness (*arthavattā*) by virtue of its extent or its essence, due to the distinction of its results;
as has been stated regarding the last two.

This has been illustrated in the passage beginning with "because of the prohibition of what is impossible" (*abhāgipratiṣedhāt*): "Fire is not to be piled on the earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in the sky. Since this injunction requires the expectation [of a specific location], the preceding statements are supplementary to it. The deprecation of the earth and so forth is for the purpose of praising gold.
Since there is no possibility [of piling fire on the earth, etc.], the prohibition is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).
As for the observation regarding the non-eternity [of the Veda] based on the passage, "Babara Prāvāhaṇi desired," that has already been refuted.

Since it has now arisen again by way of challenging the explanatory passages (arthavādas), it will be refuted by that very same refutation once the authority of the explanatory passages is established.
Or rather, it must be an injunction because it conveys something not previously known; for mere discourse is indeed purposeless.

In this context, those explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) that are recited according to rule serve as examples: "The sacrificial post is made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is indeed strength (*ūrj*), and cattle are strength; by means of strength he obtains for him strength and cattle, for the sake of securing strength.
What is its function—is it an injunction (*vidhi*), or is it also a praise (*stuti*)?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It must be an injunction, because it conveys something not previously known; for a mere statement would be purposeless.
In injunctions of this kind, there must be an injunction of a result according to the rule; for a result is indeed understood, as it will thus enjoin a new (apūrva) purpose.
Otherwise, it would be a mere statement of praise and thus useless.
Whether praised or not praised, that purpose remains exactly the same.
Moreover, the purpose "for the attainment of vigor" (ūrjo 'varuddhyai) is heard [in the text];
yet there is no word whatsoever stating that "this matter is praiseworthy. Rather, the praise is understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā).
And direct audition (śruti) is more authoritative than indication (lakṣaṇā).
If it be argued that it is "as in the world," [we reply: no.

If you think thus—that praise is purposeless and is not understood through the words themselves—then let your honors understand worldly sentences such as this: "This cow belonging to Devadatta should be purchased; for she yields much milk, has female offspring, and her progeny has not perished."
Even when it is said, "It should be bought," buyers proceed all the more eagerly because of the mention of its qualities;
and the statement "it yields much milk" is understood as a mention of its qualities.
In the same way, this will also be the case in the Veda.
Not so, because it is prior.
But it has been stated that [the word] functions as a supplementary part of the sentence.
We have already stated that it is a supplementary part of a sentence—namely, "because it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction.
Now, it was argued: "In this case, what is understood is a statement of a result, not a praise.
However, the statement of a result found here refers to the sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood.
