Furthermore, there is no sacrificial post made of Udumbara wood that has not been prescribed;
in that case, the mention of a fruit would be entirely purposeless.
If it is argued that there is no word expressing praise, [we reply:]...

In this context, by means of the statement regarding the fruit, the possession of a fruit is understood; and that which possesses a fruit is praised. Therefore, while the literal sense concerns the possession of a fruit, the second meaning—which is what is called "praise"—is what is actually apprehended.

If it is argued that this is a case of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we say no; for even in the case of secondary indication, there is indeed meaningfulness, since secondary indication is also a worldly phenomenon.
But was it not said that there is no correspondence in the Veda, since "the udumbara tree is indeed *ūrj* (vigour)"?

We reply that we state its purpose is for the sake of persuasion (*prarocanā*) by means of figurative speech (*guṇavāda*). Because it is figurative, there is correspondence. What is that? It is similarity—just as food is a means to pleasure, so too this [tree] is endowed with the power to be a means to pleasure; thus it is expressed by a word denoting praise in order to praise it. For it can indeed be called "*ūrj*" because of its connection with ripe fruit.
And in some cases the injunction would be purposeless; therefore, praise should be understood [as the intended meaning], and by analogy with that, the same applies to the others.
"The horse has its origin in water, and the reed grows in water"—since the injunction that "the horse must be made to have its origin in water" is impossible to carry out, it would be purposeless.
Therefore, a figurative praise (stuti) must necessarily be inferred: that the connection of the horse and the reeds with waters which are pacifying brings peace to the suffering of the sacrificer.
Because of that similarity, the same applies to the others—"tathā" meaning "so," and as long as there is that [similarity], so is the application.
What is that generality?
It is the impossibility of an injunction and the possibility of praise.
If an application were possible within the context, a displacement [of the mantra] should not be assumed; for, in relation to that [context], the injunction would otherwise be rendered purposeless.

And from this we see that it is praise. Why? Because they recite this: "That which is overcooked belongs to Nirṛti; that which is undercooked belongs to Rudra; that which is properly cooked belongs to the gods."
Therefore, it should be cooked without burning, because it is for the sake of the deity.
If this praise were intended for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves, then the cooked offering (*śṛta*) would be praised;
in that case, since such a connection is possible, one should not assume a displacement [of the praise].
It is called *apakarṣa* (removal) because it is drawn away.
Under the view that this is a positive injunction (*vidhi*), however, the state of being burnt (*vidagdhatā*) would be applied wherever there is an offering to Nirṛti;
if that were the case, the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be sublated.
Since there is no offering to Nirṛti in relation to the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual, the mention of "burnt" offerings would be purposeless;
therefore, it is merely a commendatory statement (stuti).
Furthermore, if it were a direct injunction (vidhi), there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

If this injunction, "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood," were accepted, and the statement "for the attainment of strength" were also accepted, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*):
namely, that "the Udumbara post is thus praised, and it is for the attainment of strength.
Therefore, just as with injunctions, the function of explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)—even those in the form of recitations (*nigadas*)—is indeed praise alone.
Or it may be the cause, because of its meaningfulness and logical consistency.

Now, regarding those statements which express a reason—such as "One offers with a winnowing basket, for with it food is prepared"—there arises a doubt: is their function praise (*stuti*) or is it a reason (*hetu*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
The preparation of food would be the cause for the oblation.

[Objection: But surely, when the relationship of cause and effect is not established, there can be no instruction regarding a cause. [Response: This is indeed true in common worldly practice; however, in the Veda, it shall be enjoined by means of a scriptural statement.
When the oblation is to be performed with a winnowing basket, it is taught that "being an instrument for preparing food" is the reason.
What is the purpose?
It is so that even other instruments for preparing food, such as a ladle or a cooking pot, might also be used to perform the oblation.
Why?
Because that [fire] also possesses purposefulness in the act of cooking food, and it is indeed possible for it to cook food;
for it is said that "this is what is done."
For there is no such thing as a "present time" for which this [term] could serve as a direct designation.
Furthermore, in the case of the cause (*hetu*), the word is used in its primary sense (*śruti*); in the case of praise (*stuti*), it is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*).
Moreover, if a ladle, a pot, and so forth do not produce food directly, they would not be called "producers of food."

If that [purpose] were non-existent, the praise of the winnowing basket would be purposeless; for even the winnowing basket does not directly produce food. Without such a purpose, the praise of the winnowing basket would not be logical.
As for the praise itself, it is based on the word, and thus there is no injunction regarding its [actual utility].

But this is not the case; for this meaning is preceded by the word: "being an instrument for preparing food is the reason. And the word states that being an instrument for preparing food is the reason for the *sūrpa* offering. This does not apply to the offering with a ladle (*darvī*) or a cooking pot (*piṭhara*), because the *sūrpa* is [designated] by the word, whereas there is no injunction (*codanā*) for the ladle, the cooking pot, and so forth.
If it is argued that the praise is for another purpose when it is redundant—
Thus, what was stated again must be refuted;
however, the meaning [of the Veda] is subordinate to an injunction, just as it is in common worldly usage.
In our position, there is a purposeful meaning; for in that case, the remainder of the sentence serves as a supplement to the injunction.

Furthermore, the corroboration occurs by way of praise, such that just as we know food is being prepared with a winnowing basket, it is understood from this very [passage] that "food is indeed prepared with a winnowing basket."
And at that time, he teaches [the word] "present" in order to praise what is not present.
This fault belongs to your own position, for you maintain that there is a prescription of a logical reason (*hetuvidhi*).
For in the case of a prescription, no other meaning of the word is perceived.
Furthermore, the Veda, while teaching about the present, could not establish a [future] purposeful result.
In our position, however, this word "other" (para) refers to something else; just as in common worldly usage one says, "The strong Devadatta overcomes Yajñadatta and others."

Even when the word "strong" is applied to one who possesses superior strength, it is not used in reference to a lion or a tiger; rather, it occurs in reference to those whose strength is inferior to that of Devadatta. Likewise, the statement "for by it food is made" is a praise of the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) on account of its superior capacity for making food, and this will be in reference to other means of making food which are inferior.

Furthermore, if the reason (*hetu*) were to remain fixed based on the specific mention, and if it were argued that this applies due to a general principle, then there would be an instability in the injunctions.
Because there is an explanatory treatise for that purpose.
Now, are mantras intended to convey meaning, or are they not intended to convey meaning?
Do they assist the sacrifice by illuminating its purpose, or merely by being uttered?
If it were merely by being uttered, then the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" would not necessarily be employed for the cutting of the grass.

If it is argued that [the mantra] functions through its denotation, then since its status as an auxiliary has been understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*), it cannot assist elsewhere; thus, even without an explicit statement, it would be employed only for the cutting of the *barhis* grass. Therefore, we understand that mantras assist by mere utterance alone.
Why? Because of the explanatory scriptures concerning their purpose (*tadarthaśāstra*).

The scripture enjoins this mantra only where it is capable of expressing a meaning, as in the statement: "He spreads the sacrificial cake [with the mantra] 'O wide-expanding one, expand widely! This statement would be meaningless if mantras assisted through the expression of their meaning;
however, if they assist by mere utterance, then their application (viniyoga) must be stated—and it has indeed been stated.
Therefore, it is not by means of expressing a meaning;
just as when a man with eyes is led by another, it is understood that he surely does not see with his eyes.
If it is argued that this will be for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), [we reply: no.

For it has been stated that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is a supplement to that which is enjoined; and when something has been enjoined by an independent [injunction], no purpose whatsoever is served by an explanatory passage. Therefore, the statement is not for the sake of an explanatory passage.
Surely, one might argue that it will serve as an exclusion (parisaṃkhyā) regarding the donkey’s bridle. But it is not capable of being an exclusion;
for in excluding [one thing], it would abandon its own purpose, assume a purpose for another, and subvert what has already been established.
Therefore, mantras do not have the intention to convey a meaning;
consequently, the form of the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" is not an authority for its application to the cutting of the sacrificial grass,
because of the fixed nature of the sentence.
For mantras possess a fixed sequence of words;

for instance, "agnimūrdhā divaḥ" (Agni is the head of heaven) and not the reverse. If their purpose were merely to convey meaning, then since the meaning would be understood even by reversing the order, the restriction [of word-order] would be purposeless.
Now, if it is argued that the purpose is for the sake of specific pronunciation— such that a rule is adopted stating that in the case of the opposite, there would be a different pronunciation—
then whichever position renders the rule meaningful is surely the correct one.
But is it not observed that rules are applied even to those words that already possess meaning?
For example: "Indra-Agni.
That [dual compound] is appropriate there because, in the opposite case, there would be no cognition of the meaning from the Buddha's teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the word *buddha*, by virtue of its recitation, a mantra becomes capable of expressing its meaning,
such as "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires. What would that [mantra] cause one who is already awakened (*buddha*) to awaken?
Now, if it is argued that they serve the purpose of a specific pronunciation, then even in the case of a cognition (*buddhi*), a specific pronunciation could be postulated.
[Objection: But surely, due to repetition, there will be a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
[Reply: In this way, you have merely resorted to our own position.
Utterance is the vocal enunciation; for that can indeed be performed, whereas the communication of meaning cannot,
since that is impossible once [the utterance] has been perceived.
Just as one does not put on a second sandal when the foot already has a sandal, because it is impossible,
since [the word] refers to what is not yet present.
In a sacrifice, that which serves as a means must be made manifest;
however, there is no such object as they describe, as in the case of [the verse]: "He who has four horns."
For there exists no sacrificial implement whatsoever that has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands;
therefore, what could the word here denote?
It is only as having the purpose of mere utterance (*uccāraṇa*) that it is plausible.

Likewise, in the case of "Do not harm me," what would one be saying even when no actual harm is occurring? [The answer is: because the connection with the object exists even in the case of an insentient being.
Indeed, they attach meaning to an insentient object—such as [in the mantra], "O herb, protect him.
Those of this kind, by means of their denotation, would intend to employ the herb for the protection of the animal;
yet it is not possible to employ that which is insentient.
However, this fault does not apply when they serve the purpose of pronunciation;
therefore, they are for the purpose of pronunciation.
"Listen, O pressing-stones! is an example.
Because there is a contradiction in meaning.
There is also a contradiction in meaning:

[the Veda says] "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space. Who could ever determine that she is the very same heaven and that it is the very same intermediate space? And if one cannot so determine, how could one be benefited by the expression?
But this contradiction does not exist when [the mantra] is merely uttered;
therefore, mantras have utterance as their purpose.
"Rudra is one; he did not stand as a second."
"Countless thousands are those Rudras who are upon the earth"— this is an illustration,
because it is not stated [in the scripture] as being like one's own recitation (svādhyāya).
At the time of Vedic study, Pūrṇikā threshes grain;
the young student threshes while reciting a mantra.
He does not practice the denotation of that mantra through it; rather, he exerts himself solely in the mastery of the sequence of syllables.
Whatever indeed serves a purpose must be practiced;
therefore, from the practice of pronunciation, we understand that the purpose lies in the pronunciation itself,
because [otherwise] it would be unintelligible.

Moreover, the meaning of certain mantras is simply impossible to understand, such as: "O Indra, that spear of yours is unfailing for us," or "Like two ploughs, they carry the burden; they are the destroyers."
And [in the mantra] "indraḥ somasya kāṇukā," what would these [words] convey? However,
there is no fault if they are for the purpose of mere pronunciation.
Therefore, mantras are for the purpose of recitation;
[however], because of their connection with impermanent things, mantras would be rendered purposeless.
Furthermore, there would indeed be an association with impermanent things in the case of mantras whose meanings are denotative,
as for example: "What do your cows do among the Kīkaṭas?"—
where the Kīkaṭas are a [specific] region.
There was a city named Naicāśākha,
and Pramaṅgada was its king.
If these [names] were intended as proper names, it would be understood that this mantra had never been experienced before the time of Pramaṅgada.
Thus, by these reasons—such as the fact that there is an explanatory śāstra regarding their meaning—the mantras do not have their literal verbal expression intended;
however, the meaning of the sentence remains undifferentiated.
To this it is said: the recitation of mantras in a sacrifice is solely for the purpose of conveying meaning.

As for what was stated—that there is no purpose in conversing with deities or the constituent parts of the sacrifice—the purpose in the sacrifice is precisely the manifestation of the sacrificial components.
How so? For indeed, when the sacrifice and its constituent parts have not been manifested, the performance of the sacrifice cannot be accomplished.
Therefore, for the sake of its accomplishment, the illumination of meaning is a great benefit of the action, and it is understood that [the word] performs this.
Consequently, there is a purpose for that which is unreal; and since that purpose is perceived, it cannot be denied—that is, that the expression of meaning is not the purpose.

Now, while [certain words] assist by expressing a meaning—such as "He takes it with four [fingers]" and so forth—let that [other type] be meaningless; we never deny that the expression of meaning is seen to be helpful.
But is that scripture (the Veda) entirely meaningless?
Certainly not.
Furthermore, the repetition of the scriptural statement is for the purpose of [indicating] a quality.
As for what was said— that because there is no word expressing conjunction (*samuccaya*), "he takes it with four" does not mean for the purpose of conjunction—

it is understood from the sentence that the act of taking must be qualified by the number four. Therefore, one who takes it with a single mantra would not be taking it according to the scriptural injunction.
Enumeration.
Or it is an explanatory statement (arthavāda).

"He spreads it wide, O wide-spreading one"—this repetition of the scriptural statement is for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), namely, "thereby he indeed causes the lord of the sacrifice to expand.
Now, one might object: this is not a supplementary part of the mantra's sentence, nor is there any purpose in praising what is already established.
True; this is neither an injunction regarding the mantra, nor is it a mere panegyric.

In this case, the spreading itself is what is being praised. The mantra, however, is merely restated here because it is already established by its very form, for the purpose of praising the spreading—namely, that the spreading is excellent when it is performed with a mantra of such a form. What, then, is the benefit?
Thus he causes the lord of the sacrifice to expand through offspring and cattle.
Is this its only fruit?
No, we say.
It is stated thus: "How will there be praise? [The answer is:
How can there be a word that causes expansion when no expansion exists?
Because of the recitation of a mantra—the Adhvaryu priest says to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) by means of a mantra, "Expand yourself."
And he who says "spread thus" spreads it; just as he who says "do" causes [someone] to do. This is not contradictory to the other [view].
As for what was said— that because the restriction of word-order possesses a purposeful meaning, the mantras do not have their literal meanings intended—
it may be that the restriction is purposeless, yet it is not the case that the perceptible is without authority.
If it is argued that the restricted recitation is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), then the postulation of an unseen result is not contradictory even in our position.
Thus, when it is understood in this way, it becomes conducive to prosperity;
therefore, there is no reproach for the disparagement of the ritual act during the formal injunction, because it is a purificatory refinement (*saṃskāra*).

Now, as for what was said— that the instruction "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters" is an impossible awakening of one who already knows, and therefore an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) results from its mere utterance—
that is not so;
even when it is understood that "it must be done," there is a purpose for [the instruction] at the time of performance, namely, to bring it to mind.

She may attain it by other means as well; therefore, the traditional teaching is for the purpose of restriction—that it must be performed by this specific means—because it is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra).
Regarding its verbal expression, it is an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
In the statement "four horns," the word is figurative when applied to what is unreal; such figurative conceptualization is based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
whereas the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from mere recitation lacks such validity.
His four officiating priests (*hotrā*) are like his horns;
"his three feet" refers to the three *savana*s;
and "his two heads" refers to the wife and the sacrificer.
"Seven hands" refers to the Vedic meters;
"bound in three ways" means bound by the three Vedas;
and "the bull" is so called because he rains down desires.
"He roars" refers to the action of making sound;
"the great god has entered into mortals" is intended with reference to human beings.
For example, it is like praising a river by saying, "The river has breasts that are ruddy geese, rows of teeth that are swans, garments of *kāśa* grass, and hair of *śaivala* moss."

Desiring to establish the similarity between the ritual implements and sentient beings for the sake of the success of the sacrifice, he indicates this through the use of vocative forms: "O herb, protect him!

and "Listen, O pressing-stones! This implies that from now on there will be the recitation of the *prātaranuvāka*, at which time even the inanimate pressing-stones would listen, let alone learned Brahmins. In this way, even inanimate pressing-stones are addressed with vocatives.
There would be no contradiction because of the quality.
The statement regarding knowledge [is not established] because of the lack of connection.
As for the objection that— since at a time when no ritual action is being performed, the student does not wish to manifest the *mantra* used for threshing,
because it is not connected to a sacrifice, and he does not wish to manifest it for the sake of assisting a sacrifice—
it has been argued that there is no practice of manifestation, but rather a practice of the syllables themselves.
It is said: because it is easy, there is no practice of illumination; and because it is difficult to grasp, there is practice regarding the syllables.
Regarding that which exists, there is subsequently non-cognition.
Even though an object exists, it may not be perceived due to negligence, laziness, and so forth;
therefore, the meaning must be inferred from the verbal root by means of grammatical rules, etymologies, and commentaries.
For example, such designations for the Aśvins as *sṛṇyeva*, *jarbharī*, and *turpharītū* are observed to be in the dual number.
From this it is understood that the hymn belongs to the Aśvins because it fulfills their desire;
furthermore, the designations of the deities, such as "jarbharī" and so forth, are appropriate,
and they are further specified by their well-known etymological meanings according to worldly usage.
Thus it is in all cases;
and the conjunction with impermanence has been explained.
"But here [in this case], there is merely a commonality of sound";
and the instruction by means of an indicative mark (liṅga) is for that purpose.

Because of the injunction, "One worships the Āgnīdhra fire with the Āgneya [mantras]," there is an instruction by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*) only for those mantras whose meaning is intended.
If they have Agni as their purpose, then they are *āgneya* on that account, not merely due to the proximity of the word "Agni.
This is the modification (*ūha*).
And the observation of modification occurs only with respect to those meanings that are intended to be expressed. What is this observation of modification?
It is: "The father does not increase; the mother does not [increase]."
It is understood that others increase;
it is directly perceived that mothers and others grow through childhood, youth, and old age.
[The opponent] asserts, however, that sound does not increase.
What, then, is the increase of a word?
It is its connection with the dual and plural numbers,
as well as with prescriptive words.
Furthermore, injunctive words restate those very mantras whose meanings are intended to be conveyed—as in the statement, "He said this very thing: 'May I live a hundred winters, a hundred years.
Since dharma has its root in verbal testimony (śabda), that which lacks such verbal authority should be disregarded.
Alternatively, inference may be a means of valid cognition because of the identity of the agent.
The alternative view introduced by "or rather" (api vā) is set aside:
memory is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), for it is indeed a form of consciousness;
why then should it be otherwise?
If it is argued that he lacks prior consciousness because of the absence of a cause,
we shall infer from the very firmness of this memory itself that there is a cause; however, that cause is not [simply] the experience, because that would be untenable.
For humans are not able to experience such matters as these in this very life;

nor is that which was experienced in another birth remembered. However, the text [of the Smṛti] may be inferred [to have a Vedic source], because of the identity of the author between the Smṛti and the Vedic subject matter.
For those born of the three *varṇas*, there is a connection with the Veda upon being so reborn.
[Objection: But they do not actually find such a text.
[Response: Even though they do not find it, they may infer its existence; for even forgetfulness is possible.

Because the prior consciousness of those who remember the three Vedas is possible, and because forgetfulness is also possible, the inference of the original text is established; thus, tradition (smṛti) is a means of valid knowledge.
However, in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded, for there is no inference when such a contradiction exists.
Now, what is the case where there is a contradiction with Śruti?
For example, the total wrapping of the Audumbarī post contradicts the Śruti injunction, "One should chant the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī.

Likewise, the practice of observing Vedic studentship (brahmacarya) for forty-eight years contradicts the injunction, "Having fathered a son and while his hair is still black, one should establish the sacred fires (agnyādheya)."

"One should not eat at the house of one who has performed a *krītarājaka* sacrifice"—this contradicts the rule that "one should eat at the sacrificer's house when the *agnīṣomīya* rite is concluded. Since the former is authoritative due to the identity of the agent (*kartṛsāmānyāt*), such being the position reached, we reply: because it is impossible [to follow both], it is understood to be a delusion.
How is there impossibility?
Because it must be touched during the performance, it is not possible for the Udgātṛ to touch the entire cloth while singing the udgītha.

Understanding that it must be touched by the Udgātṛ while singing, we say: "By what means could we set aside this conviction [of the Smṛti] through the Smṛti rule regarding the covering of the whole [body]?
And because a reason [for the Smṛti] is observed.
Out of greed, some, desiring to obtain a dwelling, wrapped the entire Audumbarī pillar;
this is the seed of that Smṛti rule.
Others, desiring to eat, practiced the custom of eating at the house of one whose king had been purchased.
Concealing their impotence, they practiced Vedic celibacy for forty-eight years;
from this it is understood that such is the traditional teaching (smṛti),
or else it constitutes a separate legal topic.
"The Adhvaryu takes the cloth used for the Vaisarjana-homa," and "They practice the giving [of the cloth] to the one who holds the sacrificial post.
Since these [Smṛti rules] share the same agent [as the Śruti], they are authoritative— this being the prima facie view— it is concluded that Smṛti is not authoritative [in this case].
In this regard, there is another root:
some practiced [these acts] out of greed, and from that this tradition (smṛti) arose;
and this is more plausible than the assumption of Vedic injunctions.
If it is argued that "it is not contradicted because it does not conflict with the teachings of the learned."
It is not so, because it is limited by the extent of the treatise.
This is not so;
for they would contradict the sequence determined by the treatise.
How so?

If one were to perform acts such as sipping water (ācamana) between the preparation of the *veda* grass-bundle and the construction of the altar (*vedi*), one would obstruct this Vedic injunction: "Having made the *veda*, one should make the *vedi*.
Furthermore, when ritual items are being performed with only the right hand, the primary rite might occasionally exceed its proper time;
by performing with both hands, one will ensure that the time for the primary rite is maintained.
Or rather, when the cause is not apprehended, those [words] employed [in a context] should be understood [as figurative].
Since no contradiction is observed among them, there would be an equal degree of disagreement.
"A sacrificial pap made of barley; boar-skin sandals; on a mat of reeds he collects the oblations for Prajāpati"—thus they recite the words "barley," "boar," and "reeds.
Regarding these, some apply the word "barley" to long-awned grain, while others apply it to *priyaṅgu* seeds;
some apply the word "boar" to a pig, while others apply it to a black bird.
Some take the word *vetasa* to mean the *vañjulaka* plant, while others take it to mean the *jambu* tree.
Since the meaning of the term is understood in both ways there, an option (*vikalpa*) applies;
however, the usage established in the technical treatises (*śāstrastha*) prevails, because that [treatise] is the source of authority for the term.
But that which is enjoined should be understood as valid, provided there is no contradiction with a means of valid cognition.
Now, there are certain words which the Āryas do not employ in any sense, yet the Mlecchas do employ in a particular sense—such as the words *pika*, *nema*, *sata*, *tāmara*, and so forth.

Regarding these, a doubt arises: should the meaning be inferred from a verbal root by means of etymological derivation (*nigama*), semantic analysis (*nirukta*), and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), or is that in which the Mlecchas employ them the true meaning of the word?
It has been stated that the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is authoritative, but not the tradition of those who are unlearned (*aśiṣṭa*).
Therefore, the determination of meaning is based on usage (*nigama*) and other criteria;
in this way, usage and the rest will possess purposeful significance.
Furthermore, there is a lack of application regarding word-meanings among those who are not refined (*aśiṣṭa*), whereas there is application among others.

Therefore, when it is argued that the meaning must be inferred from the etymological root (*dhātu*), we reply: even if something is prompted by those who are unrefined, it should be understood if it is not known to the refined (*śiṣṭa*). That which is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should not be rejected when it is being apprehended.

As for the claim that the practice of the refined is authoritative, that applies only to matters not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, as for the statement that "the refined are those who are experts in the meanings of words," [that is true].
To this it is replied: Mlecchas are more expert than others in the rearing and binding of birds.

As for the claim that [words] possess meaning through the Nigama, Nirukta, and Vyākaraṇa, their meaningfulness will apply only in those cases; it does not apply where the meaning of a word is understood even by Mlecchas.
Furthermore, if the meaning were to be determined solely through the Nigama and other such sources, the meaning of words would become unstable, and there would consequently be uncertainty.
Therefore, "pika" should be understood as the cuckoo; "nema" means half; "tāmarasa" means a lotus; and "sata" refers to a wooden vessel that is circular and has a hundred holes.
[If it is argued: "It is a manual of ritual application (prayoga-śāstra)."

In this context, the *Kalpasūtras* serve as the example—such as those characterized as the *Māśaka*, *Hāstika*, *Kauṇḍinyaka*, and so forth. Are they authoritative or not? Thus they are doubted. What is the conclusion?
We say that a treatise of this kind is indeed authoritative for its practical application (*prayoga*).
These are the words of those whose speech is truth.
How is this known?
Because there is agreement between these and the Vedic scriptures.
For those very same cups that are in the Veda are here; those very same bricks that are in the Veda are here.
Therefore, the teachers are speakers of truth, and there is a scriptural declaration: "The word of the teacher is authoritative."

If it were argued that their authority is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no fault, as it is established by another means of knowledge, namely, by verbal testimony (*vacana*).
Furthermore, they are accorded the same degree of respect as the Vedic statements;
therefore, they are authoritative.
Not so, because of the non-restriction regarding non-existence.
This is not so, because there is no restrictive rule;
this is not a correct connection, because it lacks a vowel; and because there is no supplementary statement.
As for what was said— that these are the words of those who speak the truth— that is not so,
because they are employed everywhere and because of the scriptural injunction regarding proximity.

For there is indeed a statement by the Teacher regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In all lunar days (*tithi*), it is the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). And the proximate scripture states: "One should sacrifice with the *Paurṇamāsī* [offering] on the full moon day; one should sacrifice with the *Amāvāsyā* [offering] on the new moon day.
Therefore, because their statements contradict the revealed scripture (*śruti*), they are not speakers of truth; consequently, they are not authoritative.
Because it is established by inference, that which is connected with it would be a valid means of knowledge.
The authority of inference, recollection, and established customs is accepted.
By whatever reason those [other means] are authoritative, by that very same reason these [customs], being firmly established, deserve to be authoritative.

Therefore, the *holākā* and other such rites are to be performed by the Easterners alone; the *āhnīnaibuka* and others by the Southerners alone; and the *udvṛṣabhayajña* and others by the Northerners alone.
Just as the rule for topknots is established— where some have three topknots and some have five—
or rather, it might apply to all dharmas, because that is the principle of the injunction.
Now, as for what was said— that the ritual procedure for the topknot (śikhākalpa) is established— its application [is determined] through direct observation (darśana).
The vision [of the truth] is clear through the establishment of the lineage and the establishment of the ritual of the topknot;
and because of the absence of signs, it belongs to the eternal one.
This is a sūtra following certain words.
What are those words? And for what purpose is there no fixed determination based on gender?
For example: "The Hotṛ priest is white.
That characteristic which follows the observed instance is not necessarily eternal for them;
even those who are dark-complexioned, large-bodied, and red-eyed do not all perform the Ārhnīnaibuka and other such rites.
Moreover, even those who do not possess such characteristics perform [the rites];
therefore, there is no fixed rule.
"The Hotṛ priest is white" is a direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*).
For a name [is applied] due to connection with a place.
Now, why is there no restriction based on designation?
Those who are designated as "southerners" will perform the *āhnīnaibuka* and other such rites; those who are designated as "northerners" will perform the *udvṛṣabhayajña* and other such rites.
As for those who say "those from the East," they [perform] the Holākā and other such rites;
for example, as in the statement, "The king [should sacrifice] with the Rājasūya.
This is not so.
The designation [of a practice] arises from connection with a country.
One who has departed from the southern country and resides in the east or the north certainly performs the *āhnīnaibuka* and other such rites;
northerners perform the *udvṛṣabhayajña* and others in another region, while easterners perform the *holākā* and others.
Furthermore, one who has gone to another country does not necessarily perform the duties of another place;
therefore, there is no fixed rule [of application]. However, in the case of "the king by means of the Rājasūya," the caste (jāti) is indeed fixed.
If it is argued that [the effect] would not exist in other locations;
If you think this: "If the designation were due to conjunction with a location, it would not apply to one situated in another location;
yet the designation 'Māthura' applies even to one situated in another location who is not connected with Mathurā. Therefore, the designation does not arise from conjunction with a location."
For there may indeed be the designation "yoga" [in the case of a non-yogi], as in the case of Māthura.
Even when a name is caused by connection with a place, it is not contradictory for one who has departed from that place to retain that name;
because this designation based on yoga depends merely upon the potential for connection, and not upon a past, present, or future actual connection.
For it is observed that one setting out for Mathurā is called "Māthura," as is one dwelling in Mathurā or one who has departed from Mathurā.
But he who lacks any one of these connections is not a "Mathuran. Therefore, the determination [of the Vedic text] is not by way of a name,
nor is it a property of the ritual action, like the case of the sloping ground.
Now, why is location not an auxiliary factor (*aṅga*) of the ritual action?
That which consists mostly of black clay is [the locus] for the *Āhnīnaibuka* and other such rites;
as in the rule: "One should sacrifice with the *Vaiśvadeva* on ground sloping toward the east."
But it is equal [to the action] by virtue of being a property of the agent.
Just as a characteristic such as "darkness" that is not fixed to the agent does not correspond with the actual state of things, so too the characteristic of a region is unfixed.
Even in a place consisting mostly of black soil, some do not perform [the rite], while others perform it even in a place with a different characteristic.
Therefore, there is no fixed rule based on location.
The requirement that the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice be performed on ground sloping toward the east is fixed by direct Vedic injunction;
however, because there is no scriptural rule governing the origin of the performance, there would be no restriction regarding the words [used].
Words such as *gaur*, *gāvī*, *goṇī*, and *gopotalikā* serve as examples.

There arises a doubt: just as the word *go* is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [denoting] that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, are words like *gāvī* and others likewise [means of valid cognition], or not?
In this regard, is there one single word with an uninterrupted tradition that denotes the meaning, while the others are corruptions (*apabhraṃśas*), or are all of them beginningless?
We say "all.
Why?
Because of the cognition.
For the object possessing a dewlap and so forth is indeed understood from words such as *gāvī*;
therefore, even a hundred years ago this relationship between the word and its meaning already existed, and prior to that, and even further back—thus it is beginningless.
And it is firmly established that there is no creator of this relationship.
Therefore, all [words] are correct, and all should be spoken;
for all indeed accomplish the intended meaning,
just as— *hastaḥ*, *karaḥ*, and *pāṇiḥ*.
For these [words] are uttered for the sake of meaning, not for the sake of some unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).
Indeed, there is no scriptural injunction regarding their mere utterance.
Therefore, one could not establish that only a single word is correct while the others are incorrect.
Because sound is produced through effort, it shares in the nature of being subject to error.

They produce sound with great effort: the air, rising from the navel, expanding in the chest, turning in the throat, striking the head and returning, moves through the mouth and manifests various sounds. In this regard, even the utterer might commit an error—for instance, one might fall into mud thinking "I shall fall on dry ground," or touch twice thinking "I shall touch once. Due to such errors, words like *gāvī* and others may arise; they do not necessarily possess an uninterrupted traditional lineage.
And it is unjust that there should be multiple words [for the same meaning].
Nor is it logical that all similar words, while denoting a single object, must necessarily have an uninterrupted lineage.

This is accepted merely because a cognition [of meaning] is observed; for even when the correct word (*sādhuśabda*) is understood through similarity, the cognition [of meaning] is still accounted for.
Therefore, among these, one is beginningless, while the others are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*).
In cases such as *hastaḥ*, *karaḥ*, and *pāṇiḥ*, however, because they have been taught by experts, the connection of these words with their meanings is beginningless;
in that regard, the true nature [of the meaning] arises from specific expertise.
But how, then, can reality be known therein? He says that it is possible;
for those who seek [it] become diligent.
Moreover, it is observed that for those who are diligent in their practice, non-forgetting is logically established;
this is also directly perceived, as that which is being practiced does not fall away.
Therefore, whatever those who are diligent teach must be understood as being alone correct.
And there is an incapacity [to act] because of its suitability [to the specific object].
And because it occupies only a single part, there would be a displacement of case-endings.
For this very reason, even when there is a transposition of case endings, comprehension occurs:
when a portion of the word "aśmaka" is perceived in the expression "aśmakair āgacchāmi," the word "aśmakebhyaḥ" itself is remembered;
from that, the meaning "from the Aśmakas" is apprehended.
Thus, from the perception of words such as *gāvī*, there arises the recollection of the word *go*; from that, the animal possessing a dewlap and other characteristics is understood.
Because there is no difference in usage or injunction, there is a unity of meaning due to the lack of distinction.
This is said: the individual (vyakti) is the meaning of the word.
Why? Because of the absence of injunctions for practical application.
Injunctions for application—such as touching, sprinkling, and immolation—would not be possible if the meaning were the form (ākṛti).
If it is argued that where the utterance would otherwise be purposeless, it serves to denote the individual (vyakti),
whereas elsewhere it denotes the form (ākṛti)— to this it has been replied: "It is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings."
If it is asked how there can be a cognition of a universal, [the answer is:
the configuration (*ākṛti*) will serve as the mark for the individual (*vyakti*) which is the referent of the word; "that which has such a configuration is a cow.
It is just as one who possesses a staff is called "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), even though the word "staff-bearer" does not denote the staff itself.
So it is here as well,
because of the word "substance" (dravya).

A word that denotes that which has substance as its substratum is a "substance-word" (*dravyaśabda*); in that case, there would not be a word expressing that which has substance as its substratum if the form (*ākṛti*) were the meaning of the word. [For example, one says:
"Six are to be given," "Twelve are to be given," or "Twenty-four are to be given.
Indeed, the form is not connected with numbers such as six and so forth.
Therefore, it does not denote the form;
this is also because another view is observed.
"If the animal that has been dedicated should escape, one should sacrifice another of the same color and the same age"—
if the word were expressive of the specific individual form (ākṛti), the sacrifice of another would not be possible;
for even in another sacrificial substance that is an animal, that very same form exists.
Therefore, [the word] denotes the individual;
but it is the form (ākṛti) [that is denoted], because [the individual] is for the sake of action.
But surely the piling will be performed by means of individual *śyena* bricks?

The meaning of the word *śyena* is not that which is most effective in accomplishing the action (*sādhakatama*), for it is that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) which is indicated by the word *śyena*.
Therefore, the *śyena* must be brought about by the act of piling; this is possible only if the word denotes the generic form (*ākṛti*).
But surely, in both cases, it is precisely the impossibility of action that is being indicated;
the form (ākṛti) is not the meaning of the word.
Why?
If the word-meaning were the *ākṛti* (form), ritual action would not be possible in the case of the injunction "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

Likewise, the individual (*vyakti*) cannot be the word-meaning; for if the individual were the word-meaning, ritual action itself would be impossible in the case of the injunction "one should build the *śyena*-altar" (*śyenacitaṃ cinvīta*).

As for the argument that in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains," the *ākṛti* indicates the individual as its object, it can equally be said in the other case—"one should build the *śyena*-altar"—that the individual indicates the *ākṛti* as its object.
What, then, is superior in this regard?
That the form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of the word.
If the individual (*vyakti*) were the meaning of the word, it would not be applied to another individual.
If it is then applied to another individual, then the individual is not the meaning of the word, for an individual is indeed devoid of all generalities and particularities.
It is replied: this is not a fault;
it will function toward another individual precisely as something devoid of all generalities and particularities.
If it were to apply to another individual that is devoid of all generalities and particulars, then that [individual] would indeed be a generality.

To this it is replied: no; for that object which is the substratum of both generalities and particulars is the individual (*vyakti*). And a word denoting an individual does not apply to a generality, nor does it apply to a particular.
But [the word] denotes their very substratum; therefore, its occurrence in another individual is not a fault.
For that is not a universal.
But was it not said that it is perceived as a subordinate factor?
The fact that [the object] is subordinate does not invalidate our position;
for it is perceived in every respect.
Whether it is subordinate or primary depends on the context of the meaning.
If it is uttered for its own sake, it is primary;
if, however, it is not for its own sake but solely for the sake of another, then it is secondary.
In that case, there is no operation of the word itself.

Now, it might be argued: "In the case of the word *daṇḍin* (‘staff-bearer’), the staff itself is not denoted by the word *daṇḍin*, and yet one understands [the person] as qualified by a staff. Likewise here too, the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not denoted, and yet the individual (*vyakti*) would be understood as qualified by that generic form.
This is not well said.
It is true that the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) does not directly denote the staff; however, it is not the case that there is no cognition of the staff-bearer when the staff is not cognized.
For there exists within the word "staff-bearer" the constituent part "staff," by which the staff is made known.
Therefore, it is correct that when the qualifier is perceived, the qualified is perceived.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a certain part of the word *go* denotes the generic form (*ākṛti*), while another part denotes the individual (*vyakti*), such that it is said: 'From that [part], the form is understood, but the word *go* itself does not denote the form'?
Furthermore, it is not as if the word *daṇḍin* is not applied to the staff, so that the word *go* would likewise not be applied to the form.
It is for that very reason that it has been demonstrated that the word *śyena* denotes only the configuration (*ākṛti*).

Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that in the absence of a connection with the individual *śyena*, the word *śyena* expresses the configuration because it is uttered;
however, the use of a word for an individual grain of rice (*vrīhi-vyakti*) is never observed without a connection to the configuration of rice.
Therefore, the view that the word denotes the form (ākṛti) is superior.
If it is argued that [the injunction] would not be an action, or that there is an injunction regarding a different object, or that it does not concern a substance—[these objections do not hold].
Because the performance has that as its purpose, there is no division.

Since a word has the generic form (*ākṛti*) as its meaning, its application is to that individual (*vyakti*) with which the generic form is connected; for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is heard in scripture as something to be performed upon a substance.
Of which [substance]?
Of that which is the means of sacrifice.
Since that [sprinkling] is prompted by the *apūrva*, it does not pertain to the generic form (*ākṛti*), because that would be impossible.
In this context, the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) is employed as a designation for the generic form in order to specify the substratum of the sprinkling;
for it will cause the generic form to be understood, and once the generic form is understood, it will specify the substratum of the sprinkling.
Therefore, the mention of "form" (ākṛti) is not contradicted.

Thus, in the statement "six cows are to be given as the sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā), when the number is to be applied to the substance that constitutes the fee, the word "cows" serves as a qualifier denoting the form. Likewise, in the phrase "another," there is a connection with "otherness" (anyatva) regarding the substitute for what has been lost.
In this regard, the word "animal" (paśu) denotes the form (ākṛti), and thus it will be qualified by that form.
Therefore, it is established that words such as "cow" and "horse" are denoters of the form.
It has been stated: "The purpose of the Vedic corpus (samāmnāya) is this; therefore, everything [in it] must have that [form] as its object."

They prescribe: "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*; one should sacrifice with the *balabhid*; one should sacrifice with the *abhijit*; one should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*. In this regard, there is a doubt: are words such as *udbhid* injunctions regarding accessories (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)?
Why is there this doubt? Because the sentence appears to admit both possibilities—the word *udbhidā* is connected with the verb *yajeta*.

Does it enter into a relationship through grammatical coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya)—meaning "one should accomplish the sacrifice by means of the substance called *udbhid*"? Or rather, through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—meaning "one should sacrifice with the sacrifice called *udbhid*"?
Since both ways appear possible in this sentence, a doubt arises.
This being the case, we reply:
Or rather, it may be a name, because that which is new at its origin is not injunctive.
Alternatively, the position shifts:

we maintain that this must be a name; thus it will enjoin a meaning not previously enjoined—a sacrifice other than the Jyotiṣṭoma—and the Vedic revelation (śruti) will thereby denote a distinct sacrifice.
Otherwise, the Vedic text, intending to express the *udbhid* and other such names, would imply by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that which possesses the *udbhid*, namely:
"One should effect [the result] by means of a sacrifice characterized by the *udbhid*.
To say "one should effect [the result] by means of a sacrifice" is the meaning of the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

For the sacrifice is the instrument (*karaṇa*); since *udbhid* and other such terms are also designated with the instrumental case-ending, they too are instruments. In that context, the coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is consistent when *udbhidā yāgena* (by means of the sacrifice called *udbhid*) is understood as a name of the ritual action.
If it were a word denoting a substance, the coordination would have to occur through the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).
And between the direct expression (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct expression is superior.
Therefore, it is a name for the ritual action (*karman*).
[Objection: But would not the well-established status of denoting a substance (*dravya*) be denied, while the unestablished status of denoting a ritual action (*karman*) would be asserted?
[Response: It is said: its status as denoting a ritual action follows from the use of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*).

Why? Because the third case ending occurs after a nominal stem that denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*), and the sacrifice (*yāga*) is the instrument. Therefore, we shall infer this [sacrifice] from the word;
for when there is an instruction regarding a quality (*guṇa*), its connection is primarily with the principal act.

This being the case, we reply: when there is a doubt as to whether a term is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name (*nāmadheya*), and another quality is taught, its connection is with the primary action; the meaning is that it is the name of the action.
For if it were an injunction of a quality, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
When a male animal is already established, one cannot enjoin a female animal, the animal as a result, and the variegated color (*citra*) as a quality all at once within a single sentence.

If a variegated quality (*citro guṇaḥ*) were being enjoined, it would have to be enjoined for the female [animal]; it would not be enjoined for the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice or for one desiring cattle, nor would that [quality] be enjoined for the *agnīṣomīya*.
Likewise, in the statement "the *ājya* [stotras] are fifteen-fold," the state of being fifteen-fold applies to the *ājya* stotras.

However, the *ājya* stotras do not exist unless they have been enjoined, and there is no other injunctive sentence; therefore, this very [sentence] must enjoin the *ājya* stotras and, once they are enjoined, their fifteen-fold nature.

And the relationship between the number fifteen and the *ājya* hymns is indeed understood; however, both the relationship of the *ājya* hymns with the *stotra* and their relationship with the number fifteen remain unestablished. It is impossible for a single sentence to enjoin these two distinct matters simultaneously.
But rather, it is a name for the ritual action; thus, there is no contradiction.
In that case, only the connection with a number is being enjoined.
Furthermore, by means of the words "ājyās" and "stotras," the accessory would be enjoined only through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).

Therefore, the names of these rites—prescribed by other sentences such as "they praise with the Ājyas" and "they praise with the Pṛṣṭhas"—are established. As for the claim that the name of the rites is not well-known, it is [established] through the etymological derivation of its parts: they are called *ājyāni* because of their connection (*ājigamana*) to the butter.

How is it that they are called *ājya*? Because of a statement in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Because they went to the race (*āji*), that is the reason for the *ājya*-nature of the *ājyas*."

The *pṛṣṭha* stotras are so called because of the mention of "touch" (*sparśa*). It is called the *bahiṣpavamāna* because it consists of mantras dedicated to Pavamāna and because it is connected with the exterior.
It is called *citram* (the variegated) because it consists of various substances: curd, honey, milk, ghee, parched grain, rice, and water.
Therefore, these are names of rituals of this kind.
Now, why are the *ājya* offerings, qualified by the number fifteen, not enjoined as ritual acts for the hymns? Because there is no word that expresses them as thus qualified.
And another scriptural text is that which makes this [name] known.
"One desiring heaven performs the *agnihotra*," and "He pours the *āghāra* libation"—thus they recite.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the words *agnihotra* and *āghāra* injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rites (*karmanāmadheya*)?
We say: they are injunctions of accessory qualities.
Why? Because it is understood that "the oblation (hotra) is for Agni in this [act]";
likewise, there is the expression "he pours the libation (āghāra)," referring to a substance such as clarified butter (ghṛta) capable of flowing.
In this way, common usage (prasiddhi) will be upheld.

Furthermore, there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) in the case of the *darvihoma*, and an injunction of a quality in the case of the *āghāra* at the *upāṃśuyāja*. In those instances, these two possess purposefulness and produce a specific engagement [in ritual action].
Moreover, in the view that they are injunctions of qualities, there is no figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as is the case in the statement "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*."
In the Agnihotra, the injunction of an accessory is understood through a concise statement;
likewise, in the Āghāra, the accessory is enjoined by the direct Vedic text itself in the words "he performs the Āghāra.
Therefore, it is concluded that these are indeed injunctions of accessories. This being the position reached:
And its designation [is likewise].
If it is argued that there must be an injunction because of the hearing of the qualities associated with the name;
It is heard in scripture: "One desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this an injunction regarding a quality (*guṇavidhi*), or is it the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)?
If such a doubt exists, [one might argue] that it appears to be an injunction regarding a quality.
There is no doubt; for a quality is indeed heard [in the text]. Since that quality is being understood, it is impossible to say that it does not exist.
Therefore, this is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi).
Because the two actions are equal, there is no [fault].
When there is a single word, it is like something intended for another.
But its qualities should indeed be enjoined, because there is no separation [from the archetype] in the sense of being prescribed, provided they have not been taught by another [source].
It is heard in the scriptures: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds, which is unswerving at the new moon and the full moon," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are [the terms] such as "for Agni" and "for Agni-Soma" injunctions of accessory details (*guṇavidhi*), or are they names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*)? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
If it were an injunction of qualities (guṇavidhi), multiple qualities would have to be enjoined—namely, the fire, the cake, and the eight potsherds.
Therefore, they are not injunctions of qualities.
Regarding the grass and the clarified butter, because the words are applied even when there is no consecration, they do not denote that [consecrated] substance.
Regarding *barhis*, *ājya*, and *puroḍāśa*, there is a doubt: are these words for consecrated objects (*saṃskāra-śabda*) or are they words for generic classes (*jāti-śabda*)?
We say they are words for consecrated objects.
For everywhere, people employ the word *barhis* with reference to grass that has been consecrated, and not with reference to unconsecrated grass.
The word *ājya* is applied to clarified butter (*ghṛta*) when it has been consecrated;
likewise, the word *puroḍāśa* is applied to flour-cake (*piṣṭa*) when it has been consecrated.
But is it not the case that these terms are used even for unconsecrated substances in certain regions?
Just as people say, "The cows have gone away taking the sacrificial grass (barhis)," so too do they say,
"The clarified butter is for purchase," or "My mother gives me a riddle with the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa)."
The application [of the term] to them is due to similarity, just as the word "sacrificial post" (yūpa) is applied to the "resting place" (upaśaya).

Why is this so? Because the application of a word occurs with respect to a single part; therefore, it follows that these are words for consecrated objects (saṃskāra-śabda). Such is the position reached.
[The term *prokṣaṇī* applies] to the sprinkling waters because of their connection with the purpose [of sprinkling].
It is heard in the scripture: "Place the *prokṣaṇī* waters.
Regarding that, there is a doubt concerning the word *prokṣaṇī*: is it based on a ritual preparation (*saṃskāra*), or is it based on a genus (*jāti*), or is it etymological (*yaugika*)?

In this regard, since the word is observed when the preparations are present, its status as a term for a preparation might be understood; however, because the word is applied even to that which has not been prepared, it is a term for a genus.
In a certain region, people say, "We were agitated by the sprinkling waters even though they were non-conditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Since this would [otherwise] result in [the word *āpaḥ*] being a genus-term (*jātiśabda*), it is stated that it is an etymological term (*yaugika*).
Why? Because of its connection with the meaning.
From usage, it is inferred that the aggregate of prefix, root, and suffix in the word *prokṣaṇyaḥ* has a genus (*jāti*) as its cause;

for, through its connection with the act of sprinkling, the term—consisting of prefix, root, and instrumental suffix—is established as applying to water, thereby supporting common linguistic convention.

When even other forms of sprinkling are expressed by the word *prokṣaṇa*, then [the term] will apply to water simply through its connection with that [act of sprinkling]; thus, it is not possible to assume a collective meaning [of the etymological parts].
Therefore, it is etymological (*yaugika*).

The purpose [of this interpretation] is that clarified butter (*ghṛta*) may serve as the *prokṣaṇa*; for if these were words denoting a preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), then the injunction would be "bring the *prokṣaṇī* waters."
If it is a word denoting a genus (*jātiśabda*), as in "place the ghee" (*ghṛtam āsādaya*);
if it is etymological (*yaugika*), as in "sprinkling" (*prokṣaṇa*); and likewise in the case of the "fire produced by friction" (*nirmanthya*).
"They bake bricks with the *nirmanthya* fire. Since the word *saṃskāra* is seen [as a synonym] for *nirmanthya* when it refers to something prepared,
it is also seen to apply even to that which is unprepared (*asaṃskāra*).
"By means of this being churned, we shall cook it.
Because of its connection with churning, it is established as being etymological (*yaugika*) as before.
The purpose is that, when the occasion for consecration arises, the bricks must be baked after having been consecrated.

In the case of a generic term (*jātiśabda*), [the meaning] is understood according to what is appropriate; in the case of an etymological term (*yaugika*), as in "he eats with fresh butter" (*nāvanītena*), it is understood to mean "with butter that has not long been churned.
If it is argued that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice:
Regarding the first festival among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, namely the Vaiśvadeva, there is a doubt concerning the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva":
is the word *vaiśvadeva* an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), or is it the name of a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*)?
If there is a doubt, there is no doubt.
In the case of the Vaiśvadeva [offering], there is an option;
the word "Vaiśvadeva" is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), for an injunction of a subordinate quality is indeed understood.
The Viśvedevas are prescribed in sacrifices such as the Āgneya;
in those cases, there is an option between Agni and the others on one hand and the Viśvedevas on the other.
In this way, the established usage will be meaningful.
Or rather, it is not so, because of the context and because of direct injunction; for the context does not pertain to the substance.
This is not so;

Agni and the others are prescribed for those sacrifices by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), whereas the Viśvedevas are [prescribed] by means of the syntactical connection (*vākya*) within that very context (*prakaraṇa*), and not by any other means—this is understood. Furthermore, this option (*vikalpa*) cannot be one where the injunctions are of unequal authority (*viṣama-śiṣṭa*).
For context is not capable of subverting a substance that has been directly heard [in scripture];
therefore, it is the name of a ritual action,
and there is no mutual connection of meaning.

Now, it might be argued that by the word *vaiśvadeva*, the sacrificial accessory (*yāga-guṇa*) characterized by the qualities of Agni and others is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), because the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture) belongs to the Viśvedevas therein. However, if the sacrificial accessory is indicated by the word *vaiśvadeva*, then the Viśvedevas themselves would not be enjoined. How could the word *vaiśvadeva*, uttered only once, both indicate the sacrificial accessory and enjoin the Viśvedevas? This mutual connection between the word *vaiśvadeva* and the Viśvedevas is not tenable.
Therefore, it is merely a name for the ritual action that functions as an injunction regarding a quality,
because qualities exist for the sake of another.
Furthermore, the subordinate qualities (guṇas) exist for the sake of another;
they are not capable of causing the primary element (pradhāna) to repeat its performance.
Therefore, the sacrifice must be performed once; it ought not to be repeated in accordance with the subordinate qualities.
And because they have attained the status of deities, there is no contradiction.
In that context, since thirty oblations are offered during a single principal oblation, it is not possible for the number thirty to be achieved by the oblations made into the Āhavanīya fire alone.
Therefore, it is established that [the term] is a name of the ritual action.
Those [mantras] which possess a prior [source] and serve no other purpose have their efficacy in the Vedic collection.

But for the purpose of enjoining a quality, those qualities would be meaningless in the performance [of the rite], for there is nothing meaningful with respect to that [quality] which possesses its own object.

This is not the case that these are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*). While being for the purpose of enjoining an accessory quality, they would merely enjoin a number upon the potsherds of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*);
they are not capable of enjoining the performance of the sacrifice itself.

For the state of having twelve potsherds belongs to the sacrifice by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*), whereas the eight-potsherd cakes and so forth belong to it by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*);
therefore, those latter will not apply to the sacrifice.
Moreover, since the number eight and so forth form a single syntactical unit with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), they will not apply to the sacrifice, as they set aside the context.
If they were not connected to the sacrifice, they would be meaningless; if they were connected to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), there would be no fruit [for the sacrificer].
However, as explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), their function as praise for the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is appropriate.
Therefore, they are *arthavādas*.
The remainder of that is not tenable.
Thus, that which was stated must be refuted; this is the sūtra ending with the introductory phrase:
"Because there is no distinction, they would be applicable for the purpose of praise within the context of an injunction."
If it is argued that there must be a cause;
If you view these as mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), why should the eightfold nature and so forth not be the cause for [attaining] spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and the like?
For one desiring spiritual luster, there is the cake on eight potsherds;
likewise for the subsequent [rites], according to one's desire.
How could this be?

Even if the qualities were being enjoined for the *puroḍāśa*, there would be no pointlessness, nor would the praise of the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) have to be assumed through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, the injunctions will pertain to the desires.
Because it would be purposeless, [the Veda] is not the cause; for the causes of the author are indeed prescribed for the sake of merit.
Its accomplishment.
"The sacrificer is the prastara-grass-bundle; the sacrificer is the cake baked on one potsherd," and so forth, is recited in the scripture.
In this regard, there is a doubt:
is the statement "the sacrificer is the prastara" an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi), or is it an explanatory praise (arthavāda)?
Likewise, regarding the statement "the sacrificer is the one-potsherd [cake]," what is the prima facie position? That it is an injunction of an accessory (guṇavidhi).
How could this be? It will thus establish a meaning not previously known;
otherwise, the explanatory passage (arthavāda) would be purposeless, and it is logical that it should possess purpose.
Therefore, it is an injunction.
But how is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of these two understood?
For the grass-bundle (*prastara*) or the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) are not the sacrificer.
Nor is it the case that the sacrificer is the first sacrificial cake prepared on a single potsherd, or that the grass is the first cut.
How then does a word for one thing apply to another, or for what purpose is that which is already known being mentioned?
It is said: that which is already known is mentioned for the sake of praise.
The grass-bundle (prastara) is to be placed upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) because it represents the sacrificer.
Likewise, the one-pot-sherd cake (ekakapāla), which is to be offered entirely, represents the sacrificer; thus he becomes established in heaven, for the Āhavanīya fire is heaven.
This is the [explanation of] the genus (jāti).
Conformity.
"The sacrificer is the sacrificial post"; "the sacrificial post is the sun," and so forth, is what is heard in the scripture.
Regarding this, there is a doubt as to whether it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
It is an injunction of a subordinate quality because it possesses purposeful meaning.

Because it is impossible for the sacrificer to accomplish the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or for the sacrificial post to accomplish the function of the sacrificer, and because there is no other injunction [to that effect], this is not an injunction.
The correspondence [between them] is for the purpose of praising the injunction.
The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) arises from figurative description (*guṇavāda*).
What is the quality? It is similarity.
What is the similarity? It is verticality and brilliance.
Therefore, explanatory passages (arthavādas) of this kind [are to be understood] in this manner.
Praise.
The Infinite.
It is heard in the scripture: "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi* [bricks].

Regarding this, when there is a doubt as to whether it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is an injunction because it conveys something not previously known.
To this, it is replied: if it were an injunction, the meaning would be that "one should lay down bricks accompanied by the *sṛṣṭi* mantras."

In that case, no specific distinction would be adopted regarding the bricks, such as "those of this form have creation-mantras, while those of that form do not. Consequently, all mantras containing the characteristic of creation would apply to every brick,
and other mantras that are not specifically connected [to a particular brick] would become purposeless.
Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the mantras already established by their inclusion in the Vedic collection for the purpose of laying down the bricks;
the mention of the *sṛṣṭis* is for the sake of a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding their creation.

Furthermore, if it were an injunction (*vidhi*), there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereby one would have to indicate those [bricks] which are not among the *sṛṣṭis* in the passage "they praise with one."
But surely there is also figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even in a restatement (*anuvāda*). There is no fault in employing figurative indication on the side of the restatement.
However, how can the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) apply both to those [mantras] that do not describe creation and to those that do?
By way of abundance: there, the mantras possessing the marks of creation are numerous, while those lacking such marks are few.
This is the "conjunction of marks" (liṅgasamavāya).

"He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks; he lays down the *ājyānī* bricks"—if these were injunctions, then while the *prāṇabhṛt* mantras are being laid down, there would be the uselessness (*ānarthakya*) of mantras that lack the corresponding indicative marks (*liṅga*). Therefore, they are restatements (*anuvāda*). A word for one thing may apply to another due to the presence of a common indicative mark (*liṅgasamavāya*), as in "the umbrella-bearers are going," where all those accompanied by one umbrella-bearer are indicated. However, this word *prāṇabhṛt* and the word *sṛṣṭi* do not indicate the group of mantras by abandoning their own primary meanings.
When both the words *sṛṣṭi* and *prāṇabhṛt* are applicable to a group (*gaṇa*), they are both included.
Just as, for example, by the word "umbrella-bearer" (*chatri*), used in the sense of indicating its own referent, that person who is actually carrying an umbrella is also included.
[This principle applies] in cases of doubt, based on the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣāt*).
"One places smeared pebbles"; it is heard in the scripture, "Clarified butter is indeed brilliance.
In this regard, there is a doubt:
should the pebbles be smeared with any one of the substances—clarified butter, oil, or fat—or only with clarified butter?
How is there doubt?
Because the sentence begins with the general term "ointment" (añjana) and concludes with the specific term "clarified butter" (ghṛta);
for within a single sentence, the conclusion must correspond to the beginning.

In this regard, there arises a doubt as to which is more consistent between the commencement and the conclusion: whether the universal is intended at the outset for the purpose of indicating the particular, or whether the particular at the conclusion is intended for the purpose of characterizing the universal.
Thus, when there is doubt at the outset, since there is no contradiction in a general statement, a specific meaning should not be assumed.
However, since a cognition of the general arises at the conclusion, there is a contradiction; therefore, the mention of "clarified butter" (*ghṛta*) serves to define the term.
Just as the word "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is used for both what is created and what is not created, so too "clarified butter" is said to be "clarified butter" even when it is not clarified butter.
Or rather, because it is a part of conceptual construction by virtue of its object.
It is heard in the scripture: "One portions out with the *sruva* ladle," "one portions out with the *svadhiti* knife," and "one portions out with the hand. Regarding this, there is a doubt:

should everything—whether liquid, solid, or meat—be portioned out with the *sruva*, the *svadhiti*, and the hand respectively? Or is there a distribution based on the nature of the substance, such that liquids are portioned with the *sruva*, meats with the *svadhiti*, and solids with the hand?
Since the text makes no specific distinction, there is no fixed rule.
Words denoting action have the sense of being as their primary meaning; from them, the ritual act is to be understood, for it is this meaning that is enjoined.

In the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) was established; therein, injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and traditional texts (*smṛti*) were determined according to their true nature, while subordinate injunctions (*guṇavidhi*) and names (*nāmadheya*) were examined, and it was stated that the determination of doubtful matters is achieved through the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*) or through the context (*artha*).
That must not be forgotten.

Immediately following this, the primary and secondary elements will be examined, as well as those that are distinct and those that are non-distinct; this alone is the subject to be described, and nothing else. This indeed constitutes the connection between the chapters.

Therefore, six types of distinctions between ritual acts (*karmabheda*) will be explained here: difference of words (*śabdāntara*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), number (*saṃkhyā*), quality (*guṇa*), context (*prakriyā*), and name (*nāmadheya*). This which is about to be stated is first announced as a summary of what is to follow. By stating what is already indicated, the listener’s intellect is made to grasp [the subject] easily and is concentrated; thus they call this chapter "The Characteristics of Various Ritual Acts" (*nānākarmalakṣaṇa*) with that as its primary intent. Apart from this, there is the introductory matter (*upodghāta*) and the incidental (*prasaktānuprasakta*).

In this regard, first of all, this is considered: it was stated in the first chapter that "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*)," and an injunction is a sentence that expresses an action; and within a sentence, there are the meanings of the words. In that case, is Dharma expressed by each individual word, or is it one and the same [Dharma] expressed by all [the words] together? What, then, is the prima facie position? That Dharma is [expressed] with respect to each word.

When there is only one [action], then a doubt arises: does it proceed from words denoting an action (*bhāva*), or from words denoting substances or qualities? What, then, is an action (*bhāva*)? And what are those words denoting an action? They are such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), "he gives" (*dadāti*), "he offers oblations" (*juhoti*), and so forth.
But surely these are words for sacrifice, giving, and offering; they are not words for an action. This is not so.

And these words such as *yāga* (sacrifice) are verbal nouns (*bhāva-śabda*), and from them the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) and so forth is understood, as well as the sense "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*).
Thus, one should strive in such a way that something comes into being.
