Therefore, these are verbal nouns; whereas from words denoting substances (*dravya*) or qualities (*guṇa*), there arises the cognition of a substance or a quality, not of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).
Therefore, they are not words denoting existence (*bhāva*). What, then, is the conclusion? That it applies without distinction; that is, if it is argued that the meaning of all [words] is existence.

If one perceives it in this way—that because they are words denoting existence (*bhāva*), words denoting substances or qualities are not the enjoiners of the *apūrva*—then the meaning of all [words] is existence. [The text] will state the connection between "one desiring heaven" and "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), and likewise the connection between "one practicing sorcery" and "by means of the Śyena," as well as "one desiring cattle by means of the Citrā.
Therefore, these too are expressions of existence because they possess expectancy.

Among all expressions of existence, there is no reason for a definitive distinction that only words denoting action (*karman*) are the enjoiners of the *apūrva*, and not words denoting substances or qualities.

Those things whose form is perceived when they arise in their own application are called "names" (nāma); therefore, there is no further expectation for them once they have arisen in their own application, because they are already established as such.
But those [words] for which no usage is found when their own meaning arises are verbal roots (ākhyāta).
Therefore, the meaning should be understood from them, because their usage is dependent [upon that meaning].

However, those words whose application to their own referents is not found at the time of their utterance—meaning that at the time of usage, their referent is not perceived—are called *ākhyāta*s; thus he teaches these *bhāva*-words by means of a synonymous term (*paryāyaśabda*). How is it that *bhāva*-words possess synonymy?
Since their case-endings are said to be verbal (ākhyātika), what are they? They are "he cooks," "they two cook," "they cook," and so forth.
Therefore, the apūrva should be understood from them.
Those future purposes are uttered together with past facts.

When a past fact serves as the purpose for a future thing, its purpose is seen; the production of a future purpose by means of an effort is meaningful, and since that is accomplished by the past, the purpose is perceived.
However, when a future thing has a past fact as its purpose, nothing is seen; rather, an unseen [purpose] must be postulated.
Therefore, the sacrifice is not for the sake of the substance.

Now, it might be argued that this has already been stated: [the text] will say "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) to express the connection between the seeker and the substance, and "one should effect by means of the substance" (*dravyeṇa bhāvayet*).
From this, the production (*bhāvanā*) of the purpose by means of the substance would be understood, as well as the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

It is true that [the connection] with the substance is understood through the sentence "one should effect [the result] by means of the substance," whereas the connection with the sacrifice is understood through the direct Vedic statement (śruti), namely, "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice.

However, when the connection with the sacrifice is enjoined—namely, "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice"—then at that time there is no connection with the substance, such as "one should effect [the result] by means of the substance.
Furthermore, when the connection with the substance is being enjoined, there can be no connection with the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice).

However, when something is being restated (*anūdyamāna*), it must be possible [for it to exist]; and it is not possible for both an injunction (*vidhi*) and a restatement (*anuvāda*) to occur simultaneously.

Therefore, there is a contradiction between the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*). And in the case of a contradiction, the direct statement is more authoritative (*balīyasī*). Consequently, there is no connection of the substance with the person desiring the result (*arthin*). In that context, it is untenable to claim that the substance—given the absence of a connection with the one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*)—will serve the purpose of attaining heaven; this is the reason for the definitive conclusion (*vinigamanā*) that only words denoting an action (*bhāva-śabda*) are the enjoiners of the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and not words denoting substances or qualities. When [the text says] "one should effect [the result] by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena kuryāt*), then it is indeed a word denoting the sacrifice itself.
By the term "by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices," it is indicated through metaphorical extension (*lakṣaṇā*) that a sacrifice is enjoined for both the new-moon day and the full-moon day.
But how is it understood that this *apūrva* exists?
It is said:
Furthermore, "codanā" means an instigation.

What is the purpose of this deliberation? If words denoting substances and qualities also enjoin the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), then in the event of the loss of a substance or a quality, no substitute should be taken, as in the case of the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*).
However, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the performance should be carried out by employing a substitute substance or quality;
thus, those [words] are of two kinds, being either subordinate (*guṇa*) or primary (*pradhāna*).
Those things by which a substance is not intended to be produced are primary, because the substance is subordinate to them.

This being the case, it is more reasonable to assume the fewest unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*); however, we do not perceive any decisive reason (*vinigamanā-hetu*) as to why the *apūrva* exists in one instance and not in another.

To this it is replied: those verbal roots (*bhāva-karman*) by which a substance is not intended to be refined or produced are expressive of the primary action (*pradhāna-karman*), because the substance is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*).
For the substance is subordinate, since it is that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*) for the accomplishment of the action.
But in cases where a substance is intended to be prepared, a quality should be understood [as subordinate], because that [substance] is the primary element.
But the action would apply to the mere dharma alone, because it has not yet been accomplished, just like the *prayāja* offerings.

It is heard in the scripture: "He cleanses the *sruva* ladles, he cleanses the fire, he cleanses the enclosing sticks, and he performs the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) around the *puroḍāśa* cake.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are the circumambulation with fire and the cleansing primary acts (*pradhānakarman*), or are they subsidiary acts (*guṇakarman*)?
What, then, is the prima facie view?

To this it is replied: we say that when an action of such a kind is insufficient for its visible purpose, it is called a "mere *dharma*," and in that case, it would be a primary action (*pradhāna-karma*).

Why? Because the benefit is not yet accomplished; for an action of this kind does not itself produce a benefit for the substance, whereas a substance of this kind, while being brought into existence, becomes subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). Since that [substance] is subordinate, this [action] is the primary one.
Or rather, because the scriptural statement is identical, it should possess the same characteristics as the others.
If it is argued that this is an instruction concerning a substance;

If you should think that, because a second [substance] is not seen, the substance here is the primary element—this is not so; for the accusative case occurs even when [the substance] is subordinate. For instance, it is observed in such cases as: "He offers groats" (*saktūñ juhoti*), "He offers to the Maruts" (*mārutaṃ juhoti*), and "He offers the single-pot-sherd cake" (*ekakapālaṃ juhoti*).
No, [this is not the case], because it is for the sake of that [action], as in common worldly usage, and because it is subordinate to it.
But the consecration of the *stotra* and *śastra* is like that of the *yājyā*, because they denote the deity.
However, it would be drawn away by the purpose, because the deity is subordinate to the purpose of the injunction.

If the *stotra* and *śastra* were merely acts of ritual preparation (*saṃskārakarma*), then by virtue of their purpose, they would be displaced from the deities, because the deity is subordinate to the purpose of the injunction; for the mantra is subordinate to the purpose of the deity. Therefore, when that [deity] is the primary element, it should be led wherever the primary element is; in that case, the order and proximity [of the mantras] would be obstructed. Consequently, this faulty position must be rejected.
But which, then, is that mantra?

The *pragātha* "abhi tvā śūra" belongs to Indra; since it is recited in proximity to the offering of the cup for Mahendra, it would be drawn away to wherever Indra is, or it may serve as a subordinate element (*guṇa*) for the sake of a specific quality, like the case of the barren cow (*vaśā*).

We shall not reject this position: that the *stotra* and *śastra* are indeed the acts of consecration (*saṃskārakarma*), precisely because they denote a deity. As for what was said—that there is a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pragātha*—that is not so. By the word "Indra," Mahendra will be denoted; he is the very same Indra who, by virtue of the quality of greatness, is called Mahendra. For we perceive the word "Indra" directly as a designation of a deity, and the word "great" (*maha*) as a designation of greatness, just as a king is a "great king" (*mahārāja*) and a Brahmin is a "great Brahmin" (*mahābrāhmaṇa*). It is like the case of the barren cow (*vaśā*): just as that which is a barren goat (*ajā vaśā*) belongs to all deities, and when a rite is enjoined by the words "one should sacrifice a [goat] dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavyām ālabheta*), the ritual recitations (*nigama*) use the word "goat" (*chāga*) even though the act was enjoined by the words "barren goat" (*ajāvaśā*), so too, when the deity with his qualities is enjoined, the denotation will occur by means of the name without the qualities.
"Therefore, there will be no excellence"—
this is not so, because it is inherent in the Vedic revelation.
And because of the difference in designation.

Furthermore, there is a difference in designation: "Milk much for Indra, the oblation for the gods," and "Milk much for Mahendra, the oblation for the gods. For this reason also, they are distinct deities; if there were only one deity, there would be an option between the two mantras, and the mention of the specific quality (mahat) would be purposeless.
Likewise, [the same applies] to the *yājyā* and *puroruc* verses.

This being the case, the observation of a distinction between the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses becomes intelligible. For instance, one observes the Aindra [rite] through the distinction of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses beginning with "O Indra, [grant us] winning wealth" (*endra sānasiṃ rayim*) and "We [offer] to [Indra]" (*vayam*), and one observes the Māhendra [rite] through the distinction of the verse beginning with "Great is Indra, who by his might" (*mahān indro ya ojasā*). If there were identity [of the two], they would be subject to option (*vikalpa*); in that case, there would be sublation (*bādha*) in one alternative.
This is because, in the case of the barren cow (*vaśā*), the purpose is inherently connected [to the specific deity].

As for what was stated—that when an action is enjoined by the word *ajāvaśā*, the subsequent recitation (*nigama*) may be performed using the word *chāga*—that is correct; for we perceive directly that the term *vaśā* (cow) possesses a real connection with the meaning [of the animal], as seen in the injunction, "Recite for the omentum and fat of the *chāga*," wherein whatever is a *vaśā* is indeed a *chāga*.
Therefore, on the view that [the recitation] is a preparatory act (*saṃskāra*), there would be a displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *pragātha*; hence, they are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*).
Or rather, it should be so because of its meaningfulness (*arthavattvāt*).

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position: the stotra and śastra are indeed preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarma*). As for this matter of the displacement (*utkarṣa*) of the *praghātha*, let the *praghātha* be displaced wherever Indra is, for by the indicative power (*liṅga*), both sequence (*krama*) and proximity (*sannidhi*) must necessarily be set aside;
however, this does not apply to those [verses] that are already recorded in the traditional text (*āmnāta*).
It is seen.

To this it is replied: all [hymns] possess purposefulness. The *maṇḍūkasūkta* is used in the fire-ritual (*agni*), the *akṣasūkta* in the *rājasūya*, and the *mūṣikāsūkta* in the *ekādaśinī*. All [hymns] are used in the *vācastoma*; indeed, in the *vācastoma*, all *ṛc*s, all *yajus* verses, and all *sāman* chants are employed. Likewise, it is said that one recites the *pāriplava* at the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), and similarly, "if the sun should not rise while the *āśvina* hymn is being recited, one should recite all the *dāśatayī* hymns. Therefore, there is purposefulness for those [hymns] that have been displaced [from their original context]. Consequently, the *stotra* and *śastra* are acts of consecration (*saṃskārakarman*).
Alternatively, because of their connection with the Vedic text, the two verbs *stauti* and *śaṃsati* should enjoin the origination of the actions within the context.

Alternatively, the *stotra* and *śastra* might be primary actions. Why? Because of their connection with a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). For there is a connection with the locative case: "They praise in the *kavatī* verses," "They praise in the *śipiviṣṭavatī* verses. If it were praise, then [the action] would be located in the syllables of the *kavatī* verses;
if it were illumination, then it would be located in the deity. In that case, the *kavatī* verses as the instrument would have been heard in the instrumental case, not in the locative.
Moreover, there is a connection with the Vedic revelation (śruti), as it says: "He recites the *prauga*," and "He recites the *niṣkevalya*.
Therefore, praise must be accomplished by means of that mantra; the word expressing a quality will serve the purpose of accomplishing praise and will effect an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*).
Consequently, these two are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*).

Moreover, the two verbal roots *stu* (to praise) and *śaṃs* (to recite) would have to be words denoting qualities directly, or they would have to denote the act of naming through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, they must enjoin the production of an action, that is, the production of the unseen potency (*apūrva*).
This is also because of the distinctness of the words.
By the word itself, distinctness is indeed understood; [it is said] "the Agniṣṭoma has twelve stotras and śastras," for otherwise there would not be a state of being twelve.
Since the recitation and the praise of the stotras and the śastras are one and the same, if a distinction were resorted to, then the number twelve would not be maintained.
Furthermore, that statement would be purposeless.

In the Agniṣṭut sacrifice it is heard: "The cups belong to Agni," and therein it is further stated: "They recite [the verses] dedicated to Agni. If this were a preparatory act (*saṃskārakarma*), then that [recitation] would not need to be enjoined at all.
Therefore, for this reason also, these are principal acts (*pradhānakarma*).
Furthermore, another meaning is perceived.
Regarding the statement "the *stotra* and *śastra* are indeed connected": if one *stotra* is different from the *śastra*, then there is a connection between the two.
Or, if they were not previously mentioned [as distinct], then the *stotra* would be one thing and the *śastra* another; otherwise, that which is the *stotra* would be the very same as the *śastra*.
And the designation is like that of the ritual action itself.

Furthermore, there is a designation by means of connection with the accusative case, just as in the case of a primary object (pradhānakarman), as in "he recites the prauga" and "he recites the niṣkevalya.
And there is the accomplishment of a result.

Furthermore, there is the observation of the accomplishment of a result, such as "Of that which has been praised, you are the praise," and so forth; "Possessing Indra, may we meditate; may we enjoy offspring and food"—thus the fruit of the *stotra* is restated, not that of the deity.

Therefore, the *stotra* and *śastra* are principal acts (*pradhānakarman*). Elsewhere, the purpose is established by the Sūtra: in the tenth chapter, regarding the change of deities for the cups (*graha*), there would be an application [of the *stotra* and *śastra*] because they are principal acts.
The ritual injunction and the mantra have a single purpose because they consist of the same words.
Or rather, by virtue of its capacity for ritual application, the mantra should be expressive of the name [of the deity].

The alternative view introduced by "api vā" (or rather) is set aside: a mantra of this kind would be a statement of designation (*abhidhānavacana*), because of its functional capacity (*prayogasāmarthya*). When it is employed, it possesses the capacity to convey the giving of a cow (*godāna*) and the sacrifice of a cow (*goyāga*), but not to enjoin them. Why? Because the giving of a cow has already been enjoined in the injunction regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and the sacrifice of a cow has already been enjoined in the case of the *anubandhyā* cow. If it is argued that this must be a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*), [the response follows].

No; for even if it were stated repeatedly, [the injunction] would arise from that very [source]. Even if one assumes it has the purpose of praise (stuti), it is still redundant, because the sacrifice has already been enjoined by a complete sentence accompanied by an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Therefore, a verb of this kind occurring within a mantra is not injunctive.
Among those [mantras] that impel [the ritual], there is the designation "mantra."
The word "brāhmaṇa" applies to the remainder.

Now, what is the definition of a Brāhmaṇa? The Veda consists of both Mantras and Brāhmaṇas. Since the definition of a Mantra has already been stated, the definition of a Brāhmaṇa need not be explicitly stated, as it is established by elimination; it is established simply by the statement of the definition of a Mantra. That which does not possess this [Mantra] definition is a Brāhmaṇa—thus, the Brāhmaṇa is established by elimination.

The author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), however, for the benefit of his students, has elaborated extensively, including: the use of the particle *iti*; "thus he said" (*ity āha*); "it is recorded" (*upanibaddham*); the form of a narrative (*ākhyāyikā-svarūpa*); a reason (*hetu*), as in "one offers with a winnowing basket, for by it food is prepared"; an etymology (*nirvacana*), as in "that is the essence of curdness in curd" (*tad dadhno dadhitvam*); censure (*nindā*), as in "his fires are indeed uninvested" (*upavītā vā etasyāgnayaḥ*); praise (*praśaṃsā*), as in "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity" (*vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā*); a doubt (*saṃśaya*), as in "should one offer in the Gārhapatya fire or not?"; an injunction (*vidhi*), as in "the Audumbarī post is of a height equal to the sacrificer" (*yajamāna-saṃmitaudumbarī bhavati*); the action of another (*parakṛti*), as in "he cooks beans for me alone" (*māṣān eva mahyaṃ pacati*); a past event (*purākalpa*), as in "in former times they used to assemble with firebrands" (*ulmukair ha sma pūrve samājagmuḥ*); and the assumption of restriction (*vyavadhāraṇa-kalpanā*), as in "as many horses as one might accept" (*yāvato ’śvān pratigṛhṇīyāt*).
Cause, etymological derivation, censure, praise, doubt, injunction, the action of another, ancient tradition,
restriction, and comparison— these ten are the modes of exposition for the Brāhmaṇas.
This indeed is the fixed characteristic of the injunctions in all the Vedas.

This [classification] is also mostly applicable; for there are some mantras that abound in the particle *iti*, such as "Thus, or so, is my mind," which is recorded as having been spoken thus: "He said, 'May I enjoy fortune'"; there is the form of a narrative, such as "Ugra indeed was Bhujyu"; there is a reason, such as "For they desire this from you, O Vām"; there is an etymological explanation (*nirvacana*), such as "Therefore, you are indeed waters" (*apo nu sthana*); there is censure, such as "In vain he finds food, being witless" (*mogham annaṃ vindate apracetāḥ*); there is praise, such as "Agni is the head" (*agnir mūrdhā*); there is doubt, such as "Was it below? Was it above? (*adhaḥ khidāsīt upari khidāsīt*); there is an injunction (*vidhi*), such as "One should give to those who beg" (*pṛṇīyād inn ādhamānāya*); there is the action of another (*parakṛti*), such as "He gave a thousand, ten thousand"; and there is a mythic account of the past (*purākalpa*), such as "The gods sacrificed the sacrifice with the sacrifice" (*yajñena yajñam ayajanta devāḥ*).
That which is not recited in the sacred tradition lacks the status of a mantra; for the distinction [between mantra and non-mantra] applies only to those things that are so recited.
There is a doubt regarding the *ūha* (modification), *pravara* (genealogical invocation), and *nāmadheya* (proper names): are they mantras or not?

Since they denote [their respective objects], the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are mantras. To this we reply: the status of being a mantra cannot belong to those things not included in the traditional recitation (*samāmnāya*), even though they are denotative; for denotativeness is not the cause of being a mantra. Rather, it is the usage by those who are learned (*abhiyukta*). Those which are not called "mantras" by the learned are not mantras. And since such things as these do not exist within the traditional collection of mantras, they are therefore not mantras. The practical application (*prayojana*) is this: whatever expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed when a mantra is corrupted does not apply to those that are not mantras.
Among these, the *ṛc* is that in which the arrangement of quarters is determined by the sense of the meaning.

The word *ṛc* exists in the Veda [in the passage]: "O Ahi Budhnya, protect my mantra, which the seers who know the threefold knowledge know as the Ṛks, Yajus, and Sāmans. What is the definition of an *ṛc*? Among those, an *ṛc* is that where there is a division into quarters (*pāda*) according to the sense; that mantra where there is a division made by quarters is called an *ṛc*. For example, in mantras such as "agnim īḷe," those who are learned in the tradition teach: "We study the Ṛks," "We teach the Ṛks," and "The Ṛks occur."

If it is said that [the designation of a *ṛc*] is by virtue of meaning (*arthavaśena*), then it would not apply in cases where it is by virtue of metrical form (*vṛttavaśena*), such as in "agniḥ pūrvebhir ṛṣibhiḥ. Therefore, the phrase "not by virtue of meaning" is intended to exclude cases determined by metrical form and the like; rather, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of illustration. Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way, for if it were for the purpose of excluding metrical form and so on, the sentence would be split. Consequently, wherever there is a fixed arrangement of quarters (*pāda*), that is a *ṛc*.
The designation "Sāman" applies to the Gītis (chants).

Now, what is the definition of *sāman*? A particular kind of chanting is called *sāman*. For those who are experts designate the word *sāman* for a mantra-text when it is being chanted, as they say: "We study the *sāmans*, we teach the *sāmans*, the *sāmans* proceed. And the instruction of experts is our authority. Just as one says "curd is sour" or "molasses is sweet," so too the word "chanting" applies to a mantra qualified by chanting; it should be understood that the cognition [of the term *sāman*] with respect to the mantra arises through its connection with chanting. The word *yajus* applies to the remainder.
Now, what is the definition of a *yajus*?

The definition of a *yajus* need not be stated separately, for it will be understood through the very definitions of *ṛc* and *sāman* by way of contrast: that which is neither song (*gīti*) nor composed in metrical feet (*pādabaddha*), but is recited in a continuous flow (*praśliṣṭapaṭhita*), is a *yajus*.
Now, as for what is called a *nigada*: are they *yajus* formulas, or are they something other than *yajus*?
Or rather, the *nigada* should be the fourth [type of *mantra*], because of its specific nature as a *dharma*.
And because of designation.
There is also a designation [to this effect]: "The *yajus* formulas exist, but not the *nigadas*;
the *nigadas* exist, but not the *yajus* formulas.
For this reason as well, it is a different mantra.
Or rather, they are *yajus* formulas, because they possess that characteristic form.
The *nigadas* are indeed *yajus* formulas.

Why? Because they possess that same form; their very form is identical to that of the *yajus*, namely, the continuous recitation (*praśliṣṭapāṭha*) and the distinctness from the characteristics of *ṛk* and *sāman*.
A specific ritual property [is established] by virtue of this statement.
Because of the statement—that is, because of the capacity for communication—for some *yajus* formulas there exists indeed the capacity to communicate to another person;
and also because of the meaning.
Furthermore, there is a purpose served by those [mantras] being understood by other persons; if they were uttered in a whisper, they would not cause understanding among other persons.
Therefore, the specific property [of loudness] is meaningful.
And those sacrificial formulas which are uttered loudly are called *nigadas*.

Why? Because the prefix *ni-* is a denoter of excellence (*prakarṣa*); for example, that which is red with excellence is said to be "intensely red" (*nitarāṃ rakta*). The root *gad-* has the meaning of "speaking," referring to the recitation of the text.
Indeed, this very excellence consists in being characterized by loudness.
The designation is for the sake of the qualities.

Now, as for what was said regarding "designation," that occurs even when there is identity [of substance], based on a quality (*guṇa*), just as one says, "Let the Brahmins be fed here, and the wandering mendicants there.
In the same way, those very *yajus* formulas are designated as "nigadas" by virtue of the quality of being uttered loudly.
If it is argued that this applies to all [formulas]...
If that which is recited aloud were a *nigada*, then even an *ṛc* would follow as being a *nigada*;
this is not so, because of the specific designation of the *ṛc*.

The *nigadas* are not designated as *ṛcs*, for it is said, "The *nigadas* are indeed not to be recited with the sacrificial formula (*ayājyā*); one sacrifices with the *ṛc* itself. For designations arise on the basis of distinction. It is replied: the designation is a *liṅga* (indicative mark); let the basis for its application be stated. The root *gad* functions [here] with respect to that which is not composed in metrical feet (*apādabaddha*), for that which is not composed in metrical feet is called prose (*gadya*).
A group of words constitutes a single sentence because it has a single purpose, provided that if it were divided, the parts would remain syntactically expectant.
In the case of identical [words], there would be a split in the sentence.

"Īṣe tvā, ūrje tvā," and likewise, "āyur yajñena kalpatām, prāṇo yajñena kalpatām. Here a doubt arises: are such [formulas] as these distinct sentences, or are they one? We say they are one. When it is said, "Īṣe tvā," no visible purpose is perceived; likewise with "ūrje tvā," there is only an unseen result by virtue of the power of the words. Therefore, it is logical to assume that both together constitute a single sentence; in this way, there will be an assumption of a single, minimal unseen result. Consequently, it is a single sentence.
Or rather, there is a syntactic connection (anuṣaṅga) because all [the terms] are equally connected until the completion of the sentence.

Furthermore, a sentence-remainder (*vākyaśeṣa*) is that which is heard as complete and capable [of fulfilling the sense] either after or before something that is expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*). But what duration constitutes "proximity" (*sannidhi*)? It is said: it is for as long as both [the expectant word and the remainder] are able to relate to one another. And what is this [duration]? It is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) or the intervention of a related word (*saṃbandhipadavyavāya*); for within that span, both are able to relate. Indeed, even when there is an intervention by a related word, the prior mental impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*) does not disappear precisely because of that connection.

Even where there is an intervention by another word that requires something else, a connection still exists; for the function of both must be stated, and thus the latter expects the former. If it did not expect it, one of the two would be a faulty recitation. And it is capable of being expected; therefore, just as this [word] is in proximity to one, so it is to the other, because neither is separated from the two words by unrelated terms. Since both require [the other], this much alone is the cause for the connection with the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), and not mere immediate sequence; for a connection occurs even when there is an interruption, provided there is no separation.
Therefore, there is an implication; it would not be implied because of the intervention [of other words].
"May your desirable wealth go together with the wind; may your limbs be united with the conquerors; may the lord of the sacrifice be united with his blessing."

In the phrase "Let the waters go with the wind," because of the intervention by the word ending in the plural number, "saṃ yajatrair aṅgāni" (may the limbs unite with the sacrificial vessels), the remainder "saṃ yajñapatir āśiṣā" (may the lord of the sacrifice unite with his blessing) does not attach itself. Since it is separated by one word that requires completion, the remainder "gacchatām" (let them go) [attaches to the first]. Then, because it has not entered into a connection with the subsequent word ending in the plural, "saṃ yajatrair aṅgāni," and is thus separated, it does not connect with what follows. For then a distinction is perceived: namely, that it is separated by one word. When such a distinction is perceived, the presence of the remainder of the sentence there is not tenable.
Therefore, a worldly completion of the sentence must be supplied for that which ends in a plural number and for that which follows it separated by those [intervening words].
There is a difference in action when there is a different word, because of the connection with what has been performed.

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, where it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "He offers the sacrificial fees," and "He gives gold to the Ātreya. Regarding these acts of sacrificing, giving, and offering, there arises the doubt: do they perform their function by acting together, or by acting separately? For we observe that means of accomplishment sometimes accomplish their purpose by acting together, and sometimes by acting separately. To begin with, they act together: three pressing-stones are seen supporting a single mouth [of the ladle]; but pegs on an elephant's tusk act even separately, for it is possible to hang a loop from each one individually.
Therefore, regarding the acts of sacrificing, giving, and offering oblations, a doubt arises as to whether they should be accomplished collectively or separately.

What, then, is the prima facie view? That they should be performed collectively. Why? Because it is more reasonable to assume a minimal number of unseen benefits (*adṛṣṭa*) for those [acts] whose purpose is unseen.
How so?
An object that is neither seen nor heard is understood to be non-existent;
if it does not exist, then what is seen or heard is not contradicted.
If [the two] were contradictory, it would have to be postulated; by that means, it becomes meaningful.
However, if no distinction were perceived, then not even one would be postulated.
Furthermore, the repetition of the same [injunction] would be purposeless, as there is no distinction [between the two instances].

Regarding the injunctions "he offers the *samidh* oblations" and "he offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," and so forth— the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), which is repeated five times, does it enjoin a single unseen potency (*apūrva*), or does it produce a distinct unseen potency with each repetition?
Since a difference in action was stated to arise from a difference in words, whereas here the very same word is uttered again and again,
therefore there is only one unseen potency in this case.
But surely, if it does not produce a distinct *apūrva*, it becomes purposeless.

True, it would indeed be purposeless; yet, even if uttered many times, it does not convey a different meaning. What is understood at the first utterance is precisely what is understood at the hundredth. Therefore, the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), when repeated five times, enjoins a single *apūrva*.
Furthermore, the repetition will not be purposeless, for the deity Tanūnapāt and others will be enjoined; therefore, there is a single *apūrva*.
However, the context [belongs] to the Full Moon sacrifice because its specific form is not stated [elsewhere].
And because of the perception of a distinction, there would be a lack of activity toward all [objects] when they are equal.

And if all [the elements] were equally principal, the *prayāja* offerings would not be seen in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*); yet they are indeed seen there—[as in the injunction]: "At each *prayāja*, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain. This would not be possible if the *prayāja* did not possess the quality of being subordinate to the *āgneya* [offering].
Therefore, all are not equally principal;
rather, it is a subordinate element because of its connection with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).
Or rather, there is a simultaneous injunction of the qualities, because when [the rite] is enjoined by the scripture, each [quality] would be taught as being for the sake of that [rite].
The injunctions regarding ritual action would consist of the Āgneya and other sacrifices.

Why? Because of the simultaneous teaching of multiple qualities; for you intend to enjoin several qualities here by means of a single sentence, and it is not possible to enjoin several qualities when the action has been enjoined by another word and there is no mutual connection between them.

How so? If, first of all, the intended connection is "on the full moon day there is [the offering] consisting of eight potsherds" (*paurṇamāsyām aṣṭākapālo bhavati*), then the meaning is not that "being an eight-potsherd offering, it is connected with that [full moon]. What then is it that is connected with the full moon? In that case, the verb *bhavati* ("there is") is operative; at that time, the term *āgneyaḥ* ("dedicated to Agni") also falls into proximity, but because there is no [direct] connection, it cannot be connected with this [verb], as in "the eight-potsherd offering becomes dedicated to Agni.
Alternatively, if what is intended is "the one dedicated to Agni exists on the full moon day" (*āgneyaḥ paurṇamāsyām bhavati*).
In that case, there would be no connection at all between the *āgneya* and the *puroḍāśa*.
Alternatively, if it is argued that the *āgneya* nature of the eight-potherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*) is prescribed for the full moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*),
then it must be stated by what [text] that eight-potherd cake is prescribed for that [sacrifice].
Now, in that case, the status of being an eight-potherd cake would belong to the offering to Agni; even so, this same fault remains.
Or, if "on the full moon day" were connected with both [the offerings], [that too would be problematic].
And designation is likewise [based on that].

Indeed, these formidable oblations are collected on the new moon day; by stating "the one for Agni first, the one for Indra last," it demonstrates their combination (*samuccaya*). If the offerings to Agni and the others were merely subordinate qualities (*guṇa*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*) between them.

In that case, the designation "the one for Agni first, the two for Indra last" would not be possible; furthermore, if there were an option, the sequence of the collection (*saṃbhāra-paurvāparya*) would be untenable.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
And an indicative mark (liṅga) is observed: "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day; thirteen on the new moon day.
Therefore, the Upāṃśuyāja should be like the Paurṇamāsī sacrifice.

"It is a state of redundancy (*jāmi*) in the sacrifice that two *puroḍāśa* cakes are offered consecutively; therefore, one should offer the *upāṃśuyāja* in between to avoid redundancy—Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in secret to avoid redundancy, Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in secret to avoid redundancy, Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in secret to avoid redundancy.

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the phrase "one offers the *upāṃśuyāja* in between" refer to the collection of the previously mentioned sacrifices characterized by Viṣṇu and the others, or rather to a distinct, new sacrifice?
To this it is replied: the *upāṃśuyāja* ought to be like the *Paurṇamāsī* [offering].

Why? Because of the connection with a name; for a specific sacrifice connected with a name is heard in scripture, namely that which is designated as the *upāṃśuyāja*. Furthermore, the material and the deity do not constitute its "form" (*rūpa*), and sacrifices characterized by the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśu*) already exist in the context. Therefore, it is a term denoting a collective. [Objection: But surely another distinct sacrifice, characterized by the quality of being whispered, is enjoined as having form by means of the property of whispering.

A word of such a nature cannot denote a sacrifice qualified by "inaudibility" (*upāṃśu*); for its designator would have to be *upāṃśuyāga*, which, according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, ought to take the form *upāṃśuyāja* due to the substitution of *k*. However, the word *upāṃśuyāja* is an irregular formation (*avyutpanna*). Therefore, it is not a distinct sacrifice possessing its own specific form. Even if it were merely the general term *yajati* (to sacrifice) connected with a name, we could still not recognize it as a separate sacrifice, as its deity and substance are not prescribed.
But if this were the case, it would follow that [the word] is non-expressive even of the primary acts.

Let the term *upāṃśuyāja* not be so; the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) will suffice. This being so, even if the term *upāṃśuyāja* is not literal because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is no fault. Or rather, it is an original injunction (*codanā*) because [the acts] have not been previously established.
Because of the connection with qualities.
As for what is said— that it is not known which sacrifice is designated as the *upāṃśuyāja* to which this accessory (*guṇa*) is attached, namely, "one should sacrifice silently on the full moon day"—
therefore there is no fault;
and because of the statement regarding the general rule (*prāya*).

This statement occurs in a context where the primary object (pradhānakarman) predominates; it serves to reinforce the status of the primary object. Just as, upon seeing something written in a place where the best [writing] predominates, the thought arises, "This must be the best," so too, this is not a term denoting a collective whole. [The case of] the Āghāra and Agnihotra is thus, because they lack a specific form (arūpatvāt).
Because of the connection with the term "perception" (saṃjñā).

Furthermore, there is the attachment of a name, such as "one performs the sacrifice called *agnihotra*" or "one performs the rite designated as *āghāra*"; thus, the *āghāra* and *homa* are enjoined as qualified by their respective names.

Yet, it is not understood what specific rite is this one named *āghāra*, nor which is that designated as *agnihotra*. But is it not already known? The pouring out (*āghāraṇa*) is the *āghāra*, and the offering (*havana*) is the *homa*.

If both the general category of *āghāra* and the general category of *homa* were being enjoined, then the *āghāra* and *homa* would already be previously known; therefore, they would be mere restatements (*anuvāda*).

Alternatively, if both names were previously unestablished, even then the general categories of *āghāra* and *agnihotra* could not be expressed, because a name depends upon a specific instance (*viśeṣa*). Furthermore, since that specific instance is not perceived, the injunctions for the previously unknown *āghāra* and *homa* are not tenable.

Furthermore, how could an action (kriyā) be expressed by a word denoting a means (sādhana)? For that which is the most desired object among the means is expressed by a word ending in the accusative case, whereas an action is expressed by a verbal suffix (tiṅanta).
In the view of restatement (anuvāda), the collection of actions constitutes a distinct entity; that will be the most desired object among the means.
Moreover, [the action] is not the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, even the substance and deity that are under discussion are not present in the *āghāra* offering,
by virtue of which it might possess a specific form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, these two [terms] are also collective designations (*samudāya-śabda*).
Or rather, it is an injunction because the meaning of the word pertains to the sphere of performance; its repetition, occurring in proximity to that, is for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa).

And this is not the case; that these two are collective terms [denoting the entire sacrifice], for they would then be injunctions of separate acts. Why? Because the meaning of a word is determined by its usage. The meaning of the words "he pours out" (*āghārayati*) and "he offers" (*juhoti*) is that the pouring out and the offering are to be performed; thus we understand that a separate act is being enjoined. Furthermore, the words *āghāra* and *agnihotra* are known to denote the general acts of pouring out and offering respectively; therefore, their meanings are not unknown.
Therefore, they are established as being possessed of form.

As for what was said—that because they are already enjoined by such [passages] as "he pours upwards" and "he offers with curds," these two are merely restatements (anuvāda)—this is not so; for these two cannot serve to enjoin the *homa* and the *āghāra*.

In the statements "He pours the *āghāra* upwards" and "He offers with curd," it is not meant that "the *āghāra* must be performed" or "the oblation (*homa*) must be performed"; rather, what is meant is that "the connection between the upward direction and the *āghāra* must be established," and "the connection between the curd and the oblation must be established. Therefore, because these matters have not been previously established, they are not mere restatements (*anuvāda*). [Objection: But once the connection has been enjoined, the oblation and the *āghāra* will necessarily follow as a matter of course.
This is not so; for when this [injunction] exists, there is a connection by way of prescription.
Therefore, the *homa* and *āghāra* do not follow merely from the sense of the words; rather, we say that they are prescribed as something previously unestablished (*apūrva*).
If so, by what means is the accessory (*guṇa*) prescribed? Do not say it is by the word "curd" (*dadhi*).
But was it not just stated that the operation of the quality is understood from the sentence right now?
True, this is so; however, if it is not being enjoined, how could it be understood? Its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not be apprehended.
In the absence of a means of valid cognition, there would be delusion.
If that is so, then the words *juhoti* and *āghārayati* are injunctive.
Of what, then, is there a restatement (*anuvāda*)? We say: it is a restatement of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).

If they are injunctive, and their own meanings have already been enjoined previously, for what purpose are they uttered again? There is no fault here, because they are uttered in order to enjoin the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
Therefore, regarding the injunction for a separate ritual action,
as it was stated— that there is no material or deity prescribed for the *āghāra* offering—
what is the use of a material and deity in this case, since its form is already fully determined by the expression of well-known meanings?

Furthermore, this [offering] consisted of four portions; "having poured the *āghāra* for it" indicates that clarified butter (*ājya*) is its substance. The prescription of the deity is based on the wording of the mantra: "O Indra, may the lofty sacrifice touch the sky; O Lord of the Sacrifice, may the great sacrifice be accompanied by Indra, *svāhā*!"—thus he pours the *āghāra*. In this way, it is "accompanied by Indra" (*indravān*) only if Indra is its deity. Therefore, if this is a designation of the deity for the *āghāra*, then by this [mantra] the *āghāra* is performed.
Consequently, it is established that these are distinct rites, and not merely collective names [for the same rite].

The injunction regarding the animal and the soma is due to their connection with substances; for within the context, the connection with substances would be purposeless, as it is not for the sake of a subordinate quality.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma," and therein they recite: "He cuts off first from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest. Likewise, regarding the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma," it is also stated there: "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu, he draws the cup for Mitra and Varuṇa, he draws the cup for the Aśvins," and so forth. In this regard, a doubt arises: do the words "cuts off" (avadyati) and "draws" (gṛhṇāti) merely restate the collection of acts already enjoined by the terms "sacrifices" (ālabhati) and "sacrifices" (yajati), or do they enjoin two entirely new acts?
What, then, is the established position? That it pertains to the aggregate.

Why? Because those two actions which are considered here as being enjoined by the verbs *ālabhati* (he touches) and *yajati* (he sacrifices) have already been understood through the acts of *avadyati* (he cuts off) and *gṛhṇāti* (he takes).
And an object that has already been understood is not what is enjoined.
However, it refers to the heart and other organs by the word "animal" (paśu), and to the juice by the word "Soma.

Therefore, in the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," the verb "sacrifice" (yajati) is a restatement intended to connect [the sacrifice] with the result, as in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice.
And in the injunction "one should immolate the animal," the verb "immolate" (ālabhati) is intended to establish the connection with Agni and Soma.
Moreover, the collection [of offerings] is observed in the statement, "The Adhvaryu draws these ten cups at the morning pressing.
Likewise, there is a sequence: "The Aśvin cup is drawn as the tenth, and it is offered as the third.

If two previously unestablished sacrifices were being enjoined, then the deities would have to be enjoined by means of the Indra-Vāyu and other formulas; being for the same purpose, they would necessarily be subject to option (*vikalpa*).
For example: "He binds it to a Khadira tree," "He binds it to a Palāśa tree," and "He binds it to a Rohitaka tree.

In that case, neither the observation of sequence nor the observation of conjunction would be possible; however, if this is a reference to a collective whole, then this becomes properly established when the sacrifice is performed.
Therefore, these two are restatements of a collective whole.
And the formative forces are not impellers.

Due to that distinction, there is repetition of the action; for if there were a difference [in the substance], it would be purposeless, since the distinction [of the action] is subordinate to the substance.
But the ritual action (saṃskāra) would not be distinct [from the substance], because the substance exists for the sake of another and is subordinate (guṇabhūta).

As for what is also said—that just as in the injunctions "he binds with a *khadira* [wood]" and "he binds with a *pālāśa* [wood]," the *khadira* and other woods are optional alternatives (*vikalpa*) for the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), so too the deities will be optional—this is not correct. In those cases, the *khadira* and other woods are prescribed specifically to accomplish the preparatory rite. If the deities of the cups (*graha*), such as Indra and Vāyu, were also prescribed to accomplish the sacrifice itself, then there would indeed be an option here; however, they are not so prescribed in relation to the sacrifice.
Therefore, they should be combined (*samuccīyeran*).
Because they are applied separately, there would be a distinction of ritual acts based on their number.

This being the case, we reply: there must be a distinction of rites based on the number, because the number seventeen can only be applied when the animals are separate; and that separateness of the animals is possible in the case of many sacrifices, not in a single one.

How so? The injunction (codaka) prescribes that this sacrifice is to be accomplished by means of eleven portions (avadāna); yet these [portions] are obtained from only a single animal. In that case, the seizing of a second and subsequent animals could not serve to complete the required portions; rather, while one animal is being seized, others would be seized for some unseen purpose (adṛṣṭārtha). If that were the case, since they would not serve that specific purpose, they would not be "dedicated to Prajāpati" (prājāpatya), and thus the scriptural statement "the ones dedicated to Prajāpati" (prājāpatyān) would be contradicted.

Therefore, the number seventeen, which resides in distinct units, could not be applied to a single animal; rather, there is a requirement for many sets of cuttings (avadāna) in many sacrifices. Consequently, they would take seventeen animals for seventeen sacrifices, whereby the compatibility of the number will be achieved. Therefore, there are seventeen sacrifices.
And the name [of the sacrifice] is due to its connection with the originative injunction.
"Now this is Jyotis, now this is Viśvajyotis, now this is Sarvajyotis.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: do these names merely refer back to the previously mentioned Jyotiṣṭoma to prescribe qualities such as a sacrificial fee of a thousand [coins], or are they teaching distinct rituals characterized by the features about to be described?
What is the prima facie view? That it is a prescription of qualities for the previously mentioned ritual, in order to respect the context.

[Objection: But surely these qualities will be enjoined for the Jyotis and others by the force of the sentence. [Reply: This is not a fault; these are indeed designations of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself. "Jyotis" is taken as a synonym (pratīka) for the Jyotiṣṭoma; "Viśvajyotis" refers to its lights—namely the Trivṛt and so forth—as mentioned in the supplementary part of the passage (vākyaśeṣa). Since all those belong to it, therefore the Jyotiṣṭoma is called "Viśvajyotis" and "Sarvajyotis. Thus it is established.
And because the two sentences are equal in their connection with a new (apūrva) result, there is no injunction of a mere accessory (guṇavidhi).

In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, they recite: "He pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* (whey) for the Vājins. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the *vājina* an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) within the ritual characterized by the *āmikṣā*, or is it a separate ritual characterized by the *vājina*? What is the prima facie view? That it is an injunction of an accessory. Why? Because the Viśvedevas are called upon as "Vājins" by virtue of this *āmikṣā* which is their "vāja" (strength/food); having referred to them, the *vājina* is enjoined. Therefore, both the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina* belong to the Vaiśvadeva rite.
And in that very same ritual action, there is an injunction regarding the quality of the horse (vājina).

Just as when it is stated, "One performs the Agnihotra," it is further said, "One offers with curd," or "One offers with milk"—this being the position reached, we reply: the accessory (guṇa), when connected with a deity not mentioned in the original context, must enjoin a different ritual action; for in this case, these two sentences are equal, and both are injunctive of two previously unknown sacrifices.
But how can there be a mention of a deity not previously established, when it was just stated that "the whey (vājina)" is a restatement (anuvāda) of the Viśvedevas?
To this it is replied: here, the status of the Viśvedevas as deities is established in some cases by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and in others by syntactical connection (*vākya*).
It is established by direct statement when there is a derivative designation, and by syntactical connection when there is a designation using the dative case.

Where the status of deity is established by direct Vedic statement (śruti), there is syntactic unity with the *āmikṣā*; where it is established by the dative case-ending, there it is with the *vājina*. Thus, in one case these [deities] have the status of deity through direct statement while their connection with a specific substance is through syntactic connection (*vākya*); in the other case, both are established by syntactic connection.

Thus, here there is a conflict between the direct Vedic statement (śruti) and the syntactical connection (vākya) regarding the status of the deity; and since the direct statement is stronger in the event of a conflict, it is determined that the status of deity belongs to the Viśvedevas in the sentence concerning the *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), and not in the sentence concerning the *vājina* (whey). From this it is understood that its connection is with a deity not mentioned in the original context. Therefore, it is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
However, when the word denoting the ritual act does not possess a [new] quality, then a quality would be understood therein.

It is appropriate that there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) in that case; for there is no connection with any quality not already present in the context, but there is a connection with the sacrifice (*yāga*) which is already present.
Therefore, this [previous] description is incorrect.

Alternatively, this is a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*): "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) and similar statements constitute distinct rituals (*karmāntara*), being postulated out of a desire to avoid the fault of optionality (*vikalpa*).
However, it is understood from the word "juhoti" (he offers) that this is indeed the same ritual action, not a different one.
Therefore, it is established that there is an injunction regarding a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*) in that very context, and that there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to the scriptural statement.
But on account of the mention of a fruit, it would be a separate ritual action, because a fruit is connected with a ritual action.
With reference to the Agnihotra, they recite such texts as, "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the offering of curd and the like a separate oblation from the Agnihotra oblation, or does the fruit result from the accessory (guṇa) consisting of the curd and the like? What is the prima facie view? That it is a separate oblation.
Why? Because of the mention of a fruit; for a fruit is heard here, and that is logically appropriate to the ritual action.
However, because the two sentences are not equal, it [the fruit] should be understood as pertaining to the accessory.
By the word "tu" (but), the position is reversed: it is not a separate action, but rather that the fruit results from a subordinate factor (guṇa).

How so? For these two sentences are unequal: in the sentence "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," the fruit is mentioned in connection with the action, meaning "one desiring heaven should effect [heaven] by means of the oblation"; whereas in "One desiring sensory power should offer [the oblation] with curd," the fruit is mentioned in connection with a subordinate factor.

For in this case, it is not understood that "the oblation should be performed for the sake of sensory power"; rather, it is that "the oblation with curd is [performed] by one desiring sensory power. Thus, the connection of the oblation with the curd is for the sake of sensory power, not the origination of the oblation itself; the meaning is: "Whoever should desire sensory power, he should perform the oblation with curd. Which word here expresses the human effort? We say: the word "juhuyāt" (he should sacrifice).
Among equals, it should be joined with the ritual action.

"The Agniṣṭut is a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma; having made the twenty-one-fold [stoma] its Agniṣṭoma-sāman on verses addressed to Vāyu, one desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should sacrifice with it. Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman on the Revatī verses, one desiring cattle should indeed sacrifice with this. Here, the meaning is subject to doubt: is it that cattle are the fruit resulting from the accessory (guṇa), the Vāravantīya, of that very Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma, and "one should sacrifice with this" is a mere restatement (anuvāda); or rather, is "one should sacrifice with this" an injunction for a separate ritual action (karmāntara)? What is the prima facie view? It is not a separate ritual action; the fruit results from the accessory.

Why? Because this statement, "one should sacrifice with this," refers to that which is already known [from the archetype], not to something unknown; therefore, it is not a separate injunction. It is said that "one who desires cattle should sacrifice in this manner," not that "one should sacrifice. How so? By performing the Vāravantīya [chant].
Furthermore, the phrase "of this very [sacrifice]" is a clear statement that there is no other action.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that the fruit results from the accessory (guṇa).
Now, how is there no syntactical split (*avākyabheda*) in the case of another ritual action?

[In the sentence] "Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice, having performed the *vāravantīya* chant upon the *revatī* verses," a previously unknown (*apūrva*) sacrifice is enjoined as qualified by all the qualifiers; thus, because there is a single purpose and mutual expectancy when divided, the status of being a single sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is established.
But is there not a difference in meaning, since the sacrifice is thus to be performed as something new, and the *vāravantīya* on the *revatī* verses is also something new?

We say: no; what is enjoined is a sacrifice characterized by the *vāravantīya* as its quality and the *revatī* verses as its substrate, not the production of the *vāravantīya* itself. By implication, the *vāravantīya* will be produced upon the *revatī* verses, and it is capable of being so produced. It is replied: the connection between the *revatī* verses and the *vāravantīya* would not be enjoined; in that case, other *sāmans* might occur on the *revatī* verses, and the *vāravantīya* might occur on other verses as well.

This is not a fault; for by the word "having done" (*kṛtvā*), the relationship already established is expressed as being for the sake of the sacrifice, and thus that relationship is understood. This word "having done" is capable of expressing both these meanings: completion and priority in time. Just as in the command "Bring the red one," a horse connected with the quality of redness is enjoined by the word itself to be brought, and there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), so it should be understood here as well.

Now, if a distinct sacrifice is being enjoined, how does that *vāravantīya* [song] become the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* among the *revatī* verses? It is said: by virtue of the scriptural statement, it will take the place of the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*; for what indeed can a scriptural statement not accomplish? There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that "of this very [sacrifice]" refers to a statement dependent on what immediately precedes—it will also be a figurative expression (*lakṣaṇā-śabda*) meaning "possessing these characteristics," since there is no contradiction therein.

Therefore, the result does not arise from a quality; rather, it is a distinct action that possesses this property. Thus, it is established that in such similar cases, the result is connected to the action itself.
In the case of the *saubhara* chant, because of the mention of the person (*puruṣa*), there is a connection with desire through the *nidhana*.
What, then, is the prima facie position? That another desire is enjoined in connection with the *nidhana* of the *saubhara*.

Why? Because of the mention of the person; here there is the hearing of human effort in the form "one should do. This must be stated when the relationship between the *hīṣ* sound and one desiring rain is to be established, but not when the relationship with the *saubhara-nidhana* is concerned, for in that case it is already established by the force of the injunction of performance itself, namely, "one should perform the *saubhara* along with its subsidiaries."

Therefore, from the statement "one should perform [it]," which expresses human effort, we understand that whichever position renders the expression of human effort meaningful, that is the correct position. In this case, it is meaningful; namely, that there is a fruit subsequent to the *nidhana*.
Therefore, the *saubhara* chant is one desire, and by means of the *nidhana*, a second desire [is achieved] through differentiation.

Alternatively, the word "desiring rain" (*vṛṣṭikāma*) refers to a person; that person who desires rain is designated by the term *vṛṣṭikāma*. In this view, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the means of application. In the other view, however, since the word *vṛṣṭikāma* denotes a person, it would indicate the *saubhara* chant through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, it would be a word based on indication. And between the domain of direct statement and indication, direct statement is the proper authority, not indication. Therefore, we see that the second desire pertains to the *nidhana*.
And thus there will be an abundance of fruit; therefore, there is another desire in the *nidhana*.

Since everything has already been stated as being desired, the mention of "desire" (*kāma*) would apply to that [the *nidhana*]; however, the repetition of the text is for the purpose of the *nidhana*.
Now, how is it that there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) regarding the connection of *hīṣ* with the *nidhana*?

It is said: for one desiring rain, the *saubhara* chant already exists, and the *nidhana* of the *saubhara* (i.e., the attainment of the *saubhara*) already exists; in that context, the meaning "one should employ *hīṣ*" is what is enjoined.
Therefore, there is no syntactical split, and from this it is understood that there is a restriction (*vyavasthā*) regarding the *nidhana*.

In the same way, it should be pronounced as "ūrg" and "ū". Since the entire Saubhara chant desires food (*ūrj*), rain, and heaven, the Saubhara can be indicated by means of these expressions of desire.
For what purpose is it thus indicated?
It is for the sake of the *nidhana*; that is to say, the repetition [of the term] will establish the specific *nidhana* (the meaning is that it will determine the concluding syllable).
But a quality, because it is connected with a sacrifice, should enjoin a different ritual action, since that connection is not subsidiary to anything else.

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [enjoined by the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. With reference to that, it is heard in scripture: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman, one should draw the cups beginning with the Aindravāyava; if it has the Bṛhat-sāman, those beginning with the Śukra; if it has the Jagat-sāman, those beginning with the Āgrayaṇa. In this regard, a doubt arises: is this specific order of the cups (grahāgratā) enjoined as a modification of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, or rather for a different ritual action characterized by the Rathantara-sāman or the Bṛhat-sāman?

If the Jyotiṣṭoma is denoted by the mention of the Rathantara-sāman and the Bṛhat-sāman, then it possesses this specific precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*); if it is not so denoted, then it belongs to a different ritual action (*karmāntara*).
[Objection: Just as the Jyotiṣṭoma does not have the Rathantara-sāman, so too there is no other [action] that has the Rathantara-sāman.
[Reply: It is said: this sentence will postulate a different ritual action having the Rathantara-sāman, [namely], "If the Soma sacrifice were to have the Rathantara-sāman..."
[Objection: But surely there is no injunctive word here.
[Reply: It is said—in reply—that there is this word "syāt" (it should be).

[Objection: This is not able to enjoin; because of its connection with the word "yadi" (if), such a word occurs for the purpose of indicating a cause (*nimitta*) regarding something already existing, not for the purpose of injunction (*vidhāna*).

To this we reply: regarding this sentence beginning with "sayadi," namely, "If the Soma sacrifice were to have the Rathantara-sāman," there exists an intermediate sentence within it: "The Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara-sāman. The meaning of that intermediate sentence is one thing, while the meaning of the sentence beginning with "sayadi" is another; the sentence beginning with "sayadi" is unable to enjoin [the Rathantara], since the intermediate sentence will enjoin it.
Furthermore, the existence of either the Rathantara-sāman or the Bṛhat-sāman, even when heard as a condition (*nimitta*), does not become meaningful [in this context].

Therefore, if the connection with "yadi" (if) is not intended to be expressed, and that being unintended, these two words—"the Soma sacrifice would have the Rathantara-sāman"—are able to enjoin a ritual (*kratu*) characterized by the Rathantara-sāman, then "yadi" is redundant.
[Objection: But surely we do not find the optative suffix (*liṅvibhakti*) following the root *iṣ* (to wish); rather, they recite it as following the root *sic* (to sprinkle).

Indeed, the root *siñcati* (to pour out), when uttered in this supreme form, conveys the meaning of "desire" (*kāma*), for we consider it to be used in the expression of a wish; likewise here, the phrase "if one should take the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu" means "if one should desire to take them," and consequently, "one should perform the sacrifice having the *Rathantara* as its *Sāman*.
But if this were so, there would be merely a matter of desire, and not an injunction regarding the specific priority of the cups.

It is said: just as in this worldly sentence, "If one should desire curd as a condiment, one should eat rice," because of the mention of curd as a condiment, it is understood through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with that [sentence] that "one should eat rice with curd as a condiment"; so too here, because of the mention of a specific priority of the cups (*grahāgratā*) and because of syntactic unity with that, a *rathantara-sāman* qualified by that priority of the cups is understood.

Alternatively, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) here expresses the relationship between cause and effect: a Soma sacrifice with the *rathantara-sāman* must be made the cause for the cups having the Aindravāyava cup as the first.
Therefore, because of its connection with the entire sacrifice, this accessory (guṇa) should occasion a distinct ritual act; in this way, the connection with the entire sacrifice will be meaningful.

Furthermore, there must be a prior cause (nimitta) and a subsequent effect (naimittika). How so? For the effect can exist only when the cause exists, not when it does not. And that which is yet to come is not [yet] existent. Since the *rathantara* melody is something yet to come, how could it serve as the cause for the specific priority of the cups (*grahāgratā*) belonging to a prior time?
Moreover, it is beyond doubt that the *jagatsāman* is a distinct ritual action; because of its similarity to that, it is understood that the other [rites] are also distinct actions.
Therefore, this is not an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the Jyotiṣṭoma.
However, due to the difference in characteristic marks (*liṅga*), the unity [of the rites] might be stated for the sake of a specific purpose, since they constitute a single statement of qualities.
By the word "tu" (but), the position is otherwise: it is not as was stated, that this is a different sacrifice (*kratvantara*).
How then? It is merely a specific arrangement of the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*) within the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.
Why? Because of the force of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
But has it not been stated that, by the force of the sentence, this refers to two different sacrifices—one having the *rathantara* as its *sāman* and the other having the *bṛhat* as its *sāman*?
This has already been answered: the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself possesses both the *rathantara* and the *bṛhat* *sāmans*.
Furthermore, this was refuted on the grounds that because the *jyotiṣṭoma* contains many *sāmans*, the qualification by either the *rathantara* or the *bṛhat* alone is not possible.

This is explained as follows: a qualification is applicable because the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] are optional; there exists that performance where the *rathantara* is absent, and there also exists that performance which possesses the *rathantara-sāman*. Thus, this *rathantara*, by its very existence, serves as a differentiator due to its uniqueness.
Therefore, it is in the Jyotiṣṭoma alone that there is both the *rathantara-sāman* and the *bṛhat-sāman*.

Now, as for what was said—that there must be a preceding cause (nimitta) and a subsequent effect (naimittika)—this is not necessarily so; for even a future thing can be a cause, just as the performance of agricultural and domestic tasks is undertaken because it will rain. Moreover, that [future cause] is observed in the world, whereas this [present case] is a scriptural cause (vācanika-nimitta), and thus it ought to occur exactly according to the scriptural statement.
Furthermore, this potential suffix *liṅ* occurs with reference to all three times.
Therefore, even that which is yet to come serves as the indicative mark (*nimitta*).

As for the statement "that which has the *jagat-sāman*," it refers to a distinct ritual act; by analogy with that, "that which has the *rathaṃtara-sāman*" must also be a distinct ritual act. [Objection: Because it is impossible [for the *jagat-sāman* to belong to the archetype], it constitutes a distinct ritual act; whereas the *rathaṃtara-sāman* and the *bṛhat-sāman* are designations for the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, and therefore [the *rathaṃtara-sāman* case] does not constitute a distinct ritual act.
Because it is connected with a sacrifice, the Aveṣṭi is said to have the sacrificial rite as its primary element.

When the Rājasūya exists—[as prescribed by the injunction] "A king desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) should sacrifice with the Rājasūya"—they recite, with reference to that [sacrifice], the sacrifice named Aveṣṭi: "A cake on eight potsherds for Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee," and so forth. With reference to that [Aveṣṭi], it is ordained: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed the oblation for Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should pour butter over each oblation as it is offered; if a Rājanya, [the oblation] for Indra; if a Vaiśya, [the oblation] for the Viśvedevas."

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others—who are already established [as entitled to sacrifice]—for the purpose of indicating a condition (*nimitta*), or is this sacrifice being enjoined for the Brāhmaṇas and others?
How would there be the status of a condition, and how would there be the injunction of a sacrifice?
If the word "king" (*rājan*) applies to Brāhmaṇas and others in some manner, then it would be for the purpose of indicating a condition.

Now, if [the word "rājan"] refers specifically to a Kṣatriya, then scriptural passages of this kind would indeed be indicative [of that status]. What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it serves as a defining characteristic (*nimitta*). Therefore, it is explained in this way: the word "rājan" is etymological (*yaugika*); he whose function is "rājya" (sovereignty) is a "rājan. But what, then, is the function of a king? It is the protection of the countryside and the city, and from that, as well as from their elevation, those dwelling in Āryāvarta employ the word "rājya."

Those who are learned teach that "kingship" (*rājya*) is the function of a king (*rājan*). Therefore, we understand that he whose function this is is the king. It is just as when people did not know a certain man named Udamegha, yet they knew his son as "the son of Udamegha" (*Audameghi*); they would be able to infer that he who was his father was Udamegha, because such a designation applies specifically to the son of Udamegha. In the same way, it is understood that the word "king" (*rājan*) is derived from its connection with kingship (*rājya*).

Alternatively, there would be a lack of authority for a practice that is universal when it is contradicted by another universal practice; for those local people indeed accept the universal practice. Moreover, worldly matters that are not disputed are more trustworthy than those that are disputed; thus, the conduct of those dwelling in Āryāvarta—who are devoted to the means of understanding words and meanings, who speak [correctly], and who perform rituals—is more excellent than that of the Mlecchas dwelling in the borderlands.

Therefore, the word *rājan* is etymological (*yaugika*); the scriptural mentions [of the word] serve to indicate the causal basis [for its application]. This is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) for the Rājasūya, not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
But surely, anyone who performs the protection of the country and the city is addressed by the world with the word *rājan*.

It is said: The world employs the term based on connection (*yoga*); the word *rājya* (sovereignty) is well-known in the sense of protection. But we have already stated that this word *rājya*, in the sense of protection, arises from its connection with a king (*rājan*). Therefore, the word *rājan* is the root of the conventional usage, while the word *rājya* arises from its connection with that [king]. Furthermore, the word *rājan* is applied even to a Brāhmaṇa or a Vaiśya when they possess that [quality of sovereignty]. However, they do not remember it thus: "A king is so called because of his connection with sovereignty.
As for what was said—that one who is the agent of sovereignty is a king by inference, just as the son of Audameghi is called Audameghi because his father was Udamegha.

It is said: usage based on inference is stronger; we infer that the performer of sovereignty (*rājya*) is a "king" (*rājan*), whereas we observe people using the term "king" with reference to a Kṣatriya through direct perception. Likewise, we infer the etymological connection (*yoga*) that the performer of sovereignty is a "king," while they [the grammarians] record the traditional rule (*smṛti*) that "sovereignty is the action of a king."

Those who infer [the existence of a king] do so by means of memory (*smṛti*), whereas those who remember perceive [the king] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); therefore, in that case, memory is the stronger authority. He says: "Whosoever exercises sovereignty, people apply the word 'king' to him; it is not the case that what constitutes the king's activity is sovereignty. From this we understand that connection with sovereignty (*rājya-yoga*) is the cause for the application of the word 'king,' and not that connection with a king (*rāja-yoga*) is the cause for the application of the word 'sovereignty. We do not say that we understand connection with a king to be the cause for the application of the word 'sovereignty' based on usage.
How then? Because of recollection and application; recollection is stronger than application, for recollection would be inferred from application.
This is because [recollection] is a subordinate element to everything in the context of the fire-installation (ādhāna).

They recite this: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring, a Rājanya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the mention of the Brāhmaṇa and others for the purpose of an occasion—that those who are Brāhmaṇas and so forth, when establishing the fires, should do so in spring and the other seasons—or is the establishment of the fires enjoined specifically for the Brāhmaṇas and others? How would it be for the purpose of an occasion? And how would it be an injunction for the establishment of the fires?
If the two words "brāhmaṇa" and "vasante" are mutually connected, then the mention [of the season] is for the purpose of indicating a causal condition (*nimitta*).
If, however, it is "the Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires" (*brāhmaṇa ādadhīta*), then it is the injunction for the Brāhmaṇa to perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*).
The same applies to the Rājanya and others.

Moreover, while these direct injunctions for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) exist, the injunctions regarding specific desires (*kāmaśruti*) are not able to imply another separate injunction for the establishment of the fires; rather, these [desire-injunctions] would be mere restatements of the established act of fire-establishment. If these [injunctions for the establishment of the fires] did not exist, then—failing to grasp an injunction for the establishment of the fires—the desire-injunctions, which speak of the Agnihotra and other rites that would otherwise be impossible, would necessitate the acceptance of an injunction for the establishment of the fires.
