However, since these [injunctions for the establishment of the fires] do exist, it is understood that the subsequent desire-injunctions apply specifically to those for whom the establishment of the fires has been prescribed.

To this it is said: There is indeed an injunction for the mere laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) in the scriptural text, "He who, knowing thus, lays the fire, overcomes his rival and enemy"; the mentions of the Brāhmaṇas and others will be for the purpose of specifying the occasions (*nimitta*) for that [act] already established by that text.
It is replied: This repeated mention is for the purpose of prescribing the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*).

We say no; for this sentence is distinct from the sentence enjoining the collection of materials. For the meaning of "he establishes" (*ādhatte*) is one thing, while the meaning of "he pours water" (*apa upasṛjati*) is another. Indeed, a single sentence occurs when there is the injunction of a single purpose, but these two purposes are distinct; therefore, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) here. [Objection: But is not this also a sentence: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires" (*brāhmaṇo 'gnīn ādadhīta*)? [Reply:

It is said—in this case, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) enjoins the act of establishing (*ādhāna*), which is its own word-meaning, while it praises the connection with other word-meanings, such as the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, by saying, "He who thus overcomes his rival and enemy."
[Objection: But surely you have concluded that multiple qualities are enjoined by this single sentence.

[Response: This is not a fault; for it has been stated that multiple qualities may be enjoined when the sentence is intent upon enjoining a primary act (*aguṇavidhipara*). As it is said: "But those qualities should be enjoined because they are not separated from the object of the injunction, provided they are not already taught by another. Therefore, it is established that while the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) connected with the Brāhmaṇas and others is injunctive, this [present] repetition of the mere *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is intended to introduce the injunction regarding the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*).
And in the case of the solstices, there is a separate injunction because of the attachment of a specific name.

With reference to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they prescribe: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña; one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāpya; one desiring food should sacrifice with the Saṃkramayajña. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the result arise from a mere accessory (guṇa) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa itself, or is it a distinct ritual action (karmāntara) of this kind? What is the prima facie view? That it is a distinct ritual action.

Why? Because of the attachment of a name (*saṃjñopabandhāt*). Even though, by virtue of the context and the word *yajati*, it is understood that this is indeed the previously mentioned sacrifice, nevertheless, because it does not have that specific name, it is understood that another sacrifice is to be enjoined.
Furthermore, because there is no accessory (*aguṇāt*), it is an injunction of an action (*karmacodanā*).

Furthermore, no quality (*guṇa*) is obstructed here such that the injunction would have to serve the purpose of enjoining it; and if it were not a different sacrifice, there would be sheer meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*).

Moreover, if a quality were attached [to the sacrifice], then a connection between the sacrifice and the quality would be understood, and thus its performance would be enjoined. But when no quality is attached, only the sacrifice is understood, and thus its performance is understood as being enjoined. And the sentence is complete with respect to the fruit.
Moreover, this is a different ritual action.

How so? A sentence is completed with respect to its result: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice. Thus, the sacrifice is enjoined as a means for one who desires offspring. And if it is enjoined [as such], it is a different ritual action.
Or rather, it is a modification, because of the context.

The qualification for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices alone would be of such a nature as the Dākṣāyaṇayajña and others; in this way, the context (prakaraṇa) is maintained. And this is also because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).

An indicative mark (*liṅga*) also demonstrates this same meaning: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for thirty years, if one is a performer of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice; moreover, one may sacrifice for only fifteen years, for in this very way that [thirty-year] total is accomplished; for one should sacrifice at two full moons and two new moons, for in this very way indeed that total is achieved. If the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice were merely the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves, then the purpose would be the attainment of the number thirty; thus, it is logical that it should be assisted by the attainment of that thirty-year total. Therefore, for this reason as well, it is not a separate ritual act.
The application of the designation [of "sūtra"] is based on its quality.

As for what was said—that because of the attachment of a specific name (*saṃjñopabandha*), it is a different ritual—this would be asserted as a different ritual only if the word *dākṣāyaṇa* could not be interpreted in any way as denoting the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). However, it can indeed be understood through its connection with the quality of repetition (*āvṛtti*): "going" (*ayana*) denotes repetition; those belonging to Dakṣa are the *Dākṣas*, and their "going" is the *Dākṣāyaṇa*. But who is Dakṣa? One who is energetic (*utsāhī*).
Likewise, in the case of the *sākaṃprasthāpya* sacrifice as well, "starting together" (*sahaprasthāna*) signifies a connection with a subordinate quality (*guṇa*); this applies everywhere.

If it is possible to state that there is a connection with a subordinate quality for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), why then is that very same sacrifice, being recognized [as such], said to be something else? Or why should the context (*prakaraṇa*) be sublated?
The conclusion (*samāpti*) remains the same.
And the formative act (saṃskāra) [is not enjoined] because it is not in the context [of the main ritual], and because the word is not one denoting an action.

Certain [injunctions] are studied as unattached (anārabhyādhīta): "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal"; "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a pap (caru) to Sūrya"; and regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, they also recite: "He should touch the pole" and "He offers four handfuls."

In this regard, the matter is subject to doubt: Is the act of touching (*ālambha*) in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*), and is the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*) in the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices also an injunction of an accessory; or rather, do these two not depend upon the archetype (*prakṛti*)? And when they do not depend upon the archetype, are they merely as much as is stated in the text, or are these two actions characterized by sacrifice (*yajimat*)?
Or indeed, are they merely as much as is stated, because the action is rooted in what is explicitly heard in scripture (*śruti*)?

And this is not the case, that these are injunctions of qualities for the archetypal acts; rather, another touching (*ālambha*) and another pouring out (*nirvāpa*) are enjoined. If the touching and pouring out were enjoined [as the primary acts], then those two would not be the archetypal ones enjoined. If they were not enjoined [as primary acts], then the archetypal ones would be indicated by the words "the touching and pouring out which are to be performed"; having thus indicated them, the white color and the *caru* would have to be enjoined, and both the desire for prosperity and the desire for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) would also be enjoined—thus, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Alternatively, that word which is injunctive is employed for the purpose of indicating [the thing to be enjoined]; thus, in the absence of an injunctive [word], not even a single meaning can be enjoined.

If it is argued that the same [word] will both indicate and enjoin the quality, this is not so; a relationship between indication and injunction is not logically possible between two things that are mutually related.

Now, if it is argued that the meaning of the verbal root is a restatement (anuvāda) while the suffix is intended to be enjoined—meaning that whatever "slaughter" (ālambha) there is, it must be performed with these specific qualities—then [the following applies].

Nevertheless, the archetypal (prākṛta) act would not be indicated, for there is also a worldly (laukika) grasping; if the meaning of the suffix were being restated, it would be the archetypal that is restated, since that is known as something to be performed and not the worldly one. Therefore, it is not a restatement of the archetypal; rather, as far as has been said, merely the grasping and merely the pouring out (nirvāpa) are to be performed as something new (apūrva), because the ritual action (karman) is rooted in direct Vedic revelation (śruti). For it has been stated that "action is rooted in revelation," namely, "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (codanā-lakṣaṇa). Therefore, these are distinct actions. But the root *yajati* [is used] because of the connection of these with the substance, the fruit, and the enjoyer, due to their connection with the ritual action.

As for what was said—that these are not injunctions of qualities regarding the two archetypal acts—we accept that. However, as for what was said—that only the act of touching (*ālambha*) is enjoined, or only the act of pouring out (*nirvāpa*)—we reject that; these two rites possess sacrifice (*yajimat*).

Why? Because of the connection with the substance, the fruit, and the enjoyer (i.e., the deity). Here, a connection between the substance and the deity is enjoined for one desiring prosperity and one desiring Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*).

How so? For this is not what is being said: "Then one should sacrifice a white [animal]. If only that much were said, then a connection with the white animal would be understood. But here it is said, "One should sacrifice a white [animal] dedicated to Vāyu"; therefore, a connection between the white [color] and Vāyu is enjoined. Just as in the case of "Weave a cloth," a connection between the cloth and weaving is understood to be enjoined; or in "Weave a long cloth," the length of the cloth is enjoined because of the use of the word "long," so too here, because of the use of the words "solar" (*saurya*) and "dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavya*), it is understood that the connection between the substance and the deity is what is enjoined. Otherwise, it would be understood that the word for the deity was recited by mistake.
And because no indicative mark is observed.

Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) also demonstrates this point. Having introduced the injunction "one should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra," there is the rule for enclosure: "one should sacrifice in an enclosed space. The mention of the word "sacrifices" (*yajati*) in this sentence is only intelligible if these two rites involve a sacrifice (*yajimat*).

If, on the other hand, they were merely injunctions regarding accessories (*guṇavidhāna*) in the archetype, or if they were simply as much as was stated [without a sacrifice], then the restatement by means of the word "sacrifices" would not be possible.
Therefore, we understand that they involve a sacrifice.
Because it is observed for the most part in that specific context.
This being the case, we reply: in this doubt, the act of touching (*ālambha*) is merely a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

Why? Because of its occurrence in the majority of cases (*prāyadarśanāt*). Where other purificatory acts are said to be predominant, there this one is also heard. And a determination of meaning arises from predominance; for example, when something is written in the section on "foremost things" (*agryaprāya*), it is understood to be "foremost."
But surely, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is a matter of frequent observation; how can success be achieved by this?
It is said: it must be explained how it is established through frequent observation.
And how is frequent observation a reason? When there is an attainment [of the conclusion] through logical necessity (*nyāya*).

What, then, is the reasoning? Because there is no connection with a deity, the term does not denote a sacrifice; and because it serves an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), [the statement] "the calf, being seized, will cause the cow to low" [is intended as praise].
Therefore, when this is established by such reasoning, the observation of common usage (*prāyadarśana*) serves as an indicator.
Consequently, the mere seizing (*ālambha*) is a purificatory act (*saṃskāra*).
And because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is thus rendered logical.
But that which is connected with the word "artha" has that as its meaning, because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti).
Having stated, "There is fire; there is an oblation of wild rice (naivāra-caru)," the texts further recite, "He places this oblation [upon it].

Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the oblation intended for sacrifice—meaning it should be placed there after the sacrifice has been performed—or is it intended solely for the purpose of being placed?
We say it is for the purpose of sacrifice, for the well-known function of an oblation is sacrifice, not being placed.

It is said: although it is well known that the *caru* (gruel) is for the purpose of sacrifice, nevertheless, because of the absence of a connection with a word denoting a deity and the absence of a connection with the verb *yajati* (he sacrifices), it is understood that it is not for the purpose of sacrifice.

To this it is replied: in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of that very [passage] it is heard, "The wild rice (*nīvāra*) is indeed the food of Bṛhaspati"; thus, there will be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that proximate word denoting a deity, meaning that it is to be offered as having Bṛhaspati as its deity.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that the *caru* is for the purpose of sacrifice.

This being the case, we reply: since it is conjoined with the word "object" (*artha*), which is a word for a purpose, the act of placing (*upadadhāti*) must have that [object] as its purpose; that is, the purpose of the placing.

Furthermore, the syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) of this [act of placing] with the verb *upadadhāti* is direct (*pratyakṣa*), whereas its unity with the mention of a deity is indirect (*parokṣa*) and must be inferred. For "he places the *caru*" is a direct statement, while "he places the *bārhaspatya*" is inferential.

Therefore, the entire sacrificial porridge (caru) must be placed upon the fire; if, however, any part of it were employed in the sacrifice, that which was heard [prescribed] for one purpose would be performed for another. As for the statement, "The wild rice (nīvāra) belongs to Bṛhaspati," that is a mere explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Furthermore, as for what was said—that the well-known fact of the caru being intended for sacrifice is contradicted by the syntactical context (vākya)—[it is not so].
Therefore, it is established that [the mantra] is for the purpose of placing [the offering];
however, in the case of the Pātnīvata offering, there is a restriction because of its prior occurrence.
Having prescribed the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ accompanied by the Patnīvats, this is stated: "They release the Patnīvata once it has been encircled by fire.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this release of the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ prescribed for that which has already been encircled by fire, or is it a separate sacrifice from that?

If the two words "paryagnikṛtam" (encircled by fire) and "utsṛjanti" (they release) are connected with each other, then it is the release of the offering to Tvaṣṭṛ; however, if the word "pātnīvata" is connected with the verb "utsṛjati," then it is a separate sacrifice.
What, then, is the established conclusion? That it is a different sacrifice.
Why? Because the previous [animal] belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ and is dedicated to the Patnīvat; how could that which is qualified by both attributes be referred to by the word "pātnīvata" alone?
Furthermore, if the disposal of the animal belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ were being enjoined, the qualification "paryagnikṛtam" (having been carried around the fire) would not be appropriate.

Therefore, we say: the status of being dedicated to Patnīvat is enjoined for that which has been encircled by fire; it is that very same sacrifice. This being the prima facie view, we reply: it is not a separate ritual action; rather, by the word *utsṛjati* (releases), the delimitation of the previous [action] itself is enjoined.
What will be the result of this?

First of all, it will not be necessary to assume a distinct sacrificial act (*yajimat*). Furthermore, the word *utsṛjati* (he releases), which enjoin the release by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), will not be sublated by the syntactical connection (*vākya*). In the alternative view that this is a separate ritual act, if the status of being dedicated to Pātnīvata were enjoined by the sentence, then the release—which is already established by implication—would have to be restated by the verbal root. Moreover, the dedication to Pātnīvata for the previously mentioned animal that has been encircled with fire (*paryagnikṛta*) is already known; therefore, it cannot be enjoined [again]. Consequently, there is a delimitation of the previous ritual act.

As for what was said—that if the release of the *tvāṣṭra* [animal] were being enjoined, the qualification "paryagnikṛtam" (having been carried around the fire) would not be appropriate—this is not a fault. Here, the word *pātnīvata* is simply not the primary factor (*atantram*);

it is not that which is being qualified. Therefore, the *tvāṣṭra* animal, which is characterized by both qualifications, may be referred to by the word *pātnīvata* alone through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇayā*). Thus, there is no fault. Consequently, it is established that this is a case of exclusion (*avaccheda*).
Because it lacks substantiality, it would be merely a remnant of the ritual action.

In no context whatsoever is it heard [stated]: "He who, having taken the *adābhya*, sacrifices to Soma, indeed sacrifices with an oblation upon an oblation"; likewise, "The life and breath of him depart who takes the *aṃśu*.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this a separate sacrifice consisting of the taking [of the cup], or is it an injunction for a cup-offering within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice? What is the prima facie view? That it is a separate sacrifice.
Why? Because of the connection with a previously unknown name; there is no sacrifice bearing this name in the archetype (prakṛti), nor is there any cup (graha) that could be repeated.
Therefore, it is a different sacrifice. [Objection:
But surely neither the material nor the deity is mentioned.
Let it be that there is no material or deity; the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) is directly present.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that this is a distinct ritual action, one that performs a sacrifice named *adābhya* and a sacrifice named *aṃśu*.

This being the position, we reply: when only a name is heard without a material or a deity, we say that it is merely an injunction for a specific repetition of the cup-drawings (*graha-abhyāsa*) within the Jyotiṣṭoma itself.

Why? First of all, this is the name of the *graha* (the vessel for drawing the soma), not of the sacrifice (*yajña*), because it has a direct connection with the act of drawing (*grahaṇa*), whereas the sacrifice is mediated by that act. Furthermore, the term *aṃśu* is undoubtedly the name of a *graha*, and a difference in the *grahas* does not entail a difference in the sacrifice. Nor is the material or deity mentioned here, such that the verb *gṛhṇāti* (he draws) could signify the sacrifice. As for what was said—that the word *yajati* (he sacrifices) is directly prescriptive here—it is not possible to enjoin a separate action in this way, for that word refers to a sacrifice already enjoined, as there is no distinguishing feature [to differentiate it].

Therefore, it is established that by the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is denoted, while by the words *aṃśu* and *ādabhya*, two other cup-offerings (*graha-abhyāsa*) are enjoined.
As for the fire-altar (*agni*), however, it should be understood as a name for a sacrifice (*kratu-śabda*) because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

"There is the fire; he who, knowing thus, piles the fire"—having prescribed this, it is heard: "Now, therefore, one sacrifices after the fire with the Agniṣṭoma, him with the Uktha, him with the Atirātra, him with the Ṣoḍaśin," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: does this word "fire" (agni) denote a sacrifice, such that a separate ritual action distinct from the Jyotiṣṭoma and others is enjoined by the verb "he piles" (cinute); or does it denote a substance, such that it is an injunction of an accessory (guṇa) within the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? That it denotes a sacrifice.

Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). For an indicative mark is indeed seen: "The hymn (*stotra*) of Agni, the recitation (*śastra*) of Agni," and likewise, "There are six *upasads* of the piled fire-altar (*agni*)"; from this it is understood that the word "Agni" denotes that which possesses the hymn, the recitation, and the *upasads*. All of this belongs to the sacrifice; therefore, [the word] expresses the sacrifice. [Objection: But an indicative mark is not a proof; let the direct statement (*prāpti*) be stated. To this it is replied: In the passage, "Now, therefore, he subsequently sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma to Agni," it is stated that he brings about the sacrifice, and he qualifies that [sacrifice] as "to Agni."
Therefore, it is understood that [the term] is designated as "Agni. Furthermore, the prefix *anu-* is appropriately a qualifier of the root *yaj-* only if Agni is the sacrifice;
consequently, the word *kratu* (sacrifice) would be implied.
Or rather, it may be a substance, because the injunction has that as its purpose.
Or rather, the substance might be expressed by the word "fire.
What is that substance? It is this which is the blazing [fire], for it is well-known in this context.
Indeed, this injunction "he piles" (cinute) has the purpose of piling; it cannot express the meaning of sacrificing. By means of piling, he consecrates it, placing it upon the altar.
Furthermore, the word *anu* will have the sense of "after"; that is, after the piling [of the altar] has been completed, one subsequently sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Due to its connection with that, the ritual (*kratu*) shall be designated by that name, and through it, the injunctions regarding the ritual duties (*dharma*) are established.

As for the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was stated—that the word *agni* denotes the sacrifice—that applies only to those specific statements connected with that indicative mark and not everywhere; for in those cases, because of the connection with the piled fire-altar (*cityāgni*), the word is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote the sacrifice. Therefore, there is no fault in the view that these are expressions denoting the ritual (*kratu*) which enjoin its specific properties. In a different context, there is a difference of purpose.

In the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana*, it is heard: "He performs the *agnihotra* for a month; he sacrifices with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* for a month," and so forth. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the month enjoined as the time for the established *agnihotra* and the established *darśapūrṇamāsa*, or is there an injunction for a different ritual action distinct from the established *agnihotra* and the established *darśapūrṇamāsa*? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it is an injunction of time regarding the established [rites].
Why? Because this word "māsam" (for a month) has the same form as an injunction regarding time.
How does it have the same form as an injunction regarding time? That which is known [from other sources] is "he offers the Agnihotra," whereas "for a month" is not yet known.
In this way, the words *agnihotra* and *darśapūrṇamāsa* will not be applied to a different meaning; therefore, it is an injunction regarding time.
[Objection: "In that case, would not the context of the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* be sublated? [Reply:
"Let it be sublated; for the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more powerful, and the result [of the sacrifice] occurs when there is no proximity to another ritual action."

Without reference to anything else, it is heard: "One desiring splendor should offer an eight-potherd cake to Agni; one desiring spiritual luster should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Soma; one desiring progeny should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Indra-Agni. Here a doubt arises: is the fruit enjoined for the archetypal offerings to Agni and the others, or are these distinct rituals from the archetypal ones? What is the prima facie view? That the fruit is enjoined for the archetypal offerings.
Why? Because the Agneya and other sacrifices, having been previously known, are recognized; therefore, they are restated for the purpose of connecting them with a result.
"But because there is no distinction in their proximity, the repetition is for the sake of the result."

There is the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, beginning with the injunction, "The sacrificial cake on eight potsherds is for Agni," and so forth; concerning that, it is stated: "One desiring food should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with this.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this a different ritual act from the Aveṣṭi, or is it the Aveṣṭi itself? What is the prima facie view? That it is a different ritual act, according to the previously stated reasoning. This being the case, we reply: because of its proximity, the repeated mention for the sake of a result refers to the Aveṣṭi itself, not to a different ritual act.
Why? Because of non-separation; the word "by this" (*etayā*) cannot denote another sacrifice distinct from the *Aveṣṭi*, for this word is a reference to what is proximate.
Therefore, it is the *Aveṣṭi* itself that is enjoined for one desiring food.
What is the purpose? If it is the *Aveṣṭi*, then there are the oblations beginning with the *Āgneya*.
Now, as for another ritual action, namely a sacrifice with a different oblation:
because of the reason provided by the *Āgneya* hymn, it would be understood through repetition.

Having prescribed for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices that "the cake on eight potsherds for Agni (āgneya) is not omitted at the new-moon and full-moon [sacrifices]," it is stated again: "The cake on eight potsherds for Agni occurs at the new moon. In this regard, there is a doubt: should one sacrifice with the offering to Agni twice at the new moon, or only once? What is the prima facie view? Because the mention of the *āgneya* is based on the specific context (*sūkta-hetutvāt*), it is understood through repetition; for the repeated scriptural statement of the same thing would otherwise be purposeless, as there is no distinction [between the two mentions].
But because there is no distinction [of the action] and because it is mentioned twice, it is not prescribed [as a separate injunction].
This is not so; it is not the case that the *āgneya* [offering] must be performed again.
Why? Because there is no word expressive of repetition. But surely, the *āgneya* being uttered again will enjoin another action?

We say: no; for a word that is uttered again cannot be said to have its meaning performed [anew]. Whatever was the meaning of it when first uttered, that same meaning it will have even if uttered a hundred times, not another. [Objection: But surely, enjoining again what has already been enjoined while qualifying it makes it purposeless (*anarthaka*). [Reply: Let it be purposeless as you wish, but it cannot be said to express a different meaning. Purposelessness may be logically consistent, but not the expression of a different meaning.
Therefore, one should not repeat it twice;
or rather, the repetition serves another purpose.
Alternatively, it is said that the repeated mention is not purposeless; rather, it will serve as an explanatory praise (arthavāda).

What is the purpose of the explanatory passage (arthavāda)? Since the Āgneya offering has already been enjoined by the preceding sentence together with its explanatory passage, for what other purpose would the Vedic revelation (śruti) be employed? It has been stated that a mere mention which does not serve to enjoin anything is purposeless, according to the principle: "Because the sacred tradition (āmnāya) has action as its purpose, those [passages] which do not have that as their purpose are purposeless. However, whether heard or unheard, the meaning remains exactly the same; just as a deity, whether explicitly mentioned or unmentioned, fulfills its status as a subordinate factor (aṅga), so it is in this case.

To this it is replied: Or rather, the repetition has another purpose; it is not for the sake of enjoining the *āgneya* (cake for Agni), but for the sake of enjoining the *aindrāgna* (cake for Indra-Agni). The *āgneya* cake on eight potsherds indeed exists at the new moon sacrifice, yet it does not become effective through Agni alone; rather, Agni accompanied by Indra is more efficacious. Therefore, the *aindrāgna* must be performed. As for the lifelong repetition, that is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*) because of the context (*prakaraṇa*).

In the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* it is heard: "One performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is the lifelong duration a repetition that is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), or is the lifelong duration an injunction of a restriction that is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*)?
How is it that the repetition is a property of the action, or how is it that the restriction is a property of the agent?

If the word *juhoti* (he offers) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) and *yāvajjīvam* (as long as one lives) is the injunction (*vidhi*), then the repeated performance is a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*); if it were otherwise, then the restriction would be a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*). What, then, is the prima facie position? That the repeated performance is a property of the ritual action.

Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). If this mode of expression is such that the words *juhoti* and *yajati* are restatements (*anuvāda*) and "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*) is the injunction (*vidhi*), then the context is upheld; therefore, there is repetition (*abhyāsa*). By taking it thus, the praise of the sacrificial session (*satra*) will be appropriate: "This Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa are indeed sacrificial sessions (*satra*) ending with old age," because of the commonality of their long duration. Therefore, there is repetition.
Or rather, it belongs to the agent, because of its connection with the Vedic text.

And because of the observation of an indicative mark; for if it were a property of the ritual action, it would be restricted by the introductory statement, and in that case, the other [text] would be purposeless.

And there is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Indeed, he who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should let the Full Moon or the New Moon day pass by, is cut off from the heavenly world.

How is this an indicative mark? For if the sacrificial session (*sattra*) were a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*), it would be completed within the duration of one's lifetime; in that case, there would be no passing over of the [prescribed] time.
And in that case, other things such as expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) being enjoined would be purposeless.
And it shows the completion [of the action]; for if time were the differentiator of the action, there would be a division of the action.
But because of impermanence, it would not be so.
The word *tu* (but) is used in the sense of addition (*anvācaya*), and we observe another [point]: that the duty and the restrictive rule (*niyama*) are enjoined for the agent.

If this were an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the previously mentioned oblation, then each individual prior *agnihotra* oblation would be non-obligatory (*anitya*), since it is heard in connection with a specific desire (*kāmasaṃyoga*) and no other would be obligatory; in that case, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) would be contradicted: "This sacrificial session (*satra*) is to be maintained until old age or death—namely, the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; one is released from these either by old age or by death."

How is there a contradiction? The statement regarding the support for liberation from old age and death is consistent with the position of obligatory duty (*niyamapakṣa*); however, under the position of optional desire (*kāmyapakṣa*), one would be liberated even without performing [the rite].
Furthermore, the contradiction is as explained previously.
From this as well, we see that prior practice is not enjoined as a quality.

Why? Because of contradiction; there would be a contradiction, in that the modifications (*vikāra*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, such as the Saurya and others, would have to be practiced throughout one's life.
That would mean the sense of the *anārabhyādhikaraṇa* (the section on unattached injunctions) would be abandoned.
From this also we see that there is a fixed rule; thus, the repeated practice of the sacrificial session will result in its continuous state.
However, because the duty belongs to the agent, the scriptural injunction regarding time would serve as the occasion for its performance.
If the restrictive rule (niyama) were enjoined as a property of the agent, then living would be the occasion; the rite would be prescribed when the occasion of living exists.

In that case, the rite would be completed at the performance [of the act], and thus the observation of its conclusion (vyapavarga) would become unaccounted for. Therefore, it is established that the restrictive rule is enjoined as a property of the agent.

The difference of the rite in different recensions (śākhāntara) may arise from [the following grounds]: difference of name, difference of form, repetition of a specific property, censure, incapacity, mention of completion, expiation, and the observation of another purpose.
In this context, other Vedic branches (*śākhā*)—such as the Kāṭhaka, the Kālāpaka, the Paippalādaka, and so forth—are cited as examples.

Regarding these, there arises a doubt: when a ritual such as the Agnihotra is heard of in one branch and is then heard again in another branch, does it differ from the former, or does it not differ? We observe that it must differ. Why? Because of the difference in name; one is named Kāṭhaka and the other is named Kālāpaka. Thus, due to the difference in names, there is a difference [in the ritual].

[Objection: "But surely this is the name of a text. [Reply: True; we say it is also [the name] of actions (*karman*), because there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and identical case-ending even with such actions. Furthermore, due to a difference in form (*rūpa*): in one recensional branch (*śākhā*) they prescribe the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] as having eleven potsherds (*ekādaśakapāla*), while in another they prescribe it as having twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*). Since the form is thus different, how could these not be distinct actions?

Furthermore, some followers of certain Vedic branches (*śākhins*) censure the offering after sunrise with the words: "Those who offer the *agnihotra* before sunrise, praising that which is to be praised during the day, speak falsehood every morning, for at that time the sun is not their light. Others, however, censure the offering after sunrise, saying: "If they offer when the sun has risen, it is like bringing food to a guest who has already departed. Since these [criticisms] contradict one another, they cannot be accepted by all branches; yet this does not imply a difference in the ritual action itself. Therefore, on this ground as well, there is no difference [in the sacrifice].

And because of incapacity: indeed, they would not be able to synthesize what is taught in all the recensional branches (*śākhā*); in that case, it would have to be asserted that an independent matter is being enjoined there. However, this is possible when there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*); therefore, there is a difference of ritual acts. And because of the mention of completion: even when [the rite] is not yet completed, there is a mention of its completion. Some say, "Our *agni* sacrifice is completed here," while others designate the completion of another [rite]. This would not be tenable if it were a single ritual act; for it would not be completed there, nor would it be completed elsewhere.

But [this] is logical in the case of a difference [of rites]; therefore, there is a difference. Furthermore, because of the prescription of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*): some authorities prescribe an expiatory rite for the omission of the *anudita-homa* (the offering before sunrise), while others prescribe an expiatory rite for the omission of the *udita-homa* (the offering after sunrise) or for its performance when the time has passed (*vṛddha*). If the ritual action were one and the same, such a twofold increase [in the occasion for expiation] would not be possible. But if there is a difference of rituals, then that which is the *anudita-homa* rite is "increased" (performed late) when [the sun] has risen, whereas the other [the *udita-homa*] is likewise [considered increased] when performed after the time has passed. For this reason also, there is a difference.

Furthermore, there is another indicative mark: "If one were to measure [the sacrificial post] equal to the wings [of the altar], he would approach a smaller sacrifice, a lesser progeny, fewer cattle, and less food; he would become more wretched. Then, when the measurement equal to the wings is prohibited, there is the mention of the measurement equal to the altar: "Now, if he measures it equal to the altar. This observation of the measurement equal to the altar is appropriate only if there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*); it is not possible if there were a single ritual act, because the measurement equal to the altar would then be merely optional.

How so? For some transmit the tradition that the intervals between the sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) are to be the size of a chariot-axle; if that were the case for all [sacrifices], then there would be neither the measurement of the sides nor the measurement of the altar (*vedi*). Since the observation of the measurement of the altar is not possible [under those conditions], for this reason also there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

Furthermore, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) observed: in some [recensions] of the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard, "Two [verses] of the *saṃstuta* verses shall exceed the *virāj*," while for others it is heard, "Three [verses] of the *saṃstuta* verses exceed the *virāj*. If there were a single action, there would be a contradiction; but if there are different actions, then in one Jyotiṣṭoma there are two, and in another there are three. Therefore, there is a difference of action. Moreover, in the Sārasvata sacrifice it is heard: "Those who offer the *puroḍāśa* sit down; those who offer the *sānnāyya* drive away the calves."

Those who offer the *sānnāyya* have already performed their first sacrifice; those who offer the *puroḍāśa* are the opposite. The observation regarding both groups in the *Sārasvata* sacrifice is consistent only if there is a difference in the ritual acts (*karmabheda*). If it were a single ritual act (*ekakarmatva*), all would necessarily have previously performed the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and in that case, the observed distinction would not be possible.
Or rather, it is one [act], because there is no difference in the connection, form, injunction, or name.

This is not so, as has been stated—that there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) in different recensions (*śākhā*). Rather, the ritual act is one and the same, recognized across all recensions and all Brāhmaṇas, because there is no difference in its connection with the purpose; we recognize that very same act being enjoined for the sake of that very same objective. Its form is also the same—the substance and deity are identical, and the human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*) is enjoined in exactly that manner; furthermore, the name is undifferentiated. Therefore, the recognition is that it is the same ritual act in all recensions and so forth.
It cannot be [different] by virtue of the name, because a name does not denote an injunction (*codanā*).
As for what was said—that there is a difference in names—that has been refuted by the fact that [the name] belongs to the book (*grantha*).

Now, as for what was said—that action (*karman*) is also seen to be in grammatical apposition with the name—this is not a fault; for the action is called *Kāṭhaka* and so forth because of its connection with the book, but the book is not called *Kāṭhaka* because of its connection with the action.
How is this understood? That ritual action which is associated with the *Kāṭhaka* and so forth is designated by the word "Kāṭhaka" and so on.

What follows from this? Since the ritual action is called "Kāṭhaka" or "Kālāpaka" due to its connection with a specific text, even though the action is one and the same, it will be termed "Kāṭhaka" because of its connection with the *Kāṭhaka* text, and "Kālāpaka" because of its connection with the *Kālāpaka* text.
And there should be a single performance for all.
If difference were to arise from a difference in words, then identity of action would follow from the identity of the word.

In that case, because of the designation by the word "Kāṭhaka," there would be identity among the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and the Jyotiṣṭoma, since they possess that same word; yet this is not so.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no difference.
And the designation is something produced.

This designation would be a recent one; it did not exist for it previously. Since the time when there was the preeminent teaching of Kaṭha, from that time onward it has proceeded; it is contradictory to say that there was no division before, but now there is a division.
Even if there were oneness, it is supreme.

Even when there is a single action, a difference in form occurs due to scriptural statement; and when there is such a difference in form based on scripture, one should not conclude that the action itself is different merely because the cognition of difference is absent.
Regarding knowledge, this is the rule of the Dharmaśāstra.
Now, as for that specific quality which has been mentioned, it is for the purpose of acquiring knowledge; it does not assist in ritual action.
How is this known? Because of the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth, and because of its connection with knowledge, it is not prompted by ritual action.
Its reiteration is like that of the *Āgneya* sacrifice.

Now, as for what was said—that just as on the new moon day the middle position was rejected due to the fault of redundancy regarding the *āgneya* offering, so too this [position] must be rejected because of that very same fault, namely the identity of the ritual action (*karmaikatva*)—this must be refuted.
(This concludes the introductory portion of the sūtra:
"Or rather, there is no repetition, because there is no difference in the connection with the Vedic revelation (*śruti*)."

Indeed, this is not a case of repetition; rather, this same matter—the Agnihotra and so forth—is heard again by many persons many times over. An object, even when spoken of many times by many people, does not become redundant.

If it were redundant, it would be so even when spoken of many times within a single Veda. Therefore, this is not a collection of multiple rites; this is one and the same rite, because there is no collection of distinct sentences [constituting separate acts].
And because of the non-proximity of the object.

Furthermore, the term "branch" (*śākhā*) will be appropriate due to the non-proximity of the entire meaning; the sacrifices are "branches" because they are like branches. Just as there are branches of a tree, so too here, there are branches of the Veda, which stands in the place of a tree. What is the similarity with branches? Just as there is a distribution across various locations and the entirety of flowers and fruits is not present in each single branch, so too here, the entire section on qualities (*guṇakāṇḍa*) is not present in each single [branch]. Thus, the application of the word "branch" is justified by the non-proximity of the whole meaning.
Therefore, for this reason also, the ritual action is one.
And it is not taught for the sake of a single person.

Furthermore, that *agnihotra* which is [prescribed] in the *Kāṭhaka* is not enjoined for the *Kāṭhaka* school alone; it is indeed enjoined for the *Taittirīya* as well, because there is no mention of a specific person. And whatever limb of the *agnihotra* is enjoined, it belongs to the *agnihotra* in all its states—whether it be the *agnihotra* of the *Kāṭhaka* or that of the *Taittirīyaka*—because there is no statement of distinction. Therefore, it is said that a single completed ritual action (*karman*) is taught by all the *śākhās*.
And this "completion" implies mutual observation (*saṃprekṣā*).

In this regard, people form the following supposition: "Our fire is completed here," whereas for the Maitrāyaṇīyas, the fire is completed during the *anvāroha* rites; they [the others] think, "For us, it is not completed in those [rites]. If what belongs to the Maitrāyaṇīyas were one thing and what belongs to them [the others] were another, how could they say, "For us, it is not completed in these"? Unity is established, for they too possess those [rites]. Even though there is unity, there are subsequent statements regarding censure, incapacity, and completion.

Indeed, a censure is not employed for the purpose of censuring that which is to be censured; rather, it is for the purpose of praising something other than that which is censured. In that case, the prohibition of the censured object is not understood; rather, it is for the purpose of praising something other than the censured, and thus no prohibition of the censured is implied.

However, there is an injunction for the other [alternative]; thus, regarding that single *agnihotra*, two times are enjoined as options (*vikalpyete*). Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Likewise, those who are incapable lack the power to collect the entire collection of auxiliary elements (*aṅgajāta*) prescribed even within a single Veda; whereas those who are capable possess the power to collect even additional injunctions brought from all the branches (*śākhā*). Thus, even though the ritual action is one and the same, there is no contradiction.

Likewise, even with respect to a single ritual action, the word "completed" is employed on the basis that some portion of the matter has been finished; for example, when the Adhvaryu's portion of the Jyotiṣṭoma is finished, it is said, "The Jyotiṣṭoma is completed.
An expiation [is prescribed] by reason of a specific occasion.
Or [it is so] by necessity due to the context.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.

This is not a fault; for when one has begun with the intention, "I shall offer after sunrise," and it is performed otherwise, then a fault occurs, and in that case there will be scope for an expiation. Thus, even though the ritual action is one and the same, there is no fault. The completion [of the rite] should be understood as being according to what was previously known.

In the case of the *pūrvavat* [type of injunction], there is a statement of completion: that which has been commenced is brought to its conclusion. In that context, the meaning is that "our fire-sacrifice (*agni*) is completed"—that which was commenced by us is finished; this is the intention. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not restricted, because it applies as a supplement to all [the days]; for there is no injunction for a ritual act (*karmacodanā*) therein. Therefore, there should be a designation of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) as a single whole.

As for what was said—that if [the text] says "those who previously desired to consecrate themselves," then the observation of both those who have already performed their first sacrifice and those who have not in the context of the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite) establishes a difference in ritual acts (*karmabheda*), and not that there is a single ritual act known across all recensional branches (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya*)—this is not a fault. If it were the case that "those who have consecrated themselves [perform] the *dvādaśāha*, and those who have not consecrated themselves [perform] the *dvādaśarātra*," that would indeed imply a difference; however, the *Jyotiṣṭoma* is not actually enjoined in the Sāmaveda.

What follows from this? Where it has been enjoined, it is merely restated here; therefore, even if there is a difference in ritual acts, this property called "primacy" (*prāthamya*) belongs to all *Jyotiṣṭomas*.
Therefore, even in the view that there are various distinct acts, one must necessarily assume a designation of "day" for the twelve-day rite; thus, there is no fault.

Furthermore, since the specific substances are not enjoined, there would be a lack of fixed determination for the ritual rules; [only] through a specific direction would they be determined. Therefore, this must be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*).

Furthermore, since the *ekādaśinī* (the set of eleven sacrificial animals) is not enjoined with respect to the substance [of the altar] or the fire, this rule regarding measurement by the side or the altar would not apply to the fire; for the *ekādaśinī* is never enjoined in relation to the fire. Why, then, should there be measurement by the side or measurement by the altar? Both of these are mentioned for a different purpose, namely for the sake of enjoining the *paśvekādaśinī*. If it were measured by the side, this fault would arise; however, there would be no fault in the case of measurement by the altar. Who would venture upon such a difficult conclusion—that eleven animals are to be bound to a single sacrificial post (*yūpa*)? But in the *vācastoma* and other rites, because this is a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) regarding the eleven posts, the intervals between the posts will simply be the measure of a chariot-axle. And because it is a constant restatement, even if there is no measurement by the side or measurement by the altar, the statement is still appropriate for the purpose of enjoining the *ekādaśinī*; thus, there is no fault.
Because of the prohibition of what has been prescribed, there would be an excess in one alternative.
In the case of the Sarasvata sacrifice, because of the contradiction, it should be "yadā" (when).

As for what was said—that there is a mention of both those who offer the *puroḍāśa* and those who offer the *sānnāyya* at the *Sārasvata* sacrifice—and that this is contradictory because all rituals are preceded by the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, therefore it is understood that when [the text mentions] "those who offer the *sānnāyya*" and "those who offer the *puroḍāśa*," it refers to different occasions; thus, in the *Upahavya* sacrifice, there is no counter-exception.

Now, as for what was stated—that in the Upahavya sacrifice, the prescription of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [sāmans] is already established by the archetype (prakṛti), and that even as a counter-exception (pratiprasava) it would be impossible and thus the enjoined rule would be purposeless—that must be refuted.
The sūtra ends with the introductory phrase:
"Or rather, the repetition is for the sake of a subordinate quality (guṇa)."
"When it has the Rathantara-sāman, then a white horse is the sacrificial fee; when it has the Bṛhat-sāman, then one with a golden mark on the forehead [is the fee].
And he also shows the cognition [of this].

If it were not the case that a single ritual action (*karman*) is recognized across all recensional branches (*śākhā*), how could it be that while [the rite] is fully enumerated in one branch, a subsidiary detail (*guṇa*) is prescribed in another? For example, among the Maitrāyaṇīyas, the *prayāja* offerings such as the *samit* are not enumerated; nevertheless, details are heard: "The *prayājas* are indeed the seasons; they should be offered after being brought together. Likewise, for those belonging to a branch where the mantra for taking up the stone, "Thou art the *kuṭaru*," is not recited, it is nonetheless seen among them: "He places the stone down with either 'Thou art the *kukkuṭa*' or 'Thou art the *kuṭaru*'.
Therefore, we understand that the ritual action is one and the same.
Or rather, due to the connection with the sequence, the distinctness of the injunctions should be established within a single [action].

For he who collects injunctions situated in other recensions (śākhās) obstructs the sequence prescribed in his own recension; therefore, there is a difference of ritual acts (karmabheda) among the various recensions.

However, because there is no connection with that which is contradictory, there is unity of the ritual act (aikakarmya); due to the connection [of the details] with that [single act], there would be the cognition of all the ritual acts as being enjoined.
It is said: this is not a case of conflict with those [details] prescribed in other recensions when they pertain to a single ritual action.

For sequence is not contradicted by syntactical connection (*vākya*); indeed, sequence is weak while syntactical connection is strong, and by means of syntactical connection, there is an inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of the details from other recensions.
Therefore, it is established that a single ritual action is enjoined as being cognized through all recensions and cognized through all Brāhmaṇas.
Now, therefore, follows the definition of the remainder.

The treatment of the characteristics of various ritual acts has been completed; next, we shall set forth the characteristics of the subsidiary (*śeṣa*). What is a subsidiary? For what reason is it a subsidiary? And how is it applied? It will be stated that direct assertion (*śruti*) and the other means are the causes for application, as well as their relative strength and weakness; this will be the primary focus, while other matters will be addressed by way of introduction (*upoddhāta*) and so forth. "A subsidiary is that which exists for the sake of another."

Now, what occurred there? [The principle] "But that by which a substance is intended to be acted upon, in that case a quality is understood" excludes the status of being for the sake of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) for those verbal roots (*ākhyāta*) that have a visible purpose. Here, however, the definition of all subordinate elements (*śeṣa*) is stated.
Vādari [maintains that] [the Veda is authoritative] with respect to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts.

The teacher Bādarī maintains that in this context the term *śeṣa* (subordinate) applies only to substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), and not to sacrifices (*yāga*), fruits (*phala*), or persons (*puruṣa*).

A substance exists for the sake of action; if there is an action that has a purpose, it must clearly be accomplished by means of a substance, since its accomplishment does not occur without a substance. Therefore, a substance is sought for the sake of accomplishing that [action]; thus, a substance exists for the sake of action.

A quality (*guṇa*) is capable of characterizing a specific substance (*dravya*) that has been enjoined, and there is a purpose for that characterized substance because it serves as the means for accomplishing an action.
Therefore, since it also assists the action by way of the substance, it too is indeed for the sake of the action.

That which is called a refinement (*saṃskāra*) is that upon whose arising a thing becomes fit for some purpose; since there is likewise a purpose for it when an action is to be performed, it too is for the sake of another.
Therefore, substances, qualities, and purificatory acts are subordinate because they exist for the sake of another;
Jaimini maintains that ritual actions also are subordinate, because they exist for the sake of the fruit.

The teacher Jaimini, however, considered ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) to be subsidiary (*śeṣabhūta*) as well; unlike Bādari, he did not accept the restrictive determination [that they are solely for the sake of another].
For he perceived that the sacrifice is not enjoined as something to be performed for its own sake, but rather as a means for the attainment of the result for one who desires that result.
In this way, the meaning heard in the scripture will be correctly grasped.
Furthermore, this instruction is purposeful;
he will establish this very point through the sūtras themselves in the sixth chapter.
Here, however, he establishes the subordinate status of the sacrifice precisely by means of its being for the sake of a fruit, which is already established there.
Therefore, substance, quality, and ritual action are subsidiary because they lack independent determination; the sacrifice is also subsidiary with respect to the fruit;
and the fruit is [subsidiary] because it exists for the sake of the person.
The fruit, too, is taught with reference to the person:
for one who desires, "May heaven be mine," there is the sacrifice;
it is not that heaven itself [is taught] as "may it attain itself."

Why? Because of the use of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); this [verb] occurs when the result [of the action] is intended for the agent. The sacrifice is performed with the thought: "How might the person experience the fruit of the action?"

Therefore, the fruit is heard in scripture as being for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) from the sacrifice, not for the sake of the self's own fulfillment. Consequently, it is subordinate (*śeṣabhūta*). And the person exists for the sake of the ritual action (*karma*).
The person (*puruṣa*) is also heard of as being subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) in rites such as the measuring of the *audumbarī* post;
therefore, this [statement] is not definitive: "Bādarī held that subordination (*śeṣatva*) exists in substances, qualities, and preparatory acts.

Now, in this matter, the venerable Commentator (*vṛttikāra*) has reached a final determination: the state of being subordinate with respect to the sacrifice is fixed (*niyata*) only for substances, qualities, and preparatory acts, whereas for the others, it is relative (*āpekṣika*).

The sacrifice has the status of a primary element with respect to its material, but the status of a subordinate element with respect to the fruit; the fruit has primacy with respect to the sacrifice, but subordination with respect to the person; the person has primacy with respect to the fruit, but subordination with respect to such acts as the wiping of the *audumbarī* post.
Therefore, there is a consensus regarding this determination: substances, qualities, and preparatory rites are necessarily subordinate to the sacrifice.
Their connection is established by their purpose (*artha*).
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [enjoined by] the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa.
In that context, certain duties (dharmas) are heard: pouring out [the grain], sprinkling, threshing, and so forth—these are the duties pertaining to the vegetable offering (auṣadha).
Likewise, there are the duties pertaining to the clarified butter (ājya), such as purifying by heating, melting, taking up, and placing down.
Likewise, there are also [acts] such as fetching the branch, driving the cows forward, and making the cows advance, which belong to the *sānnāyya* offering.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: should all of them be performed in relation to the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sānnāyya*, or should only those be performed where they serve a purpose? [The answer is:
But the prescribed property (dharma) should apply to all, because there is no distinction in the connection and no distinction in the context.
It is said: that which is obtained by implication (*arthāt*) would be performed only where it serves a purpose.

But since all these constituent elements (*padārthas*) are enjoined by the verbal text (*śabda*), they should not be performed only where a visible purpose is directly perceived. Where, then? They should be performed wherever they are enjoined; and it is understood that these are enjoined everywhere.
Why? Because there is no distinction in their connection and no distinction in the context.

First, for all the clarified butter (ājya), the vegetable offerings (auṣadha), and the milk offerings (sānnāyya), the connection as means and end with the transcendental result (apūrva) is undifferentiated; it is understood that when performed in one case, they become as if performed for the transcendental result in all cases.
Likewise, the context is undifferentiated; it is understood that what is prescribed in one instance is prescribed for all.

Therefore, all [subsidiaries] must be performed everywhere; as for the objection that these do not assist in every case, it is understood from the force of the injunction that they do indeed assist everywhere. And this assistance will be of an unseen (adṛṣṭa) nature. [The opponent argues: "There would be non-performance due to the loss of purpose."
This is not so; it has already been stated that all [subsidiaries] are not to be performed everywhere, for those which do not assist in a particular context do not merit performance there.
[Objection: But surely, by the force of the injunction, all will assist in every instance.
[Reply: We say no.
But the fruit [of action] occurs together with the effort; for if there were no word-meaning, it would exist even in separation.
There is no rule by which all [words] would assist in every instance;
nor do we perceive such assistance through perception and other means of knowledge.
Even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would necessarily apply only where there is an injunction by means of a word, and not otherwise.

If the recitation of the *prathan* (spreading) and other such acts within the context of the *ājya* and *sānnāyya* offerings were illogical even though they do not assist them, then an invisible benefit (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*) would have to be inferred by implication; however, those acts must necessarily be recited for the sake of the *auṣadha* (grain-offering). For the result—such as the removal of husks—is understood to occur together with the activity of threshing and so forth, and there is a purpose served by it; without that [activity], the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) cannot be accomplished. And when this is the case, the recitation within the context is meaningful.
And since there is no authority for assuming an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) when a visible purpose exists, it is not possible to assume one.

Furthermore, if the production of rice and so forth were not observed there [in the case of *ājya* and *sānnāyya*], then, because rice and so forth would be absent in their absence, the benefit would have to be regarded as the mere meaning of the word, independent of any observed benefit; consequently, even for the *ājya* and *sānnāyya*, the acts being performed would result in an unseen effect.
Therefore, acts such as spreading out (*prathana*) do not apply everywhere.
The same applies to the acts of purifying and so forth, as well as bringing the branch and so forth.

Therefore, it is not the case that all [acts] must be performed everywhere; spreading [the cake] and so forth are not for the clarified butter (ājya) or the milk-offering (sānnāyya), but only for the vegetable offering (auṣadha); purifying and so forth are for the clarified butter, not for the vegetable offering or the milk-offering; and bringing the branch and so forth are for the milk-offering, not for the clarified butter or the vegetable offering. This is established. Furthermore, because of its connection with the original injunction, the substance should be employed only for that specific purpose.

This being the case, we reply: A substance is enjoined solely for the purpose of that [action] with which it is connected by a sentence of origin; whatever substance is connected with a particular action by a sentence of origin, that action must be performed with that very substance. For example, in the injunction "one digs with the wooden sword (*sphya*)," the wooden sword serves the purpose of digging because of that sentence; therefore, that digging is not to be performed by anything other than the wooden sword. And when this is so, the wooden sword is already established [as required], and the statement "these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements" must be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that. Thus, there is a restatement of each [implement] as it is already established by its respective scriptural injunction.

For example: "He cooks in potsherds," "He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle," "He winnows with a winnowing basket," "He spreads the black antelope skin beneath the mortar," "He places the grinding stone upon the wedge," "He threshes with the mortar and pestle," and "He grinds with the lower and upper grinding stones."

By virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), all [accessories] would apply everywhere; however, by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), they apply according to that specific statement. Even the word "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*), while enjoining a purpose in a general sense, would indeed be set aside [by a specific rule], for the prescription of a particular is indirect when expressed through a general term, whereas the prescription of a particular is direct when expressed through a specific term. Therefore, it is established that whatever is connected with something by way of its origin is employed only in that very place.
When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction because the substance and the quality serve a single function.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, with reference to the purchase [of Soma], it is heard in scripture: "One purchases Soma with a red, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the quality of redness pertain to the entire context, or does it pertain only to the one-year-old cow in the act of purchase?
But how can there be a doubt when the connection with the purchase is clearly understood from the expression "one purchases with a red [cow]"?

It is said: here, indeed, the word teaches that the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*), being incorporeal, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the action, since it is pointed out in conjunction with the instrumental case-ending—which denotes an instrument—in the form "with the red one" (*aruṇayā*). And an incorporeal object cannot be the means of accomplishing an action; therefore, we understand that there is no connection between the act of buying (*krīṇāti*) and the quality of redness. Nor can it be suspected that a word, being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), will express such an impossible meaning; for such a supposition could perhaps never be tenable.

When one seeks the manner in which the authority of a statement is established, the thought arises that there must be some kind of connection. Therefore, if, upon further investigation, we perceive the capacity for a connection with the action, we shall, by virtue of syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), incorporate the quality of redness (*āruṇimā*) into the act of purchase itself.

However, if, despite being sought by those who are careful not to err, no connection whatsoever can be established, then we shall admit a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) and determine this [quality] to be a property of the context (*prakaraṇadharma*).
Thus, this matter must necessarily be investigated.
But is it not the case that this [term *aruṇā*] does not denote a quality (*guṇavacana*), but rather denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*)?
Why? Because of its connection with the feminine gender.

For these—“female,” “male,” and “neuter”—are indeed distinctions of substance; and according to the rule that "the feminine suffix is applied to that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) which refers to a female," we perceive the feminine suffix in the word *aruṇā*.

Therefore, the word *aruṇa* denotes a substance. This [position] is not sound; for it is that very same substance, when delimited by redness (*aruṇiman*), that acquires the status of being denotable by the word *aruṇa*. That same substance, when possessing other qualities, cannot be expressed by the word *aruṇa*. This word does not deviate from redness, whereas it does deviate from the substance. And it is accepted by those who possess reasons that the non-deviating [quality] is the cause [of the denotation].

Therefore, it is understood that its quality is for its own sake; thus, its status as expressing a quality (*guṇavacanatā*) is understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*). However, because the feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is observed, the inference (*anumāna*) is that the nominal stem *aruṇā* must express a substance (*dravyavacana*). Direct perception is stronger than inference; therefore, it is an expression of a quality.

How, then, is there a connection with the feminine suffix? For even an expression of a quality can possess a feminine gender (*strīliṅgatā*), just as one says "the cognition is red" (*aruṇā buddhiḥ*) and likewise "it is red" (*aruṇā*).
If it is a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), it cannot be syntactically connected with the verb *krīṇāti* (to buy).
Therefore, having effected a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), its placement must be within the entire context (*prakaraṇa*).

To this it is replied: when a word, functioning as a mere indicator of a quality (*guṇavacana*), does not obtain a connection with anything else, it then attains the status of referring to a substance (*dravyaparatā*) so that it may not be purposeless due to its lack of instruction [regarding an object]. In that state, becoming syntactically unified (*ekavākyatā*) with the proximate term *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow) which is joined with the same case-ending, it becomes a term in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). And having done so, the expression "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*) is logically established.

And this word *aruṇā* (red) functions in that [specific] state; for if it were to denote its own primary meaning [independently], being thus severed from this context, it would have no purpose even within the ritual procedure (*prakaraṇa*).
Why? Because of the very same reason why it is not connected with the act of buying (*krīṇāti*): namely, that an immaterial object cannot serve as an instrument (*sādhana*) for an action.

Nor can it be connected with substances that are the means of action; for a word denoting a quality alone is not capable of denoting a substance—this is the very same reason [given] even in the absence of a connection with the context. Even in that case, if it were to be connected, it would have to be connected either with actions or with substances that are the means of those actions; yet both of these are untenable.
Therefore, in order to avoid meaninglessness, the word *aruṇā* (red) is connected with the proximate word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow).
There is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

This is not so; for this word *aruṇā* cannot function as a qualifier of the *ekahāyanī*. What is the reason? It is uttered with the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*), and therefore, by the force of that instrumental hearing, it must be a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). For grammatical factors (*kāraka*) are connected with an action, not with a substance.
Thus, by the force of direct statement (*śruti*), it is a qualifier of the action; yet, because of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), it is a qualifier of the *ekahāyanī*.
Direct assertion (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*); therefore, there is no connection between this [the word "blue"] and the one-year-old cow.

How, then, does a connection arise here in the case of "a blue lotus"? It is said: it does arise, but it is not characterized by direct assertion; rather, it is characterized by syntactical connection. In the proximity of the word "lotus," the word "blue"—which depends upon it—enters into a single sentence with it; thus, while being uttered, it accepts a connection by not abandoning its own primary meaning, being intent on denoting a specific kind of lotus.
[Objection: But surely here too, just as in that case, the connection of the one-year-old cow with redness is established through syntactical connection (*vākya*).
[Reply: We say no; for direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection, and this direct statement expresses its connection with the action, not its connection with the quality.
If, however, the connection with the action were accepted on the strength of the direct statement, then the connection with the quality would also exist, just like the unity of the sentence.
This is not possible; for when one thing is uttered as being connected with another, no other thing situated near it can be connected with that [first] thing.

Just as in the expressions "the king's wife" and "Devadatta's man," the word *rāja* (king), though uttered for the purpose of qualifying the wife, is not connected with the man; similarly here, the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), though uttered for the purpose of qualifying the purchase (*kraya*), cannot be connected with the word *aruṇā* (red).

He says: We maintain that the word *aruṇā* (red) is connected to both [the one-year-old cow and the purchase] in order to avoid its meaninglessness; for even that which is performed for one purpose is capable of serving another purpose as well. For example, irrigation channels are constructed for the sake of rice, yet from them water is both drunk and used for ritual sipping (*upaspṛśyate*). Likewise here, the word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), being uttered for the purpose of connecting it with the purchase, is joined with the word *aruṇā*; nothing is thereby corrupted. Therefore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

This is not so; for even if this word *aruṇā* were connected with the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) so that it might not be meaningless, it would nevertheless have to find its place within the entire context.

Furthermore, the word "he buys Soma" (*somaṃ krīṇāti*) is not able to qualify it. For this [word *aruṇā*] is not uttered as a qualifier; rather, it is enjoined here as something previously unestablished (*apūrva*).
Now, it has been argued that even in this context, its connection is untenable.

It is not untenable; for when one meaning is being enjoined within a single sentence, it does not connect with another, because of the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). Indeed, the mode of expression is one when something is being enjoined, and it is another when something is being connected with a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

An object being enjoined is made known as if it were unknown; for the purpose of connecting it with a quality, it is restated as if already known. And it is not possible for that which is uttered only once to be both as if unknown and as if already known. The word *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow), when enjoined in connection with the purchase (*kraya*), would be as if unknown; yet, when connected with the word *aruṇā* (red), it would be as if already known.
However, there is no fault if there is a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), for in the context (*prakaraṇa*), other actions and other substances have already been established by other sentences.
These [words] are connected with that which is enjoined by another sentence; thus it becomes logical that while something is enjoined in one place, it is restated (anūdyate) in another sentence.
Therefore, because there is no distinction in their connection and no distinction in the context (prakaraṇa), they are to be applied to all substances within the entire context.

But has it not just been stated that there is a single effect? And that too is contradictory, for it was previously asserted that "because it is incorporeal, a quality is not connected with action," whereas now the opposite is being said—that both substance and quality have a single purpose and together accomplish the act of buying.

It is replied: this is not contradictory, nor is there an alternative; there is indeed a single effect, but there is a difference in their capacities. For the substance assists the action directly, whereas the quality is the means of qualification for the [substance].
If this is so, then a quality (*guṇa*) does not bring about the action, since it is merely a qualifier of the instrument (*sādhana*).
This is not the case; for a quality that brings about the action possesses precisely this capacity: that it should qualify the instrument.
Furthermore, the action requires a qualifier of the instrument, for the quality, acting as a mark, indicates the instrument.

If there were no mark (cihna), it could not be perceived: "Which is the means (sādhana) of the action? Consequently, we would not determine that the action is to be performed; therefore, the quality (*guṇa*) is the means of the action. And when this is the case, there is no such conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) as there is for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth. For the locus supports the agent and the others; those [factors] being unsupported are unable to bring about the action. Likewise, the agent coordinates the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the others; those [factors], being uncoordinated, are unable to bring about their respective purposes.

However, when another means is prescribed for that very same service which is the effect of the first means, there is an option (*vikalpa*), as in "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley"; both are intended for the purpose of producing the rice-grains.
[Objection: Even so, would the sentence not be split (*vākya-bheda*)?
