[Question: How so? [Answer: Because it is observed that the completion of a sentence occurs for each individual [element], as in "Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra should be fed," where the act of eating is completed for each one, and as in "he whose father and grandfather did not drink Soma."

Likewise here too, in the cases "he buys with a ruddy one" and "he buys with a one-year-old [cow]," this does not contradict our position; for even so, the quality of ruddiness will be restricted to the act of purchase itself, and not to the entire context. True, this fault does not arise; however, it follows that a purchase could be made even with a non-ruddy one-year-old cow, or with a ruddy cow that is not one-year-old. In that case, the proposition stated—that there is a restriction between the substance and the quality—would be abandoned.

In that case, we do not say there is a "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*). How so? For it is the purchase (*kraya*) that is taught as having both the substance and the redness (*aruṇimā*) as its qualifiers, not the purchase [itself] as having those two [as its qualifiers]. Furthermore, a subordinate element (*guṇa*) does not split according to each primary element (*pradhāna*); rather, a subordinate element is repeated for each primary element. And there is this illustrative example: "the completion of the sentence applies to the whole collection," such as in "The Gargas shall be fined a hundred," and likewise, "having pressed [the Soma] and offered [the oblation], they consume [it]."
Therefore, the purchase qualified by both attributes is enjoined.

To this we reply: if the quality enters into a connection as a means for the purchase, then—even though the sentence is divided—the redness will not fail to apply to this substance because it is a means for the purchase; why then is such effort made to establish a single syntactical unity?

This is explained as follows: For if the sentence were split, the purchase (*kraya*) would be understood as having the one-year-old cow (*ekāhāyanī*) as its means, while the redness (*aruṇa*) would be the means for a different purchase altogether; it would not be enjoined as a quality within that very same purchase which has the one-year-old cow as its means. In that case, since another means would be obtained by implication for that other purchase qualified by the quality of redness, the quality of redness, while qualifying that [other] means, would become connected with it. But if there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), that [problem] is avoided.
Therefore, it is rightly stated: "When there is a single purpose, there should be a restriction [of the substance] because the substance and the quality perform a single function;
that which is joined with singularity [is restricted] because of its connection with the direct scriptural statement."
Or rather, because it is the characteristic of all [dharmas], the characteristic is indeed non-distinct.

In this regard, it might be argued as follows: Since the singular number heard here applies to one substance that is already established, what else could it do other than exclude [others], unless the singular number were to exclude the second and subsequent substances? For if it did not exclude the second and subsequent substances, it would be entirely meaningless; yet it is capable of excluding the second and subsequent substances, just as in the case of "he takes the horse's halter," which excludes the donkey's halter—so too should it be understood here.

This is not so; for the statement "imām agṛbhṇān raśanām ṛtasya" (He grasped this rein of Order) is intended to express the relationship between the mantra and the horse's halter. Since the act of taking up [the halter] is already established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the word "took up," it is appropriate that the mantra serve as a restrictive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*).

Furthermore, in this case, the singular number that is heard in reference to the substance, even though it is heard, cannot function as an exclusion because it is not being enjoined. It is just as if someone, having pointed out some rice, were to say: "If any dog or cat should eat it, he must be warded off. In that instance, if the eating is enjoined as the condition (*nimitta*) and not the connection with the dog or cat, then even a crow arriving there would be warded off; for although the dog or cat is mentioned, the connection with the dog or cat is not enjoined as the condition.

Thus, here too, since the connection with oneness is not being enjoined, even though oneness is heard [in the text], one would have to cleanse the cup (*graha*) alone. Furthermore, there is this other defect: that oneness could not be restricted to the substance in the context of the cleansing and so forth. For the cleansing and so forth does not exist as a qualifier of that substance in which oneness would be restricted; rather, the cleansing and so forth is what is being enjoined here. It is not recited as a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the substance because it is already established [otherwise]; for it is impossible to enjoin it simultaneously while also uttering it as a characteristic.

For that which has a well-known relationship is capable of indicating [by secondary indication], and a word-comprehended object of this kind cannot have a well-known relationship unless it is itself enjoined. However, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) and so forth are indeed enjoined; therefore, it is not a qualifier. And if it is not a qualifier, one cannot maintain that the oneness is restricted to the substance. Thus, oneness is stated as being part of the cleansing.
In that case as well, there would be two possibilities: either oneness is primary, or the cleansing is primary; yet both of these are untenable.
First of all, the cleansing of oneness cannot be performed.
Nor does the cleansing, when performed upon the substance, benefit oneness in any way through its context.
Furthermore, there is no purpose served by assisting singularity, for it is not heard in the scripture as being subordinate.
If it is argued that singularity is subordinate with respect to the cleansing (*saṃmārga*),
that too is not the case.

How so? Because it is formless (*amūrtatvāt*); for it does not effect the cleansing (*saṃmārga*). Even if another formless thing effects an action by qualifying the instrument (*sādhana*), this cannot be the case here; for in this context, the cup (*graha*) is not for the sake of the cleansing. Rather, the cleansing is enjoined for the sake of the cup, since that [cup] possesses a purpose, whereas the cleansing would have its purpose merely to be inferred. If the cup were to assist the cleansing, then on the principle that "one assists that which assists," singularity (*ekatva*) would become an auxiliary to the cleansing.
But this is not so;
therefore, there is no connection between oneness and the sweeping.
If oneness were not intended to be expressed, why is the singular number uttered? Surely, when many things are intended to be expressed, the plural number ought to be used.

It is said: we do not deliberate whether this singular number should be uttered or should not be uttered; rather, when it is being uttered, what is to be understood? Is it that the cleansing and so forth apply to only one, or to all? And it has been established that it applies to all.

Furthermore, the expression of number is not the sole purpose of the case-ending. What then? It is also for the sake of expressing the relationship with the grammatical factor (*kāraka*); since the singularity is not intended to be significant, its utterance will serve the purpose of establishing the connection with the *kāraka*.
Therefore, it is not meaningless;
for when something is enjoined, because it is for the sake of another, it should be understood according to the literal scriptural statement.

Now, as for what was said—that just as in the injunction "one should immolate an animal," only one animal, specifically a male animal, is immolated, so it is here too—there is a reversal of this principle in the present case: here, the cleansing is for the sake of the cup (*graha*), whereas there, the animal is for the sake of the sacrifice (*yāga*).
What follows from this? He who prepares [the animal] for the sake of the sacrifice benefits the sacrifice; for a sacrifice cannot be performed with that which has not been prepared.

However, the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) should not be performed as qualified by any particular cup (*graha*), such that [the qualification] would qualify the cup and thereby benefit the cleansing; rather, this singularity of the animal (*paśu*) is taught with reference to the sacrifice (*yāga*). But was it not said: "The case-ending (*vibhakti*) expresses its own meaning, which resides in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), by direct denotation (*śruti*) itself"? [And was it not also said: "The sacrifice will enjoin this by means of the sentence (*vākya*)," and in that regard, it was stated that direct denotation is stronger than the sentence?

True; where a direct (śrauta) connection is intended to be expressed, and where it is not so intended, that which is understood from the sentence remains unrefuted. Therefore, [the rule] "one male animal is to be sacrificed" applies. Just as the singularity of the cup does not assist the cleansing and thus cannot qualify the cup, so too [the number] is not intended to be significant. Otherwise, because of the purificatory rite, there would be an indefinite application of the subordinate factors (guṇa).
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein it is heard: "He cleanses the cup with the fringe-filter. Regarding this, the following point has been understood: all cups are to be cleansed.
Now, this is being deliberated: are the camasa vessels also to be cleansed, or not?

What, then, is the prima facie position? That everything, including the *camasa* cups and so forth, is to be wiped. Why? Because there is no distinction in the connection [to the ritual] and no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*). For just as the cups (*graha*) have a connection with the transcendental result (*apūrva*), so too do the *camasa* cups; and just as the cups are within this context, so too are the *camasa* cups. Therefore, the wiping applies everywhere.
But surely the *grahas* (cups) are mentioned in the scripture; they will therefore be the performers of the cleansing for the *camasas* (bowls).

It is replied: the mention of the *grahas* is for the sake of illustration. A *graha* is a Soma-vessel—that is, any vessel into which the Soma being drawn might spill—and it is suspected that all such vessels must be cleansed. Just as when it is said, "Dinner time is here; let the dishes be cleansed," all those things that are fit for use at the meal are cleansed, and it is understood that the mention of "dishes" is intended as an indication (*lakṣaṇārtha*).

"In this case as well, it should be viewed in the same way. To this it is replied: In the world, linguistic usage is characterized by the object (*arthalakṣaṇa*); whatever object is touched by something else—whether explicitly stated or unstated—that very thing must be touched. But here in the Veda, linguistic usage is characterized by the word (*śabdalakṣaṇa*); and the word [in the text] expresses the cleansing of the cup (*graha*). In that case, while the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is available, why should the word "cup" (*graha*) be assumed through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?

It is said: This word is capable of enjoining human effort toward the act of wiping (*saṃmārjana*) through mere hearing; however, its connection with the cup (*graha*) would require syntactical connection (*vākya*), and direct statement (*śruti*) is more powerful than syntactical connection. Therefore, the word "cup" is explained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) rather than according to its literal sense. Consequently, whatever is fit for the refinement of wiping must be wiped; it does not follow that such a quality would be restricted solely to the cups. [The opponent says: "Or rather, there is restriction because the meaning is connected to the direct statement, since that [direct statement] is the authority for the word."
Or rather, the wiping (*saṃmārjana*) should apply only to the cups (*graha*), and it should not be over-extended to the bowls (*camasa*).

Why? Because the purpose is connected with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*); for the cup (*graha*) which is being heard [in the text] must not be abandoned. If it were abandoned, the very Vedic statement "the cup" would be contradicted; thus it is understood that what you say is merely the song of the careless, and this is not logical.
Therefore, by means of the word "cup," the cup is indicated (*lakṣita*), and its connection with the wiping is enjoined.
And since one cannot enjoin a connection with that [the cups] without first enjoining the act of cleansing, this word must indeed enjoin the cleansing.

Nor will the direct Vedic statement (śruti) be sublated. Why? Because the statement "he cleanses" (saṃmārṣṭi) is able to enjoin, by means of direct statement, the human effort directed toward the act of cleansing.
In that regard, there is no distinction whether the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) is performed while the cup (*graha*) is being produced, or when it is subsequently connected with another [action].
Therefore, even when there is a connection with the cups, the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) is not sublated; thus, the cleansing ought to be restricted to the cups alone.

But, it may be argued: since there is no difference in the connection with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) and no difference in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would follow that the cleansing applies to the *camasa* vessels as well; it was not stated that its injunction is restricted to the cups alone.

To this it is replied: those possessing the context (prakaraṇa) are able to enjoin [a property] there by establishing syntactic unity (ekavākyatā), but not without establishing such unity. And that [unity] is inferred from the context; however, this [present case], on the other hand, is directly perceived (pratyakṣā) along with the word "cup" (graha). Therefore, there is no injunction within the context. Furthermore, regarding the connection between the cup and its singleness, [the word] cannot enjoin [it] while abandoning its own primary meaning. Thus, there is a disparity between this and the injunction of the singleness of the cup.

As for what was said—that just as in the case of "the dishes should be cleaned," there is an indication (lakṣaṇā), so it is here too—that has been refuted by the principle: "In the world, indication is for the sake of action; however, in the Veda, it is for the sake of the word.
[This applies] because of the futility [of the literal sense] with respect to its subsidiaries.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificial post (yūpa) of the Vājapeya is seventeen aratnis long.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the measurement of seventeen aratnis apply to the *ūrdhvapātra* (the upper vessel) of the Vājapeya, or does it apply to the sacrificial post for the animal victim?
What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it applies to the *ūrdhvapātra*.

Why? Because the Vājapeya has no sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Therefore, it must apply to that vessel belonging to the Vājapeya which resembles a sacrificial post; and there exists the *ṣoḍaśin* vessel, which, because it is made of *khadira* wood and is upright, resembles a sacrificial post. When it is applied there, the word "Vājapeya" occurs in its primary sense (*āñjasyena*). Otherwise, it would be understood that the word "Vājapeya" is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) for the animal sacrifice that is a subsidiary (*aṅga*) of the Vājapeya. [Objection: But even in your view, the word "sacrificial post" would have to be used figuratively for the upright vessel. [Reply: It is said: in any case, we cannot escape the use of figurative language.
In my view, however, the context of the Vājapeya sacrifice is preserved; therefore, it should be applied to the *ūrdhvapātra* vessel.
But if it were a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because of the lack of connection with the ritual action.
In the section on the *prayāja* offerings within the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, it is heard in the scriptural text: "He offers while stepping forward, for the sake of victory.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the stepping forward apply only to the *prayāja* offerings, or to the entire sacrificial context (*prakaraṇa*)?

What, then, is the prima facie view? We say that since the stepping forward is a quality of the agent, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because one action cannot be connected with another action.
The act of approaching (*abhikramaṇa*) is formless; it cannot accomplish the act of offering (*havana*). Therefore, it does not form a single syntactical unit with that [offering].
Consequently, it is inserted into the entire context (*prakaraṇa*), because there is no distinction in its connection and no distinction in the context.
But surely, by this very same reason, it would not be inserted elsewhere either?
It is said: [the act] will be connected with persons elsewhere.
But would it not also be connected with persons in the case of the *prayāja* offerings?
This is not so; for the word "he offers" (*juhoti*) is capable of enjoining the effort of a person regarding the act of pouring, but not a connection with the person's stepping forward.
[Objection: But surely, in other cases as well, there is no injunction regarding the connection with the person's stepping forward (*abhikramaṇa*).

[Response: This is not a fault; for in other cases, since its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) is already established by its mention within the context (*prakaraṇa*), the injunctive statement of performance (*prayogavacana*) will declare its necessity of being performed. Therefore, the stepping forward is to be included in the entire context.
But that which has a requirement [for completion] should be considered a single sentence, for it is not finished by what precedes it.
But when there is doubt, a split of the sentence would occur because of the intervention [of another element].

In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the Sāmidhenī verses are taught in the seventh and eighth Brāhmaṇa sections; the Nivids in the ninth; the optional forms of the Sāmidhenīs in the tenth—specifying that for such-and-such a desire one should recite this many verses, and for such-and-such a desire that many; and in the eleventh, the wearing of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is prescribed: "He wears it over the left shoulder; thus he makes it the mark of the gods. In this regard, there is a doubt: should one wear the sacred thread only while reciting the Sāmidhenīs, or should it be worn by one who performs all the ritual acts within the context?

Whence arises the doubt? The *upavīta* is recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenī* verses; yet it is not known whether this occurs while that context is still active or once it has ceased.
The twelve-fold *upasads*, however, are a property of the *ahīna* sacrifices within the context of the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
Therefore, a doubt arises.

Regarding this doubt, what is the prima facie position? The context of the *sāmidhenī* verses has not ceased; therein the *upavīta* is enjoined. Why? Because of the statement of immediate sequence following the optional (*kāmya*) forms of the *sāmidhenī* verses; while the *sāmidhenīs* are revolving in the mind, they enjoin the *upavīta*. And the *upavīta*, which is merely a particular arrangement of the garment, is an accessory (*guṇa*) belonging to the agent.

When the question arises, "By doing what must that [act] be performed?", there is an expectancy for the meaning of the thing to be done (*padārthākāṅkṣā*). In that context, having entered into syntactic unity with the *sāmidhenī* passage—which is present in the intellect and not remote—the word "he wears the sacred thread" (*upavyayate*) is understood to enjoin the wearing of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) in relation to the *sāmidhenīs*. Alternatively, one might understand the preceding thing to be done through another means such as meditation and thereby produce the meaning of the sentence.

That sentence-meaning would be non-Vedic, based on human intellect, or it would be like a sentence-meaning produced by taking a verb from one section and a noun from another; it would be of such a kind where one produces a sentence-meaning after having understood the preceding word-meaning through some other means, such as meditation.
Therefore, it is determined that there can be no syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) when interrupted by unrelated meanings.
Consequently, the *upavīta* does not form a single syntactical unit with the *sāmidhenī* verses.

[Objection: But surely, since the *upavīta* is recited in the proximity of the various forms of the *sāmidhenī* verses that have just been understood, it must therefore be connected with those *sāmidhenīs*. [Reply:
We say no; for the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *sāmidhenīs* has already passed away due to the intervention of the *nivid* formulas.
Indeed, by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*),...

The various options for the *sāmidhenī* verses pertain to the optional rites (*kāmya*), and they do not follow from the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, by the statement of these options, the *sāmidhenīs* do not become part of the primary ritual context. For in that case, the statement does not mean "they are to be recited"; rather, it means "they are to be connected with specific numbers," and even that is established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), not by context (*prakaraṇa*).

In that regard, among the *sāmidhenī* verses which are not the primary subject, there is no syntactic unity for a quality that lacks a connection with the *sāmidhenīs*; therefore, it has no relation to them.
Consequently, it is established that whatever is to be performed within the context (*prakaraṇa*) must be done while wearing the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavītin*).
Furthermore, because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there would be no mutual relationship between equals.
This being the case, we reply: because the qualities are equal, there is no mutual connection between the Pavamāna oblations and the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya).
Just as the establishment is a quality of the fire for the purpose of consecration, so too the Pavamāna oblations are qualities belonging to the fire itself.
What, then, would be their mutual connection?

As for what was said—that [the mantras] are recited in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*)—even though they are so recited, nevertheless, by overriding the context, they belong to the fire (*agni*) through syntactical connection (*vākya*). What is the syntactical connection here? It is: "In that he offers into the *āhavanīya* fire, thereby that [fire] becomes his desired and gratified.
And because there is no mutual relationship of purpose between them.
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The two Vārtraghni verses are recited at the Full Moon sacrifice; the two Vṛdhanvatī verses at the New Moon sacrifice.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the duality of the invitatory verses (anuvākyā) apply to the primary sacrifices, or to the two Ājyabhāga offerings?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it applies to the primary sacrifices.
Why? Because of the mention together with the *paurṇamāsī* (full-moon sacrifice) and the mention together with the *amāvāsyā* (new-moon sacrifice).
The *paurṇamāsī* and the *amāvāsyā* are the primary sacrifices, not the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Therefore, it follows from the direct statement that [the rule applies] to the primary sacrifice.
There is no injunction regarding the immediate [retribution].

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "He clenches his fists, restrains his speech, and announces the initiated [sacrificer]"; likewise, "He washes his hands" and "He spreads the grass-bundle. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are the clenching of the fists and the restraint of speech for the purpose of the announcement, or do they find their place in the entire context? Likewise, is the washing of the hands for the purpose of spreading the grass-bundle, or is it for performing all the ritual acts within the context?

What, then, is the established conclusion? The non-moving of the hands is for the purpose of preparing the hands; the restraint of speech is for the purpose of preparing the person. When one is addressing [the gods], he becomes single-minded and performs the ritual acts. Thus, there arises an expectancy as to which specific acts these two preparations pertain to. Since this expectancy exists, it is satisfied by immediate proximity (*ānantarya*). Therefore, by virtue of immediate proximity, the restraint of speech and the clenching of the fists are for the purpose of the announcement (*āvedana*), and the non-moving of the hands is for the purpose of spreading the *ulaparāja* grass.
This is because the sentences are complete in themselves.
A single sentence is that which is complete with its own respective collection of words; so it is with another, and so with all those that have been cited.
Therefore, there are clearly two distinct meanings, and since there is no expectancy for further supplementation upon division, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Consequently, because there is no distinction in their connection and no distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), they must be inserted into the entire context.
But the remainder, being conjoined with qualities, would be perceived as common [to all], because there is no mutual connection among them.
Alternatively, because of the connection with the purpose, the mention of a quality is for the sake of definition, due to the relationship of the indicative mark with that purpose.
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the alternative view; rather, the fourfold division should apply to the cake dedicated to Agni alone, as it cannot be common to both.

Why? Because of the connection with the purpose: there is a connection with the deity Agni for that which has a single deity, but not for those with two deities, namely the one dedicated to Agni-Soma and the one dedicated to Indra-Agni.

Why is this so? For one whose deities are Agni and Soma, the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is performed as qualified by both attributes; for such a person, Agni is a deity only in relation to Soma, not independently. And for that [deity] which is Agni in relation to Soma, the *taddhita* suffix does not arise, because that suffix is prescribed only for those [words] that are semantically independent (*samartha*). Furthermore, that which is dependent (*sāpekṣa*) is not semantically independent. Therefore, there can be no designation of a dual-deity offering (*dvidevatya*) by means of a word ending in a *taddhita* suffix whose deity is Agni alone and independent.

Therefore, the fourfold division occurs only where Agni is the deity independently; for the connection of the possessive suffix (taddhita) with the meaning of the deity-sign occurs through semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), not when such competency is absent.

Now, as for what was said—that just as the cutting off of the *prāśitra* portion is performed for all [deities], so too is the fourfold division—it is appropriate that in the case of the *prāśitra*, the connection is made specifically there, as in the rule: "He cuts off the *prāśitra* of the *āgneya* [cake].
How then is it to be understood in the case of: "He divides the head of the *āgneya*"? [It refers to the specific cake dedicated to Agni.]

For there is one statement, "He cuts off the *prāśitra*," and a second, "He divides the head of the offering to Agni (*āgneya*). From this, it is understood that he cuts from the head of the *āgneya* [offering]; however, there is no restriction as to whether it is from the head of another [offering] or from something else.
If, however, there were not an offering dedicated solely to Agni there, then even an offering dedicated to two deities would have been accepted in order to avoid its purposelessness.

Since mantras possess the capacity to express a meaning, they should function as subsidiaries (*śeṣa*) through that expressive power; therefore, their connection with the original rite is established by their eternal association with the meaning.
In this context, the mantras are the examples—such as "I cut the seat for the gods" (bahir devasadanaṃ dāmi) and so forth.
Is the application of mantras restricted solely to their primary denotation, or is it also applicable to their secondary (gauṇa) meaning?
Furthermore, what is the primary meaning, and what is the secondary?
It is said: that which is understood from the word alone is the first meaning, the primary one; it is called "primary" (mukhya) because it is like the face (mukha).

But that which is understood from the primary meaning through some connection is, because it occurs later, like the hindquarters (jaghana), thus "secondary" (jaghanya); and because of its connection with a quality, it is "figurative" (gauṇa).
To this it is replied: there is a distinction here; a young boy is not understood from the word "fire."
How is this understood? It has been stated: "It is illogical for a single word to have multiple meanings.

Why is the reverse not the case? It is said: we observe that people understand the word *agni* as referring to fire even while disregarding the notion of a young boy (*māṇavaka*); however, we do not observe them understanding a young boy from the word *agni* while disregarding fire.
Why is this so? Because wherever something similar to fire is intended to be expressed, the word "fire" is invariably applied there.
Therefore, this [word] is seen to have departed from [actual] similarity.
Consequently, similarity to fire is the cause for its application; and that similarity is not perceived unless the blazing [fire] itself has been perceived.
Therefore, the word "fire" has the flame as its primary cause (nimitta), not the boy;
consequently, it is primary (mukhya) with respect to the flame, not the boy.
In exactly the same way, the word "barhis" has the grass as its primary cause, not the cognition of something resembling grass.
Thus, since there is this duality, it is appropriate to investigate whether the word’s application is primarily intended or whether it is also intended in a secondary sense.
What, then, is the prima facie position? Its application is both primary and secondary.
Why? Because both are possible; both grass and that which resembles grass can be conveyed by the word *barhis*—grass directly, and that which resembles grass through the cognition of grass.

And whatever indeed can be made known by the word *barhis*, which serves as a means for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), all that must be made known, because there is no reason for a restrictive selection (*vinigamanā*).
This being the position reached, we reply: the mantra should be employed only in its primary sense, not in a secondary one.
Why? Because both are impossible; for, due to its recitation within the context (*prakaraṇa*), it enters into syntactic unity with the principal rite.
In this regard, the following point arises: that which one might be able to accomplish by means of this mantra, one should accomplish in that manner.

And since this [mantra] is capable of assisting through its connection with the expression of the primary meaning, it is not possible for it to express a secondary (gauṇa) meaning; therefore, there is no application [of the mantra] to a secondary sense.
But surely, from the cognition of the primary sense, the secondary sense can be made known?
This is true; since its purposeful utility is fulfilled solely through the communication of the primary meaning, there is no evidence for its application toward a secondary sense.
Rather, the charge of pointlessness is averted by the application to the primary sense; once pointlessness has been averted, the expression of a secondary sense does not follow.
For a word does not express a secondary sense without first expressing the primary one.
Therefore, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it should not be applied in a secondary sense;
because it is a purificatory act (saṃskāraka), it would not apply where there is no injunction (acodita).

Now, as for what was said—that there will be no displacement (utkarṣa) of the consecratory formulas (anumantraṇa) addressed to Pūṣan and others—it is indeed appropriate that they be displaced. For a mantra is a means of consecration; since it would be purposeless in the absence of something to be consecrated, it shall be led to where it has a purpose. And there will be no fault whatsoever.
However, by virtue of a specific scriptural injunction, the Aindrī verse may be used even though it does not correspond to its literal meaning.
What, then, is established? By implication, it is the attendance upon Indra, because attendance upon the householder is impossible.
If it is asked how the accusative case ending [is justified] here, it is either because the intended object is not what is primarily meant, or because it emphasizes the mere relationship.
Alternatively, the word "gārhapatya" qualifies the act of attendance (upasthāna) due to their connection;
therefore, the attendance qualified by the gārhapatya fire must be performed for the sake of Indra.
And since the gārhapatya fire qualifies it by way of location, the primary function of the mantras remains [to serve that very purpose].
This being the case, we reply: on account of the scriptural statement, however, the *aindrī* verse would be used in a non-literal sense.
It is not the case that this standing near (*upasthāna*) is for the sake of Indra; rather, the *aindrī* verse would be used in a non-literal sense.

Why? Because of the force of the scriptural statement. This scriptural statement exists: "One stands near the *gārhapatya* fire with the *aindrī* verse. Here, the accusative case-ending in *gārhapatyam* expresses predominance. What indeed could a scriptural statement not accomplish? There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement.
Therefore, the act of standing near [the fire] is for the sake of the Gārhapatya;
or rather, the designation may be based on a secondary quality (guṇa), because the relationship [between the name and the object] is not established by the scripture itself.

To this it is replied: "Or rather, there may be designation by way of a quality (guṇa), because the relationship [of the word] is not based on scriptural injunction. Although this sentence is not the cause for establishing the relationship between the word and its meaning, nevertheless, it is possible to effect the designation of the Gārhapatya fire by means of this word "Indra. Why? Because of the connection with a quality, this designation will be figurative (gauṇa); for designation occurs even by way of a quality, as in "Devadatta is a lion" or "The boy is fire."

In the same way, here too, the word "Indra" will apply to the *gārhapatya* fire even though it is not Indra; for it possesses a similarity to Indra, in that just as Indra is a means for the sacrifice, so too is the *gārhapatya*. Alternatively, one becomes "Indra" from the root *ind*, which signifies the act of ruling; and the *gārhapatya* also possesses sovereignty (*aiśvaryatva*) over its own function.
Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that the meaning conveyed by the word "Indra" will, once understood, convey the *gārhapatya* either through similarity or through sovereignty.
If it is argued that there is likewise an invocation [of the deity], we reply as follows.
There is no injunction regarding time, because it has already been enjoined.
This is not the case—that it is taught [to be used] with respect to the act of killing.
What then? It would be a characteristic of time.

Why? Because in the phrase "he calls out three times," the number three is what is enjoined here; if the mantra were enjoined in this very sentence, the sentence would be split due to the injunction of multiple qualities.
Therefore, the connection is not "thus striking," but rather "striking, he calls. But [one might object]:
even in this view, both the mantra and the time are being enjoined; would that not result in the same fault?
We say no; at the very time of threshing, the *haviṣkṛt* must be summoned for that purpose, and it is this connection alone that is being restated here.
Only the threefold repetition is enjoined as a new rule.
As for the claim that the word is intended to indicate time—that is not so.

This is not a fault, for this is indeed worldly indication (lakṣaṇā). Moreover, the mantra is already established for the purpose of summoning by its very form; that too is merely being restated. And the threshing, enjoined by another sentence, is capable of indicating the time.
Therefore, it should be employed for the purpose of summoning.
Because of the absence of qualities.
This is a *padottara* (subsequent-word) sūtra.

Now, why does it not state that the act of threshing (*avahan-ti*) [is designated] from the quality [of making the oblation]? For threshing indeed makes the oblation (*havis-karoti*), and therefore it is the "oblation-maker" (*haviskṛt*). What will be the result of this? Since the mantra for the act of threshing is already established by its very form, [the sūtra] will merely prescribe the threefold repetition; thus, there will be no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

To this it is replied: since the designation based on secondary qualities (*gauṇam abhidhānam*) is not possible when those qualities are absent, [the wife] does not understand "I am being summoned. In that case, the summoning would serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
However, when the sacrificer's wife is the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), the summoning serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, it is not a *hanti*-mantra;
this is also established by the indicative mark (*liṅga*).

And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Speech (*vāk*) is indeed the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*); it is speech that he thus invokes. Now, there is no similarity between speech and the act of threshing (*avahanti*), but there is a similarity with the sacrificer’s wife, for she is female, and the word *vāk* is a feminine noun; whereas the act of threshing is neither female, nor male, nor neuter. [Objection: But surely there is also a feminine word for threshing, namely *kriyā* (action).
To this we reply: It is not necessarily the case that the word for threshing is feminine; it also has a masculine form, namely *avaghāta*.
There is also the neuter gender-sign; furthermore, there is the word "action" (*karman*).
Moreover, there is similarity with the wife (*patnī*) in her own form, and with the act of threshing (*avahanti*) through its external form, namely the word.
Therefore, the gender-sign is more appropriate when the wife is the *haviṣkṛt* (the preparer of the oblation).
And there would be a contradiction of the injunction in the case of such an instruction.
Likewise regarding rising and departing.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard: "Rising, he recites: 'O Āgnīdhra, distribute the fires! and likewise, "He releases his speech with the words, 'Prepare the vow! In this regard, there is a doubt: is the instruction regarding the two mantras intended for the acts of rising and releasing speech, or is the connection intended for the sake of timing?
In this case, the principle of the preceding section is extended by analogy: whatever was the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) there is the prima facie view here;
whatever was the established conclusion (siddhānta) there is the established conclusion here.
The prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that one recites "O Agnīdh, the fires! while rising, and releases speech with "Make the vow!
However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the connection is that one recites while rising because there is no indication [to the contrary];
and when "Make the vow" is uttered, one releases speech.
The prima facie view is based on the explicit statement (*vākya*), while the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
For although it is possible to say, by means of the act of rising, "O Āgnīdhra, spread the fires," implying that "the fire is kindled by rising" and "the fire is carried forth";
and [although] the phrase "perform the vow" (*vrataṃ kṛṇuta*) is a designation of speech; [nevertheless, the conclusion holds].
Nevertheless, since the statement would otherwise have an invisible (adṛṣṭa) purpose, one should not assume that the two mantras serve the purposes of rising and releasing speech.
And if such an assumption were made, another prescribed mantra—"Those which belong to the cattle, or the bull of speech"—would be contradicted.

Furthermore, if the two mantras were enjoined for the sake of rising and the release of speech, they would serve an invisible purpose; however, if used for the purpose of commanding, they serve a visible purpose.
In this case, it is logical that the definition [of the time] is indeed by means of those characteristics;
for in the *sūktavāka*, there is an injunction regarding time because [the mantra] serves another purpose.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One offers the prastara-bundle with the Sūktavāka.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Sūktavāka enjoined as part of the procedure for the prastara-bundle, or is this a designation of time?
To this it is said: it is a designation of time.

Why? Because the *sūktavāka* serves the purpose of proclaiming the deities; because it lacks the capacity with respect to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *prastara*; and because the *prastara* serves the purpose of supporting the offering-ladle (*sruc*).
Or rather, it is an injunction, for the word "offering-verse" (*yājyā*) is not used without cause.

Or rather, the instruction would apply to the mantra with respect to the context of the *prastara* (grass-bundle); in this way, the meaning is established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), because of the connection with the instrumental case ending in the phrase "with the *sūktavāka*. Otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), namely: "one should throw the *prastara* by means of the *sūktavāka* as an indicator. And by doing so, the term "offering verse" (*yājyā*) becomes appropriate: the *sūktavāka* itself is the offering verse, and the *prastara* is the oblation.
Thus, it serves the purpose of indicating the deity, due to its connection with that [deity].

As for what was said—that the *sūktavāka* is capable of proclaiming the deities, but not of [functioning within] the context of the *prastara* (grass-bundle)—it is replied: No; for even if these [other factors] exist, it would ultimately result only in the proclamation of the deities. [For one might argue: "Agni and the others have already been worshipped with the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth; therefore, the sacrificer, by merely praying for longevity and other blessings, shall obtain them from that very [proclamation]."

It is said: since there is a connection in both ways, it should be employed in the ritual act of striking; thus, the indicative power (*liṅga*) will not be sublated, and the syntactical connection (*vākya*) will be upheld.
Alternatively, in the phrase "Agni has enjoyed this oblation," the *prastara* (grass-bundle) itself is indicated as the oblation;
in this way, the use of the word "this" (*idam*), which denotes something proximate, will be justified.
If it is argued that it is a performance, then, like the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, it would be a consecration of both.
Because the teaching is complete in both cases, the term "all" is used.
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One casts the prastara-bundle with the Sūktavāka.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the entire Sūktavāka be employed at the Full Moon sacrifice and the entire one at the New Moon sacrifice, or should it be used by extracting portions according to their respective capacities?
To this it is replied: the whole is to be recited in both cases.

Why? Because the entire mantra is called the *sūktavāka*; if it were lacking even a single word, it would not be the *sūktavāka*, and in that case, the offering would not have been performed with the *sūktavāka*.
Therefore, the entire *sūktavāka* must be recited in both cases.
Or rather, it should be according to the purpose, because it is a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for what remains.
Those words which denote the deities of the Full Moon sacrifice should be employed at the Full Moon sacrifice, not at the New Moon sacrifice;
those which denote the deities of the New Moon sacrifice should be employed at the New Moon sacrifice, not at the Full Moon sacrifice.
It has been stated that mantras assist by consecrating the subsidiary matter (śeṣa), and not otherwise.

Therefore, those [subsidiary acts] which assist in a particular [main rite] should be employed in that [rite]; thus, not all [subsidiaries] are to be performed at the Full Moon sacrifice, nor all at the New Moon sacrifice.
[Objection: This is because of a specific scriptural injunction.
To this it is replied: because there is no distinction between the two contexts, the word "entire" applies to both.
This term "entire" (*kṛtsna*) refers to both the full moon and the new moon sacrifices, because both are within the context; thus, that which is "entire" is said to belong to both, part by part.

This is not so, for there is no connection with the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for those things that are mutually dependent. Indeed, the procedure is not heard as being qualified by these [sacrifices], but rather these [sacrifices] are understood as being qualified by the procedure.

Why? Because the constituent acts (*itikartavyatā*) are not enjoined with respect to the ritual action (*karman*); rather, their injunction is with respect to the result. However, the constituent acts are enjoined for the sake of the ritual actions; in that case, since there is no difference in proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), no distinction is perceived as to which act is enjoined for which purpose and which is not. Furthermore, because all are indicated as means (*sādhana*), and because of the proximity of the constituent acts, and because of this specific scriptural statement (*vacana*), and because the indicative mark of the context (*prakaraṇaliṅga*) is non-distinctive, the entire context belongs to each individual [act] once it has become independent, not to one that is still requiring assistance.

Therefore, the entire *sūktavāka* is taught with respect to each [deity]. Even though there is a division among the principal acts (*pradhāna*), it must be employed in its entirety; thus, even those words which are meaningless in a particular context must be employed there for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because of the injunction "one strikes with the *sūktavāka*. There is no excessive burden for the scriptural statement, as they will effect the designation of those deities through some secondary quality (*guṇa*).
Due to indicative mark (*liṅga*), order (*krama*), and name (*samākhyāna*), the recitation is connected with the optional rites (*kāmya*).
What, then, is the prima facie position? Whatever belongs to Indra-Agni, Vaiśvānara, Agni-Soma, and Jātavedas—in all those cases, these should be the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.
Why? Because of their indicative mark (*liṅga*).
But will not the order (*krama*) and the name (*samākhyāna*) serve as the specific determinants?
True; nevertheless, the indicative power (*liṅga*) is capable of subverting both the order (*krama*) and the name (*samākhyā*).

This being the position reached, we reply: on account of the indicative power, the order, and the name, it is understood that these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses belong to those very optional rites (*kāmyāḥ*). For whatever is the order of these actions, that same is the order of these *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; therefore, they are subsidiary (*śeṣabhūta*) to those [rites] alone. But was it not said that the indicative power is more powerful?

This is true; however, in this case, the name (*samākhyā*) is more powerful. For these [verses] do not attain the status of *ṛc* for these optional rites (*kāmya-karman*) merely through their being named as such, nor for rites occurring in different locations. Why? Because without the name, the very fact that these are *ṛc*s used as *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses would not even be known; how much less could they be the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for rites in different locations? Furthermore, this name indicates that they are the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the optional rites alone, not for all rites.

If the designation (samākhyā) is not respected, these [mantras] would not even possess the status of being *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*; if it is respected, then they belong only to the optional (*kāmya*) rites.
For it is designated as such: "The Section of Optional *Yājyā* and *Anuvākyā* Mantras.
Furthermore, within the context of a specific injunction, there is an injunction for mantras even in those not so designated, because they have been taught [as belonging there].
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "He worships the Āgnīdhra shed with a verse addressed to Agni, the Sadas with one addressed to Indra, and the Havirdhāna shed with one addressed to Viṣṇu.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the worship be performed with verses of such indicative marks (liṅga) that are already present in the context (prakṛta), or should verses of such indicative marks be brought in from the Daśatayas?
But surely, by virtue of the power of the context (prakaraṇa), it is proper to accept those verses already present.

It is said: "No," for indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). [The opponent] says: "In the event of a conflict, context would be sublated by indicative power; however, there is no conflict between these two. We do not sublate the indicative power by adopting the contextual [mantra] as possessing that indicative power while desiring to favor the context.
But if we were to adopt the contextual [mantra] as lacking that indicative power, then we would indeed sublate the indicative power."

"We shall accomplish both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*). This is not so; the conviction arises from the indicative mark that it "must be performed even with the *dāśataya* [verses]," for even the *dāśataya* verses can be designated by the term "Agni-verses" (*āgneyī*). That conviction produced by the indicative mark is assumed to be false only because of deference to the context. If it conforms to the context, it is assumed to be false; if it does not conform to the context, it is correct. Therefore, there is a contradiction.
And in case of conflict, the context is weaker;
or rather, that which is designated by it [the name] prevails over both the context and the logical connection.
That which is designated by that name—namely, the one specifically called *jyotiṣṭoma*—must be understood [as the referent].

Why? Because of both the context (*prakaraṇa*) and logical consistency (*upapatti*). For it is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*), and it is logical to have a cognition of what is already under discussion.
How so? It is not possible to enjoin the application of the mantra with respect to the *jyotiṣṭoma*, precisely because it is already established.

However, the prescription of a specific function is logical because that specific function has not been previously established; furthermore, if it were prescribed in the *Daśataya* collection independently of the context, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
[The injunction] "and he should perform the *upasthāna*" [is understood] through the indicative power (*liṅga*) in this manner.
Furthermore, the instruction would be purposeless because it lacks a connection with that which possesses a fruit; for the *upasthāna* itself does not possess a fruit.
But would it not rather be an auxiliary to the Jyotiṣṭoma by virtue of the context?

If the connection between the *upasthāna* (ritual attendance) and the Jyotiṣṭoma were intended, then the *upasthāna* would be taught as part of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and through the context, it would form a single syntactical unit with it.
However, when the connection of the *mantra* with the *upasthāna* is intended in all instances of *upasthāna*, then the *mantra* applies there, overriding the context.
The context cannot serve as a qualifier; for if it were connected to both, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

In our position, however, this fault does not arise: by means of that which—whether the *Āgneya* or the *Aindra*—is employed in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, a specific act of standing near (*upasthāna*) is enjoined as belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, while everything else is restated (*anūdita*). Thus, no fault occurs.

Alternatively, only the mere connection with the *agnīdhra*, the *havirdhāna*, and the *sadas* is enjoined; the word "he worships" (*upatiṣṭhate*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*), meaning that one approaches the *agnīdhra* with this mantra. Therefore, only those mantras of this kind that are relevant to the context should be adopted, because all [of them] have been taught.
As for what was said—that "those which have been taught are indeed the *prakṛta* [archetypal] ones because they serve another purpose"—that is replied to as follows:
this has already been answered.

Furthermore, it is not the case that none have been taught; rather, when the entire collection of hymns (*vācāstoma*) is being recited at the *āśvina-śastra*, the sun does not set. Therefore, there is no distinction regarding the *prakṛta*.
Therefore, only that which is under discussion [in the context] is to be understood;
by both indicative mark (liṅga) and name (samākhyā), the section has the purpose of [prescribing] the consumption [of the Soma].
The mantra for consumption is heard: "Enter me indeed for long life, for health, for the increase of wealth, for splendor, and for good progeny!
Come, O Vasu, O Purovasu; you are dear to my heart. With the arms of the Aśvins, may I hold you fast.
O divine Soma, with clear vision may I look upon you, the beholder of men."

"Stir my limbs, O Lord of Bay Horses; do not let my groups thirst. Be auspicious to me as you attend the Seven Seers; do not descend below my navel. May Vāk (Speech), the delightful, the victorious banner of sacrifices, being pleased, satisfy herself with Soma. Of the group accompanied by the Vasus, the group accompanied by the Rudras, the group accompanied by the Ādityas—O divine Soma, knower of the mind, of the morning pressing, the midday pressing, and the third pressing, of that which has the *gāyatrī* metre, the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the *jagatī* metre, offered into the fire, drunk by Indra, drunk by Narāśaṃsa, drunk by the Fathers, full of sweetness, having been invited, I, being invited, partake"—and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should this entire section (anuvāka) be applied to the act of eating, or is some part of it to be applied elsewhere? What is the prima facie view? On account of both indicative mark (liṅga) and name (samākhyā), the entire section is for the purpose of eating; the whole anuvāka is to be applied to the act of eating. Why? Because the word "I eat" (bhakṣayāmi) is clearly to be applied to the act of eating; this word is capable of expressing eating and nothing else.
Furthermore, his other words are indeed expressions qualifying "eating," and they are employed wherever the word "I eat" occurs.
It is replied: it has already been stated that all these are qualifiers of the specific aspects of eating.
He says: even so, the sentence would be split, because it is impossible to express the qualifier and the qualified simultaneously.
It is replied: "We do not intend to express the qualifiers; rather, a single object qualified by the qualifiers—such as eating, looking at, and so forth—is intended to be expressed.

This is not correct, because it would mean that the words expressing the qualifiers do not intend their own literal meanings, yet are instead intent upon qualifying the act of eating; thus, they would have to be understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And when there is a choice between direct denotation (*śruti*) and secondary indication, direct denotation is the proper course, not secondary indication. Therefore, this is not a single sentence.

To this it is replied: although many meanings such as "seizing" and so forth are understood here, not all of them are intended; rather, only "eating" (bhakṣaṇa) is what must be communicated. For that alone is directly stated (śruta), whereas the qualifiers are unstated (aśruta); there is no purpose in those [qualifiers] being understood. Furthermore, a single sentence consists of as much of a collection of words as has a single purpose.
Therefore, since this is one sentence for the purpose of a qualified eating, it must be applied to the act of eating.
And there is a designation: "the *bhakṣānuvāka*. Furthermore, it is the entire *anuvāka*, not merely a part of it.
Now, one might object: "But a designation is a worldly term; how can it restrict a Vedic subsidiary (*aṅga*)?
Even though it is a worldly term, nevertheless its connection with the *anuvāka* is beginningless.

What follows from this if it is so? This follows: one recites the *anuvāka* mentioned in connection with eating; and such mention occurs only when there is a relationship, just as we infer a relationship from the mention of "cook" and "reaper.

[The opponent] says: "In matters of this kind, the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is not to be understood through inference alone; it is understood only from an injunction (*vidhi*), and not otherwise; and a name (*samākhyā*) is not an injunctive authority. To this it is replied: "A name will bring the two related things into proximity within the mind, and the statement of performance (*prayogavacana*) will enjoin them."
Therefore, the entire section (anuvāka) should be employed for the act of consumption;
however, there is an extraction (apakarṣa) of it from that context due to its form and the instruction [of the mantra], because the purpose has already been enjoined.

This is not so; the entire anuvāka is not enjoined for the act of consuming. Rather, by virtue of its form, the sentence beginning with "ehi" and ending with "sajūs" would be enjoined for the act of taking up [the cup], while the portion beginning with "nṛcakṣasam" and ending with "avakhyeṣam" would be enjoined for the act of looking.

Why? Because that sentence would have its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) in this way; otherwise, it would have a figurative meaning (*lakṣaṇārthatā*). And it is logical for it to have its primary meaning, not a figurative one. It is replied: "It has already been stated that there is no purpose whatsoever in the denotation of qualifiers.
To this it is said: These are not qualifiers at all; rather, these [acts] such as *grahaṇa* (taking) and so forth are expressed by their own respective sentences as entirely distinct [actions].

Why is this so? Because there is indeed a purpose for them; for they have been enjoined—some by separate sentences and some by implication—and these must necessarily be made manifest. These sentences will manifest them, and their form possesses the capacity to manifest them; therefore, because they serve multiple purposes, it is said that they do not constitute a single sentence.
[Objection: But surely these [words] must have the form to serve as supplements to the sentence concerning eating.
[Reply: It is said: Certainly they do have that form, but these are not imagined to be qualifiers of that [eating].

For what reason would they be thus for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*)? Whether with the stated or unstated qualifiers, the meaning remains exactly the same; otherwise, they would manifest the acts of seizing and so forth, and thus they would be for the sake of a visible result (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
Therefore, on account of both the form and the instruction, there would be a displacement of certain [mantras] here.
Because of the mention of qualities such as "low-pitched" (*mandra*) and so forth, it should be a single mantra, since those two are connected to a single purpose.

This being the case, we reply: because of the mention of qualities, there should be a single mantra beginning with "mandra," for satisfaction (*tṛpti*) is mentioned as a qualification of the act of eating. Thus, [the mantra is]: "I eat; may speech be satisfied. Now, one might object: "tṛpyatu" (let it be satisfied) is one word, while "tarpsyati" (it will be satisfied) is another; this [latter] is a future form used as a subordinate adjunct (*upapada*) to an action. In that case, there is a connection between two actions: "I eat; speech will be satisfied."
But here, there is no connection whatsoever between "I eat" and "let [him] be satisfied.
It is said in reply: for this is not understood as an injunction (*vidhi*) in the sense of "let [him] be satisfied.
Where, then? Either in the sense of a request (*prārthanā*) or in the sense of the time being appropriate (*prāptakāla*).

If the connection is made as "If I eat, speech will be satisfied," or alternatively, "If I eat, it is the time arrived for the satisfaction of speech," then, because of this relationship between qualifier and qualified within a single purpose, the unity of the sentence—and consequently the unity of the mantra—is established.
[Objection: But these two sentences are already self-contained; they are rendered expectant only by breaking their original form.

To this it is replied: even if these two sentences, having distinct meanings and being syntactically independent, were to express two separate matters, nevertheless, since the visible purpose is the manifestation of the act of eating and not that of satiating, they must indeed have a single purpose. How much more so when it is understood that [the latter] exists in a subordinate (guṇa) relationship? Therefore, because it expresses a subordinate quality, "mandra" and the rest should constitute a single mantra.
Because of the specification of a particular gender, those offerings not dedicated to Indra lack the status of being accompanied by mantras, even when the ritual procedure is otherwise identical.
This very mantra serves as the illustration: here, there exist offerings belonging both to Indra and not to Indra, and there are also corresponding consumptions (bhakṣaṇa) of them.

In this regard, a doubt arises: is the mantra used for both the offerings to Indra and those not to Indra, or is the mantra used only for the offerings to Indra, while the consumption of those not to Indra is performed without a mantra?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That the consumption of those not to Indra is without a mantra.

Why? Because these offerings have the same ritual injunction; among them, the mantra "of that drunk by Indra" (indrasya pītasya) is unable to denote what has not been drunk by Indra. Furthermore, modification (ūha) is not possible within a common context, because in the absence of an explicit scriptural statement, it cannot express anything other than its own meaning. Therefore, in such cases, the consumption is to be performed without a mantra. Or rather, it should be according to the respective deity, for the text shows that [the offering] has that as its archetype.
Alternatively, it should be indicated by modification (*ūha*) according to the respective deity. Why? Because the *dhruva* cups constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Which, then, are the *dhruva* cups? Those belonging to the opening of the pressings (*savanamukhīya*) during the performance of the *śukra* and *manthin* draughts; they belong to Indra, and their offering constitutes the archetype, while the others are modifications (*vikṛti*).
How is this understood? For the text demonstrates that they are the archetype.

How so? Because [the rule] "one modifies the consumption mantra in the *ṣoḍaśin* at the *atirātra* sacrifice by [specifying it as] being in the *anuṣṭubh* meter" applies here. What is the evidence for this? The word "modifies" (*namati*) indicates a transformation. This point remains established for now as an unfinished matter; therefore, once this is settled, another inquiry will follow.
Furthermore, when the cups are refilled, there is a secondary indication for all [the deities], because of their twofold distinction.
What, then, is the established conclusion? That in the case of the cups being filled again, there is a designation for all [the deities].

Why? Because of the presence of two remnants; for in each cup there are two remnants. In the archetype, it was stated that "the remnant belongs to whichever [deity] the offering was made, and [the draught] drunk by him is [his]. Here too, it must be stated in exactly the same way.
Therefore, in each cup, there is the observation of two [deities];
or, because of the removal [of one], there is no observation of the first.
We consider the remnant of the deity to whom [the oblation] was offered to have been removed.
Why? Because that which remains in the vessel is addressed for Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others.

How is this so? It is said: Mitra, Varuṇa, and the others are indeed the ones being worshipped. For example, when Devadatta is eating the teacher’s leftovers and gives the remainder to Pūrṇaka, Pūrṇaka perceives it as "Devadatta’s leftovers" and eats them as such, not as "the teacher’s leftovers."
Therefore, Indra is not to be understood as the deity of the *prasthita* cup;
rather, there would be a removal [of the deity] because of the act of taking [the cup].
But for the offering to Pātnīvata, it is as before.

There is the *pātnīvata* cup; for it is said, "One draws the *pātnīvata* from the *āgrayaṇa* vessel using the *upāṃśu* cup. The remnants of the cups dedicated to dual deities have been poured into the *āgrayaṇa* jar, and from that, the *pātnīvata* is drawn.
Now, when the *pātnīvata* has been offered and its remnant is being consumed, a doubt arises: should Indra, Vāyu, and the others be mentioned [as secondary deities], or not?
What, then, is the prima facie position? They should be mentioned.
For that [remainder] belongs to them just as it does to the deity for whom the offering was originally intended;
or rather, by the act of taking [the portion], it would be set aside [for them].

For that remnant is taken here, but not as it was previously; for in that case, it was mentioned by way of being the characteristic of the vessel, and Soma was not intended to be drawn. But here, in the injunction "he draws from the Āgrayaṇa," the Soma residing in the vessel is indicated for the purpose of offering to the deity about to be worshipped. Now, one might object: "In the vessel there is both the Āgrayaṇa and what is not Āgrayaṇa; therefore, that which is drawn from that [portion] which is the Āgrayaṇa is the Pātnīvata, whereas that which is drawn from the *saṃpāta* (the residue) is not the Pātnīvata."

It is said: the Āgrayaṇa is the source (apādāna); therefore, whatever departs from it—whether it be Āgrayaṇa or non-Āgrayaṇa—all that belongs to Pātnīvata, for all of this has departed from the Āgrayaṇa.

He says: "A portion of that which was previously drunk by the former deity existed [therein]; thus, by way of its past state, it shall belong [to Pātnīvata]. It is replied: "In the archetype (prakṛti), no designation was made by way of its past state; here too, it should not be done in that same manner."

Moreover, in that case [of the *aindravāyava* cup], it is stated that Indra is the deity, and his status as having Indra as the deity has not been removed; however, in this case [of the *vaiśvadeva* cup], the connection with the previous deity has departed.
Therefore, the previous deity should not be indicated here. But one should indicate Tvaṣṭṛ, because of the drinking.
But because they are incomparable, it could not be so.

This is not so; we take scripture as our authority, and whatever the scripture says is authoritative for us. The scripture states that Agni Patnīvān has a drink, but it mentions Tvaṣṭṛ’s mere accompaniment. For since accompaniment cannot be established unless there is an act of performance, a drink for Tvaṣṭṛ is inferred.
[Objection: But is not a drink for Tvaṣṭṛ enjoined? [Reply:
True, it is enjoined by the wording of the mantra, not by a direct injunction (codanā).

For there is an injunction: "One takes the Pātnīvata [cup]. However, in common worldly practice, having observed that a task must be done, one performs it even if it has not been explicitly enjoined; and this is determined from worldly experience, not by a scriptural statement such as "the Soma has been made for Tvaṣṭṛ.
And [the rule regarding the thirty-fold cup] is because it exists for the sake of another.

But is it not the case that in the injunction (*codanā*), Agni alone accompanied by his wives (*patnīvān*) is heard as the deity? True, in the injunction Agni accompanied by his wives is heard as the deity, but other deities are not excluded. What follows from this being so? This follows: the thirty-three deities mentioned in the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*) are understood in the injunction as being non-contradictory.

This being the case, we reply: the thirty-three gods are not to be indicated here. In this mantra, Agni is not requested to be the invoker, the server, or the one who satiates; nor is any purpose accomplished by sacrificing to the thirty-three gods.
Who, then, is to be sacrificed to? The one accompanied by his wife (patnīvat).
Whence is this so? For he is enjoined thus: "He takes the Pātnīvata cup. [Objection:
But is there not here a mention of the thirty-three deities based on the wording of the mantra?
[Reply: It is said in response: they are mentioned for the sake of another purpose.
How so? For that which has not been offered does not belong to Agni, nor is it possible for there to be a gift of what belongs to another.

Therefore, the statement "give these to the thirty-three deities" is inconsistent; rather, by this [formula], the giving is declared to be to Agni. How so? For the Lord (Īśāna) causes the substance to linger; thus, by mentioning this lingering here, he makes it understood that "you are the Lord of this."
But was it not said that the injunction prohibits what is based on the wording of a mantra?
It is replied: it has already been stated that even such a basis in the wording of a mantra does not exist;
moreover, it is understood from the context that the injunction prohibits it.

For the word *patnīvat* is not dependent [on another term] in the same way as the word *patnī*; rather, it is characterized by the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Therefore, the deity is simply *patnīvat*.
Furthermore, the mantra must be interpreted in accordance with the force of this injunction.
Consequently, the mantra must be exactly as we have described it; thus, Agni is designated as *patnīvat* through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "O Agni, *patnīvat*."
Therefore, Agni alone is to be recognized [as the deity], and not thirty-three deities;
and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is like the agent.
But there is a prohibition against desire because it leads everywhere.

The answer to this established position is stated: This is not so; as for what was said—that the consumption should be performed with a mantra through modification (*ūha*)—the consumption should be performed without a mantra.
Why? It is said: because the rule of application (*samānavidhāna*) is identical, there is no relationship of archetype and ectype (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) here.

How so? Because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is the same. As for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was mentioned—the prohibition of the metre—it is explained thus: since the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) applies the *jagatī* metre, when the *anuṣṭubh* metre is obtained in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup], the modification of the consumption mantra is justified even within the identical rule of application.

As for what was stated—that Soma is drawn and measured for Indra—and that these are not distinct sacrifices, some for Indra and some not for Indra, but rather specific repetitions of a single sacrifice; and that the ritual properties (dharmas) do not belong to the specific repetitions because they are subordinate, but rather all these are properties of the sacrifice itself;
therefore, the properties of Soma and Soma himself are enjoined for the entire sacrifice.

And as for the statement that "Indra is drawn and measured," since there is a recitation of mantras for Indra, the drawing must be manifested by means of the mantra, whereas for the other deities, it is by means of meditation and so forth.

Therefore, for those offerings not dedicated to Indra, the consumption [of the remnant] is without a mantra; however, in the case of the offering to Indra-Agni, it should be accompanied by a mantra because of the presence of the indicative mark (liṅga).
This being the case, it is considered: there is a Soma offering for Indra and Agni, as expressed in the injunction, "He takes the Aindrāgna [cup].

Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the consumption accompanied by a mantra, or is it without a mantra? What is the prima facie view? There should be a mantra for the Aindrāgna [offering], because that which has Indra and Agni as its deity does not have Indra alone; yet it is possible to designate it as "drunk by Indra" (*indrapīta*). For that of which one part has been drunk by Indra is "drunk by Indra"; and of that [Soma] which is being drunk by both Indra and Agni, one part has indeed been drunk by Indra.
Therefore, there is eating accompanied by a mantra; or rather, it is like a division from another deity in the case of a single [substance].
No other part of it is drunk by Indra, nor does that [other part] become "drunk" merely because another part was drunk by Indra; therefore, this word "indrapīta" is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*).

Just as there is no connection with the sense of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) for a term that is still expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*), such as "Indra is its deity," so too a compound like *indrapītasya* is not possible for something that remains expectant. As it has been said: "Or rather, there is a restriction based on the connection with the meaning.
[The opponent] says: But surely this has already been settled by that very same section (*adhikaraṇa*)!
Why, then, is it considered again?
It is said: that which has already been deliberated upon there is indeed established.
How, then, is it deliberated upon? [It is shown that] for one who still has an expectation, there can be no connection with the deity.

The prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that there is no connection with a deity here; the subsequent view (uttara-pakṣa) is that there is a connection with drinking alone here, and that where drinking is performed by two [entities], the connection with a deity belongs to one of them. Therefore, it is not a redundant statement.
And the meter is like the deity.

In this mantra, the phrase "gāyatrachandasaḥ" (of the Gāyatrī metre) is mentioned; regarding this, there is a doubt: does the mantra apply to Soma when it possesses only one metre, or even when it possesses various metres? It is replied: the metre is like the deity. Just as there is no mantra when Indra is accompanied by another [deity], so too there would be no mantra when the Soma has multiple metres. For in this case as well, a compound consisting of the term "gāyatrachandasaḥ" along with its qualifier is not possible.
Or rather, because they do not exist in all [the Vedas], they belong to a single *chandas*.

Or rather, the mantra should apply to all [soma-pressings]. Why? Because of the absence of any [soma] consisting of a single metre; indeed, there is no soma at all that consists of a single metre. Therefore, since this [soma] is of such a nature, the specific metre serves as its qualification. Consequently, the mantra should apply to the soma that possesses multiple metres.
According to Aitiśāyana, there is a single mantra for all [the cups], because they are consumed as a matter of devotion; for it is the entitlement to the Soma-pressings that is the essential factor.
Based on the Vedic revelation, there would be an entitlement from birth.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice it is heard: "The Ṛc is recited loudly, the Sāman loudly, the Yajus in a low voice.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: do these words apply with reference to the *jāti* (class/type) of Ṛc and so forth, or with reference to the Veda? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They should apply with reference to the *jāti*.

Why? Because of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). From the mere hearing of these words, we understand the *jāti* (generic class); therefore, the quality of being whispered (*upāṃśutva*) is connected with that which is governed by the *jāti*. There is no word that governs the Vedas as a whole. Furthermore, for those *ṛc*s that have transcended the *Ṛgveda*, there will be the loud recitation (*uccaiḥ*) in the *Yajurveda*; otherwise, both properties would be optional alternatives for that very same *ṛc*, and in one case, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*).

Moreover, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is thus preserved; otherwise, if there were a connection with the Veda, the quality of being whispered would apply to the entire sacrifice (*kratu*), regardless of the specific context.
Therefore, these words have their application restricted to what is born [from them];
or rather, it is the Veda [that is meant], because of the observation of the majority of cases.
And because of an indicative mark.
There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this meaning, namely that words such as *ṛc* and so forth are capable of denoting the Veda: "By the *ṛc*s the god moves in the sky at dawn;
by the Yajurveda he stands at midday;
by the Sāmaveda he is magnified at sunset."

Regarding the statement, "The sun moves with three Vedas that are not empty," after mentioning two Vedas and the word *ṛk* in the first three quarters [of the verse], he concludes in the fourth quarter with a plural form: "The sun moves with three Vedas that are not empty. Thus, he shows that the word *ṛk* is a synonym for "Veda. From this as well, we see that these words have the Veda as their subject matter.
And because of the instruction on the Dharma, there is indeed no connection with a material substance.
Furthermore, there is the instruction regarding the *sāman* as "the *sāman* is loud," which is appropriate under the view that it pertains to the Veda;
