for if it pertained to the [specific] *jāti*, the loudness of the *sāman* would already be established by the loudness of the *ṛc*. Its connection with the substance (*dravya*) of the *sāman* itself need not be understood [as the primary meaning]. Therefore, these [terms] pertain to the Veda.
Moreover, the designation "knower of the threefold knowledge" (*trayīvidya*) applies to one who knows that [Veda].
If it is argued that in the case of a transgression, one should act according to what was heard [in the scriptures]:

Now, as for what was said—that for those *ṛc*s which have transcended the *Ṛgveda*, there will be loudness (*uccais-tva*) even in the *Yajurveda*—and regarding that, it was stated that according to my view the performance will be exactly as heard [in the text], that must now be refuted.
This concludes the introductory portion of the sūtra:
"Not so, because [the quality] is included in the whole."

This is not a fault. Since loudness applies to the entire Ṛgveda and low-voiced recitation applies to the entire Yajurveda, it does not matter if a verse that has transgressed into the Ṛgveda from elsewhere is recited in a low voice within the Yajurveda.
Being a property of the Veda, it is a property of the *ṛc*; and the Veda is not connected with two distinct properties.
Because of its connection with the Veda, it cannot be set aside by the context (*prakaraṇa*).

As for what was said—that the context (prakaraṇa) would thus be favored—there will be no fault when the context is set aside by the sentence (vākya) due to its connection with the Veda; for in a conflict between the subordinate and the principal, the connection with the Veda belongs to the principal, because it exists for the sake of that [principal].

There is the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), as stated in the text: "He who, knowing thus, consecrates the fire. This belongs to the Yajurveda; therein they prescribe the singing of Sāmans: "He who, knowing thus, sings the *Vāravantīya*," "He who, knowing thus, sings the *Yajñāyajñīya*," and "He who, knowing thus, sings the *Vāmadevya*.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: at the fire-consecration, should the Sāman-singing be performed loudly (*uccais*) or in a low voice (*upāṃśu*)?

This being the case, we reply: one may either override the primary [element] for the sake of the subordinate, or follow the subordinate for the sake of the primary; however, it is logical that the subordinate should be overridden and the primary should be upheld. Why? Because the subordinate exists for the sake of the primary. One engages in the subordinate with the thought, "How might the primary be endowed with its quality through the performance of the subordinate? But if, by the engagement in the subordinate, the primary suffers a loss of its quality, then the very purpose of engaging in the subordinate is not achieved.
Now, if one thinks, "I shall make the primary act possess its quality," and while engaging with the quality, causes the quality of the quality to fall away, his own purpose is not lost.

This [primary act] does not engage in order to make the quality possess its quality; for the quality is the chanting of the *sāman*, while the primary act is the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration). Since the *ādhāna* belongs to the Yajurveda, its quality is low-voiced recitation (*upāṃśutā*). That [quality] sublates the loudness (*uccais-tva*) which is the property of the group belonging to the Sāmaveda. Therefore, the *sāmans* should be chanted in a low voice.
Because both are heard [in scripture] in abundance.

In the Yajurveda they recite the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Likewise, in the Sāmaveda there is this very same recitation. And when the cognition has already been produced once, a second hearing occurs for the sake of a subordinate element (guṇa). In this regard, there is a doubt: is the Yajurvedic recitation for the sake of the action, and the Sāmavedic for the sake of the subordinate element, or is it the reverse?
Whichever recensional text (āmnāna) serves the purpose of ritual action, its specific rules (dharma) shall apply.
What, then, is the prima facie position? There is no certainty as to whether the Sāmavedic or the Yajurvedic text serves the purpose of the action, because no distinction is perceived.
[The rule] is not restricted by the context (prakaraṇa), because there is a requirement for the procedure (itikartavyatā).
The causes of application (viniyoga) have been stated as *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya*.

*Śruti* is the accusative case-ending, as in "the *gārhapatya* [fire] by means of the *aindrī* [verse]. *Liṅga* is the capacity of the words in mantras, as in "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods. *Vākya* is, for example, "he buys [the soma] with a red [cow].
Now, are these the only causes of application? No, it is said.

The introduction is made by the very question, "What is another reason? And it is indeed introduced by a question, as in: "What is the name of this river?", "What is the name of this slope?", or "What is this fruit?
Furthermore, the sequence follows from the similarity of location.
And the designation is likewise [justified] because it has that as its referent.
Now, are there only these many grounds for application?
No, it is said.
And what else? There would also be "designation" (samākhyā) in this way.
What is the cause of application (*viniyoga*)?

It is *samākhyā* (name/designation), which occurs when a relationship exists, as in the cases of "cook" (*pācaka*) or "reaper" (*lāvaka*). There, upon perceiving the word "cook," it is understood that he has a connection with the act of cooking; so it is also in the case of the Veda. Upon perceiving a word that designates an uncreated relationship with its object, there arises a conviction regarding that relationship.

What is the example and the purpose here? The actions designated by the name *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu) are to be performed by the Adhvaryu, and those designated as *hautra* (pertaining to the Hotṛ) by the Hotṛ;
this is both the example and the purpose. [Now follows the rule:

"In the case of a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*), each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding because of its remoteness from the purpose."

What, then, is the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) here? What is the indicative mark (*liṅga*)? The direct scriptural statement is the hearing of the word "gārhapatya"; the indicative mark, moreover, is the capacity of the word "Indra" to denote a specific deity, as in the mantra: "Never art thou barren, O Indra; never dost thou fail the donor. Now, what is called a sentence (*vākya*)? A sentence is a collection of words that express a meaning together. If this is so, then this too is a sentence—"With the *aindrī* [verse] he worships the *gārhapatya* fire"—and this too is a sentence: "Never art thou barren... In both cases, the words express a meaning by acting in concert.

Therefore, this deliberation concerns sentence against sentence, not word against indicative mark (*liṅga*); or rather, if one were to distinguish between word, indicative mark, and sentence, it would be: "This is the difference between word and sentence," and "This is the difference between indicative mark and sentence.

If that is so, then what must be deliberated here are the conflicting indicative mark and sentence, not the word and the indicative mark. Because the word *indra* has the capacity to denote a specific deity, Indra is to be worshipped if the indicative mark is stronger;
but if it is the sentence, then the Gārhapatya fire is to be worshipped.

For this sentence—"one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse"—is not so [as it appears]. Even though this is a sentence (*vākya*), there is also direct statement (*śruti*) here; however, that which is the direct statement here is contradicted by the indicative power (*liṅga*), not the sentence.

How so? For even though the indicative power is stronger, the phrase "one worships with the Aindrī" must enter into syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word "Gārhapatya"; for if it did not do so, then it would be contradicted by the indicative power.
However, that meaning which is understood from the direct statement (*śruti*) regarding the *gārhapatya* fire is set aside when the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more powerful.
It [the *gārhapatya*] would not then be connected with the act of worship; for in that case, the word *gārhapatya* would either denote Indra or the vicinity of the fire.
But if the direct statement is indeed the authoritative means of knowledge, then the worship of Indra understood through the indicative mark would be sublated.
Therefore, this contradiction is between *śruti* and *liṅga* alone, not between *liṅga* and *vākya*.
Alternatively, here there is no predominance of Indra or predominance of Gārhapatya for the act of worship (*upasthāna*) due to syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*).

How then [is the predominance determined]? The predominance of Indra arises because the mantra contains the word "Indra," while the predominance of Gārhapatya arises from the hearing of the accusative case ending.
Therefore, there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).

To this, it is replied: when a certain matter is mentioned in proximity to a subject that possesses a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), it is understood that this matter serves as a means (*sādhana*) for that subject.
When it is doubted as to how exactly it will provide assistance, the determination arises through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Since that for which something is capable can be employed there, therefore *liṅga* (indicative power) constitutes a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no reason for deciding between them regarding the authority of *liṅga*.

Therefore, these two causes possess equal force: by *liṅga*, Indra is to be attended upon [with the mantra] "kadā cana starīr asi," while by *śruti* (direct statement), the Gārhapatya fire is [to be attended upon].
Indeed, we also arrive at this very conclusion because there is no contradiction:

even a stronger reason is capable of subverting a weaker one only when they are in conflict, not when they are not in conflict; and here there is no contradiction whatsoever, such that one might worship Indra with this mantra while also worshipping the Gārhapatya fire.
This being the case, we reply: between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the direct scriptural statement is more powerful.
Why? Because of the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣāt*).
What is this "remoteness of the meaning"? Remoteness of the meaning is *arthaviprakarṣa*. But what is "meaning" (*artha*)? It is the meaning of the direct audition (*śruti*).
"One worships the *gārhapatya* fire" is the meaning directly conveyed by the Vedic text (*śruti*), whereas "Indra is to be worshipped" is remote.
How so? It is not heard in the scripture that Indra is to be worshipped by means of this mantra, "Never art thou barren.
Even though Indra possesses the capacity to be denoted by the words, because there is no such scriptural injunction, it is understood that Indra is not to be worshipped.

But has it not been said: "It is understood to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) because of its mention in the context (*prakaraṇa*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is determined by its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*)"?
This is not so; for it has already been stated: "Since Dharma has the Word as its sole source, that which is not based on the Word should be disregarded.
Both this context and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) are themselves based on the Word.
Furthermore, in the case of an object characterized in this way, which lies beyond the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), determination is not possible without verbal testimony (*śabda*).
Therefore, we consider that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is more remote than the directly heard word (*śruti*).
If this is so, then even where there is no conflicting *śruti*, there can still be no determination of the meaning from the *liṅga*.
In that case, this very thing—that the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—does not even exist;

how then could it contradict the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)? We say that in such a situation, even the deliberation regarding which of the two—the direct statement or the indicative mark—is more powerful is simply untenable.
Furthermore, an alternative interpretation (vikalpa) is improper, and such an alternative is indeed improper.

For in that case, non-existence would have to be treated as if it were permanent; for when it is heard in the scripture, "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse," if non-existence is postulated as an alternative, then what is not heard becomes accepted, and what is heard is abandoned.
Whatever fault there is in discarding the meaning of what is heard, the same fault applies to the postulation of what is not heard, for in both cases established tradition is subverted.

Therefore, because an option (vikalpa) is illogical, we understand that between direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga), the direct statement is stronger. What is the example for a conflict between indicative mark and syntactical connection (vākya)? It is: "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well with a stream of ghee.
Sit upon it, O immortal one; take thy stand, O essence of rice, being well-disposed."

In this matter there is a doubt: should the entire mantra be employed both for the spreading [of the grass] and for the placing of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), or should that which ends with "I fashion" (kalpayāmi) be used for the spreading, while that beginning with "on it sit" (tasmin sīda) and so forth be used for the placing of the cake?

If the syntactical unity (vākya) is more powerful, then the whole mantra is to be used in both cases. How so? With reference to the words "I fashion well," the portion beginning with "on it sit" enters into a single syntactical unity with the preceding part—namely, "that which I fashion, on that let it sit."

Now, if *liṅga* (indicative power) is stronger, then [the mantra] "I prepare" (*kalpayāmi*) is used for the preparation of the seat (*sadanakaraṇa*). How so? Because the phrase "I make a pleasant seat for you" (*syonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*) is capable of expressing the preparation of the seat. In that context, the phrase "sit upon it" (*tasmin sīda*) is also employed for the act of placing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and thus it is applied to the act of seating.

What, then, is the prima facie position? These two means of proof are of equal strength; for while it has been stated that direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*), it has not been stated that indicative mark is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*). Alternatively, syntactical connection itself is stronger than indicative mark. Why? Because that [syntactical connection] is even sublated by direct statement, whereas a stronger cause cannot be sublated.
Therefore, we determine its fragility; for that which is obstructed by one thing can also be obstructed by another.
The capacity of the mantra "yat syonam te" to directly denote the act of preparing a seat is primary (*mukhya*).
However, the capacity of the mantra "tasmin sīda," which enters into a single syntactical unit with the preceding one, is secondary (*jaghanya*).

Thus, in this case, because the capacity for expression of the first mantra [is already present], its application to the act of spreading (*upastaraṇa*) is stated; therefore, the meaning of the direct statement (*śruti*) is proximate to the indicative power (*liṅga*). But for the latter [mantra], since the capacity for expression must first be produced, the meaning of the direct statement occurs only after that; thus, it becomes remote, being separated by the indicative power. Likewise, for the latter [mantra] regarding the act of placing (*sādana*), [the application] is proximate, while for the former it is separated by the indicative power.

Therefore, between the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the syntactical connection (*vākya*), which are both remote from the actual purpose, the indicative mark is more powerful. Consequently, although the word "syonam" (pleasant) might—because it is required by what follows—be employed for the act of settling as well, nevertheless, having set aside the syntactical connection, it must be applied specifically to the act of spreading. And the phrase "tasmin sīda" (sit upon that) belongs to the act of settling.

Furthermore, for that which has entered into a single syntactical unit with what follows, there is no visible purpose whatsoever; however, the communication of the act of spreading is indeed a visible purpose.
Why? Because the spreading [of the grass] and the placing [of the oblation] are both directly stated in scripture.
Thus, there is an indication of the subsequent placing, but not a syntactic unity with the preceding [act].
Nor do these two fail to perform their respective functions separately without a syntactic unity with the preceding and subsequent [acts].

Therefore, the preceding [evidence] should be applied to the preceding [object], and the succeeding to the succeeding. Now, as for what was said—that since it is set aside by direct statement (*śruti*), it must also be set aside by syntactical connection (*vākya*)—this is not so. For it is not logical that what has already been set aside should be further set aside by another; rather, what has been set aside should be favored so that it may have purposeful meaning. With respect to direct statement, its meaning is remote; with respect to syntactical connection, its meaning is proximate. Therefore, indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger.
Now, [one may ask]: "What happens when there is a conflict between syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*)?
But what, then, is called "context"? Context is the statement of that which is to be performed, which requires an explanation of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
For it is the commencement of that act of stating; it does not depend on a subsequent injunction (*vidhyanta*) beginning with an initial injunction (*vidhi*).
The statement has already been made.
What is an example of a contradiction between those two? It is the *sūktavāka* recitation.
For in that context, both the deities of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and the deities of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) are prescribed, and they do not admit of syntactic unity with one another.

In this matter, by virtue of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the word *indrāgnī*, that term must be displaced from its use at the Full Moon sacrifice and employed at the New Moon sacrifice. Now, a doubt arises regarding its remainder—the portion beginning with "they have both increased" and "they have both become greater"—as to whether it should be employed as many times as it is recited in the *sūktavāka* for both the Full Moon and the New Moon sacrifices, on the grounds that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is more powerful; or whether it should be employed only where the word *indrāgnī* has been displaced and taken there, on the grounds that the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is more powerful.
Such is the doubt in all such cases.

This being the case, we reply: syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). Why? Because of the remoteness of the meaning (*arthaviprakarṣa*). What is this remoteness of meaning here? In a sentence, each individual word, when analyzed, remains expectant; only the whole becomes complete. Thus, the status of being a single sentence is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) there, whereas in the case of context, it is not directly perceived.

How so? When that which is complete falls near a [text] that requires an understanding of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the expectancy of that subject matter (*prakṛta*) is understood; it is inferred that they do not constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyabhūta*).

And having postulated the capacity for expression based on their being a single syntactical unit, the conceptualization arises: "This, when expressed, becomes thus. This is the remoteness of meaning here: that *śruti* (direct statement) is proximate to the sentence, whereas *prakaraṇa* (context) is remote.

Therefore, regarding the injunction "one casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," when those words denoting the deities of the Full Moon sacrifice and those denoting the deities of the New Moon sacrifice are extracted for separate use, the remaining portions of the *sūktavāka* must also be extracted for use. Consequently, even if—by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*)—it might be inferred that the remnants of the words denoting the Full Moon deities form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the words denoting the New Moon deities, there is nevertheless a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of their connection with the words denoting the New Moon deities themselves; and where there is a contradiction with what is directly perceived, inference is not possible.
Furthermore, once a context has become meaningful, it is impossible to impose expectancy upon those [words] that have already achieved syntactic completeness (*nirākāṅkṣā*).

Now, as for what was said—that since it is sublated even by indicative power (*liṅga*), it must therefore also be sublated by context (*prakaraṇa*)—that is not so. One should understand that whatever is sublated by one thing is inherently fragile and will be sublated elsewhere as well.

If it were fragile, it would not have been a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) at all. However, the power of one thing is relative to something else: the sentence has the power to sublate the context with respect to itself, but not with respect to the indicative mark (*liṅga*). This is because, with respect to the indicative mark, this context has a more remote object, whereas with respect to the sentence, it has a more proximate object; therefore, the context is sublated by the sentence. To this prima facie view, we reply: context is stronger than order (*krama*).

Why? Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*). What here constitutes the remoteness of the purpose? It is because that which possesses a context (*prakaraṇavat*) is expectant (*sākāṅkṣatvāt*); thus, syntactic unity (*ekavākyatvam*) can be established even with something recited in proximity to it that is complete in itself. However, this is not the case for that which possesses a fixed order (*kramavat*), [which requires] what is recited in its specific sequence (*krameṇāmnātena*). For "order" (*krama*) is merely the recitation of many items being recited in a particular proximity.

In that case, by the force of the recitation in a particular proximity, it must be understood that even though it is not perceived, there exists a state of expectancy in that which is recited in proximity to what possesses the order.

In the case of *prakaraṇa* (context), however, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) belonging to that which possesses the context; and it is not possible for that which possesses the context and that which possesses the sequence (*krama*) to have syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) simultaneously regarding what is recited (*āmnāta*). Thus, there is a contradiction. In that regard, the direct perception of expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*) within the context is capable of subverting the inferential [indication] of the sequence, because syntactic unity arises from expectancy; from syntactic unity comes the capacity for expression (*abhidhāna-sāmarthya*); and from that capacity comes the meaning of the direct Vedic text (*śruti-artha*). Therefore, the meaning of the direct text as derived from *prakaraṇa* is proximate, whereas that of *krama* is remote.

Therefore, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is stronger than both the sequence (*krama*) and the syntactical connection (*karaṇa*). Now, as for what was said—that since it is set aside even by the syntactical connection, it must therefore be set aside by something else as well—that is not so; for it is right to favor that which has been set aside, rather than setting aside that which has already been set aside.
This being the case, we reply: *krama* (order) is more powerful. Why? Because of the remoteness of the purpose (*arthaviprakarṣāt*).

What, then, is the remoteness of the purpose here? When it is already ascertained by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) that [a passage] forms a single syntactical unit with something else, then regarding that which is recited in proximity, one must postulate a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*), and it is not understood as forming a single syntactical unit; furthermore, a common worldly word is *samākhyā* (name/designation).
Furthermore, the world is not an authority regarding such matters;
therefore, it is argued that order is more powerful.

If this were so, then in cases characterized by such [features], application would indeed occur according to order; however, order is not more powerful than the proximity of meaning (*arthāviprakarṣāt*).

How so? For there is a deliberation regarding the relative strength of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and this being the case, the name (*samākhyā*) is not a means of valid cognition because the word is worldly; thus, it is the person who possesses the status of a means of valid cognition.

This is not a fault, for here the status of being an auxiliary part is not understood through the authority of the person; rather, it is the fact that "the word *pauroḍāśika* belongs to this section" that is established here by the authority of the person.

And in this matter, the person is the authority, just as the recitation in the sequence of the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice is based on human authority; just as the context (*prakaraṇa*) constitutes syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*); and just as this word "Veda" [is so designated].

For these matters, which are not objects of the senses, are not possible [to be known] otherwise; among these, those who are experts possess authority, whereas those experts are not authorities regarding things that are beyond the reach of the senses.
Therefore, the name (*samākhyā*) is the cause [of determination]; and since it is a cause, its relative strength must be examined.
It is replied: then the remoteness of meaning (arthaviprakarṣa) of the name must be stated.
This is the remoteness of meaning:

the connection with the *sāṃnāyya* is taught by its being recited in the [ritual] sequence (*krama*), whereas it is not taught by the name; rather, having perceived the word being uttered, it is inferred through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that it "surely exists" [there].
Therefore, because it is remote from the meaning of the previously mentioned Veda, the name is sublated by the sequence;
or rather, "Ahīna" is used figuratively due to the context.
With reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma, they recite: "There are exactly three upasad days for the Sāhna, and twelve for the Ahīna.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the state of having twelve upasads belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma or to the Ahīna?
What, then, is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Why? Because of the context; in this way, the context is upheld.
[Objection: But is it not set aside by the syntactical statement (vākya)?
[Reply: It is not set aside; we shall explain that the word *ahīna* refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Why? Because it is not deficient (*ahīna*); it is not deficient in terms of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), ritual performances (*kratukaraṇa*), or results (*phala*). Therefore, the Jyotiṣṭoma is *ahīna*.
By the word "or" (*vā*), doubt is set aside.
However, because of the lack of connection with the primary [sacrifice], it should therefore be extracted from that.
The twelve *upasads* would be displaced.
Why? Because of their lack of connection with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
How is there no connection? Because the syntactical unity with the *Ahīna* sacrifice is directly perceived.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is figuratively called an *ahīna*?
[Reply: No, it is said; for when the primary meaning is possible, one ought not to adopt a figurative sense.
[Objection: But surely it will be a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*)?
We say: no; for if that were the case, the word *ahīna* would have been accented on the first syllable, yet this word has its accent on the middle syllable.
Therefore, setting aside the context, it is a characteristic of the *ahīna*.
Moreover, there is a specific designation: "There are three *upasads* for the *sāhna*, but twelve for the *ahīna*."

If the *sāhna* sacrifice were one thing and the *ahīna* sacrifice another, then such a designation would be possible; and since there is indeed a statement of such a designation—namely, "of the *ahīna*"—or because the injunction [prescribes] it as being associated with duality or plurality.
If it is argued that [the rule] applies to what is performed for the sake of a purpose within a fortnight;
If you think that the two *pratipad* verses should be displaced [from their original context], this is not so;
for the context would then be contradicted.
If it is argued, "Let it be contradicted, since there is no connection [of these verses] with two sacrificers or with many sacrificers in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma," [we reply: no.

Even in the absence of an explicit statement, there will effectively be two sacrificers: he who is unable to perform it alone shall undertake it with assistance. Since the sacrifice must necessarily be performed, the sacrificer will take an assistant, even if this sets aside some established rule, in accordance with the principle that "it should be performed as far as possible.
Thus, the two *pratipad* verses will apply within the context of the ritual; therefore, they should not be displaced.
[This is because] in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is a connection with only one [sacrificer].
For the Jyotiṣṭoma is the archetype (*prakṛti*); its ritual details (*dharma*) are directly enjoined there and are not obtained from anywhere else by means of the extended injunction (*codaka*).
What follows from this? If it is so, those [details] heard directly in the text cannot be sublated.

However, in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), those [details] obtained through the *codaka*—being inferential (*ānumānika*)—would be sublatable; for the singularity of the agent in the Jyotiṣṭoma, being directly heard in the text, is not sublated by implication (*sāmarthya*).
For even where the necessity of performance is heard, there too only a single sacrificer is heard—namely, "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring.
Therefore, these two feet (the *pratipad* verses) must be displaced from the Jyotiṣṭoma;
and the tail (*jāghanī*) likewise, because it is a single part [of the animal].
In the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "They perform the joint offerings with the tail of the sacrificial animal.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this injunction part of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, or is it part of the Animal Sacrifice?
How would it apply to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and how would it apply to the Animal Sacrifice?

If the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are prescribed in relation to the tail (*jāghanī*), then there is a displacement [of the offering]; but if the tail is prescribed in relation to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, then it remains within the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices themselves. What is the prima facie view? There is displacement. Why is this displaced? Because the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are prescribed in relation to the tail.

How so? The injunction for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings is derived from direct scriptural statement (*śabda*), whereas that for the *jāghanī* (tail) is derived from syntactical connection (*vākya*); and direct scriptural statement is more powerful than syntactical connection.
Furthermore, [the tail] is a primary injunction because it conveys something not previously established.
Or rather, the tail (jāghanī) is enjoined as a subordinate element (guṇa) of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.

Why? Because it is something not previously established (apūrvatvāt); the tail has not been previously established as a subordinate element of the Patnīsaṃyājas. In that case, while the Patnīsaṃyājas are enjoined by their own specific terms, their connection with the tail is not yet enjoined. And where a connection is being enjoined, there the enjoining of one of the two relates to the other; the connection itself is an inseparable consequence.

Alternatively, regarding the prescription of a relationship: where both related members are necessarily present as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there the relationship is prescribed by its own word. However, where only one is a defining characteristic, there one member is defined and the other is prescribed. And here, the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings serve as the defining characteristic. How is this understood? Because of the connection with the *patnīs*, not every sacrifice is intended; rather, only that specific sacrifice is defined for which the *patnīs* serve as the instrumental means.

Now, why is it that the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are not prescribed by taking the tail (*jāghanī*) as the indicator? It is because the wives cannot be prescribed for this new sacrifice; however, if the tail were taken as the indicator while the sacrifice together with the wives were being prescribed, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
But here, there exists a sacrifice already prescribed together with the wives, which is indicated by the wives.
Therefore, the tail is prescribed by taking the sacrifice as the indicator.

As for the argument that the injunction regarding the tail (*jāghanī*) is by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), while the injunction regarding the sacrifice is by means of direct statement (*śruti*), it has been stated here that an injunction of the sacrifice is not possible in this case, because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, there is an injunction of the tail.
If this is so, then in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifice would be deficient without the tail; therefore, there is no displacement (*anutkarṣa*).
If it is argued that it is a partial [application], then:
Now, as for what was said— that because the tail is a single part, it will not employ the entire animal, and therefore there must be a displacement (utkarṣa)— that must be refuted:
"Because the archetype is not established by scripture."

The tail (jāghanī) is not mentioned in the scriptural injunction regarding the *prakṛti* (archetypal form) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as "the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are to be performed with the tail obtained from the animal. Rather,
it is the tail in general that is enjoined without qualification.
It can occur even when being brought from a purchase at the New and Full Moon sacrifices; therefore, there is no displacement [of the rite].
The *saṃtardana* (joining together) should apply to the archetype, just like the purchase, because there is no loss of purpose.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, with reference to the two pressing-boards, it is heard in scripture: "In a long Soma sacrifice, one should join them together for the sake of stability.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the joining belong to the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, or rather to those Soma sacrifices that take a long time?
It is said in reply: this [joining] does not have its purpose lost in the archetype (prakṛti); therefore, it should not be displaced [from the Jyotiṣṭoma].

He asks: "But is it not also heard that there is no joining together? For it is said, 'The two [stones] remain unjoined. It is replied: "It will be an option, like the purchase; just as there is an option among such statements as 'he purchases with gold' and 'he purchases with a cow,' so here too there will be an option—either joining together or not joining together.
Or rather, there is a displacement [of the rule], because of the mention of a specific distinction.
Or rather, [the distinction] is due to the agent, because that [distinction] has him as its cause.
Or rather, the *saṃtardana* (the joining together) should not be extracted from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
In this way, the context (*prakaraṇa*) is upheld, and the term *dīrghasoma* will be based on the agent: the *soma* of a long [tall] sacrificer is the "long *soma*.
Or else, it would be based on the sacrifice itself, because [otherwise] the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable.

And this is not the case—that its placement is in the Jyotiṣṭoma; rather, it should be performed during a long-duration Soma sacrifice. The length belongs to the sacrifice itself, not to the performer. Why? Because the explanatory passage (arthavāda) would otherwise be untenable. The phrase "for support" (dhṛtyai) is an arthavāda, meaning "for the sake of holding. Since, in a long-duration Soma sacrifice, the pressing stones strike repeatedly, there is a danger that the two wooden boards used for pressing the Soma might split; thus, the arthavāda "for support" becomes meaningful. Therefore, it is an *utkarṣa* (a displacement to another context). Furthermore, the sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthās*) are like the performers, because the purpose of support is no different.
This is a sūtra consisting of subsequent words.
What are those words? [They are: "Now, for what reason is there no application to the *saṃsthās*? If that were so, the context would be upheld, as well as the term "long *soma*.
For *soma* in the *saṃsthās* such as the *ukthya* and others is indeed of long duration in comparison to the *agniṣṭoma*.

It is said: even though the *saṃsthās* (sacrificial forms) involve a long duration of time, an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the *soma* is not applicable there, because the *soma* remains exactly that much, according to the injunction "one measures out ten handfuls. In that case, there is no difference in the act of holding; therefore, [the passage] must be transferred [to another context]. Alternatively, it applies to the *ukthya* and other sacrifices, because the substance [of the *soma*] exists there.

And this is not the case—that there is an "extraction" (utkarṣa). Because it is supported by the context, there is no extraction; furthermore, the term *dīrghasoma* is appropriate because of its long duration, and even in that case, the Soma is more than that of the Agniṣṭoma, for the offerings (*pradāna*) indeed increase.
These [offerings] cannot be increased unless the substance to be offered (*pradeya*) is increased.
The word "cup" (*graha*) applies when the cup is full; therefore, it is impossible to take cups that are deficient.
Therefore, when there is a fear of falling away, it is necessary to aspire toward steadfastness; thus, the use of the term "by steadfastness" (dhṛtyā) is appropriate.
If it is argued that praise is useless because there is no distinction [between the two states], [we reply: no.

If you think that even in the case of the *saṃsthās* (the sacrificial terminuses), the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is appropriate because of the increase in the substance to be offered (*pradeya*), this is not so; for the praise would then be entirely purposeless. Why? Because there is no difference regarding the Soma: as much Soma as is used in the *agniṣṭoma*, just as much is used in the *ukthya* and other *saṃsthās*; thus, in the *ukthya* and others as well, only ten handfuls of Soma are to be taken.
[Objection: But surely the substance to be offered will increase by implication (*arthāt*).

How could that [soma] which consists of ten handfuls be increased? Furthermore, because of the restriction on the number of joints by the term "three-jointed," it is not possible to take up [soma] with many joints; therefore, due to this specific requirement of retention (*dhāraṇā*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would be untenable in the case of the *saṃsthā* sacrifices. Consequently, there must be a displacement (*utkarṣa*).
This is so because [the *saṃsthās*] are non-permanent (*anityatva*).
That which is associated with a number should pertain to the sacrifice, because of the context.

In the context of the *pravargya* rite in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, it is traditionally recited: "One should not perform the *pravargya* at the first sacrifice; one may perform it at the second or the third. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the prohibition apply to all performances of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, or is the prohibition restricted to the first performance?
What, then, is the prima facie view? The prohibition applies to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* [in general].
Why? Because of its connection with sacrifice; by the word "first," the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is denoted.

For it has a connection with being "first," as it is recited thus: "This indeed is the first of sacrifices, namely the Jyotiṣṭoma; having not sacrificed with this, one should not sacrifice with another.
Since it is the first among sacrifices, the Jyotiṣṭoma is denoted by the word "first," and in this way the context is upheld, provided that this statement refers to the sacrifice.
Therefore, the prohibition accompanied by a specific number would prohibit the *pravargya* rite for the *Jyotiṣṭoma*;
or rather, it is occasional (*naimittika*), because of its connection with the agent, since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) has that as its cause.

Now, as for what was said—that because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *jyotiṣṭoma*, it must be a statement regarding that [sacrifice]—that has been refuted by the fact that the coreferentiality is based on metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

As for the coreferentiality with the word *yajña* in the expression "the first sacrifice" (*prathamayajña*), that too does not contradict our position, because the word *yajña* denotes a sacrificial rite (*yāga*) in general. [The rule:
"The grinding of the offering for Pūṣan should be understood as applying to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because there is no injunction for it in the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*)."

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they recite: "Therefore Pūṣan has ground as his share, for he is toothless. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the grinding for Pūṣan belong to the archetype (prakṛti), or to the ectype (vikṛti)? What is the prima facie view? That it belongs to the archetype.
Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*). [Objection:
But surely, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), they do not prescribe Pūṣan as the deity of any sacrificial offering (*havis*).
[Reply: It is said: the word "Pūṣan" will denote some archetypal deity.
That [is] for all purposes, because there is no distinction.
It has been stated that the grinding (peṣaṇa) prescribed for the Pūṣan-oblation in the archetype applies to the ectype as well.

In this regard, there is a doubt: does it apply to the cooked rice (caru), the animal sacrifice (paśu), and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), or only to the cooked rice? What, then, is the prima facie view? It should apply everywhere—to the cooked rice, the animal sacrifice, and the sacrificial cake.
Why? Because there is no distinction; no specific distinction is relied upon, therefore it applies everywhere.

Or rather, [it applies] in the case of the *caru*; it is implied for the *puroḍāśa* by the sense of the text, but it would not apply to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) because of a contradiction in the purpose.
In the case of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), the grinding would be enjoined for the sake of the offering to Pūṣan.

As for the cake (*puroḍāśa*), grinding is already established by the very nature of the thing; therefore, there is no need for a scriptural statement to that effect so long as the cake is produced. Furthermore, it would not apply to the animal sacrifice, because if the heart and other organs were ground, their specific forms would be destroyed.

What is the fault in that? [The rule] "he cuts from the heart first" would not allow for a portion to be cut from the heart; likewise, other portions would not be cut according to what is prescribed in the scripture.
But could one not cut portions even from hearts and so forth made of flour?
We say no; the heart and so forth are shapes (*ākṛti*), not pieces of flesh. This has already been stated: the meaning of a word is the shape.

Even if it were made in that same form, they might still be confused regarding the place for its removal; therefore, the statement is for the purpose of ensuring that the grinding of the offering to Pūṣan shall take place in the *caru*.
[Objection: "But this would apply even to the *caru*."
No, because it is the name of a cooking vessel.

To this it is replied: It is true that the word *caru* is employed for rice that has been clearly cooked, as in the expression "a *caru* of clearly cooked [rice] is offered"; however, its being clearly cooked is not the primary cause [of the application of the term]. If being clearly cooked were the cause, it would not be used for what is prepared from flour. Yet it is indeed used there as well, as in "a flour-*caru* is being prepared. Therefore, there is another commonality between these two which serves as the cause; this is what is meant by the statement: "Not so, because it is the name of the cooking process," and thus there is no contradiction regarding the *caru*.
How so? Because it is a name for a cooking process; this word "caru" is a name for the act of cooking.

The term "caru" is denotative of that which is produced by cooking with internal heat without the liquid being drained away. For that reason, speakers apply the word "caru" to both ground rice porridge and solid, non-liquid rice.

The purpose is exactly as stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): that grinding (*peṣaṇa*) applies even to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it applies only to the *caru*.
This is because there is a single connection with one [element].
It has been stated that the grinding of the offering for Pūṣan occurs only in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) when it is a *caru*.
Now, a doubt arises: does this apply only to an offering for Pūṣan dedicated to a single deity, or even to one dedicated to two deities?

What is an example of a dual-deity offering? In the Rājasūya, there are the two offerings connected with the three [deities] on the northern altar: a cake on eleven potsherds for Soma and Pūṣan, and a *caru* for Indra and Pūṣan, with a dark-colored animal as the sacrificial fee; among these, the offering to Indra and Pūṣan serves as the example.
What is established? That the grinding applies only to that which has a single deity.
Why? Because of the connection with the singular alone, as in the case of the fourfold division;
and because of the contradiction of ritual properties.

In the case of an offering intended for two deities, there would be a conflict regarding the ritual rule: grinding applies to Pūṣan, but not to the other deity. In that situation, if the portion of Pūṣan were ground, the portion of the other deity would remain unground;
consequently, the cooking would be uneven, and since the word *caru* (cooked sacrificial rice) is based on the act of cooking, that term would be contradicted.
Alternatively, if one considers this to be non-conflicting, they might grind the portion of the other deity as well.
There would be confusion regarding the portions.

What is the fault in that? A portion belonging to one [deity] might be offered to another; thus it would be done contrary to what was prescribed. Therefore, for this reason as well, there must be grinding even when the offering is dedicated to a single deity.
Or rather, it should apply even when there is a companion, because it is based on the deity.

This grinding is heard as being for the sake of a deity: "Pūṣan is to have his portion ground. And that portion becomes "ground" even when it is part of a portion belonging to two deities; this is not like the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*), for there, the derivative suffix [in *caturdhā*] applies to what is independent, not to what is accompanied by another. Likewise, the compound *indrapīta* ("drunk by Indra") also applies to what is independent, not to what is accompanied by another.

In this case, however, the compound *prapiṣṭa-śabda* forms a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *bhāga* as its external referent (*anyapadārtha*). This [compound] also occurs only when the members are semantically connected (*samartha*); yet, there is no such defect here regarding the offering for two deities (*dvidevatya*).
Therefore, whether it is an offering for a single deity or for two deities, that portion of the *caru* must indeed be ground.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
An indicative mark (*liṅga*) is also as follows: "Therefore Pūṣan has the ground portion, for he is toothless"—this shows that the grinding is for the sake of the deity through praise.
Likewise, [the text] shows the state of being half-ground in the passage: "One desiring cattle should offer a *caru* to Soma-Pūṣan, half-ground.
Similarly, [the text] shows that the grinding is indeed for the sake of the deity in the passage: "Half is ground and half is unground, because it belongs to two deities."

Because of the explicit statement, there is grinding of all [grains] with respect to that [sacrifice], since it is governed by scripture; however, due to the absence of purpose, there is no grinding in the case of the two-caru offering.

This is a subsequent sentence (*padottara-sūtra*). Why is it not the case that this is not a statement [to the effect] "it is not half-grounded"? It is said in reply: if this were a statement, then, having merely referred to the offering to Soma-Pūṣan (*saumāpauṣṇa*), it would enjoin grinding in all cases—namely, in the case of the cooked rice (*caru*), the animal victim (*paśu*), and the cake (*puroḍāśa*). In that case, since both the connection with the *caru* and the connection with being half-grounded would be enjoined for the offering to Soma-Pūṣan, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, in every case where there is an offering to Soma-Pūṣan, there is the grinding of the edge [of the grain]. With respect to that—specifically with respect to the mere offering to Soma-Pūṣan—this grinding is established by scripture. Since, in the case of a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), total grinding would follow as a matter of course, and since in the case of an animal or a cooked rice offering (caru) there would be no purpose for grinding, this statement [of the scripture] must serve its purpose [only] in those cases.

In that context, the word "caru" would not be intended in its literal sense; it would have to be assumed as being merely illustrative. However, under the view that this is a restatement of grinding, this contradiction does not arise. Therefore, this indeed constitutes an indicative mark (liṅga). But surely, in the case of the animal, there is no grinding for fear of destroying its limbs?

We say: no; for in the case of half-pounding, there would be no destruction of the integrity of the substance, as the portion not pounded will still be offered; furthermore, the pounding would serve only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Alternatively, since it is a property of the substance (*arthadharma*), it would apply to both [deities] like the *aindrāgna* sacrifice; however, this is not the case because it has not been so enjoined.

The grinding of the offering for Pūṣan ought to apply to a sacrifice dedicated to a single deity, not to one dedicated to Indra and Pūṣan. Why? Because this is not enjoined as a property of the deity—that the portion of Pūṣan must be used ground—but rather it is a property of the purpose (the sacrificial substance).
What, then, is the meaning? It is sacrifice.
How is this understood? [From the fact that] it is not a property of the deity.
It is said: for she has no share [in the offering].
Even if, for some reason, there were a portion [of the grain], even so, grinding cannot be the duty of the deity, for it would be purposeless in that case, as it is not a property of the sacrifice.
How then will that which is recited in a different context become a property of the sacrifice?
It is said: because of its connection with the sentence.
But is it not the case that this connection is heard in scripture as being with the deity, and not with the sacrifice?
It is replied: it has already been stated that there is no connection with the deity because [the deity] lacks a share and because [such a connection] would be purposeless.
Nevertheless, it must be explained how the connection with the sacrifice nonetheless comes about.

This is explained as follows: that which is relinquished with reference to Pūṣan is the "portion" (bhāga) of Pūṣan here; that substance whose relinquishment has Pūṣan as its deity is [the portion]. However, in the offering to Indra and Pūṣan (aindrāpauṣṇa), Pūṣan is not the deity, and thus that *caru* is not connected to Pūṣan by way of ownership.
Therefore, in the offering to Indra and Pūṣan, there is no connection whatsoever between Pūṣan and the *caru*; rather, it becomes a portion intended for him only when Pūṣan alone is the deity.

How so? It is a well-known principle that whatever is intended for someone constitutes that person's portion. Therefore, even if Pūṣan, by his own utterance, becomes a benefactor by performing an utterance that assists Indra and Pūṣan, nevertheless he is not said to have a "portion" in the offering dedicated to two deities, because there was no such intention.
The grinding of the sacrificial pap (caru) is performed when the deity is Pūṣan alone, not in the case of offerings to two deities such as those dedicated to Indra and Pūṣan;
the fact that [Pūṣan] does not eat is merely a reason [for this].
As for what was said— that "he is toothless" shows the duty of the deity—
this is a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), which is applicable even in the other view;
the [primary] statement is paramount.
The rule "nivīta" is a duty pertaining to humans, because the word has that as its primary meaning.

It is prescribed in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "The *nivīta* is for humans, the *prācīnāvīta* is for the ancestors, and the *upavīta* is for the gods; he wears the *upavīta*, for he thus assumes the mark of the gods. Regarding the statement "the *nivīta* is for humans," there is a doubt: is this an injunction (*vidhi*) or a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*)? If it is an injunction, is it a duty pertaining to the person (*puruṣadharma*) or a duty pertaining to the ritual act (*karmadharma*)? Furthermore, does the injunction apply to that [context] where humans are mentioned, or does it find its place in a ritual act where humans are the primary factor?

What is established? That it is an injunction and a human duty (*puruṣadharma*). If it is indeed an injunction, then by enjoining such a previously unknown matter (*apūrva-artha*), it becomes purposeful; otherwise, it would be a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and thus useless. If it is an injunction, then "the *nivīta* is for humans" is a statement where the person is the primary element (*puruṣapradhāna-nirdeśa*). How is this understood? Here, humans are not being enjoined; rather, the *nivīta* is enjoined for humans. Furthermore, that which is not enjoined cannot be a subsidiary element (*aṅga*).
If humans were also enjoined [as the referents], the sentence would be split;
therefore, the *nivīta* is an aid for humans.
But surely, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is an aid for the New and Full Moon sacrifices?

For a sentence is indeed more powerful than context. Furthermore, since the relationship of the factors of action (*kāraka*) is intended to be expressed when humans are subordinate, the instrumental case would be used; however, this genitive case indicates a general relationship (*saṃbandha*). In that case, the mention of "humans" would not need to be made at all regarding those who are subordinate. That [act] would be performed by humans alone [even without the word], whereas it must be mentioned in the view where humans are the primary factor.
Or it is a figurative designation, because the object actually exists.
An *apadeśa* is the statement of something already known;
this is not an injunction (*vidhi*),
but rather a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Why? Because the meaning is already established.

The meaning is indeed already attained: that which is "worn across the neck" (nivīta) belongs to humans; for humans generally perform their own purposes while wearing it thus. Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda).
However, it would be an injunction (vidhi) because it conveys something not previously known.

It must indeed be an injunction (*vidhi*), for only thus does it possess a purpose; otherwise, it would be a mere statement devoid of meaning. A restatement (*anuvāda*) refers to what has already occurred previously, but this is unprecedented (*apūrva*): that it must be performed as a rule. Therefore, it should be a property of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
As for what was stated—that it is an injunction (vidhi)—that is accepted.
However, as for the claim that it is a duty of humans (manuṣyadharma), that is not approved.

This is a duty pertaining to the ritual (kratudharma) because of the context; for this is stated precisely while duties mostly relating to ritual acts are being discussed, and therefore it is a duty of the ritual act.
Because it is a supplementary statement to a preceding sentence.
The supplementary statement for "nivītaṃ manuṣyāṇām" (the *nivīta* [mode] is for men) is its designation (*samākhyā*), namely "Ādhvaryava" (pertaining to the Adhvaryu).
If it is a subsidiary element of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then it must be performed by the Adhvaryu;
in that case, the designation will be supported.
In that context, whatever is connected with it [is included], because there is no prohibition.
Or rather, when that [the subordinate] is predominant, the other [the principal] is counted as equal because it exists for the sake of that [subordinate].

This is not the case—that it should find its place in the context [of the general ritual]. Rather, the *nivīta* should apply to a rite where humans are the primary agents, such as the *ātithya* (guest-reception) ceremony.
Why? Because they are enumerated as equals; these are enumerated as being on equal footing.

As for the statement, "The *upavīta* belongs to the gods; he invests himself with the *upavīta*," that prescribes the *upavīta* for the two rites under discussion, the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

As for the statement, "The *prācīnāvīta* [mode of wearing the sacred thread] belongs to the ancestors (*pitṛs*)," it prescribes the *prācīnāvīta* for a rite where the ancestors are the primary focus. Furthermore, as for the statement, "The *nivīta* [mode] belongs to human beings," that also prescribes it independently for the *ātithya* (guest-reception) rite.
How is this understood? It is understood that it prescribes it for a rite where human beings are the primary focus.

Because of the connection with the word "of humans" (*manuṣyāṇām*) ending in the genitive case, [the result] would apply only to humans themselves, and not to that which has humans as its primary object.

It is replied: if it were assumed to belong to humans, a separate result would have to be postulated; however, if it belongs to that which has humans as its primary object, the genitive case will be justified, the relationship will be thus established, and no separate result need be postulated.

Thus it has been said: "In the case of equal [factors], there would be a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Now, [one might argue that] having first attained syntactic unity with the human agent as the primary factor, it will then attain syntactic unity again with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices under discussion. For two relationships are not enjoined in a single sentence; if they were, the sentence would indeed be split.

Because the other mention of "man" is for the purpose of connecting with the *nivīta*, it will form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that very [term] by means of the directly perceived word; and since it possesses meaning through that single syntactical unit, a connection with the context (*prakṛta*) is not to be assumed.
Therefore, setting aside the context, it should be applied to the *ātithya* sacrifice.
Or rather, it is an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) because of the context.
This is not so—that it is an injunction and that it concerns an action where humans are the primary agents.
Here, the connection with humans is heard in the phrase "of humans" (*manuṣyāṇām*); there is no connection with an action where humans are the primary agents.
And if humans were the primary agents, a separate fruit would have to be postulated.
But it might be connected with the act of hospitality, which is not specifically indicated, is not the subject matter at hand, and must be inferred.
What fault is there in that? It would be displaced from its context, even though such a connection is possible there. If it is asked, "How is such a connection possible? [the answer follows].

This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda); by praising what is relevant to the context, it will be applicable within that very section. If it were an injunction (vidhi), it would have to be displaced [from its context].
Therefore, it is not an injunction regarding rites where humans are the primary agents, because it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction.
And the division of directions is likewise [established], because the relationship [between words] has meaning as its cause.
What, then, is the prima facie position? The division of directions is likewise [to be considered], because the relationship [of the directions] has its basis in the purpose [of the action].
This division of directions is to be deliberated upon just like the *nivīta* [wearing of the sacred thread].

Whatever was the prima facie argument regarding the *nivīta*, that is the prima facie argument here; whatever was the intermediate [position], that is the intermediate [position] here; and whatever was the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), that is the final conclusion here.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because the passage has a meaningful purpose and is connected with humans, it is a duty for humans;

it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the fact that humans perform their tasks facing west or north, with the sun behind them and looking upwards. The other position is that it is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*), and by virtue of conforming to the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is a duty of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; specifically, to conform to both the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context, it finds its place within the Jyotiṣṭoma in the activity of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) where humans are the primary agents.

Another opinion holds that because the sentences are distinct, they should be included in the section on hospitality (*ātithya*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended to support the context, since its syntactic unity with the injunction "he makes the eastern hall" (*prācīnavaṃśaṃ karoti*) is directly established.
The same applies to [the passages concerning] what is broken at the joint (*paruṣi dita*), what is full (*pūrṇa*), and what is burnt (*vidagdha*).

What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? These [rites] are also like that: whatever was the prima facie position regarding the *nivīta* is the prima facie position for these; whatever was the middle [position] is the middle; and whatever was the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is the very same final conclusion here.
The prima facie position is that these are injunctions and constitute duties for humans, because they serve a purpose and are connected with humans.

Regarding the upper and lower parts, there is simplicity due to the absence of restriction; because it is uncooked, it is "fierce" (*raudra*) due to its rawness; and even when full, there is simplicity due to its smoothness.

Thus, the subsequent position is that clarified butter placed on the head of men is merely for their benefit, and because its purpose has already been established, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Another position is that it is an injunction (*vidhi*), and based on the predominance of ritual duties and the name [of the rite], it is a duty of the ritual action (*karmadharma*).
Yet another position is that it applies to the *anvāhārya* rice and the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), as this favors both the syntactical connection (*vākya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*).
It cannot be a separate injunction (*vidhi*) because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
It is rather an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*), because within the context it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction.

These [passages] form a single syntactical unit with such injunctions as: "He cuts [the hair] at each joint," "He takes [the hair] from above the opening," "He anoints it with fresh butter," and "It should be cooked without being scorched."
Therefore, these are not injunctions but explanatory passages (arthavādas).
An act not connected with a sacrifice would be a permanent restatement (nityānuvāda) because of its connection [with the ritual context].
Is it not the case that this Śruti is the source of that Smṛti?
This [Śruti] cannot possibly be its source;
for if it were based upon that [Smṛti], it would have been recorded as belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, yet its instructors appear only at the time of the initiation (upanayana).
Moreover, they teach that this is a property of the person; therefore, this Smṛti does not derive from this Śruti.
Or rather, it is an injunction because of a different connection.
This injunction regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices—"one should not speak untruth"—is an original mandate (*vidhi*), not a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Why? Because of a difference in connection (*saṃyogāntara*).

In the case of the Smṛti rule, the person's connection is with the performance of a restrictive observance (*niyama*); here, however, the person's connection is with the prohibition of a specific action (*padārtha-pratiṣedha*).
How can that which is heard as one thing be a restatement (anuvāda) of another? Therefore, this is an injunction (vidhi) for a prohibition.
[The opponent] says: "We accept this, that it is an injunction;
however, we maintain that it is a duty of the person (puruṣadharma), because human effort is explicitly stated in the scripture."

To this we reply: in all verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), the performance of an action (*kriyānuṣṭhāna*) is heard, but no *kāraka* (participant in the action) whatsoever. How is this understood? From the suffix (*pratyaya*), for it is from the suffix that we perceive the action as something to be performed. The opponent says: According to the teacher’s instruction that "the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) together express the meaning of the suffix," it is understood that the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are the word-meanings (*śabdārtha*). For the teachers prescribe the suffixes *śap* in the sense of the agent and *yag* in the sense of the object; thus they enumerate the agent and the object as the meanings of the suffix. Therefore, the agent and the object are the word-meanings.
It is said: the meaning of a word does not arise from the statement of a teacher or the author of a sūtra; rather, it is understood through the suffix (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, it is understood that an action (*kriyā*), once perceived as something to be performed, causes the factors of action (*kāraka*) to be understood.
Moreover, the teachers do not say that either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) is the meaning of the suffix.

But surely the verbal suffix (lakāra) is heard in reference to both the agent and the object? It is not heard in reference to the agent or the object as such; rather, there is another statement therein: "the singular number [is used] for one, the dual number for two, and the plural number for many. In that context, the connection is made thus: "when there is one agent, when there are two agents, or when there are many agents," and so forth.

In this way, the relationship of oneness and so forth pertains to the action (*karman*). In that context, it is not the case that [the suffix occurs] "when there is one agent" (*kartari bhavaty ekasmiṃś ca*).
How then? It means that the singular number (*ekavacana*) occurs when there is one agent, that is, when there is oneness of the agent.
Thus it is in the case of duality and plurality, as well as in the case of the object of the action (*karman*).
When explained in this way, the meaning of the Sūtra is shown to be in accordance with worldly logic,
and the very syllables of the Sūtra become consistent with reason.
This is also the traditional authority (*āgama*): when singularity and so forth are the meanings of the case-endings, then [the notions of] object and so forth function as qualifiers.

Now, one might object: "The singular number is used because of the singularity of the agent, the dual number because of the duality of the agent, and the plural number because of the plurality of the agent.
Therefore, it is understood that the agent is certainly the meaning of the word."
It is said: this cannot be established through inference; rather, it is perceived directly that the agent is understood precisely from the comprehension of the action to be performed.
That [perception] is not sublated by anything whatsoever.

When there is an indication in the singular number, the oneness of the agent is understood; when there is an indication in the dual number, the duality of the agent; and when there is an indication in the plural number, the plurality of the agent.

That too is perception; which among these could possibly sublate inference? Just as when a word expresses a form (kṛti), a dual number indicates a plurality of substances, while a singular number indicates the unity of a substance, so it should be understood here as well.
Therefore, it is not based on direct scriptural statement (śruti); and if it is not based on scriptural statement, it will not sublate the context (prakaraṇa).

As for the argument that human effort would be rendered useless under the view that it is a property of the ritual action (karmadharma), because its necessity is already expressed by the injunction of performance (prayogavacana)—[that objection is refuted].

To this it is said: An auxiliary (*aṅga*) would be grasped by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), but that which is not enjoined cannot be an auxiliary; therefore, for the sake of being an auxiliary, it must be enjoined—even under this view.
Hence we consider that this prohibition refers to what belongs to the context.

Therefore, that which is an auxiliary is such that untruth (*anṛta*) must not be spoken; thus, whatever has been resolved upon (*saṃkalpita*) is the auxiliary, and that alone must be performed. Having resolved upon rice (*vrīhi*), one should not offer an oblation made of barley (*yava*).
He says: "If falsehood must not be spoken in either case, then what is the purpose of this deliberation?

It is replied: In the former position (*pakṣa*), it is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*); in the event of a lapse there, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is that prescribed by the *Smṛti*. In the final view (*siddhānta*), it is a duty of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; in the event of a lapse there, the expiation is that belonging to the Yajurveda.
Like the *Ahīna* sacrifice, [the rule] pertains to the person because it is for his sake.

[Objection: But surely the context (*prakaraṇa*) would be contradicted. [Reply: Let the context be contradicted; however, the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is what contradicts it here, because of its connection with the person who is yawning. From the context, it is understood that [the rite] is taught for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; from the syntactical connection, it belongs to the yawner. And the syntactical connection is stronger than the context.
Therefore, it should be displaced [from the context].
They also declare a fruit: "He indeed establishes the out-breath and in-breath within himself. And that connection [with the fruit] is sublated;

therefore, it is a property of the person (puruṣadharma) and should be extracted from the context, like the *ahīna* sacrifice. Just as the number twelve of the *upasads* is extracted from the context due to its connection with the *ahīna*, so too is the statement "may strength and wisdom [dwell] in me" extracted from the context because of its connection with the one who is yawning.
Or rather, due to the distinction of context, that [quality] belonging to the qualified [substance] is a refinement (saṃskāra), like a substance.
He says: It is understood as "the rite of human consecration" (*puruṣasaṃskārakarma*), but not as being performed only by one who performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Why? For even one who yawns elsewhere than at the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices is indeed denoted by the word "one who is yawning.
And it has been stated that [the application] is not restricted by the context (*prakaraṇa*); therefore, it is displaced [from its original context].

To this it is replied: It is not excluded at all; however, there is no purpose served by that [exclusion] being expressed in Sanskrit. But surely, in this context, there is likewise no purpose served by the refinement of the person?
It is said: the refined person will perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
He says: "Even if there is a displacement [of the ritual], the consecrated person will perform another [ritual].

It is replied: "The consecration does not become a subordinate element (*guṇa*) for another [ritual], because that other is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛtatvāt*. He says: "Even for the subject under discussion, it is not a subordinate element, because it is understood from the syntactical statement (*vākya*) to be a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*)."
It is said: Because it would otherwise be purposeless, it is understood that this is not a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*).

Therefore, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices under discussion, and not with any other fruit-bearing rite, due to the absence of a context (*prakaraṇa*). Consequently, there is no displacement (*utkarṣa*).

As for the objection that, on this view, if one were to say "it should be performed within the context," the statement regarding performance would have its literal meaning unintended; [the reply is: in that case, it will be a restatement (*anuvāda*), since there is no purpose in enjoining a connection with the person.
It is set aside because of the designation.
Now, as for what was described—that just as the twelve-fold *upasads* are displaced, so too should this [the *dvādaśāha*] be displaced—it is replied:
for that [twelve-fold nature] is designated by the scriptural statement (*vākya*) for the *ahīnas*, and the *ahīnas* possess results;

moreover, the word *ahīna* does not apply to the *jyotiṣṭoma* because it would be used figuratively, and because of the specific designation: "There are three *upasads* for the *sāhna* sacrifice, and twelve for the *ahīna*."
Therefore, it is appropriate that the twelve-fold attendance (*dvādaśopasattā*) is extracted from its context;
however, in this case, there is no connection with the person (*puruṣa*), because it would serve no purpose, and because there is nothing else in the context that possesses such a purpose.
Furthermore, in the case of the *Śaṃyu* [rite], it is because of the complete surrender of everything.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The gods indeed said to Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya, 'Carry our oblation. Having introduced this, the following statement occurs: 'What shall be mine from my offspring? They replied: 'He who threatens a Brāhmaṇa, him you shall cause to suffer for a hundred years; he who strikes him, him for a thousand years; he who draws blood, for as many years as the number of dust particles that are moistened by the spilling [of blood], for so many years he shall not know the world of the ancestors. Therefore, one should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa, nor strike him, nor draw his blood."
[Objection: But surely there should be insertion into the context, as in the case of one who is being consecrated by the *jañjabhyamāna* rite?
[Reply: No, it is said; for in that case a result would have to be assumed, whereas here it is already established.

For here there is an injunctive suffix: "one should cause to suffer with a hundred," "one should cause to suffer with a thousand," "one may know the heavenly world"—therefore, such a type of injunction must indeed be displaced from its context.
Because there is no prior exclusion for one who wears soiled clothes.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One should not converse with one wearing soiled clothes; one should not eat her food. In this regard, there is a doubt: is this a prohibition of conversing with one wearing soiled clothes as part of the Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual, or is it a prohibition for a person in all circumstances? What is the prima facie view? On account of the context, it is a rule of prohibition pertaining to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
And because of the prohibition against food.

And there is a prohibition regarding food: "One should not eat her food; indeed, food is for a woman [only] as an ointment. This is a prohibition against sexual intercourse that is enjoined; and since it is not applicable within the context [of the sacrifice], it is determined to be a duty of the person (puruṣadharma), extracted from the context.
But when it occurs outside of a context, it is a duty of that [person], because of that distinction.
It is heard in a passage not connected to a specific ritual context: "Therefore, gold should be worn; [one who wears it] becomes fair-complexioned, while his rival becomes ill-favored.
Also: "One should be well-dressed; thus one maintains beauty.
In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this a property of the ritual context (*prakaraṇadharma*) or a property of the person (*puruṣadharma*)?
To this it is replied: But that [injunction] is a property of the person, because of its distinction from the context; such a thing must be a property of the person.
Why? Because there is a distinction between this and what is recited within the context—it is not recited within the context.
If it were recited outside of any specific context, it would be a property of all contexts.
Recitation outside of its specific context would not produce any particular result;
therefore, such a thing is a duty of the person (puruṣadharma).
