However, because it lacks a material substance (adravyatva), it must be a subsidiary (śeṣa) [to a ritual action].
Because of the connection with the Veda.

The connection with the Veda as "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" is appropriate for that which is subordinate; for it is by the Adhvaryu that the subordinate element is performed, and it is not a duty of the person [in general], since the Adhvaryu is the performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites along with their subsidiaries.
Therefore, duties of this kind are indeed properties of the ritual action.
And because of the connection with the substance.
Furthermore, the instruction here refers to the substance, because of its connection with the accusative case in the phrase "gold is to be worn.
And the purification of a substance is purposeful under the view that it is a subsidiary part of a ritual act, whereas it would be useless if it were a duty pertaining to the person.
Alternatively, there may be a connection for this [wearing] with the fruit [of the sacrifice], like the connection [of other accessories]; therefore, it is a ritual act—so says Ātiśāyana.
Or rather, the meaning is that the connection of such things with the result would be a property of the person; for if it were a property of the gold or the cloth, it would be purposeless.
[Objection: But surely the ritual act will be accomplished by means of the consecrated gold or cloth.
[Reply: This is not so; as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the gold, it could not assist the ritual act.
Because of the absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means of proof, [the *durvarṇa* mantra] is not an auxiliary part of the ritual action.
Therefore, there is a connection with a fruit for those mantras of this class, such as "thereby his rival becomes ill-colored.
Since they are not within a specific context (*aprakaraṇe*), they are subsidiary to all rituals because there is no distinction.

In this context, the offerings associated with ritual actions, such as the *jayas* and others, serve as the illustration. For instance, there are injunctions such as: "One should offer the *jayas* in whatever rite one intends to perform," "He offers the *rāṣṭrabhṛts*," and "He offers the *abhyātānas*.
Regarding these, the question arises: are they subsidiary to all actions, including agriculture and the like, or only to Vedic rituals such as the *agnihotra*?
Their status as subsidiaries (śeṣatva), however, follows from their connection with known rites and from the absence of any mention of a separate fruit.
What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are subsidiaries to all rites, because no specific distinction is stated.
But the oblations (homās) should be restricted [to the Āhavanīya fire], because of their connection with the Āhavanīya.
And the remainder [is established] from the traditional designation.
For this reason as well, we see that they are subsidiary to the Vedic rites.

Why? Because of the designation (*sāmakhyāna*). For the *jayas* and other such rites, being recited in the Veda designated as "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*), will be performed by the Adhvaryu priest.

Since the Adhvaryu is absent in activities such as plowing, if these rites were performed by someone other than the Adhvaryu, they would contradict the designation; therefore, they are subsidiary to the Vedic rites.
However, because of a defect, the expiatory rite (iṣṭi) should apply to the worldly fire; for according to the scripture, there would be no defect in the case of the Vedic fire.
There is the Aśvapratigraheṣṭi sacrifice: "Varuṇa indeed seizes him who accepts a horse; as many horses as he may accept, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should he present.
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the sacrifice pertain to the acceptance of a horse in a worldly context, or in a Vedic context?
What, then, is the worldly acceptance of a horse, and what is the Vedic?
Whether one is begging in the world or not begging, wherever one receives a horse, there is the worldly acceptance of a horse.
There is also the Vedic [acceptance], such as the thousand horses given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice, and "the cow and the horse" in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
But is it not the case that even in the Vedic acceptance, sin accrues to one who accepts from someone from whom one ought not to accept?

It is said: This would indeed be so if the sacrifice were intended for the one who performs the acceptance; however, we shall explain in the subsequent section how that [intention] actually belongs to the causal agent. Therefore, it is established in this section only that there is no sacrifice in the case of the acceptance of a horse as enjoined by the Veda. Consequently, it should be understood as a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because otherwise [the injunction] would be untenable; therefore, it is to be recognized as part of the sacrifice.

Now, if evil (*pāpa*) were expressed by the word *varuṇa* on the grounds that its intended meaning is "it chooses" (*vṛṇīte*), then, having abandoned the established conventional meaning, there would be mere conceptual difficulty: one would have to say that Varuṇa is denoted by the word *varuṇa* because he "chooses. In that case, even in the sacrificial acceptance of a gift, one would be "seized by Varuṇa" due to the distress caused by guarding, nourishing, or worrying about it; this position would not be tenable—namely, that it refers to the acceptance of a horse in common worldly usage—and the established conventional meaning would be contradicted.

Therefore, this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*); it is a commendation by way of comparison, to the effect that as long as there is benefit in being released from Varuṇa for one seized by Varuṇa, so too is this [the acceptance of the horse].

The acceptance of this [horse] is like being seized by Varuṇa; the sacrifice is like the rite for his release. Just as the release of one seized by Varuṇa must necessarily be performed, so too is this [acceptance]. Therefore, it should be understood as applying to the Vedic sacrifice.
For in the case of a worldly [gift], a fruit would have to be imagined, whereas in the Vedic context, it will become an auxiliary part of that [act] in which the acceptance of the horse occurs.

Since a syntactic unity with the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is possible through their connection, and because a direct syntactic unity with the statement of a fruit is lighter than an indirect one, it is logical that the sacrifice belongs to the Vedic gift.
And that which is not enjoined [is established] through the differentiation of actions.
It should belong to the officiating priest on account of the indicative mark.
This [result] does not belong to the recipient, but rather to the causal agent (hetukartṛ).
Why? Because of an indicative mark (liṅga).
What is the indicative mark? It is the connection of the preceding words with the subsequent words according to their respective meanings.

This is heard [in the scripture]: "Prajāpati gave a horse to Varuṇa," where Prajāpati is celebrated as the giver of the horse and Varuṇa as the recipient; [it continues], "he (sa) was afflicted by his own deity. The word "he" (sa), being dependent, requires the previously mentioned remainder of the sentence; since "he" refers back to Prajāpati, it forms a single syntactical unit with that. Furthermore, due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the reference must be understood as referring to Prajāpati alone, and not to Varuṇa, because of the lack of coreferentiality (vaiyadhikaraṇya).
"He was rent asunder"—this also refers back to Prajāpati who was the subject previously mentioned, and thus forms a single syntactical unit with that;

"he saw this four-potherd oblation to Varuṇa"—this is Prajāpati himself; "he offered it"—this is Prajāpati himself; "thereupon he was released from the noose of Varuṇa"—it was Prajāpati who was released.

"Varuṇa seizes him"—this is a statement of reason (*hetvapadeśa*). Because Prajāpati, having given a horse to Varuṇa, became afflicted with dropsy (*paridīrṇa*), therefore Varuṇa seizes whoever accepts—that is, gives—a horse; he becomes afflicted. Since he was released by means of an offering to Varuṇa (*vāruṇa*), therefore even by another who gives a horse, an offering to Varuṇa must be performed; thus the *vāruṇī* sacrifice for the giver of the horse is praised, and it is enjoined as something to be done by this verb.
Therefore, "having given a horse, one should perform the *vāruṇī* sacrifice."
Moreover, one would have to assume many inconsistencies, such as that Prajāpati led a horse to Varuṇa, or that he accepted the horse from Varuṇa.

The word "accepts" (*pratigṛhṇāti*) is capable of expressing the meaning "causes to accept" (*pratigrāhayati*) by whatever capacity it may have. For whoever performs that action, and by whomsoever the action is accomplished even through an indirect means (*praṇāḍyā*), he can be called the agent (*kartṛ*) of that action. Just as one who arranges the use of six ploughs is said to "plough with six ploughs," even though he does not perform the actual scratching of the soil himself, because he performs what is conducive to that;
so too here, he who gives performs what is conducive to acceptance.
Therefore, it can be said that "the giver accepts."
Therefore, having determined this, it is established that one who gives is said to "receive," and for him there is the Vāruṇī sacrifice;
and the case of the mishap from drinking is likewise.
But there would be a fault in the case of the Vedic [text], whereas in the case of the worldly [text], there would be no fault because of the meaning.
This [consequence] may occur in the case of a Vedic drink, but not in the case of a worldly one.

Why? Because of a fault; for here a connection with a fault is heard in scripture: "He is deprived of his senses and his vigor. But in the case of a worldly drink, when it is consumed for the purpose of balancing the bodily humors (*dhātu-sāmya*) and so forth, nothing is faulty; indeed, in the world they drink it specifically for the sake of vomiting.

Moreover, even if this is an explanatory passage (arthavāda), nevertheless, in order to avoid the postulation of a separate result, it is logical to assume that [the action] belongs to the Veda itself;
for there is no distinction in this regard across all cases.
Or rather, it belongs to the owner, because it exists for his sake.
Or rather, it should belong to both masters.

Why? Because it is for their sake; the ritual action is for the sake of the sacrificers, and since the Soma is vomited there, that Saumendra rite which occurs here is also indeed for their sake alone.

For this [rite] is heard as being for the benefit of one who has vomited Soma; it can benefit the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who has vomited Soma, not the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). For that is not a rite intended for the sake of the priest in which Soma is vomited.
Now, if it is argued: "The priests belonging to the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ who have vomited Soma will perform [the rite] in their own fires."

That being the case, if [the rite] were not a subsidiary part of the ritual action of one whose Soma has been vomited, nor of the Adhvaryu or Hotṛ priest who has vomited the Soma, then the Adhvaryu and others—who are entirely subordinate [to the sacrificer]—would not obtain the fruit while having it performed by their own priests.
Furthermore, that which is performed for their sake would not serve the benefit of the sacrificer; therefore, the rite should not be performed for the priests in the event of vomiting.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
And there is an indicative mark [in the scripture] regarding one who vomits the Soma:
"He who vomits the Soma is deprived of the drinking of Soma.

Since the sacrificer is the one whose ritual action becomes defective when the consecration of the Soma is ruined, he would be deprived; in no way could there be such deprivation for the officiating priests.
The connection would be with the act of vomiting, as in "the officiating priests of whom [the sacrificer] vomits the Soma," and not with the person who vomits the Soma, as in "he who vomits the Soma.
Therefore, we see from this also that when the sacrificer vomits, the offering is dedicated to Soma and Indra;
for there is a complete offering of the oblation because it is intended for that purpose.
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein it is recited: "That which belongs to Agni, the cake on eight potsherds, is never omitted at the new moon and the full moon.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the entire oblation be offered to Agni, or should some be set aside and only a portion be offered? What is the prima facie view? The entire oblation should be offered.
Why? Because it is for that purpose;
there is the injunction, "The cake dedicated to Agni (Āgneya) must be prepared.
Therefore, everything must be offered.
But because there is no removal, it should be the remainder.
Having extracted [the portion], it is a non-extraction;

for it is heard [in scripture]: "He cuts off twice from the oblation. There is also another statement: "He offers the double-portioned [oblation]. Therefore, only the double-portioned amount should be offered, while the remainder is to be left over.
Or rather, it is a means, because it has that as its purpose.

And this is not the case—that only two portions are to be offered, or that whatever one offers must be consecrated by cutting it twice. What is enjoined regarding the offering is merely the act of cutting twice; the offering of what has not been cut twice is not prohibited. Furthermore, since the entire substance is to be offered, this alone is logical, and not otherwise. However, because the ritual action has already been performed [by the cutting], the offering should be made once, since the substance is subordinate to the action.

How is it that the substance is not primary, such that there would be no repetition? Because the fruit arises from the sacrifice; for when there is the mention of both the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished, the accomplished is taught for the sake of the to-be-accomplished. Furthermore, no perceptible benefit to the substance is produced by the sacrifice. Therefore, having offered two portions, the remainder must be set aside.

As for what was said—that because of the statement "the oblation belongs to Agni," it is understood that the whole must be offered—therein the connection with the offering is inferential, whereas here, in the case of the two-fold cutting, it is directly perceived. Moreover, even when there is no connection with the whole, the use of the suffix -taddhita is justified; therefore, it should be accepted [that only a portion is offered]. Indeed, "belonging to Agni" (āgneya) is the general rule, while "one offers the two-fold cutting" (dvyavadānaṃ juhoti) is the specific exception.
Therefore, something must be left over;
for it is because of the observation of a remainder [that this is known].

From the statement "he cuts off the *iḍā* from the remnant" and "he performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from the remnant," we see that there is indeed a remnant, because these are restatements (*anuvāda*).
Since they are not the primary motivators (*aprayojaka*), the offerings should be made from a single [remnant], because the remnant is a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*).
There are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein there are the subsidiary acts, such as the eating of the iḍā-portion, the prāśitra, the sauviṣṭakṛt, and so forth.

In this regard, a doubt arises: should these be performed from each individual oblation, or from only one oblation? What is the prima facie view? They should be performed from only one, because they do not serve as the motive for the oblations; the subsidiary acts are not the motive for the oblations.

If they were employed for the sake of the remaining rites, then all [the materials] would be employed, and thus they would have to be prepared for all of them; however, these have other purposes and need not necessarily be applied to the remaining rites.
Nevertheless, due to proximity, they must be performed from some [source], for the remnant is indeed the means for these, and because they have already been consecrated.
And because the primary substance has been consecrated by such a preparatory rite even once, it need not be performed again from another [substance];
or rather, it must be performed for all [the substances], since there is no distinction between the causes and the purpose of the consecration is for their sake.

The ritual acts with the remnants (śeṣakāryāṇi) should be performed from all the oblations (havirbhyaḥ). Why? Because there is no difference in the underlying reason; whatever is the reason for performing the ritual acts with the remnant of one oblation is the same for all of them. For that remnant must be disposed of; if it were not disposed of for any particular one, that oblation would be abandoned without having received the refinement (saṃskāra) provided by that disposal. Therefore, the acts should be performed from all of them.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
If [it were derived] from one [element], there would be no distinction regarding the fulfillment of desires as one wishes.
Now, let us consider the alternative:
if they were to arise from a single [cause], would they then arise from "any" [cause] whatsoever, or from the "first"? What is the prima facie position? That they arise from any cause whatsoever.
Why? Because no specific distinction is relied upon;
therefore, there is no fixed rule.
Or rather, it is because [the primary] occurs at an earlier time.
Or rather, they should be performed starting from the primary [offering].

Why? Because of their prior occurrence; thus, when they are to be performed, there is no obstruction of the occasion (*nimitta*). Since there is no obstruction of the occasion, that which is contingent upon it (*naimittika*) must be performed. Therefore, once the first has been performed, there is an obstruction of the occasion for the second and subsequent ones, and thus they are not performed.
Therefore, [the rites] should be performed by the principal [priests] alone;
since there is no mention of eating, the word "giving" refers to a purchase.
And because of familiarity with that.
"This indeed is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices"—because of this praise of the sacrificial fee, we consider it to be for the purpose of hiring [the priests];
or rather, it is for the purpose of consumption, because of the equality regarding the substance.
This division is for the purpose of consumption.
Why? Because there is an absence of giving.
How is there an absence? For only one who possesses power is able to give.
It is not due to a lack of authority.
How is there no authority? For it has been resolved by the sacrificer that "this belongs to the deity," and the learned do not deal with what has been resolved for the deity as if it were their own.
Therefore, for one who follows the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it is impossible to exercise independent authority; hence, there can be no purchase (*parikraya*).

Now, as for what was said—that it is not heard [in the scripture] that "it must be consumed," and that the fault incurred in abandoning what is explicitly stated is equal to the fault in postulating what is not stated—it is replied:

through such expressions as "this is for Brahmā," there is a connection between the portions and Brahmā and the others; therein, either the portions would benefit Brahmā and the others, or Brahmā and the others would benefit the portions.

No visible benefit is observed for the Brahman and others by means of the portions [of food] which merely assist them; however, a visible benefit can be produced in some way for the Brahman and others by the portions when they are being consumed as assistance.
Therefore, the division [of the food] is for the purpose of consumption.
If it is asked, "What, then, is this benefit? [the answer follows].
Those who are satisfied possess the capacity to complete the remainder of their karmic tasks;
thus, from this declaration, there is praise for giving.
Now, as for the statement "because of the praise of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā)," that is due to the commonality of the designation; it will apply even when there is no purpose of purchase.
And because of the connection with all [the priests] through the clarified butter (ājya).

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; regarding them, it is heard in the scripture: "One cuts off [a portion] for the Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half," and likewise, "One invokes the Iḍā," as well as other remaining rites such as the cutting off of the Prāśitra.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the Sviṣṭakṛt and the Iḍā be cut off from the clarified butter (*ājya*), which is the substance of the Upāṃśuyāja, or not?
What is the prima facie view? That they should be cut off.
Why? Because of the connection with all [the offerings], since they are recited in a common context, the subsidiary rites belong to all of them.
Moreover, there is a connection with all, as it says: "That which one cuts off from all the sacrificial oblations.
Therefore, the subsidiary rites are performed even from the clarified butter (*ājya*).
And because of the cause.

The reason is heard [in scripture]: "The gods indeed said to Sviṣṭakṛt, 'Carry our oblation. He said, 'Let me choose a boon; let there be a portion for me. They said, 'Choose it. He said, 'From the northern half alone, one should cut off for me a single portion each time. This same reason is proclaimed in the explanatory passage (arthavāda) both for the other [portions] and for the clarified butter (ājya). Therefore, from the clarified butter also, a portion should be cut off.
This is because of the word *samavatta* (the collected portion) being used in reference to a single [substance].
And because the explanatory passage concerning the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is seen in the context of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Regarding the *dhruvā* butter, there is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) concerning the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "Having made each successive portioning, one replenishes the *dhruvā*; having made the portioning for the *sviṣṭakṛt*, one does not replenish the *dhruvā*. For there is no subsequent oblation to be offered after that. This demonstrates the purpose of the replenishing: namely, that one will offer another oblation after that. Once the *sauviṣṭakṛta* rite is completed, since there is no further oblation, it should not be replenished.
It indicates that there is a re-sprinkling (pratyabhighāraṇa) in the *dhruvā* vessel for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
however, this would not be the case because [the substance] is not left over, since its entirety has been taken up. Thus, there is no remainder because of the taking of the whole.
It is not so; the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* must be cut from the permanent clarified butter (*dhrauvājya*).
Why? Because there is no remnant. Why is there no remnant for this? Because of the taking of the whole.
Because it is common [to all], it would not apply to the Dhruva [pole-star].

He says: "In that case, there will be a remnant of the clarified butter (ājya) in the juhū-spoon, just as with the cups (camasa), because of the injunction regarding Soma in the cups and the draught-vessels (graha).
To this, he replies:
"And because [the butter] has been offered from the juhū, and because that [offering] is connected with the oblation (homa)."
First of all, there is no remnant in the *dhruvā* vessel, as it has been stated that the *upāṃśuyāja* is common to both [offerings].
Now, why is it that the ritual action regarding the remnant is not performed with what remains in the *juhū*—just as there is a remnant in the *camasa* cup intended for the *homa*?
It is replied: whatever was taken into the *juhū*, all of that is connected with the *homa*; therefore, there is no remnant in the *juhū*.
If it is argued that it is like the *camasa* [cup].
Thus, what was stated again must be refuted:
[it is not so] because it contradicts the Vedic injunction and because it involves the preparation of the sacrificial oblation.
Because the topic concerns what has arisen, the word "all" is used [only] when it exists.

Now, as for what was said—"that which one cuts off from all the oblations"—it is replied: this is said with reference to the remnant that has been produced, not without qualification; therefore, "from all" means from all those remnants that are present here, just as in the cases "all the rice has been eaten" or "all the Brahmins have eaten," where the word "all" depends on the context, so it is here as well.
This is the conclusion regarding the specific class [of remnants].

Now, as for what was said—that if the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation were not to be taken from the clarified butter (*ājya*) by virtue of the extended injunction (*codaka*), then the term *samavatta* (the "collected portion") would not be applicable to the mere cooked rice (*caru*) that is to be offered—it is replied:

even if there is no further ritual function for the *ājya*, the term *samavatta* is still appropriate because it refers to a specific class of substance, namely with reference to both the class of boiled rice (*odana*) and the class of clarified butter (*ājya*).
For it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), and a restatement should be understood according to its possible application.
The final [letter] is for the purpose of negating the vowel *a*.

Now, as for what was said—that the pouring over the *dhruvā* vessel indicates its purpose is for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—that is not for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, because of the absence of any remnant; this has already been stated.
Therefore, this is its true meaning: [the pouring is for the purpose of replenishing the *dhruvā*].

For it is not the case that one would not preserve [the remnant] with the thought, "I am about to offer an oblation from this"; if another oblation were to be offered from the *dhruvā* vessel, it should not be replenished.
Indeed, the *dhruvā* would be depleted; it is not preserved because there is no other oblation [to follow], so what is the use of replenishing it?
The same applies to the *sviṣṭakṛt* and the *iḍā* at the *sākaṃprasthāyīya* sacrifice.
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the Sviṣṭakṛt and the Iḍā exist [in this rite], or do they not?
We say: they do exist.
Why? Because the Sākaṃprasthāyīya is indeed a modification (vikāra) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
This being the position, we reply: it does not exist [as a modification]. Why? Because of its non-remainder (aśeṣatva); and non-remainder results from the taking of everything.

How so? It is heard there as follows: "Having performed the two *ājyabhāga* offerings and having offered the *āgneya* cake, and having handed over the two ladles (*srucau*) at the *āgnīdhra* altar, he says [the formula] while stepping forward together with the water-pots.
Therefore, the disposal of the remnants does not take place from that point.
And the same applies to the cups (*graha*) in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice.
And the statement regarding the remainder is likewise.
This very principle supports the statement regarding the "remainder" (*ucchiṣṭa*).

Since it says, "he leaves it over; he does not offer everything," this prohibition is understood to apply when a complete offering would otherwise be required. Furthermore, because it is expressly stated in the scripture, there is no *sviṣṭakṛt* or *iḍā* portion, as it is declared that this [remnant] has another use: "One should hire a Brāhmaṇa as a drinker of the remnant. There is also an express scriptural application for the other remnant: "They sprinkle it upon the *śatātṛṇā* grass."
If the substance were one, then because of the distinction between the acts, the rites would have to be performed for each individual act.

There is the Sarvapṛṣṭheṣṭi sacrifice: [consisting of offerings] to Indra associated with the Rathaṃtara, to Indra associated with the Bṛhat, to Indra associated with the Vairūpa, to Indra associated with the Vairāja, and to Indra associated with the Śākvara. In this context, the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is common to all these rites. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the Sviṣṭakṛt and Iḍā offerings be performed for each individual rite, or only once?

What is established? That [the ritual act] must be performed for each individual action, because of the favor accorded by the injunction; even when there is a single substance, there is a multiplicity of actions.
And because the remnant is undivided, it is not distinguished with respect to all [the actions].
But in the case of the offering to Indra and Vāyu, there should be a consumption [of the remnant] for each ritual act, because of a specific scriptural statement.

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, [enjoined by the rule]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Regarding that, there is a doubt concerning the Aindravāyava cup: is there a single consumption, or is there a double? Since it is for the purpose of consecrating the Soma, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there should be a single consumption; however, we reply: in the case of the Aindravāyava, one must consume it twice.

Why? Because of a scriptural statement; for there is this statement: "He consumes the draught for Indra and Vāyu twice, for he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call for it twice. There is no overburdening of a scriptural statement. Since there is no such statement regarding the Soma [in general], no consumption [of it] is prescribed.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they recite [cups] of Soma;
regarding them, there is a doubt: should their remnant be consumed, or not? What is the prima facie view? There is no consumption of Soma [in these cases].
Why? Because there is no statement; it is not possible to determine the act of eating in the absence of a statement.
Therefore, the remainder of the Soma is not to be consumed.
Or rather, it may be so, because of the observation of another purpose.
But since these statements are based on what has not been previously established, they should be according to the instruction.
But surely this is merely a visual observation; the actual attainment must be stated.
It is replied: in that case, there will be explicit scriptural statements:
"He consumes the Āśvina cup as a complete circumambulation."
Therefore, the phrase "he hears from all directions" prescribes a specific manner of eating;
since this is not previously established, it is not appropriate to treat it as a mere restatement of the act of eating.
Moreover, by prescribing such a novel matter, the passage will possess purposeful meaning.
Therefore, wherever a specific act of eating is heard [in the scripture], it applies only there and does not extend too far;
for in the case of the cups (camasa), the designation [of the priests] is based on that very connection.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, it is heard in scripture: "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward; let that of the Brahman go forward; let those of the Udgātṛs go forward; let that of the Sacrificer go forward; let those of the Sadasyas go forward. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is there a consumption [of the Soma] for the Camasins, or not? What is the prima facie view? We say: no; it has already been stated that [the rule] does not over-extend.
This being the case, we reply: there is consumption in the cups (*camasa*).

Why? Because of the designation (*samākhyā*); for they are designated by the names "the Hotṛ’s cup," "the Brahman’s cup," and "the Udgātṛ’s cup. Where the Hotṛ has consumed, will consume, or has consumed, that is the Hotṛ’s cup. If the Hotṛ were not to consume therein, it would not be the Hotṛ’s cup.
Therefore, it is called a "camasa.

Now, if [the term] were to depend on [actions such as] carving and so forth, then, because the relationship [with the material] would be denied, it would not be a camasa at all; rather, it would be a different substance altogether.

And for this reason, it prohibits the non-Brahmin from consuming Soma; [the text says]: "If he should officiate at a sacrifice for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, and if he should desire to consume Soma, he should fetch Nyagrodha-piths, grind them, mix them with curd, and offer that as the portion to him, not Soma. This shows the exclusion of the consumption [of Soma].
This very suspicion regarding consumption is justified only if there is a consumption by the Camasins; therefore, we consider that such consumption exists.
[Furthermore,] the Udgātṛ's cup belongs to one person alone, because of the connection with the direct scriptural statement (śruti).

Objection: But the plural number is heard; therefore, many should consume [the soma]. Response: It is true that the plural number is heard, but it belongs to the nominal stem *udgātṛ* (singer). If that were intended to be significant, it would express a plurality of *udgātṛ*s; however, there is only one *udgātṛ*. Therefore, even though the plural number is heard there, it cannot effect a division of the *udgātṛ*.
Consequently, the plural number is not intended to be significant; for this [interpretation] is based on inference, namely, that "the cup belongs to many."
How so? When a nominal stem refers to many things, the plural number is used; and here the plural is indeed seen, as in "of the *udgātṛ*s" (*prodgātṝṇām*).
Therefore, the inference is certainly that the cup belongs to many. However, perception shows that there is only one *udgātṛ*, neither a second nor a third.
Moreover, direct perception (pratyakṣa) would be a stronger authority than inference (anumāna).
Therefore, the cup belongs to one person, and that [cup] belongs to the Udgātṛ.
Or rather, all [the priests] [share it], because of the connection with all.
Or else all [the chanters] might consume [the portion]; since the singular number is used while one *udgātṛ* is consuming, it is understood that the plural number was recited by mistake.
For that [plural] is neither being restated nor being enjoined.
[Objection: But even if all were consuming, the word *udgātṛ* would still be understood as a mistake.
It is said: first of all, even the sense of a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) will be possible, as in the case of "the Udgātṛ and others";
or rather, it refers to those who perform the Stotras, because of their connection with that [action] and because of the frequent occurrence of the plural form.
But all [the Vedas] should be [considered as the source], because of their connection with the Veda; on account of this reason, it would be a single part.
Therefore, four persons connected with the office of the Udgātṛ should consume from the Udgātṛ’s cup.

Even where there is a specific reason, the Subrahmaṇya is included among the Udgātṛs; for example, as in the statement "the Udgātṛs, having sat down, praise with the Sāman," which refers to those performing the stotra, so too is this statement: "The Udgātṛs should not speak out [the name] at the last [verse], for this is the last," which applies only to those excluding the Subrahmaṇya. There is no consumption for the Grāvastut, because it is not prescribed.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is a person among the Hotṛ’s assistants named Grāvastut.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: should he consume the Soma, or not?
It is said: the Grāvastut should not consume it.
Why? Because they do not prescribe its consumption. Thinking that the Hāriyojana [cup] is the domain of the Camasins, he said this: "Its consumption is not prescribed.
Or rather, it belongs to the Hāriyojana because of the connection with the whole.
Or rather, because of the proximity of the *camasins*.
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that there is a consumption [of the Soma] by the Grāvastut priest at the Hāriyojana cup; rather, only those who possess cups (camasins) have authority therein, not everyone.

How so? This distribution belongs to the cup-possessors: having referred to the cup-possessors as they consume other cups—just as it says, "they consume the cup"—it speaks specifically of the cup-possessors alone, and then states, "all of them indeed desire this Hāriyojana cup."

This is indeed a single sentence, because of the use of the word "atha" in the phrase "atha etasya," which refers back to what has immediately preceded it. Furthermore, the word "eva" in "atha sarva eva" implies, by the force of its meaning, a reference to all those previously mentioned. Therefore, we consider that this forms a single syntactical unit with the preceding passage: "As the cup-bearers consume [the Soma] from their respective cups, so do they consume from this Hāriyojana cup. Consequently, this distribution applies to the cup-bearers who are present: as elsewhere they consume from their own individual cups, but in the case of the Hāriyojana, "all" consume from it.
But since all [the cups] possess the character of being prescribed by rule, the scriptural mention of the *camasa* (cup) is for the sake of that [rule].
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.

It is not the case that only the *camasins* desire [the cup] at the *hāriyojana* [rite]; rather, all are enjoined regarding the *hāriyojana*, for it says "all partake," and it is not possible to enjoin a connection such as "only the *camasins* [partake].
For two novel connections cannot be enjoined within this single sentence.
Therefore, there is another mode of expression:
"And one should consume [the portion] after the *vaṣaṭ*-call."
Now, is the name alone the sole cause for consuming [the Soma]? We say: no; one should also consume on account of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call is also a cause for consumption.

How so? Because of a scriptural statement; for it is heard thus: "The first consumption belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*-call. Since consumption itself has not yet been established, this word does not intend to enjoin priority; rather, it enjoins the very act of consumption as qualified by priority. And [there is also the cause] from the oblation (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*).
Because of the direct instruction regarding the cups, the procedure for the remaining [vessels] is unmanifested.

The following is heard [in the scripture]: "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward; let that of the Brahman go forward; let that of the Udgātṛs go forward. In this regard, there is a doubt: should those who perform the oblation and the pressing in the cups, as well as the utterers of the *vaṣaṭ* call, consume [the soma], or not?
What is the prima facie view? They should not consume it, because the cups are explicitly prescribed for the cup-bearers (*camasin*).

By specific injunctions such as "Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward," and by the general statement regarding those who perform the oblation and the pressing—namely, that "the Soma which is to be consecrated by consumption shall be [consumed] in the cups by the cup-holders"—then where will another occasion for [the consumption] arise? Where will the unmanifest general occasion occur? It will occur in the remainder, where there are no cup-holders.
Or rather, because of the absence of a cause, there would be no designation of the cups, since the agent is designated by that [general rule].
And because another [use] is seen in the case of the *camasa* cup.
Furthermore, [the text] indicates other cup-holders (camasin) in relation to the cup (camasa): "He hands over the cups to the cup-attendant (camasādhvaryu);
he brings them to the one who utters the vaṣaṭ-call.

For indeed, only one's own cup is brought to the one who utters the vaṣaṭ-call; therefore, the observation of bringing many [cups] would not be possible if the one who utters the vaṣaṭ-call and the others were not to consume [the soma] from the cups.
Therefore, [it is said] "they eat.
Now, where many eat from a single vessel, what is the sequence there?
It is said:
In a single vessel, the Adhvaryu priest should consume first, in due order.
For the sequence for consuming belongs to him in whose hand the Soma is;
or it belongs to the Hotṛ, according to the wording of the mantra.

Or rather, the Hotṛ priest should consume first, because of the wording of the mantra; for the wording of the mantra is thus: "Even before the Hotṛ, they have attained the eating of the oblation," and likewise: "Like a Hotṛ, drink first for us.
And it is so because of this direct statement.
And because of the sequence of their causes.
For the first *vaṣaṭ*-utterance is the occasion for the *hotṛ*, and from that, the oblation is the occasion for the *adhvaryu*.

And because of the sequence of the occasions, there is a conformity to the order in the sequence of the things occasioned. The consumption [of the portion] is permitted by virtue of a specific scriptural statement.

Now, regarding the case where the Soma in a single vessel is consumed by more than one person: should it be consumed there after having requested permission, or without having requested permission, or only after having requested permission?
Since the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) suggests that no fixed rule applies, it is stated: "It must be consumed after having requested permission.
Why? Because of a scriptural statement; for this statement exists: "Therefore, Soma is not to be drunk by one who has not been invited (*anupahūta*)."
The invitation and the request for permission constitute this sūtra on attainment.
Since it is established that one must consume [the food] only after being permitted, the question arises: should one seek permission using worldly speech or Vedic speech?
Since it might be argued that there is no fixed rule regarding this according to worldly practice, the following is stated:
one should seek permission by saying "He has been invited; may you invite [him] as well," because of the indicative mark [of the text].
In that case, the response follows from the meaning.

This has been understood: one should seek permission with the words "You are invited; please be invited. Now, there is a doubt regarding the response: is the response to be worldly, or is it this very [Vedic] formula? What is the prima facie view? This is Vedic, as it is employed for the purpose of answering a question.
Another worldly response would be appropriate here;
this being the case, we say: in this instance, this very [response] is the answer.
But is it not the case that "upahūyasva" (be invited) possesses the characteristic of a question?
It is said: that which is its predecessor and is capable of being the response, "Upahūta" (Invoked), shall serve the function of the response.

He says: this traditional recitation is inverted; for there ought to be the question first, and then the response. It is said: by virtue of the sense, it shall serve the function of the response first; for the sense is more powerful than the sequence.
Because of the assembly of those who share a single vessel.
When the *yājyā* is removed, the *bhakṣa* (consumption) is also removed, just like the *pravara*.

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein, regarding the seasonal offerings (ṛtuyāga), it is heard in the scripture: "The sacrificer [performs] the *yājyā*; he gives the direction, 'O Hotṛ, recite the offering-verse for this,' and having himself accomplished [the rite], he sacrifices.

When he sacrifices himself, a doubt arises: does he have a portion to consume (*bhakṣa*), or not? To this it is replied: when the *yājyā* is removed, the consumption should not be removed; however, the consumption would belong to the Hotṛ alone, and not to the sacrificer.
Why? Because the *yājyā* is one thing and the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*) is another; and when one thing is removed, another is not thereby removed.
Just as when that very *yājyā* is removed, the *pravara* is not removed, so it is in this case as well.
Or rather, [the *pravara* remains] because of the arrival of the cause for the sacrificer (*yaṣṭṛ*).
Or rather, the portion should belong to the sacrificer.
Why? Because of the arrival of the cause; the cause of the consumption is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, and that arrives when the *yājyā* verse arrives.
For it is heard in scripture thus: "He utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the *yājyā*."

But has it not been said that even when the sacrifice is being performed by the sacrificer, the Hotṛ utters the *vaṣaṭ*? This is no solution; for one must sacrifice without pausing (*anavānatā*), and the sacrifice is accomplished by the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, not by the *yājyā* mantra alone.
Therefore, the sacrificer must not pause until the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance; if someone else were to utter the *vaṣaṭ*, the sacrificer would have to pause.

And he should not perform the sacrifice; for he is enjoined to sacrifice when it is time for the sacrifice to be performed, not merely when the word "sacrifice" is uttered. This is because the injunction "he sacrifices, sitting down himself" prescribes the performance of the sacrifice along with its ancillaries while seated. Furthermore, since the Pravara (the invocation of ancestors) has already commenced, it cannot be omitted.
The fruit-cup is an occasional modification of the consumption [of Soma], because of its connection with the Vedic text.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard in scripture: "If he should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya, and if he should desire to consume Soma, having fetched fruits of the Nyagrodha tree, having crushed them, and having mixed them with curds, he should offer that as the portion for him to consume, but not the Soma.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the fruit-cup (phalacamas) a modification of the consumption (bhakṣa), or is it a modification of the sacrifice (ijyā)?
Does the meaning of the text imply that one should consume the fruit-cup, or that one should sacrifice with the fruit-cup?

What is established? The fruit-cup (phalacamasa) is a modification of the consumption (bhakṣavikāra) occasioned by a specific cause, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the scripturally heard act of consuming, as in "one should give him the consumption. It is not the case that there is a word stating "one should sacrifice with it"; therefore, it is a modification of the consumption.
Or rather, it is a modification of the sacrifice (ijyāvikāra), because the consecration (saṃskāra) is for the sake of that [sacrifice].
He asks: "How can there be a modification of the sacrifice when there is no connection with the root *yaj*?
It is replied: "There is indeed a connection with the root *yaj*.
How so?"

If one were to officiate at a sacrifice for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, one should crush the shoots of the *nyagrodha* tree and offer them to him as a sacrificial portion (*bhakṣa*); this is understood to mean "in order to officiate.

For if there were a connection with the act of consuming, the former [the crushing] would not be connected with the latter [the offering], [as it would imply]: "If one wishes to purify the Soma by means of consumption, one should purify it with the *nyagrodha* shoots.
Therefore, there is no connection with consumption.
For the sacrifice is the subject under discussion; it will be connected with that, and thus there will be no fault.

[Objection: Is it not understood from the statement "one should give him a portion to eat" that it is a means for eating, and not a means for the sacrifice, because of its immediate proximity to the word "eating"? [Reply: It is said:
since the connection [with eating] would be purposeless when it is already being heard [in another context], it is stated that the connection is with the subject under discussion.

But how is there a connection with eating? For whatever substance of the sacrifice is to be eaten, that becomes [the object] through the extended application (*codaka*); therefore, it obtains a connection with eating. And by means of the connection with eating, the very connection with the sacrifice is indicated: if one sacrifices with it, then it becomes an object of eating. Therefore, from the mention of eating, it is understood all the more clearly that one sacrifices with it; such is this construction involving an intermediate step.

The meaning is that one should offer him a portion to consume; that is, one should act in such a way that he becomes a consumer of that portion. And if he performs the sacrifice with it, then he becomes a consumer of that portion.
Therefore, he must sacrifice with it;
this follows from the fact of the oblation (*homa*).
There is a statement regarding a specific oblation: "When they offer the other cups, then he offers this one, having struck it with a young blade of darbha grass.
Since there is a modification of the sacrifice, the mention of the "young blade of darbha grass" as an accessory for the act of offering becomes intelligible.
Therefore, this too is a modification of the sacrifice.
And because it occurs at the same time as the *camasa* cups.
"When they draw up other cups, then they draw up this cup"—
this observation of the drawing up [of the cup] is appropriate when there is a modification of the sacrifice (*ijyā*), not when there is a modification of the consumption (*bhakṣa*).
Therefore, it is also a modification of the sacrifice.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
From this also we see that it is a modification of the sacrifice (ijyāvikāra). Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).

What is the indicative mark? It is the restatement of the prohibition of Soma: "One should give him the draught (bhakṣa), not the Soma. If there is a modification of the sacrifice, the Soma is not consumed.
Therefore, we see that it is a modification of the sacrifice (ijyāvikāra),
because of the commonality among those who enter [the ritual].
Or rather, they are Brahmins because their names are identical.
Or rather, Brāhmaṇas should follow after the Rājanya’s cup.

How so? The injunction—"A hundred Brāhmaṇas consume the Soma"—by means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), expresses a number residing specifically in the Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, there are a hundred Brāhmaṇas; for the purpose of their consumption, ten are assigned to each individual cup as they approach.
Therefore, ten Brahmins from among a hundred Brahmins should follow after the cup of the Rājanya;
this applies to all [Brahmins] because there is no specific context [restricting it].

Something is stated without reference to a specific context: "He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood cuts [the portion] with the very essence of the meters; his oblations become full of essence. And:
"He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood does not hear an evil report," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: do the *khadira* nature of the *sruva* and the *parṇa* nature of the *juhū* apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*), or to both the archetype and the ectype (*vikṛti*)?
What is established? That such [injunctions] apply to all purposes, because they do not occur within a specific context; rather, they pertain to both the archetype (prakṛti) and the ectype (vikṛti).
Why? Because they are not heard within the context of any particular rite; therefore, by virtue of the syntactical statement (vākya), they would apply everywhere.
Or rather, they belong to the archetype alone, because they are not repeated.

Or rather, the vessels mentioned as independent injunctions (anārabhyādhīta) should enter into the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti). Why? Because of the avoidance of redundancy; thus, there will be no redundancy. What is the fault in redundancy? We say it is impossibility—for that which exists both in the archetype and in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) must already exist in the archetype.

If it exists in the archetype (prakṛti), it reaches the ectype (vikṛti) by the force of the extended injunction (codaka) itself; therefore, it does not require a non-contextual injunction (anārabhyavidhi). Consequently, because there is no such requirement, the non-contextual injunction does not prescribe it there. For this reason we say: it serves only the purpose of the archetype.
Let that [injunction] be set aside, as it is already obtained through the verbal statement.
If it is argued that [the object is known] from perception:

If the general rule (*anārabhyavidhi*) is stronger than the extended application (*codaka*), then once [the rite] has been established by the general rule, it does not require the extended application; and when the modified (*vaikṛta*) rite is thus devoid of requirement, the extended application does not apply at all.

In that case, the observation of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth would be impossible; yet the *prayāja*s and others are indeed observed in certain instances, such as: "At each *prayāja*, one offers a *kṛṣṇala*.
If, on the other hand, the extended application is stronger, then this observation is logically accounted for.
Therefore, the injunction not connected to a specific context pertains to the meaning of the root;
it is not [restricted] because of the unity of purpose with the injunctive statement.
It does not have the sense of *prakṛti* (archetype); we say it has the sense of "all" (*sarva*), because it is recited outside of any specific context (*aprakaraṇa*).
As for what was said—that there is no *codaka* (injunctive force of transfer) for that which is already rendered self-sufficient by an *anārabhyavidhi* (independent injunction)—that is not tenable.

For an *anārabhyavidhi* does not render an injunctive requirement (*codanā*) self-sufficient; indeed, when the *codaka* is already present, the quality of being made of *khadira* wood cannot be enjoined for the *sruva* ladle by means of an *anārabhyavidhi*.

In the absence of a primary injunction (*codaka*), there is no non-contextual injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*) either; nor does a non-contextual injunction bring about the *sruva* ladle or its being made of *khadira* wood.
Why? Because an injunction has a single purpose.
For an injunction has a single purpose, namely: "He whose *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood... [is successful].

And in this case, neither the *sruva* spoon nor its being made of *khadira* wood is both enjoined; rather, this scriptural statement [only] prescribes the *khadira* nature for that which is already a *sruva*, and that [status as a *sruva*] is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).

Therefore, the *codaka* exists; for, because it is directly perceived by the sentence of the general injunction (*anārabhyavidhi*), it causes [the application of the *khadira* wood] to everything else, excluding that [specific *sruva*].
Consequently, the *anārabhyavidhi* serves the purpose of both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modification (*vikṛti*).
If it is argued that there is origination;

If you see it thus—that their origin is similar to that of the archetypal injunctions (*prakṛti-vidhi*), wherein the subsidiaries are stated both concisely and in detail: "He offers five *prayāja*s" is the concise statement;
"He offers the *samidh*s," and so forth, is the detailed statement;
here too, "For whom the *sruva* ladle is made of *khadira* wood," and so forth, is the detail, while "For whom the *sruva* is of such a form" is the concise statement.

A rule of this kind is observed in the *prakṛti* (archetype); this one is also of this kind; therefore, it belongs to the *prakṛti*. This is an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*).
Therefore, the rule not prescribed in a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*) has the *prakṛti* as its object.
No, because they are equal.
This is not so.

For an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) of this kind is not a means of proof; there is merely a similarity here with the procedure of the archetype (*prakṛti*), but there is no authoritative evidence that "this occurs in the archetype.

Furthermore, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) are prescribed both concisely and in detail: "He offers three oblations" is the concise form, while "The gods [know] his devotion, his devotion" is the detailed form.

Therefore, even the rules concerning modifications (*vaikṛta*) are equal to those not specifically prescribed (*anārabhyavidhi*); thus, this is no reason for [the rule] to apply only to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
However, because the purpose of the injunction must be fulfilled in its entirety, and because there would otherwise be a contradiction with the primary [rite], the rule applies to the archetype.

The general rule (*anārabhyavidhi*) is not connected with that primary modified sacrifice (*vaikṛta-mukhya*). In the conflict between the general rule being a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) for that modified sacrifice and its application to the archetype (*prakṛti*), the general rule will not apply to the archetypal supplementary statement once it has been obtained through the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*). Therefore, the general rule is for the purpose of the archetype.
But due to the specific context, it would be contradictory in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).

Without reference to anything specific, a measure for the *sāmidhenī* verses is traditionally taught: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenīs*. In this regard, there is a doubt: does this apply to the archetype (*prakṛti*) or to the modified form (*vikṛti*)?

What is the prima facie view? By the previous principle, it is established that it applies to the archetype; however, fifteen [verses] are traditionally taught for the archetype, and therefore there is an option between the two.
But the occasional [rite] belongs to the archetype; its modification [belongs to the ectype] because of a specific connection.

It is prescribed in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "One desiring cattle should fetch [the water] with a milking vessel (godohana)"; likewise, regarding the sacrificial post (yūpa) in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is heard: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should make it of Bilva wood. Regarding such cases, there is a doubt: does it find its place in the archetype (prakṛti) or in the ectype (vikṛti)? What is the prima facie view? It is in the ectype; for the archetypes are already satisfied by other vessels and other sacrificial posts.

This being the case, we reply: the occasional (naimittika) element is inserted into the archetype (prakṛti), because it is enjoined in connection with a specific occasion (nimitta). The *khadira*, *pālāśa*, and *rauhitaka* woods are mentioned without distinction, as is the *camasa* cup; whereas the *godohana* vessel and the *bilva* wood are specifically prescribed. And a general rule is set aside by a specific injunction. Context (*prakaraṇa*) is the general factor, while connection with an occasion (*nimittasaṃyoga*) is the specific factor. That which is obtained through the general [context] is indirect, being based on indication (*lakṣaṇā*); whereas that which is obtained through the specific [injunction] is direct, being based on explicit statement (*śruti*). And explicit statement is stronger than indication, and the direct is stronger than the indirect.
Therefore, it should occur in the archetype itself;
the establishment of the sacred fires is for the sake of the sacrifice, because of the context.
Or rather, it is not so, because those [mantras] have that as their purpose.

For the Pavamāna-iṣṭis have the fires as their purpose; if the fire were for the sake of the sacrifice, then the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya) would benefit the sacrifices. However, the sacrifices are themselves fruitless, and therefore the establishment of the fires intended for them would also be fruitless.
But how is it that the Pavamāna-iṣṭis have the fires as their purpose? Precisely because [the sacrifices] lack a further purpose, whereas the fires possess utility.
The *iṣṭis* should indeed be performed for the sake of the elemental fires (*bhūta-agni*).
Therefore, the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) is for the purpose of the *pavamāna-iṣṭis*.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

It indicates the *liṅga* (indicative mark), as in the case of the Pavamāna-iṣṭis being for the sake of the fire. What is the *liṅga*? "This animal, namely the fire once established, indeed decays; therefore, one should offer these oblations of the Agnyādheya after a year. By that, it does not decay, and by that he makes it new again; thus it is not [merely] subtle.
This is for the sake of the primary ritual (*prakṛti*), just as other *ārambhavāda* (independent injunctions) function.

Regarding this *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires), there arises a doubt: does it serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*), or does it serve the purpose of all rituals (*sarvakarma*)? What is the prima facie view? It is said: it serves the purpose of the archetype. Why? For the same reason that other *anārabhyavāda* (independent) injunctions serve the purpose of the archetype.
Or rather, it is for all purposes, because the injunction has its own specific time.

Furthermore, its own time is prescribed; that [time] need not be separately enjoined, because whenever there is the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma, then this [rite] must be performed—and that is during the spring. Likewise, whenever there is the performance of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, then it must be performed.
Then it would be either the full moon day or the new moon day.
However, it should not be performed when the primary sacrifice is being carried out for a purpose other than its own; in that case, the mention of time would be appropriate.
Therefore, it is not for the sake of the primary sacrifice.
For these [offerings], Agni should be the deity by virtue of the original model, just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.
There are the Pavamāna sacrifices, such as "To Agni Pavamāna," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the Pavamāna sacrifices be performed in a fire that has been consecrated by the Pavamāna sacrifices, or not?
What is the prima facie view? Indeed, for those Pavamāna sacrifices, the fire consecrated by the Pavamāna sacrifices would be the archetype (prakṛti).

Why? Because of the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*), as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings; just as the *prayāja*s occur by virtue of the extended injunction, so too the fires consecrated by the *pavamāna* sacrifices should likewise occur.
Or rather, it is not so, because those [sacrifices] have that [consecration] as their purpose.
The procedure for the animal sacrifice is common to all, because there is no distinction in the context.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma—namely, "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma"—as well as the Savanīya and the Anubandhya animals.

There are also the ritual duties pertaining to the animal, such as the formal dedication (*upākaraṇa*), the leading forward (*upānayana*), the sprinkling with water (*prokṣaṇa*), the binding, the tethering to the sacrificial post (*yūpa-niyojana*), the immolation (*saṃjñapana*), and the dismemberment (*viśasana*).
Do these apply to all three—the Agniṣomīya, the Savanīya, and the Anubandhya—or to the Agniṣomīya and the Savanīya, or to the Agniṣomīya alone?
What is established? [That the animal rites apply] without distinction to all animals.

How is there no distinction? All animals are mentioned within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma; since they have entered that context, all the characteristics (*dharma*) of the animal sacrifice are connected to them, and there is no distinction among them therein.
And because of their position, [the characteristics belong] to the preceding [rite].
As for what was said—that [the mantras] are for the sake of the *savanīya* due to the context—we accept that; and by virtue of the sequence, they belong to the *agnīṣomīya*.

For its sequence is recited on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*), therefore they belong to both. However, according to some, the mention of "tomorrow" (*śvas*) there is for the purpose of indicating a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

For certain reciters of the Vedic branches (*śākhins*), there is a scriptural injunction for the *savanīya* animals [to be offered] on the following day; with reference to that, this repeated mention of them is for the sake of a secondary quality (*guṇa*).
What, then, is the quality for the sake of which this scriptural statement exists? It is said:

after enumerating the animals, having stated the fault in not knowing them—“Just as a fish, when unrecognized, shakes off the people [who catch it], so too these, being unrecognizable, shake off the people”—the scriptural statement enacts the performance of the omentum (*vapā*) as a secondary quality by means of a question: “How do the pressings (*savana*) become possessed of animals through these? This scriptural statement is for that purpose, because it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the performance of the omentum.

What follows from this? If that is so, it is not the case that the animal-ritual details (paśudharma) belong to the *savanīya* offerings by virtue of context (*prakaraṇa*), but rather they belong specifically to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice by virtue of sequence (*krama*).

What, then, is that scriptural injunction (*āmnāna*) regarding the horse? It is: "Having taken the *āśvina* cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted rope, one dedicates the *āgneya* *savanīya* animal.
If it is argued that, by this, there is an injunction of time for [the ritual] which has been displaced [to a later point], [we reply: no.
Not so, because it occupies only one part [of the whole].
This is not so; these [acts] are indeed for the sake of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] according to their sequence.
For the recitation at the time of the Āśvina [cup] is for the purpose of injunction;
in this case, if it were for the purpose of a subordinate quality (guṇa), the sentence would be split, but not if it is for the purpose of an injunction.
For it is not possible that there is an injunction regarding the time for that which has been postponed by the performance of the omentum-offering (*vapāpracāra*).

Since the substance of the omentum is but a single part [of the animal], the preliminary rite (*upākaraṇa*) would not be postponed because of its direct connection (*saṃnipātī*) with the consecration of the omentum.
If it is argued that this is so "for the sake of the purpose" (*arthena*), [we reply: no.
He said: "In that case, the time for one who has been elevated by the purpose (artha) is prescribed.
For it is heard in the scripture: 'Having covered [the wound] with his fist, he should remain seated after the extraction of the omentum until the offering of the omentum.

On the previous day, having covered the extraction of the omentum with his fist, he would not be able to remain seated for such a long duration; therefore, he must necessarily perform activities such as eating and moving about."
Not so, because it would contradict the Vedic revelation.

This is not so; for if it were thus, there would be a contradiction with the Veda, and there is no contradiction with the Veda, as [the fire] will be covered by a handful of grass or a handful of leaves.
Now, the term *āste* (he sits) occurs in the sense of sitting down;
but it does not necessarily refer only to sitting down, as it is also seen in the sense of remaining indifferent (*audāsīnya*).

For example: "Having taken hold of the domestic [fires], he remains," or "Having taken hold of the fields, he remains"—this occurs even without an explicit instruction, signifying the cessation of activity.

Here too, having covered [the fire] with a handful of grass or a handful of leaves, he will remain until the offering of the omentum (*vapā*). Therefore, the mention of the time of the Āśvina cup is for the purpose of an injunction; the characteristics of the animal sacrifice do not belong to the context of the *savanīya* offerings. Consequently, they are not for the sake of the *savanīya* offerings.
But because the preceding formative force has that [attainment] as its purpose, it is established from that position.

Since there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for the *savanīya* offerings, this must belong to the preceding *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice by virtue of the same reason previously stated—namely, *sthāna* (position).
This preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) is prompted by the animal sacrifice, not by the *jyotiṣṭoma*; for if it were prompted by the *jyotiṣṭoma*, there would be no distinction regarding the animals.
Indeed, the animal sacrifices themselves are capable of prompting the ritual duties because they possess their own *apūrva* (transcendental result), and they likewise possess their own *prakaraṇa*.
Therefore, by virtue of the sequence, these are the properties of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice];
this is also because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).
Furthermore, we see that the rites pertaining to the animal belong to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice.
Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*).

There is an indicative mark for this meaning: "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing; with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at the midday pressing"—this shows the animal-cake-offering.

Otherwise, if the procedure were identical for all animals, the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), being intended as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the two deities Agni and Soma, would—by virtue of its functional capacity—belong only to the *agnīṣomīya* animal and not to the *savanīya*, because those two deities are absent in the latter; and the scripture indeed indicates this.
Therefore, they are for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya*.
[The objection that] "there is no injunction for them as a subordinate element" is refuted.
This is a sutra that follows the previous word.

[The opponent] says: "Is it not the case that the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is for the purpose of covering the gaps? We say: "No. There is no injunction for it as a subordinate element; there is no injunction for it as being for the purpose of covering the gaps, for it has been stated that it is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

Therefore, they are for the purpose of consecrating the deity; therefore, since they serve the purpose of the Agniṣomīya [animal], the observation of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) at the Savanīya sacrifice is logically consistent, but not if they were common to both.
Therefore, the animal-ritual duties (paśudharma) are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya.
Because of the difference in time between the two milkings, the boiled milk (śṛta) would be unconnected [to the other].
There is the evening milking, and likewise there is the morning milking.
However, there are certain duties pertaining to the milking, such as the fetching of branches, the driving forth of the cows, the sprinkling [of water], the milking of the cows, and so forth.
Do these have the evening milking as their purpose, or do they serve the purpose of both?
What, then, is the prima facie position? The milk of those two [milking sessions] that has not been joined with the ritual properties should be boiled.
Why? Because they prescribe the sequence for the evening milking on the Upavasatha day, beginning with the fetching of the branch; and the evening milking takes place on that very day.
Therefore, by virtue of this sequence, the properties of the milking pertain to the purpose of the evening milking.
Or rather, because there is no distinction between the contexts, the rule regarding time applies to that which is connected with it.

For the context (*prakaraṇa*) is common to both; just as it applies to the curd, so too does it apply to the milk. Moreover, context is stronger than sequence (*krama*); therefore, the properties of the *doha* (milking) pertain to both. Furthermore, the recitation of the evening milking does not take place on the preceding day; when, then? On the following day.

How so? They prescribe thus: "The curds for Indra on the new moon day; the milk for Indra on the new moon day. For on the new moon day, both [substances] along with their auxiliary parts are enjoined.
This evening milking is performed on the previous day by implication; this is the very nature of curds, that what is commenced on the previous day is completed on the following day.
Therefore, the claim that the sequence of the evening milking is prescribed is simply not the case.
Therefore, the properties of *dohada* serve both purposes;
likewise, the mention of the cups (*graha*) occurs within another extraction (*savana*).
And the girdle [is used] because of the observation of an indicative mark.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, concerning which it is stated: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
In that context, a rope is mentioned, as well as the properties of the rope: "It is threefold," "it is made of darbha grass," and "it must be made of pounded [grass].
Regarding this, a doubt arises: are these properties common to both the rope of the Agni-Soma animal and the rope of the Savanīya animal, or do they belong to the rope of the Agni-Soma animal alone?
What is established? From the context, it is the rope of the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice].
That which is taught at a distance is unconnected with others because of its proximity [to the specific rite].

Regarding that which remains distant from the Jyotiṣṭoma—such as the Aṃśu and Adābhya cups mentioned in the section on the *aupasadānuvākyās*—there arises a doubt: should the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the cups prescribed for the Jyotiṣṭoma be performed here, or not? What is the prima facie view? They should not be performed, because they are not in proximity; just as, by the statement "he mixes the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa with milk," the mixing applies only to the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa and not to all of them.
Thus, this category of phenomena belongs only to those situated in the specific context (prakaraṇa), and not to all;
or rather, it is connected [to them] because the remainder has that as its purpose and is caused by it.
One should abide by the detailed explanation.

As for what was said—that "one mixes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup with milk"—that is appropriate because of the explicit scriptural statement regarding mixing; there, the context is set aside and a specific determination is made. But here it is the opposite: in that case, the context applies to all cups, while the sentence applies to specific ones; here, however, the sentence applies to all cups, while the context applies to specific ones.
Therefore, even for that which is not situated within a specific context, they are "dharmas," just as in the case of the subsidiary parts of the fire-altar (*agni*).
Without reference to the fire-altar (*agni*), it is said: "One lays down the *citriṇī* bricks; one lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks; one lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks.

However, within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the fire-altar, there exist properties of the bricks, such as: "One should make the brick unbroken and not black," and likewise, "One should join the bricks with ashes."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should these ritual duties (dharmas) be performed for those [rites] recited outside of a specific context, or not? What is the prima facie view? They should not be performed. Why? Because they are not in proximity (asaṃnidhāna). To this, it is replied: a subsidiary of the fire-altar (agnyaṅga) of such a kind should be treated exactly like that, just as in the case of the cups (grahas).
For a sentence is stronger than context,
since these bricks serve the purpose of the fire-altar;
because they are unequal, the occasional rite would not have the same injunction.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, it is heard: "If he should officiate for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya, and if he should desire him to consume Soma, having fetched Nyagrodha shoots, having crushed them, and having mixed them with curds, he should give that to him as the portion to be consumed, not the Soma.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are properties of the Soma, such as measuring, bringing down, purchasing, pressing, and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: are these properties common to both the Soma and the fruit-cup (phalacamasa), or are they properties of the Soma [only], while the fruit-cup [partakes of them] because it is a modification (vikāra) of it?

The purpose of this discussion regarding the subject matter is to determine whether those who desire specific qualities (guṇakāma) are entitled to participate. What is the prima facie view? That they are equally entitled to the injunction because there is no division of the context. To this, it is replied: an incidental rite (*naimittika*) of this kind would not have the same injunction as the primary one. Why? Because of inequality; the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is not equal to the *soma*. The *soma* is prescribed as a constant (*nityavat*), whereas the fruit-cup is incidental (*naimittika*).

What follows from this? If it were so, even the ritual details (*dharma*) prescribed as if they were permanent could not be treated as if they were non-permanent. If they were common [to both], then a purpose not previously undertaken would have to be enjoined there. Furthermore, the *phalacamasa* (the fruit-cup) is occasional; it adopts the ritual details of the *soma*. In that case, since the ritual details would already be common [to both], they would be said to be "redundant" (*dvirukta*).
Therefore, they do not have the same ritual application;
and a substitute is likewise [not of the same application].
In the same way, because the purpose is one and the same.

This is not so—the substitute does not have an identical injunction; it would be like that [original], just as it is heard in scripture, and there is no relationship of original and modification (prakṛti-vikāra).
Why? Because the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*) is the cause for the properties of rice to apply to the individual instance of rice.
And it is not heard in scripture that the nature of *nīvāra* takes the place of the nature of rice; therefore, there is no relationship of original and modification.
How, then, do the ritual properties (dharmas) exist in wild rice (nīvāra)?
It is said: those individual grains of rice (vrīhi-vyakti) which are delimited by the nature of rice exist in the wild rice;
for their sake, those properties are performed. And this rule applies equally to those individuals and to other individuals belonging to the genus rice.
What is their equality? It is that both are characterized by the nature of rice (*vrīhitva*).
Therefore, they are subject to the same injunction (*samānavidhāna*), and because they are not defined by separate scriptural rules (*aśāstralakṣaṇatvāt*).
For this reason as well, there is no relationship of original and modification between the substitute and that which is directly enjoined in the scripture.
Why? Because the substitute is characterized by its purpose; indeed, a substitute is employed for the sake of the purpose.
