And it cannot be understood from the purpose alone that "the state of being *nīvāra* takes the place of the state of being *vrīhi*."
Therefore, there is no relationship of original and modification between the substitute and that which is directly enjoined;
thus, the mention of the quality is for the purpose of restriction.
But the sacrificial sessions (saṃsthās) have identical injunctions, because there is no distinction in their context.
There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein the terminuses (saṃsthās) are recited as the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, and the Atirātra.
In that context, there are ritual duties (dharmas) such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others.

Regarding these, a doubt arises: are the ritual duties beginning with the Dīkṣaṇīyā stated with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma in all its terminuses, or are they intended specifically for the Agniṣṭoma terminus?
What is established? That the injunction is common to all sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*).

Why? Because there is no distinction in the context; there is no specific feature in the context by which it could be known that [the injunction] refers specifically to the *agniṣṭoma* terminus. Therefore, the terminuses have a common injunction.
And the designation is as if they were equal.

Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "At the Agniṣṭoma, one should sacrifice a goat dedicated to Agni; at the Ukthya, a second [goat] dedicated to Indra and Agni; at the Ṣoḍaśin, a third, a ram dedicated to Indra. This observation of a second and a third animal is consistent with their being subject to the same rule (*sāmānavidhya*). For in the Ukthya, there are two occasions: the Agniṣṭoma-stotra and the Ukthya-stotra; in that case, there are two contingent offerings (*naimittika*), namely the animal for Agni and the one for Indra and Agni. Therefore, the observation of a second animal is appropriate there. The same applies to the Ṣoḍaśin and the Atirātra.

If, however, there were a relationship of original material and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), then the *āgneya* [offering], which is obtained by extension (*atideśa*) from the *aindrāgna* and others that are explicitly heard in the scripture,
would be sublated; in that case, the observation of a second [offering] and so forth would not be possible, yet it does occur.
Therefore, the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites are the properties (*dharmas*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma in all its states;
however, when there is a connection with specific desires, they belong to the modified forms (*vikāras*), because that [desire] is common to the permanent form.

This is not so; they do not have an identical injunction. What then? The Ukthya and other forms are modifications of the sacrifice; for the ritual duties such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others are prescribed with the Agniṣṭoma form as the established basis.
Why? Because the Ukthya and other forms are heard of in connection with specific desires.

"One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya; one desiring vigor should praise with the Ṣoḍaśin; one desiring progeny should sacrifice with the Atirātra. When an optional (kāmya) accessory is heard in scripture, it enters by modifying the permanent (nitya) purpose.

How so? Because in such optional cases, the accomplishment of the fruit results from the accessory itself: "One desiring cattle should take the Ukthya" means that one should take it in such a way that cattle come to be, not because one desires the Jyotiṣṭoma, nor because one desires the taking of the Ukthya. This is the meaning.
How so?
In that case, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) must necessarily be expected; because of its proximity, it is understood that the procedure belongs to the obligatory rite (*nitya*).
Now, why is it not common [to both]? Because it is enjoined as if it were obligatory: whenever there is a *Jyotiṣṭoma*, at that very time there is the initiation (*dīkṣā*).

But when one desires cattle at the Jyotiṣṭoma, then there are the Ukthya terminuses; the ritual duties (dharmas) of the Jyotiṣṭoma must always be performed, yet at one time the Ukthya terminuses occur. In that case, the duties of the Jyotiṣṭoma must always be performed, and it was previously stated that these are for the sake of the Ukthya and other terminuses. This contradicts the subsequent [statement] if they are not always for the sake of the Ukthya and others. Or, if they are for the sake of the Ukthya and others but not always, both [positions] are mutually contradictory. Therefore, [the duty] is not common to all.

If that which is non-eternal were to have an eternal scriptural injunction, then that non-eternal act would be performed as if it were eternal, and in that case, the eternal scriptural injunction would be sublated.
Therefore, [the rule applies] to the Jyotiṣṭoma established as an eternal rite, not to the optional forms such as the Ukthya and others.
Alternatively, because of the double mention, they will belong to the archetype (prakṛti).
But because of the scriptural statement, there is a combination.

Now, as for what was said—that the mention of a second and a third [offering] is possible only if there is a common injunction (samānavidhi) and not otherwise—that will be a mere statement (vacana), not an actual observation (darśana).
For in the Ukthya sacrifice, a second offering to Indra-Agni is enjoined; likewise, in the Ṣoḍaśin, a third offering to Indra is enjoined.
Furthermore, this is because of the prohibition of the previous indicative marks (liṅgas).
From this also we see that there is a relationship of material cause and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*).

Why? Because of the negation of the previous indicative marks (*liṅga*). For if [the *agniṣṭoma*] were the original form, then the observation of the absence of the oblation—namely, "if it is an *ukthya*, he anoints the enclosing-sticks, he does not offer"—would not occur; for when the occasion has arisen, there would be uniformity of rule (*sāmānavidhya*) due to the authority of the scriptural statement.
The designation of one [among many] is due to a specific quality.
Now, as for what was said regarding "designation":
this designation by a quality not pertaining to it belongs to the very same person who is qualified, according to the reasoning already stated;
and the mention of the Agniṣṭoma is a mere restatement (anuvāda).
Due to the distinction of context, it is not connected with the primary [sacrifice].
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the properties of the sacrificial grass, as well as the altar (*vedi*) and the properties of the altar.
In this regard, there is a doubt: do the sacrificial grass and its properties, and so forth, belong to the primary sacrifice alone, or to both the subsidiaries and the primary?

What, then, is the prima facie view? Because of the specific context (*prakaraṇa*), that which is not specifically connected [to a particular part] belongs to the primary; thus, properties of this kind pertain to the primary alone.

Why? Because of the distinction of context; for the context belongs to the primary acts, not to the subsidiaries, and their connection is through the context; therefore, it pertains to the primary act.
Or rather, [the subsidiaries belong] to all [the primary acts], because being a subsidiary is not occasioned by that [specific primary].

These ritual properties (dharmas) belong to all subsidiaries (aṅga) and primaries (pradhāna); here, subsidiarity does not arise from the context (prakaraṇa), for that is characterized by utility (upakāra).
Whatever benefits something is subsidiary to it, and these properties benefit all subsidiaries and primaries.

How is this understood? From the syntactical statement (vākya): "He places the oblations on the altar. From the statement, only the oblations in general are understood; the primary oblations [are understood] from the context.
And a direct statement (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*); therefore, [the rule] "he places the sacrificial offerings on the *barhis* grass" applies.
[The opponent] says: "If context is set aside by a direct statement, then in common worldly usage these ritual properties (*dharma*) would also be said to belong to the *barhis* grass.
What is the fault in that? It follows that these properties must be performed everywhere."
It is said: from the context, it is understood that these are indeed auxiliaries to the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices;
therefore, they should not be performed in worldly (secular) rites. [Objection: "But [they may apply] even remotely?"

In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña as well, [the act] would be connected with the properties of the sacrificial grass (barhis), for that [offering] also takes place upon the sacrificial grass, and there is a purpose for it to be with the sacrificial grass.
That too would be like the properties prescribed for distant [rites].
But it is not so, for that statement is for the sake of that [specific purpose].

The sacrificial grass (barhis) for that [Piṇḍapitṛyajña] does not possess these ritual properties (dharma), for the single sentence [prescribing them] is connected with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therefore, the ritual properties are auxiliaries to the Darśapūrṇamāsa, and they apply only where there is something for the sake of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, not elsewhere.
Consequently, these properties will not belong to the sacrificial grass of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).

There is an indicative mark (liṅga) that shows this; it says: "He indeed sprinkles the *dhruvā* first, for from there he is about to offer the two initial *ājyabhāga* portions. This demonstrates that the purpose of the sprinkling is for the sake of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
However, because of the connection with a fruit, [the action] is connected to the master as the primary element.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the shaving of hair and beard, milk-vows, and ascetic practices are prescribed.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: do they serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, or do they serve the purpose of the principal rite alone? What, then, is the prima facie view? That they serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite; this is established by the previous reasoning, as well as because of their connection with the desire to perform [the sacrifice].
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "Thirty-six steps long toward the east, twenty-four at the front, thirty at the rear—this much we are able [to prepare].
Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this altar for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal rite, or is it for the sake of the principal rite alone?
What, then, is the prima facie view? It is for the sake of the principal rite, because of its connection with the desire to perform [the sacrifice].
What is the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)? It is the thought, "I shall be able to do this much.

This [desire] is heard for the sake of that which is desired to be done—namely, "we shall be able to perform this"—and it is the primary action (*pradhāna*) that is desired to be performed, not the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*).
For the primary action possesses the fruit, whereas the auxiliaries do not.
By means of such a designation.
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; regarding them, it is heard in scripture: "One should touch the Pūrṇamāsī with the Caturhotṛ formula, and the Amāvāsyā with the Pañcahotṛ formula.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is the touching for the sake of both the subsidiaries and the principal, or for the sake of the principal alone?
What, then, is the prima facie view? It is for the sake of the principal, because these are names of the principal sacrifices—namely, "Pūrṇamāsī" and "Amāvāsyā."
Therefore, there is the touching of the principal [offering];
since the scriptural statement of the fruit applies to that which is joined with it, there should be a desire to perform all [the rites].
Because it denotes qualities, the denotation [of a word] pertains to all objects.

As for what was said—that because the words *paurṇamāsī* and *amāvāsyā* denote the primary [sacrifices], there is the touching (*abhimarśana*) of the primary oblations—this is not so; there would also be the touching of the subsidiary oblations. Why? Because of the mention of a quality (*guṇa*); for the touching is designated as a "quality" (*guṇa*).

What is that designation? It is that which calls it *abhimarśana* (touching). Since the words *paurṇamāsīm* and *amāvāsyām* end in the accusative case, it follows that "the *abhimarśana* must be performed for the sake of the *Paurṇamāsī*," and "the *abhimarśana* must be performed for the sake of the *Amāvāsyā*. Therefore, wherever its performance benefits either the *Paurṇamāsī* or the *Amāvāsyā*, there it should be performed.
Whatever is connected with the *Paurṇamāsī* or the *Amāvāsyā*, whether directly or through an indirect channel (*praṇāḍyā*), the *abhimarśana* performed in those instances benefits them both.
Therefore, [the rites] must be performed for both the primary oblations and the subsidiary oblations;
however, the initiation fee belongs to the primary sacrifice because of a specific scriptural injunction.
And because cessation is observed.
It demonstrates the cessation of the initiations.

How so? [The text says]: "O Adhvaryu, since you have purchased the animal, what is its initiation? "That which he offers the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ-oblation—that is its initiation. Even in the absence of an actual initiation, there is this statement.
Therefore, the initiatory fee belongs to the subsidiaries.
Likewise, the sacrificial altar belongs to the sacrificial post.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, [as stated]: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, with reference to the sacrificial post (yūpa), it is heard: "The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt; if one were to fix it within the altar, it would burn him up; if outside the altar, it would not be secured. Therefore, he fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar; thus it is both secured and does not burn him up."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the altar (*vedi*) enjoined as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) by the phrase "within the altar" (*antarvedi*), or is it stated for the purpose of defining a location, namely that "half [of the post] is within the altar and half is outside the altar"?
How is it a subordinate part of the post, or how is it a definition of location?

If the connection between the half of the post and the interior of the altar is intended, then the post must be made connected to the altar; in that case, it is by way of being a subordinate part of the post.
Now, that place where half of the area being measured is within the altar and half is outside is taught; therefore, it is a designation by way of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*).
Or rather, it refers to the location itself, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the word *āśiṣya*.
Or rather, it is merely a location that is indicated by the word "altar" (*vedi*), and not the altar as a subordinate part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Why? Because of its syntactic unity with what is not to be enjoined; for the syntactic unity with the statement, "He fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar," exists only if there is an indication of a location. If, on the other hand, the mention of the altar were made because it is a subordinate part of the post, then the mention of "outside the altar" would not be something to be enjoined. If the altar were being taught as a subordinate part of the post, then the utterance of "half outside the altar" would serve no purpose whatsoever.
Furthermore, if one were to prescribe even the location outside the altar as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
Therefore, when the altar is designated as a subordinate part of the sacrificial post, the term "outside the altar" must by no means be prescribed.

If, however, it is a designation of a location (*deśalakṣaṇā*), then since a specific location is being designated, the word *bahirvedi* must necessarily be stated; for if it were not stated, it would be understood that the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is in some place whatsoever within the interior of the altar (*vedi*). But when the word *bahirvedi* is heard, that location where, as it is being measured, one half is inside the altar and one half is outside the altar is intended to be designated. And since that [location] cannot be designated without the word *bahirvedi*, it must necessarily be taught.

Therefore, it is called "characterized by place" (*deśalakṣaṇā*), because of the statement regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses: "They recite those [verses] as the *sāmidhenīs* for the two *havirdhāna* carts. Thus, these are the *sāmidhenīs*.
Or rather, the direct perception of the Soma's functional activity consists merely in its location.

Now, why is it that the following connection is not accepted: "The connection with the *sāmidhenī* verses belongs to that very *havirdhāna* cart in which they press the Soma"? This cannot be so; for in this way, two distinct matters would have to be enjoined: the connection with the *havirdhāna* in general and the connection with a specific *havirdhāna*. In that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Therefore, the connection is not thus;
and the designation is likewise.
And the designation is likewise exactly as we have taught in our reasoning: "The Havirdhāna shed is for the sake of Soma.
Since the fruit of the scripture accrues to the performer, because he is characterized by that [action], therefore it should be performed by oneself.

But in the case of renunciation, because it is the primary act, the one who performs the subsidiary rites is the one who performs the primary act; therefore, it may be performed by another or by oneself.
There is primacy in the act of relinquishment (utsarga). How so? He who performs the relinquishment has thereby accomplished everything.
How so? Relinquishment is the purchase (parikraya); by means of it, all [the officiants] perform the infinite [rites].
Therefore, for one who performs the purchase [of services], everything becomes as if done by himself.
Consequently, he should perform the mere act of relinquishment himself; the remainder may be performed by another or by himself.
Or rather, it must be another, because of the scriptural injunction regarding purchase and because of the prohibition against [acting for] one's own self.
The performer of the remainder must be someone else. Why? Because hiring is prescribed;
when many types of persons are applicable, hiring is the fixed rule.
Therefore, all ritual acts must be performed by those who have been hired for a fee.
Furthermore, hiring oneself is a contradiction;

for if one were to perform them oneself, the act would be performed by one who has not been hired, which would render the scriptural injunction regarding hiring meaningless, or else it would have to be admitted that its purpose is merely transcendental (adṛṣṭa).
Therefore, the remaining ritual acts should be performed by others who have been hired;
however, by performing the *utsarga* (the final disposal) oneself, everything becomes performed by oneself.
In that case, the number of performers would be determined by the requirements of the purpose, as there is no restrictive rule due to the absence of specification.
In that case, regarding the duties to be performed by those hired, there would be no restriction on the number of performers.
Why? Because there is no distinction; no specific rule concerning the number of performers is prescribed in the sacred tradition.
Their number is determined by the purpose: one should select as many as are required to accomplish that particular procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Or rather, because of the difference in scriptural injunctions, there should be separate [offerings] for each name.
As many as there are names of performers heard in connection with ritual actions—so many distinct [actions] are to be chosen; and these are the hearings of the names:
"The Adhvaryu divides the cakes," "The Pratiprasthātṛ offers the Manthin," "The Neṣṭṛ leads the wife forward," and "The Unnetṛ draws up the cups."

Likewise: the *prastotṛ* chants the *prastāva*, the *udgātṛ* sings the *udgītha*, the *pratihartṛ* performs the *pratihāra*, the *subrahmaṇya* recites the *subrahmaṇyā*, the *hotṛ* recites the *prātaranuvāka*, the *maitrāvaruṇa* issues the directions (*preṣya*) and recites the responses (*anucāha*), the *acchāvāka* offers the sacrifice (*yajati*), and the *grāvastotrīya* recites the verses.
There is need for these many ritual acts; therefore, those [priests] must necessarily be chosen to perform these as prescribed by the sacred texts, for no other entity exists apart from these.
Even that which is not taught by direct statement is understood through its name (*samākhyā*).
"Therefore, one should choose from among these many.
If it is argued that this is because there is a distinction between the ritual acts (*karman*) for each [deity], [we reply: no.
For indeed, in the case of non-arising...

This is not so; for at the time of the origin of persons—that is, when persons are being produced—their designations differ: "he chooses a Brāhmaṇa," "he chooses a Hotṛ," "he chooses an Udgātṛ," "he chooses an Adhvaryu," and so forth. Therefore, there is a need for those who bear such names in the performance of the ritual, and they must necessarily be chosen. Consequently, the mention of them in the act of choosing is not an injunction.
Because there is no purpose [for it], it is not a mere restatement (anuvāda).
For the Veda would not say "so many [priests] are to be chosen," as that would be entirely meaningless;
moreover, this [text] is capable of conveying a specific number.
Therefore, this statement is for the purpose of making known that specific number which pertains to them;
consequently, sixteen performers are to be chosen, and the Soma sacrifice should likewise have that many performers.
The same applies to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices as well.
And the *camasādhvaryu*s [are distinct from the priests], because they are designated by means of them.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are the Camasādhvaryus, as it is said: "One should choose the Camasādhvaryus.
Regarding them, there is a doubt: are they any one of these [already mentioned], or are they different from these?
What, then, is the prima facie view? Since only this many have been enumerated, they must be any one of these very ones.
This being the position, we reply: there should be other *camasādhvaryu*s, distinct from those [already enumerated].

Why? Because of their designation by them; for these are designated by those who have been enumerated—namely, "the *camasādhvaryu*s of the central performers" (*madhyataḥkārin*) and "the *camasādhvaryu*s of the *hotraka* priests.
Moreover, because the plural is heard in the original injunction of their appointment.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: is there no restriction—whether one, two, or many—or must there be many? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) being that there is no restriction, it is stated in reply: "There must be many. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of plurality at their origin; for in the originative injunction "the Camasādhvaryus," there is a mention of plurality. Therefore, there must be many. Furthermore, the number ten is established by the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
And [the word] *śamitṛ* [is distinct] because of the difference in the verbal root.

There is the *śamitṛ*—the injunction "one should initiate the *śamitṛ*. Is he one among those already mentioned, or is he someone other than them? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since he is mentioned in the context of their selection, he must be one among them; this being the position, it is said in reply: "And the *śamitṛ*, because of the difference in designation. The designation differs, such that "this rite is to be performed by one with this specific name"; therefore, one who bears that specific name must be produced [for the occasion].
From the mention of this [number], an increase in the number [of priests] is understood; therefore, there should be another *śamitṛ*.

Moreover, there is the statement: "The *kloman* and the *vaikartana* belong to the *śamitṛ*; he should give them to a Brāhmaṇa if he be a Brāhmaṇa"—this implies a suspicion that [the *śamitṛ*] might not be a Brāhmaṇa, which is not applicable in the case of a priest (*ṛtvij*). Furthermore, because of the context, there is no connection with the original injunction [for such a role].
And the Upagas [are included] because of the observation of their characteristic marks.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are those called *upagās*. Since they indicate an increase in number through a difference in terminology, it follows that they must be distinct from the Adhvaryu and the others; this being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: some of them must be among those very same [priests]. Why? Because they are enumerated within the original injunction (*utpatti*) and because the term is etymological (*yaugika*).
There is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this: "The Adhvaryu should not sing as an *upagā*. If they were different from these [priests], he would not have prohibited the Adhvaryu.

Because [the act] has not been attained; since, however, he prohibits it, we understand from this that it refers to one of those specifically mentioned in the context of its origin. But the seller is different, because his action is not enjoined.

There is a seller of Soma; regarding this, there is a doubt: is he one of the [officiating priests] such as the Adhvaryu and others, or is he other than them? What is the prima facie view? Since they are enumerated, it follows that he is one of them. To this we reply: "But the seller should be another. For the selling is not enjoined, whereas the buying is enjoined; the selling occurs there only by implication. Furthermore, the Adhvaryu and others are appointed to perform the constituent acts of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, but the selling of the Jyotiṣṭoma is not heard of in the scripture.
Therefore, he is not one of the Adhvaryu and others.
All [the priests] possess the status of officiating priest (ṛtvij) because there is no distinction regarding their performance of ritual duties.
Regarding these persons who are mentioned in connection with the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, are they all officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or only some among them? What is the prima facie view? All of them.
Why? Because of their functional activity; since all of them perform the means for the sacrifice, therefore all of them "sacrifice" during the ritual.

Those who sacrifice at the seasonal sacrifices (ṛtu) are the officiating priests (ṛtvij); no specific distinction is adopted such that "only these sacrifice at the seasons" would define them as ṛtvijas, while "these do not" would exclude others.
Therefore, all [participants] possess the status of being ṛtvijas.
But is it not the case that an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā) is heard in the text: "For the Saumya Adhvara, the sacrificial rite, there are seventeen ṛtvijas"?
It is said: since there are many faults in [interpreting this as] an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), this must be an analytical statement (avayutyavāda);
or rather, it is not [an exclusive specification] because of the enumeration.

Nor indeed are all [the priests]. Why? Because of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyāna*). For it is heard thus: "In the Soma-sacrifice, the ritual performance (*yajñakratu*), there are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). This is not an injunction (*vidhi*), because a greater number [of priests] is already established; nor is it a restatement (*anuvāda*), because it would serve no purpose.
And if it were not even an exclusive specification, it would be utterly meaningless.

He says: But surely, even when the additional priests are being excluded, the exclusion does not apply [to them], for they do not fail to sacrifice at the proper time; nor would those sacrificing at the proper time cease to be *ṛtvij*s. It is replied:

True, it is not that they are not connected with the word *ṛtvij* because of the exclusion; rather, by the force of the exclusion, they do not perform the duties of an *ṛtvij*. What, then, is the duty of an *ṛtvij*? Namely: "The *ṛtvij*s fast," "He chooses the *ṛtvij*s," and "He gives the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the *ṛtvij*s."

He asks: "What is the duty of the *ṛtvij*s (sacrificial priests), how could that not apply to some who possess the word *ṛtvij*? It is replied: "In that case, this word *ṛtvij* is of two kinds: one based on the performance of the seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtuyajana*), and one based on being chosen and supported (*varaṇabharaṇa*). Among these, the application of the term based on the sacrifice would be redundant; therefore, the term is understood as being based on being chosen and supported. He asks: "But surely this results in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): those who are *ṛtvij*s are the ones to be chosen, and those who are chosen are the *ṛtvij*s; thus there is mutual dependence."

It is said in reply: For the meaning of "one should choose the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīte*) is not that those who are already officiating priests are to be chosen. How then? It means that by the act of choosing, they become officiating priests; in this way, the use of the accusative case will be appropriate, as in the expression "one chooses the Adhvaryu. Furthermore, the act of choosing will thus serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*).
If it is argued that [it is known] by means of a fortnight;

If you think thus—that this is stated according to the aforementioned position, whereas according to the position of partial application (*avayutyavāda*), there are seventeen priests—then that must be refuted; it is not the case that all [of them] lack qualification.

This is not so; for here the statement is not intended to apply to all persons, such that there would be a partial exclusion (*avayutyavāda*) with respect to them. A partial exclusion occurs where a higher number is mentioned, as in the case of the twelve-potsherd cake where it is said, "that which is eight-potsherd"; but here no higher number is mentioned. Therefore, this is not a partial exclusion.
But there is a restrictive rule regarding the sacrificial fees, because of their connection with the Vedic revelation.
It has been established that there are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Now this is considered: who are those seventeen? What is the prima facie view? It is ignorance [of their specific identities].

This being the case, we reply: there is indeed a restriction by means of the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), because of the connection with the Vedic text; they should be restricted through their association with the sacrificial fees. For it is thus recorded in scripture: "He gives the sacrificial fee to the priests. Having stated this, in a subsequent passage concerning the sequence of giving the sacrificial fees, specific individuals such as the Brahman and others are heard of: "He gives first to the Āgnīdhra, then to the Brahman, then to so-and-so and so-and-so"—only certain specific persons are mentioned. Those who are thus mentioned are the priests (*ṛtvij*); therefore, no others besides them can be [intended].
Thus, the restriction is by means of the sacrificial fees.
And having stated their status as sacrificers, because of the prescription of initiation for them.

Having stated, "Those who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are the sacrificers (*yajamāna*)," the text demonstrates the initiation (*dīkṣā*) in a subsequent passage concerning the sequence of initiation for the Brahman and the others.
How so? "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the *Gṛhapati*, initiates the Brahman; then the Udgātṛ; then the Hotṛ.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated him, initiates the 'half-sharers': the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin of the Brahman, the Prastotṛ of the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa of the Hotṛ."

Then the Neṣṭṛ, having initiated him, initiates the third group: the Āgnīdhra for the Brahman, the Pratihartṛ for the Udgātṛ, and the Acchāvāka for the Hotṛ. Then the Unnetṛ, having initiated him, initiates the fourth group: the Potṛ for the Brahman, the Subrahmaṇya for the Udgātṛ, and the Grāvastut for the Hotṛ.
Then another Brāhmaṇa initiates him, or a religious student (brahmacārī) sent by his teacher.
And initiation (*dīkṣā*) is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer;
therefore, there are seventeen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), beginning with the Brahman,
because they share the commonality of performing the ritual action, with the master (*svāmin*) as the seventeenth.
They are for one's own purpose because they have been employed, and the fires are [for their own purpose] because they have their own specific time.
It has been established that there are seventeen priests for the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, including the master.

Now, a doubt arises here: should all human duties be performed by them, and all fire-related duties by the fires, such as the Gārhapatya and others; or is there some restriction? What, then, is the prima facie view? They are for all purposes because they have been appointed, and the fires are for their own specific times; therefore, those who have been chosen should be available for every human duty, and the fires for every fire-related duty.

Why? Because they are required by those ritual acts; their individual mention is a restatement (anuvāda) [of what is already established], since the fires have their own time and are for the sake of all purposes—this has been understood.
"Because of that connection, there should be a restriction of the ritual act, since the connection must be purposeful."

Through that connection—that is, through the connection with a specific person—it would be determined: those [rites] which are designated by a particular person must be performed by him; in this way, their connection with a person will be meaningful.
Thus, the *ādhvaryava* is to be performed by the *adhvaryu*, the *hautra* by the *hotṛ*, and the *audgātra* by the *udgātṛ*.
This is the specification [of duties] based on the designation of the instruction.
Is this the general rule—that everything declared by those who have declared it must be performed?
We say: no; for there is a specific direction based on that instruction and because of a particular designation.
As for the instruction: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the directions and recites after [the Hotṛ]."
The designation is "potrīyā" and "neṣṭrīyā";
this is an exception to the [general rule of] designation.
And there is a scriptural indication to that effect.
The recitation of the *praiṣas* belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa, because of the direct instruction.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, according to the text: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, they recite: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest issues the directions and also recites the invitatory verses. In this regard, a doubt arises: should the Maitrāvaruṇa perform all recitations and all directions, or only those cases where a direction follows a recitation?
What, then, is the prima facie position? [He should be the Maitrāvaruṇa] at all recitations (*anuvacana*), because there is no distinction;
for no specific distinction is adopted such that "the Maitrāvaruṇa is for this recitation, but not for that.
Therefore, he should be the Maitrāvaruṇa at all recitations and at all directions (*praiṣa*).
Or rather, it is the section concerning the *puro'nuvākyā*, because of its proximity to the *praiṣa*.

Or rather, the Maitrāvaruṇa priest should recite the *puro'nuvākya*. Why? Because the Maitrāvaruṇa acts where both the command (*praiṣa*) and the *anuṣākya* are spoken together; he does not act where there is only the *anuṣākya*, nor where there is only the command. He should be present only where both are combined.

For they prescribe that [function] for the two combined, stating: "Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa gives the direction and also recites after"; from the word "and" (ca), it is understood that this refers to the two combined.
This is because the Hotṛ is seen [to perform it] during the Prātaranuvāka.
For this reason as well, we see that the Maitrāvaruṇa is not present at all recitations (*anuvacana*s).
Why? Because [the text] indicates the Hotṛ in relation to the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*).
How so? "When he should overhear the Hotṛ while he is reciting the morning litany, then the Adhvaryu should take [the draught]. Thus it is said.
Therefore, the Maitrāvaruṇa does not [participate] in all recitations;
rather, the Camasādhvaryus [participate] in the cups, because of their designation.
There are the cup-attendants (camasādhvaryus), and regarding them there is a doubt: should the cup-attendants offer the cups, or should the Adhvaryu?
We say: the cup-attendants. Why? Because they perform the duties of the Adhvaryu with respect to the cups; therefore, they are called "cup-attendants," and thus it is they who should offer.
Or rather, the Adhvaryu [should do it], because that is the logical rule.

Or rather, the Adhvaryu himself should offer the oblation; for this is the logical rule: that which is an Adhvaryu-function must be performed by the Adhvaryu, and the oblation is an Adhvaryu-function; therefore, the Adhvaryu should offer it. [Objection:
But surely the Camasādhvaryus will offer it, because of the specific designation "Camasādhvaryus.
[Reply: No, it is said in response: they are called Camasādhvaryus because they act like Adhvaryus with respect to the cups (camasa).
If the Adhvaryu offers with them, then the Camasādhvaryus must also offer with them;
if the Camasādhvaryus offer, not the Adhvaryu,
then those Camasādhvaryus would not be like him.
Therefore, they should not offer oblations;
for another [practice] is observed in the case of the *camasa* cup.
If they are unable [to do so], they should rely upon them.

Now, how is the designation "Camasādhvaryus" (Chamberlain-Priests) to be understood? It is said: they should be recognized as such in cases of incapacity; when the Adhvaryu is unable to offer the oblation because he is otherwise occupied, then, by virtue of the designation, they shall offer it.
Because of the instruction of the Veda, as before, when there is a difference in the Veda, they should act according to the instruction.
There is a sacrifice called Śyena prescribed in the Audgātra [section], and the Vājapeya in the Ādhvaryava [section].

In this regard, a doubt arises: should the constituent elements (padārtha) of the Śyena be performed by the Udgātṛs alone, and those of the Vājapeya by the Adhvaryus alone; or rather, in both cases, by all the officiating priests (ṛtvij)?

What is established? [The view] from the instruction of the Veda, meaning from the designation (*samākhyāna*), as before; just as, because of the designation "Adhvaryava," the Adhvaryu performs the ritual items, even so, when there is a difference between Vedas, they should be performed according to the instruction: whatever is taught in a Veda designated by a certain [priest], its ritual items must be performed by that very [priest].
That [Veda] is taught there together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*).
Therefore, in the Śyena sacrifice, the ritual items are to be performed by the Udgātṛs, and in the Vājapeya, by the Adhvaryus.

Or rather, because of that [Vedic] mention, it would be one's own duty (svadharma) by virtue of the force of the qualification; thus, it remains unmanifested along with its subsidiaries in the remainder.

Because of that inclusion—that is, because of the inclusion of the archetypal (prakṛti) properties—the own-property (svadharma) would be connected with its own properties obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer). It is heard [in scripture] that "one should perform it together with the subsidiaries by virtue of the power of the *codaka*"; and those subsidiaries, which exist in the Jyotiṣṭoma, are required there.
In that regard, in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are no priests; therefore, this [new rite] has syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with them.
But surely, the name (*samākhyā*) is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the *codaka* is inferential (*ānumānika*).
It is said: True, the designation is indeed perceptible, but it is worldly.

In that case, one would have to infer a Vedic word and then establish syntactic unity with it; however, in the case of the *codaka* (the general transfer rule), there is syntactic unity with a directly perceived procedure (*itikartavyatā*) studied in a remote context.
Therefore, the *codaka* is more powerful.
As for what was stated—that it is "due to the name" (samākhyāna)—to that it is replied:
the unmanifested [element] will be designated by the name in the remainder.
Regarding that ritual item which is not obtained through the extended application (codaka), there will be a restrictive rule based on its name.
Just as in the Śyena sacrifice, [the text] says "piercing with thorns," meaning the Udgātṛs will pierce; and in the Vājapeya, it says "striking with bags of chaff," meaning the Adhvaryus will strike.
The hiring of priests is the work of the master, because the ritual action exists for his sake.
There is the matter of purchase: in the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are one hundred and twelve [cows], and in the Darśapūrṇamāsa, there is the *anvāhārya* rice.

In this regard, a doubt arises: are the priests to be purchased by the Adhvaryu, or by the master (the sacrificer)? What is the prima facie view? Based on the technical name (*samākhyāna*), it follows that they are to be purchased by the Adhvaryu; to this we reply: purchasing is the duty of the master.
It is understood that he performs it himself.
Why? Because the ritual action is for his sake; for the sacrificer desires the fruit, and whoever desires the fruit must perform it himself.
If he hires others, then it is understood that he himself performs everything.
Now, if one does not purchase [the Soma], one should not perform everything;
therefore, because of the scriptural statement, "The owner purchases [it]," the other [rites] would belong [to the sacrificer].
Is this the general rule? No, it is said: "In the case of others, it would be so because of a specific scriptural statement.
Where there is a scriptural statement, there the purchase (parikraya) takes place by virtue of the authority of that statement, as in:
"He who should lay down this brick should give three boons."
But the ritual preparations (saṃskāras) would be restricted according to the Veda, based on the capacity of the person, just like the ritual acts themselves.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "He shaves his hair and beard, he cleans his teeth, he cuts his nails, he bathes. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are such acts to be performed by the Adhvaryu, or by the sacrificer? What is the prima facie view? They should be performed by the Adhvaryu; for purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are restricted according to the Veda, because of the designation (samākhyā), just like other ritual actions. Just as other items prescribed in a particular Veda are performed by the person designated by that Veda's name, so too are these [acts].
But the acts performed by the sacrificer [are included], because he is the primary agent, just like the ritual action itself.
Or rather, they should be performed by the sacrificer.
Why? Because the person is the primary factor.
How is the person the primary factor? It is understood that the fruit of the action is intended for the agent; therefore, [the rites] produce in the person the capacity to perform the ritual act.

Nor does anyone purchase men for the sake of that performance of action by which capacity is produced; rather, one purchases them for the sake of the desired objects. Whatever capacity belongs to someone through whatever means, that must be performed by that very person, just like the primary object (*karmavat*). Just as in the case of the primary object, the purposes of the sacrificer accrue to the man [employed], so it is here as well.
And because of the designation.

And there is the designation of the *parasmaipada* [ending]—as in "he anoints him" (*tam abhyanakti*) and "he anoints with a reed-shaft" (*śareṣīkayānakti*). It is understood that another person performs the anointing (*añjana*) and the subsequent smearing (*abhyañjana*) for the sacrificer;
thus, it is indicated as being subordinate (*guṇatva*).
And because [the object] exists in relation to the injunction (*codanā*).
By "injunction" (codanā), we mean the *apūrva*—the unseen potency; with respect to that *apūrva*, the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) are prescribed.

Since they are impossible in relation to the substances themselves, they are postulated [to apply] to them; and in the absence of proximate substances, they would apply to remote ones. However, when they are possible in relation to a proximate substance, they should not be applied to remote ones, because their purpose has already been fulfilled.
Therefore, they belong to the sacrificer.
Because they are incomparable, they would be of unequal status.
This is a sūtra that follows the preceding word.

Now, why do they not have the same application (*samānavidhāna*)? For, because it is prescribed without distinction, they would apply to every person whatsoever. To this it is said: this is not a prescription common to all persons.

Why? Because they are unequal; these [priests] are unequal with respect to this injunction. What is the inequality? That which is prescribed for the sacrificer is not prescribed for the officiating priests.
How is it understood that it is prescribed for the sacrificer? By implication: it would apply in the case of one's own performance.
[Objection: But surely they are prescribed for the officiating priests as well, since there is no distinction [between them and the sacrificer].
[Response: We see that they are not prescribed for them because there is no purpose [in their performance by the priests].

How is there an absence of purpose? When performed by the officiating priests, [the rites] are neither performed nor caused to be performed by the sacrificer; for the act of hiring (parikraya) is not for the sake of that [performance by the priests].
Furthermore, things produced by oneself do not benefit one who seeks them;

therefore, they are purposeless. Consequently, they are not prescribed for the officiating priests (ṛtvij). This constitutes the difference [between the two cases]. Therefore, they are not subject to the same rule (samānavidhāna).
And austerity [is effective] because it results in the attainment of its fruit, as is seen in the world.
Regarding austerity (tapas), it is heard in the texts: "He does not eat for two days," "He does not eat for three days.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the austerity that of the officiating priest (ārtvija) or that of the sacrificer (yājamāna)? What is the prima facie view? On account of the designation (samākhyāna), it follows that the austerity belongs to the officiating priest.
This being the case, we reply: austerity belongs to the sacrificer. Why? Because it is for the sake of accomplishing the fruit; austerity is for the purpose of achieving the fruit.
The fruit of the sacrifice is accomplished by one who has perfected his austerity.

How is this understood? For austerity is suffering, and suffering is the fruit of unrighteousness (*adharma*); unrighteousness acts as an obstacle to the fruit of sacrifice. Since it is detrimental to one's welfare, as long as it exists, welfare cannot arise; therefore, it must be removed. Furthermore, righteousness and unrighteousness are counteracted by the experience of their fruits.
Therefore, it is taught that righteousness [leads] to the experience of the fruit of suffering.
"That suffering which is to be produced by him—that is this [suffering].

In this way, the purpose is seen; one need not postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). For, once that [unseen] result has been exhausted through the enjoyment of its fruit, the sacrifice—being unimpeded by unrighteousness (*adharma*)—will yield its fruit. Furthermore, the accomplishment of the fruit belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), not to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, austerity (*tapas*) is a duty of the sacrificer.
And the remainder of the sentence is likewise.

The remainder of the passage also illuminates this very point: "When indeed nothing remains within a person, when the blackness vanishes from his eyes, then he is most fit for sacrifice (*medhyatama*).
When there is fasting, then one is worthy of sacrifice (*medhārha*).

Sacrifice (*medha*) is a ritual (*yajña*), and a ritual is renunciation (*tyāga*); the remainder of the passage implies that one who is capable of performing renunciation through austerity is being described, for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is one who renounces.
Therefore, on account of the scriptural statement, "Austerity belongs to the sacrificer," it would belong to the others as well.
And because it is a quality, there would be no fixed restriction by means of the Veda.

Now, as for what was said—that because of the designation (*samākhyāna*), the austerity belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)—it is not grasped by the designation because it is a subordinate factor (*guṇatva*). Where a person stands in a subordinate position, there the designation is restrictive.
Or likewise, it is heard in the *Śyena* sacrifice: "The officiating priests proceed wearing red turbans and red garments.
Similarly, it is heard in the *Vājapeya*: "The officiating priests proceed wearing golden garlands."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the red turbans be worn by the Udgātṛs in the Śyena sacrifice, and the golden garlands by the Adhvaryus in the Vājapeya, or should both be performed by all the officiating priests? What, then, is the prima facie view? On account of the specific designation (samākhyā), the red turbans are for the Udgātṛs in the Śyena, and the golden garlands are for the Adhvaryus in the Vājapeya.

This being the case, we reply: because it is a subordinate quality (*guṇatva*), there would be no restriction by means of the Veda. The red turban and the golden garland are subordinate qualities, while the person is the primary element (*pradhāna*). Therefore, the red turban and the golden garland are heard in scripture as qualifications of the person, not as things to be performed; hence, the person is the primary element. What follows from this? If this is so, it has been stated that when persons are the primary elements, the name (*samākhyā*) is not a restrictive factor.

Moreover, because it is heard as a subordinate element (*guṇatva*), it is understood that this rule applies to all priests; for a subordinate element taught in proximity to a principal (*pradhāna*) is prescribed for each principal.

In that case, how could that which is obtained by direct statement (*vacana*) be restricted by a name (*samākhyā*), even though such a name exists? Therefore, in both cases, a duty of this kind must be performed by all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Likewise, [the application of] desire [is determined] due to its connection with the purpose.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, they recite: "If he should desire, 'May Parjanya rain,' then he should measure out the Sadas-altar low.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this desire that of the officiating priest (ārtvija), or is it that of the sacrificer (yājamāna)? What is the point of this? Is it "if the Adhvaryu should desire," or rather "if the sacrificer [should desire]"? Such is the uncertainty.
What is established? That the desire belongs to the officiating priest (*ārtvija*), because of the designation (*samākhyāna*).
The Adhvaryu is the subject under discussion as the one who desires; he is connected by the sentence with the verb "he should measure.
Therefore, the desire belongs to the officiating priest.
This being the case, we reply: the desire should be such as the austerity; that is to say, the desire belongs to the sacrificer.
Why? Because of the connection with the purpose; for it is understood that the sacrificer is connected with the fruit of the sacrifice together with its constituent parts.

Because of the distinction of verbal suffixes (*upagraha*): from the specific verbal suffix in "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and because of the specific suffix in "the Adhvaryu should measure [the post]," it is understood that [the action] is for the sake of another.
Now, as for what was said—that there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the person who has the need due to the context—it is replied:
even so, there is syntactic unity with the contextual sentence, namely, "when the sacrificer desires [it], he should measure."
On account of the designation of others, it should be so.

Where there is a specific designation, there the desire belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), as in the case: "Whatever desire he desires for himself or for the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), that he brings about by singing. If [the phrase] "for himself" were to be interpreted as "for the sacrificer," then both the mention of the "sacrificer" and the word "or" (*vā*) would be rendered purposeless. Therefore, it is understood from the designation of the "sacrificer" that the Udgātṛ refers specifically to himself.
And the mantras that do not perform an action are likewise [to be understood].
In this context, formulas of this kind serve as examples: "O Agni, giver of life, give me life," and "O Agni, you are the giver of luster, give me luster.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: are they to be recited by the officiating priests (*ārlijya*) or by the sacrificer (*yājamāna*)?
Based on the formal designation (*samākhyāna*), it is initially concluded that they are to be recited by the officiating priests.
This being the case, we reply: these mantras should be understood in the same way as the *kāma* [mantra]; thus, a word denoting the self is appropriate.

In [the mantra] "May there be life for me, may there be luster for me," the fruit of the ritual action is expressed by such terms as "life" and "luster," meaning "O Agni, accomplish the fruit of my ritual action for me.
Here, that fruit of the ritual action is proclaimed for the sake of instilling enthusiasm; and it is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who is emboldened by it, not anyone else.

That which is the fruit of the ritual action for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) is not for the sake of the fire-altar (*agni*), for that is already established. That which belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is for the sake of the fire-altar; and since that is not yet established, it must be prayed for—that which generates enthusiasm for the sake of ensuring the ritual's non-deficiency.
Even when the officiating priest exerts himself regarding what is already established, he exerts himself solely for the sake of the fruit of the ritual action belonging to the sacrificer.
In that case, a word denoting the self is not appropriate; however, when a word denoting the self is applied to the sacrificer, it becomes non-figurative. Therefore, they belong to the sacrificer.
Furthermore, this is seen from their appearance in the absence [of the officiating priests].
Furthermore, in the event of separation from the fires, there is a ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) during travel, performed while remaining right here with the words, "Thee, O Agni, who art there.
Moreover, one who has gone abroad does not become a priest (*ṛtvij*) for the fires; this term is a designation for one who performs the ritual action.

However, the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) remains the sacrificer even when away from the fires; having made arrangements for the *agnihotra*, he departs on his journey, and it is possible for him to perform the act of renunciation (*tyāga*) even while staying in a foreign land.
By stating that very specific form of attendance for one who has gone abroad, it shows the attendance of the sacrificer; therefore, those of this kind should belong to the sacrificer.
In the case of those [rites] prescribed for two [sacrificers], both [should attend], because there is purposefulness in the prescription for two.
There are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein, two sets of mantras are prescribed: those in the Ādhvaryava section and those in the Yājamāna section.

These include the mantras by which the clarified butter (ājya) is taken, such as "I take thee for the restraint and support of the five winds," and likewise the mantras for spreading the ladles, such as "With the impulse of strength, I spread the two ladles.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are these to be performed by both [the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer], or by the Adhvaryu alone?
What is the prima facie view? That they belong to the Adhvaryu because of the designation (*samākhyāna*).

This being the prima facie view, it is said: both should employ them. Why? Because the recitation by two is purposeful; since the designation is made for two, both are understood to be the performers. Therefore, the two should recite.
The Adhvaryu [thinks], "I shall perform according to what has been revealed by this [mantra]," and the sacrificer [thinks], "I shall not be negligent.
Furthermore, the recitation occurs when there is knowledge, for one who is ignorant is not authorized [to perform the rite].

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He causes the sacrificer to recite the *kḷpti* formulas; he causes the sacrificer to recite the *ujjit* formulas. Here there is a doubt: should everyone, both the learned and the ignorant, be made to recite, or only the learned? What is the prima facie view? Since there is no distinction specified, both the learned and the ignorant should be made to recite.
Objection: From the injunction "one should study the Veda," it follows that the entire Veda must be studied, and one is not authorized to study merely a portion of the Veda.
Response: It is said that the study of the Veda is to be performed for the sake of knowing the sacrificial rites (*kratu*).

In that case, when one sacrifice is to be performed, knowledge of another sacrifice does not serve a visible purpose; therefore, knowledge of other sacrifices need not be taken into account regarding the qualification [for a specific rite]. There is a separate text for each sacrifice so that all sacrifices may be known. Since it is heard in scripture that the entire Veda must be studied individually, one who knows his own subject matter (svapadārtha) is qualified. Thus, for one who does not know his own subject matter, there is no ritual action at all; how could such a person be made to recite? Therefore, it is rightly said: "Only one who knows [the text] should be made to recite."
On account of the designation "pertaining to the sacrificer," the ritual acts should belong to the sacrificer.
"He girds the wife and sets down the sprinkling waters and the clarified butter; these twelve items, in pairs, [are prescribed] for the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Here a doubt arises: are these the duties of the Adhvaryu, or are they the duties of the sacrificer? What is the prima facie view? Because of the designation [of the section], these duties should belong to the sacrificer.
It is understood that these belong to the sacrificer because of their specific designation, just as [one speaks of] the *potrīya* or the *neṣṭrīya*.
Or rather, they belong to the Adhvaryu, for the designation is preceded by the logic that he is the one for whose sake [the rite is performed].
Or rather, the *adhvaryu* should perform these [actions], for it is understood from the designation (*samākhyā*) that the *adhvaryu* is hired for that purpose.

All these constituent elements (*padārtha*) are recited as belonging to the *adhvaryu* alone; however, their "pairing" (*dvandvatā*) is stated to belong to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and "pairing" consists in performing the actions in close proximity.
In that case, while the *adhvaryu* will perform the constituent elements, it is impossible for the sacrificer to effect this proximity.

In that case, when there is a conflict between the subordinate element and its quality, the quality of being a collective whole (dvandvatā) must be set aside on the grounds that [the former] exists for the sake of that [latter].
Therefore, these ritual acts belong to the Adhvaryu.
In the event of a contradiction, the instrumental factor prevails due to a specific connection; the other [belongs to the one] from whom their distinction arises.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma; for its sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there are two mantras used for the act of encircling it (*parivyāṇa*). One, "Thou art the encircler" (*parivīr asi*), belongs to the Adhvaryu and is an *injunction* (*karaṇa*); the other, "The youth well-clothed" (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*), belongs to the Hotṛ and is a *recitation following the action* (*kriyamāṇānuvādī*).

When these two mantras have been extended to the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana by a series of transfer rules (*codaka*), a doubt arises: which one is it? In that context, a summary of the priests' functions is prescribed: "He who is the Hotṛ, he is the Adhvaryu. Does the Hotṛ perform the Adhvaryu’s *injunction-mantra*, or the Hotṛ’s *recitation-mantra*? What is the prima facie view? There is no fixed rule.

This being the position reached, it is replied: in case of conflict, the instrumental [formula] should be used—namely, the *ādhvaryava* "parivīr asi"—and not the *hotṛ*'s descriptive formula of the action in progress, "yuvā suvāsāḥ.
Why? Because of a specific connection (*samavāya-viśeṣa*).

There are two connections here: the *hotṛ*'s connection with the *hautra* rites through the extended application (*codaka*), and the connection with the *ādhvaryava* rites through direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇa*)—namely, "He who is the *hotṛ* is the *adhvaryu*."
Thus, the act is explicitly enjoined for the *adhvaryu*’s duty, and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is more authoritative than inference (*anumāna*).
Therefore, the *hotṛ* should perform the *ādhvaryava* rite "parivīr asi.

Now, who would perform the conflicting *hautra* rite? Another person [should do so], whichever one among them has a specific qualification; that is, another person who is a subordinate assistant (*hotṛpuruṣa*) who is otherwise unoccupied, or one who possesses a specific distinction of primary importance.
And because, in the case of the *praiṣa* (directions), the authority belongs to another.

There are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein, the directions (praiṣas) are handed down: "Place the sprinkling waters, prepare the fuel and the sacrificial grass, cleanse the ladles, gird the wife, and bring the clarified butter.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is it the case that the one who utters the direction is the same as the one who performs the action directed, or is the one who utters the direction different from the one who performs the action directed?
What is the prima facie view? That the person who utters the direction and the person who performs the action directed are one and the same.
Why? Because of the designation [of the person] and because it is not heard that "another" [is meant].
But surely, an injunction to oneself is contradictory.
It is said in reply: there will be no injunction; we shall explain that the *loṭ* suffix is used in the sense of the time having arrived (*prāptakāla*).

He says: Even when the time has arrived, the middle and other persons are established only when *yuṣmad* and so forth are the governing words (*upapada*); it is not a refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāra*). It is replied: When there is the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), the middle and others occur in relation to *yuṣmad* and so forth; when one intends to say "the time has arrived for you," then the middle person occurs only for *yuṣmad*, and not for *asmad* or the remainder. However, when only this much is intended to be expressed—namely, that "the time for the action has arrived"—and not "for you" or "for me," then the middle and others ought not to occur in accordance with *yuṣmad* and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not possible to intend to express both of these simultaneously—that "the time for the word-meaning has arrived" and "and yours"—for in that case, the sentence would be split.
Therefore, one can only say either "your time [has come]" once the time for the word-meaning is already known, or "the time for the word-meaning [has come]" once "yours" is already known.

In that context, the time for the ritual action (*padārtha*) must be stated, but not the time for the person denoted by "you" (*yuṣmad-artha*), because there is a purpose in remembering that [action]; for it is understood as something to be performed, whereas the person denoted by "you" is not so. Therefore, based on the designation (*samākhyā*), both the command (*praiṣa*) and the object of the command belong to the Adhvaryu alone.
As for the Adhvaryu, [his presence] is established through direct observation (*darśana*).

Now, this being the case, a doubt arises: should the Adhvaryu direct the Agnīdhra, or should the Agnīdhra direct the Adhvaryu? Since there is no specific rule, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed restriction. To this we reply: the Adhvaryu should be the one who carries out the purpose of the direction previously mentioned. Why? Because of a scriptural observation (*darśana*). There is such an observation: "He should hold the wooden sword (*sphya*) crosswise; if he were to hold it lengthwise, the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the thunderbolt would strike down the Adhvaryu. Thus, the wooden sword is in the hand of him who gives the direction.
"He might injure the Adhvaryu with the wooden sword"—this indicates that one Adhvaryu is distinct from the one who gives the command;
therefore, the Āgnīdhra should give the command to the Adhvaryu.
Or rather, the term is used figuratively because of the similarity of their functions.
The fruit belongs to the officiating priests because it serves a purpose in relation to the instruments of action.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they prescribe: "With the mantra, 'O Agni, may there be splendor for me in the invocations,' he first encloses the fire. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the fruit of the rite be prayed for for the officiating priest (ṛtvij), as in "O Agni, may there be splendor for me in the invocations," or rather for the sacrificer (yajamāna)? What is the prima facie view? That it should be for the Adhvaryu alone.

Why? Because in this way the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) will be respected; otherwise, there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereby [the word] would indicate the sacrificer by means of the self.
Therefore, the fruit must be desired for the officiating priest.
What is the meaning? Through this fuel-stick being held, the sacrifice will become possible in the fire.
In this regard, the statement of the *adhvaryu* priest is: "In these contests, in places of rivalry, I shall be resplendent," and likewise, "I shall be full of enthusiasm";
or rather, it belongs to the master (*svāmin*), because the purpose is for his sake.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) also demonstrates this point; for it says: "Whatever benediction (*āśis*) the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) invoke, that belongs to the sacrificer alone. This shows that the benediction has the sacrificer as its purpose.
Therefore, we also say: the fruit of the sacrificer is what should be invoked.
Thus, the purpose is exactly as stated in the prima facie position (*pakṣa*).
But the fruit of those [actions] exists for the sake of karma, because it possesses purpose with respect to its master.
And because of designation.

And where there is a designation, there the office of the officiating priest (*ārvtijam*) applies. Below the southern *havirdhāna* cart, there are four *uparava* holes, which are openings leading inward with intervals between them; having inserted his hands there, the Adhvaryu asks the sacrificer, "What is here? He replies, "Blessing. The Adhvaryu responds, "May that be ours together. Thus there is a designation between the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
The statement "May that be ours together" is the speech of both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer.
Therefore, it should be understood that the fruit here is to be prayed for by the Adhvaryu priest.
Since there is no distinction in the context, the preparation of the substance pertains to all ritual acts.

Regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there are the properties of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the properties of the altar (*vedi*). Concerning these, a doubt arises: do they serve the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice, or only the primary sacrifice?

Since they belong to the context (*prakaraṇa*), it follows that they serve the primary sacrifice. This being the position reached, it is said: it is not so; the preparation of materials serves the purpose of both the subsidiaries and the primary sacrifice. Just as has been explained, this [prima facie] position is stated for the sake of what is to be said subsequently.
But because of the specific instruction, there is no entitlement for the modified *apūrva*.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, according to the injunction: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, it is heard in the scripture: "He strews the pit for the sacrificial post with sacrificial grass (barhis) and anoints the sacrificial post with clarified butter (ājya).
In this regard, a doubt arises: should the archetypal (prakṛta) duties pertaining to the clarified butter and the sacrificial grass be performed for those two, or not?
What is established? That [the ritual acts] must be performed.

Why? Because the sentence is indeed the prescriber of the properties for *barhis* in general and *ājya* in general; that same sentence is obtained here as well through the force of the extended application (*codaka*).
And this *barhis* and *ājya* are not without purpose.
"Therefore, the ritual duties (dharmas) should be performed here [in the modification].

This being the position reached, we reply: because of the specific instruction, there is no application of new (apūrva) duties in the modification; these duties are specifically prescribed for the archetype (prakṛti), where they assist the primary act through the two archetypal functions of the clarified butter (ājya) and the sacrificial grass (barhis).
And those duties which assist the primary act are what are extended (atidiśyante) here.
For the primary act requires the injunction, not the subsidiary details;

for the primary act has a commonality with the injunction, whereas the subsidiary details do not. And in case of conflict, because of the specific nature of the revealed scripture (śruti), the [application of] the subsidiary details remains unmanifest.

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they prescribe: "He makes two purifiers (pavitra) of darbha grass, with unbroken tips, the length of a span (prādeśa)," and likewise: "The two separators (vidhṛti) are purifiers, one cubit (aratni) long; or else from something other [than the sacrificial grass]. In this regard, there is a doubt: are the two separators and the two purifiers to be made from the sacrificial grass (barhis) intended for strewing the altar, or from something else?
What, then, is the prima facie view? They should serve the purpose of the sacrificial grass used for strewing the altar.

What is the reason? Because that [fire] is the subject under discussion, and since all sacrificial grasses (*barhis*) are without distinction, the fires serve their purpose; therefore, [the fire should be taken] from that.
This being the position reached, we reply: it should be procured from another source.
Why? Because of contradiction.

How is there a contradiction? For it is heard [in scripture]: "One spreads the altar-grass in three ways or five ways. Now, how could that [grass] by which it is spread be made into the *vidhṛti* and the *pavitra*? Indeed, it is not possible for one thing to serve both for spreading and for the *vidhṛti-pavitra*.
Thus, both this prescribed statement and the possession of multiple functions would be asserted as impossible.
Therefore, it should not be made from that [same material].
If it is not from that [specific source], then from where? Such an unmanifested remainder exists; there is a sacrificial grass (barhis) called *paribhojanīya*, and from that it should be performed.
However, the removal of a portion [of the grass] occurs because of its connection with what is already present.
In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the subsidiary element serves all purposes, just as in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti).
They declare this: "The optional sacrifices (kāmyā iṣṭayaḥ) for the purpose of sacrifice must indeed be performed in a low voice (upāṃśu).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the low-voiced nature intended for both the subsidiaries (aṅga) and the principal acts (pradhāna), or is it intended for the principal acts alone? What is the prima facie view? The subsidiary [rule] should apply to everything in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because there is no distinction between subsidiaries and principals, just as in the model sacrifice (prakṛti); just as in the model sacrifice the properties of the altar (vedi-dharma) and the properties of the clarified butter (ājya-dharma) are for the sake of both subsidiaries and principals, so it is here as well.
Or rather, the primary meaning [is intended], because the subsidiary part is not enjoined.
In the absence of [the primary], it applies to its subsidiaries due to the distinction of proximity.

In the Śyena sacrifice, it is heard: "The clarified butter is fresh butter. Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the fresh butter belong to the primary rite or to the subsidiary rites? What is the prima facie view? It belongs to the primary rite, for that is the context; thus, by the authority of the scriptural statement, the primary rite is to be accomplished with fresh butter.
This being the case, we reply: there would be an impossibility of the subsidiaries (aṅgas) of that [sacrifice], namely the subsidiaries of the Śyena.
How is there an impossibility? Because the primary sacrifice has soma as its substance.
But surely, on account of the scriptural injunction, clarified butter (navanīta) will be used.
The meaning of the sentence is not that "there is no clarified butter (navanīta) in the Śyena sacrifice.

What then? It is the connection between the clarified butter and the *navanīta* that is enjoined—namely, that "in the Śyena, the clarified butter is *navanīta*"—while the connection between the Śyena and the clarified butter is merely restated (*anūdyate*).
Furthermore, there is no direct connection between the Śyena and the clarified butter; rather, such a connection exists between the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the Śyena and the clarified butter.
For one who possesses [the butter], fresh butter is prescribed as a restatement (anuvāda) because of its specific proximity.
If it is argued that the same applies to the fire-laying (ādhāna) rite as well:
If it were seen thus—that butter belongs to the parts of the Śyena sacrifice—then it would also apply to the Pavamāna offerings at the Ādhāna (fire-laying).
For those [offerings] also assist the Śyena, since the Śyena is accomplished in the fire consecrated by them.
[But this is not so], because the subsidiary part does not belong to that context, as its cause lies elsewhere.
Or because at that time there is the observation of indicative marks.
This is now being deliberated: is the fresh butter (navanīta) for those subsidiaries performed at the time of the Soma-pressing, or for all of them?
It should be for those at the time of the pressing, because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
This is heard in scripture: "He immolates the animals together."

Furthermore, there is a statement: "In place of the Agniṣomīya [animal sacrifice], there is the Agniṣomīya cake; in place of the Anubandhyā [cow], there is the Maitrāvaruṇī [cow]. This shows two substitutions being heard in the text; therefore, it is understood that the statement regarding the Śyena [sacrifice] prescribes a specific modification for the auxiliary rites belonging to the time of the Soma-pressing (sutyā). Or rather, [the rule applies] to all [auxiliaries] without distinction.
The clarified butter (navanīta) should belong to all the subsidiaries.
Why? Because there is no distinction; since there is no specific qualification, it belongs to all the subsidiaries.
This is a scriptural indication supporting the stated principle.
But the meat belongs to the Savanīya offerings, because of the specific injunction.
The Śākya sacrifice lasts for thirty-six years.

Regarding this, they recite: "At the conclusion of each day, the householder goes out hunting; the *tarasa* (raw flesh) portions of whatever wild animals he kills there become the *puroḍāśa* cakes for the *savanīya* offerings.
In this regard, there is a doubt: do the *tarasa* portions take the place of both the *savanīya* cakes and other possible *puroḍāśa* cakes, or do they take the place of the *savanīya* cakes alone?

What is the prima facie view? That all *puroḍāśa* cakes would consist of meat; for it is not possible both to enjoin that the *puroḍāśas* consist of meat and to qualify those *puroḍāśas* by means of the word "savanīya," since in that case the sentence would be split. This being the prima facie view, it is replied: meat, however, should belong to the *savanīyas*; the statement "the *savanīyas* are made of tarasa" is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Why is this so? Because the term *savanīya* cannot function as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for all *puroḍāśas*, whereas the term *puroḍāśa* is applicable to the *savanīyas*.
Therefore, the word *puroḍāśa* is the restatement.
Consequently, meat is prescribed in place of the *dhānās* and other offerings belonging to the *savanīyas*, on the basis of the remainder of the injunction.
If it is argued that devotion is improper when [the teacher] is absent;

If you should think: "In the case of the *savanīya* offerings, the word *puroḍāśa* will be a restatement (*anuvāda*)," [we reply]: the word *puroḍāśa* does not apply to parched grains (*dhānā*) and the like; moreover, figurative usage (*bhakti*) is improper when the primary sense is possible.
This would be so because it possesses the characteristic marks of the archetype (*prakṛti*), as in the case of the *vairāja* chant.

In the archetype, the *jyotiṣṭoma*, this term "puroḍāśa" is used figuratively for the parched grains (*dhānā*) and so forth; since it is employed there with reference to what is proximate, here too it will be used only figuratively.
For in this case as well, those [grains] are proximate by virtue of the term "savanīya.
