Just as the application of a word occurs in the archetype through a connection of indicative marks (*liṅga*), so it does in the ectype—as in the expressions, "the umbrella-bearers are going" or "the banner-bearers are going."

For example—just as in the case of "the Ukthya has the Vairūpa-sāman" and "the Ekaviṃśa Ṣoḍaśī has the Vairāja-sāman," it is understood from the word *sāman*, which is a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), that [the rites] have the Vairūpa-pṛṣṭha and Vairāja-pṛṣṭha [stotras];
so too here, it follows that the Savanīya offerings consist of meat.
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*).
In the third chapter, the definition of the application of subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*) through direct statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name was stated.

Now, here, it is investigated whether something is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); that is, what is for the sake of the sacrifice and what is for the sake of the person? Furthermore, even the investigation regarding the instigating and non-instigating [acts], the injunctions concerning results, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and the distinction between subsidiaries and primary acts, is precisely this investigation into what is for the sake of the sacrifice and what is for the sake of the person.
How so? A subsidiary is for the sake of the sacrifice; a primary act is for the sake of the person.
The injunction regarding the fruit (phalavidhi) is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), while the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is for the sake of the ritual (kratvartha).
A certain [injunction] is instigating (prayojaka) when it serves the purpose of the person, and non-instigating (aprayojaka) when it serves the purpose of the ritual.
Therefore, it has been aphorized that there is a desire to know (jijñāsā) both that which is for the sake of the ritual and that which is for the sake of the person.
In this regard, the words *atha* and *ataḥ* have already been explained in the very first sūtra of the first chapter.
The word *atha* refers back to the previously mentioned definition of the application of the remaining [subsidiaries].
The word *ataḥ* introduces the specific inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) and what serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
That which exists for the sake of a ritual is "for the purpose of the ritual" (*kratvartha*); that which exists for the sake of a person is "for the purpose of the person" (*puruṣārtha*).

The word *jijñāsā* is also understood in that same context—as the desire to know (*jñātum icchā*). Thus, this is the introductory aphorism: "The desire to know [the difference] between that which is for the purpose of the ritual and that which is for the purpose of the person."
Whatever a person finds pleasure in, there arises a desire for it, because [desire] is not distinct from the characteristic of the object.

Or rather, the Sūtra is explained as follows: regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed—"He strews [the grass] so that it is not seen through; he thus makes him not seen through by means of offspring and cattle. Likewise: "For one desiring cattle, he should make the altar with removable soil; for one desiring cattle, he should make the Veda [grass-bundle] knee-high; for one desiring cattle, he should carry forward the water with a milking vessel," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: are such items as these for the sake of the sacrifice (kratvartha) or for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha)? What is the prima facie view? That they are for the sake of the sacrifice.

Why? Because a visible benefit to the sacrifice is seen from them: the carrying away of the loose soil (*purīṣa*) and the strewing of the altar (*vedi*). As it has been said—“Bādari [holds that these apply] to substances, qualities, and purificatory acts” (*Dravyaguṇasaṃskāreṣu Bādari*).

Therefore, the prima facie view is that they are for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). This being the position, we reply: “That in which there is pleasure for a person is indeed for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); pleasure is produced by them; therefore, these are for the sake of the person.”
But was it not said that a visible benefit to the sacrifice is observed?
It is replied: True, it is observed; however, they are not mentioned for the sake of benefiting the sacrifice, but rather these are heard in relation to [specific] results.
And that which benefits something is not necessarily its subordinate (śeṣa).

It has been stated that "whatever is heard to exist for the sake of another is its subordinate (śeṣa)," according to the principle: "The subordinate exists because it serves another's purpose. This being the position reached, we reply: [the ritual action] is for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha). When this object of the word has been performed, pleasure arises for the person; therefore, his desire for it is characterized by its purpose, namely for the sake of maintaining the body. For one whose body is maintained, it is evident that he possesses material wealth.
Furthermore, sacrifice is heard in scripture as belonging to one who possesses a body; therefore, it is stated that there is an application of a substance already in existence.

The acquisition of a substance is not grasped by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), for even without the word expressing the acquisition of a substance, the sacrifice is indeed accomplished. Therefore, the appropriation of a substance is for the sake of the person.
Now, as for what was said—that the statement of a restrictive rule (niyama) is purposeless because the possession of property serves the human goal—it is replied:
the status of serving the human goal is not overturned by that much.

For that [status] is directly perceived (pratyakṣa), whereas you describe it through inference (parokṣa) based on logical reasoning; and that which is inferred cannot sublate what is directly perceived.
Therefore, based on that restrictive statement, one may indeed postulate another unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), but not at the expense of abandoning what is seen (*dṛṣṭa*).

Consequently, since wealth is acquired for the sake of that which is a man’s purpose—namely, pleasure—then when it is said that "a sacrifice must be performed with rice," it makes no difference whether the rice was acquired for the sake of pleasure or acquired for the sake of the ritual;
for rice acquired for the sake of pleasure is simply rice, and rice acquired for the sake of the ritual is also simply rice.
Therefore, the acquisition of property is not included within the injunction for performance (*prayoga-codanā*).

Now, as for what was said—that in your view the restriction forms a single syntactical unit with an inferred or non-contextual word, whereas in our view it does so with a directly perceived injunction of performance—this is not a fault; for in our view as well, it is with the directly perceived act of eating (*bhujin*), and not with the statement of the result (*phala-vacana*).
How, then, is it understood that the unseen result (adṛṣṭa) arises from restriction? It is just as in your own position.
He says: In our position, because of the syntactic unity with that which possesses a fruit, it is understood that it assists that which possesses a fruit.

It is said: even in our position, it is only that which possesses a fruit that forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*). However, this is the distinction: for you, the fruit is scriptural (*śruta*), whereas for me, it is perceptible (*dṛṣṭa*).
Now, as for the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that was stated—that ritual action is heard in connection with house-burning and so forth—it is replied:

even if the acquisition of property is not for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), nevertheless, when burning is the occasion (*nimitta*), the injunction of the *jāmavatī* verses and others for the sake of a result or for the status of being an auxiliary to the ritual action is indeed logical.

Therefore, the acquisition of wealth is for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha), for it is inseparable from pleasure. Upon its relinquishment, ritual acts serve the human goal, because the scripture is beyond doubt; nor is wealth intended to be discarded, since it is connected with that purpose. Thus, the mention of the person (puruṣa) in relation to the action is due to this connection with that purpose.
In this context, the vows of Prajāpati serve as the illustration—such as, "One should not look at the rising sun, nor the setting sun," and so forth.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are the vows of Prajāpati for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), or are they for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*)? What is the prima facie view? They are for the sake of the sacrifice.
Why? Because in this way, it will not be necessary to postulate a fruit [of the action]. [Objection:
But surely their fruit is indeed heard in scripture, for it is said, "By this much he becomes free from sin.
[Reply: It is said in response—this statement is not intended to convey a fruit; this word is merely a description of the present state.

Therefore, since it has been established that the sun is to be looked upon [at the time of its rising], this prohibition might apply there, or perhaps some restriction regarding the setting sun exists as a subsidiary part of a ritual act (*karmāṅga*).

This being the position reached, we reply: in that case, when that [restriction] is set aside, the abandonment of pleasure would also follow; thus, such acts would become for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), rather than being for the sake of the ritual act itself.
These are taught for the agent, not for the sake of the ritual act.

The connection intended [by the scripture] is that which exists between the agent who has attained the object and the action; it is not the case that a non-existent connection with the object is being enjoined.

Furthermore, the scripture is beyond doubt and is a more authoritative means of knowledge than even the words of one's father or mother, for one gains conviction through it directly, as it stands in the place of the senses.
Nor is any visible benefit produced for the substance by such [connections] as these.
Therefore, because of its connection with that human purpose, it is the person who is heard [as the agent] in an action of this kind.
Moreover, the human effort would be uttered merely to indicate the injunction of the ritual elements, while itself being unintended [as the primary object];
for, since there is no distinction in the scripture, the results would follow exactly as they are heard in the text.
It is said: If this were so, then these [acts] would also be for the sake of the person—such as "he offers the *samidh*," "he offers to *tanūnapāt*," "one should not speak untruth," and so forth.
For here too there is a mention of human effort, and here too no material substance is intended to be prepared.
Or rather, because no cause [for preparation] is perceived, the purpose [of the act] is not connected to that [preparation].

Or rather, this is not the case; for it would follow that even the *samidh* offerings and the like serve the purpose of the person. If no specific cause were perceived, the *prājāpatya-vratas* would have to be considered for the sake of the person. In that regard, no cause such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or the like is perceived by which they could be understood as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the ritual acts; therefore, they serve the purpose of the person. There is no connection between the ritual act and the *prājāpatya-vratas*.
In this case, however, the reason is taken to be what is called "context" (*prakaraṇa*), by which it is understood that [the acts] are for the sake of the ritual;
therefore, the comparison is unequal, and the human effort involved is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) when this is the case.
And so it is with things that have become like the world.
But substances should be offered without distinction, because otherwise they would be purposeless.

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recorded there: "The wooden sword (sphya), the potsherds (kapāla), the Agnihotra-ladle (agnihotrahavaṇī), the winnowing basket (śūrpa), the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina), the yoke-pin (śamyā), the mortar (ulūkhalam), the pestle (musalam), the lower grinding stone (dṛṣad), and the upper grinding stone (upalā)—these indeed are the ten sacrificial implements (yajñāyudha).
In this regard, a doubt arises:

are these substances to be offered as oblations, or are they to be connected with their respective purposes? To establish this, it must be considered whether this is an injunction (vidhi) or a restatement (anuvāda).
If there is an injunction (*vidhi*), there is a prescription; if there is a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is a connection according to the actual facts.
What is the conclusion? That it is an injunction; for in that case there is a specific purpose in the performance [of the rite], whereas otherwise it would be a mere statement devoid of purpose.
Furthermore, in the case of a prescription, the term "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudha*) is supported, meaning they are the weapons of the sacrifice, the means of accomplishing the sacrifice.
Otherwise, by direct hearing (*śravaṇa*), the winnowing baskets and other items would become the instruments (*āyudha*) of the sacrifice through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Furthermore, the number [ten] is thus made consistent because of its connection with a single sacrifice; otherwise, due to the connection with multiple objects, the number ten would not be consistent.
Therefore, they should be given; what is enjoined without distinction ought to belong to the principal rite by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
But the connection of substances is with their own respective purposes, because they serve distinct purposes; therefore, they should be used according to the literal scriptural injunction.
And they are exhorted to perform purposeful actions.
In rites for specific purposes, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and the like are enjoined; these too would be subject to option (*vikalpa*).

In that case, there is sublation (*bādha*), not combination (*samuccaya*), because the sacrificial cake and the others are connected with the act of sacrifice independently, as are the wooden sword (*sphya*) and the other implements.

Likewise, they are enjoined for ritual acts for a purpose; they are enjoined for the concluding rite—[as it is said]: "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires with the fires and with the sacrificial vessels.
If [the vessels] were given away [at the time of death], they would not exist there [for that purpose]; therefore, for this reason also, they should not be given away.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga): "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day.
For this reason as well, it is a restatement (anuvāda).
In that case, singularity is not a constituent part of the sacrifice, because it is subordinate to the purpose.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, according to the text: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Likewise, [there is]: "He yokes two oxen," and similarly, in the Aśvamedha: "He sacrifices kapiñjala birds for the spring.
In this regard, a doubt arises: are the singular number, the dual number, and the plural number intended to be significant, or are they not intended to be significant?

The meaning is that, in this context, singularity—which is not a constituent part of the sacrifice—is not intended to be expressed, because the object is subordinate; neither the number is subordinate to the animal (*ālambha*), nor is it subordinate to the binding (*niyojana*).
To what, then, does it belong? It belongs to the animal, the two oxen, and the *kapiñjala* birds.

For the case-ending, by virtue of direct audition (*śruti*), expresses the meaning of number as residing in the meaning of the nominal stem; it could express it as a constituent of the sacrifice only through syntactical connection (*vākya*), and direct audition is more powerful than syntactical connection.
Therefore, it is not intended as a constituent part of the sacrifice.
He says: "Let it not be a constituent part of the sacrifice; nevertheless, it may still be intended as a constituent part of the animal and so forth.

It is replied: No; for whether the constituent part of the animal and so forth is mentioned or not mentioned, there is no purpose served by it, since the purpose lies in the constituent part of the sacrifice being unimpaired.
For even when a limb of the animal or other such component has failed, the sacrifice remains entirely unimpaired; and the fruit arises from the sacrifice, not from the animal or its parts.

Therefore, there is no purpose served by the quality of the animal—whether unknown or known—and thus that quality is not intended to be expressed. For it is said that only that which serves a purpose is intended to be expressed. This is also because of the use of a single [Vedic] accent.
If it is argued that it is perceived:

If you view it thus—that the number is not intended to be expressed—that is not correct; for the number is perceived as being an integral part of the verbal expression, just as when it is said, "Bring the animal," only one is brought; when "the two animals," two are brought; and when "the animals," many are brought. And that which is perceived is the meaning of the word. Therefore, it is understood from the word itself that the number is an integral part of the sacrifice; and what is understood from the word does not become unintended except for a specific reason. It is not the case that it is non-verbal, because its authority is established by the word, as in the previous case.
This is not so; while it is true that [oneness] is perceived, this perception of the meaning of the word is not due to a defect such as delusion.

Why is this? For it is understood from the syntactical connection (*vākya*) that [the singular number] is a subordinate element of the sacrifice (*yajñāṅga*), and the syntactical connection is sublated by direct statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, this [notion that the sacrifice is one] is not the literal meaning of the word, because of the oneness [of the substance].
For even the meaning of a word is understood, as in the case of "the one in front runs.
That person is called "the one in front" because there is another [behind him]; thus, when "the one in front" is mentioned, the other is understood.
However, the other is not understood merely from hearing the words "the one in front runs."

In this case as well, "the animal" (*paśum*) is understood as a singular entity, but not in reference to the sacrifice. For just as when "previously" (*pūrvam*) is stated, another [time] is merely understood and not enjoined for any purpose, so too here the number is merely perceived; it is not enjoined as something to be performed in the sacrifice, nor is it enjoined in reference to the animal.

If it is asked, "Why is it not prescribed with reference to the animal?"—because there is no prescriptive element (vidhāyaka). It might be argued that the verbal form (ākhyāta-śabda) will be the prescriptive element; however, this too is untenable, because while that [verbal form] is the prescriber of the connection between the substance and the deity—as in "one should sacrifice" (*ālabheta*)—it is not capable of prescribing the relationship between number and the numbered object.
For in that case, the sentence would be split;
therefore, the number is not intended to be expressed.
However, it is perceived like the word itself, for when that [word] occurs, its cognition is observed, just as it is for others.

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position. This is not so—that number is not heard by means of a word in the sacrifice—because it is perceived in the meaning expressed by the verb. In common usage, when one says "bring the animal" (*paśum ānaya*) with the singular ending, the act of bringing qualified by the singularity of the animal is understood; when one says "animals" (*paśu*) [with the dual], that which is qualified by duality is understood. For in that case, singularity departs and duality arises.
And when something arises upon the addition of another element, it is understood that the latter is the meaning of the former.

His knowledge is as follows: just as with other words, when it is said, "Bring the horse," the bringing of a horse is understood; when it is said, "Bring the cow," the bringing of a cow is understood. Therein, the horse recedes and the cow arises; by this it is known that the referent of the word "horse" is the horse, and the referent of the word "cow" is the cow.

As for what was said—that the meaning of the sentence is sublated by the direct Vedic statement—it is replied: the direct statement does not say that "the meaning of the sentence does not exist"; rather, it merely expresses the number inherent in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Such a number is not enjoined in the sacrifice by means of the sentence; for the meaning of the nominal stem is connected with what is expressed by the verb (*ākhyāta*), as is the meaning of the case ending (*vibhakti*) as well.
Thus, the act of offering (*ālambha*) is understood as qualified by those specific attributes; in that case, because there is a single purpose, it is logical that it constitutes a single sentence.

For if the number were being enjoined with respect to the animal, a single verbal form would not be able to enjoin both the meaning of the verb and the relationship between the number and the thing numbered.
Therefore, the number is intended to be significant in the sacrifice.
And there is a scriptural indication to that effect.
And there is also an indicative mark to that effect.

And by doing so, the gender (liṅga), which shares the same phonetic form [as the word], will also be intended; in that case, this observation becomes applicable: "In spring, at dawn, one sacrifices a black-necked animal dedicated to Agni; in summer, at midday, a lioness dedicated to Indra; in autumn, in the afternoon, a white animal dedicated to Bṛhaspati. There it is heard: "They are pregnant," and since pregnancy is a quality of females, it will thus indicate females. Likewise: "The horse, the bull, the ram, the goat, and the man—these are dedicated to Prajāpati."
In this regard, it is heard [in the Veda]: "They are to be with testicles, because they possess the male organ.
Possessing testicles is a quality of males; thus, it indicates the attainment of the status of a male.
Or, it may be a separate topic (*adhikaraṇa*); and so, regarding the "mark" (*liṅga*), the section on number (*saṃkhyā*) is seen to apply by analogy to the section on the mark.

The gender is not intended to be significant, because the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is set aside by direct statement (*śruti*); nor does it constitute a "gender-indicator" (*liṅga*) merely because it is heard as if it were intended.
For example, in the case of "A female cow is the *somakrayaṇī* (the cow for purchasing Soma)," although the word for female is used, the gender is understood to be unintended.

[Objection: But why is a male deer not brought when one says, "Bring a *mṛgī* (female deer)"? [Response: It is not so; that [intentionality] is not based on the word itself, just as in the case of "The one in front is running."
The meaning would be understood as existing without distinction among all substrata.
In this context, the items dependent [on the sacrifice] are the examples; the *uttama-prayāja*, the *paśupuroḍāśa*, and the *sviṣṭakṛt*—these sacrifices are the examples.
Regarding these, there is a doubt:
is the mere act of sacrificing a refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the deity, or is an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced in the deity by the sacrifice?

What is established? Since the meaning of existence is understood without distinction in respect to substrates, therefore, in the case of such verbal roots as these, the meaning of existence must be understood as something new (apūrva), because there is no distinction from other verbal forms such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti*. This has already been stated: "That which has come into being (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being (*bhavya*). However, there is no commencement [of action] in the case of an injunction (*codanā*), because [the result] is distinct; for it is not enjoined by anything else.
Or rather, there may be a desire to produce a substance; for the state of being subordinate (guṇabhāva) arises from relying on the fact that the action is subordinate to the purpose.

Or rather, there may be an *apūrva* (unseen potency) from this [act of abandonment], even though there is a desire to prepare the deity; for in that case, the sacrifice is subordinate to the purpose of preparing the deity, and the deity is remembered therein by means of the mantra through the presentation of the substance.

While that visible purpose is being accomplished by the mantra, another abandonment is heard of which has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Since it has no visible effect, it is understood that this *apūrva* resides in the deity because it is based upon the deity.
Therefore, there is a disparity between the purpose and the substances and actions.

The third subject has been transcended; from this point forward, the equality and inequality regarding the purpose and utility of substances and ritual acts will be explained. In some cases there is equality, and in others there is inequality: for instance, there is inequality between *āmikṣā* and *vājina*; there is inequality between the purchase and the dust; and there is equality between the staff held by the Maitrāvaruṇa priest and that held by the sacrificer. Thus it should be observed in each respective case—both equality and inequality. [Objection: Since they all result in a single accomplishment, everything should be equal.

In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the whey (*vājina*) for the Vājin deities.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the pouring of curds into heated milk serve to produce both the *āmikṣā* and the *vājina*, or only the *āmikṣā*? What is the prima facie view? That it serves to produce both.

Why? Because it is understood that when something is performed, that which is accomplished as a result and serves a purpose is the motivator (*prayojaka*) for that action. And when the bringing of curd is performed, both results are accomplished: the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk) and, from that very same act, the *yājñika* (the sacrificial offering). Therefore, the bringing would be performed for the sake of either one if there were a reason for a definitive determination (*vinigamanā*). Since no such distinction is perceived, it is understood that the bringing is for the sake of both.

Therefore, this single production is impelled by both [the milk and the curds]; thus, because the essence of the production consists in their conjunction, the *āmikṣā* (curdled milk) would be the primary element.
This is not the case; both are not the motivators. It is the *āmikṣā* that is the motivator.
Why? Because here, that which is produced from the curd and milk is not the sacrificial offering (*havis*).
If that were the offering, it would follow as a specific distinction that both [the curd and milk] are produced from those two [substances] themselves.
What, then, is the oblation (*havis*)? It is milk mixed with curds. Why is this so? Because it is said, "That [mixture] belongs to the Viśvedevas," not that which is produced from it.

He says: when curd is added to heated milk, two things occur—the milk is mixed with the curd, and it is separated from the whey (*vājina*). In that case, the intended action is the mixing, not the separation.

Why is this so? It is said: the mixing with the curd is expressed by the word (*śābda*), whereas the separation of the milk from the whey is not expressed by the word (*aśābda*); furthermore, a pronoun attains syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word mentioned previously.

In the alternative view, the addition of curds to the milk would be for the purpose of distinguishing the whey (*vājina*); and when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the direct statement is more authoritative.
Therefore, the addition of curds is for the sake of the *āmikṣā*, and the word *āmikṣā* here is a restatement (*anuvāda*), since that alone is called *āmikṣā* where curds are added to heated milk.
Consequently, the *āmikṣā* is the motivator (*prayojikā*), while the whey is not a motivator.
And because of the designation by the primary term.

Furthermore, it is not logical that both [the presence of a purpose and the absence of a purpose] should be the motivators. There is no statement here to the effect that "this is the motivator" and "this is not. Since an instruction would be meaningless in the absence of a motivator, a motivator is therefore postulated.
In that case, once a single motivator has been established such that the instruction becomes meaningful, another cannot also be a motivator.
Nor is any distinction perceived between them.

How is this understood? From the praise of the primary term; for it is logical to praise the primary term. However, because of its priority, the knowledge that it is the motivator arises first. Once that motivator exists, since the charge of purposelessness has been refuted, the second [term] is not a motivator either. Furthermore, curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) is the first, while whey (*vājina*) is the second; therefore, curdled milk is the motivator. The act of preparing the vessel is not a motivator for the leading forth, because it is for the sake of another purpose.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, yellow-eyed, one-year-old cow.
Therein, another [scriptural injunction] is heard: "He follows her for six steps," and likewise, "He takes up the seventh step.
Another [injunction] is this: "When they move the two Havirdhāna carts eastward, then he should anoint the axle with that [cow]."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is the leading of the Soma-purchasing cow for the purpose of the foot-dust, or is it prompted by the purchase itself? What is the prima facie view? From the act of leading, both are accomplished—the purchase and the footprint; therefore, both are the motivators. For no distinction is perceived between them; as it has been said: "Because they are produced from a single source, everything should be equal."
This being the case, we reply: "The act of placing [the Soma] on the foot is not the motivator.
Why? Because the leading [of the Soma] is for the sake of the purchase; for without the leading, the purchase in a specific location would not be possible.
Therefore, it is understood that the leading is motivated by the purchase.
If it is prompted by the purchase (*kraya*), it cannot possibly be prompted by the foot-step (*pada*) as well.

But what is the purpose of this inquiry? If both [the purchase and the foot-step] were the prompters of the leading of the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), then when the seventh foot-step of the one-year-old cow is placed upon the pressing-stone (*grāvan*), the one-year-old cow would have to be led again for the sake of that seventh step. However, if the foot-step is not the prompter, then the one-year-old cow need not be made to walk out six more steps.

Furthermore, the act of expressing the meaning (*arthābhidhāna*) occurs because of its connection with what is yet to come; since that [future result] is the cause, the action is enjoined for that purpose.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One bakes the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) on the potsherds," and likewise, "With the cake-potsherd, one scatters the husks. Regarding this, there is a doubt: do both—the baking of the cake and the scattering of the husks—motivate the use of the potsherds, or is it only the baking that motivates them, not the scattering of the husks? What is the prima facie view? Since there is no reason for a decisive conclusion, both motivate their use.
Because the animal is not to be slaughtered, blood and excrement do not constitute ritual action.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Regarding that, it is heard in the scripture: "He cuts off first from the heart, then from the tongue," and so forth;
likewise, "He discards the blood, he throws away the dung, and he removes the thick parts of the entrails."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the sacrifice with the portions (avadāna) such as the heart constitute the motivator for the animal, or is the complete cutting out [of the organs] and the removal of the blood also a motivator? What is the prima facie view? Because they arise from a single performance, all should be equal; that is, both are motivators.

This being the case, we reply: the dung and blood are not the purpose (prayojaka) for the animal sacrifice. For the slaughter of the animal is not for their sake; it is stated that "he strikes once and discards the blood," without specifying whether it is the animal's or another's. The animal belongs to Agni and Soma by virtue of the direct statement (*vākya*): "He who is initiated, he slaughters the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. The dung and blood would belong to the animal by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), but context is sublated by direct statement. [Objection: But these two, the dung and blood, are to be disposed of (*pratipādya*); therefore, the determination is that they belong to the animal intended for the sacrifice and not to any other.
If this is so, then [the mention of] dung and blood is non-essential (*aprayojaka*).

What is the purpose [of this discussion]? When there is parity [between the two], in the absence of dung and blood, another animal must be sacrificed; however, if dung and blood were non-essential, they would be omitted.
Furthermore, because the substance consists of a single part, it is connected with what exists at the time of its origin.
In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One cuts off [the portion] for Sviṣṭakṛt from the northern half.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Āgneya sacrifice the motivator (prayojaka) of the cake, while the Sviṣṭakṛt is not a motivator, or are both motivators? What is the prima facie view? Since they are produced from a single substance, all [portions] should be equal.

This being the case, we reply: a substance consisting of a single part of this kind would not be a motivator [of action]. Why? Because of the connection with what already exists. It is not the case that an action upon a single part motivates the whole; rather, the meaning is that a single part of an existing whole is to be taken up, and not that one should take up the whole itself. For example, when it is said, "Give him a piece of sugarcane," or "Give him a fragment of a sweetmeat," it is understood that one should not take up the entire sugarcane, but rather take a piece from the existing sugarcane, or take a fragment from the existing sweetmeat.

Therefore, the substance intended for another purpose should be taken from its northern half; and since there exists a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) intended for Agni, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is not a motivator [for the preparation of the cake]. This is because of the specific designation that "another portion is for that purpose."
Not so, because of the proximity of what remains.

This is not so; for that which remains is already present. That which, if not produced, would cause the purpose to fail, is produced by implication (*arthāt*). Since the remainder is already present, the taking from the upper half is accomplished.
Therefore, a substance should not be produced by implication; rather, one should take from the upper half of that very substance which is already present for another purpose.
For it is heard [in the scripture] that "the northern half" belongs to the Sviṣṭakṛt, but it is not specified as "the northern half of this particular substance.

And a linguistic usage does not occur by this much alone, for every northern half belongs to something; thus, it requires a proximate referent, and what is proximate is that which serves another purpose.
Therefore, the sacrifice to the Sviṣṭakṛt is performed from the substance that serves another purpose.
And therefore, it is not a non-efficient [reason].

As for what was said—that "one who is not the owner cannot give"—it is replied: this relinquishment (*utsarga*) is scripturally enjoined for the purpose of transferring the remainder; that can indeed be performed.
For giving (*dāna*) is the establishment of another's ownership preceded by relinquishment; that cannot be done by one who is not the owner.
From the performance of action.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.

There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*): "Because he cuts portions from all the sacrificial oblations (*havir*), therefore this food of manifold forms is collected within the stomach. If the sacrifice were performed from a substance already present for the sake of another [rite], then it is logical that portions would be cut from all of them, since there is no distinction in their proximity; however, if it were the motivator (*prayojaka*), one would have to cut only from a single one.
Therefore, for this reason as well, it is not the motivator.
Likewise, there is this further indicative mark: "He cuts off the *iḍā* from the remnant; he offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the remnant.
Now, one might argue that this is an injunction (*vidhi*).
We say it is not; for there is no injunctive suffix here, as this is merely a statement of an existing fact (*vartamānāpadeśa*).
In the case of the sprinkling (abhighāraṇa), because of the distance [between the substances], there should be a separation of vessels, as in the case of the after-offerings (anuyāja).
Nor is it due to being an unfit recipient; rather, unfitness arises from being only a partial [recipient].
Alternatively, the omenta of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati should not be sprinkled with clarified butter.
Why? Because there is no remnant. If it is asked how there is no remnant:
Because it is not a fit vessel.
How is it not a fit vessel? Because it is a single part; for that remnant is a single part of the clarified butter (ājya) taken for the purpose of the *prayāja* offerings.
What follows from this? If this is so, then an action pertaining to a single part, when prescribed in scripture, does not enjoin the whole as something to be taken up (*upādeya*).
And because the simultaneous application [of the two] is due to their being causes.

And because the sprinkling [of ghee] serves as the cause, there is a commendatory statement: "He immolates them together. "The morning pressing is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha); since the animals are immolated at the morning pressing, he thus immolates them at a sacred ford, for the sake of their having a common origin and for the purpose of the sprinkling of the omenta. By thus supporting the sprinkling of the omenta through a different purpose, [the author] shows that [the sprinkling] does not exist here [in the case of the cooked meat]. And this is because of the observation of its absence.

Indeed, it also demonstrates the absence of the act of sprinkling: "The omentum is rough (savya) at this time when it has not been sprinkled; the Brahmasāman is indeed the Brahman; in that one offers [the victim] to the Brahmasāman, by that it is no longer rough, by that it is sprinkled.
The word *savya* is used for that which is dry; thus, "the omentum is rough" indicates its state of being unsprinkled.
The mention of "rough" occurs only when [the sprinkling] is absent.

He said: "This is not the correct view; for this statement regarding the left hand occurs only when there is indeed an act of sprinkling (abhighāraṇa), since there is another sprinkling of the omentum (vapā)—namely, 'he spreads clarified butter, [places] a piece of gold, [and then] the omentum; he then sprinkles it.'"

While that [sprinkling] exists, how could they be dry? And he says: "Therefore, it cannot be understood that those omenta appear dry; hence, there must certainly be sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings. Since this sprinkling is perceptually evident, the observation that "they are dry" is an illusion.
[The opponent objects: "That is not so."

If it is seen thus, then the statement "the left [hand] when there is pouring over" is not a non-indicative mark; it is not a non-indicative mark, for this is its statement: that which performs the act of lubricating.
Which is that? It is the first, for the first indeed performs the lubrication, not the second.

That [quality] belongs to what is already unctuous, and no further unctuousing is performed upon what is already unctuous. This is just as there is a common saying in the world: "When we emerged from the wilderness, we ate unctuous food at Devadatta’s house; by that, we were made non-arid," even though other unctuous foods were available. Thus, because there is an absence of that which makes something non-arid—the act of pouring over—it is appropriate to say it is "arid"; but this being the case, such a statement would not be appropriate. Therefore, for this reason also, there is no pouring over of the *prājāpatya* offerings with the remnants of the *prayāja* oblations.
It may be so, because of its primacy.
This is a sutra that follows upon the previous statement:
if the expression "together with" (*savyā*) were untenable due to the absence of a first [member], then it would be tenable because another first member exists.
Which one is that? It is that which is subsequent to the time when it is being cooked and prior to the time when it has been removed from the heat.

To this it is replied: It might be so if there were a primary [purpose] for the sprinkling with the remains of the *prayāja* offerings; however, since that very [primary purpose] is absent, this [objection] is untenable. Even though there is sprinkling while the cake is being baked and after it has been removed from the fire, that which occurs while it is being baked is consumed by the flames of the fire, and that which occurs after it has been removed is destroyed by the particles of the fire and the particles of heat. Thus, that [cake] remains indeed dry. But this [sprinkling] with the remains of the *prayāja* is performed when it is cold; that makes it oily. Therefore, the sprinkling performed at the time of offering—which is done to what has already become oily—does not provide further oiliness.

It has been stated that this [practice] is justified by the mention of the left hand due to the absence of both the moistening and the sprinkling; therefore, the remnant of the *prayāja* offerings is not retained.
However, the act of pouring together (*samānayana*) should be primary, because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "Having passed over the iḍā, he brings [the butter] together toward the barhis.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: does this bringing together (samānayana) motivate the properties of the clarified butter, or is it not a motivator? What is the prima facie view? That it is not a motivator.

Why? Because this [clarified butter] is brought as a single portion of the clarified butter intended for the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings; thus, by the previous reasoning, its lack of independent purpose (*aprayojakatā*) would follow. To this it is replied: "The bringing [of the butter] is primary because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the indicative mark? It is stated in the *Ātithyā* ritual: "There are four portions of clarified butter, for one is not about to perform the *anuyājas* here. If the bringing were for the sake of the *prayājas*, then only one four-portioned measure would be brought there.

There is even one [oblation] for the *anuyāja* offerings; therefore, when [the text says], "Then the *iḍā* of the *ātithya* is concluded," the absence of *anuyāja*s implies that one *caturgṛhīta* portion must be taken in the *upabhṛt* ladle for the purpose of bringing [the butter] together, but not for the purpose of the *anuyāja*s themselves.

In that case, the observation of many *caturgṛhīta*s becomes logical; otherwise, in the absence of *anuyāja*s, no *caturgṛhīta* would be taken in the *upabhṛt* at all, and thus the plural number in the expression "the *caturgṛhīta*s" would be untenable.
Therefore, the bringing together [of the butter] is the motive [for the action].
For when the reason lacks efficacy in the statement.
Now, why is it that this statement—"the clarified butter is not taken four times"—is not [accepted]?
It is said in reply: for if there were such a statement, the reason would be rendered ineffective, since one is not about to perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) here.
When it is understood that the act of pouring together (*samānayana*) is not for the sake of the fore-offerings (*prayāja*), then the statement [is made].

When it is a statement [of fact], then the absence of the *anuyāja* offerings is not the cause; for if there were no cause, the explanatory formula (*nigada*) stating "he will indeed not perform the *anuyājas*" would be inappropriate.
Therefore, the bringing together [of the butter] for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings is the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the butter in the *aupabhṛta* ladle.

What is the practical consequence? If the bringing together is for the sake of the *anuyājas*, then as much as is required for the *prayājas*—namely, half of the *aupabhṛta* butter—should be brought together; but if it were not motivated by that purpose, there would be no necessity for either exactly half or that specific amount.
In that case, the arising would be undifferentiated.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One takes four portions in the *juhū* ladle; one takes eight portions in the *upabhṛt* ladle. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are both the *jauhava* (the portion in the *juhū*) and the *aupabhṛta* (the portion in the *upabhṛt*) intended for both purposes—that is, for both the *prayāja* offerings and the *anuyāja* offerings—or is the *jauhava* for the *prayājas* and the *aupabhṛta* for the *anuyājas*? Or rather, is the *aupabhṛta* for both the *prayājas* and the *anuyājas*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Both are intended for both purposes.
Why? Because whatever is performed with clarified butter ought to be for that very purpose, as there is no distinction;
in this context, the *jauhava* [clarified butter] is intended for the purpose of excluding the *anuyāja* offerings.

He says: "Is it not the case that there is no statement here for the purpose of prohibiting the *anuyāja* offerings, since this—'he takes it from the *prayāja*s'—is an instruction regarding the *prayāja*s, and lacks the capacity to prohibit the *anuyāja*s?
It is replied: We do not say that this is a prohibitive statement.

However, in the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*), there is no connection with a specific purpose for the *ājya* offerings; by this statement, the *jauhava* [clarified butter] is made the purpose for the *prayāja* offerings, whereas its status as the purpose for the *anuyāja* offerings is not understood because of the absence of such a statement. Thus, it is said that this statement is for the purpose of prohibiting [the use of *jauhava*] in the *anuyāja*.
If it is argued that the same applies to the *aupabhṛta* [butter]:

If it is argued that [the *jauhava*] is seen [to be for the *anuyājas*], such that the *jauhava* is prohibited from the *anuyājas* while the *aupabhṛta* is for both purposes—let the *jauhava* be for the sake of the *prayājas*, but the *aupabhṛta* is not for both purposes.
That too would be so, just as the *jauhava* is.
How so? This also is heard to be for the sake of the *anuyājas* alone: "That which he takes in the *upabhṛt*, he takes for the *anuyājas*; for the *anuyājas* are the meters (*chandas*)."
As for the claim that this [ladle] is intended for the *anuyāja* offerings:
it would be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) because of the prohibition regarding the *juhū*.
Then, it is eightfold because of the scriptural statement.
It is heard in the scripture: "One takes eight [ladlefuls] in the *upabhṛt*.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is that butter in the *upabhṛt* consecrated by the taking with the number eight, or is the number four a subordinate quality belonging to two takings?
What, then, is the prima facie view? The number eight is the subordinate quality, not the number four belonging to two [takings].

Why? Because the number eight is heard directly; the number four is indicated by the number eight. And when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), direct statement is the more authoritative. Therefore, this is the taking [of the offering] with the number eight.
Furthermore, it is because of the favoring of the *jauhava* [clarified butter].
But in the case of two [vessels], the efficacy of the cause and the act of bringing together are equal.

The word *tu* (but) sets aside the previous position. These two [portions] are each taken four times; in this way, the reason is established for the *ātithyā* sacrifice: "The clarified butter portions are taken four times at a time, for one is not about to perform the *anuyāja* offerings here. Even if the *anuyāja* offerings were absent, this butter in the *upabhṛt* ladle would still be taken eight times. When the number eight is a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), then the plural form "the clarified butter portions" (*ājyāni*)—referring to two [sets] of four-times-taken portions—is appropriate.
Therefore, there are two [sets] of four-times-taken portions.

He says: "This is the indicative mark (liṅga); let the rule of application (prāpti) be stated. That is now explained: it is stated without reference to a specific context (anārabhya), namely, "one offers with four ladlings" (caturgṛhītaṃ juhoti) in all oblations. Therefore, even in the case of the fore-offerings (prayāja) and after-offerings (anuyāja), that [rule] cannot be set aside by the "eight ladlings" (aṣṭagṛhīta), because their spheres of application are different. For the "eight ladlings" apply to the act of taking [the butter], while the "four ladlings" apply to the act of offering; indeed, it is possible that the eight ladlings might be taken and the four ladlings offered. Thus, in this case, the state of being eight pertains to the taking.
How can one accomplish two offerings of four portions each? Therefore, these two [portions] of four portions each are taken when eight portions are being taken;
no one can accomplish two portions of four each without first taking eight portions. Therefore, these are two portions of four each.
But the *svaru* is not produced for multiple purposes, because its own term denotes its specific function.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, according to the injunction: "When one who has been initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, it is prescribed: "He binds [the animal] to a post made of Khadira wood; he binds it to a Pālāśa post; he binds it to a Rohita post. In proximity to that, another rule is taught: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*; he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Now, a doubt arises: should the *svaru* be produced separately from the sacrificial post, or should a splinter that is produced as a byproduct while the post is being fashioned be taken?

In this regard, we must first examine this: is the *svaru* the motivator (*prayojaka*) for the production of the cutting and so forth, or is it not the motivator? If it is the motivator, then it would be produced separately from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
If it is not the motivator, then the splinter (*śakala*), being produced as a byproduct of the sacrificial post being fashioned, will be taken up [as the *svaru*].
How, then, could it be the motivator? Or how could it not be the motivator?

If this is the mode of expression—that which is denoted by the word *svaru* is the object to be brought into being—how so? By means of specific procedures such as the act of selecting (*joṣaṇa*) and so forth.
Consequently, when it is said, "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*," that which is understood to be the *svaru* will be taken up; therefore, it is the motivator (*prayojaka*).

Now, if it is understood thus—"he anoints the animal with the *svaru*," where the *svaru* itself is not yet known—only this much is understood of it: "anointing is performed by means of it. Furthermore, [the text] "he makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post" (*yūpa*) assigns a portion of the post to the function of anointing. Therefore, it is not a motive for action (*aprayojaka*).
Moreover, one might suspect [it refers to] a different species [of wood].
From this as well, it is understood that the *svaru* originates from an independent [piece of wood].
Why? Because there arises a suspicion regarding a different species, namely another tree.

How so? "One should not make the *svaru* from anything else; if one were to make the *svaru* from another tree, others would follow after his world; therefore, one makes the *svaru* from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Thus it is said.

For when a post (yūpa) is being prepared, there can be no suspicion that it is of a different species when it comes to its cutting; for at that time, a chip of the post (yūpa-śakala) is employed for the function of the sacrificial stake (svaru). Therefore, the svaru must be produced separately from the post.
Alternatively, it is a part of that [post], because its status as a svaru is caused by that [connection].

But has it not been said that here a part of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*), while the production of the *svaru* is [enjoined] by direct statement (*śruti*), and direct statement is stronger than syntactical connection?
It is replied: True, it is so; however, in that case, the word "of the sacrificial post" (*yūpasya*) would have its meaning unintended.
Therein, both direct statement and syntactical connection would be sublated.

But in our view, nothing is intended to be non-literal; the statement "he makes the *svaru*" will be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of its own meaning, and a splinter of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*) will be enjoined. It is understood that the word *svaru* is applied metaphorically (*upacarita*) to the splinter for the purpose of anointing, and the well-known etymological derivation (*avayava-prasiddhi*) will convey this meaning. For there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Now, why is it called *svaru*? Because from this [post] it is cut off, and thus this becomes like its own (*sva*) wound (*āru*), therefore it is called *svaru*."
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the whole.
And because it is seen at each sacrificial post.

For this reason as well, the *svaru* is not produced separately. Why? Because it is observed in the context of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice that there is one for each sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as it says: "Having anointed the animals in order with the *svarus*, he hides each respective splinter of the post within its own loop of the middle cord. This demonstrates the plurality of *svarus*. If the *svaru* were produced separately [as a single item], then a single one would suffice to accomplish the purpose throughout the *ekādaśinī* by means of a common procedure (*tantra*).

However, regarding the taking [of a chip] from that which has not yet been produced as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), since in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the anointing was performed with a chip from its own post (*svayūpa-śakala*), the extended injunction (*codaka*) likewise brings about the use of a chip from its own post even in the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice; thus, the plurality [of chips] becomes logically established.

Furthermore, the taking of a chip from its own post is determined by the taking of the archetypal one, in the sense that "just as this archetypal one is, so should this one be taken, not something different.
Therefore, the *svaru* is not the motivator (*prayojaka*) for its production.
The word "karoti" (he does) is used in the sense of taking up.
Now, as for what was said—that its production is expressed by the word, so that the word "makes" (*karoti*) will be appropriate in the expression "he makes the *svaru*"—it is replied:

the word "makes" will apply to the act of taking up; "he makes the *svaru*" means "he takes up the *svaru*. Just as the word "makes" is used in the sense of taking up in such expressions as "he makes [fuel] from wood" or "he makes [cakes] from cow-dung," so too should it be understood here.
Because that [the sacrifice] is the primary subject in the section.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, with reference to the sacrificial branch (śākhā), it is heard in the scripture: "He brings [the branch] from the east," "He brings it from the north," and "He brings it from the northeast.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this a statement concerning directions (digvāda), or is it a statement concerning the branch (śākhāvāda)? The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is a statement concerning directions, because in that case the word is used in its primary sense (śruti); whereas in the case of a statement concerning the branch, it would involve figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, it is called the "discussion on the direction.

This being the case, we reply: it is the "discussion on the branch. Why? If the meaning were that "the eastern direction is to be brought," then that would be an impossible task; or if the meaning were that "one should bring [something] toward the eastern direction," then the question arises, "What is to be brought? Since the word "branch" (śākhā) does not occur in the sentence, this connection is untenable.
Now, as for the phrase "the branch under discussion," it is logical that the word "eastern" (*prācī*) should be connected to that very [branch].

Why? Because the syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) of the verb "to carry" (*harati*) with the word "eastern" is directly perceived (*pratyakṣā*), whereas its connection with the word "branch" would have to be based on the context (*prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, in either case here, the word "eastern" could only indicate the branch under discussion or the direction through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*); it is not appropriate for it to indicate the place of the sacrificial site (*vihāradeśa*), since the direction is not what is primarily desired (*anīpsitatvāt*), whereas the place of the sacrificial site is what is most desired.
Because that [branch] is the primary object, the separation [of the twig] should be performed with the *upaveṣa*; that constitutes the disparity.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recited in the scriptural tradition: "Having stripped the branch from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa* (the fire-stirring stick).

Regarding this, a doubt arises as to the meaning: is both the branch and the *upaveṣa* the motive for the cutting of the branch, or is the branch the motive and the *upaveṣa* a by-product? What is the prima facie view? Both are produced from the cutting—the branch and the base of the branch—and both serve a purpose.

The driving away of the calves and so forth will be performed with the tip [of the branch], while the *upaveṣa* (fire-stirring stick) is made from the base; since there is no distinction between them in this regard, both would be the efficient cause (*prayojaka*).

This being the prima facie view, it is replied: we say that it concerns the branch, because that is the primary object; since the branch is the primary object, the separation [of the calf] should be effected by means of the *upaveṣa*.
That which is produced as a byproduct of the branch is what is taken [as the *upaveṣa*].
How is its predominance established? From the use of the accusative case in the expression "having trimmed the branch" (śākhāṃ parivāsya).
But is it not the case that there is also an accusative in "he makes the upaveṣa" (upaveṣaṃ karoti)? It is said in reply: that [upaveṣa] is not the object of the verb "to trim" (parivāsayati).

To what, then, does it belong? It belongs to the root [of the *karīra* plant]. But is it not the case that, because it is the subject under discussion, the "root" (*mūla*) is connected with the word "upaveṣa"?
It is said in reply: there would be a contradiction if it were connected to both.
Furthermore, in case of conflict, a direct statement (vākya) is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa).
Even if it were connected with what is proximate, it would still follow that it is employed by the branch (śākhā).
Therefore, it is established that the enclosing-stick (paridhi) does not necessitate the act of cutting.
This is the discrepancy here;
and because of the departure from the Vedic revelation.

In such cases as "he drives away the calves with the branch," "he brings the cows together with the branch," and "he milks [the cow] with the branch," the *upaveṣa* (the small twig used for driving) has no function; therefore, the word "branch" does not apply to it.
For they do not call its root a "branch.
What follows from this? Wherever the word "branch" occurs in this manner, the cutting is for that specific purpose, because of the use of the accusative case.

Furthermore, even if the word "branch" were to apply to the root, even so, the root would not be included among those things designated by the word "branch," because it is excluded from the category of branches. And the cutting is performed for the sake of that which is done with a consecrated branch;
moreover, the placing [of the wood] is not performed with one that has been excluded from the root.
Therefore, the cutting [of the branch] is not for that purpose.
What is the point? According to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), a branch should be produced even on the full moon day;
according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should not be produced in that manner.
But in the case of taking away, the term *juhoti* (he offers) is used because of the commonality of the act of joining and because substances are subordinate to a purpose.

[The opponent] says: "In each of those cases, the branch is subordinate; therefore, its disposal is proper. Otherwise, the consequence would be that [the branch] possesses multiple subordinate statuses.

[The author] replies: "Because substances are subsidiary to a purpose, substances are taught as being subsidiary precisely to that which is intended to be produced through their origination; for that which has already come into being (bhūta) is taught for the sake of that which is yet to be brought into being (bhavya).
Therefore, it is logical that substances indeed possess multiple subordinate statuses."
Or rather, there is the application of the word [to the universal], because that [the universal] is the primary referent.
Alternatively, the performance is the felling of the branch, because the word has that as its primary meaning;
here, the word has the branch as its primary referent. Why? Because the accusative case ending is not heard.
"But surely that second case applies only to the *prastara* [grass-bundle], not to the *śākhā* [branch]. It is replied: "The sense of the accusative applies to both the *prastara* and the *śākhā*.
How so? Because of their equal connection; it is only when the *śākhā* is also thrown in that the *prastara* becomes truly 'thrown' (*prahṛta*)."
In this context, the word *saha* denotes equality of status (*tulyayoga*).
If the *prastara* (grass-bundle) were the primary element in the act of throwing, and the *śākhā* (branch) were merely a qualifier of the *prastara*, then there would be no equality of status.
Therefore, whatever function the accusative case serves for the *prastara*, it serves for the *śākhā* as well; consequently, the *śākhā* is the primary element.
Moreover, in various instances, the branch is subordinate; when it is being disposed of elsewhere, there is no multiplicity of subordinate purposes.

What fault is there in this? One would be abandoning a visible purpose to postulate an invisible one. By removing the branch whose purpose has been fulfilled, the clearing of the altar results in the visible purpose of facilitating movement; however, by striking [the branch], not even the slightest visible result exists. Therefore, its disposal as a ritual act of realization (*pratipatti*) is logical.
If it is argued that this applies even to the object;
He said: "But surely the accusative case occurs even when something is subordinate, as in the case of *saktu*, *māruta*, and *ekakapāla* offerings.
[The reply is: No, because that [usage] does not apply here, and because the purpose has already been accomplished.

This is not comparable to the case of groats (*saktu*) and the like, because those [cases] have no application elsewhere, whereas here, by means of the branch, another purpose such as the driving away of the calf (*vatsāpākaraṇa*) has already been accomplished.
He says: "But surely this illustration of the groats and so forth, along with its resolution, is redundant.
It is replied: Redundancy is not a great fault; wholesome advice should be understood even if repeated many times. People avoid repetition only out of fear of increasing the length of the text.
However, those who fear the non-apprehension of the meaning highly value what is stated again and again.

What is the purpose of this deliberation? If it is an act for the sake of a specific result (*arthakarma*), then the *śākhā* (branch) should be produced even on the full moon day; if, however, it is a disposal (*pratipatti*), then it should not be produced.
Because there is no connection with its production, there should be a division of the *praṇītā* waters, just as in the case of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed: "He brings forward the water; for water is indeed faith (śraddhā); having obtained faith itself, he performs the sacrifice. In both cases, there is an operation involving the water brought forward (*praṇītā*): "He mixes the sacrificial oblations with the *praṇītā* waters," and likewise, "He pours out the *praṇītā* waters within the altar. Here a doubt arises: are both mixing and pouring out the motivators (*prayojaka*) for these waters, or is the pouring out merely a disposal (*pratipatti*) of those waters intended for the purpose of mixing? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? There is no connection of these [waters] at their origin with any specific purpose; rather, they are connected with both purposes once they have been produced.

Therefore, no distinction is perceived; since no distinction is perceived, this division of the purposes of both [types of butter]—that some is for the mixing [of the dough] and some is for the pouring out—is like the case of the *ājya* (clarified butter), as in the statement: "Indeed, all that *ājya* which is taken in the *dhruvā* vessel is for the sake of the entire sacrifice.
Or rather, those intended for the purpose of mixing are the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the others, because they are subordinate to that [mixing].

The *praṇītā* waters are for the purpose of kneading (*saṃyavana*). Why? Because of the use of the instrumental case, water is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) in the act of kneading; and because of the use of the accusative case, it has primacy (*prādhānya*) in the act of pouring out (*ninayana*).
The purpose of this inquiry is that in the absence of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), there is an absence of the *praṇītā* waters, as is the case with the *payasyā* offering.
The handing over of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is like the throwing [of the grass-bundle], because its purpose has already been fulfilled.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "Speech indeed departed from the gods, not remaining for the sacrifice; she entered the trees. This is that speech which speaks in the trees—[the speech] which is in the drum, which is in the flute, and which is in the lute. When he gives the staff to the consecrated one, he truly secures speech; when the Soma has been purchased, he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa. The phrase "he gives the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa" is the illustrative example.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the handing over of the staff—which is subsidiary to the holding by the initiated—to the Maitrāvaruṇa a disposal (*pratipatti*), or is it a purposeful act (*arthakarma*)? What is the prima facie view? The giving of the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa is a disposal.
Why? Because its purpose has been fulfilled through its being held by the initiated.

The phrase "they initiate with the staff" implies that the disposal (*pratipatti*) of that which has become a subordinate element (*śeṣabhūta*) elsewhere is what is logically required; just as in the case of "he throws the black antelope horn into the pit," the throwing away is the disposal of that which was subordinate during the act of scratching, so too should it be understood here.
Furthermore, the accusative case-ending is used for the staff.
Therefore, it possesses primacy.
Or rather, it is a purposeful action because of its connection with an agent, like a garland.
Now, as for what was said—that the priority of the staff follows from the absence of the accusative case—it is replied:
the accusative should be understood here according to the rule "and likewise that which is not desired [as a result] is [expressed by the accusative].
Why? Because of the use of the dative case in reference to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
For the dative case occurs in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and the recipient is that which is intended by means of the object (*karman*).
In this context, it is understood that Maitrāvaruṇa is more intended than the staff;
this is because [the dative] is seen to be used when connected with an object.
The statement "the staff-bearer recites the directions" is a restatement; by this, he displays the staff while performing the ritual action.
This is appropriate if it serves a specific purpose.

However, if it were a mere disposal (pratipatti), the staff would have been given to the Maitrāvaruṇa and then discarded once its function was fulfilled; since its task would be completed, there would be no further need for it, and thus it should not be retained.

In this regard, the following scriptural indications are not tenable: "He should say to the Maitrāvaruṇa, 'The snake bites you,' for he is like a snake"; and likewise, "Or, 'Strike with the club' (muśalyan vāha).
Furthermore, the word *muśala* is well-known to denote a staff, as in the expression, "Where indeed would the students (*māṇavaka*) carrying clubs descend into the Gaṅgā?
Therefore, it is also a ritual action (*arthakarma*).

In the case of origination, that which is connected with something for its sake [is subordinate] because it is the cause of the scriptural statement; therefore, when that [subordinate element] moves toward another purpose, there should be a performance [of the rite] because it remains a subsidiary.

Alternatively—this constitutes a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntaram*). The prima facie view (*pūrvaḥ pakṣaḥ*) is that both scratching with the horn and throwing it away are equally instrumental causes (*prayojaka*), because "since they result in a single accomplishment, everything should be equal.
The final view (*uttaraḥ pakṣaḥ*) is as follows: in the case of scratching, the horn has a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) due to its being indicated by the instrumental case;
whereas in the case of throwing it away, due to its being indicated by the accusative case and because it serves no other purpose elsewhere, it possesses primary importance (*prādhānya*).
And because its purpose has been fulfilled by the rites pertaining to Soma.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice there is the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), [prescribed by the text]: "They descend for the *avabhṛtha* with a cake on one potsherd dedicated to Varuṇa. Regarding this, it is recited: "That which is the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs) of the sacrifice, the pressing-stones, the *undubara* wood, and the two pressing-boards—these are seized by Varuṇa; therefore, they go to the *avabhṛtha* with whatever substance is smeared with Soma. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the going to the *avabhṛtha* with the substances smeared with Soma a *pratipatti* (disposal), or is it an *arthakarma* (a primary act)?
What, then, is established? That it is a *pratipatti* (a disposal).

Why? Because their purpose has been fulfilled; these substances have served their respective purposes here and there, and for them, proceeding to the *avabhṛtha* (final purificatory bath) as a *pratipatti* is logical.
Or rather, it is a primary act (*arthakarma*), because of its connection with a specific designation.
Or rather, it is the performance [of the rite], because that is logical; thus there is the scriptural mention of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) for the sake of the region.
Or it is a preparatory act (*pratipatti*).
Why? Precisely because of that same principle.

For this is the principle: when something that has served its purpose in one place is prescribed for another, then here, if the substance smeared with *soma* were enjoined as the instrument for the *avabhṛtha*, it would therefore be a primary act (*arthakarma*).
Now, if the act of going [to the water] is enjoined as being smeared with Soma, then it is a disposal (*pratipatti*).

For in this case, what is smeared with Soma is not enjoined in relation to the *avabhṛtha* bath; for if that were so, the connection between the *avabhṛtha* and what is smeared with Soma would have to be enjoined by the verb "they descend" (*abhyavayanti*).

In that case, the injunction would be by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*), and not by direct assertion (*śruti*); whereas when the act of going is enjoined by this [verb], the injunction is by direct assertion.
That [conclusion] is accepted; moreover, direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*), therefore there is a ritual application (*pratipatti*).

Now, as for what was said—that it is because of the connection with the designation of a primary act (*arthakarman*)—to that we reply: this being the case, the Vedic mention of the *avabhṛtha* (final purificatory bath) has the purpose of indicating a location. In the phrase "they go to the *avabhṛtha*," one indicates a location by means of the *avabhṛtha*, meaning "they go to that location where the *avabhṛtha* takes place."
Therefore, it is a performance;
there is no injunction regarding the agent, place, or time, because they are eternally inherent in the performance.
Or rather, the scriptural statement is for the purpose of restriction.
It is said: this is not a restatement (*anuvāda*), for a mere restatement is purposeless.
If it is an injunction (*vidhi*), it will thus bring about a previously unknown matter (*apūrva*); therefore, it is an injunction.
[Objection: But surely it is already established because it is a constituent part of the performance (*prayoga*).
It is said: the scriptural statement will serve as a restrictive rule (*niyama*).
What is this restriction? It is the restriction of that which was unrestricted. As a constituent part of the ritual performance, all locations are applicable, but not simultaneously.
When it is level, then it is not uneven; when it is uneven, then it is not level.

This very [equal] is both attained and unattained; when it is not attained, that position necessitates an injunction. Therefore, even when there is a desire to perform an unequal act, the equal is enjoined.
Consequently, since the non-attainment of the unequal occurs when there is an injunction, the equal is enjoined.
The same applies to the others as well; therefore, it is an injunction.
Likewise, in the case of substances, there is a mention of qualities because of their connection with the originative injunction.
And because that [volition] is predominant among the formative forces (saṃskāra).
This is also a point of discussion regarding legal injunctions (*adhikaraṇāpradeśa*).

In connection with the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it is heard in the scripture: "One threshes the rice-grains (*vrīhi*)," and "One grinds the rice-particles (*taṇḍula*). Regarding this, is there a doubt as to whether these two are original injunctions (*vidhi*) or mere restatements (*anuvāda*)?

When the doubt arises that they are restatements because the actions are already established by worldly necessity, the conclusion is reached that they are indeed injunctions because they serve the purpose of restriction (*niyama*).
The injunction to sacrifice pertains to the action involving a substance and a deity, because its purpose is fulfilled in the aggregate.
Because it is heard stated thus, the *juhoti* sacrifice should consist of pouring [the offering] in addition [to the other actions].

Now, what is the defining characteristic of the root *hu* (to sacrifice)? When the meaning expressed by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is stated, the word *juhoti* is heard as being used when there is an addition of pouring [libations].
Therefore, *juhoti* is simply the root *yaj* with the addition of pouring; for in common worldly usage, people speak of someone in such a manner as "he has sacrificed (*huta*) by means of this."

Even in the Veda, that which is enjoined by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is restated by means of the root *hu* (to offer): "One should cause a warrior to sacrifice with the Caturhotṛ formula; having prepared the clarified butter taken in four portions, he should recite the Caturhotṛ formula; he should offer one half with the first ladle-full and the other half with the latter.
Now, what is the defining characteristic of the act of giving (*dadāti*)?
It is the removal of one's own ownership and the establishment of a connection with another's ownership.
In all cases of *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti*, the act of relinquishment (*utsarga*) is common.

Among them, *yajati* consists merely of relinquishment directed toward a deity; *juhoti* is that same act with the addition of pouring (*āsecana*); and *dadāti* is the establishment of a connection with another as owner, preceded by relinquishment—this is the distinction between them.
Because an injunction (*vidhi*) culminates in the completion of an action, there would be an extension of the injunction to other matters.
