What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since there is no scriptural injunction that imposes a restriction, there is no fixed order.

This being the case, we reply: they must be regulated by sequence within a single sacrifice. Why? Because they are subordinate to that [sacrifice]. For the subordination of ritual elements is understood from the sentence; just as in the cases "one should bathe," "one should anoint," and "one should eat," the performance of these acts is understood to follow a specific sequence according to the sentence.

Just as when matters concerning invisible results are being taught, someone might say: "Incense should be offered to the deity, flowers should be scattered, he should be anointed with sandalwood, and an oblation should be presented to him; when this is done, the deity becomes pleased. Another person replies to him: "It is not so; incense should not be given first; rather, flowers should be scattered first. This [second person] thinks: "He has stated that the offering of incense must come first."
Therefore, this sequence of theirs is based on explicit scriptural statement.
If it is argued that it is not based on the word, [we reply] that it would indeed be so, because it is expressed by the words of the sentence.
If you view it thus, then in this way being understood, the sequence itself would be non-verbal.
How so? The meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of the words, and from the words only the word-meanings are understood, not the sequence.

This might be so if the hearing of a collection of word-meanings were the conveyor of the [sentence] meaning; however, it is not the aggregate that conveys it, as was stated in the passage: "The mention of those [word-meanings] which have come into being is for the sake of the action."

Therefore, since there is no word expressive of sequence, this sequence is understood only through delusion. In this way, the non-existence of the *apūrva* will be supported; otherwise, even that would be displaced like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*). And [the author] will demonstrate this: "He cuts from the heart first, then from the tongue, then from the chest."
If the order of recitation were restrictive, then this [rule] should not be enjoined; for if the order of recitation were restrictive, it would be obtained from that very order of recitation.

Or rather, there would be an inference based on purpose: since the sacrifice is a single unit and exists for the sake of another, its connection is with its own specific purpose; therefore, it should be expressed by its own word.
And likewise, there is the observation of another meaning.
And thus he shows another purpose: he places the *ṛtavyā* bricks in reverse order; he recites the *ṣoḍaśin* chant in reverse order;
the cup for the Aśvins is drawn as the tenth, yet it is offered as the third.
If the placing [of the ladles] and the recitation were not governed by a fixed order, then the mention of their transposition would be purposeless;

for there is no way that they could not be transposed. Likewise, the reference to the third offering of the Āśvina cup would not be possible if there were a fixed rule according to the order of the text.

Furthermore, regarding the injunction that "one practicing sorcery should offer in reverse order, for he thus drives back his [victim's] vital breaths," which indicates the regular order while prescribing the reverse, this is only logical if the performance follows the order of the text.

Otherwise, everything would be in direct order (*anuloma*), and the observation of reverse order (*pratiloma*) would not be possible. Furthermore, when it is stated that "one brings back the fourth and the last," and then it is said, "having passed over the *iḍā*, one brings back the *barhis*," this indicates that the *barhis* occupies the fourth position; this is only consistent if the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is the regulating factor.
This is because, according to the principle of *pravṛtti*, among qualities performed simultaneously, the sequence follows the commencement of the first.
This being the case, we reply: since the first [item] has been commenced, the second and subsequent items must likewise be commenced from that very point.

Why is this so? Because of the commencement of that; for all items must not be separated from the time of the principal act, as the principal is either what is intended to be performed or the occasion for their performance.

For there is an injunction stating that "the principal [act] must be performed together with the constituent elements"; however, because many constituent elements are enumerated, a separation [of the principal act from each element] is inevitable. Nevertheless, one must necessarily allow a separation only by as many [intervening acts] as are required so that the constituent element can be performed without being interrupted; it must not be separated by more than that. If one were to begin the second constituent element from another point, one would separate it by even more [intervening acts], and thus one would contradict the injunction regarding the performance order (*prayogavacana*).
[Objection: But if that were the case, would there not be some [interruption] separated by only a few [steps]?

[Reply: It is said: by abandoning those interruptions that are permitted, some superior quality arises; therefore, from the very point where the preceding member of the compound was begun, from that same point the subsequent one should be commenced.
[Objection: "The whole" (sarva) [is the term to be used].

If you think that because of its proximity to the primary act, it is favored by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), then the entire section on subsidiaries (*guṇakāṇḍa*) must be completed within a single [performance], as in the case of the *saurya* and other such rites;
for it has not yet been performed.
This is not so; for in that case, the simultaneous performance itself would not be carried out.
If it is argued that this is like other sacrifices (*kratu*), [we reply: no.
Now, as for what was said—that it is as in the case of other sacrifices such as the Saurya and others—that must be refuted:
"No, because of the lack of connection."
For them, no sequence is obtained from the meaning that could be restricted;
for a restriction must pertain to subsidiaries (aṅga), whereas for that which does not rest upon a subsidiary, its status as a subsidiary would have to be postulated [de novo].
Furthermore, [the order is determined] by position (sthāna) because of its connection with the originative injunction.
Since it would follow that the restriction here is established merely by the order of recitation in the traditional text (samāmnāya), resulting in tautology, it is explained otherwise:
"And because of position, due to connection with the origin."

In the Sādyaska sacrifice, it is heard: "He offers the animals together. Regarding this, the following point has been established: the offering of all three occurs at the time of the Savanīya. Now, in this case, by virtue of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), should the Agnīṣomīya be offered first, or, by virtue of the order of position (*sthānakrama*), should the Savanīya be offered first?
What is established? That the Agniṣomīya comes first.
Why? Because of the order of recitation.
This being the case, we reply: the Savanīya comes first, because of its position.
If the Agniṣomīya were to occur first, the position of the Savanīya would be obstructed;
for [the text] says, "Having drawn the Āśvina cup, one should encircle the sacrificial post with a threefold cord.
But would not the order of recitation be violated even in the other case?
Let it be set aside; for the word "together" (saha) is traditionally recited for the purpose of prohibiting that [order], and the position of the Āśvina cup is not prohibited.
Therefore, it should not be set aside, because the subsidiaries follow the order of the principal, as they exist for its sake.
But in the case of the original form (prakṛti), because it is expressed by its own word, it should be understood according to the respective order.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the ritual details for the vegetable offerings (oṣadhi) are prescribed first, followed by those for the clarified butter (ājya).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the ritual details for the clarified butter be performed first according to the order of the principal acts (mukhyakrama), or according to the order of the textual recitation (pāṭhakrama)? [The prima facie view is:
according to the favor of the order of the principal acts, the details of the clarified butter should come first.

This being the position, we reply: in the archetype (prakṛti), the order should be understood according to the recitation; for their own words constitute that order of recitation, and it would be sublated if it were performed otherwise.

Furthermore, the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) is the subsumer of simultaneity; when the constituent elements (padārtha) are brought into proximity according to their own order, that injunction will not be sublated.
Moreover, the word "own" refers to the order of recitation, as in the rule: "One's own Veda (svādhyāya) is to be studied."
The syntactic unity with the injunction of performance according to the primary order is subtle;
however, in case of conflict, it should be determined by the mantra, because of the capacity of the form of the performance; therefore, that is the place of origin.
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the mantra-text for the Āgneya offering comes first, while that of the Brāhmaṇa follows later.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: which textual order is more authoritative?
It is said in reply: there is no fixed rule, because there is no scriptural injunction that establishes such a rule.
By virtue of that statement, in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), it should be according to the principal [element].

There is a sacrifice named Adhvarakalpā, for which it is prescribed: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu; Sarasvatī should have a portion of clarified butter; there should be a pap for Bṛhaspati. In this regard, a doubt arises: should the ritual details (*dharmāḥ*) of the Bārhaspatya offering—which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the Āgneya—be performed first, because the extended injunction (*codaka*) is stronger than the performance-injunction (*prayogavacana*)? Or rather, is the performance-injunction stronger than the extended injunction, [making the details of the Upāṃśuyāja—the modification of which the Bārhaspatya is a variant—to be performed first]?
What is established? In this modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the procedure should follow the primary elements, because of the scriptural statement regarding them;
for in the modified sacrifice, the sequence of those [elements] is directly stated.

Therefore, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) is indeed perceptible as it summarizes those things that are present, whereas the properties of those [elements] are inferential, since they are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).

Therefore, the explicit statement of the application (prayogavacana) is more powerful as it is directly perceived; by it, the inferred injunction (codaka) is sublated. Or, in case of conflict, according to the connection with the archetype (prakṛti), it should be as in the archetype.
Because the modification possesses the nature of the original form, it should take place at that same time, as prescribed by tradition.

Among the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Sākamedha is the third festival (parvan). Its constituent parts are: an eight-potherd cake for Agni Anīkavat in the morning; a pap (caru) for the Maruts Sāṃtapana at midday; and boiled rice in the milk of all [the cows] for the Maruts Gṛhamedhin in the evening. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these offerings (iṣṭis) to be performed over two days, or are they to be completed on a single day (sadyaskālā)? What is the prima facie view? A modified sacrifice (vikṛti) ought to follow the time of its model (prakṛti), just as it is taught; just as the model is stated, so should the modification be.
For that [sacrifice] has the nature of the archetype; therefore, whatever modification there may be ought to have a duration of two days.
Alternatively, if it were performed immediately in connection with a specific sequence of time, there would be a loss of the archetypal characteristics due to the inference of a different injunction.
If it is argued that there is an extension of time;

If you see it thus—that [the sacrifice] is prescribed with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) for the midday and the evening as well—then there will be a displacement (*utkarṣa*), so that it may be performed with its parts at these times.
Nor is there any sublation of the two-day duration; one would commence the *Anīkavat* on the morning of the first day and perform the sacrifice on the morning of the second.
Likewise, the *Sāṃtapanīyā* will be commenced on the previous day at midday and performed on the following day at midday.
Likewise, in the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, the commencement takes place on the previous day in the evening, while the sacrifice itself occurs on the following day in the evening.
Now, it was argued that from the sentence (vākya) only a single day is understood;
to this it is replied: for the meaning of a sentence arises from the capacity of the meanings of its constituent words.
Nor is there here any semantic force in the word-meanings by which a single day could be understood;
it is not [understood] through connection with that.
This is not so.
Why? Because of their connection; the principal acts are heard in scripture as being connected with their subsidiaries at a single time.
How so? For the principal act together with its subsidiaries is heard to be performed in the morning, and likewise at midday and in the evening.
The auxiliary parts [are not restricted] to the morning time and so forth;
for in that case, since the auxiliaries would belong to one time and the primary rites to another, the sacrifice would not have been performed with its auxiliaries at those times.
Therefore, these modified sacrifices (vikṛtis) must indeed be performed on the same day.

Moreover, it is heard in scripture: "One should perform the Sākamedha sacrifices for two days. This is appropriate for those [Sākamedhas] that have an immediate time (sadyaskāla), because the subsidiaries follow the time of the principal, as has been stated regarding displacement (utkarṣa).

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "They proceed with the after-offerings (anuyāja) after the Āgnimāruta [offering]"; this is an upward displacement (utkarṣa). Likewise, in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, it is said: "They perform the fore-offerings (prayāja) while the animal stands"; this is a downward displacement (apakarṣa). In this regard, there is a doubt: at the time of upward displacement, is only the after-offering displaced, and at the time of downward displacement, is only the fore-offering displaced; or rather, at the time of upward displacement, is everything from the after-offering onwards displaced, and at the time of downward displacement, is everything up to the fore-offering displaced?
What, then, is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? It should be as much as has been stated: that in cases of upward and downward displacement, only the specific elements mentioned are displaced.
Why? Because the subsidiaries have the time of the principal as their own time;
thus, the other subsidiaries will likewise have the time of the principal. In that case, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which establishes their simultaneity, will be upheld.
Or rather, because of the connection starting from that [first] point, there would be an extraction ending with that [last] point.
In that case, [the sequence] would be understood as beginning with the first in the case of an ascending order, and ending with the last in the case of a descending order.
Why? Because of the connection.

That which is recited after the *anuyāja* offerings is performed after the *anuyāja*s by virtue of the force of the textual order (*pāṭha*), overriding what was obtained through the performance injunction (*prayoga-vacana*) as being intermediate to the principal rite; likewise, whatever follows that is placed after that.
Thus, when one [factor] is elevated, it elevates the entire category of qualities; likewise, when it is depressed, it depresses them.
This is according to the sequence of those whose time has been determined.

This being the case, we reply: for those items whose time is determined by their performance (*pravṛtti*), there must be a restriction based on that performance; for one indeed restricts the preceding item while it is being performed. That [subsequent item] is recorded after it, and thus it is to be performed later.
However, in the case of the *saumika* item—the *pracaraṇī-homa*—the sequence is set aside by a direct scriptural injunction.

Furthermore, the *alaṃkaraṇa* (adorning) of the *bahiṣpavamāna* is prescribed after [the *nirvapaṇa*]; therefore, the ritual act preceding that belongs to the end of the *nirvapaṇa* and other such rites.
Consequently, the subsequent Soma-related acts are to be performed.
This is also because of the contradiction with the verbal injunction.
Furthermore, the verbal form would be contradicted; for if one were told "decorate," he would instead undertake acts such as sprinkling.
In our view, however, when told "decorate," he will understand only the act of decorating.
In that regard, since the time for decorating has arrived, the imperative ending (*loṭ*) expressing the arrival of the proper time will be favored.
Therefore, in this case, the order is that of the primary performance (prāvṛttika);
however, because there is no connection [with the original context], that very modified element (vaikṛta) would be drawn forward.

This being the case, we reply: that which is additional in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), when it is postponed, cannot cause the postponement of even those elements preceding it, such as the carrying forward of the fire and Soma (agnīṣomapraṇayana) and so forth.

Why? Because of the lack of connection (asaṃyoga). The ritual action concerning the sacrificial post (yūpakarma) belongs to the animal sacrifice (pāśuka), while that which precedes it belongs to the Soma sacrifice (saumika);
there is no mutual relationship between the two.
An item belonging to the Soma sacrifice is neither an auxiliary to the animal sacrifice nor to the animal itself.
For if it were an auxiliary to those two, then its sequence—by assisting that which assists them—would be subordinate to them.
But this is not the case; therefore, there is no rule regarding their mutual sequence.
Therefore, only the sacrificial post (yūpa) is drawn forward.
Moreover, since the word has fulfilled its purpose by being drawn forward only for the post, there will be no subversion of the own-order (svakrama) of the Soma-related rites.
And one should not draw forward what is incidental (prāsaṅgika), because of the lack of connection.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "After the Āgnimāruta [offering], they proceed with the after-offerings (anuyājas). There arises a doubt: when the after-offerings are displaced, do they displace the two oblations belonging to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, or not? [The answer is:
because of their connection, they do displace them.
And likewise, it was unprecedented.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the altar (vedi) is prescribed to be prepared after the covering of the oblation materials.

However, in the case of the New Moon sacrifice (Amāvāsyā), it is drawn forward [in time], as it is stated: "On the day before the Amāvāsyā, one prepares the altar. Regarding this, there arises a doubt: when that [altar] is drawn forward, does it draw forward the ritual elements (padārtha) that precede it, or not?
It is said: "Because of the connection, one draws [the details] back.

This being the position reached, we reply: likewise, as in the case of the *apūrva* (novelty). In the original *Amāvāsyā* sacrifice, the preparation of the altar (*vedi*) is prescribed on the previous day, while the covering of the sacrificial oblation (*havir-abhivāsana*) occurs on the following day for both [the *Darśa* and *Pūrṇamāsa*].

There is no basis—such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) or any other means of proof—for the claim that the altar must be prepared on the *Amāvāsyā* day immediately after performing the covering of the oblation.

Therefore, the rites ending with the *abhivāsana* (the covering of the fire) should not be postponed. If the *abhivāsana* were postponed, the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) would be reduced to ashes.

However, one should postpone the *sāṃtapanīyā* offering; the *agnihotra* should follow it, because otherwise there would be a deficiency in the ritual sequence, as in the case of the *savana* offerings.
And because there is no intervention.

In this way, the Sāṃtapanīya will not be separated from the Agnihotra; thus, the sequence will be maintained. For it is heard as a fault regarding the breaking of sequence: "The sacrifice is indeed cut off from the ritual when the procedure (tantra) of one is undertaken while the procedure of another is already extended. However, because there is no connection [between them], one should not postpone [the Sāṃtapanīya].
The Sāṃtapanīyā is not an auxiliary of the Agnihotra, nor is the Agnihotra an auxiliary of the Sāṃtapanīyā.
Therefore, that [Sāṃtapanīyā] need not be performed prior to the Agnihotra; consequently, the Agnihotra need not be postponed.
This is also because the occasion [for the Sāṃtapanīyā] has already arrived.
Now, as for what was said— that it should be postponed like the *savana*s— it is replied:
the postponement of the *savana*s occurs because of their connection [to them].
For the pressing is indeed connected with the pressing because of its connection to a single sacrifice; thus it is displaced, as is the Ṣoḍaśin, due to its association with the Ukthya.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma, regarding the Ṣoḍaśin, it is heard in scripture: "One draws that [cup] after the Ukthyas. When, due to a divine or human obstacle, the Ukthyas are postponed, there arises a doubt: should the Ṣoḍaśin then be postponed as well, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should not be postponed.
Why? Because in this way, the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra will be performed at its own proper time; for it assists the *ṣoḍaśin* stotra when the sun has risen.
Therefore, there is no displacement [of the stotra].
In the case of a conjunction of principal acts, the subsidiary elements of each one should constitute the entire ritual action.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "One should immolate seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati. And in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the ritual duties for the animal are prescribed and extended to this case by the rule of transfer (codaka). Regarding these, a doubt arises: should one perform all the duties for the first animal from beginning to end, and then start again from the beginning for the second; or rather, should all the duties for the first be performed first, and then those for the second?
What is the prima facie view? That all the duties should be completed for each individual animal one by one.
Why? For the sake of favoring the proximity of the primary acts; otherwise, the proximity of the primary acts would be disrupted.
Just as when many horses have been received and there are sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) for them, there is no sequential performance (anusamaya) by kind, so it is here as well.
Or rather, all [the cakes] are of one kind, because the sequence has already been established.
A simultaneous performance (*ekajātīyānusamaya*) must be carried out.

What will happen by doing so? Simultaneity (*sahatva*) will be maintained; that simultaneity is heard [in the scripture]: "Having performed the *vaiśvadevī* sacrifice, they proceed with the animal sacrifices," which implies the performance of the animal sacrifices at one and the same time. But if this is the case, would not the subsequent ritual act be separated from the preceding ritual act by the operation of another animal sacrifice?
This is not a fault; even so, the sequence is indeed established.
That very operation which occurs in the case of another animal is itself [the same here], it is not a different entity; there is no intervention by a separate category of thing.
The repetition arises from the cause.
Now, as for what was said—that when there are many sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), there can be no *anusamaya* (sequential performance) of those of the same kind—that must be refuted.

To this it is replied: It is appropriate in that case because of the underlying reason; for if *anusamaya* of the same kind were performed, once the placing on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) of a thousand [cakes] had been done, the first one would burn, and its [required subsequent action] could not be performed first.
Or rather, this is a different topic (*adhikaraṇa*).
Repetition occurs because of a specific cause.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when accepting many thousands of horses, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) should be performed [once for all]. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that one must follow the sequence of the sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*).
And in the cases of the handfuls, the potsherds, the cuttings, the collyrium, the anointing, the shaving, and the purifications, it is done with a single [performance].
But all [the factors] have a single function because they possess that quality.

However, one should perform [the ritual] after completing all [the parts], for the offering of a single handful (*muṣṭi*) is not the constituent element (*padārtha*), since the act of offering (*nirvāpa*) possesses the number four.
How is there the number four? Because of the connection of the word "four" with the verb "to offer"; thus, together with the action, it is logical to enjoin multiple qualities.
Otherwise, if there were a connection with the handful, a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result.
And it would follow that the act of pouring out [the oblation] is merely a subordinate part [of the rite].
The same applies to the placing [of the potsherds] and so forth, because of the injunction: "He pours out [the offering] on eight potsherds, on eleven potsherds.
Likewise, in such cases as "he cuts off twice," "he anoints thrice," and "he purifies with twenty-one [stalks]," numbers and other such qualities become attributes of the action.
Therefore, the sequence [of the ritual] is according to the collection [of parts].
But when [the parts] are conjoined, by virtue of the context, that would be a subsidiary part of the other, because the latter has that as its purpose.
But on account of the scriptural statement, the rites beginning with the anointing should extend up to the end of the encircling.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, regarding the animal offering to Agni and Soma, the ritual acts such as the anointing of the sacrificial post (yūpa) are prescribed. When these acts are extended to a set of eleven posts (yūpaikādaśinī), a doubt arises: is there a sequential performance (anusamaya) for each individual act, such as the anointing, or is it from the beginning with the anointing up to the end with the encircling (parivyāṇa)? What is the prima facie view? The acts beginning with the anointing should extend up to the encircling. Why? Because of a scriptural injunction; for there is this scriptural statement: "The sacrificer should not touch the post after the anointing until the encircling."

Furthermore, it is not possible to perform the *anusamaya* (successive performance) by means of collyrium and so forth when there are many [sacrificial posts], nor is it possible to refrain from discharging them.
Therefore, the *anusamaya* concludes with the binding (*parivyāṇa*).
Or rather, there may be a non-discharge for a specific reason, as in the case of the increase of the vessels (*pātravṛddhi*).

The statement regarding the performance (*prayoga-vacana*), which brings about simultaneous action (*sahatva*), will be accepted as providing assistance; thus, there is a sequential performance according to the individual items (*padārtha*).
Furthermore, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), non-abandonment (*anavasarga*) is established by implication, meaning that the sacrificer provides assistance to the Adhvaryu.
In this way, the non-abandonment serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*); otherwise, it would have only an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).
Furthermore, the injunction does not bring about anything by implication.

Therefore, one should release [the animal] for the purpose of raising another sacrificial post (*yūpa*), just as when it is said, "He performs the after-sacrifices with speckled butter," a vessel is separately prepared by implication for its holding.
Or rather, since it is established by the word itself, the other case is merely a logical inference; the enlargement of the vessel occurs by implication.

Nor is there a sequential performance (anusamaya) according to each individual ritual act (padārtha); rather, the sequential performance should be according to the group of acts ending with the encircling (parivyāṇa).

For in the archetype (prakṛti), there is no relinquishing [of the post] due to the nature of the verbal injunction; indeed, even without the sacrificer, the Adhvaryu is able to raise the sacrificial post.
If it is argued that this is for the sake of convenience (saukarya):
The word "injunction" would be sublated; for in this way, it would be restricted to a visible purpose alone, just as facing east is restricted to eating.
Therefore, because [the simultaneous performance] is impossible, there is sequential performance according to the section on constituent elements (*padārtha*).
Furthermore, the prescriptive statement (*prayogavacana*) is merely a logical principle; the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) is stronger than that.
The increase of the sacrificial vessel, however, should be performed according to the purpose;
in the case of a herd of animals, one should set aside a portion for each individual animal because of their singularity.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there are animals dedicated to Prajāpati.

Regarding them, a doubt arises: should one take the portions for the deities from each individual animal, then the portions for Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt, and then the portions for the *iḍā* goddess; or should there be a sequential grouping (*anusamaya*) by deities—meaning the portions for the deities from all animals together, then the portions for Sviṣṭakṛt, and then the portions for the *iḍā*?

What, then, is the established position? One should cut off the entirety of each [animal] and then offer it, because of the scriptural statement in the archetype; this same rule, by means of the extended application (*codaka*), applies to the *prājāpatya* offerings as well, since they share the same ritual procedure with the deities.
And because the mantra possesses meaningfulness.
In this way, the *manotā* mantra will constitute a single ritual procedure (*tantra*); otherwise, it would have to occur in rotation.

Therefore, there is [one set of] mantras for the deities for the offerings to the deities, for the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offerings for the *sauviṣṭakṛta* offerings, and for the *aiḍa* offerings for the *aiḍa* offerings.
In the case of various seeds, there is only one mortar, because it is sufficient for all.

In the Rājasūya sacrifice there is an offering of various grains (*nānābījeṣṭi*), such as: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Gṛhapati of *sūti* grains; a pap of *śyāmāka* to Soma Vanaspati," and so forth. However, the archetypal act of threshing (*prākṛtāvahanti*) is also present therein. Regarding this, a doubt arises: should there be a single mortar used in succession for these, or should there be many mortars used simultaneously?

Whence arises this doubt? If the spreading of the black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) and so forth are distinct ritual acts (*padārtha*), then there is a difference [of performance]. But if the spreading of the black antelope skin and so forth, up to the preparation of the rice grains (*taṇḍula-nirvṛtti*), constitute a single ritual act, then there is a *tantra* (common performance). What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it is one.
Why? Because it exists through alternation (*paryāyeṇa*).
Since [the result] is established by the appropriation of one [cause], the appropriation of a second would be purposeless.
Therefore, it is a "tantra" (a single, continuous system).
Or rather, there is an increase [in the number of observances], because the sequence of restrictive rules is for that purpose.

There would be an increase in the number of mortars, for a fixed sequence established by the textual recitation is appropriate only when there is simultaneity; furthermore, there is a sequential performance of the constituent acts (*padārtha*), and the acts such as spreading [the grass] below are distinct acts because they conclude with the act of pressing (*yatībhāva*) and are denoted by the words "spreading below" and so forth.
Therefore, there is an increase.
Or rather, there is only one mortar, because the act of threshing exists for the sake of that [single purpose], namely, the state of being rice-grains (*taṇḍulabhāva*).

There would be a single mortar used in turn; for there is only one set of items, beginning with the spreading [of the grain] and ending with the husked rice. The spreading and so forth are the commencement of the act of threshing (*hanti*), and everything up to the husking (*phalīkaraṇa*) is its remainder, since the purpose of the threshing is the production of rice. In this way, the spreading and so forth, as well as the threshing, will not have a transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
Therefore, it is a *tantra* (a common performance).
But in the case of a modification, there should be a distinction of vessels for the after-offerings (anuyāja), because of the difference in purpose.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma; regarding this, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs the after-sacrifices (anuyājas) with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya). In this regard, a doubt arises: is there a single vessel for holding both the clarified butter (ājya) and the speckled butter for the fore-sacrifices (prayājas) and after-sacrifices, or are they distinct? What is the prima facie view? That there is one. Why? Because in the archetype (prakṛti), there is one; as in the archetype, so here too, there ought to be one.
Now, it might be argued that since *pṛṣadājya* is indeed *ājya*, its being mixed does not constitute a fault.
This is not so; for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the purpose of the purification (*utpavana*) and inspection (*avekṣaṇa*) is precisely this: that the *ājya* remains unmixed with any other substance.
If this is the case, then it is untenable that the *prayāja* offerings should be performed with *pṛṣadājya*.
Moreover, this being the case, a certain portion of the oblation must necessarily be set aside.

And it is not possible to take what remains for the sake of the *anuyāja*s once the function of the *prayāja*s has been completed; for in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the taking [of the portions] occurs at one and the same time, and here too it must be performed at one and the same time.

Therefore, it is called "the breaking of the vessel. Since the subject matter has been previously mentioned, that which is not previously mentioned would occur at the end; for there is no mention of a supplementary part (śeṣa) for what has not been enjoined.
In the *Agnau Nakṣatreṣṭi*, it is heard [in the scripture]: "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Agni Kṛttikā.
There, the oblations are prescribed as follows: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to the Kṛttikās! and so forth.
However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there are the *Nāriṣṭa* oblations.

In this regard, there is a doubt: whether the *nāriṣṭa* oblations come first, or the *upahoma*s. To resolve this doubt, it is said: the archetypal (*prākṛta*) should come first, and the modified (*vaikṛta*) should be at the end. Why? Because the supplement (*śeṣa*) is prescribed for that which has been enjoined and completed, just as a toy is provided for a son who has already been born.

According to Ātreya, there should be immediate succession with the primary; because the scriptural statement is identical, and since there is no verbal indication [of interruption], there would be an intervention by the archetypal elements.
Ātreya held the view that the immediate sequence belongs to the modified (vaikṛta) rite; however, the original (prākṛta) rite should be performed afterwards.
Since the recitation of the modified rite occurs immediately after the principal [rite], the *upahomas* should come first and then the *nāriṣṭhahomas*.
There would be an interruption of the original rites, because they are not explicitly heard [in the text].
But Bādarāyaṇa holds that they [are the breaths], because among them [the term] is primarily used.

The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, held the view that the performance of the modified (*vaikṛta*) elements occurs at the end. Why? Because they are grasped by the word denoting the primary act (*pradhāna*). The archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries are grasped by the word denoting the primary; for those archetypal subsidiaries are indeed grasped by that word denoting the primary. And this [modified element] follows after that word denoting the primary, such as: "He offers here with [the formula], 'To Agni, svāhā! To the Kṛttikās, svāhā! and so forth.
Therefore, according to the directly perceived sequence, the *upahoma*s (supplementary offerings) come after the *nāriṣṭa* offerings.
And by that [reasoning], there is the observation of another meaning.
Moreover, another passage also demonstrates this same point: "First [comes] the rite of the sacrifice, then one approaches the fire; this is the rite of the fire-altar.
This shows that the performance of what is mentioned later must occur later.

However, because the location for the preceding rites has already been established, that same location should apply to them; thus, the other view is merely a logical inference based on direct connection.
And that which is before the Prakṛti.

"There is the fire; he who, knowing thus, piles the fire"—in this context, it is traditionally taught that prior to the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering there are the *sāvitra* oblations, the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā*), the bricks, and the animal sacrifice.
Should those very rites be performed first, or rather the *dīkṣaṇīyā*?
What is the prima facie view? That the performance of the modified rites (*vaikṛta*) occurs at the end, according to the principle "but at the end, [it is] Bādarāyaṇa's.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: first come the Sāvitra oblations, the bricks, the animal sacrifice, and the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā*).

Why? Because of the direct textual recitation (*pratyakṣapāṭha*); furthermore, the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* is prescribed there, and prior to that, the Sāvitra oblations, the bricks, the animal sacrifice, and the preparation of the fire-pan are mentioned.
Therefore, their preliminary application occurs first;
if there were a conjunction, it would occur at the end as previously described.
This being the case, we reply: the consecratory rites (*dīkṣita-saṃskāra*) must be performed first.
Why? Because both the textual order (*pāṭha-krama*) relative to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice and the extended application (*codaka*) indicate that they are to be performed after the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*.
As for their mutual internal order, there is no direct textual sequence—as there was for the preparation of the fire-pan (*ukhā-sambharaṇa*)—that establishes their priority.

However, there is the prior recitation of the preparatory acts (*saṃskāra*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), whereas in the ectype (*vikṛti*), the fastening of the gold plate (*rukmapratimocana*) is recited later; therefore, the sequence should be exactly as stated, with the ectype occurring at the end.
Now, for what purpose is a conflict (*saṃnipāta*) suspected? Is this not an evident conflict? This statement regarding a conflict is made concerning something that is not actually doubtful.
For example:
"The Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and have sacrificed with many sacrifices—if the scriptures were authoritative, they would have attained the supreme goal. Thus it is said.
Therefore, there is no fault;
an increase [in the number of deities] due to the differentiation of the ritual acts should be taught for each case, like the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).
Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is heard in the scripture: "He performs eleven *prayāja* offerings; he performs eleven *anuyāja* offerings.

Regarding the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, it is heard: "He performs nine *prayāja* offerings; he performs nine *anuyāja* offerings. Regarding the fire-altar (*agni*), it is heard: "There are six *upasad*s."

In this regard, there is a doubt: does the number eleven apply to each *prayāja* and to each *anuyāja*, as well as the number nine in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, and the number six for the *upasads* in the *Agniṣṭoma*, or is the number to be accomplished collectively for all? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That the number is distinct with each principal act.
Why? Because those acts are distinct, and the number is heard in connection with each of those principal acts.

Furthermore, when subordinate elements (guṇas) are enjoined in proximity to principal elements (pradhānas), they differ with each principal element; just as in the injunction "one sacrifices the after-sacrifices with speckled butter," the quality of being speckled differs for each after-sacrifice, so it is here as well.
Or rather, because it is a number pertaining to all, a modification (vikāra) should be understood.
But they would increase from their own respective positions because they have been established in their proper sequence.
Regarding the *upasad* rites, there is a doubt:
does the repetition follow the pattern of a "beaten stick" (*daṇḍakalitavat*), or do they increase from their own place?
What, then, is the prima facie view? This is the rule for things that are to be repeated: namely, the pattern of a beaten stick.

For when it is said, "Recite the section three times," one begins from the beginning, completes it, and then begins again from the beginning; therefore, the repetition is like that of a staff-stroke (daṇḍakalita).

This being the prima facie view, we reply: it ought to increase from its own place. Why? Because the sequence has already been established. The sequence is established in the *upasads*: having performed the first, the middle one must be performed, and after that the last. Thus, the repetition should proceed from its own position.

In that regard, if there were a repetition like that of a "flogged stick" (daṇḍakalitavat), then having performed the last [note], when one proceeds again to the practice of the first, that increase would be placed in the wrong position. In the case of an increase in its own proper place, this fault does not occur.
Therefore, the increase occurs in its own proper place.
The *dhāyyā* verses should be placed between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī* verses, because they represent the intermediate space between heaven and earth.
Or the word "that" [is used].
Alternatively, those verses designated by the term *dhāyyā* ought to exist there;

for there is a conventional usage (*saṃstava*) with that specific word, and from such usage comes the injunction, as in: "The two *pṛthupājavatī* verses are *dhāyyās*," and "The *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses are *dhāyyās*.
But what indeed are these things called *dhāyyās*? We do not find any established meaning for this word.

It is said: the *sāmidhenīs* are to be meditated upon. Why? Because there is this statement of the venerable Pāṇini: "The forms *pāyya*, *sāṃnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* [are used] in the senses of measure, oblation, dwelling, and *sāmidhenī* verses respectively. From this statement, we infer a corresponding Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
[Question: In which *sāmidhenī* verses?

It is said: because there is no distinction, it is understood that [the term *dhāyyā*] applies to all [verses]. However, here, since it is stated that they should be *dhāyyās* between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī*, and since the word *dhāyyā* is not mentioned in relation to all *sāmidhenīs*, it is understood that the word *dhāyyā* refers specifically to certain distinguished *sāmidhenīs*.
Because they are seen at the end of the Uṣṇih and Kakubh meters.

The employment of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters is observed at the end [of the litany]: "If one were to conclude with a *jagatī*, he would reach the end of the sacrifice; but since he concludes with a *triṣṭubh*, he does not reach the end.
Now, is it not the case that the *triṣṭubh* is seen here at the end, and not the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*?
It is said in reply: this [text] refers to the *triṣṭubh* itself as being the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*.

How so? Because at the end of the praise it says, "The *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor," [the author] has employed a metaphorical treatment of the cause as if it were the effect, stating that "the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* are the vigor of the *triṣṭubh*."
When the *stoma* is increased, the additional verses (*āgantu*) should be inserted in the *bahiṣpavamāna* before the *paryāsa*, for it is so established in the case of the *dvādaśāha*.

There are sacrifices characterized by increased *stomas*: "They should cause one who desires offspring to sacrifice with an Atirātra having the twenty-one-fold [stoma]; one who desires vigor with the twenty-seven-fold; and one who desires stability with the thirty-three-fold.
In that regard, it will be stated that the completion of the number is achieved through traditional scripture (*āgama*).
Now, a doubt arises concerning the *bahiṣpavamāna* when the modified [verses] are being brought forward.
Should the modifications (*vaikṛta*) be inserted at the end, or prior to the *paryāsa*? What is the prima facie view? The adventitious elements (*āgantavaḥ*) should be placed before the *paryāsa*;
for it is so observed in the *dvādaśāha*: "There are two *ṛc*s, the *stotrīya* and the *anurūpa*, and there are *ṛc*s containing the word 'vṛṣan'."
Since it is stated that "the final *ṛc* is the *paryāsa*," here too, there must be insertions (*āgantu*) prior to the *paryāsa*;
furthermore, "*paryāsa*" is a designation for the end.
Furthermore, the word *prayāsa* is seen in common usage to denote "the end," as in the expressions *kṣetraparyāsa* (the boundary of a field) and *nadīparyāsa* (the mouth of a river).
Thus, the *paryāsa* will be placed at the end;
or rather, it is stated [here] at the end.
Or rather, such a modification should occur at the end;
for it has been stated, "But at the end, according to Bādarāyaṇa.
However, on account of the explicit scriptural statement, it applies to the twelve-day sacrifice.
Now, as for what was said—that it is observed in the case of the *dvādaśāha*—that must be refuted.

To this it is replied: it occurs in the *dvādaśāha* because of a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*): "There are two *ṛcas*, a *stotrīya* and an *anurūpa*; there are *ṛcas* containing the word *vṛṣan*; the final *ṛca* is the *paryāsa*.
For indeed, there is no burden too great for a scriptural statement.
And it is not subject to transformation by that.
Nor is this a transformation of that [object], such that one could perceive the properties from it; for even if there were such a transformation, [the cognition] would be something entirely new.

Even that which is a modification of it should be placed at the very end. Why? Because of the unprecedented nature [of the rule]: the *vṛṣaṇvat* triplets [are prescribed] before the *paryāsa*; whatever is stated by explicit statement is authoritative, and one does not resort to what is merely similar. However, one should place them at the end of the two subsequent [sections].
Or rather, [the rule applies] to the *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters because of a specific scriptural statement.
The insertion [of verses] occurs within the *gāyatrī*, *bṛhatī*, and *anuṣṭubh* meters.
Why? Because of a scriptural statement: "There are indeed three bellies of the sacrifice: the *gāyatrī*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *anuṣṭubh*.
For it is said, "In these alone they insert [verses], and from these alone they extract them"; thus, there is no objection.
Therefore, there is no insertion of these at the end;
the *graheṣṭaka* belongs to the *aupānuvākya* section and should be a subsidiary part of the piling (*citi*) of the Soma-pressing (*savana*).
Or rather, it is a remainder of the kratu and the fire-altar, because they are enjoined, whereas there is no injunction for the sequence.
The fire-altar (agni) would be subordinate to the ritual action (kratv-aṅga).
Why? Because it is enjoined; for it is heard in scripture that "the fire-altar is to be built," as in the statement, "He who, knowing thus, builds the fire-altar.

It is not the act of piling (citi) itself that is to be performed; rather, it is heard that the fire-altar is to be built by means of the piling of bricks, because of the use of the accusative case in the word "agnim" (the fire-altar).

Likewise, just as there is a connection between the *adābhya* cup and the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) in the statement "having taken the *adābhya*, one sacrifices to Soma," so too is there a connection for the *aṃśu* cup.

Therefore, having established a single connection with the sacrifice, the word becomes fulfilled in its purpose, having brought about the relationship that was heard in the text. Similarly, having established a single connection with the fire-altar (*agni*), one would consider the task complete; for the altar-piling (*citi*) and the pressing (*savana*) are not enjoined as things to be performed independently, since their mention is for the sake of another purpose.

What is the purpose? If they are subsidiary to the *savana* (pressing) and the *citi* (piling), there would be a drawing of the cup at every pressing and the laying of bricks at every piling. If they are subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratu*) and the fire-altar (*agni*), the drawing and laying would occur only once.
They should be at the end [of the sequence], because there is no intervention.

In the *Aupānuvākya* it is heard: "He lays down the *citriṇī* bricks; he lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks. Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these to be laid down in the fifth layer, or in the middle one? What is the prima facie view? These bricks, having a fixed sequence, must be laid down in the fifth layer itself; no others should be interposed between them.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
Or rather, the final layer is the sowing; one lays down the other bricks [only] because of a specific scriptural statement.
However, in the middle layer, the bricks possessing Brāhmaṇa formulas are used because of a direct injunction.
These [bricks] do not belong to the final layer;
rather, to which one then? To the middle one.
Why? Because these bricks possess Brāhmaṇa explanations, and it is the middle layer that is prescribed for them.
"Whichever brick one may recognize as having a Brāhmaṇa description, that one should place in the middle layer.

[Objection: But are not all bricks indeed accompanied by Brāhmaṇa descriptions? [Reply: No, he says, because of others [being excluded] on account of their indicative marks (*liṅga*), their order (*krama*), and their designation (*samākhyāna*).
Therefore, these [bricks] should not be at the end,
because that [Lokampṛṇā brick] is for the purpose of completing it prior to the Lokampṛṇā.
In the *Aupānuvākya* section, bricks are prescribed: "He lays down the *vajriṇī* bricks; he lays down the *citriṇī* bricks; he lays down the *bhūteṣṭakā* bricks.
Regarding this, it has been established that they are to be laid down in the middle layer (*citā*).
In this regard, there is a doubt: are they to be placed before the *lokāṃpṛṇā* brick, or after it?
What is the conclusion reached? "But at the end, [it belongs] to Bādarāyaṇa.

This being the position reached, it is said: prior to the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick, because its purpose is to complete that [altar]; for its purpose of completion is heard in scripture: "Whatever of this is deficient, whatever is a gap, that he fills with this; fill the world, fill the gap!
And because the matter is not previously established, it is understood that this is indeed an injunction by way of praise.
Therefore, it should be performed prior to the *lokaṃpṛṇā* brick;
for the ritual action is performed upon the prepared site, since that is the purpose of the preparatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
At the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), there are the Pavamāna-iṣṭis;
and there are fixed rites, such as the Agnihotra and others, as well as non-fixed rites, such as those dedicated to Indra and Agni (aindrāgna) and others.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the ritual acts be undertaken after performing the Pavamāneṣṭis, or immediately upon the fires having been established? What is the prima facie view? That they should be undertaken immediately upon the fires having been established. Why? Because one becomes capable of performing the ritual acts upon those fires as soon as they have been established, just as it is said: "One who has established the sacred fires should not offer wet wood."
And it indicates this: "They pursue the fire with the Agnihotra as soon as it has been created"; this shows that the Agnihotra is to be performed immediately upon the fires being established.
Therefore, one need not wait for the Pavamāna offerings.
This being the position reached, we reply: the rites should proceed when the fires have been consecrated by the Pavamāna offerings.

Why? Because the consecrations (saṃskāras) have that as their purpose; these terms such as *āhavanīya* and so forth are words for consecrations. In the absence of any [other] consecration, there would be a disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *āhavanīya* and other fires. Therefore, rituals are to be performed in fires that have been consecrated. Immediately following this is the rule regarding the vow (*vrata*), because it has become part of that [consecration].

As for the statement, "One who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) should not offer wet wood," and so forth—it is appropriate that this is prescribed for those who have just established the fires; that is called the vow of the āhitāgni.
And he becomes an āhitāgni immediately upon the establishment of the fires.
Therefore, the vow should follow immediately after that, because it consists of that [state],
and because there is a scriptural indication to that effect previously.

Now, as for what was stated—that the Agnihotra is shown to be performed immediately after the fires have been established, prior to the Iṣṭis—what is the refutation of that? This is the end of the introductory portion of the Sūtra: "Or it is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), because the matter [it describes] already exists."
This is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). Why? Because the primary meaning exists; for in that case, there is indeed another Agnihotra oblation altogether.
The exponents of Brahman deliberate: "How should the Agnihotra be offered? Should it not be offered?

If one were to offer with a sacrificial formula (*yajus*), one would offer the oblations in a manner contrary to what was before; if one were not to offer at all, the fire would depart. Therefore, it should be offered silently (*tūṣṇīm*).
This explanatory passage (arthavāda) is for the purpose of praising that silent oblation (tūṣṇīṃ homa),
and because it would otherwise contradict logical reasoning.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction of the established principle (*nyāyavipratiṣedha*).

If the Agnihotra and other rites were to follow immediately [after initiation], then the principle previously stated—that "they [the initiations] do not have that [the rites] as their purpose"—would be contradicted. Therefore, the ritual acts should take place once [the person] has been consecrated.
But for one who has piled the fire-altar, it is appropriate [to perform the rite], because the occasion for its performance has arrived.

"One who has piled the fire-altar (agnicit) should not run while it rains, nor should he approach a woman; therefore, one who has piled the fire-altar must not eat birds"—such items are heard [in the scriptures]. Regarding these, there is a doubt: are they to be performed immediately upon the mere piling of the altar, or at the conclusion of the sacrifice? What is the prima facie view? That they are to be performed immediately upon the mere piling.

"One who has piled the fire-altar" (agnicit) refers to one who has performed the piling; for such a person, the [rites] prescribed for one who has piled the altar apply immediately thereafter. Since the occasion has arisen, the contingent rite must be performed.
Therefore, it should be done immediately. Alternatively, it may be at the end of the sacrifice, because there is no statement regarding its performance [at that specific time].
For in this context, the injunctive statement brings about those ritual items which serve the purpose of the sacrifice;
however, these [acts] do not serve the purpose of the sacrifice, for they serve the purpose of the person.
How so? In the case of a prohibition, the person is heard as the subject, as in "one should not run while it rains," "one should not approach a woman," and so forth.
Nor are these [acts] established as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), such that their prohibition would benefit the sacrifice. [Objection:

But surely they are also for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), since they are heard [to be enjoined] for one who has performed the piling of the altar (*citavān*); thus, they would apply immediately after the piling.
[Reply: We say no.
Because Agni is not specified as being the object of the action.

The piling (*cayana*) is for the sake of the fire; that which serves as assistance to the fire while it performs its own function is "for that purpose. And what is its own purpose? It is the accomplishment of the sacrifice (*yāga*); and once the sacrifice is accomplished, it becomes assisted by the piling.
Therefore, when the sacrifice is accomplished, one is an "Agnicit" (one who has piled the fire-altar), and by that [act], the rite is concluded.
One becomes initiated through the announcement by another, because initiation is connected with all [the officiants].
Or rather, it should be performed at the end of the sacrifice, for its purpose is connected to that [result] without distinction.
Or rather, one should become initiated at the conclusion of the *iṣṭi*, for that initiation is for the sake of that [conclusion].

How so? That [initiation] belongs to one who is about to be initiated but is not yet initiated; if he becomes initiated at a time subsequent to it, then it belongs to one who is about to be initiated.

Therefore, it is understood from the sentence that he becomes initiated at that time. Once the ritual act which is the cause of initiation has been accomplished, why should he not be considered initiated? For the sentence, being independent, makes known that he is initiated.

As for the connection with initiation (*dīkṣā*) in the statement "he initiates [him] with a staff" (*daṇḍena dīkṣayati*): how could that [initiation] exist in the state of being already initiated? Therefore, we understand it to mean that he brings about the state of being initiated by means of the staff itself.
As for the objection that the word "initiated" does not appear immediately thereafter—
The non-employment of a word is not the reason for the absence of its referent;
even when the referent exists, the word may not be employed due to the absence of an occasion for its use.
Furthermore, that he is initiated is understood from another sentence: "One who is about to be initiated should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu."
And as for the fact that the word "dīkṣita" (initiated) occurs at the time of the announcement:

even at the end of the *iṣṭi*, this [designation] is not contradictory for one who has been initiated, nor is the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*) contradictory; because it is understood that there is one cause of initiation, and that he brings about the state of being initiated by means of other [rites].
And the name (*samākhyāna*) is likewise.
Moreover, we see from this that [the sacrifice] is for the purpose of the initiation (*dīkṣaṇā*), and the performance occurs at the end of the *iṣṭi*.
Why? Because "the designation (*samākhyāna*) is like that," just as the principle has been taught.
How so? The designation "initiatory" (*dīkṣaṇīyā*) indicates its being for that purpose, just as in the cases of "for bathing" (*snānīya*) or "for eating" (*bhojanīya*).
And from this we see that the sacrifice is for the purpose of initiation, and the commencement [of the main rite] occurs at the conclusion of the sacrifice;
just as with the auxiliary parts, there is a fixed sequence among the sacrifices.
In this context, the optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*) serve as the illustration;

these include such offerings as "one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," as well as the *gavāmayana* and other rites, the *soma* sacrifices, the *saumya* and other animal sacrifices, and the animal sacrifices themselves.
Regarding these, there is a doubt: should they be performed in the very same order in which they were studied, or is there no fixed rule?
What, then, is the established position? The sequence of the sacrifices that exists in the textual recitation ought to be the very same in their performance.
In this way, the order of the text will be respected; otherwise, the order of the text would be subverted. Lest that happen, they must be performed in that sequence.
Not so, because there is no connection [between the order of the text and the order of performance].
Or rather, this sequence would not be restricted.
Why? Because there is no connection.
There are separate injunctions for the performance of these individual rites, and they serve to bring together their own respective constituent elements.
That which is not beneficial to another does not relate to it either sequentially or non-sequentially.
For one who benefits someone, a sequence exists in relation to that assistance.
However, these actions do not benefit one another.
Therefore, this sequence does not function as an auxiliary;
consequently, there is no connection [between them],
and also because they are objects of desire.
These actions are performed for the sake of desires, and desires arise in a sequence; therefore, because the cause is not sequential, [the actions] do not possess a sequence.
If it is argued that this is not so because [the sequence] would be purposeless—
That which was stated in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is now stated again in order to refute it;
thus, the recitation will become meaningful in this sequence.
This concludes the sūtra up to the point of this introductory remark (ābhāṣānta).
It might be so, because it is for the sake of knowledge, just as [the *sarvasvāra* sacrifice is] in the case of others.

The sequential recitation may indeed be purposeful, even though there is no practical application for the sequence itself, because it serves the purpose of acquiring knowledge; for in the case of knowledge intended for the understanding of ritual action, an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) based on that sequence will necessarily arise. Just as in your own view, regarding those [sections] following the *Sarvasvāra* sacrifice—even for one who holds the position that sequence is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the rite—an unseen purpose must certainly be postulated for the sequence of those sections following the *Sarvasvāra*, which occurs in connection with the *Sarvasvāra*. As for the phrase "by this," it refers to the *Agniṣṭoma* due to the context (*prakaraṇa*).
And because of an indicative mark.

There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*); it is heard there: "He for whom there are one hundred and ninety *stotrīyā*s. For indeed, the *agniṣṭoma* has one hundred and ninety *stotrīyā*s. How so? The *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the *ājya* [stotras] are fifteen-fold, and there are four of them.
That makes sixty-nine.
The Mādhyandina Pavamāna consists of fifteen [verses]; by that, there are eighty-four.
The Pṛṣṭhas consist of seventeen [verses] each; these four amount to sixty-eight, which together with the eighty-four make one hundred and fifty-two.
The Ārbhava Pavamāna consists of seventeen [verses]; by that, there are one hundred and sixty-nine.
"The Yajñāyajñīya [Sāman] has twenty-one [verses]"—this constitutes one hundred and ninety verses for the Agniṣṭoma; therefore it is also called the Agniṣṭoma.
Now, as for the phrase "by another," this refers to the proximity of the other sacrificial terminuses (saṃsthās).

Now, regarding the phrase "by another," does this refer to the *saṃsthās* (terminuses), or rather to the one-day (*ekāha*) and other sacrifices which are modifications of the Jyotiṣṭoma? What is the initial position? It refers to the *saṃsthās*.
Why? Because of proximity; the *saṃsthās* are proximate within that context, and it is their discussion that serves to support the context.
For the arising and the departure from that fundamental nature are not possible among equals.
Or it is praise, because there is no wandering about.

If this is so, then there is no discussion regarding their modifications; in that case, there is neither a displacement (*vihāra*) nor an application (*āpatti*), because [the animals] belong to the *jyotiṣṭoma* by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*) and other such factors. For if cows and the like were to be displaced, the context and other factors would be sublated. An application [of them elsewhere] would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, this is merely a commendation (*praśaṃsā*), since there is an absence of both displacement and application. Or rather, it follows from the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), for a commendation does not occur without cause.
To this it is replied: even if the occurrence (*āpatti*) and the performance (*vihāra*) are not explicitly enjoined here, they are nevertheless enjoined by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer).
Whatever is to be performed in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is understood that those same acts must also be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*) due to the statement of the *codaka*.
Therefore, it is understood that the occurrence and performance take place there through some other [means] as well, just as they do in the case of the occurrence and performance themselves.
For praise would not occur without cause; therefore, this praise has the purpose of indicating how that other [element] might be characterized by such praise.
Or rather, it is because of the connection with the sacrifice in the case of a single-stoma rite.
It is heard in the scripture: "Having sacrificed with this [rite], one should then sacrifice with another.
Regarding that, the following point has been established: that this refers to the modifications (vikāra) of that [original rite].
Now, a doubt arises: does this apply to a rite consisting of a single stoma, or to one consisting of multiple stomas?

What is established? That the statement refers to that which has a single *stoma*. Why? Because of its connection with the sacrificial rite (*kratu*); for there is a connection with the rite in the case of a single *stoma*: "He who resorts to another sacrificial rite while being the *trivṛt* kind illumines it; he who is the *pañcadaśa* kind [illumines] it; he who is the *saptadaśa* kind [illumines] it; he who is the *ekaviṃśa* kind [illumines] it.
The *trivṛt* and the others are those having a single *stoma*.
Therefore, this is their doctrine;
or rather, because there is a specific injunction for all of them, it is a praise of the *stomas*.
That which is sequential is [determined] by both the meaning and the word, because of the specific nature of the audition and because of the predominance of the meaning.
Here is an investigation regarding the sublation of the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) by both the order of the Vedic text (śrutikrama) and the order of meaning (arthakrama).

Is the order of recitation equal to those two, or is it sublated by them? What is the prima facie view? These two are of equal strength, for the order of recitation is also a cause, as are the order of the text and the order of meaning.
And there is no distinction whatsoever regarding their authoritative status; therefore, there is no fixed rule.
This being the position reached, we reply: the order of the text is indeed set aside by direct Vedic statement (śruti) and by the purpose (artha).
Why? Because of the specific force of the direct statement and because of the priority of the purpose.

What is this distinction of direct statement (*śruti*)? Where there is a direct statement, there perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the cause; whereas the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is inferential (*ānumānika*). Through the order of recitation, there is recollection, and it is understood that "it must be performed in this way. Its performance occurs solely on the basis of its purposeful efficacy (*arthavattva*), which serves as the supporting reason. By contrast, through direct statement, the performance itself is understood directly from perception in the form: "it is to be thus."
Likewise, it is by way of the meaning.

Why? Because the meaning is paramount; for everything is for the sake of the meaning, and since everything is performed to bring about the primary purpose, the literal recitation is set aside by those two.

What is the example and what is the purpose? In the Śruti, the Āśvina cup is drawn as the tenth, yet it says, "one offers that as the third. If the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) were stronger, the offering would be of the third; however, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is of the tenth. Regarding the meaning (*artha*), the Agnihotra oblation is enjoined first, and the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) afterwards.
It must be performed in this way if the order of recitation were more authoritative.
In the established conclusion (siddhānta), the cooking comes first, followed by the oblation;
as for the sequence of the portions, the sprinkling with clarified butter, and the placing [on the altar], it should follow the order of their performance.

There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices. In that context, first the ritual properties of the curd (dadhi) are prescribed, and afterwards those of the Āgneya [cake]; yet the offering (pradāna) of the Āgneya comes first.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the portions (avadāna), sprinkling (abhighāraṇa), and placing (āsādana) of the curd be performed first according to the order of procedure (prāvṛttika-krama), or should they be performed first for the Āgneya according to the order of the principal acts (mukhya-krama)? What is the prima facie view? That there is no fixed rule.
This being the case, we reply: in the case of the portions to be cut off (avadāna) and so forth, the order of precedence is first that of the curd, according to the sequence of the procedure.
Why? Because, when this is accepted, no other intervening factor will be postulated as more significant than those already permitted; moreover, it indicates that the curd is indeed to be given first.
Or rather, the order follows the actual offering, because that is the purpose of the action.

Or rather, the acts should be performed according to the order of offering (*pradāna*); that is, for whichever [deity] the offering comes first, its portions (*avadāna*) come first—therefore, those of the Āgneya [offering].

Why? Because the acts beginning with the cutting of portions are governed by the injunction for the offering; it has been stated that these acts commence with the offering and are not separate ritual items (*padārtha*) in themselves.
Both the sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) and the cutting of portions are performed solely with the desire to make that offering.
Even the placing [of the offering] is for the purpose of giving; it is the preparation for the act of giving. In this way, there is a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatā).
Therefore, the performance of the auxiliary rites follows the primary order.
This is also because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅga).

There is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for this meaning: "He indeed first sprinkles the *dhruvā* [ladle], because he is about to offer the two primary portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) immediately thereafter.
Therefore, the rule is established by the order of the principal acts.
From the explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*), it follows that the *iṣṭi* must come first.
The precedence of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice has been taught.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the precedence of the *iṣṭi* and the precedence of the *soma* sacrifice optional alternatives, or is it that the precedence of the *iṣṭi* alone must be observed?
What is the prima facie view? It should be the precedence of the *iṣṭi* alone.

Why? Because of a scriptural statement (*vacana*). This statement exists: "The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the chariot of the gods; he who, having sacrificed with the New and Full Moon sacrifices, then sacrifices with Soma, rests at the end of his journey on the excellent chariot-track of the gods. There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement. Therefore, the performance of the *iṣṭi* must necessarily precede [the Soma sacrifice].

Furthermore, according to some, the Soma sacrifice [must follow] the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), because of the scriptural injunction regarding the passing of the seasons and constellations; for otherwise, that [injunction] would be rendered meaningless by the end of the [Soma] sacrifice.
And because it expresses that purpose, it does not [apply] without distinction; therefore, it has that as its purpose.
Furthermore, there is immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna).
Why? Because of the statement to that effect: "He who shall sacrifice with Soma should establish the fires.

For he establishes the fires intending to sacrifice with all [rites], including the Soma sacrifice, the Agnihotra, and so forth; if there were no specific reference to the Soma sacrifice, the phrase "for the sake of the Soma" would not be meaningful.
This would be the distinction: namely, that there is immediate succession between the Soma sacrifice and the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*).
Furthermore, since the time for the *pavamāna* oblations is prescribed for one who does not intend to perform the Soma sacrifice, there might arise a doubt regarding their immediate succession.

The time for the Pavamāna offerings of one who is not intending to perform a Soma sacrifice is specified by the rule: "He who, not intending to perform a Soma sacrifice, should establish the sacred fires (agnyādheya), he should offer the oblations before a year [has passed]. Indeed, there is no one who does not intend to perform a sacrifice, since it is prescribed for everyone.
Therefore, it is understood that the phrase "one not intending to perform a sacrifice" refers to one who intends to perform it immediately thereafter.
For such a person, there is the Iṣṭi; and when the purpose is that [Iṣṭi], the Soma sacrifice must come first.
This is described as the sūtra on purpose (*prayojana*).
The legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) is concluded.
What is the purpose of this reflection? It is the desire of one who does not intend to sacrifice with *soma* to perform the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) without a specific motive.

If, however, it were for that purpose [the Agnihotra], then the Soma sacrifice would come first; but if the establishment of the fires (ādhāna) is for the sake of the Soma sacrifice, then the Soma sacrifice would indeed precede it.
Because of its displacement, the Soma sacrifice would belong to the Brāhmaṇa.
There is the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires), and in that regard, this principle has been established: namely, that it must be preceded either by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice or by a *soma* sacrifice.

Now there arises a doubt: is it that for all three social classes (*varṇas*) the sacrifice must be preceded by an *iṣṭi* or a *soma*, or is it that only for the Brāhmaṇa must it be preceded by a *soma*, or is it that only the Full Moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) is postponed, while for the Brāhmaṇa both ritual options remain available?
Or rather, is this a separate rite that occurs after the *soma* sacrifice, or is only one oblation (*havis*) postponed, while for the Brāhmaṇa both options indeed remain available?
What is established? That for the three social classes (varṇas), the sacrifice is preceded either by the iṣṭi or by the soma.
Why? Because there is no distinction;
we perceive no specific difference whatsoever.
This being the case, we reply: for a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice should come first.

Why? Because of its exaltation; for an exaltation is heard in scripture: "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed of the nature of Agni as his deity; having sacrificed with Soma, he becomes one whose deity is Agni-Soma.
That which is the Paurṇamāsa oblation—therein he should subsequently offer it; then he becomes possessed of both deities."
For what word indeed would not be effective?
Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Soma sacrifice must necessarily come first.
Or rather, it is the Full Moon sacrifice [that comes first], because of its connection with the direct Vedic injunction.
As for what was stated—that for a Brāhmaṇa there is only the sequence beginning with Soma—that is not so; for him as well, both ritual procedures (kalpa) are valid.
Why? Because there is no distinction; indeed, no specific distinction regarding the two procedures is recorded for the Brāhmaṇa.
But was it not just now stated that there is a superiority for the Brāhmaṇa?
We say: no; for in that case, there is only the displacement of the *paurṇamāsī* sacrifice itself.

There is a direct scriptural connection (*śruti-saṃyoga*) with the *paurṇamāsī* in the text, "That which is this *paurṇamāsa* oblation," and where there is a statement, it is based on that statement; in such a case, logical inference (*nyāya*) does not apply.
When one part of two equal things is displaced, surely the other part must also be displaced.
Or rather, because everything has but a single function.

As for the claim that only the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) is displaced, that is not so; rather, there is a displacement of the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa ritual, for only in this way is there a connection with the fruit [of the action]. Otherwise, there would be no fruit.
