Since the full-moon sacrifice is but one part [of the whole], if only that part were displaced, there would be no fruit for the remainder performed earlier, because it is but a single part. And since it would be fruitless, even what has been prescribed would not be performed.
When the whole is being extracted, the result follows;
therefore, by implication, there is an extraction of the entire collection, so that the complete instruction may be meaningful.
Consequently, there is an extraction of everything, and thus for a Brāhmaṇa, Soma-sacrifice must indeed come first.
Or rather, there may be a positive injunction for that purpose.

This is not the case; since there is no statement regarding the whole [sacrifice] in this manner, one should not assume an "exaltation" (utkarṣa) of it. Therefore, this is a different rite altogether with that name, which should take place after the Soma sacrifice. In this way, an unmentioned fruit for a single part will not have to be postulated.
Furthermore, the name is common to both rites, just as in the case of "akṣas," "pādas," or "māṣas."

Alternatively, it may be that another distinct rite possessing the characteristics of the Full Moon sacrifice is enjoined; this would be an injunction of a separate action, which, by virtue of the direct Vedic statement (śruti), overrides the syntactical connection (vākya). Therefore, it is a distinct rite.
However, on account of the context (prakaraṇa), it should be understood as a [mere] time.
It would exist at its own time, because there is no contradiction.
"He who, intending to sacrifice with Soma, establishes the sacred fires (agny-ādheya), need not wait for a season nor for a lunar mansion.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this a sublation of a specific time for the establishment of the fires, or for the Soma sacrifice? What is the prima facie view? It is a sublation of the time for the establishment of the fires; the Soma sacrifice should take place at its own proper time.

Why? Because there is no contradiction. The fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is a subsidiary (*aṅga*); therefore, it is logical that its time should be set aside, not that of the primary (*pradhāna*). And it will be stated later that "in a conflict between a subsidiary and a quality, the subsidiary prevails because it exists for the sake of that [primary].
Alternatively, there is a removal of the time for the installation, because it may be performed at any time.
Or rather, there would be a displacement of the time for the Soma sacrifice because of the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna).

Why? Because the establishment of the fires may take place at any time; there is no restriction regarding time for the establishment of the fires, as it is said: "On whatever day faith may come upon him, on that day he should establish the fires.
That which is prohibited [here] is something that was not even applicable to the establishment of the fires.
Therefore, there is a sublation of the time for the Soma sacrifice;
for according to the scriptural statement, the Paurṇamāsī [sacrifice] for a Brāhmaṇa occurs after the Soma sacrifice.
The answer to the established position is as follows:
It is not the case that both the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices in their entirety are postponed beyond the Soma sacrifice; rather, only the Pūrṇamāsa is postponed.

Why? Because of a scriptural statement. This is the scriptural statement: "Whatever that Pūrṇamāsa oblation is, one should then offer it subsequently. There is no overburdening for a scriptural statement.
Therefore, only the full-moon sacrifice (*paurṇamāsī*) would be displaced.
As for the objection that there is no fruit [for the individual], the fruit will indeed arise from the aggregate itself, because this is understood from the scriptural statement.
Therefore, there is no fault.
One [is established] by the force of the word, prior to the complete prescription.
Or rather, only one oblation should be postponed, not the entire Paurṇamāsī sacrifice.

Why? Because of the force of the scriptural statement; the text is capable of postponing only one oblation, as it is heard in the scripture: "That which is this Paurṇamāsa oblation. To the extent that there is a verbal injunction, to that extent can it be postponed by that injunction, and nothing else. Prior to the Soma sacrifice, the entire [Paurṇamāsī] is prescribed.
Therefore, that which is displaced by the verbal injunction must occur after the Soma sacrifice, while that which is not displaced ought to occur before it.
Consequently, one oblation is to be displaced; for a Brāhmaṇa, both ritual procedures are applicable.
However, in the absence of a specific designation, the cake-offering (puroḍāśa) applies because the deity associated with it is present.
If it is argued that clarified butter is also [to be offered], [we reply: no.
If you say, "Because it is dedicated to Agni and Soma, it is a *puroḍāśa*," then the clarified butter (*ājya*) is also dedicated to Agni and Soma;
therefore, that too would have to be displaced [from its position].
It is not so, because of the presence of mixed deities, as in the case of the offering to Indra and Agni.
For clarified butter (ājya) has mixed deities— namely, those dedicated to Agni-Soma, Prajāpati, and Viṣṇu—
whereas the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is dedicated to Agni-Soma alone.
However, there is no mention here of a mixed deity, for the existence of a mixed deity is only conceivable prior [to the division].
Even though at that time the sacrificer is not yet fit for Agni-Soma as their deity, he will nevertheless indeed offer clarified butter as the oblation; he will sacrifice to Prajāpati, or to Viṣṇu.
Therefore, the fact of being "for Agni-Soma" (agnīṣomīyatva) cannot be the reason for its upward movement.

Just as the fourfold division (caturdhākaraṇa) applies to the offering for Indra-Agni because it has mixed deities, so too in that case, it cannot be said to be "for Agni" alone; for a suffix denoting a derivative relationship (taddhita) does not arise from words that are semantically expectant [of another].
Thus, here, the word *agnīṣomīya* cannot denote the clarified butter (*ājya*), for that [butter] belongs to Agni and Soma.
Therefore, it is possible for the sacrificer to perform it beforehand.

Consequently, the fact that it belongs to Agni and Soma is not the reason for the sacrificer’s displacement; rather, it has been stated that this is due to the commonality of the grasping of a deity shared by both, just as in the case of the *aindrāgna* offering.
Because the time of the modification (vikṛti) is that of the archetype (prakṛti), the modification is subsequent to the same-day performance; for both of these are directly taught by scripture.
In this context, the modified sacrifices (*vaikṛta-karman*) serve as the examples, such as "one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," and so forth.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are these modifications (*vikṛti*) to be performed on the same day (*sadyaskāla*), or over two days (*dvyahakāla*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? A modification receives the archetypal properties (*dharmān prākṛtān*) through the extended injunction (*codaka*); therefore, those properties are inferential, whereas the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) is a different time.

Whether it be grasped by way of the archetype (*prakṛti*) or by way of the modification (*vikṛti*), in the event that both are impossible, the time of one or the other must be abandoned; in that case, it is logical that the inferred time of the modification should be abandoned, and not the directly heard time of the archetype.
Therefore, these modifications should be performed on the same day (*sadyaskālā*);
however, regarding the two-day interval (*dvaiyahakālya*), it should be according to the rule.
When performed on two days, it becomes accomplished according to the rule; therefore, there should be a two-day period.

In this way, the injunction (*codaka*) is properly accommodated, for it is heard in the archetype (*prakṛti*): "On the previous day he takes up the fire; on the following day he sacrifices to the deity.
Therefore, one rite should be completed over two days; having commenced on that very day, one should conclude it on the subsequent day.
From the statement, there would be simultaneity.
The modifications of the *sāṃnāyya* and the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] take place after the *soma* sacrifice, just like the archetype.

In this context, the modifications of the *sāṃnāyya* and the modifications of the *agnīṣomīya* serve as examples. First, regarding the modifications of the *sāṃnāyya*, such as the *āmikṣā* and the animal sacrifice; and regarding the modifications of the *agnīṣomīya*, such as: "A Brāhmaṇa desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a cake of *śyāmāka* grain on eleven potsherds to Agni and Soma in the spring," and so forth.

In this matter, there is a doubt: are these [to be performed] both before and after the *soma* sacrifice, or only after it? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? They are both before and after, because no specific distinction is perceived.

This being the case, we reply: they should take place after the Soma sacrifice. For their archetype (*prakṛti*) occurs after the Soma; by the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*), these too must occur after the Soma. As for the *sānnāyya*, it is established by a direct scriptural statement (*vacana*): "One who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should offer the *sānnāyya*. Regarding the *agnīṣomīya* [animal sacrifice] as well, [the scripture says]: "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed Agni-Soma by deity; having sacrificed with the Soma, he becomes so. Therefore, one should subsequently offer that very oblation which belongs to the Full Moon; at that time, he becomes possessed of both deities. Since its archetype occurs after the Soma, its modification (*vikṛti*) likewise ought to occur after the Soma.
Likewise, the products of Soma [are connected] with the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
When substances are conjoined with an action, they are related as qualities.
It is traditionally taught: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt: is heaven subordinate and the ritual action primary, or is the ritual action subordinate and heaven primary?
Why is there this doubt? Because here both "one desiring heaven" is specified, as well as "should sacrifice."

In this context, a relationship between the desire for heaven (*svargakāma*) and the sacrifice (*yāga*) is understood. Regarding that relationship, an inquiry arises as to whether the sacrifice is connected as a means (*sādhana*) or as an end to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

In that regard, if the sacrifice is enjoined as something to be performed by the person desiring heaven—meaning "the sacrifice must be performed by one who desires heaven"—it is understood that it is fulfilled for one characterized by the desire for heaven.

The desire for heaven is taught there with respect to the sacrifice; therefore, it is accomplished by that [sacrifice] and not by anything else. A person who desires heaven is capable of accomplishing the sacrifice.

Now, if the desire of one who desires heaven is enjoined as something to be performed (*kartavyatā*), then the "to-be-performed-ness" is qualified by the sacrifice, and thus the sacrifice is accepted as the means of accomplishment.

And this meaning of both [the sacrifice and the desire] is understood from a single uttered sentence—namely, that "either the sacrifice is to be performed" or "the desire is [to be attained]"—yet this cannot occur simultaneously; for when there is the desire, there is not the sacrifice, and when there is the sacrifice, there is not the desire, due to the difference in the mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*). Thus, the doubt is justified.
What, then, is the established position? That heaven (*svarga*) is subordinate (*guṇataḥ*) and the ritual action (*karman*) is primary (*pradhānataḥ*).

Regarding this, they explain that heaven is a substance (*dravya*). How is this understood? For all words, common usage (*laukika-prayoga*) is the means for knowing their meaning; and in that common usage, the word "heaven" is observed to denote a substance: "Heaven is fine silken garments," "Heaven is sandalwood," and "Heaven is women aged sixteen."
Whatever substance is accompanied by pleasure, that is denoted by the word "svarga.

Because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word], we consider that the substance accompanied by pleasure is *svarga*. If it is argued that the application of the word is based on analogy (*upamāna*), [we reply: for this cannot be an analogy, because there is nothing established in the world that is not itself comparable, to which this [comparison] could refer; therefore, it is not an analogy.

Therefore, [some claim] that heaven (*svarga*) is a substance (*dravya*). He says "no"; rather, pleasure (*prīti*) is heaven, not a substance, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For that very same substance, in certain states, the word "heaven" does not denote it; however, there is no state in which it does not denote pleasure.

Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the word "heaven" (*svarga*) refers to pleasure. Now, it may be objected that in common worldly usage the word "heaven" is well-known as a specific place where there is neither heat nor cold, neither hunger nor thirst, neither discontent nor fatigue; only those who have performed meritorious deeds go there after death, and no others.

To this it is replied: if some were to go there without dying and return without being reborn, then that region would not be of such a nature as to be perceptible; rather, it would be known through inference.
If it is argued that certain other perfected beings (*siddhas*) have seen it and described it, we reply:
there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that, namely, that such perfected beings exist and that they would speak of having seen it.
Therefore, such a place simply does not exist.
But is it not understood from common worldly usage, from narratives, and from the Veda that heaven is indeed such a place?
That is not so; because humans have no connection with such a place, their words lack authority.
Even a narrative (ākhyāna) is not to be respected because it is composed by a human author.

Even a Vedic narrative concerning heaven (*svarga*) does not exist as something intended to enjoin an action; rather, it forms a single syntactical unit with another injunction and is intended as a praise (*stuti*).

Even if such a place [heaven] were to exist by implication from the mere hearing of the word "pleasure," there would still be no contradiction with our position, since the word *svarga* denotes that which brings about delight.
Because there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) for that region [of heaven], how could the word "heaven" (*svarga*) be its designator?

When heaven is a substance (*dravya*) consisting of pleasure, we say: "In the connection of substances with an action, they are related as subordinate factors (*guṇa*). Here, it is heard in scripture that "a sacrifice is to be performed by one who desires heaven.

In that case, a necessary relationship exists between heaven and the sacrifice; therein, heaven is the accomplished substance (*bhūta-dravya*), and the sacrifice is the action to be accomplished (*bhavya-karman*).

It is logical that an existing thing (bhūta) exists for the sake of something yet to be accomplished (bhavya), because its purpose is perceptible; however, it is not the case that something yet to be accomplished exists for the sake of an existing thing, for in that case, a perceptible benefit would be abandoned.
Moreover, [the former] is not a means of accomplishment [for the latter], because it exists for the sake of that [latter].
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
Therefore, they describe it as follows: pleasure is heaven.
Why? Because you have stated that the word "heaven" applies to a substance characterized by pleasure.
If this is so, then he ought first to abide in joy;
for he does not deviate from that,
whereas he does deviate from material wealth.

When that very substance which is the means of pleasure is denoted by the word "heaven" (svarga), it is only when that same substance ceases to be a means of pleasure that it is no longer designated by the word "heaven.
Therefore, this word denotes pleasure itself.

As for what was said regarding the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin), even in that case, the word [for the staff] produces a cognition of the staff within the person bearing the staff; the word "staff" is contained therein, and it is that [contained word] which is the designator of the staff.
In this context, however, the word "heaven" (svarga) alone is the designator of pleasure.

[Objection: But surely the sacrifice is heard as something to be performed. [Reply: It is said: True, it is heard as something to be performed; yet desire (kāma) is also understood as something to be performed.
He says: [The injunction] is by direct statement (*śruti*) for the sacrifice, and by syntactical connection (*vākya*) for the desire.
Nor can it be for both, because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

It is replied: although the sacrifice is heard as something to be performed, nevertheless it is not to be performed; for only that which bestows pleasure is to be performed, whereas the sacrifice bestows pain.
Therefore, it should not be performed based on direct perception, for it causes suffering when perceived directly.
It is argued that because of the scriptural injunction regarding its performance, it becomes a source of happiness through inference.
To this it is replied: inference is not a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts direct perception.
Therefore, the sacrifice should not be performed if it is not for the sake of [the deity's] gratification.
If it is argued that it will be connected with another statement regarding the fruit, it is replied:
even if it were so connected, being unenjoined, it cannot be understood as possessing a fruit merely by virtue of being mentioned in proximity.

Therefore, so that it may not be purposeless, heaven is understood as that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*); and since human effort is distinguished by the sacrifice, the sacrifice must be its instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, it has been well said: "The sacrifice is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), while heaven is primary (*pradhānabhūta*).
For because of the connection with each respective object, the relationship is indeed through the action; therefore, there must be an instruction regarding the action (*karma*).
What follows if heaven is not taught [as the result]? This follows:
for a quality (guṇa) that is neither taught nor attained through the primary purpose does not exist as such.
Therefore, heaven is the primary [result], while the ritual action is the subordinate [means].
Moreover, the statement that "he for whom heaven is desired should perform a sacrifice" seems incoherent, as it would imply desiring one thing while performing another.
If it is argued that this is understood through the connection that "from that [sacrifice], heaven arises," we reply:
for those who hold verbal testimony to be the sole authority, comprehension cannot be justified without the word itself.

We understand this relationship from the sentence itself; for example, if one were to say, "One desiring to fetch firewood should go to the forest," one would say that the capacity of going to the forest to fetch firewood is established there by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, if it is thought that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) will arise so that the instruction may not be purposeless, it is replied: this capacity does not belong to the purposelessness of the instruction, such that, in the absence of a statement of the result, the pleasure resulting from the sacrifice could be understood as its fruit.
Granted that this [injunction] may be purposeless, it never follows that its efficacy arises;
for the taking up of water by one desiring to burn does not produce a power of burning simply because it is purposeless when there is no burning.
Alternatively, its purposefulness will be established by resorting to another position, namely, that a sacrifice is enjoined for one who desires heaven.
Since ritual action is for the sake of its fruit, the scripture must apply to all who are qualified.
They recite this: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this stated with reference to every existing being whatsoever, or is it stated with reference to those who are capable? What is the prima facie view? It applies to all, because there is no distinction made.

[Objection: But trees and the like do not desire anything; how could they have the qualification [for ritual action]? [Response: It is said: let there be no [qualification] for insentient beings, but one might say "one should sacrifice" with reference to animals.
[Objection: But even animals do not desire anything.
[Response: We say no; they do desire happiness, for it is observed thus: those tormented by heat approach the shade, and those afflicted by cold approach the sunlight.
[Objection: "But surely those who are unable to perform the ritual in its entirety are not entitled [to the sacrifice].

[Reply: It is said: some are indeed able to perform the sacrifice; therefore, injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) will entitle those who are capable. However, the injunctions regarding the *viṣṇukrama* steps and so forth will not entitle those who are incapable. In that case, one for whom the *viṣṇukrama* steps and so forth have not been taught will simply perform the sacrifice; what fault is there in that? Even the appropriation of property exists through metaphorical usage, as in "the village of the gods," "the village of the elephant," or "the village of the bull. Thus, it certainly exists.
Therefore, even non-human beings who are capable possess the qualification [for ritual action].
Alternatively, because of the connection with the scriptural injunction, the mandate is understood to apply in its entirety to the agent.
The word "or" (vā) excludes the alternative position.
This is not the case, namely that animals and others also possess the qualification [for ritual action].
Then for whom is it? For one who is capable of fully accomplishing the ritual act.
Furthermore, animals and the like are not able to fully accomplish such action; therefore, for them, action is not a means to happiness.
How could that which cannot be performed be a means?

It is not [possible] for the gods, because there is no other deity [to whom one might offer]; for it is not possible to renounce oneself, as that would not even constitute a renunciation. Nor is it [possible] for the sages, because there is no lineage of sages [to whom one might offer].
Bhṛgu and others do not belong to the same lineage as [the later] Bhṛgus and others, nor is their capacity [to know such things] perceptible.
But has it not been said: "We see animals who desire fruits in another time, such as dogs and hawks fasting on the fourteenth and eighth days"?
It is replied: they do not fast because they desire fruits in another birth.
How is this understood? Because of the absence of Vedic study; for those who study the Veda know this: "Having performed this action, one attains this fruit in the hereafter.
But these [barbarians] do not study the Veda, nor the Smṛti scriptures, nor do they learn it from others.
Therefore, they do not know dharma.
How could those who are ignorant perform [the fast]? Therefore, they do not observe the fast for the sake of dharma.
For what purpose, then, is their fasting? It is said: it is due to an illness from which they have no appetite.
But how can an illness occur at a fixed time? It is said: there are indeed illnesses with fixed times, such as tertian and quartan fevers.
Therefore, the qualification belongs to human beings. Furthermore, animals do not possess property, for they are never seen to use property according to their own will;
thus, they lack mastery over wealth.
As for the expressions "village of gods" (*devagrāma*) or "village of elephants" (*hastigrāma*), those are merely figurative designations (*upacāramātra*).
Therefore, for this reason as well, animals lack the qualification [for Vedic rites].

Furthermore, as for those indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as "The gods, indeed, performed a sacrificial session" (*devā vai satram āsata*), these are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) intended to praise the injunction; for in all of them, another injunction exists.
Furthermore, an injunction does not form a single syntactical unit with another injunction, because their modes of expression differ.

Rather, that is a praise: "In this manner indeed should the sacrificial sessions (*satra*) be performed, since even the gods sit [in them] once they have accomplished their purpose; even animals, though lacking consciousness, sit [therein]; and even insentient trees [sit there]. How much more so, then, should learned humans do so!"

The purpose has been stated regarding the position [of the opponent]. Some say that a ritual lasting a thousand years need not necessarily be calculated in terms of days, because such a lifespan is possible for deities and others during the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). In the established conclusion (siddhānta), however, even if it were possible there, it must be calculated in terms of days alone.
We shall explain that further below.
Aitiśāyana maintains that [the rite] is connected with males because of the mention of a specific gender.
And because it is stated as such, the mention of a fault applies only when [the truth] is not understood.

When an embryo is killed before it has been discerned [as male or female], the designation "bhrūṇahatyā" (the killing of a learned person/embryo) applies; therefore, by killing an undiscerned embryo, one becomes a "bhrūṇahan" (a killer of an embryo).

A "bhrūṇahan" is the worst of evildoers. He who benefits both worlds is the "bhrūṇa"; the killer of that [benefactor] is a "bhrūṇahan. The "bhrūṇahan" is the killer of the sacrifice (*yajña*); he is the one who commits the slaughter of the means of the sacrifice.
Therefore, he designates the sacrifice by the word "bhrūṇa."
For he indeed either sustains everything or brings about prosperity;
therefore, the "bhrūṇahan" is one who destroys the sacrifice. Because it refers to a male [fetus], this descriptive restatement (anuvāda) is appropriate.

When an embryo is killed while its sex is unknown, it is possible that a male might be killed; in that case, since the one entitled to perform the sacrifice has been killed, the destruction of the sacrifice would constitute *bhrūṇahatyā* (the killing of an embryo).
Otherwise, if both were eligible [for the ritual], then there would be a "sacrificial slaughter" (yajñavadha) both when [the victim] is known and when it is unknown;
in that case, one would have to assume that the mention of "unknown" is non-essential (atantra).
Therefore, the masculine case-ending is intended to express its meaning.

Likewise, "having killed an Ātreyī, one becomes a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan). They say that an Ātreyī is a woman who has conceived; she is called an Ātreyī because an embryo exists within her womb (*kukṣi*). From this also, the qualification of the male is understood. Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice an animal," only a male animal is sacrificed because of the specification of the gender (*liṅga*).
In this case as well, it should be viewed in the same way.

This being the position reached, we reply: But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that it refers to the genus (jāti), because there is no distinction; therefore, a woman also should be understood [as eligible], since the meaning of the genus is not different [for either sex].
If it is argued that [the feminine suffix] is removed by means of a case ending, that is not so.
Why? Because, since it expresses the masculine, it lacks the power to exclude the feminine.
If it is argued that the restatement [of the word] "man" (*pumsaḥ*) with a case-ending is purposeless, we say no;

for even if it were purposeless, there would still be no exclusion of women (*strīnivṛtti*). In the case of an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*), there is the loss of one's own primary meaning, the assumption of a foreign meaning, and the sublation of what was already established. Furthermore, it is not purposeless, because it serves the purpose of specific indication (*nirdeśārthatvāt*).
Therefore, a woman also should be understood [as eligible], because the meaning of the genus is not distinguished;
she is enjoined just as the text declares.
As for the scriptural mention of a fault when an embryo is killed while unperceived, and the mention of an *ātreyī* woman as being associated with a male, that must be explained away.
Here it is said: the statement "by an unperceived embryo" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended for praise, and [the rule] "an *ātreyī* is not to be killed" [is likewise].
Thus, an embryo must not be killed, since even by one who is indistinct [in gender], one becomes a sinner.

A masculine case-ending, even when heard, is not capable of excluding the feminine; how much less so, then, can a gender whose meaning is unknown serve as an exclusion? Likewise, the mention of the Ātreyas is for the purpose of praising their lineage.
Nor is a woman who has conceived a child an *ātreyī*, for this is a [patronymic] lineage name (*gotra*).

Indeed, this secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix does not arise here from the word *atri*; for a secondary derivative arises only when there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), and the word *atri* lacks such competency in this context.

But because men possess property, they would [be liable]; for that which is connected with property [is liable]. Women, however, lack property due to buying and selling, since they share a common status with property itself.

But the entitlement [to perform rituals] belongs to men, because they possess property; for men possess property, whereas women do not. This ritual action is connected with property, as in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley. Why? Because women lack property due to buying and selling; for women are connected with buying and selling: they are sold by the father and bought by the husband. And because they have been sold, they have no ownership over their father's wealth; and because they have been bought, they have no ownership over their husband's wealth.
For a sale is indeed heard of in the texts: "One should give a hundred [cows] plus an extra chariot to one who has a daughter," and "In the Ārṣa rite, a pair of cattle.
And since this is for a visible purpose, it cannot be for an invisible purpose when it serves the act of bending down (in prostration).
Thus, women possess a commonality with material objects.
And likewise, there is the observation of another fact.
The statement, "She who, having been purchased by her husband, then acts with others," demonstrates the fact of her being purchased;
because she exists for his sake, the action [of purchase] exists for his sake.
He said, "She will perform the sacrifice with whatever wealth she has acquired through this increase in her wages or through spinning.
It is replied: even that is not her own property; for when she belongs to another, then whatever belongs to her also belongs to him alone.
Moreover, she must perform work for her master; she ought not to abandon that and perform her own private work.
Whatever is acquired by her through another means ought to belong to the husband alone;
thus the law records:
"The wife, the slave, and the son—all of these are entirely without property."
Whatever they acquire for you, that wealth belongs to you alone.
But because there is no distinction in the enthusiasm for the fruit.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the [previous] position.

This is not the case—that a woman is without wealth—for she is indeed possessed of property, because there is no difference in her zeal for the fruit; and on the authority of the Smṛti, she must be independent even when desiring the fruit, because of a specific Vedic statement: "One who desires the fruit should sacrifice.
If, while following the Smṛti, she were dependent and without wealth, then when it is said "one should sacrifice," she would not sacrifice.
In that case, the revealed scripture (śruti) would be sublated by the traditional law (smṛti);
and this is not logical.
Therefore, one who desires the fruit, disregarding the traditional law as non-authoritative, should acquire the substance and perform the sacrifice.
And because it is inherent with its object.
Moreover, she possesses a state of inseparable union with her husband through their shared purpose.
Thus, at the time of giving her away in marriage, a formal agreement is made: "She must not transgress in matters of dharma, artha, or kāma.
As for what is said—that wives and others are without property—even that notion of propertylessness, though it may be recorded in tradition, is indeed unjust, because it contradicts the Veda.
Therefore, in this manner, a lack of independence is stated for the purpose of establishing conventional usage;
[it serves] to show that the nature of purchase is merely a legal convention.
As for the fact that "purchase" (kraya) is mentioned in the scripture, that is merely a technical term for a religious duty (dharmamātra), not an actual purchase;
for a purchase consists of bargaining over high and low prices,
whereas this is a fixed gift of a hundred [cows] regardless of whether the girl is beautiful or unattractive.
Moreover, they do not approve of a sale that is based on Smṛti if it contradicts Śruti;
therefore, this [gift] is not a sale.
He also demonstrates that [the recipient] possesses ownership over it.
The wife indeed has authority over the nuptial property; thus, it is performed with the husband's own consent and approval.

Likewise, they perform the *saṃyājana* offerings for the wives with the *bhasad* (the rectum), for the wives possess the power of the *bhasad*; or rather, by means of the *bhasad*, they obtain mastery over the houses of others.
However, because of the specific scriptural statement regarding those who possess their own property, there should be a single performance of the rite.
Thus far, it remains established that both husband and wife possess [the capacity for] wealth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the wife sacrifice separately and the sacrificer separately, or should they sacrifice together? What is the prima facie view? That they should do so separately.
Why? Because the singular number is intended to be significant.
The agent is heard in the scripture as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) by virtue of being the one to be enjoined;
therefore, the singular number is intended to be significant. Just as two persons should not perform the sacrifice together, so it should be understood here as well.

[Objection: "Surely, for a male sacrificer, the clarified butter (ājya) will be that which has been looked upon by the sacrificer; and for a female sacrificer, it will be that which has been looked upon by the wife.

[Reply: No, he says, this is not a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the beholder. If it were a refinement of the beholder, then it would be so. But this is a refinement of the clarified butter, and the two beholders are merely subordinate factors (*guṇabhūta*). In that case, if either one is absent, there is necessarily a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*); and the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) requires the inclusion of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhārī*)."
In this regard, it might be argued that a woman acting as the sacrificer will hire a man to look at the clarified butter (*ājya*), and a man will hire a woman to look at it.

But that is not so; for the term *patnī* (wife) signifies the mistress of the sacrifice, not one who has been hired. Furthermore, *patnī* is a relative term, and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) is the master, not one who has been hired.
Therefore, the karma of this kind is one and the same for both woman and man;
and this is also because of the observation of indicative marks.
Furthermore, an indicative mark (liṅga) is indeed observed: "He girds the wife with the yoktra, and the sacrificer with the girdle, for the sake of forming a couple.

If a woman and a man are together in one place, the distinction between the yoktra and the girdle as well as the praise of their being a couple is understood from the sentence; this is appropriate in a rite where a woman and a man are the means of accomplishment, and not otherwise.
However, because she has been purchased, her status as an owner is spoken of figuratively.
But because of the desire for the fruit, there is a connection [with it] by way of ownership.

This is not so; purchase is primary, while ownership is secondary. For that Smṛti rule is for the sake of the fruit [of the sacrifice], and thus it will not be respected [as absolute]; according to the Smṛti, she would be without ownership, but according to the Śruti, she possesses ownership. And the scripture shows her to be possessed of the fruit.
"May the husband and wife go together by virtue of their good deed;
yoked as the two bearers of the sacrifice, being in harmony, may they cast away their enemies and attain undecaying light in heaven"—this verse shows the fruit for the couple.
Therefore, it is established that both are authorized [to perform the rite].
And there is a double laying [of the fires], as in the case of the two sacrifices.
There is the rite of establishing the sacred fires, as it is said: "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire.
Regarding this, they prescribe: "Wearing linen garments, the two should establish the fire. In this regard, there is a point of doubt: should two persons establish the fire, or only one person?
How does the doubt arise? It is said: here it is heard, "The two, wearing [wool], should establish the fires.

In that context, since the statement is already established by the sense of the matter, it is heard again; therefore, the doubt arises as to whether this is for the purpose of connecting the masculine gender, or for the purpose of enjoining the linen cloth (*kṣauma*).
Since both possibilities exist, there is doubt: if it is for the purpose of connecting the gender, then two men would perform the establishment of the fires.

Now, for the purpose of connecting [the word] with linen, one says: "the two wearing" (*vasānau*). This is not merely in the masculine gender; it is expressive of both female and male, just as *kukkuṭa* (cock) and *kukkuṭī* (hen) are *kukkuṭau*, or *śūkara* (boar) and *śūkarī* (sow) are *śūkarau*.
Likewise, *vasāna* (wearing) and *vasānā* (wearing) would be *vasānau*.

To this it is replied: where there is no specific meaning, nor a specific context, and there is an injunctive word rather than a restatement (*anuvāda*), two males are understood; for example, when told "bring two," one brings two males. When told "bring two [feminine]," one brings two females; therefore, it is understood that the dual ending in *e* denotes females, and likewise, the dual ending in *au* denotes two males.
Regarding the fact that the form ending in *au* is now seen when applied to both a woman and a man, is it the case that a man accompanied by another is the cause, or a woman accompanied by another?
It is said: [the suffix] is seen [to apply] when a man is accompanied by another, as in "bring the two Brāhmaṇas"; here too, the meaning is a man accompanied by another.
Therefore, it is understood that the cause is the man.
Here it is asked: "Is it not understood from the very observation here that [the word] denotes both female and male?

To this it is replied: This has already been stated—that it is improper for a single word to have multiple meanings; therefore, its meaning will be 'a male accompanied by another,' and it would be improper [to take it] as 'female and male.
Now, in the injunction regarding a male accompanied by another, who else could be the companion?"

Because a woman cannot be denoted [by the term "the other"], and because a second [partner] is necessarily implied, "the other" refers to a man who has a companion; likewise, the one is accompanied by the other, and the other is also accompanied by the one—thus, only two men are understood to be taken.
Therefore, it is said that here, two men are prescribed for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) rite.
But is it not the case that grammarians record a dual form ending in *-au* as denoting both a woman and a man?
We say that this is not a traditional rule (*smṛti*). [The opponent] says: "We shall infer a traditional rule from the statement of the Blessed Pāṇini, namely, *pumān striyā*.
It is replied: No; the statement of Pāṇini regarding *kukkuṭau* does not mean that the dual ending *-au* denotes both male and female.

How, then, is it so? Where there is a co-utterance of both female and male, one might think that because it is "a man with a companion," the vowel *au* would apply to the form ending in *a*; or because it is "a woman with a companion," the vowel *e* would apply.
However, Pāṇini’s rule states that in such a case the word for "man" (*pumśabda*) is correct, not the word for "woman.
Furthermore, he says "the masculine remains" (*pumān śiṣyate*), by which it is understood all the more clearly that the vowel *au* is the designator of the male.

Therefore, the entitlement belongs to two men. [The opponent] asks: "Will she (the sentence) indeed enjoin that? It is replied: She is able to enjoin the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) as expressed by its own word, because the *ādhāna* is heard [in the text] and is already enjoined; however, since [the injunction of the *ādhāna*] would otherwise be purposeless, the phrase "wearing [two garments]" (*vasānau*) is able to enjoin it through syntactical connection (*vākya*), for there exists a relationship between the two wearing [garments] and the *ādhāna*. In that case, its own primary meaning is not entirely abandoned. But if one were to enjoin the relationship with the wearing of linen (*kṣauma*), while discarding the *ādhāna* by saying "they two should perform the *ādhāna*" (*ādadhīyātām*), one would utterly abandon the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

Furthermore, when a mark closely connected to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is to be enjoined, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is not capable of enjoining a remote connection with wearing linen (*kṣaumavasāna*), because of the remoteness of the meaning.

Moreover, if one were to set aside the direct statement and enjoin a connection with wearing linen, then the linen would become an accessory (*aṅga*) of the person wearing it, rather than an accessory of the *ādhāna*.
In that case, since the *ādhāna* would not be defective even in the absence of linen, the *ādhāna* could be performed even when linen is lacking.

He asks: "In that case, what purpose is intended by the quality of wearing [the garment]? It is said: "None at all; for this very reason, this position is abandoned. He asks: "How then is the scriptural mention of wearing linen (*kṣauma*) to be understood now? It is said: "It is not possible to enjoin both the linen and the gender-mark (*liṅga*); for in that way, the sentence would be split."

Therefore, the word *kṣauma* (linen) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding two [garments] that are not linen; and since clothing is already established by implication, the meaning is "two men wearing [clothing].
And these, for one who is moving about, are generally soiled and resemble linen, or the garments of one who is moving about become noisy.
Therefore, the entitlement belongs to two men.
But because it is an injunction of an accessory, the word "second" should refer to the wife.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.

This is not so—that which was said, that two men should establish the fires; rather, only one should establish them. For it is said, "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fire in spring," and the singular number is intended to be significant.
Therefore, only one person should establish the sacred fires. [Objection: But this statement says that "two men should establish the fires.

[Response: No, he says, because it is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇa*). In this sentence, the injunction of the linen cloth (*kṣauma*) is what is logical; for in this way, a previously unknown matter (*apūrva-artha*) is enjoined, and a specific restriction is indeed understood.
Otherwise, the mention of *kṣauma* would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and a mere statement would be purposeless.

Furthermore, a restatement occurs only when there is an alternative position (*pakṣa*), yet this word does not denote a single alternative. And if it were used in a figurative sense (*gauṇatva*), the similarity would have to be common to both.
Therefore, one might understand that study is enjoined even without a reason [for the gender].

To this it is said: "Surely two males are to be enjoined; and if they were enjoined, there would be no injunction for the linen cloth (*kṣauma*), for in that case there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, the two males are understood through direct audition (*śruti*), whereas the linen cloth is understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*); thus, the former two would sublate the latter. To this it is replied: the two males are not to be enjoined; rather, a male accompanied by a second is already established here, and he is merely restated (*anūdyate*).
How so? In this context, one man is heard; his wife would constitute the second [person].
Furthermore, that which is already understood prior to the statement cannot be the object of an injunction.
Therefore, this is an injunction regarding the linen garment (*kṣauma*), and there is no split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).
Regarding her, it is said that she possesses blessings and celibacy because of her incomparability.

In such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," it has been stated that there is joint entitlement for both the woman and the man.

Now, a doubt arises: must the wife perform all the duties pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), or only those specifically mentioned, namely the *āśis* (benedictions) and celibacy (*brahmacarya*)? What is the prima facie view? All the duties pertaining to the sacrificer should belong to the wife as well, for she too is a sacrificer, and thus they are equal.
"Therefore, everything belongs to her.

This being the position reached, we reply: only that which has been explicitly stated for her applies, because of the authority of the scriptural statement; namely, the benediction and the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Why? Because of their inequality; for women and men are unequal—the sacrificer is a man and is learned, while the wife is a woman and is unlearned.
The four castes [are equal] because there is no distinction.

Rites such as the *agnihotra* serve as the example; regarding them, there is a doubt: do they belong to all four castes, or to the three castes excluding the *śūdra*? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? The Veda issues injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" and "one should offer oblations" with reference to the four castes. Why? Because there is no distinction; for no specific qualification is mentioned.
Therefore, the Śūdra does not [participate].

Or rather, because of the specific instruction regarding the three [castes], there would be no connection for him in the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) or in the sacrifices; thus Ātreya maintains that the scriptural mention refers only to the Brāhmaṇa.

The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position; rather, there would be entitlement for the three [castes]. Why? Because of the specification in the *agnyādheya* (the ritual of establishing the sacred fires). In the *agnyādheya*, there is a specification of the three: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fires in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. Since there is no scriptural injunction (*śruti*) regarding the establishment of fires for a Śūdra, the Śūdra is without the sacred fires (*anagni*) and is thus incapable of performing the *agnihotra* and other such rites. Therefore, in passages such as "One desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," there is no scriptural basis that would grant entitlement to the Śūdra.

That [injunction] proceeds with reference only to Brāhmaṇas and the other [twice-born classes], for they alone are capable because they possess the sacred fires; the Āhavanīya and other fires do not belong to a Śūdra, because they are not prescribed for him, and because terms such as "Āhavanīya" denote consecrated ritual preparations.
Therefore, Ātreya held that the Śūdra is not entitled to perform the Agnihotra and other such rites.
Bādari, however, maintains that because the [mention of the Śūdra] is for the purpose of indicating a specific occasion (nimitta), there should be entitlement for all.

As for what was said—that the Śūdra has no entitlement—that is not so; for it is stated that "one should sacrifice" with reference to every seeker of results, and in the absence of a prohibitory statement, the Śūdra would not be excluded.

As for the claim that he is incapable due to the absence of sacred fires (agni), he would indeed possess such fires as they are obtained through necessity, because they are encompassed by the scriptural injunctions regarding desire (kāmaśruti).
Moreover, from the observation of other passages, one should understand the matter according to the literal text.

The alternative view (*api vā*) is set aside. [The ritual] should be understood exactly according to what is heard in the scripture; for in the context of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), Brāhmaṇas and others are mentioned. Therefore, the consecration has Brāhmaṇas and others as its performers, and because of the mention of spring and other seasons, it has spring and so forth as its time. And thus, this enumeration applies only to those excluding the Śūdra: "One should perform the *Bārhadgira* as the *brahmasāman* for a Brāhmaṇa, the *Pārthuraśya* for a Rājanya (Kṣatriya), and the *Rāyovājīya* for a Vaiśya"; they do not prescribe a *sāman* for the Śūdra.

Likewise, there is the milk-vow for a Brāhmaṇa, gruel for a Rājanya, and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for a Vaiśya; similarly, at the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), a Brāhmaṇa should establish the fire at eight steps, a Rājanya at eleven, and a Vaiśya at twelve.
Thus, even if a ritual action were performed by a Śūdra, it would be fruitless if it lacked the Brahma-sāman, the vow, and the [measured] steps.
Therefore, a Śūdra should neither offer oblations nor perform sacrifices.
But because of the specific instruction, it would apply in one case.
This is not so; [the opponent argues] that because a Śūdra lacks sacred fires, he has no entitlement to the Agnihotra and other such rites.

[The proponent replies: For there is indeed the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) for a Śūdra, as the scripture states in general terms, "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire. This [general rule] will also serve as a provision for specific occasions; therefore, the scripture ought to be understood as granting entitlement to all.
If it is argued that [the Veda] is not [authoritative] because of its defects;

Now, as for what was said—that the ritual action of a Śūdra, being devoid of the *brahmasāman*, the vow, and the formal commencement (*aprakrama*), would not achieve its fruit even if performed because it is deficient—this must be refuted; for [the action] is optional (*kāmya*).

This is the rebuttal: because it is subject to desire, the Śūdra will desire [to perform it]. The *abhīvarta* is a *brahmasāman*; indeed, it is taught without reference to anything specific and without distinction, stating, "One should place it on what is measured by the eye. Thus, for those whose commencement is unrestricted, the Śūdra is restricted [from it].
Regarding the vow as well, it is determined from the observation of the connection, "Curdled milk (*mastu*) for the Śūdra," that curdled milk alone belongs to the Śūdra.
Therefore, all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) would be entitled [to perform the sacrifice].
And because among the formative forces (saṃskāra), that [volition] is predominant.
Furthermore, a distinction is understood regarding the vow; for in the vow, the person is primary.

What follows from this fact that the person is primary? This follows: a sacrament (saṃskāra) whose primary referent is the person cannot, if it is not extended [to others], exclude that person's entitlement [to the rite].
How so?

For when it is stated, "One should sacrifice," with reference to one who desires heaven, how is it understood that a Śūdra desiring that [heaven] is not addressed? For does he not perform that part of the sacrifice which is to be accomplished by a person? If you say it is because of the vow (*vrata*), no; for that [vow] is prescribed for the sake of generating capacity (*sāmarthya*) only for the one to whom it is addressed. Without it, that person alone lacks the capacity, not anyone else.
For this indeed is the nature of being an auxiliary to the vow (*vrata*): that it renders the performer capable.
But he who has a need for that [vow] accomplishes the sacrifice without depending upon it at all.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no exclusion of the Śūdra.
Or rather, because of the instruction in the Veda, it should be understood as applying to those who are not Śūdras.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the desire for qualities;
There is a purpose for the quality of study: a Śūdra, though not initiated, might approach [a teacher] of his own accord and seek instruction; thus, his capacity will be produced.
Since the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) is for that purpose, the Vedic text regarding the person refers to knowledge.

It is said: this mention of the "person" (*puruṣa*) occurs only in reference to knowledge (*vidyā*), because the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*) has that as its purpose. One is brought into the presence of the teacher for the sake of knowledge, not for some invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭa*), nor to build a wall; such is this mention of the person in relation to knowledge. How is this understood? This [act] is designated as "making one a teacher" (*ācāryakaraṇa*). Why? Because of the observation of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). The root *nī* (to lead) is used in the sense of making one a teacher; therefore, through its connection with that purpose, initiation is prompted by the act of making one a teacher. And one becomes a teacher by teaching the Veda.

Therefore, the study of the Veda is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas and the other [twice-born classes], but the study of the Veda is not prescribed for the Śūdra; thus, because he lacks the Veda, the Śūdra is incapable and is not entitled [to perform sacrifices]. If it is argued that this is not so because of the mention of knowledge (vidyā), [we reply: no.
Due to a lack of medical knowledge, there would be failure in the performance of the ritual action.

And this is not the case, that a Śūdra would study; for his study is prohibited by the rule, "A Śūdra must not study. Even if he were to study, his study would not bear fruit, and a fault would arise. Therefore, it is established that the Śūdra is unlearned (*avaidya*), and thus there is an absence [of qualification] regarding ritual action. Furthermore, even if he were established as learned, because he lacks the sacred fires (*anagnitva*), there would still be an absence of qualification for ritual action.
Now, how is it that [the Veda] does not establish the non-existence of fire?

For the scriptural injunctions regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) pertain to Brāhmaṇas and the other castes. But is it not the case that the sentence, "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire," is the injunction for the act of establishing the fire itself?
In that regard, it is understood that statements such as "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires in spring" have the purpose of indicating a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
To this it is replied: from the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires," an injunction is understood;

whereas from the commendatory passage (*stuti*) "He who, knowing thus, establishes the sacred fires," [the injunction] is merely inferential (*ānumānika*) and is weaker than the directly revealed *śruti*.
Therefore, the statements are prescriptive; hence, there is no entitlement for a Śūdra.
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose.
Among these three, it is endowed with substance, because action is established through substance.
Regarding the Agnihotra and other such rites, there is a doubt: does one who lacks property have the entitlement, or not?
It is said: among the three [classes], only one endowed with property is entitled, not one lacking property.
Why? Because one lacking property is unable to perform a rite that requires the use of materials.
Therefore, that which is not a substance has no entitlement [to ritual action].
However, this would not be the case because of impermanence; for, by implication, there is a connection with a substance.
It cannot be as you have stated—that there is no eligibility for one who lacks property (*adravya*).
Why? Because it is impermanent; the conjunction with property is impermanent, for there is no person who is by birth alone without property.
There exists a means by which one becomes possessed of property.
The word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is denotative of one who is capable of sacrificing; it does not authorize one who is in no way able to accomplish the sacrifice.
However, it does not exclude one who is able [to perform it] in some manner.
Furthermore, by implication, there will be a connection with wealth, for it is impossible that one should live without property.
Therefore, the connection with the substance arises from the purpose itself;
and one who is deficient in a limb is subject to that same rule.
Regarding the *agnihotra* and other such rites, there arises a doubt concerning one who is deficient in limbs: is he entitled [to perform them], or not?
In this case as well, there is an extension of the preceding section of discussion.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that he is not entitled because he is incapable; the final view (*siddhānta*) is that he is entitled because his capacity exists.
This is now stated: "And one who is deficient in a limb possesses that same property. What is its property? It is the property of lacking substance (*adravyadharma*).
Why? Because of its eternal connection [to that state] from the very moment of its arising.

However, regarding one whose physical deficiency is incurable, there arises an inquiry: is he entitled [to perform sacrifices], or not? Having reached the preliminary conclusion (*pūrva-pakṣa*) that he is entitled by virtue of the preceding section, we reply: he is not entitled. Why? Because of a lack of capacity; he is unable to sacrifice in any manner whatsoever. Therefore, his entitlement is not understood.
For one who lacks three ancestral lineages (*ṛṣi*), there would be exclusion.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "He chooses an ancestral lineage (ārṣeya); he chooses one, he chooses two, he chooses three; he does not choose four, nor does he choose more than five.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is one who lacks an ancestral lineage (atryārṣeya) entitled [to perform the sacrifice], or not?
What is the prima facie view? That even one who lacks an ancestral lineage is entitled.

Why? Because the statement "he chooses the *ārṣeya* (lineage)" is a general injunction; therefore, he will choose either one or two, and that is shown by the texts: "he chooses one" and "he chooses two. Likewise, it prohibits: "he does not choose four," and "he does not choose more than five.
For a prohibition of what has not been established as possible is not appropriate.
Therefore, even one who lacks three *ṛṣis* (*atryārṣeya*) would be entitled [to perform the sacrifice].
On account of the statement regarding the chariot-maker, this [fire] belongs to him at the establishment of the sacred fires, because it is supplementary to everything.
In connection with the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna), it is heard in scripture: "The chariot-maker (rathakāra) should establish the fires during the rainy season.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the chariot-maker one belonging to the three [higher] castes, or is he one outside the three castes?
What is the prima facie view? This establishment of the fires belongs to a chariot-maker who is outside the three castes.

Why? Because of the scriptural statement; for there is nothing that a scriptural statement cannot accomplish. Furthermore, in this context of the fire-consecration (ādhāna), all those who do not belong to the three higher castes are excluded, as the consecration has been prescribed specifically for Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas. By process of elimination, the chariot-maker (rathakāra) must be one who does not belong to these three castes. Or rather, he is rightly [considered] so because of his connection with the specific ritual work, since the Śūdra is otherwise prohibited [from such rites].

Or it might be logical that the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*) belongs to the three higher castes, for he is specifically designated by his work with chariots; whereas a Śūdra is excluded because of his incapacity.
Therefore, the chariot-maker should belong to the three higher castes.
However, this cannot be so, because [the specific qualification] is due to the absence of [other] duties.

There is no chariot-maker belonging to the three [twice-born] castes, for his livelihood by means of crafts is prohibited; however, there is one who does not belong to the three castes. Therefore, on the authority of this scriptural statement, he shall perform the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*). And [the injunction would otherwise be] purposeless due to its connection [with an impossible person].

The *vasantā* (spring) and other seasons are fixed for the Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes]; if the rainy season (*varṣā*) were prescribed with reference to them, it would result in meaninglessness due to a lack of connection.
Therefore, the *rathakāra* (chariot-maker) here is one who does not belong to the three [twice-born] castes.
[Objection: "If it is argued that this is for the sake of a specific quality (*guṇa*)."

If you see it thus—that there is no chariot-maker belonging to the three [upper] castes because his livelihood as an artisan is prohibited—then there will be some chariot-maker by way of secondary quality (*guṇārthena*) or by way of a false designation (*vaitathyena*); for him, this *ādheya* (the act of kindling) is understood.
The fact that [the term] is not a primary cause (*animittatva*) has been stated.
We have already stated that these scriptural injunctions do not have the purpose of establishing a causal basis (*nimitta*). What follows from this, if they do not serve as a causal basis?

It follows from this that they are *prāpaka* (providing what is not yet obtained), because the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet been obtained; however, a *prāpaka* that merely restates what is already obtained would be redundant. Therefore, it will apply to one for whom [the rite] has not yet been obtained.
Now, it might be argued that this [mention of the rains] will serve as a single indicative mark (*nimitta*).
This is not tenable; for how could that which is connected with spring and so forth be connected with the rainy season?

Furthermore, in the view that it is an injunction of acquisition (*prāpaka-pakṣa*), the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) is enjoined by direct statement (*śruti*); whereas in the view that it is an indicative mark (*nimitta-pakṣa*), the rainy season would have to be enjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*), and direct statement is more powerful than syntactical connection.
Therefore, this kindling of the sacred fires belongs to one who is not a member of the three [upper] castes;
however, the Saudhanvanas may be understood [to be eligible] because of their low status as indicated by the wording of the mantra.
The *sthapati* should be a *niṣāda*, because of the force of the word.

"One should offer a *caru* oblation to Rudra in the middle of the dwelling; where Rudra might destroy the offspring"—having introduced this sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), it is stated: "One should cause the *niṣādasthapati* to sacrifice with this. Regarding the *niṣādasthapati*, there is a doubt: is he one of those already entitled [to perform sacrifices], or is he someone else entirely?

We say he is one of those already entitled, for he is capable, owing to his learning and possession of the sacred fires (*agni*); whereas the other is incapable, owing to his lack of learning and lack of sacred fires.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark.
A mark is seen; the mention of "the peak on the south" indicates the property of the Niṣādas.
For the peak is beneficial only to the Niṣādas, not to the Āryas; thus, it belongs to the Niṣādas alone.
Since each [rite] achieves its purpose for a specific person, that person alone would have the entitlement to it.
"One should cause one desiring offspring to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite; those desiring prosperity should undertake it.

Likewise, "In such and such cases, those having such-and-such desires should undertake the sacrificial session (*sattra*); at least seventeen and at most twenty-four should sit for the sacrificial session.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: does the entitlement to the *sattra* belong to each individual seeking the entire fruit, or does the entitlement belong to the assembly (*parṣad*) seeking the fruit?

He says: "But surely those who desire [the results] are indicated as being distinguished by a large number; how then can there be entitlement for them individually? It is replied: The injunctions such as "those desiring supernatural power" (*ṛddhikāmāḥ*) apply to all those characterized by such powers, whether collectively or individually. It is not possible to restrict them to a specific [group] by means of the plural number; therefore, a doubt arises as to whether it refers to each individual or to the assembly (*parṣad*). What, then, is the prima facie view? An individual is not capable of performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*) that requires many agents; rather, we understand that the assembly itself is the agent seeking the result.
Furthermore, there is no fruit for one who does not act, nor is a single person called the agent; therefore, the fruit belongs to all collectively.

While it might be argued that each individual receives a portion of the fruit, such that the middle [portion] would constitute the entire fruit—this being the position reached—we reply: for each respective seeker, the entire fruit is accomplished through the *sattra*.

Why? Because from [the performance of] each individual human purpose, success arises; when performed together, every single one accomplishes the human purpose by way of a common procedure (*tantra*), and the fruit belongs to the agents, with each being an agent here.
Furthermore, just as there may be the perception of existence due to connection with origination, so too would the state of being exist without division.

Furthermore, it is not contradictory that a single action is performed by many. If it is argued that this is contradictory because, once the action has been performed by one, what would a second person do? To this it is replied: such a fault applies only to performance in succession (*paryāyeṇa*); however, in the case of simultaneous performance (*tantra*), there is sometimes a possibility [of its occurrence]. Just as the perception of a being might occur, so too would the state of existence (*bhāva*) exist without division; just as the sight of a single being—such as an elephant or a horse—is fully accomplished by each individual observer.

In the same way, there may be a common procedure (*tantra*) in a sacrificial session (*satra*); the substance belongs to all [the sacrificers], and the Adhvaryu throws it over the central Āhavanīya fire. In that case, all the performers act through a common procedure.
Moreover, there is no connection with a number produced [subsequently] here; rather, the ritual action is connected with the number by its very origin.

For if that which has already arisen were to be conjoined, then the statement "for the sake of multiple connections" would be understood; however, this is not the case in the conjunction of what is arising.
Therefore, each individual [act] is connected with the entire fruit.
Since the word "person" (puruṣa) is heard in relation to the performance (prayoga), there may be performance according to one's desire.
What is established? One may perform the application according to one's desire.

Why? Because of the mention of the person; for a person is heard [in the text]. Once the word has fulfilled its purpose by enjoining the sacrifice for the person, it does not preclude the sacrifice being performed by one, two, or many.
That person is not enjoined in the sacrifice itself with the instruction, "he shall bring the sacrifice to completion," or "he shall bring about the fruit through the sacrifice."
How, then, is it? [The person is intended] so that one may obtain the fruit through sacrifice.
The person is not a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) either of the sacrifice or of the production of the fruit.
For if he were a subordinate factor of the sacrifice or of the production of the fruit, then the number, being a subordinate quality (*guṇabhūta*), would delimit that subordinate factor, the person.

Furthermore, if it were to illuminate the person as a constituent part, it would be connected to the person solely by way of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and not by way of expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).

In that case, the expression of number would be unintended; for this statement, being made with reference to every person who is a seeker and capable, cannot be qualified by a single [singular] verbal ending.

And how is there primacy of the person (*puruṣaprādhānya*)? There is no purpose served by the production of the fruit, nor by the production of the sacrifice; rather, the self, being connected to the fruit, is desired by everyone, and for its sake the ritual must be performed. Otherwise, even if it were enjoined, it would not be performed, and in that case the meaning of the scriptural statement would be rendered void. Therefore, there would be freedom of choice (*yāthākāmya*): one, two, or many might perform the sacrifice.

And thus it shows: "For you two are the lords of heaven"—this one should use as the *pratipad* for two sacrificers; "these drops have been poured forth"—this for many sacrificers. This demonstrates the performance of sacrifice for both two and for many.
If it is argued that the status of the Vedic revelation applies to each individual purpose...
It is not for the sake of the subordinate element, because it has not been stated as such; rather, since the agent is the primary factor, it serves a different purpose.

This is not so; for when the person is the primary element for the sake of that [action], the person is not perceived as a subordinate member. Indeed, we do not perceive it as such when the logical principle is not stated, since the state of being primary arises from the state of being subordinate, and here the agent is the primary element because the statement must have purpose. Therefore, a subordinate status for the agent is not tenable, because the injunction is a single unitary whole.

For there is indeed only one injunctive impulsion (*codanā*); if it enjoins either the production of the fruit or the production of the sacrifice, then the agent does not act for his own sake; but when [the impulsion] is for his own sake, then the sacrifice or the fruit exists for that purpose.

And this does not occur simultaneously—namely, that one [element] has its own purpose while the other has that [first element] as its purpose, or vice versa—as is understood in the case of the statement, "Devadatta shoots arrows with both arms. It is not simultaneous; for when he shoots with the right hand, at that time he bends the back of the bow with the left, and it is not understood that he shoots with that [left hand] as well, because it is occupied elsewhere. Likewise, when the person (puruṣa) is primary, then the subordinate status (guṇabhāva) of the sacrifice or the fruit is understood.
Because it is occupied elsewhere in that case, the primacy of those two is also not understood.
Therefore, the person does not have a subordinate status (guṇabhāva) either with respect to the sacrifice or its fruit;
hence, there would be freedom of choice (yāthākāmya), such that one, two, or many might perform the sacrifice.

Or rather, because of the connection with the desire [for the fruit], it is taught for the sake of performance, for the scriptural injunction is directed toward each purpose, like the case of the horns.

The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position: the agent would be taught for the sake of the performance [of the rite], not for his own benefit. How so? The meaning of the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice") is either "one should perform the sacrifice" or "one should effect [something] by means of the sacrifice"; thus, only the manifestation of existence is understood, not that the agent is the creator (*dhātṛ*) of the fruit. Furthermore, the word *svargakāmaḥ* ("desirous of heaven") denotes merely one who desires heaven; it does not depend upon a distinction as to whether [that desire] belongs to oneself or to another. And in such matters, we take the word itself as our authority.

How, then, is desire understood to be connected to the self? It is through the connection [itself]: even when not explicitly stated by a word, one who desires a result desires that result for oneself alone, not for another. However, where both meanings must be expressed, an injunction is heard for each meaning separately; as in: "He scratches with the black antelope horn" and "He throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit. Where there are thus two scriptural injunctions, both subordination (*guṇabhāva*) and primacy (*prādhānya*) are understood.
But in this case, there are not two such injunctive scriptural texts.

Rather, the person is heard as a subordinate element in the phrase "one should bring about [the result]"; therein, the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the object (*karman*).

However, due to the connection [with the result], the person is primary; for no one has a need for pleasure that has merely arisen, but rather the purpose belongs to the self through its connection with pleasure.
Therefore, from that connection, the predominance of the person is understood, not from the Vedic text itself;
hence, the number of the person, who is subordinate, is intended to be significant.
If it is argued that this might apply to something else—

If you view it thus, then in that case, if one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) desires the heaven of another, then even while desiring the heaven of another, a different person would perform the sacrifice.
In that situation, the previously stated principle—that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer"—would be overturned;
for there would be a connection with an object other than one's own.

It is not that one should not sacrifice because [the text says] "one desiring heaven for another," nor is it that the word "desiring heaven" does not denote another person. How, then, [is it interpreted]? It means that such a person does not obtain the fruit.
But how is there a non-attainment of the fruit? Because of the hearing of a specific grammatical designation (upagraha), namely, "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*).

Or, regarding the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires, "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the fire in the spring," then the gerundive suffix in that scriptural statement of desire is merely a restatement; for one who desires a result is the occasion [for the action]. If this is argued:

If you think thus—that the word "desirer of heaven" (*svargakāma*) is not denotative, that another person should not sacrifice because there would be no fruit, and that this [sacrificer] does not perform the sacrifice—then one should sacrifice out of a desire for the fruit of the *sūktavāka*. For the Hotṛ will designate the instigator [of the rite], saying, "This sacrificer desires long life," and so forth. Furthermore, there is an injunction regarding the fruit in the rule: "With the *sūktavāka*, he casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle]. If this is an injunction of a fruit based on the wording of the mantra, then the *prastara* is cast with the *sūktavāka*; otherwise, an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated.

Therefore, for the sake of an incidental result, it is not the case that one person desiring heaven should perform a sacrifice intended for another; this is because [the sacrifice] is obligatory (nitya).
This is not the case; for that which is the primary fruit of an action must also be its incidental fruit, so that the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is accomplished for one's own sake.

Indeed, there is no distinction regarding the self-interest of the *ādhāna*; whether it be the primary fruit or the incidental fruit, everything must accrue to the establisher. Furthermore, the status of being both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) would be contradicted: if one were to sacrifice desiring long life and such, then it would not be obligatory; if it is obligatory, then one does not desire long life and such.
Therefore, the established rule should not be overturned, nor is the person enjoined as the primary element; rather, his singularity is intended [by the author] because he is subordinate.
Therefore, one alone should sacrifice. If it is argued that the ritual act is likewise [to be performed by many], [we reply: no.

Now, as for what was stated—that it shows the sacrifice for two and for many, saying "Since you two are the lords of heaven," one should employ the *pratipad* for two sacrificers, and "These drops have been poured forth," one should employ the *pratipad* for many sacrificers; and that by prescribing the *pratipad* in rites with two or many sacrificers, the rite would thus be appropriately joined—that must be refuted.
[The answer is: "No, because of the lack of connection."
