This is not so; for there exists a combined ritual performed by two sacrificers and by many sacrificers, as established by scriptural statement, just like the *ahīna* sacrifices. In those cases, the prescription of the *pratipad* will be meaningful.
Therefore, "one should sacrifice" [is the rule].
However, it may be restricted by the commencement, because the commencement is the cause for the performance of the action.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the object desired by the seeker is what is here stated as being that which ought to be performed?

[Response: This is not so; for that would be the meaning of the sentence as a whole (*vākyārtha*), whereas the fact that the sacrifice itself is to be performed is understood through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, once a sacrifice has been commenced by one desiring a village, it must be brought to completion.

The statement expressing the desire for a village and so forth serves as the *nimitta* (the causal occasion). And when an occasion has arisen, that which is to be performed is prescribed; even if that occasion has perished, it must still be performed. One must complete what has been commenced, for that which has perished does not become non-existent. Furthermore, the arising [of the desire] is the occasion, not its continued existence. Therefore, even when the desire for the fruit has passed away, what has been commenced must be brought to completion.

For the commencement of an action is the cause for the action itself, and that [commencement] is likewise the cause for its completion. Alternatively, there is no fixed rule regarding the means because of the desire for the result, just as in the case of an action not yet undertaken.
Or rather, because it is caused by that [desire], the restriction would be the cause of the agent.
For the commencement is indeed the cause of completion. How so? It would be the cause for the agent [to achieve his goal].

What is the reason? Because of the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatā*); for the learned do not censure one who completes a task of such a kind once it has been begun, saying, "This man is unreliable and unfit to associate with. And censure by the learned is a fault.
Therefore, one should complete [the rite] starting from that point.
He asks: "But for what reason do the learned ones censure it?
It is said in reply: "They censure it simply by asking, 'What is the use of our knowing the underlying cause?'"
In this world, ritual actions are like the Vedas; from them arises the knowledge of the Supreme Person.

Someone approaches a house with either a cart or a chariot; his desire for its fruit has vanished, yet he obtains the fruit. In this regard, there is a doubt: must it necessarily be completed by him, or may it also be abandoned according to his will? What is the prima facie view? Actions of this kind in the world, once commenced, must be brought to completion; just as those belonging to the Veda, so too must they be completed as a matter of necessity.
Why? Because from that [comes] the knowledge of the presiding deity (*adhipuruṣa-jñāna*), and from that it ought to follow the knowledge of that person (*tatpuruṣa-jñāna*).

Why? From the scripture (*śāstra*); for the scripture of carpenters is handed down in tradition, and therein the activity of deities is admitted—such as "these deities are in the eastern direction" and "those others are in the other directions. If there is censure by the learned when the activity of deities undertaken for the sake of the scripture remains incomplete, so too should it be here.
And even in the case of a transgression, they [follow] the scripture.

And when those worldly people commit an offense, those carpenters hand down a penance-scripture (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*), stating: "The broken arm of Indra must be bound with *āra* grass, and a *brāhmaṇa* must be fed milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Now, if this penance were for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it would not exist without a scripture;
and if it were for the sake of avoiding a contingency (*prasaṅga-parihāra*), then it is understood that even in that case, it is indeed based on an unseen principle.

But acquisition [of a property] occurs without the authority of a scriptural rule; the scripture would not be the means of its conceptualization. Therefore, it should be understood through the purpose (artha), for a scriptural rule is meaningful only when [the matter] has not already been established by other means.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
We say that their acquisition [of this knowledge] is without a formal treatise (*aśāstrā*).
You infer a treatise from this Smṛti; however, there is no Smṛti without a treatise, nor is a manual for carpenters possible without a Smṛti.

Therefore it is said: in this case there exists a traditional recollection (*smṛti*) that "this work, such as house-building and the like, becomes beautiful," but not that "some unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) arises from this work.
Furthermore, that beauty can be known even without a scripture; having known it, it is then recollected.
Therefore, the scripture is not the source of this recollection.
It must be postulated:
if [the practice] could not be obtained without the scripture, then it would be postulated that the scripture has purpose here.

Therefore, this is not stated in the scripture; and regarding what is stated in the scripture, the learned censure one who abandons it entirely once it has been partially performed, as well as one who relies upon a deity.
[Objection: But surely even here the deities are accepted [as the objects], in the sense that "in this direction this deity will be sacrificed to, and in that direction that one.

[Reply: It is said in response: the deities are traditionally remembered (smṛta) as being subordinate to the person, not subordinate to the cup; therefore, there is no fault. However, because the scriptures possess purposefulness, the human goal is enjoined; since those two [the cup and the person] do not coincide, if they were treated as identical, there would be a transgression of the injunction.

In this case, however, there is a lack of co-occurrence between those two: here an action is prohibited, whereas no non-action is enjoined. For one who eats *kalañja* does not fail to transgress the prohibition; but here, one who looks at the sun does not fail to transgress an injunction, for looking at it is not prohibited. In that other case, a restriction (*niyama*) is taught, and he who performs that restriction becomes connected with the fruit [of the rite]. But here, *kalañja* and the like are prohibited. How is this understood? Because there is no statement here introducing the subject as "this is his vow" (*vratam*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the expression "it should not be eaten" is not a mental operation; rather, the word "it should be eaten" denotes that eating is to be performed, and the word "not" negates that very act by direct audition (*śruti*). In this way, the well-known conventional meaning is upheld; otherwise, there would be metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And when there is a conflict between direct audition and metaphorical indication, direct audition is the proper course, not metaphorical indication.
Therefore, in this case, it is a prohibition.
It is said: "Let it be granted that there is indeed a prohibition; however, no fault is heard [stated] in this regard.
Therefore, even though it is prohibited, it should be performed. If it is argued that [a fault] will be inferred, we say no, because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).

If it should be argued that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a valid means of knowledge because otherwise the instruction would result in being purposeless—this is not so; for even a purposeless instruction is possible due to ignorance.
Therefore, one should not postulate such a defect.

It is said: True, it need not be inferred; rather, it is already established. How so? Immediately thereafter, the learned (śiṣṭas) would avoid him, saying, "He has fallen from the fruits of ritual action. And this is a great fault, that the learned avoid him.

Therefore, *kalañja* and such things must certainly not be eaten. Just as one should not give a finger to a snake—because the fault [of being bitten] is observed there, a finger is certainly not given to a snake, nor is a thorn stepped upon with the foot—so too is this case.
But those things which are prescribed therein should be performed by the father.

In this context, the items prescribed by the *Smṛtis* serve as examples, as do established customs involving specific rules, such as: "The teacher must be followed and saluted; one who is advanced in age must be met with rising and shown respect. Regarding these, a doubt arises: are these items for those who have merely been born, or for those who have been initiated (*upanīta*)? What is the prima facie view? They are for those who have merely been born, because the instruction is given without qualification.

Why? Because those [rites] are prescribed for the person, and a person exists from the very moment of birth; therefore, these items belong to those who are born. This being the position reached, we reply:
"Or rather, because they are equal to the Veda, they should be performed by means of the appropriate method."
The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position.
They may proceed by means of the *upāya* (the preparatory rite), proceeding together with the initiation (*upanayana*), because of their equality with the Veda.
For it has been stated that the *smṛti* is equal to the Veda, since it is precisely Vedic matters that are recorded in the *smṛti*.
The Vedic subjects are prescribed for the period subsequent to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*); and these Smṛti subjects are indeed Vedic. Therefore, they belong to the period after initiation.
Because they do not constitute a part of a ritual action, their repeated practice is enjoined as being for the benefit of the person.

The scripture declares: "As long as one lives, one should offer the Agnihotra; as long as one lives, one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. It has been stated that this sacrifice is enjoined for the sake of the person (puruṣārtha), and not as a repetitive subsidiary part of a ritual act.

Now, a doubt arises here: should it be offered continuously, or not continuously? What is the prima facie view? Since it is taught with reference to the person, it should be performed continuously, as in the sense of "this person [should do it] continuously."

Now, it is indeed heard in scripture that "the Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk" and "at dawn in the morning," and that "one should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsa on the full moon day" and "with the Amāvāsya on the new moon day.
This performance [of the rite] does not require the inclusion of all its constituent parts (*aṅga*).
Therefore, there is no fault if only the time is omitted.
Because it is impossible for that [to exist] therein, by implication.

This is not the case; that one must offer the oblation thinking "sacrifice, sacrifice" does not mean that one should sacrifice continuously. Rather, it is said that one should sacrifice in such a way as one is able, and it is not possible to do so without interruption, for one must necessarily attend to food and recreation.
Therefore, one should sacrifice constantly at times that do not conflict with one's needs;
it is not prescribed that sacrifices be performed at specific fixed times.
The determination of time is made from the observation of the signs of time.

There is also an indicative mark [in the scripture]: "He who, being a performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, should let the Full Moon or the New Moon day pass by, is indeed cut off from the heavenly world.
If the oblation were to be performed at all times, then what would there be to pass by?
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no constant repetition.
Since these are innate, one should proceed by means of traditional scripture (āgama).

"The Agnihotra is to be offered at dusk; it is to be offered at dawn in the morning. Likewise: "One should sacrifice with the Paurṇamāsa on the full moon day; one should sacrifice with the Āmāvāsya on the new moon day. In this regard, there is a doubt: should it be offered once at dusk, or at every dusk? Likewise, should it be offered once at dawn in the morning, or at every dawn? Similarly, should it be performed once on the full moon or new moon day, or whenever that time recurs? What is the prima facie view? Having been performed once, the word has fulfilled its purpose; there is no rule for repetition.
For there is indeed the observation of an indicative mark.

"One who, being a performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should let the full moon or the new moon day pass by, is indeed severed from the heavenly world"—thus [the text] shows the performance [of the rites] whenever the time arrives;
likewise for those [acts] employed within the sacrifice.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "One offers when [the vessel] has broken; one offers when it has spilled. Regarding this, there is a doubt: having offered once when it has broken or spilled, is the purpose fulfilled, or must one offer for every instance of breaking and for every instance of spilling?

In this matter, there is an extension of the principle from the preceding section: whatever was the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) previously is the prima facie view here, and whatever was the final conclusion (uttara-pakṣa) there is the final conclusion here.

The prima facie view is that having performed [the rite] once, one has achieved the purpose; the final view is that there must be a repeated performance because it serves as a causal occasion (*nimitta*). Such would be the case regarding those rites undertaken according to traditional practice (*ācāra*), because they have the person as their aim (*puruṣārtha*).
But for the Brāhmaṇa, there is a threefold debt consisting of the Soma sacrifice, sacred learning, and progeny, because of the connection with the statement regarding debts.
The following is heard [in the scriptures]: "One should sacrifice with Soma," "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception," and "One should procreate offspring.
In this regard, there is a doubt: are these obligatory (nitya) or non-obligatory (anitya)? What is the prima facie view? They are non-obligatory because they are connected with specific desires.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: for the Brāhmaṇas and others, the Soma-sacrifices and so forth are obligatory (*nitya*). Why? Because there is a connection with the statement regarding debts (*ṛṇavākya*): "Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born burdened with three debts—to the gods by sacrifice, to the seers by the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), and to the ancestors by progeny. And, "He is indeed free from debt when he has sacrificed, lived as a student, and has offspring. Such praise of debts pertains to those duties that must necessarily be performed; therefore, they are obligatory. [Objection: But an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is not a proof; let a logical argument (*nyāya*) be stated of which this is the indicator.

It is said: there are distinct sentences for these [acts] that are not connected with desire, such as "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives.
Likewise, "One should study the Veda," and likewise, "Offspring must be produced."

Thus, when permanence has been established, this becomes the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Now, one might object: "Indeed, the Brāhmaṇa is mentioned in the passage, 'Verily, the Brāhmaṇa is being born...

To this it is replied: although there is a mention of the Brāhmaṇa in this statement, it does not enjoin a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the rule already enjoined by those statements unconnected with desire, for the purpose of praising the portions to be cut off (*avadāna*); therefore, by the mention of the Brāhmaṇa here, no non-restriction for the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya is understood.
The mention of the "Brāhmaṇa," however, is for the sake of illustration—meaning that whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya who is being born, as well as one who is already born;
the application [of the rite] should occur when there is full capacity, because the instruction refers to such a state.

In the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* it is heard: "One performs the *agnihotra* as long as one lives; one should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives. Thus, the *agnihotra* is obligatory (*nitya*), and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are also obligatory.

In this regard, there arises a doubt concerning that second [injunction] which is heard without reference to desire (*akāmaśravaṇa*), distinct from the hearing of desire (*kāmaśravaṇa*): does the entitlement belong only to one who is able to perform the rite in its entirety, or should it be performed even if deficient in its constituent parts?
In the eleventh [book], regarding the first hearing (śravaṇa) connected with desire, it will be considered along with its subsidiaries; here, in the obligatory hearing, it is the second.
Or rather, it may apply even to a single part, for when the principal is accomplished, the purpose is fulfilled, while the other is merely a subsidiary because it exists for the sake of that.
The phrase "or even" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position.

Even if only a single part of the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) were performed, the primary rite (*pradhāna*) would indeed be carried out; for whether the rite is performed with all its auxiliaries or without them, the intended result is accomplished through the primary rite alone. The employment of all the auxiliaries merely results in a secondary benefit (*guṇa*). What is this benefit? From the performance with all auxiliaries, heaven (*svarga*) is fully realized; from the primary rite alone, there is this other fruit.
Therefore, one begins with the thought, "I shall perform the rite with all its constituent parts for the sake of attaining heaven.
Even if one is unable to perform some of the parts, the fruit will still result from the principal act when it is endowed with even a portion of the subsidiary qualities.
Consequently, he prescribes the performance of the principal act alone, not that of the subsidiaries.

The primary ritual entities designated by the terms *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *agnihotra* have other constituent parts (*aṅga*) for their purpose; furthermore, there is a fault in the non-performance of those [primary acts]. Therefore, there must be a distinction based on that, because of the connection with the primary act.

A fault is heard in scripture regarding the omission of the primary [rite]: "He who, being a performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should omit either the full moon or the new moon day, is indeed cut off from the heavenly world. By stating this fault in the omission of the primary rite, [the text] demonstrates its obligatory nature.
However, Jaimini maintains that there is no difference between the rites, because the injunction for performance is one; thus, there would be an instruction for all [the constituent parts].
Because the purpose is distinct, it would apply even when only one [mantra] is used, as in the case of other sacrifices.
The meaning is that even when only a single constituent part (*aṅga*) is employed, the fruit may arise even from what is deficient. Why? Because the purpose is distinct (*vyapavargitva*).
The principal act (*pradhāna*) is distinct from its constituents; here, the fruit arises from that which is designated as the *agnihotra* and from that which is designated as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
For that indeed is taught as something to be performed:

that which is taught for the full moon day is the *Paurṇamāsī* sacrifice; that which is [taught] for the new moon day is the *Sāmāvāsyā*; and that which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni, which remains unfailing on both the new moon and the full moon days.
Therefore, there is a sacrificial cake for Agni and for Agni-Soma, and clarified butter for Agni-Soma and the others on the full moon day.
Regarding the Āgneya, Sāṃnāyya, and other rites on the new moon day:

as for what was said—that because of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering] on the full moon day" and "one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering] on the new moon day," the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* denotes the rite together with its subsidiaries (*sāṅga*)—this is not so; for it is only when the purpose of the *darśa* and the purpose of the *pūrṇamāsa* are already established that the rite, along with its subsidiaries, is enjoined for the sake of the result.
Therefore, that which is denoted by the term *agnihotra* and that which is denoted by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* do not include their constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
Rather, it is the *agnihotra* itself—and likewise the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices—that is enjoined here as something to be performed.
Consequently, even when deficient in its constituent parts, the *agnihotra* and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* must indeed be performed.

Just as in other sacrifices—whether archetypal (prakṛti) or modified (vikṛti)—the properties of one do not belong to another, so too the properties of that which is connected with desire cannot belong to that which is eternal;
for we observe the completion [of the rite] even when there is a transgression of the injunction.

Furthermore, it shows completion even in the event of defects in the performance of the rite; by stating "it should be offered in whatever manner it may be," it demonstrates the completion of that which is deficient.
This is also evident from the prescription of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).

Furthermore, expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are prescribed for the transgression of injunctions; they are subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) of the rite triggered by a specific occasion (*nimitta*), as in the rule, "One should offer an oblation when [the vessel] is broken. If the rite were defective and thus fruitless, what purpose would there be in its subsidiary elements? Therefore, the performance of rites must be carried out even when they are defective.
And this applies likewise to rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), because of the existence of a desire for the result.

Regarding such passages as "One desiring offspring should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a pap to Sūrya," and "One desiring a village should offer the Sāṃgrāhāyaṇī sacrifice to the Viśvedevas," a doubt arises: does even a deficient rite yield its fruit, or only one that is non-deficient? What is the prima facie view? It should be so in the case of optional rites—that even a deficient rite yields its fruit.
Why? Because of the presence of the desire [for the result].

If even that which is deficient in its constituent parts is indeed fruitful, then one who merely desires the result will be entitled [to perform the rite]; otherwise, a general term would have to be restricted to a specific case without any further qualification.
If it is argued that he is not entitled because of incapacity, we reply:

he may be unable to perform the rite with all its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), but he is capable of performing the principal act alone; therefore, he shall be entitled with respect to the principal act alone.
But because there is no connection [to a result], it cannot be so; for an injunction has the word as its sole authority.
And because there is no transgression in the non-performance [of such acts].
And here, it is not stated that there is a transgression for the mere principal [act] when it is not performed, as is the case with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Therefore, for this reason also, an action characterized in such a manner must not be performed if it is deficient.
Because actions are dependent [on substances], there would be a distinction in the case of another substance.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is prescribed with the *puroḍāśa* cake, and it is heard in the scripture that this *puroḍāśa* must be made of *vrīhi* rice. In this regard, it is considered: if the sacrifice were performed with a *puroḍāśa* made of *nīvāra* grain, would it be that very same sacrifice, or would it be another? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? There would be a distinction due to the difference in substance; it would be a different sacrifice.
Why? Because it is dependent; for a distinction is understood from the difference in the substratum:
"This one, which has *nīvāra* as its substratum, is different from that which has rice (*vrīhi*) as its substratum.
The difference in the substratum is indeed quite evident, and due to that difference, the form is also understood to be distinct.
Therefore, [some argue] that the sacrifice is something other than the substance.

However, because there is no distinction and because the word for its form is inseparable [from the substance], there should be identity of action, as in the case of "cowness"; and it would be a name, like the word "existent" (*sat*).
Is it not clear that there is a difference in the substrata?
It is said: we indeed admit that the substrata are distinct, but the supported [quality] does not differ because of that difference in substrata, since they are different.
For when a garland or a garment is distinct, a difference in the person is not perceived merely because of that difference in the substrata.
If it is argued that its self is also distinct,
this is not so; for only those who perceive a distinction can speak in such a manner,
and no distinction of this [self] is perceived.
Because the Veda is the authoritative means of knowledge, in the absence of cultured persons (śiṣṭa), there is no tradition [to rely upon] from others, since they are not cultured.
The obligatory rites such as the Agnihotra serve as the example.

In these, when there is a deficiency of the prescribed substance, a doubt arises: should the performance be carried out by taking a substitute, or should the rite be abandoned at that point? What is the prima facie view? In the absence of the prescribed [substance], there is no introduction of another; therefore, it should be abandoned at that very point.

Why? Because it would be improper; that which is prescribed as having rice and barley as its constituent qualities and is productive of fruit becomes fruitless when performed with wild rice (nīvāra) as its constituent quality.
Therefore, that [performance] must be abandoned at that very point.
And because there is an injunction in certain cases.
In some cases, it is prescribed: "If one does not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants.
If the performance were to be carried out by taking a substitute, this would not have been prescribed; yet it is prescribed.
Therefore, where something is not prescribed, there can be no substitute.
Or rather, it is scripture, because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction.
Or rather, it is the scriptural authority (*āgama*) for the substance to be substituted.

Why? Because there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction (*codanā*); for the purpose enjoined by the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajati-codanā*) does not differ whether it is performed with rice (*vrīhi*) or wild rice (*nīvāra*). Furthermore, the sacrifice must necessarily be performed in both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*anitya*) rites once they have been commenced.
In some cases, however, an injunction serves the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*).

Now, as for what was said—that [the substitute is used] because of an injunction in certain cases—it is replied: an injunction in certain cases is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). When many similar substances are available in the absence of *soma*, a restriction is made: "Only *pūtīka* plants are to be pressed.
Therefore, the performance of the rite must be carried out by taking up a substitute.
For that [desire] is eternal, since it is indeed the desire to perform that [action].
But how is it understood that this statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*) alone?
It is said: because *pūtīka* plants are already obtained.
And how are they obtained? Because there is a desire to perform that [substitute]; for we shall explain that in that context there is a desire to achieve similarity.
And because they were obtained through the desire to perform that [substitute], the *pūtīka* plants are [the material] for that [rite].
Therefore, that [substitution] is constant; it is understood that this statement is for the purpose of restriction, meaning it is constant.
[This applies] except in the case of the deity, the fire, the word, and the action, because of their connection with other purposes.
This being the case, we reply: there should be no substitute in the event of the absence of the deity, the fire, the word, or the action.
Why? Because of their connection to a different purpose; that which is substituted would be something other than these, and it would not be able to accomplish their specific purpose.

And what is their purpose? First, the deity accomplishes the purpose by way of being the object of dedication; having dedicated [the offering] to Agni, the cake on eight potsherds is offered on the full moon and the new moon days.

And that which is prescribed for other oblations does not constitute the New and Full Moon sacrifices [thereby]. In that case, another [deity] being designated would not fulfill the purpose of the deity as heard in the scripture. For when another [deity] is being designated, the New and Full Moon sacrifices do not take place.
Therefore, a deity is not substituted.
Likewise, when it is said, "One offers in the Āhavanīya," if the Āhavanīya fire is lost, no other fire or any other substance should be substituted.
Why? Because of its connection with a different purpose; that which is substituted does not function for the specific purpose of the Āhavanīya.
How so? The effect of the Āhavanīya fire is unseen; that which occurs when an offering is made upon the Āhavanīya does not occur when it is made upon anything else.

For that [effect] is not grasped by the word "yajati" (he sacrifices) through its inherent capacity as belonging to that upon which one sacrifices; for the location upon which something is sacrificed does not provide any assistance to the act of sacrificing itself.
Therefore, there can be no substitute for the fire.

In the case of a lapse in the performance of a rite, there is no substitution of another rite, because it is connected with a different purpose. The Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices must be performed as possessing both the *samidh* and the *yajis*; if another [rite] were performed instead, they would not possess those two.
Therefore, there is no substitute for the action. And the same applies to the deity, because the action exists for its sake.
There is another distinction regarding the deity by virtue of which it cannot be substituted: that which is called a "deity" is that for whose sake something is enjoined;
another [entity] being substituted in its place would not be the deity.
For that which is enjoined becomes the deity, not that which is not enjoined, and this term is a relative one.
Whichever deity for whose sake an offering is enjoined is the deity of that [offering] alone, and not of another.
"Deity" is a relative term, not a generic term.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there can be no substitute for a deity.
For that [practice] is prohibited without distinction by the revealed scripture.
Likewise, because the fruit belongs to the owner, since the fruit is connected to the action.
Rituals such as the Agnihotra serve as the examples. Regarding these, when the master fails to perform them, a doubt arises: should another be appointed as a substitute or not?
What is the prima facie view? That a substitute should be appointed.
Why? Because scripture (āgama) [establishes this], as there is no difference in the meaning of the injunction (codanā).
This being the position reached, we reply: it should be so for the owner;
what does this mean? That there is no substitute (pratinidhi).
Why? Because of the connection with the fruit.
He who, being desirous of the result, hires the officiating priests by means of his own relinquishment, and he who relinquishes what is to be given from himself—he is the master (*svāmin*).

If he were to be replaced by a substitute, that person would have to perform everything that must be done by the master; and while performing all that, he would be the master himself, not a substitute.
For he alone is connected with the fruit who performs the relinquishment; he becomes the possessor of the fruit.
Thus it has been said: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer."
Therefore, there can be no substitute for the master;
however, if many [priests] have begun their work, one may bring in another to avoid deficiency.
Sacrificial sessions (*satra*) are cited as the example, such as the rule: "At least seventeen persons should perform a sacrificial session.
When one of those masters behaves improperly, a doubt arises: should another be substituted for him there, or not?
What is the prima facie view? That there is no substitute for the master.

This being the case, we reply: when a rite involving many sacrificers has commenced and some master has failed to perform his duty, one should bring in another. Why? Because in this way there is no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*). The number seventeen and so forth residing in the masters is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that rite; without it, the rite becomes deficient. Therefore, to accomplish that [number], another must be brought in.
But we shall argue that the number resides in the masters, whereas the person being brought in is not himself a master.
"Therefore, it is impossible to take that number as a basis.
It is replied: "It will not pertain to the owner;
for indeed, it is not possible to make it so."
But this can be done: that those items which belong to the masters should be performed here by at least seventeen persons—this will be established.
Therefore, a substitute must be appointed there;
he would be the master because of his connection with that role.

Now, while he is approaching, a doubt arises: is he a master or a laborer? What is the prima facie view? He should be a master. Why? Because of that connection; there is a connection with that status of mastership.
For he who is brought in is made the master; if another is made the master when the original master has failed in his duty, then he becomes a substitute.
Therefore, he is called "the master.
Or rather, he is a laborer because of being hired for wages.
Or rather, he would be a laborer.
Why? Because of being hired; for he has been employed by those learned masters as a hired servant, and one who is being paid is not a master.
He who obtains the fruit is the master; he who exists for the benefit of another is a laborer, and he does not obtain the fruit at all.

Why is this so? For he who begins and completes [an action] is the one who possesses the fruit; for this is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*): it denotes the period from the commencement until the final completion.
But do they not perform that [action] with a deficiency there, due to the absence of seventeen masters?
Therefore, they too are not masters; and if they are not masters, they do not obtain the fruit.

It is said in reply: it is not heard in the scripture that "there should be no fewer than seventeen in the attainment of the fruit"; rather, the number is not a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*) in the acquisition of the fruit.

What then? It pertains to the ritual acts (*padārtha*): "The ritual acts to be performed by the sacrificer must be done by no fewer than seventeen. And these acts are performed by a substitute; and even though [the substitute] does not obtain the fruit, they nevertheless bring in another person in order to make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
And for the one who is brought in, there is no purpose served by that [substitution].
And because the fruit is seen in that [state].
And when he has gone to his destined state, [the text] demonstrates the fruit, showing that even for one who dies while consecrated (dīkṣita), there is a fruit;
therefore, he is a "performer of the ritual" (karmakara). He would possess those qualities because of his connection with the ritual.
For that desire to act is indeed common [to all].
It is established that when a prescribed substance is unavailable, one should employ a substitute after taking it up.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should the performance be carried out by taking up just any substance whatsoever, or should it be a similar one? What is the prima facie view? That one should take up just anything.
This being the case, we reply: wherever the universal (sāmānya) is apprehended, that which is similar should be adopted.

Why? Because all words denote the form (ākṛti). And although the form is heard as being a subordinate factor (aṅga), nevertheless its status as a subordinate factor toward the action is not direct. Rather, the substance (dravya), which is the means of accomplishing the action and is obtained as a subordinate factor by implication, enters into the status of a subordinate factor toward the action by delimiting [the form]. And since the specific instances (viśeṣa) of the individual are delimited by the form, those specific instances become the subordinate factors.

Now, when that specific form has been lost, the substance implied by the purpose must indeed be taken; and since that substance which, when taken as similar [to the original], includes some of those particular qualities is what constitutes the "gain" in that context, a substance similar to it must be adopted.

Therefore, in the absence of rice (*vrīhi*), wild rice (*nīvāra*) is to be used as a substitute. However, because of the explicit scriptural injunction, there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding whichever [substance] was first employed.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is an animal dedicated to Agni and Soma, concerning which it is stated: "When one who is consecrated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, it is heard: "He binds the animal to a post made of Khadira wood; he binds it to a Pālāśa post; he binds it to a Rauhitaka post. In this regard, suppose that once a ritual performance has begun with a Khadira post as its specific quality, the Khadira post is destroyed. There arises a doubt: should an alternative [post] be adopted, or one similar to the Khadira?
What is the prima facie view? That an alternative should be adopted.

Why? Because that [palāśa] is indeed prescribed; however, one similar to *khadira* is not prescribed. Therefore, there should be the adoption of the optional alternative. This being the position reached, we reply: when there is an option, that which has been employed should be adopted as its substitute. That which was employed in a particular performance is specifically indicated; it is a constituent part (*aṅga*), whereas the optional alternative is not a constituent part.

In a performance where *khadira* has been resorted to, the *palāśa* and *rauhitaka* are not constituent parts; they cannot be used at the very time when *khadira* is available, and what is impossible is not prescribed by scripture.

Therefore, when the *khadira* tree is already employed [as the sacrificial post], the other two [types of wood] should not be adopted, because they do not constitute constituent parts (*aṅga*) [of the rite]. One must seek something similar to the *khadira*.
If it is argued that this is "not based on the word" (*aśabdam*), [we reply as follows:]

If you think that what is similar to *khadira* wood is to be adopted, then this becomes something not sanctioned by scripture (*aśabda*). Therefore, because it possesses the status of being prescribed by scripture, it is to be adopted as an option;
it is not so because of its lack of being a constituent part (*anaṅgatva*).

And because of the scriptural statement, it is improper [to substitute] in the absence [of the primary]; for there is no substitute when that [primary] is absent, due to its lack of similarity to the other.
They prescribe this: "If one should not find Soma, one should press Pūtīka plants.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is this an injunction for the case of absence [of Soma], or is it a restrictive rule concerning a substitute? What is the prima facie view? It is an injunction for the case of absence.

Why? Because of the injunction; for a substitute is not enjoined. A means is employed of its own accord for the sake of accomplishing what is to be accomplished, but this [substitute] is itself enjoined; it becomes purposeful only in relation to another alternative procedure.
Therefore, it is not a substitute.
It is not a substitute because of equality.

This is now considered: when the prescribed substance has been taken but is lost, it is established that one should proceed by taking a substitute. When that substituted material is also destroyed, then should something similar to the substitute be taken, or something similar to the original substance that was taken and lost? What is the prima facie view? When the substitute is lost, something similar to it should be taken, according to the previous principle.
This being the position, we reply: there should be no substitute for a substitute.

Why? Because of their equality. Just as that former one was substituted out of a desire to perform what is heard [in the scripture], and not out of a desire for a substitute, so too this one is [substituted] out of a desire to perform what is heard, and not out of a desire for a substitute.
Therefore, something similar to a substitute should not be taken; rather, for that which has been lost after being taken, only a similar [item] to the original itself should be sought.
This would be so because it is restricted by the definition of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*).
No, for it is the desire for that [which constitutes desire].

This is not so; for there is no desire for the individual *pūtīka* plants themselves. What is being enjoined is that which constitutes the similarity to Soma found in the *pūtīkas*. For if the prescription of *pūtīkas* were for a purpose other than the visible one, and if a dissimilar substance were prescribed, an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) result would have to be assumed.
Therefore, that substance which possesses that [quality] should be taken even if it is not a *pūtīka*, and one should not pay heed to the similarity to *pūtīkas*.
When the primary [substance] is obtained, the primary is to be used; for its acquisition occurs only in the absence of that [primary].

Now, in a case where one has set out to take a substitute because the primary substance was lost upon being heard [of its requirement], but then discovers that very primary substance itself—should one take the substitute or that very primary substance?
What, then, is the prima facie view? The substitute should be taken; for by taking the substitute, he remains true to his resolve, since he had already resolved upon it.
Therefore, a substitute must be employed.
This being the case, we reply: when the primary [alternative] is available, one should adopt that very one.

For a secondary option (*anukalpa*) or a substitute (*pratinidhi*) exists only in the absence of what is prescribed by scripture (*śruta*); for while all individual instances are complete in the scriptural injunction, they are incomplete in a substitute.

As for what was said regarding the fault of a difference in intention (*saṃkalpa*), that applies either to cases where [the substitute] is prescribed in scripture or to cases involving the censure of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).
If it is argued that [the fault applies] even when [the action] has already proceeded;

Now, in the case of rituals such as the Agnihotra, when there is a substitution of a material because the scripturally prescribed substance has been lost, and some purificatory rites have already been performed with that substitute, if that very scripturally prescribed substance should be found, should the scripturally prescribed one be adopted, or should the ritual be completed with that very substitute? What is the prima facie view? The scripturally prescribed substance should be adopted, even though [the rite] has already commenced.
For it has been stated: "For there is the acquisition [of the original], because of its absence [at the time of the substitute]."
Therefore, there should be no substitution,
because it would be purposeless.

This is not so. For when, in the absence of *khadira* wood, an animal has been tied to a *kadara* tree, and one subsequently finds *khadira* wood, what would one do with that *khadira* once the purpose has already been fulfilled? Indeed, the procurement of *khadira* is for the sake of the purpose, not for the sake of procuring *khadira* itself.
Therefore, that which is explicitly stated in the scripture (*śruta*) should not be discarded.
In a conflict between the substance and the refinement, the substance prevails, because the refinement is for its sake.

When the ritual involving animals has commenced, at the time for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), there is a large *kadara* tree available that is capable of undergoing the preparatory rites such as carving, while there is also *khadira* wood which is not of such a quality.
In this case, what should be taken?
One should take the *kadara*, so that the preparatory rites will not be lost.
In a conflict between the purpose and the substance, the purpose prevails; because [the ritual] arises even in the absence of the substance, substances are subordinate to the purpose.
At the time for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a *khadira* tree branch is not capable of ensuring the animal's lack of timidity, whereas a *kadara* substance is capable of that.
In this regard, there is a doubt: should the *khadira* substance be taken up, or the *kadara* substance?

He says: the *khadira* substance [should be used], for that is what is heard in the scripture; by taking that, one performs what is prescribed by the sacred text, whereas with a substitute (*pratinidhi*), one would be performing what is not heard in the scripture.

Therefore, it should not be substituted. This being the position reached, we reply: when there is a conflict between the purpose and the substance, one must attend to the purpose; for the substance is taken up for the sake of that purpose, so that the animal will not be lacking in vigor. One should not take up the substance itself [if it fails its function]; by taking up *kadara* wood, one subverts the scriptural injunction regarding the substance, whereas by taking up *khadira* wood, one favors the purpose. By taking up *khadira*, one subverts both [the substance and the purpose].

Therefore, a substitute substance (kadaradravya) should be adopted, for it is said that its production occurs in the absence of the primary substance; the production of a substitute has been explained, as substances are subordinate to the purpose.
Furthermore, the injunction itself would apply even to a single part [of the substitute].

Alternatively, because the purpose is achievable, the rite may be accomplished by a single part; for purposes are indivisible, and the other [parts] are merely subordinate qualities since they exist for the sake of that [purpose].
The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position.

The primary act alone should be accomplished by means of a portion of the rice grains. Why? Because the purpose can be achieved; that purpose which exists here and for which the action is required is what must first be fulfilled. If the remaining subsidiary acts cannot be performed, the quality of the primary act must not be subverted for the sake of conforming to the subsidiaries.
For that alone is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) which assists the primary (*pradhāna*), not that which functions to its detriment.
And in this case, if the subsidiary rites (*śeṣakāryāṇi*) were performed, they would destroy the quality of being rice (*vrīhitva*) in the primary.
Moreover, the quality of being rice is heard to be directly an auxiliary to the primary in the injunction: "One should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*).
Therefore, no compliance with them should be made; for this [substitution] would only occur if there were no distinction between the auxiliary and the principal, yet such a distinction does exist.
Consequently, there can be no substitute.
Likewise, there is also an observation of another purpose: "That very [substance], in whatever state it may be, should be offered."
In the case of the destruction of two portions [of the sacrificial substance], the rite should be performed with the remainder, because that is its purpose.

In connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds which is offered by one who is fasting on the new-moon day or the full-moon day. In that regard, if only the two portions (dvyavadāna) that have been set aside are spoiled, there arises a doubt: should another portion be cut from the remainder, or not? What is the prima facie view?
If two portions are destroyed, one should offer again from the remainder.

Why? Because it is for that purpose; for that oblation is intended for the fire, as the sacrifice must be accomplished for Agni. When those two portions are lost, the sacrifice itself remains necessarily to be performed, and the purpose is fulfilled by the sacrifice. Since that [sacrifice] is accomplished exactly as prescribed when performed with the offering to Agni, why should it not be performed?
"Therefore, it should be drawn from the remainder," or "one should bring in another [substance] because of the specific instruction."

Alternatively, if one should procure another oblation, it should not be sliced from the remnant. Why? Because of the specific instruction; for there is indeed an instruction: "It should be sliced from the middle and from the eastern half. Furthermore, the double-slice is connected to the offering, as it is stated: "One offers the double-slice."
In that case, the remnant left over is for the purpose of qualifying the middle and the eastern half.
If that which was connected with the oblation were destroyed, then what is performed with the remnant would be done without the middle and the eastern half.
[Objection: But surely, from that which remains after the portion has been cut off, one will take [the portions] from the middle and the eastern half?
It is said: that which is the middle and the eastern half of the whole has been prescribed, not the other part.

Another says: "Because of the mention of the remainder," for that which remains is indeed mentioned for the other remaining rites (*śeṣakārya*). That is not tenable, for those remaining rites do not necessitate the sacrificial oblations (*havir*), nor should an oblation whose purpose has not yet ceased be disposed of elsewhere.
Therefore, this is not the meaning;
rather, it should belong to those who partake of the remainder, because of their specific qualification as a cause.

Now, if that which has been cut off for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is lost, should one then take a portion from the remaining substance or not? What is the prima facie view? One should again take a portion from the remainder. Why? Because in this case, a portion is not taken from the entire northern half.
Of what, then? Of that which is present; for when there is a purpose, that which is present is to be offered. Therefore, when the offering is made, the scriptural injunction is fulfilled.
Consequently, it should be offered from the remnant. Because of this specific designation, the consumption of the remnant is to be performed by others, just as in the case of the primary offerings.
There are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein are the portions for consumption at the times of the Prāśitra, the fourfold division, and the Śaṃyuvāka.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: are the consumers of these [portions] distinct [from those mentioned], or are they included within the context [of the sacrifice]? What is the prima facie view? The consumption of the remnants should be performed by others who do not stand within the context.

Why? Because of the specific mention (*nirdeśāt*). For the Adhvaryu and others are specifically mentioned in connection with the consumption of the *iḍā*: "The five, with the sacrificer as the fifth, consume the *iḍā*. Since all [participants] would otherwise be understood as consumers, this specific mention is made for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). It means: "These [five] alone should consume the *iḍā*. This is just as when, regarding the whole sacrifice, there is a general rule that it consists of eight potsherds, yet only the two portions (*dvyavadāna*) are heard; it is not an injunction because [the portion] is already established, nor is it a restatement because it would be purposeless; rather, it serves a purposeful exclusion. Thus, this is an exclusion for these [five].

Moreover, if those very [animals] were to be eaten, there would be a fault in the Aśvamedha sacrifice because of the great number of the portions to be eaten; they might die while eating, or [the rite would fail] because of the gathering together of all [the animals].
Or rather, it should be consumed by all those who are present in the context;
for that consumption is for the purpose of consecrating the persons, so that the consecrated persons may perform the ritual actions.
Since there is no criterion for selection among them, as many as are assembled in the context should all consume it.
The purpose of the detailed exposition is for the sake of its excellence.
In the case of the primary element, there is direct scriptural indication (*śruti*).
As for the fact that only two portions are specified in the primary injunction, that is for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) on the authority of the scriptural statement.

For there is no injunction of anything previously unknown (*apūrva*) therein; rather, it is the sacrificer who is enjoined here. When there is a doubt between an injunction (*vidhi*) and an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), the injunction is superior.

In that case, the word retains its own literal meaning (*svārtha*); whereas in the case of exclusion, there are three faults: the abandonment of one's own meaning, the acceptance of a non-literal meaning, and the sublation of what was already established.
Therefore, only the ordinary [priests] should consume [the portions].
If it is argued that [this rule] has a purpose:
Now, as for what was said—that there would be a contradiction in the Aśvamedha sacrifice because of the multiplicity of the portions to be consumed—that must be refuted.
And it is not so, because it would contradict the Vedic injunction.
In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, they will not consume everything; for if they were to consume everything, they would not complete the Aśvamedha.
In that case, the direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) regarding the Aśvamedha, being contradicted, sets aside the consumption of everything obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).
However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is no such contradiction.
Therefore, they should all eat what has been prepared;
because the purpose is fulfilled, the expiation applies even if only one part is eaten.
But it does not apply to the entirety [of the sacrifice], because of the deficiency; for that is its purpose.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
There should be no expiation when [the vessel] is broken entirely,
for expiation is intended for the purpose of restoring what has been destroyed.
Why?

Because there is a purpose for this [breaking] itself, not for the oblation; the expiation is performed with the thought, "The ritual application will be carried out with that which has been consecrated by it.
Furthermore, it is not possible to carry out the ritual application with that which has been reduced to powder.
Therefore, expiation would be purposeless.
However, a ritual performance can be accomplished with that which has been consecrated even if it is broken in one part; therefore, there should be expiation when it is broken in one part.

Or rather, there should be [expiation], because the occasion for it has occurred. It is not a permanent attribute [of the vessel] because of its constant connection [to the rite]; for it is not for the sake of a subordinate quality, since that [quality] is impermanent.
And because qualities exist for the sake of another, there must be a substratum [for them], as stated [in the Sūtra].

There is no merit in the mere mention [of the vessel]; it must serve a purposeful function. By virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), everything is for the sake of the primary rite. Even though it is distinct, the broken vessel is not taught as being the substratum (*ādhāra*).
For if the broken vessel were the substratum, another oblation (*homa*) would not be enjoined.
For in that case, it would be understood that a distinct quality belongs to the *pradhāna* itself;
therein, the connection with the *āhavanīya* fire would be sublated.
If it is argued that there is an option (*vikalpa*) due to the scriptural statement, [we reply: no.
No, because it is possible as a cause (nimitta), and because the oblation (homa) is enjoined by direct Vedic statement (śruti).
When the oblation is enjoined, it is by way of direct statement; when the broken [vessel] is a subordinate quality (guṇa), it is by way of syntactical connection (vākya).
Therefore, the broken [vessel] is not the substratum.

If it were argued that even in the view that [the moonrise] is the occasion (*nimitta*), there is no separate oblation, but rather the occasion is prescribed for the very oblation under discussion—that is not so; for that which is not being enjoined as a subordinate element is called an "occasion.
If it were indeed enjoined, it would not be an occasion at all.
And if that for which it is the cause were also to be designated, then, since two things would be being designated, there could be no relationship between them at all.
Furthermore, "one should perform the piercing" is not what is being enjoined here;
rather, once the piercing has been accomplished, whatever else is heard [in the text] is what is enjoined.
If it is argued that this is for the sake of distinction;
Because it is a remnant.

It is not logical for [the act of offering] to be a subsidiary part of the breaking; nor can that [broken vessel] be joined together by means of a burnt offering (*homa*) or a mantra. Even if it were joined with clay, the cognition that it is broken would never depart. Furthermore, it would be useless in the event of total destruction.
And regarding total destruction, it is heard [in scripture]: "The broken potsherd flows away in the waters. In that case, the consecration would be purposeless.
But surely, after being lifted out from there, it will be placed back [on the altar].
We say: no; for they prescribe, "One places another [potsherd] down."
Therefore, the act of offering in the case of "one offers when [the ladle] is broken" is an incidental subsidiary of the ritual;
however, in the case of a *kṣāma* (a vessel that has become charred), it would apply to the burning of the whole, because the destruction of a single part is unavoidable.
Or it may be from seeing [the teacher] in one part [of the body].
And this is not the case—that there is an expiation for the burning of the whole; it ought to occur when even a single part is consumed.
For what is called "consumption" (kṣāṇa) is indeed the occurrence of the causal condition; and the consumption of even a single part is indeed consumption.
If it were not performed there, the *śruti* (the revealed scripture) would not be followed;
and this is not logical.
Moreover, it shows: "When that oblation is completed, then one should offer this very oblation"; by this, it indicates the completion (*saṃsthāna*) with that very oblation.
That is not tenable for every single moment;
therefore, only a portion [of the offense] is extinguished by penance.
Or rather, this is because the application of the cause [for penance] is obtained from another scriptural authority.
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case, as was stated, that expiation applies even for a partial transgression;
rather, expiation applies only when the entire [transgression] has been exhausted.
For the occasion specified in the scripture—that "the two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas) are to be burnt"—refers to the burning of the whole, not of a single part;
and it does not apply when only one portion is burnt, because that partial burning is unavoidable.
As for what was said—that completion is seen with a burnt oblation, as expressed by the rule "when that oblation is finished"—[that refers to a different context].
It is said: the expiation is prescribed when the *saṃsthā* (completion) is the cause.
Even when that completion is brought about by another oblation, the expiation still applies; thus there is no fault.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the word "oblation" (*havis*) [in the rule], [we reply: no.
If it is argued that [the rite] is concluded with another oblation,
this is not so;
because of the word "that oblation" (taddhavis), the term "that oblation" is used here.

Regarding the statement, "When that oblation is completed," if it were to be completed with another oblation, the term "that oblation" (taddhavis) would not be appropriate. Therefore, because it would otherwise be illogical,
the word "oblation" (havis) must refer to the sacrifice itself, due to its connection with the characteristic mark [of that sacrifice].
The word *havis* might refer to the sacrifice;
[the meaning would be] "that *havis* should be completed," i.e., "the ritual action characterized by that *havis* should be completed.
But surely a secondary sense is accepted only in the absence of a primary one, and not otherwise?
It is said: this is simply the absence of a primary [application].
How so?
For if it were to be established that "that rite is performed with that oblation," the sentence would be split.
And [the term] would be non-expressive;
for it is the action itself that is completed, not the oblation, which is therefore the occasion [for the rite].
Thus, "that oblation" is a restatement (anuvāda).
If it is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*), then it is understood that the expiation applies even when the ritual action involving other oblations has been completed.
But how can the word *havis* (oblation) refer to the ritual action?

It is because of its connection with the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of that action; the action connected with the oblation is understood by the word *havis* due to its association with the oblation, just as a lion is indicated by the act of forceful behavior associated with Devadatta.
In this way, the ritual act is also characterized by the oblation;
therefore, there is an expiation when the entire [oblation] is spoiled. If it is argued that "it must be according to the scriptural injunction," [we reply: no.
To this we reply: it must apply to both. Why? Because it ought to be according to the scriptural text; whatever is heard in the text, that is what is understood.

It is heard in the scripture that the affliction applies to both; and what is explicitly stated in the scripture ought to be intended as significant. Otherwise, just as "the oblation" refers to one thing, so too "both oblations" would refer to the same single entity.
Therefore, the five-platter offering is prescribed upon the affliction of both.
It is not [the case] because of being characterized by that [affliction], for the occurrence [of the rite] is based on a specific cause.
This is not so;
for *upapāta* is a substance connected with misfortune (*ārti*), and it is the cause thereof.
Its characteristic is the sacrificial offering (*havis*) and the misfortune; these two, both individually and collectively, constitute the occasion (*nimitta*).

For it is not possible to qualify [the offering] by means of the word "both" (*ubhaya*); for if it were so qualified, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), as in: "When the oblation (*havis*) is spoiled, there is a five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*)," and "And that [offering] is of both oblations.
But is not the connection between the oblation and its spoilage also established by means of a sentence?
It is said: the cessation of distress (*ārtinirvṛtti*) is also understood there;

and that [cessation] is [understood] through direct statement (*śruti*). If the oblation (*havis*) were connected to both [the deity and the purpose], the direct statement would be excessively weakened. Therefore, the connection being brought about is not what is indicated.
How, then, is the word "both" (ubhaya) used?
The expression "both" is a constant restatement (nityānuvāda), applicable whether one [of the two] has been damaged or the other.
Therefore it is said: "for whom both sacrificial offerings (havir) should suffer damage."

Now, why is it that the affliction (*ārti*) qualified by two words is not understood as the occasion (*nimitta*), [as in the case of the rule]: "for whom the oblation (*havis*) qualified by both qualities should suffer affliction"? To this it is said: First, how do you conceive of it—that the affliction qualified by a qualified object is the occasion? He replies: Because of the proximity (*saṃnidhāna*) of the qualified object, the qualified object is present within the affliction.
What, then, would be the case if it were so?
From that, it would be understood that the cause is suffering characterized by both [aspects].
To this it is replied: first, this "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya) ought to be questioned.
For even if a specific object is present for someone,
why would that person not be driven away by blows with sticks for possessing something non-specific?
What does it matter if he is not driven away?
From this it follows that even pain occurring in an undistinguished state becomes the cause for the *pañcaśarāva* offering.
[Objection: But will not the word "both" (*ubhaya*) qualify the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)? [Reply:
No; since it is not syntactically connected with the word "oblation," it is unable to qualify it.

If it is argued that it will connect [with the verb] due to proximity (*ānantarya*), even so, it is not capable [of doing so], for it does not bring about cessation (*nivṛtti*). He says: because it expresses a specific quality (*viśeṣa*), it will be the producer of that [cessation], just as in the case of the command, "Let a white cow be brought."
No; for when it is stated thus, they bring the black cow. The word "white" excludes this cow from those that are black and so forth.
Moreover, even though both words are connected with the oblation, a distress characterized by both [qualities] is not at all understood.
What is the reason? The word "oblation" (havis) is connected with the phrase "he shall not suffer distress" (nārtim ārcchet).
In that case, even though both words are present, the affliction (*ārti*) is connected only with as much meaning as the word *havis* possesses;
and that meaning there is not qualified [by anything else].
Therefore, affliction qualified by both is not the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).
Now, it might be argued that the connection of both [the oblation and the person] is with the oblation qualified by distress (*ārti*).
That too is not tenable;
for the phrase "one should not suffer distress" is not employed as a qualification of the oblation.
What then?

If the *pañcaśarāva* were accepted as the cause (*nimitta*) [of the rite], and if a simultaneous connection between both [the *pañcaśarāva*] and the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) in the event of its destruction were admitted, the sentence would be split (*vākya-bheda*).

Alternatively, if it were connected with that which is characterized by the form of the oblation—namely, "one should perform [the rite] if there should be destruction"—then it would subsequently have to be connected again with the word "both" (*ubhaya*), which is qualified by the oblation.
Even so, the sentence would be split;
therefore, distress characterized by both is not the occasioning factor.
Alternatively, if it were the case that "whatever has the form of an oblation is characterized by both," then distress would not be qualified by the oblation.
If it is argued that, since the occasion [of the ritual] is not distinguished by the oblation, the word "both" will qualify the oblation—this is not tenable.
How so?

It would indeed be qualified in this way: "that which is of the nature of an oblation and is both"; but in that case, it must further be stated: "if that which is of the nature of an oblation and is both is [also] ruined."

How could the affliction (*ārti*) be connected with that which is qualified? Furthermore, the two words "oblation" (*havis*) would not be uttered for the purpose of qualifying the affliction. On the other hand, if they were not uttered again, then even if the word "oblation" were not uttered by way of *tantra* (simultaneous application) to indicate the affliction as residing in both, the indication of the affliction would be non-specific, and the indication of "both" would likewise be non-specific.
When something already specified is intended to be further qualified, it must be mentioned again;
in that case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Thus, if the word "both" were connected with the verb "to suffer damage," it would not qualify the oblation; consequently, the damage to the unqualified oblation would become the occasion for the rite.

If, on the other hand, it were connected with the word *havis* (oblation), then either the word *havis* would have to be uttered again along with it for the sake of connecting it with "ruin" (*ārti*), or it would have to be pointed out by the pronoun *tat* (that) as "this very thing"; in that case, there would be the same fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
Furthermore, if both were to be taken as things to be enjoined (*upādeya*), there would be no purpose in their being mutual qualifiers;
rather, both would have to be uttered for the purpose of qualifying "ruin."
In that case, suffering qualified by either one will not be the cause;
however, if it were the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it would be qualified by either one—this is the distinction.
And the same applies to the offering (*homa*), the pressing (*abhiṣava*), and the consumption (*bhakṣaṇa*).
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "Having pressed with the stones in the Havirdhāna shed, having offered in the Āhavanīya fire, and having gone back westward, they consume the portions in the Sadas.
Therein, the pressing is stated by another statement, and the offering by the root *yajati*;
these two are not themselves enjoined, nor is their sequence [enjoined].
For that [consumption] is indeed obtained through the very force of the meaning.
Therefore, consumption by the same agent as the offering (*homa*) and the pressing (*abhiṣava*) is enjoined;
that is, once the pressing has been performed and the offering made, the consumption must be performed by those same agents.
In this regard, there is this doubt:
must he alone who performs both [actions] consume [the portion], or may it be consumed by either one as well? What is the prima facie view?
The offering, the pressing, and the consumption should likewise be [treated] in the same manner as the impairment of the sacrificial oblation.
How so?
It is not connected in this way: "having pressed [the Soma], then having offered it, then one should consume it."
By this [passage], the sequence of the pressing and the offering is not being stated, such that "those who, having pressed, offer, they consume.
For in that case, the sentence would be split: "having pressed, they consume" and "having offered, they consume.
Therefore, there is no mutual connection between the offering and the pressing; thus, the consumption may be connected with either one of them.
Others also say that they consume [the soma] after having pressed it; therefore,
consumption occurs by means of either one of these two conditions,
or by both, for there is no specific scriptural injunction (dharmaśāstra) regarding those two.
The re-establishment of the sacred fires is like the preparation of cooked rice.

In the Agnihotra it is heard: "If both fires of one who has set out [on a journey] should go out at sunset, or if they should rise at sunrise, for him the re-establishment of the fires (punarādheya) alone is the expiation.
Regarding this there is a doubt:
is the re-establishment required upon the going out of either one, or only upon the going out of both?
What is established?

The re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) should be like the case of cooked rice (*odana*); just as the *pañcaśarāva* offering occurs when either one of the two fires is extinguished, so too the re-establishment ought to occur upon the extinction of either one, because otherwise there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). For the connection is exactly as follows: "I shall sacrifice here; I shall perform good deeds here."
Or rather, it would belong to both [the agent and the object] because of the production of a substance.

When a substance has been destroyed, the re-establishment of that very same substance constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) here. Its visible purpose is: "How may the substance exist?"—thus the re-establishment (*punarādheya*) is performed. In this regard, the rule is: two fires arise together, not separately.
Therefore, if one of them is extinguished, it is not possible to establish only one.
It would be defective.
Now, if he were to establish a second [fire],
and if that were the Āhavanīya;
In that case, since another *āhavanīya* fire already exists for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), it would not serve for that oblation.

That which is produced specifically for the purpose of the oblation is the *āhavanīya*, because this is a term denoting a consecration (*saṃskāra*). And a term denoting a consecration cannot apply in the absence of even a single consecration.

This [production] is indeed a consecration, namely the state of being for the sake of the oblation, as it is heard in the scripture: "one offers in the *āhavanīya*. If one [fire] has gone out and another is being established, there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*); for in both cases, there is certainly a deficiency.
Therefore, when one [fire] has gone out, it is not the case that the fire must be re-established, because that would be impossible;
however, the five-portioned oblation (*pañcaśarāva*) should serve as a substitute, since there is a scriptural injunction regarding the substance.
Or rather, it is the injunction itself that prescribes the substance and the deity, for these two would otherwise be inexpressible.
Alternatively, the sacrifice is a distinct ritual act based on a specific occasion, serving as an injunction for the material and the deity.
Here, the material and the deity are explicitly heard in the text: "One should prepare a five-portioned oblation for Indra.
Otherwise, the term "for Indra" (aindram) would have to be understood as a scribal error.
In the case of the *aindra* and *māhendra* [offerings], the restatement according to their actual meaning would have to be "the *aindra*";
for those two deities cannot be restated by means of the word *aindra* when they are not [directly] expressible [by it].
Alternatively, if [the word *aindra*] were used as a qualifier, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
But was it not said that direct Vedic statement (śruti) is more powerful?
True, this is so; however, in the other alternative, the direct statement would be even more sublated, because the word "Aindra" is not a restrictive factor.
He should cause him to be removed from his position.
Or rather, it is a rule concerning the constituent parts [of the sacrifice], because of its connection with a specific occasion.
Or rather, this is prescribed as an auxiliary (aṅga).
When the occasion of the destruction of the sacrificial oblation (haviḥ) arises as the cause (nimitta), a sacrifice is heard [in scripture]; in that case, three possibilities present themselves:
either an independent fruit is to be postulated for the occasion, or its purpose is that which belongs to the new-moon day (amāvāsyā), or it is an auxiliary to that [new-moon sacrifice].
First of all, it cannot be independent, because the result is something to be accomplished;
it is not [independent] in relation to the function of the new moon sacrifice.
What is the reason?

Because it is not heard; for it is not heard that "it exists in its effect. Nor is there a determination toward any one of these three positions even by means of an instruction on what is to be done (*kartavyopadeśa*); rather, an instruction on what is to be done is possible only when those [other] positions are intended.
As for the Viśvajit sacrifice, its existence would pertain to an action not yet undertaken.

This is handed down in tradition: "He who pledges himself to all deities and to all *pṛṣṭha* chants, he should sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra, which includes all *pṛṣṭhas* and for which the entire property is given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasa-dakṣiṇā*). He thereby ransoms himself from all deities and from all *pṛṣṭhas*. The Viśvajit is prescribed there upon the occasion of pledging oneself to everything. In this regard, there is a doubt.
Does the Viśvajit belong to one who, having resolved upon everything, employs everything, or to one who does not employ it?
What, then, is the prima facie position? It belongs to both the one who employs it and the one who does not, because there is no distinction made.
Or rather, [it applies] to one who employs [the mantra].
Why?
Because it has been stated that a factor of this kind is indeed a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the ritual action with respect to its cause (*nimitta*).
How could that [offering] be a constituent part for one who does not employ it?
Furthermore, it is because of the statement regarding its redemption.
Thus it is heard there: "In that he ransoms himself, he ransoms himself from all deities and from all *pṛṣṭha* chants.
And praise by way of a ransom is not appropriate when [the sacrifice] has already commenced;
therefore, the Viśvajit occurs when [the sacrifice] has not commenced.
Now, why is the connection not made in this way:
"Having resolved to perform a satra, one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit"?
For in that case, the relationship between the Viśvajit and the satra would be understood as occurring at the time of the formal resolve (*āgoraṇa*).
It is not so; for if the *satra* were qualified by the *āgoraṇa*, there would be a remote construction (*vyavahita-kalpanā*) in the connection between the *satra* and the *viśvajit*.
