Moreover, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) connects the *viśvajit* with the person—as in "A person should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*"—and not with the *satra*.
[The text] says "the *viśvajit* sacrifice of the *satra*" and "having made the *āgūra*."
In this way, the hearing [of the injunction] becomes meaningful;
however, if it were a subordinate part of the sacrifice (*satrāṅga*), its meaning would already be established and need not be stated.
Furthermore, it is impossible to enjoin immediate sequence after the resolve (*āgoraṇa*) in the case of the injunction "having resolved, one should sacrifice" (*āgūrya yajeta*).

For that which is not expressed by the words would have to be resorted to; however, the state of having a common agent is indeed expressed by the word, and since the occurrence at a prior time is established by the sense of the matter, it need not be explicitly stated.
Therefore, the connection with the Viśvajit sacrifice is only with the term "having made a vow" (*āgūrya*).
Thus, if one, having made a vow, does not perform the Sattra sacrifice, for him there is the Viśvajit.
Upon the birth of a calf, there should be an injunction for the observance of a vow.
Or time [is the cause] through its connection with that which has arisen, as previously stated.
This time is prescribed for that which has already been established by another statement as previously described.
Why?
Because it is a connection with what has already arisen; this is a connection of the vow with what has already arisen, not a connection with its origination.
How so?
A vow was previously prescribed, consisting of abstaining from beans and meat and consuming plenty of clarified butter;
yet the time for it was not specified.
Therefore, it is a prescription regarding time;
and also because the purpose [of the action] is not limited.

Furthermore, the meaning here cannot be precisely determined. Regarding the statement "one enters upon the vow with the calf," does it mean that the calf itself must be the object of the vow so that the vow is entered upon by means of the calf? Or does it mean that one should perform the vow while holding the calf in one's hand? Or rather, that one should enter upon the vow after having brought the calf near?
Thus, the meaning of the scriptural injunction remains unsettled;
for what is specified here is the instrument (*karaṇa*), not the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

This much has been stated: "One should perform the vow of the calf-attainment. How so? This remains expectant of a specific detail; the matter is not determined as to what is performed with the calf during the vow.
Or rather, [the phrase] "whatever it may be" means this:

if the calf were connected with the vow (*vrata*), it would become something desired for its own sake and would thus attain the status of being an end in itself; however, the third case ending clarifies that it is for the sake of another, for that ending occurs when there is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*).
Therefore, for this reason as well, the conjunction has time as its purpose;
however, the calf, because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti), should be an auxiliary to that [time].
But time would not be [determined] by scriptural injunction.
But this is merely a specification of time; the calf is not enjoined as a constituent part [of the sacrifice].
This is not an injunction, such as: "At the full moon they undertake the vow with sacrificial grass (barhis)," or "At the new moon, with a calf."
How is this understood?
Because it forms a single syntactical unit with an injunction; furthermore, an injunction is recorded later on: "Before the calves are driven away, let the husband and wife eat.
If this too were an injunction, there would be a split in the sentence.
And restatement occurs with respect to an object that has already come into being; moreover, the calf's state of being a limb is not unattained, but rather the time [for milking] is unattained.
Furthermore, [the suffix] is meaningless when connected with an action.
Furthermore, the calf cannot be employed as a sacrificial offering here; since it is connected with the ritual action, no purpose can be served by the calf [in that role].
Therefore, for this reason also, the calf is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Moreover, there is no mention of its own specific term [as an offering].
And this is not stated: that one will consume the cooked calf of the entire [sacrifice]. Nor is a word for this meaning heard in its own right;
the word "calf" (*vatsa*) is a term for a physical form and does not apply to meat.
Therefore, this is the time.
If it is time, then [the rule applies] to the side of the *saṃnayya* offering, because of its connection with that indicative mark.
Or rather, because both have the time as their purpose, they should be understood [together].

The word "or" (vā) sets aside the alternative position; it does not apply only to the case of one who performs the *saṃnayya* sacrifice, for this time-period would also apply to one who does not perform the *saṃnayya*.
Why?
Because it serves the purpose of indicating the time; there is no purpose served by the driving away of the calves in relation to the *vrata* milk.
However, time is indeed required, and that for which there is a requirement therein is indicated.
But how is the driving away of the calves for the sake of time? Because it serves another purpose;
for they are driven away for the sake of milk, and thus it becomes something with a visible purpose; otherwise, it would have an invisible purpose.
Therefore, the driving away of the calf is not heard in the scripture as something to be adopted [as a primary act].

As for what was said—that because of its connection with that indicative mark (*liṅga*), it applies only to the case of one who prepares the *saṃnāya*—that is not so; for even one who does not prepare the *saṃnāya* avoids the loss of the [prescribed] time.

Even for one who does not have the *sāṃnāyya* offering, there would be no *vatsāpākaraṇa* (the driving away of the calves) at all, but not even the time for the *vatsāpākaraṇa*; and it is the time that we require, not the *vatsāpākaraṇa* itself. It is like saying, "One should arrive at the time of the conch-blast.
Even in a village where the conch is not blown, that same time exists; thus, the arrival will not be precluded.
In the same way here also, even though there is no removal of the calf at that time, the vow being broken at that time shall not be abandoned;
it is like the branch [being placed] on the prastara-bunch for the purpose of the āśrayaṇa-offering.
Or rather, it is a rule regarding time, because both [the agent and the object] exist.
And because it does not have the purpose of producing a latent impression (saṃskāra) of that [object].
Furthermore, no visible benefit is rendered to the prastara by means of the branch;
wood does not serve as a benefit for grass that is being burned,
whereas grass might indeed benefit the wood.
Therefore, the branch is not for the sake of the prastara;
and for that reason, it would exist even in its separation from the prastara.

What is the purpose [of this discussion]? Even if the branch (*śākhā*) were a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*) of the grass-bundle (*prastara*), it would still be disposed of (*pratipādyate*) at the time of the throwing of the grass-bundle.
It is said in response: if the branch were a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the grass-bundle as it is being thrown, then it could not be thrown without the grass-bundle;
however, if it is a subordinate element, it may be thrown even without the grass-bundle.

We have stated that [the branch] is to be struck at the time of the *prastara*; therefore, it would exist even in the absence of the *prastara*. For that very reason, even when the *prastara* is absent, there should be the striking of the branch;
and the *upaveṣa* would also exist as an alternative.
In the case of prosperity (abhyudaya), there should be an injunction for sacrifice due to a lapse in time, as in the case of the five-platter offering (pañcaśarāva).

Regarding this, they declare: "Verily, he is deprived of offspring and cattle, and he causes his rival to prosper, for whom the moon rises after the sacrificial oblation has already been set aside. In such a case, one should divide the rice grains into three parts: those that are of medium size, from these one should offer a cake on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa*) to Agni Dātṛ; those that are the largest, from these a pap (*caru*) of curdled milk to Indra Pradātṛ; and those that are the smallest, from these a pap of boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. In this regard, there is a doubt.
Is this another sacrifice enjoined due to the lapse of time, or is it the removal of the deity from those very rites under discussion when a specific occasion arises?
Or rather, it is a removal, because [the deity] is already present.
Or else, there would be the removal of the deity.
Why?
Because [the actions] exist; for the actions under discussion do indeed exist, and while they exist, a further connection of the oblation with a deity is not possible.
Since there would be no basis for postulating a separate sacrifice,
it is not another sacrifice; rather, different deities are prescribed for those very same oblations,
because words possess that very nature.
These words are of the same nature as those that exclude a deity; for those [words] which are intermediate, another deity is prescribed.

In that case, the substance is already established, and it is the deity that is not yet established which is being prescribed. But how, when the purpose is the prescription of a deity, might the fault of prescribing multiple qualities not arise?
It is said: not indeed is more than one quality enjoined in any single sentence here.
In the case of "one should divide the rice grains," only the act of dividing is enjoined; everything else is merely restated (anūdyate). Therefore, there is no fault.

For those that are of medium size, Agni is prescribed as the deity, while other elements such as the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) are merely restated. For those that are largest, Indra accompanied by curds is prescribed as the deity in this sentence.
Since the cooking is already established by the sense of the matter, the state of being a *caru*—along with the implied locative sense—is likewise restated in this sentence.
Those that are the smallest, when combined with the boiled [milk], have Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa prescribed as their deity; everything else is merely restated.
Therefore, there is no fault, because the repeated practice of curdling is observed.
Because it is something not previously established, there should be an injunction.

Now, as for what was said—that in the sacrifice for one desiring cattle (*paśukāmeṣṭi*), there is a separate ritual act, namely: "He who desires cattle, having sacrificed on the new moon day, should drive away the calves"—that must be refuted.
To this it is replied: It is appropriate that in that case there is the injunction of a separate ritual act.
Why?

Because it is something not previously established (*apūrva*). No sacrifice previously obtained exists there; for this [injunction] is commenced only after that [sacrifice] has been completed with the words "having sacrificed on the new moon day" (*amāvāsyām iṣṭvā*).

In that context, the word *nirvapati* (he offers), which is connected with a material and a deity, implies the act of sacrificing (*yajati*), because the relationship between a material and a deity cannot exist without an act of relinquishment (*utsarga*).

But it is not so here; for here, the sacrifice is understood as being the subject under discussion, and since only the connection with a deity is enjoined for the substance already existing within that very sacrifice, no fault arises.
Because of the defect in the milk, the five-platter offering (*pañcaśarāva*) is prescribed, while the other remains unblemished.
If it is argued that the same applies to the *sāṃnyāyya* offering as well.
If you view it thus, then there is a fault even in the *sāṃnyāyya* offering;
for that too is defective because it is corrupted by the lapse of its proper time during the *abhyudaya* sacrifice.
It is not non-defective, for the cause is indeed no different.
This is not so; for while in the case of the five dishes there was a defective substance, here exactly that same [substance] remains.
But is it not corrupted by the lapse of time?
It is not corrupted, for the cause is no different.
The prescription for expiation is applicable even when [the milk] has turned sour; likewise, it applies when there is a lapse of time, even if the substance itself is not spoiled.
For while the ritual injunction regarding the deity can be performed for that which has been prepared out of season, it cannot be performed for that which has already perished.
Thus, the scriptural mention of "boiled" (*śṛta*) serves as a defining characteristic.

Now, as for what was said—that at the primary substance no deity is heard in the text "the *caru* is cooked," and that there is no statement regarding it because the cooking has not been performed at the time of the *abhyudaya* (transference of the sacrifice)—that must be refuted.

To this it is replied: this mention of "cooked" (*śṛta*) is for the purpose of a secondary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); the term "cooked" serves to characterize the ritual properties (*dharma*), meaning "possessing the properties associated with the cooked.
As in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*, because there is no specific statement, it remains according to the original form (*yathāprakṛti*).
Regarding that very same prosperity, there is a doubt:
does the displacement of the deity occur even in the case of the *upāṃśuyāja*, or not? What is the prima facie view?
The *upāṃśuyāja* should be performed according to the original model.

Why? Because there is no specific injunction; whereas for the other [cups] there is an explicit statement: "For Agni Dātṛ, the cakes of the middle-sized grains; for Indra Pradātṛ, a pap in curd of the largest grains; for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, a pap in boiled milk of the smallest grains."
This does not apply to the *upāṃśuyāja*;
therefore, it should follow the respective deity [of each offering]. Or rather, there is a displacement [of the formula] according to the procedure, as in the case of the other offerings.
It should take place when [the oblation] has been poured out, because of its connection with that.
In this very example, there is a doubt:

if the *abhyudaya* (the rising of the moon) is understood to have occurred after the oblation has been set aside (*nirupta*), then it is the *Abhyuditeṣṭi*; or is it [the case] even if it occurs before the oblation has been set aside? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
The *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice should take place when the offering has been poured out and [the moon] has risen.
Why? Because of its connection with that; for there is a connection with the pouring out, as expressed in the text: "for whom the oblation has been poured out."
Therefore, this injunction does not apply when [the oblation] has not been poured out;
or rather, it applies once the occasion for it has already arisen.
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.
This injunction would apply merely to the commencement of the ritual procedure at an improper time;

for the occasion [for the rite] is already established by that much alone, since the mention of the "oblation" (*havis*) in the phrase "whose oblation the sun rises upon" serves as a defining characteristic.
In the rule "for whom the oblation rises," the rising characterized by the oblation is the occasion; it characterizes the oblation as something already set in motion, not as something inactive.
Therefore, when it is said "the oblation rises," it is understood that the oblation which has been set in motion rises.
Indeed, it cannot be qualified by the phrase "that which has been poured out."
For in that case, the sentence would be split;

if one were to require the condition "for whom the oblation has been set aside, not for whom it has not been set aside," then it would be impossible to enjoin that "the oblation rises. Therefore, the sacrifice is to be performed even when the oblation has not been set aside.
The other is merely a characteristic.

Now, as for what was said—that there is a connection with the "offered" (nirupta), namely "he whose oblation has been offered"—this term "offered" is merely a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa); the meaning is that [the rite] has proceeded toward some particular substance.
And thus there is the observation of another purpose.
Moreover, another passage also demonstrates this point: "If the moon should rise while the oblation has not yet been taken up, that [oblation] is indeed already determined.

Then this is the procedure for the vow: they take the milk of the previous day and make it into curds as the curdling agent for the oblation; they let the calves loose, and then they drive them away again; in the afternoon, he drives them away with a branch of a *parṇa* tree."

"Just as the *āmāvāsya* oblation is well-known from its very beginning, even so is this [case]. If, however, one should not desire to observe the vow, or if the moon should rise over the oblation already taken up, then one should act otherwise: 'having once husked these very rice grains'—thus, by prescribing another rule for when the oblation has not been taken up, he shows the expiation for when the moon rises over it whether it has been taken up or not yet poured out. Regarding the case where it rises while not yet poured out, Āśmarathya says one should pour out [the offering] for the original deities, because of the removal [of the old grains] once they have become rice."
Ālekhana, however, belongs to those [karmans] that pertain to the higher realms, because it effects the removal of the deity.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
The teacher Ālekhana thought that one should offer [the oblation] to those deities who partake of the ritual action performed after [the initial offering].
Why?

Because the removal of the deity is caused by that [untimely action]: since the removal of the deity is caused by the commencement of the ritual procedure at an improper time, therefore, once the deity has been removed, the portions for the *vyūrdhva* deities must be set aside.
Once they have been set aside, there is no removal of the handfuls, because those [handfuls] are subordinate to that [deity].
For the conjunction with that which is non-ordinary occurs because it occupies its place.
The offering should not be made from the original [grains];
from which ones, then?
From the modified ones.
Why?

Because a connection with a specific, non-archetypal deity is heard in the scripture, not with the one already authorized. By the injunction "one should divide the rice-grains into three parts," it is prescribed that [the offering] is to be set aside from the archetypal deities and offered to the modified ones; these [modified deities] now occupy their place.
Therefore, once the offering has been set aside, the previous deities have ceased, and other deities have arisen.
Therefore, the remainder of the pouring out (nirvāpa) should be performed by means of the modified [grains],
because of the absence of the other.
Because the other half associated with a deity is absent, there can be no offering (nirvāpa) associated with that deity.
If one half were for one deity and the other half for another deity, there would be no offering at all belonging to either deity.
Therefore, the offering must be made silently; necessarily, in one case or the other, there is a distinction in the mental resolve (saṃkalpa).
Because of its connection with the *sāṃnāyya* offering, it should not belong to one who does not perform the *sāṃnāyya*.
The *abhyūḍheṣṭi* itself is the illustrative example.
In that context, it is heard: "a caru in curd," and "a caru in boiled milk.
Therein arises a doubt.
Does the expiation apply specifically to one who performs the *saṃnayya* sacrifice when an *abhyudaya* (oversight) occurs, or does it apply without distinction? What is the prima facie view?
The expiation applies to one who performs the *saṃnayya* sacrifice when an *abhyudaya* occurs.
Why?

Because of the connection with the *sāṃnāyya* offering; for there is indeed a connection with the *sāṃnāyya*, as seen in the injunctions "the oblation (*caru*) in boiled milk" and "the oblation in curd. Due to the absence of boiled milk and so forth, it cannot belong to one who does not perform the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, for in that case there would be a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*).
Or rather, because of the connection with the grain-oblation (*auṣadha*), it belongs to both.
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position.

It should apply to both [the *saṃnayant* and the *asaṃnayant*], not to the *saṃnayant* alone, because of the connection with the vegetable offering (*auṣadha*). There is a connection with the vegetable offering in the words, "those which are of medium size, those which are largest, and those which are smallest," and that [connection] can be made even by one who is not a *saṃnayant*.
Therefore, in the absence of a specific reason, it should not be excluded for one who is not a *saṃnayant*.
"The penance applies to both sides.
[Objection: "No, because of the deficiency [in one case]."
Regarding what was stated— that because there is an absence of curd and boiled milk for one who does not perform the *asaṃnayata* rite, there is no status as their substratum,
and therefore there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in that position— that must be refuted: "No,
because it is not a consecration of those [substances]."
In the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice, it occurs upon the conclusion of the purchase [of the Soma], because of its connection with the distribution [of the wealth].

They prescribe this: "If those who have been consecrated for a sacrificial session (*sattra*) should then break off from it, they should divide the Soma and perform the *Viśvajit* Atirātra sacrifice, consisting of all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and having the gift of all one's possessions as the sacrificial fee.
In this regard, there is a doubt:
does the *Viśvajit* apply upon the breaking off of one who has already purchased the King (Soma), or upon one who has merely commenced the rite?
What is the conclusion? The Viśvajit [sacrifice] should take place when the [Soma] has been purchased.
Why?
Because of the distribution [of Soma] and its conjunction [with the sacrifice], it is said: "Having divided the Soma, they should perform the Viśvajit.
For those who rise [to perform the Viśvajit] when the King (Soma) has not been purchased would incur a deficiency due to the absence of the division of Soma.
Therefore, those who rise [to perform the Viśvajit] after the King has been purchased should perform the Viśvajit.
Or, because the cause has been attained once activity has commenced.
The other Vedic revelation has as its purpose the communication of instruction.

Now, as for what was said—that if they were to rise while the King [Soma] has not been purchased, they would render the rite defective due to the absence of distribution—that must be refuted. To this it is replied: distribution is not being enjoined here.
For in that case, the sentence would be split:
"In the Sāṃnyūti rite, they should sacrifice with the Viśvajit, having made a division of the Soma"— thus, "having divided" (*apabhajya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).
If it is asked, "How is this obtained?"—the answer is that for those rising from their purpose, there occurs a division of wealth.

This division of all substances is indicated by the division of the *soma*; having divided the *soma*, one divides the other substances. Thus, the other scriptural statement serves the purpose of an injunction.
Therefore, whether the purchase has been performed or not, the Viśvajit sacrifice is for those who rise [from the sacrificial session] when the king [is present],
because there is no specific restriction regarding the duration of the consecration.
But it should be the twelve-day sacrifice, on account of the indicative mark.
The measure should be taken as exactly twelve days. Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), which means by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
What is the capacity [of this injunction]?
It is stated as a permanent rule (*nityavat*) that "one consecrated for twelve nights should seek wages," not as an optional one (*pākṣika*).
Performing that very same permanent act, one is unable to adopt any other measure [of time].
Therefore, the measure of twelve days alone should be fixed; other measures will apply to the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), so these [other measures] are not purposeless.
Regarding the full moon day (paurṇamāsī), there is no fixed rule because there is no specific distinction.
In the Gavām Ayana it is heard: "They should undergo initiation four days before the full moon.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
of which full moon?
What is established?
That there is no fixed rule regarding the full moon day.
Why?
Because there is no distinction; no word expressing a specific [qualification] is employed here.
However, due to immediate sequence, it would be Caitrī.
The *Vaikāṣṭakā* occurs in the month of Māgha, according to scriptural authority.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position. This is not the case; it is not [the case that] Caitrī [is the name].
What then?
"It is the Māghī [full moon].
Why?
Because of the scriptural mention of Ekāṣṭakā; for indeed, the mention of Ekāṣṭakā occurs in connection with the purchase [of Soma].
"For them, the purchase [of the Soma] falls on the Ekāṣṭakā.
Therefore, for one who has been initiated four days before the full moon of Māgha, the purchase can be performed on the Ekāṣṭakā, but not on the Caitrī.
This is what is called "capacity" (sāmarthya) as an indicative mark (liṅga); it serves to sublate the syntactical connection (vākya).
"Therefore, it is the full moon day of Māgha.
[Objection: "Are there not others as well?"
If you think, "The full moon day of Māgha [is the Ekāṣṭakā], and thus the purchase will coincide with the Ekāṣṭakā," that is not so;
for not all eighth days are Ekāṣṭakās, as there are twelve Ekāṣṭakās. Therefore, there is no fault. Nor is it [the Ekāṣṭakā] merely by way of figurative usage, for it is so known in the world.
This is not so; for the term *ekāṣṭakā* is used figuratively with respect to the other eighth days.
This one, which occurs on the full moon of Māgha, is the primary [meaning], and between the primary and the secondary, the understanding applies to the primary.
Therefore, it is only the full moon of Māgha [that is intended].
And [the initiation is successful] through grace even in the event of an offense during the consecration.
The night which people welcome like a cow approaching them,
she who is the mistress of the year— may she be auspicious to us.
"Thus, [he offers] to Aṣṭakā, the bestower of wealth, svāhā!"— this indicates that the eighth day of the month of Māgha is the Ekāṣṭakā,
because of the subsequent sprouting at the time of rising.
And he shows the subsequent growth following that arising:
"When they arise, the herbs and the trees arise. Thus, he shows the arising in spring;
in that [season], the herbs and the trees indeed arise.
For this reason also, she is restricted;
and all genders apply to her.
"Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day undergo initiation at a time of distress for the year.
A "distressed" time is one when people are afflicted;
and they are afflicted by the cold.
Therefore, the eighth day of the month of Māgha is called *ekāṣṭakā*.
Likewise, it is said: "Those who undergo initiation on the *ekāṣṭakā* undergo initiation at the [two] divisions of the year.
By the word "division" (*vyasta*), the turning of the solstice (*ayanaparivṛtti*) is meant.
Likewise, [the text] says, "Not rejoicing in the waters, they descend for the *avabhṛtha* bath"; if this were meant for the full moon of Caitra, those initiated would have to descend while rejoicing.

Therefore, it must be the full moon of Māgha. Since the time for initiation has been specifically prescribed, there is no postponement of the fixed rites even if that time is exceeded, because their own proper time has already arrived.
This is heard [in scripture]: "Therefore, one who is initiated does not give, does not cook, and does not offer oblations"; thus they recite in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
However, if by force of divine or human circumstances the time for initiation is postponed, a doubt arises there:
is there a postponement of the giving, the offering of oblations, and the cooking, or not?
What is established?

There is no suspension [of the obligatory rites]. For giving, oblations, and cooking are indeed obligatory for as long as one lives, according to scriptural injunctions such as "one performs the *agnihotra* throughout one's life. An exception to these is made only on those days during which the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice with all its auxiliary parts is prescribed; on other days, they must be performed.
After the time of the performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma*, they remain unrestricted.
Therefore, they must be performed, for their time has arrived;
or rather, there should be a postponement because of the state of being initiated, for the reason is no different.
By the word "or" (vā), the position is reversed.
As for what was said—that there is no such excellence—that is not so;
they are indeed to be excelled.
Why?
Because of his state as one initiated (*dīkṣita*). These [acts] are forbidden for one who is initiated, not for one at a time when he is not initiated;
for in that case there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereas according to our view, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the authority.
And prior to the avabhṛtha bath, this person remains a consecrated one (dīkṣita) alone;
for the cause is no different—whatever [cause] existed at the time of the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma, that same cause persists even after it has passed.
For in both cases, the state of being consecrated is indeed the cause.
Therefore, their excellence [is established];
in that case, no supplementary oblation (pratihoma) is prescribed, as was the case with the preceding ones.

In that context, when the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice is being extended and the oblations have not yet been performed, should the oblations be performed by counting them one by one, or not? What is the prima facie view? The oblations should be performed by counting them.
What is the reason? For those oblations have been prescribed as necessarily to be performed;
even if they are delayed, they must certainly be performed.
For in this way, their status as necessary duties will be upheld.
Only the principal act is fixed; here, no regard for time need be observed, because it is like the current of a river.

Even if the times have passed, one should perform the principal acts by counting those that were omitted, just as in the case of what must necessarily be done—such as eating, paying wages, and so forth—which, when omitted, is performed after counting the days of neglect. This case is exactly the same.

This being the case, we reply: in that situation, no compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*) is prescribed, just as with the previous cases. One should perform what ought to be done, not what ought not to be done. And these [oblations] are not to be performed because they have been prohibited; just as there is no compensatory oblation for the previous ones when they were left undone due to the lapse of time, so it is with these as well.
This is also because of the primacy of the time factor.
Furthermore, time is of primary importance because it is heard [in the scriptures] as a causal condition (*nimitta*);
in its absence, that which is enjoined simply does not come into being.
Even if only the principal act were to be regulated, it would still be so only when the time—the causal condition—is present.
And that [impurity], which is comparable to the current of a river, has passed with the lapse of time; therefore, no *pratihoma* (substitutive oblation) should be performed.
Furthermore, because of the prohibition, this applies after the *avabhṛtha* bath until the subsequent sacrifice.
After the *avabhṛtha* bath and before the *udavasānīyā* offering, regarding those oblations that have been omitted due to some divine or human obstacle,
a doubt arises as to whether a compensatory oblation (*pratihoma*) should be performed or not. What is the prima facie view?

"One should perform them," [the opponent argues], "for he has then become one whose initiation (dīkṣā) is released; for the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is intended for the purpose of releasing the initiations. Therefore, they ought to be performed, yet they have not been performed. To this we reply: after the avabhṛtha and before the udavasānīyā offering, there should be no compensatory oblation (pratihoma) for those [initiations] that have passed away.
Why?

Because of a prohibition; for there is indeed a prohibition: "The Agnihotra is to be offered with this sacrifice performed for the re-establishment of the fires," which is a prohibition of the offering prior to the *udavasānīyā* [concluding rite].
As long as the *udavasānīyā* is postponed, so long does the prohibition remain in force.
Thus, there is a direct scriptural statement (śruti); otherwise, there would be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, since those [offerings] were not to be performed and were not performed, there should be no compensatory oblation (pratihoma).
If there were a compensatory oblation, then the evening Agnihotra and the subsequent offerings should be offered.
But at the morning [pressing] of the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice.

When the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice has been established and the Soma offerings have been completed, there arises a doubt regarding the oblations: should they be performed with the evening *agnihotra*, or with the morning one? What is the prima facie view?
That it should be with the evening *agnihotra*, as was stated in the preceding section; thus, by the general rule, it is established that this applies everywhere.

Thus it is stated regarding what has been obtained: "But in the case of the *ṣoḍaśin*, [the rites] are performed in the morning. Since, when the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is completed, the morning *agnihotra* and other rites have been passed over, they must be commenced starting precisely from the morning *agnihotra*. This expiation applies everywhere within the ritual context because the nature of the fault is common to all cases.
Or rather, it is because the word [is used] in its specific context as the cause [of the cognition].
The expiation occurs precisely when the vessel is broken or spilled within the context of the ritual procedure.
Why?
Because it is based on scriptural authority; thus, these oblations form a single syntactical unit with that original purpose.
Therefore, the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), which is the subject under discussion, is the means for conveying the sacrifice accompanied by the *homa*;
if this is so, it will be purposeful through its assistance to that [sacrifice]. Otherwise, even without the sentence, one would have to postulate a result.
Therefore, since the sentence is set aside precisely because of the absence of a result, the context (*prakaraṇa*) must be accepted.
And it is not a modification of that.
Furthermore, neither the Agnihotra nor the Jyotiṣṭoma is a modification (*vikāra*) of those [two sacrifices];
nor is it a modification of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
If it were a modification of them, then there would also have to be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in that case when [the offering] is spilled or broken.
One should understand that whatever is unfit for the Aryas to eat when it has been cast into the water [for purification] is likewise unfit.
Since the scripture prescribes expiation for each part separately, there is no expiation when the offenses occur simultaneously.

When there is a simultaneous interruption (apaccheda) of both the Prastotṛ and the Udgātṛ, or of the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ, what expiation (prāyaścitta) should there be in that case? Or should there be none? Such is the doubt that arises.
What, then, is the initial position (pūrvapakṣa)?
There is no expiation when [the two disconnections] occur simultaneously.
Why?
Because of the scriptural teaching of division; they prescribe expiation only when the disconnections are separate.

This division is one of severance, and it is accomplished by both [the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ]; yet here, when the act is being performed by only one, an expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed for either the Udgātṛ or the Pratihartṛ.
And that which is performed together with another cannot be considered performed by one alone.
For if it were performed by one alone, then since it would have been accomplished by him, what would the other do?
Therefore, there is no simultaneous expiation for two [impurities] that have been severed;
or rather, since the occasion has arisen, there may be a single [expiation] consisting merely of the time.
In that case, because of the contradiction, there should be an option.
If the simultaneous disqualification (apaccheda) of both the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ occurs, there arises a doubt:
is there an option between the absence of sacrificial fees (adākṣiṇya) and the giving away of all one's possessions (sarvasva), or is it a combination (samuccaya)? What is the prima facie view?
In this case, there should be an option due to the contradiction;
for these two alternatives are indeed contradictory: giving away one's entire property and the absence of a sacrificial fee.
Therefore, an option must prevail.
Or else, in another application, there would be the favoring of both.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the alternative position.
This is not the case, namely that there is an option (*vikalpa*), because both are prescribed;
thus, the injunction regarding the performance (*prayogavacana*) which involves the inclusion of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhārī*) is rendered consistent.
For if there were an option (*vikalpa*), there would be a contradiction; therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*).
As for what was said—that there is an option because of contradiction—it is replied:
in another performance, both might be favored; thus it is said, "one should sacrifice again."
His application is twofold; therein, in one application, there is one eon,
and in the other, there will be another.
Thus there is no contradiction; therefore, both are expiations.
And it is not [the case that they are alternatives] because of their connection with a single [act].
In a sequence of preceding and succeeding [rules], the preceding one is weaker, as in the case of the original state.

Where there is a successive occurrence of two disconnections (apaccheda), a doubt arises as to whether the expiation (prāyaścitta) is occasioned by the earlier event or by the later one. What is the prima facie position?
The earlier one is stronger; for when that occasional rite which is applicable upon the earlier disconnection has occurred, it is impossible to perform that which is contradictory to it.
Nor is it impossible for that which is worthy of instruction to be attained as prior knowledge; thus there is no doubt.
Therefore, another effect produced without contradicting that [prior knowledge] is not contradictory.
Where, then, would that [effect] reside?
In this case, there is only the indicative mark (*nimitta*).
Therefore, the prior cognition is stronger.
This being the position reached, we reply: in a sequence of prior and posterior, the prior would be weaker.
Why?
Because regarding the meaning that is said to be "to be accomplished" by means of a verb, it is understood therein that it must be done "in such a way as it is possible";
and that can only be accomplished by subverting a prior cognition, not otherwise.
Therefore, the meaning of the word is that one must perform this [act] after having sublated the prior cognition.
Now, it might be argued that this is possible regarding the prior cognition: that another, contradictory cognition will arise, and that [prior one] is false;
for since that [prior cognition] has not come to be, it cannot be relied upon as being "this" or "that."
And it is not the case that, while that [subsequent cognition] is unrefuted, the prior cognition cannot occur;

therefore, it will remain unrefuted. But when that [subsequent cognition] arises, it arises precisely as something that sublates the prior cognition. Once that [prior cognition] has been sublated, it is unable to sublate the subsequent one, just as in the case of the primary nature (*prakṛti*).

For wherever that which is archetypal (*prākṛta*) is sublated by that which is modified (*vaikṛta*), this is precisely the reason: a modified [element] cannot come into being without having sublated the prior cognition; and the archetypal is prior, because it is required in the modification (*vikṛti*). If the Udgātṛ were the junior [priest], one should give away all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) at the Punaryajña, just as in the other case.
When the *pratihartṛ*'s disconnection occurs first and then that of the *udgātṛ*, one must perform the sacrifice again after having sacrificed with a non-fee (*adakṣiṇā*).
In this regard, there is a doubt:
at the repeated sacrifice, should one give one hundred and twelve [cows], or rather one's entire property (*sarvasva*)?
What is obtained? One thousand two hundred.
Why?
For it is thus handed down in tradition: "In that case, one should give what one would have given in the previous [sacrifice].
And in the previous performance, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself was established.
Therefore, [the fee here] is one hundred and twelve.
This being the case, we reply: in that sacrifice again, one should give everything, just as in the other, the preceding day, one gave one's entire property.
If it is asked how there is "everything" in that case, it is because of the interruption of the *pratihartṛ*.
If the *pratihartṛ* priest is deprived [of his share] during the performance, one must give away all one's possessions (*sarvasva*), setting aside the [usual] one hundred and twelve [cows].
But was he not already intending to give those one hundred and twelve on the previous day?
True; however, by the gift of all one's possessions, both [the previous and the current requirements] are fulfilled.
Therefore, that [fine] must be paid. Now, one might object: "Is not the entire property [to be given] even before reaching twelve hundred?
This is not so; when the twelve hundred are the prescribed amount, the entire property is indeed more than that.
Moreover, on the previous day, one is not yet about to give the twelve hundred;
rather, one says "I will give this much" regarding that which is to be given at a later time.
Since the twelve hundred is not actually given on the previous day, it is understood that one is not [then] "about to give" it; that is a false cognition, whereas the transaction is based on reality.
In a multi-day sacrificial session (ahargaṇa), that day on which the interruption occurs should be repeated, because each ritual act is distinct.

When there occurs on some day of a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) the disconnection of the Udgātṛ priest, then a doubt arises: does the entire session repeat, or only that specific day? What is the prima facie view?
The entire series of days [is required].
Why?
Because without the subsequent days, it would then become defective; therefore, the series itself must be repeated.
This being the case, we reply: that very sacrifice in which the interruption occurs should be repeated.
Why?

Because of the distinctness of the acts; these acts are separate, and one day is not a subordinate part of another. Furthermore, from the word "having sacrificed" (*iṣṭvā*), it is understood that the sacrifice is completed, not that it is completed along with its subsidiaries.
Those other days which will assist by way of providing help certainly exist;
therefore, they will provide assistance.
Consequently, that very [rite] should be repeated.
In a combined sacrifice, because there is no deficiency, those of equal ritual status should perform it just as they would in their original form.
Sattras are cited as examples: "At least seventeen should perform a sattra," "Those who, knowing thus, perform a sattra," and "Those who, knowing thus, enter upon a sattra.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
is there a joint entitlement for those of identical ritual procedure (*kalpa*) and those of different ritual procedures, or only for those of identical ritual procedure?
Who, then, are those of the same ritual procedure (*samānakalpa*)?

For the Kṣatriyas, the Atris, the Badhryaśvas, the Vasiṣṭhas, the Vainyas, and the Śunakas, as well as the Kaṇvas, the Kaśyapas, and the Saṃkṛtis, the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*; for the others, it is the *tanūnapāt*.
Thus, some belong to the *nārāśaṃsa* procedure, while others belong to the *tanūnapāt* procedure.
In this regard, what first presents itself? Among many sacrificers assembled together, only those who have identical ritual rules (*kalpa*) should perform the sacrificial session (*satra*) jointly.
Why?
Because of the absence of deficiency; otherwise, for that person whose ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is not fully integrated, there would be a deficiency.
Just as in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*) itself, there is an absence of fruit due to a lack of excellence, so it would be here as well.
Or rather, by virtue of the scriptural statement, it should be like the case of the head.
Or rather, it is not so, because it is not a general statement made outside of a specific context.
This is not so; as for what was said—that those belonging to different *kalpas* are also entitled [to perform sacrifices]—only those belonging to the same *kalpa* should be entitled.
Why?
Because of the absence of deficiency (*avaiguṇya*).

Now, as for what was said—that it will be established even through deficiency because of the scriptural statement—that is not so, because it is an *anārabhyavāda* (a statement not made in reference to a specific context). For that [deficiency] is postulated on account of the statement, provided that when it is not postulated, the statement becomes purposeless.

If this were stated in reference to those performing different ritual procedures (*bhinnakalpa*), then the statement would indeed become purposeless, and thus the *sattra* sacrifice would have to be admitted even for those with different procedures; however, this is not stated in reference to those with different procedures.
This statement will have its meaningful application among those belonging to the same ritual manual (*kalpa*);
therefore, there is no entitlement for those belonging to different manuals.
Or rather, it may be so because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, as in the case of the *audumbarī* post.
No, because that is the primary factor.
This is not so, because that [liberation] is the primary aim; for this ritual procedure has the human goal as its purpose. How so?
For Vasiṣṭha and others, the *nārāśaṃsa* is a constituent part (*yajñāṅga*) of the sacrifice.
And whatever is a constituent part of someone's sacrifice, the fruit-yielding action belongs to him together with that part.
Therefore, the connection is made in this way: for the Vasiṣṭhas, the action accompanied by the *nārāśaṃsa* becomes fruit-yielding.
Because the Audumbarī post exists for the sake of another, like a sacrificial potsherd.
Now, as for what was described— that "as with the Audumbarī post, so it is here"—
the Audumbarī exists for the sake of another (pārārthya), while the sacrificer is heard in scripture as a subordinate element (guṇatva).
But surely, even in that case, the injunction of performance (prayogavacana) would establish the predominance of the person?
This is not a fault; for even though this [post] is measured by a single sacrificer, it becomes "measured by all sacrificers" [collectively].
However, in this case, when one person's [share] is taken, that of all is not thereby taken.

Therefore, the *audumbarī* post exists for the sake of another, like the potsherds (*kapāla*). Just as in the case of the rule, "They strew the husks with the cake-potsherd," where the husks are to be strewn using a potsherd intended for another purpose, so too is this [the *audumbarī*] understood.
If it is argued that [the object] is [perceived] by another [means of knowledge as well]:
Because it is not one, because it lacks authority, and because the word is indivisible.
To this it is replied: the sacrificer does not become subject to another performance.
However, there is no specific distinction in the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) from which a restriction could arise based on that term.
What then?
Because singularity is intended to be expressed, the sacrificial duties (*yājamāna*) are not to be performed by two people; therefore, no other person is brought in.
[The opponent] says: "In that case, let there be someone else for all the sacrificial duties.
[The author] replies: Not so; for the statement concerning the sacrifice refers to one who possesses a desire (*kāmin*), and it prescribes the sacrifice together with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).
And the word "sacrificer" (yajamāna) is undivided here in the context of the measuring of the Udumbara post;
therefore, there shall be no other [designation].

However, due to the conjunction [of specific conditions], there would be a disruption of the occasion [for the application of the term], as in the case of the Bṛhat and Rathantara [chants], because they are taught as being distinct when performed by Vasiṣṭha.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
If there were many sacrificers, there would be an obstruction of the occasion due to their coming together.
Why?
Because it is prescribed as a distinct case, the *nārāśaṃsa* is the occasional (*naimittika*) offering in a performance performed by Vasiṣṭha;
in another case, the *tanūnapāt* is the occasional offering.
Since both are now the performers acting in cooperation, the accomplishment [of the rite] occurs through their joint effort, not by one alone.
Therefore, [the agent] is not independent.

And if, O Vāsiṣṭha, the agent is not independent, then for that reason, the motive for that [action] should not be performed there, nor should the motive for the other; for both would be mutually obstructed, as in the case of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*. For example, when it is said, "The *pṛṣṭha* chant consists of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*," it is neither accomplished by means of the *bṛhat* alone nor by means of the *rathantara* alone; thus, in that case, neither the *bṛhat* nor the *rathantara* serves as the motive.
It is the same here as well.
Alternatively, because of the connection with the whole, there should be understood to be no contradiction, due to the relationship [of the person] as an owner.
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) sets aside the previous position.
There is a connection of the whole [sacrifice] with the agent as a single unit; therefore, there is no obstruction to the occasional rites (naimittika).
But how is it that the performance must be done in its entirety?

Because of the connection by way of ownership; for in relation to the ritual action, there is a connection of Vasiṣṭha and the others as sole owners. The ritual action is beneficial to the persons, for it is capable of producing the fruit for each individual.
Therefore, each one is the performer of the whole, and thus that entire occasional rite accrues to him. It is just as when it is said, "Let it be given to the tip [of the nose] alone."
Even though she is the mother of both Tuṇḍa and Piṭṭha, she is nevertheless given [the offering] to her;
for she is his mother in its entirety,
since motherhood is not distributed [partially].
The same should be understood here as well.
Therefore, there is no entitlement for those who do not belong to the same ritual manual (*kalpa*).
When two *sāman*s are connected with a portion through an increase in ritual action, they are related as subordinate elements; therefore, in that case, there would be an obstruction.
Now, as for what was said—that it is "like the Bṛhat and Rathantara"—that must be refuted.
In the case of the two Sāmans, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, there is a connection with a portion [of the rite] through the increase of the occasional ritual action;
for in that case, both are the means of accomplishment, not just one.
In that case, however, the connection with the two *sāmans* is through only a portion of the *stotra*, not with the entire *stotra*.

For there, the *sāman* is heard as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), while the *stotra* is the primary element (*pradhāna*). Therefore, in that instance, there would be an obstruction [to the performance].
But because of the scriptural statement, there is a conjunction of two; therefore, one [hand] possesses the nature of being a hand.
But because of the absence of an object, it could not be so.
By the word "tu" (but), the position is reversed:
it would not be thus, that there are two domestic priests.
Why?
Because of the absence of purpose; this matter—that there are two domestic priests—does not exist at all.

For it is heard in scripture that for a single king, only one domestic priest is to be accepted, as in the injunction "he appoints a domestic priest" (*purohitaṃ karoti*); thus, singularity is intended to be expressed.
But was it not said [by you] that this is due to the explicit statement?
It is replied: this cannot be established by the mere statement, because the word *purohita* has its cause in a formal consecration (*saṃskāra*).
Even if one were appointed, he would not be a *purohita*.
Furthermore, since the meanings [of the words] are distinct, there is no connection with that which is heard [in the text].
Furthermore, the distinctness of the purposes is heard in scripture: there is praise of splendor for the Brāhmaṇa and praise of valor for the Rājanya.
By these two castes, their connection with those respective fruits is restated.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there are not two family priests.
Because it is a subordinate part of the hand, its lack of connection [to the sacrifice] would be understood.

Now, as for what was said—that for this very reason a single person has two hands—that is logical, because the hand is a subordinate limb (*pratyaṅga*); specifically, the left hand is a subordinate limb of the right hand for the purpose of forming the *añjali*. Without it, the *añjali* itself would not exist.
For one does not say "a joined-palms gesture (añjali) made with two right hands.
Therefore, there should be both a king and a domestic priest (purohita).
But is it not the case that in that context, "the two royal priests"—meaning the king and the priest—should perform the sacrifice?
It is said: those two do not both desire union (*sāyujya*).
That king acts with a single purpose together with his domestic priest (*purohita*), but the priest does not [act] with another priest.

For both of them, when performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) against the king, are called "domestic priests" (*purohita*); for they do not so desire [union], since the word *purohita* refers to a consecrated office (*saṃskāra*).

[Objection: But surely there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in your view. [Reply: It is said: even by means of figurative indication, linguistic usage occurs in the absence of direct denotation (*śruti*), as in "he stands on the fire" or "he stands in the pit.
Therefore, [the compound] *rājapurohitau* [is justified as meaning] "the king and the domestic priest."
Sacrifices are for all social classes without distinction.
And because of the observation of an indicative mark.
Furthermore, we see that there are three sacrifices.
Why?
Because of the observation of indicative marks.
What is the indicative mark?

It is stated thus: "One should perform the Bārhadgira as the Brahmasāman for a Brāhmaṇa, the Pārthuraśya for a Rājanya, and the Rāyovājīya for a Vaiśya. This statement regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) is intended to enjoin the Brahmasāman; within that context, there is mention of Rājanyas and Vaiśyas. Therefore, from this also, it follows that all social classes (varṇas) have the entitlement [to perform the sacrifice].
Because neither the Brāhmaṇas nor the other two [classes] possess the qualification for the office of officiating priest (*ārṭvijya*).
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
This is not the case—that [the result accrues] to all three castes.
What then?
It should belong to the Brāhmaṇas alone. Why? Because the other two [castes] lack the qualification for officiating as priests (ārtvijya).

For the performance of the priestly office (*ārṭvijya*) is prohibited for the other two castes, the *rājanya* and the *vaiśya*; moreover, [the sacrifice] would be defective without the priestly office performed by them personally. Therefore, it should belong to the *brāhmaṇas* alone.
If it is argued that this is because of a scriptural statement:
For ownership is not indeed enjoined.
Or they may belong to the Gārhapatya fire, since there is no prohibition against it.
The Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya will exist as persons entitled to the status of the *gārhapatya* fire, and there is no requirement for them to act as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) therein;
therefore, there is no contradiction for them. Or rather, it is not so, because of the contradiction with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*).

And this is not the case, that the two—the Rājanya and the Vaiśya—should perform the duties of the Gārhapatya; for there would be a contradiction with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*). For instance, regarding the cup of the sacrificer (*yajamāna-camasa*), some say it consists of *soma*, while others say it consists of fruit.
Likewise, regarding the *Brahmasāman*: the *Bārhadgira* is for the Brāhmaṇas, the *Pārthuraśma* for the Rājanyas, and the *Rāyovājīya* for the Vaiśyas.
Therefore, even this [claim] that "the establishment belongs to the householder" is not tenable;
for, because the others possess ownership, there is a scriptural indication regarding the Ahīna sacrifice.
Now, as for what was stated—that it is because of the observation of an indicative mark—that must be refuted.
To this it is replied: he will refer to the *ahīna* sacrifice itself by the term *sattra*, because the status of being the master is prescribed for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Therefore, because the officiating priests possess ownership [of the sacrifice], a *sattra* is not possible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
thus, the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*) applies to the *ahīna* [sacrifice].
Or rather, it is because of the restriction that the *brahman* office belongs only to those of the Vasiṣṭha lineage.

This being the case, we reply: because of the restriction regarding the office of the Brahman priest for the Vāsiṣṭhas, the sacrificial session (sattra) should belong to the Vāsiṣṭhas and not to others.
Why?

Because there is a restriction on the office of the Brahman priest, stating that "the Brahman priest must be a Vāsiṣṭha"; therefore, the sacrificial session should belong to the Vāsiṣṭhas and those who follow the same ritual manual (kalpa).
Or rather, because there is a counter-exception for all of them.
Or rather, it should be a sacrificial session (*satra*) for all [the officiants], because there is no distinction [stated].
But is it not said that "one belonging to the Vasiṣṭha lineage is the Brahman priest"?
No, he says.
It is further stated: "Whoever should study the *stomabhāga*, he alone may become the *brahman* priest.

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of this instruction for the Vāsiṣṭhas now?"—it is for the sake of praising the *stomabhāga*: that even one who is not a Vāsiṣṭha, if he studies the *stomabhāgas*, is capable of performing the duties of a Vāsiṣṭha.
Due to the restriction on the office of the *hotṛ* priest by Viśvāmitra, those of the Bhr̥gu, Śunaka, and Vasiṣṭha lineages are ineligible.
There would be no eligibility for Bhṛgu and others.
Why? Because the office of the *hotṛ* priest is restricted to one of the Viśvāmitra lineage, as it is prescribed that "Viśvāmitra becomes the *hotṛ*."
Therefore, the entitlement belongs to the Vaiśvāmitras and those who share the same ritual manual (kalpa) with them;
because of the sovereignty over the sacrificial fire-altar (vihāra), it would apply even to those who do not maintain the [three] sacred fires (anagnīn).
The sacrificial sessions (*satra*) themselves serve as the examples: "Those who, knowing thus, perform the sacrificial session," and "Those who, knowing thus, enter upon the sacrificial session.
Regarding these, there is a doubt:
do they belong to those who possess the sacred fires (*sāgnīnām*) and those who do not (*anagnīnām*), or only to those who possess the sacred fires?
What is established? That it applies to both those who maintain the sacred fires and those who do not.
Why?
Because of the ownership of the monastery;
for even a monastery belonging to another is capable of benefiting everyone.
For it must be maintained by him, since its success is achieved through whatever belongs to him, whether his own or that of another.
Therefore, it ought to apply even to those who do not maintain the sacred fires;
and because it is seen [to be so] in the case of the Sārasvata sacrifice.
And there is a scriptural observation in the Sārasvata Sattra:
"Those who perform a Sattra without having established the sacred fires go to the heavenly world by means of others' chariots.
This indicates that there is a Sattra for those who have not established the sacred fires.
For this reason also [it applies] to all,
and because of the prescription of expiatory rites.

An expiation is prescribed: "One whose consecrated fires have become mixed with other fires should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Vivici"; this shows that there is an expiation for the mixing of fires.
This [expiation] would apply in the case of those who have not maintained their fires, and not otherwise.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there are sacrificial sessions (*satra*) even for those who do not maintain the sacred fires.
Because for those who maintain the sacred fires, the *iṣṭi* sacrifice comes first.
And because it is motivated by one's own self-interest.

And the fires are employed for one's own purpose. How so? Because of the specific verbal suffix; for there is indeed a specific verbal suffix [indicating the agent], namely, "one should establish the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*).
Therefore, there is no accomplishment for one [rite] by means of the fires belonging to another, even though the fires are for the sake of the sacrifice;
moreover, the text indicates the act of "pouring together" (saṃnivāpa).

Regarding the statement, "Those intending to offer the Sāvitra oblations should combine [the fires]," it is understood from this that those possessing the sacred fires (agnimant) perform the Satra sacrifices.
Thus, having resolved the doubt concerning the indicative mark (liṅga), another matter is considered in the remaining section of the discussion:
since the Juhū and other vessels are not specifically prescribed [for all], there would be a doubt; in such a case, one should understand that there is freedom of choice (yathākāmī).

Should the sacrificial vessels, such as the *juhū* and others, be taken from the possession of some specific sacrificer for the performance [of the rite], or should other common [vessels] be used? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
The performance should be carried out by taking [the vessels] from the possession of any sacrificer whatsoever.
Why?
Because a sacrificer does not employ his own vessel;
rather, the performance must be carried out with one's own vessel.
Therefore, others should sacrifice using the vessels belonging to another;
or rather, they should use other common vessels, because of the prohibition and because it was ordained by the scripture.
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position.
This is not so; for other vessels must be made common [to all].
Why?
Because of a contradiction; a contradiction arises.

It may happen that those vessels have been taken up [for use], and then the death of some sacrificer should occur. In that case, there would be a contradiction between the rules: "They burn the one who has maintained the sacred fires with the fires and with the sacrificial vessels," and [the rule regarding the disposal of the vessels]. If they were to burn him with those [vessels], the sacrifice of the others would be obstructed.

If they were to complete the sacrifice with those [bones], the funeral rites for the other [deceased] would be subverted; however, if other common materials are employed, nothing at all would be contradicted.
Therefore, it should be done in that manner.
An expiation (prāyaścitta) may be performed in times of distress.
Now, the refutation of the previously stated logical mark (liṅga) is being stated:
an expiation (prāyaścitta) will be postulated for our position.
How so?

If those traveling or staying in a forest or wilderness should become terrified due to fear of bandits or wild beasts, or should be overtaken by a forest fire, that situation shall constitute an occasion for expiation. Alternatively, according to the classification of persons, there may be a restriction on the performers in the case of a modified sacrifice because the sacrifice has them as its qualifying attribute; in the absence of such a qualification, there would be entitlement for others in each individual case.

The lower *kalpas*—namely, rites characterized as the *Āgrayaṇeṣṭi*, the animal sacrifice (*paśu*), and so forth, in which there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses—are the subject of this discussion. Regarding these, a doubt arises:
do all three social classes (*varṇas*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform these rites, or is it for the *vaiśya* alone? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
In this modified sacrifice (vikṛti), the agent would be restricted by the rule for the person (puruṣakalpa).
Why?
Because this is a sacrifice such as the Adhvarakalpa, characterized by this specific number.
And this number has been stated for the Vaiśya; therefore, only the Vaiśya is capable of performing this ritual action in its entirety.
This ritual action consists of seventeen constituent parts, and that state of being seventeenfold, if performed by one who is not a Vaiśya, is improper.
For that [number] is not enjoined with respect to others.

Therefore, because of a lack of capacity, one would not be entitled [to perform the sacrifice] for Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, just as [the entitlement does not extend to them] in the case of a specific sacrifice [prescribed by gender]. This is also because of the indicative mark (liṅga).
And there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely that the number seventeen belongs to the Vaiśya, as in the statement, "The Vaiśya is seventeen.
Therefore, the number seventeen belongs to the Vaiśya;

hence, such types of rites belong to the Vaiśya alone, just as there is a specific sacrifice for the Vaiśya, namely, "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," because of its connection with the Vaiśya.
Thus, the state of being seventeen belongs to that very [sacrifice].

Or rather, it does not; because of the distinctness of the connection, and because the accessory (guṇa) has the sacrifice as its primary object, for the injunction is indeed unconnected [to any other].
In the case of a sacrifice, because it is subordinate to that [sacrifice], it would be restricted by way of specification.
Now, as for what was said— that it is just as in the Vaiśyastoma, so it is here too— that is appropriate in that case, because the sacrifice of a Vaiśya is explicitly heard [in the scripture]. There,
it would be restricted by the very specific injunction.
Therefore, there is no fault in that case;
for in the act of giving one's own [gift], everything is without distinction.
Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice, they declare: "He gives away his entire property.

In this regard, there is a doubt: should everything that is denoted by the word "property" (sva)—such as mother, father, and so forth—be given away, or should only that which is called "property" by virtue of one's ownership be given? What is the prima facie view?
Since there is no distinction made, [the property] of the mother, father, and so forth must also be given.
Now, it is said that "giving" consists of the cessation of one's own ownership and the establishment of another's ownership;
in that case, it would be impossible to cease one's ownership over the father and others.
For it is not the case that a father somehow ceases to be a father.
It is said: it is true that he does not cease to be a father;
however, he can be made subject to the authority of another, and giving consists in the transfer of ownership to another.
And by implication, there is the renunciation of ownership;
therefore, "everything should be given," because for one who is the master [of it], it is possible, whereas for another, it is impossible.
By the word "or" (vā), the position is reversed:
that which becomes one's own property through the exercise of authority is alone to be given, and nothing else.
Why?
Because it is possible for one who possesses mastery [over them], whereas it is impossible for another;
for indeed, it is not possible for fathers and others to renounce their ownership (*svatva*).
To this it is replied: this word *sva* denotes each of "one's own," "wealth," and "kinsmen" individually, not as a collective whole.

In that regard, once the state of "all-inclusiveness" (*sarvatā*) regarding one's own property has been established and the purpose of the scriptural injunction fulfilled, all-inclusiveness should not be imagined to extend to kinsmen who cannot be given away, nor should the literal meaning of the scripture be subverted. Furthermore, when cows and other such items belonging to oneself are obtained through the *codaka* (the general rule), the state of all-inclusiveness pertaining to one's own property must necessarily be adopted. Once that has been adopted, the purpose of the scripture is accomplished; therefore, there is no reason to include kinsmen, and thus fathers and others should not be given.
Therefore, only that over which one possesses ownership by virtue of lordship is to be given;
land, however, cannot be so given, because it is common to all without distinction.
Right here there is a doubt regarding the gift of all things: should the earth be given, or not?
What, then, is intended by "earth" in this context? It is that globe of the earth composed of clay and not consisting of other substances, and not merely a field or soil.
In this regard, what is the conclusion?
It should be given without distinction;
for the word "one's own" (*sva*) applies there by virtue of the connection with ownership, and it is possible to relinquish one's own ownership through a mental act of intention.
This being the case, we reply: the earth is not the deity.
Why?
Because humans are seen to be the lords of fields, not of the entire terrestrial globe.
Furthermore, because it is not produced [by causes], there would consequently be a distinction [between them].
Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt:
should the horse and other such items be given as gifts, or not? What is the prima facie position?
Since everything has been prescribed, it follows that horses should be given.
This being the position reached, we reply: that for which giving is improper should not be given, as is the case with horses;
for their giving is indeed improper.

For this is indeed the distinction of horses from other substances: that their gift is prohibited, as it is specifically enjoined in the Viśvajit sacrifice, "He does not give maned animals, nor does he accept those with teeth in both jaws.
Therefore, horses should not be given.
Furthermore, because they are permanent, there can be no connection between them and impermanent things.
What, then, is the established conclusion?

That finished articles should be given; for in that way, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) regarding the method of giving is upheld, whereas otherwise, it would be merely a syntactical connection (*vākya*).
And between these two, the direct statement is more authoritative.
"Therefore, finished articles should be given.
This being the position reached, we reply: because of their permanence, there is no connection with impermanent things; the word "and" (ca) is used for a supplementary reference.
It has been stated that horses should not be given, and it is further stated that finished articles should not be given either.
For in the Viśvajit sacrifice, the giving of gifts, being permanent, is restated as it is obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction).
However, manufactured articles (*kṛtabhāṇḍaka*) are impermanent; it is not possible to bring all such things together when the Viśvajit is being performed.

In that case, there would be [giving] of manufactured articles, but not of what is permanent; yet that [giving] is enjoined by the *codaka* as something permanent, not as being connected to a specific occasion (*nimitta*).

Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted: that the rule regarding the objects to be given applies only to those [objects] already obtained; and when the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is impossible, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) must indeed be adopted. Consequently, finished vessels (*kṛtabhāṇḍaka*) should not be given. And a Śūdra [is excluded] because of the nature of the Dharmaśāstra.
At the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), whatever belongs to oneself should be understood as such, because of its connection with the act of giving.
Regarding the Viśvajit sacrifice itself, there is a doubt:

must that which exists prior to the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) necessarily be set aside for the time of the fee, and furthermore, must even what will exist in the future—though not yet arrived—at the time of the fee be given? Or is it that only that which exists at the very time of the fee is to be given? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
Even that which was one's own property previously and subsequently should be given, because the injunction for giving pertains to one's own property in general.
This being the case, we reply: only that which is one's own property at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is to be given, not that which was one's own before or after.
Why?
Having referred here to one's own [property], its entirety is enjoined;
and since that gift is already established at the time of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it is referred to at that very time.
Therefore, what exists at the time of the sacrificial fee is what must be given.
Because it is not exhaustive, that [conclusion] would be the end; for action is established by means of substance.
Regarding that very Viśvajit sacrifice, there is a doubt:
should the Viśvajit be abandoned at the very time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), or should everything not be given, but rather the sacrifice be brought to completion? What is the prima facie view?
"It must be relinquished.
Why?
Because it is not exhaustive.
How is there completeness? In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one gives away "all one's possessions" (sarvasva). And it is not possible to complete [the rite] without material substance.
Therefore, that [substance] must be included within it.
Or rather, it should be a residual rite, because it is directly enjoined as part of the sacrifice.
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position.

There should be a residue of the ritual action; not everything should be given away as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the time of its distribution. As much as is required to complete that ritual action must be left over. Why?
Because the completion of the sacrifice is directly enjoined.
The completion of the sacrifice is directly taught by the injunction: "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit"; that is to say, having commenced the Viśvajit, one should bring it to completion.
The meaning is that whatever can be given by one who completes [the sacrifice], all of that must be given.
Therefore, that [conclusion] must not be abandoned;
likewise, there is a scriptural indication to this effect.

And by taking it in this way, the observation of another purpose becomes consistent; for the statement, "Having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he covers himself with the skin of a calf," is only possible if there is a remainder.
However, if there were no remainder, the subsequent rite would have to be performed by taking [the skin] in its entirety, which would be inconsistent.
Because non-appropriation is eternal.
But the act of taking is impermanent, while the remaining karma is permanent;
for a connection between these two is not logically possible.
Therefore, something must remain over.
But because of the specific instruction regarding the initiations (dīkṣās), there is a connection with what is not for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore, there would be no contradiction.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
It is not the case that something must be left over;
rather, the specific assignment occurs during the consecrations (*dīkṣā*) within the *jyotiṣṭoma* itself, which is the archetype (*prakṛti*).
This is obtained here by the *codaka* (the rule of extension): "this is for the sake of the sacrifice, this is for the purpose of eating, and this is for the purpose of propitiation.
Therefore, in this context, that which is to be given for the purpose of propitiation undergoes this modification called "universality" (*sarvatā*). Why is this so?
Since "he gives his own" is restated as a reference (*anuvāda*), it is enjoined (*vidhīyate*) in its entirety.
Therefore, the giving of what ought not to be given is not enjoined, nor is that which is to be given for the purpose of consumption or for the sake of the sacrifice [enjoined].
Consequently, there will be no contradiction.
And in the case of the *ahargaṇa* sacrifice, its specific characteristics should apply [to all days], because there is no distinction among them.
Or, one may offer twelve hundred [oblations] as in the original rite.
"Or one hundred and twelve [cows] should be given.
It should be performed according to the archetype (prakṛti),
and the Jyotiṣṭoma is that archetype.
In that case, the ritual details are prescribed; however, in the Viśvajit sacrifice, they are not understood to apply in their entirety.
Therefore, it might be argued that "one hundred and twelve [cows] should be given here.
But this cannot be so, because the quality does not belong to that.
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
It cannot be thus.
Why?
Because the quality of "one hundred and twelve" does not belong to the Viśvajit;
for here, the adoption of the ritual details is by means of the name.
Therefore, it will pertain to the Viśvajit, and not to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
An indicative mark (liṅga) also indeed shows this. What is the indicative mark?
