It is as follows: "He who does not give everything in the Viśvajit is deprived of his cattle"—this shows that the giving of one's entire property is mandatory in the context of a multi-day sacrifice (ahargaṇa).
Being a transformation, it would [be identical] on both sides because there is no distinction.
"In the Viśvajit sacrifice, one gives away all one's possessions.

In this regard, there is a point of doubt: does the entitlement to perform the Viśvajit belong even to one who possesses twelve hundred [cows], or more, or less, or does it belong only to one who possesses the full amount or more? What is the prima facie view?
Since it is a modification, there is no distinction between the two;
no specific distinction is adopted such that one has more than twelve hundred and the other has less.
Therefore, everyone has the entitlement to the Viśvajit sacrifice;
or rather, it is an additional entitlement because of the counter-exception.
And this is not the case, that everyone has the entitlement to the Viśvajit sacrifice.
To whom, then?
To one who possesses twelve hundred [cows], or more.
Why?
Because of the counter-exception;
for in the Jyotiṣṭoma, a counter-exception regarding the giving away of one's entire property is indeed stated.
Having prescribed one hundred and twelve [cows], he says: "By this much indeed the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are to be brought, or else by their entire property.
This means that if they do not desire [to come] for this much, they must be brought even by means of their entire property.
Therefore, if they do not desire [to come] for one hundred and twelve, they will certainly not desire it for less than that.

Therefore, one hundred and twelve [cows] is prescribed for the Jyotiṣṭoma; however, since both that and "one's entire property" (sarvasva) are applicable here, one alternative is restricted by the rule: "one's entire property must be given."

This is not an injunction, because it is already established; rather, that which is established in an indefinite manner is here being restricted. And if it is so restricted, then as it is there, so it is here.
And in that case, one's entire property—whether consisting of twelve hundred or more—is required;
here too it is exactly the same.
Therefore, one who possesses less wealth has no entitlement.
And because of favor, as in the case of the feet.
In the case of the unlimited, there is a prohibition of numbering the remainder, because that is what is heard in the scripture.

In the context of the fire-consecration (ādhāna), it is heard in scripture: "One [cow] is to be given; six are to be given; twelve are to be given; twenty-four are to be given; a hundred is to be given; a thousand is to be given; an unlimited amount is to be given. Regarding this, there is a doubt:

does the injunction enjoin a prohibition—that whatever is limited, such as "one is to be given" and so forth, should not be given—or is "unlimited" (aparimita) a specific thing, and the giving of that is enjoined?
What is established? We say that when an indefinite number is heard, the number belonging to the remainder—one and so forth—which is to be counted, is prohibited.
Why?

Because that [word] is heard; since the word "limited" (parimita) is heard, a numbered quantity is understood. And that [number] begins with one, and its negation is performed by the word "na. In this way, the meaning heard in the text is maintained; otherwise, the conventional usage of the word "unlimited" (aparimita) would have to be abandoned.
The meaning of this [term] might be conceived as plurality through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Therefore, it is a prohibition of what is not measured;
or else, it is another alternative, because they are enumerated as being equal.
But surely there is no conventional usage here; this is a definition.
That which is much cannot be measured;
therefore, "muchness" is defined by way of its being immeasurable.

And that is not so; for when there are many things whose measure is impossible to determine, the word is conventionally established in the sense of "much. Thus, when it is said, "His wealth is immeasurable," it is understood to mean "it is much," just as with the words *kuśala* or *pravīṇa*.

When many qualities of a *kuśa* (reed) are present, the word *kuśala* arises specifically in the sense of "skillfulness"; thus, it is a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*). And when many qualities of a *vīṇā-vāda* (lute-player) are present, the word *pravīṇa*, which denotes one who is "skilled," is likewise said to be conventional.
Therefore, even though there is a basis in etymological definition (*lakṣaṇātva*), the word *rohati* [arises] by virtue of the power of traditional usage (*śrutisāmarthyāt*).

Therefore, by virtue of the established conventional meaning of the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*), the etymological derivation from its parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*) is sublated in the case of the word *aparimita*, just as in the case of the word *aśvakarṇa*.
Hence, [the rule] "after a kalpa" [is stated].
There is no fixed restriction because there is no specific distinction.
It has been established that "after an immeasurable number of eons" [means] beyond a thousand;
however, a doubt now arises: is "immeasurable" less than a thousand, or more than a thousand?
What, then, is the position reached?
There is no fixed rule, because there is no distinction;
for here, no specific distinction regarding the number is adopted, such as whether it is less than a thousand or more.
If no specific rule is followed, then it is well as it has been done;
therefore, there is no fixed restriction.
Or rather, there may be an addition, because the others are present for the sake of multiple purposes.
The phrase "or" serves to exclude that alternative.
This is not the case—that there should be more or less than a thousand.
What then?
"It is indeed more.
Why?
Because the word *aparimita* has many meanings; for it has been stated that people employ this word in reference to many things.
Plurality is relative; something is called "many" only in relation to something else that is greater than it.
In the absence of such a relation, this term is incomplete, just as the word "son" exists only in relation to someone and not otherwise.
In this case, the determination is made in relation to what is under discussion and what is proximate; and a thousand is what is proximate.
Therefore, it is greater than that, immeasurable;
and the explanatory passage (arthavāda) is likewise.
How is it so?
In that context, the term "excellent" (utkṛṣṭa) indeed means "immeasurable" (aparimita); this demonstrates the deficiency of [the number] one thousand.
Furthermore, the recounting of the deeds of others and ancient legends would constitute a human attribute, for such recitation is for the sake of a specific purpose.
And because there is a prohibition when that [word] has been uttered.

A prohibition of such a kind of injunction occurs in the form "one should not do it thus"; and a prohibition is logically applicable only to that which has been previously occasioned. Therefore, these are indeed injunctions.
Or rather, by virtue of the specific mention, it should possess those characteristics, just like the five-fold portioning (pañcāvatta).

This rule is understood as being of such a nature that it pertains to the human condition (*manuṣyadharma*). However, because specific lineages (*gotra*) are mentioned therein, it is understood that this duty belongs to those [lineages] alone.

For it is known from praise that "this must be performed," and that [praise] is heard in reference to specific lineages; therefore, it must be performed by those of those lineages alone, just like the five-fold portioning (*pañcāvatta*). Just as in the case of "the five-fold portioning belongs to the Jamadagnis," it applies only to those of that lineage, so it is here as well.
But in the case of an injunction, there must be instruction because of its connection with the Veda.
Or rather, it is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) because it is supplementary to an injunction; therefore, it must be a constant restatement (nityānuvāda).
This position is also excluded by the word "or" (vā).
This is neither a rule for those of that lineage, nor a rule for human beings in general, nor indeed a mandatory injunction; rather, this is an explanatory praise (arthavāda).
Why?

Because it is supplementary to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatvāt*). For in this context, they cite another injunction: in the case of the *parakṛti* (example of another's action), "Therefore, one should eat only forest-grown [food]"; and in the case of the *purākalpa* (ancient precedent), "They should offer [the oblation] by churning fire specifically in the fires of the householder.
And there can be no syntactic unity (*ekavākyabhāva*) between two such injunctions.
For when two statements—one concerning a "deed of another" (parakṛti) and one concerning a "past event" (purākalpa)—are connected with an injunction, their mode of expression is one thing;
but it is quite another when they function for the purpose of praise.
And both cannot possibly occur simultaneously.
Therefore, it is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda),
because a lifespan of a thousand years is impossible among human beings.
Or rather, it should be a duty for humans because of their qualification for that [rite].
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to exclude that alternative position;
it means that the qualification belongs to humans alone, not to Gandharvas and the like.
Why is this so?
Because of that qualification, it has been established that the scripture is intended for human beings;
for they alone are capable of fully carrying out the prescribed injunctions as described.
An objection is raised: "But humans do not possess such a lifespan."
It is said that they will attain a long life through elixirs;
this is not so, because of their lack of efficacy.
Because no relationship [between them] is observed.
For such a connection between longevity and elixirs has never been observed before; and in the absence of an observation of a connection, there can be no inference.
[Objection: But will it not be an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)?
For we do observe the causes of even a small degree of stability.

When practiced in this way, these [exercises] will become most vigorous and produce stability of the body. Although there is the saying that "man has a lifespan of a hundred years," a longer life is indeed observed. To this it is replied: this is not an absolute rule; they may sometimes produce a certain degree and amount of bodily stability, but not necessarily beyond the previously unobserved limit. Just as those who walk, through practice, reach a certain degree and amount of stride as their steps increase, yet even while practicing, men would not cover a distance of one *yojana* in a single lifetime.
Likewise here too, because there is no [established] connection, it is doubtful whether they would attain a lifespan of a thousand years or not.

If it is doubtful, then inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nor can an unperceived object be accepted without a means of knowledge.
Therefore, it has been stated by the words of a person that, beyond doubt, there are no such long-lived beings.
"How then?
[To this] Kārṣṇājini says: "It would be a family tradition," because [the two] cannot coexist in one person.
Or rather, because of the connection with the whole, there should be the performance of only one [mantra].
For the fruit of the scripture is attained by the performer, and only he who is capable of carrying out the injunction in its entirety is entitled [to perform it].
Therefore, the family tradition (kulakalpa) is not tenable.
How, then, is it determined that "Dharma is [known] through tradition alone"?
It is heard thus: "One's own Vedic study (svādhyāya) is to be performed."
If that is so, then this must be concluded: "By the authority of the scriptural statement, the lifespan of those performing this action increases.
But that is not the case, because there is a lack of valid evidence;
for regarding this matter, there is neither the scriptural word nor any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Is it not then a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since otherwise there would be meaninglessness?
It is replied: "There is no meaninglessness, for the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) will arise from the mere recitation itself.
For it is simpler to postulate an unseen result in a general sense than to postulate a specific unseen result such as 'through this ritual act, one's lifespan is increased.'"
Alternatively, one must simply accept the meaninglessness [of the statement], for a result not supported by logic should not be postulated.

If it were argued that "two hundred and fifty will be initiated [for the Sattra] and they will complete it in four years," even so, the fixed limit would be violated, as it is stated: "They should perform the Sattra with a minimum of seventeen and a maximum of twenty-four."

If it is argued that the measure [of the Veda] will be reduced in order to avoid the meaninglessness of the word, that is incorrect; for there is a fruit resulting from its study. Therefore, this is not a valid hypothesis.
How, then? It is thus:
Lāvukāyana says that because of the contradiction, one or the other of the two qualities must prevail.
In this case, one of the two terms must be figurative: either the word "year" when it refers to less than a year, or the word "fifty-five. Why is this so?
Because of contradiction; for there would indeed be a contradiction when both are prescribed.
How so?
Because the sentence would then be split.
If there are fifty-five triplets, they are not years;
if the years are triplets, they are not fifty-five.
Therefore, because of this contradiction, the teacher Lāvukāyana considered that one of the two statements must be figurative.
The mention of the "teacher" is for the sake of honor, not for the purpose of prohibiting oneself;
[the period is] one year because of its being subject to change.
This has been stated: one of the two is figurative.
Having determined that, it is said:
the expression "year" is figurative.
Why?

Because it is variable; for the word "year" (*saṃvatsara*) is indeed variable: it may refer to the solar year (*sāvana*) consisting of calculated days, or to that characterized by cold, heat, and rain, or even to the lunar year (*cāndramasa*).
It is possible to assume that such a definition is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
But this term "fifty-five" is a denoter of an object whose quantity is specifically manifest; it does not apply when even one is lacking.
That [term] would be the base form, because of its governing context.

This position, too, is not tenable; for here, too, the same fault applies. There is no living [long enough] until this could be arranged with due regard for marriage, the sacred fires, the Soma sacrifice, and the preceding [stages]. Therefore, if this were performed, one's lifespan would be exhausted even before it was completed.
And thus, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be assumed to result from study alone.
In that case, since the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is the archetype (*prakṛti*), there will be fifty-two twelve-day sacrifices;
and thus it is seen [in scripture]: "The twelve nights are indeed the image (*pratimā*) of the year.
In this way, that fault will not occur.
It is not so, because in that context the word "year" (saṃvatsara) is directly connected with the word "image" (pratimā).
Furthermore, it is stated that there are "fifty-five triplets" (trivṛt), and the term "triplet" is observed to refer to a day in the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), not to the twelve-night rite.
Therefore, it is not so.
Or rather, it is the days [that are meant], because they are specifically enumerated.

Because it is preceded by an *iṣṭi*, the oblation (*homa*) should not be a subsidiary of a sacrifice (*akratuśeṣa*), but rather should take place in consecrated fires; for even though it is an independent rite (*apūrva*), the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is a prerequisite for all [rites].

In this context, it is prescribed among the Caturhotṛ formulas: "One desiring progeny should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with the Caturhotṛ; having taken clarified butter in four portions, he should recite the Caturhotṛ formula; he should offer one half with the first portion and the other half with the subsequent one.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
are such [offerings] to be made only when the fires have been consecrated by the Pavamāna-iṣṭis, or even when they have not been so consecrated?
Likewise, the alternative position that will be mentioned later shall also be examined.
What, then, is the prima facie view?
Such an oblation, even if it is not a subsidiary of a sacrifice, should be performed using consecrated fires alone.

Although the *darvihomas* are unprecedented and do not require any ritual details (*dharma*) from elsewhere, nevertheless, the *āhavanīya* fire and other such elements require the oblations and so forth, according to scriptural injunctions such as, "When one offers in the *āhavanīya*, by that [act] he becomes pleased with him who is desired.
Thus, since all oblations are preceded by an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, those of this class must reside in consecrated fires.
However, the praise [of these oblations] as being of the nature of an *iṣṭi* indicates that the *caturhotṛ* formulas are to be employed even in unconsecrated fires.

Now, it may be argued that an indicative mark (liṅga) is not a means of proof, and that a direct scriptural statement (prāpti) must be stated. To this it is replied: "But there is instruction because [the matter] is not previously established."
In that case, this will be an injunction for those [rites] that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice; this will be the performance for one who has not established the sacred fires.
Thus the statement will be purposeful.
Otherwise, it would be a mere assertion devoid of meaning, whereas this [statement] possesses the capacity to function as an injunction.
Therefore, the rule applies to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) because it is common to all without distinction.
He says: "This is understood as an injunction.
As for the statement, "of those not subsidiary to a sacrifice," that is not so; for it refers to all the Caturhotṛ-homas, both those subsidiary to sacrifices and those not subsidiary to sacrifices.
Why?
Because there is no distinction, this duty is not stated to apply only to those who have the sacrifice as a remainder (*kratvaśeṣa*), nor to those who do not have the sacrifice as a remainder;
therefore, it applies to all.
Alternatively, because of the absence of the sacrifice, for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is an instruction regarding the non-remainder of beings.
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position.
This rule applies only to those [acts] that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice, not to those that are subsidiary to a sacrifice.
Why?
Because for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there is an absence of sacrifices (*kratu*);
for indeed, no sacrifices exist for one who has not established the fires.
And a constituent part of a sacrifice, when employed by itself, could serve no purpose whatsoever.
Nor can another fruit for this [act] be postulated, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the statement has another purpose as well;
moreover, it is not possible to postulate a sacrifice for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) on the basis of this statement.
Therefore, this rule applies to those [rites] that are not subsidiary to a sacrifice;
or rather, it refers to the muttering of prayers, because they do not involve contact with fire.
By the word "or" (vā), the position is reversed:
such offerings as these would not take place in the case of unconditioned fires.
Why?
Because the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) is subsidiary to everything.
[Objection: But this is a direct scriptural statement: "This is the sacrifice for one who has not established the fires.
[Response: We say no; this will be like the purpose of a *japa* (muttered prayer).

Those [acts] whose form is recitation (japa) are for them [only] an explanatory praise (arthavāda), not for all the *caturhotṛ* formulas; in this way, there will be purposefulness for such statements as "he offers in the Āhavanīya fire. However, since it is praised as an *iṣṭi*, it would be a homa, because of its connection with the fire which is not introduced [as a subordinate element], and because the others cannot be so designated.
As for what was said— that this rite of one who has not established the sacred fires is equal to an *iṣṭi*, and that this statement refers to the *japas*—
that is not so; this is not the correct interpretation of the sentence.
This ritual act of one who has not maintained the sacred fires is equivalent to an *iṣṭi* sacrifice.
What is the reason?
A mere restatement of similarity would be purposeless.

In the other case, the injunction is purposeful: "This sacrifice belongs to one who has not established the sacred fires. Since this is a praise of that sacrifice, it is actually a statement regarding the oblations themselves.
How so?
An *iṣṭi* is a sacrifice (*yāga*); that same [sacrifice], when augmented by the act of pouring (*āsecanādhika*), is a *homa*.
As for what was stated—that the *āhavanīya* fire is for the purpose of all *homas*—that is not so; for it is said specifically with reference to the *caturhotṛ* offerings.
However, since the oblations are prescribed without distinction, they will apply to other [sacrifices] because they are impossible in the case of the *caturhotṛ* offerings. Furthermore,
when the *caturhotṛ* offerings are being performed by one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the *āhavanīya* fire is not a constituent part [of the rite].
For both [offerings], it is like the sacrifice to the ancestors (piṭṛyajña).
Or rather, it is an instruction for one who has not established the sacred fires, because there is no connection with the fires mentioned without reference to a specific context.
And this is not the case, that the *caturhotṛ* formulas would apply to both;
how so?
For this is an instruction concerning one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*).

This person is qualified by the statement "this is the *veṣṭi* for one who has not established the sacred fires," and not one who has established the fires, due to the force of that specific designation. Furthermore, since [the qualification] is exhausted as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) in that very context, it does not conflict with the rule "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire. It has already been stated that the injunction "one offers in the *āhavanīya*" is not spoken solely with reference to the *caturhotṛ* offerings.
Therefore, such oblations belong only to one who has not established the sacred fires; their mention again here refers specifically to one engaged in the Pitṛyajña.

Now, as for what was said—that it is "like the Pitṛyajña"—that is appropriate in the case of the Pitṛyajña. There, regarding one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there is this further statement: "It should also be performed by one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). This statement implies that even for one who has not established the sacred fires, he performs the *Anvāhāryaka* [offering]; however, in this present case, there is no such statement.
The single instruction is mandatory: "Or this [is for] one who has not established the sacred fires.
There is no word "also" (api) here;
therefore, this is not equal to the Pitṛyajña.
One should establish the sacred fires after having performed the initiation ceremony, because of the connection with the oblation.
It should be performed either with the Sthapati sacrifice or in the common fire, because it follows the sequence of learning and ritual action.
And this is not the case, that one must offer the oblation only after having established [the fires] of such a kind.
What then? It should proceed with those that are merely worldly (laukika).
Why?
Because they follow the sequence of knowledge and ritual action;
these oblations are for the purpose of acquiring knowledge.
Furthermore, eligibility for the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) belongs to one who possesses knowledge, by virtue of [that] capacity.
Therefore, it is not possible for these [rites] to occur after the time of the fire-laying, as in the case of the *Sthapati-īṣṭi*. And the fire-laying is connected with the taking of a wife.
Furthermore, the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is heard in scripture as being connected with a wife;
and the taking of a wife occurs after the time of acquiring knowledge.
Therefore, for this reason also, the priority of the establishment of the fires is not tenable.
And after the consecration, there is no ritual action, for its connection is indeed with those [specific] actions.
If it is argued that it is like the *śrāddha* [rite];

And here he says: that which was stated—that just as the Piṇḍapitṛyajña belongs both to one who has maintained the sacred fires and to one who has not, so too does the taking of a wife—must be refuted;
for there is no contradiction with the revealed scripture (Śruti).

It is not so, for there would be a contradiction with scripture (*śrutivipratiṣedha*). If this marriage rite were performed after the time of acquiring knowledge—as it is heard [in other texts]—then to say it is performed earlier is contradictory.

If it is argued that this is something entirely different from what follows from the sense of the matter, we say no; this is merely a restriction of the time for that which is already established by the sense of the matter.
And the initiation ceremony is for the sake of ritual action;
it would be prohibited in the case of a second [wife].
Furthermore, because it serves all purposes, one should not employ it for the sake of a son alone.
Now it might be argued: "Before the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*), it will serve the purpose of ritual action (*karman*), and after it, it will serve the purpose of offspring (*apatya*);
therefore, this being so, nothing will be in contradiction with it.
To this we reply: it is not so.
For that [marriage] is for one's own sake; it will not serve merely the purpose of producing offspring.
As it has been said: "Because there is no difference in the zeal for the fruit.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no taking of a second wife.
Moreover, it is thus remembered in the tradition: "One must not transgress with respect to duty, wealth, and pleasure.
If [marriage were permitted] in this way, one would be transgressing;
therefore, there is no taking of a second wife.
There is only one wife, who serves both for the sake of ritual action and for the sake of offspring;
furthermore, her acquisition occurs subsequent to the acquisition of sacred knowledge.
Therefore, these oblations are not to be performed in fires consecrated by the *ādheya* rite.
But from the drinking of soma comes the attainment of a second [birth]; therefore, one should marry.
This is accepted: that prior to initiation there is no wife.
However, what was stated—that there is only one wife—is not tolerated, because according to the Smṛti, she must not be transgressed against in matters of dharma, artha, and kāma.

And it is likewise recorded in the Smṛti that one should not take another wife while already possessing a spouse endowed with both virtue and progeny; however, in the absence of either of these qualities, one may take another.
Therefore, he whose wife is neither endowed with virtue nor endowed with progeny may take another.

And he cited "from drinking the Soma" as an explanatory statement (arthavāda); by saying "the Soma-drinker did not desire a second wife," he indicates that there was indeed a second wife. However, because it is observed in the context of the Pitṛyajña, it should be understood as applying to the period prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna).

Now, how is it that there are two times for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña)? It is said: for a scriptural statement is seen there, namely, "It should be performed even by one who has not established the sacred fires."
Therefore, the Pitṛyajña takes place prior to the Ādhāna.
The Sthapati-iṣṭi, like the Prayājas, would necessitate the performance of the Agnyādheya; however, because it serves that specific purpose, it should be concluded [upon its own completion].
Or rather, it should take place in the common fire, because the rite of formal installation (ādhāna) is not subsidiary to all [fires].
The phrase "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position.
It would apply to worldly fires, not to consecrated ones.
Why?
Because the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is not subsidiary to all [rites].
The sacred fires (*agni*) are subsidiary to all rites, and their establishment (*ādhāna*) is a subsidiary to those [fires], not a subsidiary to the rites themselves.

Since there is an absence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth, the establishment is not prompted by the rites; rather, by the force of syntactical connection (*vākya*), it is prompted by the fires.
And that which is enjoined for the New and Full Moon sacrifices is obtained through the *codaka* (transference rule), not that which is enjoined for the specific substance.

Therefore, the *Sthapati-iṣṭi* is performed in worldly fires. And the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) is likewise [performed in worldly fires], because the time for the formal establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) has not yet arrived.

Rites for the gods are to be performed during the northern course of the sun, during the first half of the month, and on auspicious days, because they are recorded in the Smṛtis and because other scriptural passages indicate this meaning.
Divine rites (daivāni karmāṇi) are exemplified by those beginning with the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
Regarding these, there is a doubt:
are divine rites to be performed at an unrestricted time, or rather during the northern course of the sun (udagayana), the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa), and on auspicious days (puṇyāha)?
When it might be thought that [the time] is indefinite, it is stated: "during the northern solstice and so forth.
Why?
Because they remember it thus: "In those times, [the rites] belong to the gods."
And there is the doctrine that [the year] is the form of the gods:
"The northern course of the sun, the bright fortnight, and the day—this indeed is the form of the gods.
Yet we do not know the form of the gods and so forth.
If, however, the rites for the gods are performed at these times, then the mention of "form" (rūpa) becomes intelligible through this connection.
Furthermore, this sentence shows another purpose: "The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors.
Therefore, the rites for the gods should be performed at these times.
And on the day [of the new moon], there is the completion of the ritual action.
Furthermore, there is a specific distinction regarding the day: since the entire ritual action can be performed only during the day, one will not perform it at night;
however, this is not the case for the other ancestral rites (pitrāṇi).
Śrāddha and other rites should be performed during the latter fortnight and in the afternoon, because there are Smṛti rules and observations of other purposes [to that effect];
and when [the required materials] are not available, one may beg or purchase them, as is done in the world.
This is recited in the Jyotiṣṭoma: "For twelve nights, having been initiated, one should seek wages," and likewise, "One purchases the Soma.
In this regard, there is a doubt.
Should one who does not possess wages seek them, and one who does not possess Soma purchase it—this being so whether [the means] exist or do not exist?
What is the prima facie view?
Seeking [wages] and purchasing [Soma] should occur when the wages and the Soma are not present.
Why?
Because begging and purchasing are for the purpose of obtaining something that exists as a substantial entity; since that [entity] is already present, such acts are useless.
And what is stated to be useless should not be performed, even if it has been enjoined.
Therefore, it would exist even when [the object] is non-existent, as is seen in the world. Just as in the world, one who has no wealth begs and buys,
so too should it be understood here.
Or rather, it must be fixed, because it possesses meaning.
Likewise, [one should avoid] eating, the call for the slaughter, covering, the *saṃjñapta* offering, and the *dveṣa* offering.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "Milk is the fast-food for the Brāhmaṇa, gruel for the Rājanya, and curdled milk for the Vaiśya.
Likewise, in the Darśapūrṇamāsa there is an injunction: "Place the sprinkling waters; set down the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the ladles; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter.
Similarly, in the Vājapeya it is heard: "The garment is made of darbha grass."

At the animal sacrifice, there is the *saṃjñaptahoma* (the oblation upon the immolation), with the mantra: "If the animal has made a sound, or if it has struck with its feet, may Agni release me from that sin entirely.
Likewise, there is the statement: "He who hates us and whom we hate.
These are the illustrative citations.
In this regard, this is an extension of the legal topic (*adhikaraṇātideśa*). Whatever was the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the preceding topic, that is the prima facie position here;
whatever was the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) there, that is the final conclusion here.

"One should perform [the rite] even when [the object] is not present" is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa); "or rather, it is necessarily [performed] because it possesses purpose" is the final view (uttara-pakṣa).
This same principle applies here that was applied previously.
But that which is purposeless would be impermanent.
In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "At midday or in the latter part of the night, one observes the vow. Regarding this, there is a doubt:
Is the vow restricted to the latter part of the night, or is it unrestricted?
What is the prima facie position? That it must necessarily possess meaning.
This being the case, we reply: but [if it were so], it would be meaningless and non-eternal.
When one thinks, "At this time my vow will be digested," then one should observe the vow.
But if one indeed thinks, "It will not be properly digested," then that vow being performed would be useless.

For if the sacrificer were to die due to indigestion, there would be a failure of the ritual procedure (*tantra*); and when there is a failure of the ritual procedure, there is a total failure of everything.
Therefore, the vow is not fixed as to the time it must be observed;
there is no restriction regarding the injunction for the animal sacrifice because there is no specific distinction made.
Or rather, it is a goat, because of the wording of the mantra.
The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position.
This is not the case;
namely, that the nature of an animal (paśutva) is to be employed in just any substance whatsoever.
There exists a restrictive cause for what is to be offered, namely the wording of the mantra:
"Recite the invitatory verse for the fat of the goat for Agni. A mantra capable of manifesting the goat is thus recorded in the tradition.
If the goat were not to be taken up [as the victim], then the employment of that which is capable of manifesting it would be purposeless.
From this it is understood that [the text] prescribes the ritual offering with reference to a goat;
thus, it is a rule for the restriction of the substance based on the wording of the mantra.
No, for that would contradict the primary injunction (*codanā*).
If it is argued that [the rule] applies as in the case of the *ārṣeya* (lineage).
If you think thus— that the state of being an animal (*paśutva*) should not be taken from animals other [than those specified]—
just as in the case where it is said, "He chooses a lineage-ancestor (*ārṣeya*)," or "He chooses three," the general scriptural statement (*sāmānyaśruti*) is restricted to exactly three;
that is, the specific number three is intended, while others are not intended.
Similarly here too, it is intended to designate the state of being a sacrificial animal (*paśutva*) as referring specifically to the goat (*chāga*), and not to other particulars.
No; for in that case, [the goat] has not been enjoined.
This is not so;
for in that case, the substance is to be relinquished as it was not specifically enjoined by the wording of the mantra,
whereas in the case of the choosing [of the bride], it is indeed enjoined.
In that context, since the connection with the number three has been enjoined in relation to the choosing (*varaṇa*), no other number is performed.
Furthermore, from the word *ārṣeya* as well, it follows that one who is not of noble lineage (*anārṣeya*) is excluded;
for it is the power of the word "three" which restricts the word *ārṣeya* to the scope of that specific number.
In this case, there is no efficacy of the mantra;
therefore, there is no restriction.
Or rather, there is a restriction, because the effect is one; for since the purpose is distinct, there is a distinction due to their being denoted as separate entities.

There is no restriction [on the meaning], because it is a different object; its distinctness [from the word] is established by both the difference in the word *vyatireka* and the difference in the word *anya*.
Or there is no restriction:
any animal whatsoever may be taken, because they are distinct entities.

"Animality" (*paśutva*) is one entity, and "goatness" (*chāgatva*) is another entity; here there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between these two meanings, not between the two words.
How, then, is another meaning understood?
From difference and from the difference of words; for there is indeed a difference, such as "some animal is not a goat," and likewise the difference of words is "the goat is an animal."
A difference in meaning is logically justified by a difference in words, because they coexist within a single sentence, as in "Bring the animal, the goat.
Otherwise, since the purpose would be accomplished by either one alone, the other would not coexist in the sentence; yet it does coexist.
Therefore, being a sacrificial animal (*paśutva*) is one thing, and being a goat (*chāgatva*) is another.
Consequently, there is no restriction, and any sacrificial animal whatsoever may be employed.
[Objection: But by employing a horse, we would certainly not be abandoning the wording of the mantra.
That very horse will become a goat;
that horse whose movement is cut off is a goat (*chāga*), for the word *chāga* is well-established as being derived from the roots *chid* (to cut) and *gam* (to go).
This is evident both from its form and its characteristic mark.
It is heard that in some cases they will be castrated;
if this were not stated explicitly, then [the rule] would apply only to those who are not castrated.
Therefore, even a horse whose movement has been cut off will be designated by the term "goat" (chāga) as a name for its ritual function.
To this it is replied:
In the case of the goat, there is no mention of the ritual action, because of its form and gender.
In the case of the word *chāga*, its meaning as "action" (the act of going) is not possible through either form or gender;

for the word *chāga* does not denote the act of cutting off movement. This is because it is a conventional whole (*samudāya*) well-known in a different sense [namely, a goat], and it should not be subverted by the etymological derivation of its individual parts.
Therefore, a horse is not a *chāga*.
Because the form is different, there would be no word for "genus."
It is not a modification, because it is innate.
This too is a subsequent word.
Here, the word "chāga" (goat) is a modification of "aśva" (horse) and so forth;
something from among the horse and others is uttered here, and nothing else at all.
Therefore, [the claim] that "the horse is also a goat" is not correct; because [the relationship] is innate (*autpattika*).
For it has been stated that the relationship between a name and its named object is innate, and thus a modification of the designation is not possible.
Therefore, the goat is not the horse;
hence, the goat alone should be taken.
That [substitution] is contingent, because no quality of the animal has been prescribed.
This sūtra follows immediately after the preceding one.
Now, why does the word "goat" (chāga) not signify the cause of a hole?
It is heard thus: "At this time, the animal is indeed hollow."
As for the statement, "When they cut out the omentum," it is said: "No," because the quality of being perforated has not been enjoined regarding the animal;
for it is enjoined that "one should sacrifice an animal without defective limbs."
Therefore, the sacrificial animal is one that is flawless.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that the established meaning of a whole is not sublated by the meanings of its individual parts.
Consequently, only a goat is to be taken as the victim, and not horses or other animals.
Or rather, because the word denotes the genus (jāti) and because it possesses both the sense of being predominant therein and semantic efficacy.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used for emphasis.
Since the conventional meaning of a whole is not sublated by the conventional meaning of its parts,
therefore the word "chāga" denotes the genus (*jāti*) alone.
Thus, since the meaningfulness of the aggregate will be supported, the statement regarding that majority is appropriate.
In the phrase "Recite for the *vapās* and *medas* of all the gods, the *uṣra*s, the goats, and the rams," the statement regarding the majority of the genus (*jāti*) is appropriate;
for even by means of a majority, a restriction is established, just as when one sees something written mostly concerning fire, the cognition arises: "This is fire."
Therefore, only a goat should be taken.
This being a hypothetical deliberation (*kṛtvācintā*), no further purpose need be stated.

Since the remaining [animals] are based on the authority of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), their application would occur according to their respective eligibility when there is a distinction among the primary [options].

By the first six chapters, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for rituals such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*—whose specific duties are directly prescribed—has been considered. Now, by the subsequent [six chapters], it is intended to consider those rituals such as the *aindrāgna*, whose procedures are not directly prescribed.

In that regard, if the duties prescribed in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices are applicable to all rituals, then by those very duties the *aindrāgna* and others are also declared to possess those duties and must be performed accordingly.
There is no purpose for the subsequent group of six.

Now, whatever [rites] are mentioned in the context of a particular [rite], they are already included therein; therefore, rites such as those for Indra and Agni (aindrāgna) are devoid of ritual details (adharmaka). Regarding these, the question arises: do they possess ritual details, or not?
And when they exist, [one must know] who they are, how many there are, and how they are to be practiced;
for that purpose, the subsequent group of six chapters should be set forth.
Therein, first by means of the seventh chapter, it is stated that "dharmas exist."
By the eighth [chapter], it is shown that "these belong to him";
by the ninth, that "they should be employed in this manner";
and by the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth, that "only this many should be employed, and no more than this."
Or, because there is no division in the sense of origination, there would be a single nature, just as in the case of a sentient being.
It is said: this is an unequal comparison.
In that case, the properties are prescribed by virtue of their connection with the universal "cow," as in:
"A cow must not be touched with the foot."
In this case, however, the properties (dharmas) are enjoined in connection with specific sacrifices,
such as "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" and "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma.
These [properties] ought to belong to the apūrva only when it is connected with a specific sacrifice, not everywhere.
To this we reply: [the injunction is] "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices in this manner.
If the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) were itself being enjoined, it could not be connected with the ritual details (*dharmas*).
For there can be no mutual connection between two things that are both being enjoined.
And since it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), it must, by virtue of being non-specific, be a restatement of all sacrifices;
therefore, the ritual properties (*dharmas*) belong to all of them.
[Objection: But will not the term *darśapūrṇamāsa* serve as a specifier?
The term "Darśapūrṇamāsa" cannot qualify the sacrifice;
for this [term] must be either an injunction (*vidhi*) or a restatement (*anuvāda*). When it is a restatement, its purpose is to establish a connection with ritual properties (*dharma*).
And that connection with the dharma is established only by way of a restatement (anuvāda) of the sacrifice [itself], namely:
"One should perform the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices in this manner, and not others.
It is not possible for it to be so.
For what reason? Because its meaning is not the exclusion of anything else.
[Objection: But will it not function as an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)? [Response: An exclusive specification is not appropriate here.
If the application of *dharma* to all sacrifices in general had already been established by another statement, then this repetition would serve to perform a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*).
However, if there were no such prior application, then for a single sentence to both establish the application and exclude everything else would be an excessive burden.
This is not a fault.
We shall not establish the connection of the dharmas by means of the explicit statement;
rather, by what?
By the context.
How so?
When the duty to act has been enjoined, there arises an expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*), namely, "How should one do it?
It is through the context (*prakaraṇa*) that the ritual details (*dharma*) become connected, [showing] that "One should do it in this way."
This is not possible;
for when the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are enjoined as things to be performed, there is no expectancy for a procedure (itikartavyatā) at all,
because their procedure is already well-known.
If there were no expectancy for the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), then the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself would not exist.
For it has been stated: "That which is not connected [by direct statement or other means] is [connected] by virtue of the context, because of the requirement for the manner of performance.
If that is so, then the ritual properties (*dharmas*) are not enjoined here in relation to the sacrifice at all.
Nor is the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) enjoined here.
What then?

Having referred to a sacrifice qualified by the two words "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām yajeta*), the ritual duties are prescribed therein, as in: "One should sacrifice by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices in this manner."
Even so, the restatement "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" would not be appropriate,
because the sense of the instrumental case is not established;
a restatement refers to what has been previously mentioned, yet the instrumental sense here is something new.
Therefore, that [injunction] must necessarily be formulated.
And when it is being formulated, something entirely unrelated results—namely, that "the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are the instrument of the root *yaji*.
Consequently, let that very first position stand: that there is an injunction of the ritual properties (*dharma*) by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the sacrifice.
But is it not the case that even there, the phrase "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" is not connected [to the result]?
Because they are supplementary to the injunction, they would remain restricted by their difference, since at the time of their origination they are subordinate elements.

The meaning is that the collection of dharma (the Vedic corpus) is a subsidiary part, a single portion, of the injunction regarding action; for example: "One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" by means of this procedure beginning with the laying of the fires (*agnyādheya*). In that injunction, the subordinate status of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is heard; the word "New and Full Moon" denotes the act of sacrificing.
Here, the status of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is heard for the root *yaj*.
One should perform something else by means of the aggregate of sacrifices known as the Darśapūrṇamāsa;
that which is other than that is enjoined as something to be performed, not the sacrifice itself,
and that is the *apūrva*.
But surely a result is heard in this sentence: "One who desires heaven should strive. Therefore, that [heaven] must be what is to be accomplished.
True, it is heard; however, it is not brought about by the sacrifice.
When the sacrifice has perished, that [result] comes into being;
however, the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is produced by it.
Therefore, its necessity for performance is stated.
That which has the status of being something to be performed is connected with its procedure (itikartavyatā).
Therefore, the dharmas have the apūrva as their purpose;
and there is a distinction among those apūrvas.
Therefore, due to that distinction, the properties (dharmas) are determined according to their respective contexts.
Even so, the productive urge (bhāvanā) is established in a general sense by the direct Vedic statement (śruti), and in a specific sense by the syntactical connection (vākya);
and these two do not occur simultaneously.
If that is so, then in this case the literal meaning of the word (*śrutyartha*) is not accepted at all.
What then?
It is the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*).
What is the reason?
If the literal meaning of the Vedic text were accepted, the word "Darśapūrṇamāsa" would become redundant,
and the verb "yajati" (he sacrifices) would be a mere restatement.
Because the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices consist of the act of sacrificing (*yajati*),
and because the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* is used in grammatical apposition with *yajati*,
it would be understood as universal [applying to all sacrifices] due to its connection with the definition of existence.
As for the phrase "like the word 'satva'": here, a property is heard in relation to the form of the cow,
because the form (ākṛti) is the meaning of the word.

And since that [individual] is not possible there, this form (ākṛti) is understood to have as its meaning the characteristic of the individual substance (piṇḍa) with which it coexists, just as in the expression "cows in the Ganges.
And since that coexistence is common to all individual substances, it is established for all individual substances.
Therefore, that [rule] would be understood as universal.
But here, because the sacrifice (yajati) is heard as being subordinate, the ritual properties (dharmas) are not heard in relation to the sacrifice itself.
What then?
"Unprecedented" (apūrva) refers to the reason being stated in this manner;
therefore, it is not to be presented [as a valid probans], just like the case of "existence" (sattva).
But because there is no differentiation, it could not be thus.
Now, it may be objected that because the sacrifice is transitory, it is incapable of yielding fruit at a later time;
in that case, it has already been stated that the dharmas performed therein are simply incapable [of producing results].
To this, a counter-argument is now presented by challenging the principle established therein.
This will be like the drinking of oil:

just as the drinking of oil or ghee, even though it is perishable, produces fruits such as intelligence, memory, strength, and nourishment at a later time, so too will the sacrifice produce its results; what need have we for a postulated *apūrva* that is neither seen nor heard?
And having two meanings is contradictory.

This being the case, all ritual elements (dharmas) serve all purposes. Thus, since the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and other such rites exist in sacrifices to Indra-Agni and others, their appearance in the solar (saurya) rite is logically justified.
"At each fore-offering (prayāja), he offers a kṛṣṇala.
Otherwise, both the fore-offerings would have to be enjoined,
as well as the offering of the kṛṣṇala within those fore-offerings.
And thus it would have two purposes;
and having two purposes is contradictory. Therefore, the ritual properties (dharmas) are enjoined by the sacrifice (yajati).
Or, because there is no injunction regarding the origin [of the rite], the activity would occur only upon a [separate] injunction; consequently, there would be a division of the ritual acts.
Or else, like the name itself, all dharmas would exist by virtue of their commonality.

Moreover, there are those who follow the Aruṇaparāśara branch. Among their ancillary texts, there exists a Brāhmaṇa in the form of a Smṛti, which begins with: "Whatever are the ritual rules for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, all those apply to all iṣṭis and to the Agniṣomīya," continuing until: "all primary and modified sacrifices, as far as they are not explicitly stated."
And this sequential enumeration indicates precisely this principle:
therefore, even though [the ritual] is prompted by the *apūrva* (unseen potency), all ritual properties (*dharma*) serve all purposes.

However, because the purpose (*artha*) is undivided, it might be so in the case of the verbal designations; yet, because the application follows the previous [pattern], and because the action is to be brought about by the word, there would be a non-application of the remaining [properties] due to their division.
First, the rebuttal by way of description is stated.
Regarding what was said, "like the Vāhīkas," we reply: because the object is undivided, it would be so in the case of designations.
The object is the state of being a Vāhīka, which is the connection with that region; that is undivided.
The meaning is that it is present in all [sensations] that carry [the flow of experience].
Furthermore, the specific pleasure caused by that [sensation] is not caused by the person (puruṣa).
How is this known?
Because the application [of the term] is based on what precedes it.
Here, the application is based on what has preceded; many Vāhīkas and non-Vāhīkas have been fed [in this manner].
There, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is known that this dislike for barley-food is caused by the region, not caused by the person.

Therefore, it should be so in the case of designations such as "Vāhīka" and others. Now, in this context, the fact that the action is to be brought about by the word cannot be known from any other source.
Of what [element] are these the "unprecedented" (apūrva) properties?
Furthermore, properties are established and understood through verbal testimony;
and since there is a distinction among those that are unprecedented, it would follow that what is prescribed for one [context] would not apply elsewhere among the remaining [elements].
If it is argued that it is memory;
Now, as for what was said— that it is memory—
what is the rebuttal to that?
No, because it is as before.

This recollection (*smṛti*) is based on what precedes it; it will state that the *codaka* (the injunction) is the grasper of the ritual elements (*dharma*), or that "the end of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) is like the archetype (*prakṛti*). Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those ritual elements already brought forward by that [injunction].
This [injunction] is preceded by logic; it does not enjoin things that have not already been reached. For this reason, the systematic arrangement of dharmas occurs through this very logic.
Since the meaning is to be brought about by the word, and because it is bound to the specific context, its existence would otherwise [occur] only through the word itself.
This is the sūtra of conclusion (*nigamana*). Conclusion is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*).

This is what is being said: since it is thus, therefore, because the object—such as the placing of the firewood (*agnyanvādhāna*) and so forth—is to be brought about by words (*śabdabhāvya*), and because it is bound to each respective context, its existence must occur through the word alone, and not otherwise.

"Just as Gandharvas or Apsarases cause one to go mad—whosoever goes mad, it is indeed these Gandharvas and Apsarases who are the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* (the 'sustainers of the kingdom')—one offers with the words, 'To him, svāhā! To them, svāhā! This is the instruction for the *udvāha* (marriage) regarding the *rāṣṭrabhṛts* that arise in the section on the fire-ritual:
'He offers these *rāṣṭrabhṛts*; he offers the *abhyātānas*.'"
In this statement, there is the principle that "rites should be established according to their respective eligibility.
This being the case, rites such as those dedicated to Indra and Agni (aindrāgna) would be non-dharmic [for certain persons]. For that reason, the subsequent six chapters must be commenced.

"The established rule is that *atideśa* (extended application) is that by which, from a primary ritual act, there occurs an extension of its properties (*dharmapradeśa*) to other acts similar to it. And this [extension] occurs either by name (*nāman*) or by a direct statement (*vacana*)."
In that regard, names are of three kinds: those that are designative (*atideśaka*), action-names (*karmanāman*), formation-names (*saṃskāranāman*), and derivative (*yaugika*).
Furthermore, verbal expression is of two kinds: that which is directly heard (*pratyakṣaśruta*) and that which is inferential (*ānumānika*).
Of these two, the inferential will be explained below.
Now, however, that which is directly heard [in the scripture] is being considered:
there is a one-day sacrifice named *iṣu*, and another called *śyena*;
both of these are employed for malevolent purposes (*ābhicārika*).
In that context, having prescribed certain dharmas, [the text] says: "The rest is the same as the Śyena.
This is now considered:
Is this a restatement (anuvāda) or an injunction (vidhi)?

If it is an injunction, then there is an extended application (*atideśa*); it extends the characteristics of the *śyena* sacrifice to the *iṣu* sacrifice. If, however, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*), then there is no such extension.
In this regard, what is the prima facie position? That is introduced by the Sūtra itself:
"Since it is the same as the preceding, there would be an injunction regarding that which has already arisen."
Furthermore, the expression "what else" is not possible in the absence [of something else];
and the word *itara* (the other) is not applicable when something is not present, for it occurs only when there is something proximate.
For example: "Let the other support be given."
When it is said, "Let another blanket be given," that which is at hand is given, not merely any cloak or merely any blanket.
And those [elements] belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are what are at hand;
therefore, the discussion concerns them.
And this is their restatement:
"For they are prescribed by the *codaka*," if it is argued that [this applies] to the *śyena*.
If you think this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the elements belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma,
it is not so; rather,
it is an injunction (*vidhi*) of the specific characteristics of the Śyena sacrifice, such as the red turban and other such attributes.
Why?
Because of the force of the mention of the *śyena*.
In this way, the mention of the *śyena* will be purposeful, by qualifying the ritual details (*dharma*).
Otherwise, it would be meaningless;
for those [rites] are common to all one-day sacrifices (ekāha), multi-day sacrifices (ahīna), and sacrificial sessions (sattra).
In that case, just as it would be stated, "the rest is the same," so too [it would be understood that] "the rest is the same as the Śyena."
Not because of non-proximity.
This doctrine of the Śyenavaiśeṣikas is not tenable.
Why?
Because of non-proximity.
This word "other" (itara) applies to what is proximate, and the Vaiśeṣikas are not proximate to the word "hawk" (śyena).
As for the claim that the word "hawk" is a Vaiśeṣika term, if it were an injunction (vidhi), its lack of specificity (avaśeṣikatva) would be a defect;
however, under the view of a restatement (anuvāda), nothing at all is being enjoined—so what could it qualify?
Since the elements belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma are common to all [sacrifices], it is appropriate that they are restated as belonging to the Śyena as well;
therefore, this is indeed a restatement of those very elements belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Alternatively, if—on account of its being a new injunction (apūrva)—the other [Śyena] were for a different purpose, then the term expressive of that [Jyotiṣṭoma] would be identical [to the one used here].
The phrase "or rather" (*api vā*) indicates the adoption of an alternative position.
This is an injunction for the Śyena-specific [rites], whereas it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Why?
Because it is unprecedented;
thus it will enjoin an unprecedented matter,
and in that way it will produce a specific mode of activity.
Being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), it would be purposeless as it does not produce any specific activity.
[Objection: But this word "other" (*itara*) refers to what is proximate.
[Reply: It is said in response: "other" has the sense of "additional"; thus, "the same other" means "the same plus something additional."
[Objection: But surely this [term] denotes only what is proximate, and does not have an additional meaning.
[Reply: It is said: it is not merely denotative of the proximate;
it also expresses that which is not proximate, provided it is similar to what was previously mentioned.
And as for the remainder:

when the word *itarat* (the other) is employed after a sequence of garments—such as "Let a woolen blanket be given to Devadatta, silk to Viṣṇumitra, linen to Yajñadatta, and the other [item] to Caitra"—then only a garment is given, not gold or silver.
Here, after enumerating the ritual duties (*dharma*) that exceed those pertaining to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the word *itarat* is employed.
Therefore, even here he ought to state only what is additional;
thus he becomes one who speaks of the additional.
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the Vaiśvadeva offerings—the oblations beginning with those for Agni—have been prescribed along with their explanatory passages (arthavādas).

And their specific ritual details (*dharmas*) have been stated. Having prescribed the sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) exclusively for the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, the explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*) belonging to the Vaiśvadeva section is extended (*atidiśyate*) to them by the statement: "These five oblations have these very [Vaiśvadeva] explanatory passages; those others have [their own] explanatory passages. In this regard, does this extension apply merely to the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), or to the entire section (*kāṇḍa*) including both the explanatory passage and the injunction (*vidhi*)?
But how can there be an extension (*atideśa*) of a mere explanatory statement (*arthavāda*)?
For example: "And the trees are like the Pampā nest.
What, then, are injunctions (*vidhi*), and what are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*)?

The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is tied in three bundles, the fuel-stick (*idhma*) is tied in three bundles, there are nine *prayāja* offerings and nine *anuyāja* offerings—such are the injunctions (*vidhi*).
"These oblations are slayers of enemies" (*vārtaghnāni*)—such are the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
Regarding this, it is said:
In the five *saṃcaras*, there is an extension by way of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) because of proximity.
Moreover, even in the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, some of the Vaiśvadeva ritual properties are prescribed, such as, "They churn the fire; there are *prasū* plants.

If the injunctions themselves were extended by analogy (*atideśa*), the restatement of those [properties] already established by that extension would be purposeless. Therefore, it is the specific details that are extended.
Therefore, there is an extension of the explanatory passage (arthavāda),
because everything possesses a single word-meaning.
This is not so; it is not merely the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that is extended, but rather the entire section (*kāṇḍa*), including the injunctions and the explanatory passages. Why?
"Because of the identity of the word" means because of the commonality of the word;
this word "Brāhmaṇa" is the same for both the injunctions (vidhi) and the explanatory passages (arthavāda).
If he grasps the explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) as they are, and likewise grasps the injunctions (*vidhi*), he extends those [injunctions] by analogy as well.
As for the claim that there is no connection between the injunctions and the sacrificial offerings (*havir*):
although there is no relationship of the enjoiner and the enjoined, there will be a relationship characterized by mutual assistance (*upakāra*).
What is the benefit?
It is that which ordains their constituent parts.
If there is such a connection, then it is logical that by the direct audition of the word "Brāhmaṇa," there should be an extension of all [details].
And because of the observation of indicative marks.
And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) demonstrates the extension (*atideśa*) of the injunctions.
What is the indicative mark?

In the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, it says: "They offer thirty oblations of whey (*vājina*) for the fulfillment of the oblations and for the sake of reaching the number thirty. Thus, it shows thirty oblations in the Varuṇapraghāsa.
If the injunctions were not extended [by analogy], they would not exist;
therefore, they are extended.
If it is argued that this is not so because they are already prescribed in the original recitation—
Regarding what was stated, namely "because of the prescribed traditional teaching," what is the rebuttal? The sūtra ends with the word "ābhāṣa. [The answer is:
No, because it serves another purpose.
To this it is replied: even though there is an extension of the injunction (*vidhyatideśa*), the mention of the churning of the fire and so forth is not purposeless;
it will serve the purpose of the other oblation, namely the *mārutī* offering belonging to the southern sacrificial enclosure.
Therefore, this is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no extension of the injunctions.
And the same applies to the Ekakapāla and the Aindrāgna offerings.

In the Vaiśvadeva [parvan], a cake on one potsherd (ekakapāla) is prescribed for Viśvedevas, and a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth; likewise, in the Varuṇapraghāsas, there is a cake on one potsherd for Ka.
Furthermore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, and curdled milk (āmikṣā) for the Maruts.

Similarly, in the Sākamedhas, two cakes on one potsherd for Indra and Agni are prescribed: a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, an oblation of boiled rice (caru) for Indra the slayer of Vṛtra, and a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.
In this regard, it is traditionally taught:
"O Brahmin, this is the offering to Indra and Agni; O Brahmin, this is the one-potsherd offering; O Brahmin, as for the others and the rest [of the offerings].
To this it is said: the one-potsherd and the offering to Indra and Agni are like that, just as the five *saṃcara* offerings are.
Here too, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the section (*kāṇḍa*) together with its rules and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).
It is by that very same principle;
this is a *prāptisūtra* for the purpose of the subsequent deliberation.

The model for the cakes baked on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) in the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice is that of the *Vaiśvadeva*, because in the *Avabhṛtha* we observe the non-transference of the entire oblation and because there is an explicit injunction for a single double-portion (*sakṛd dvyavadāna*).

In the Sākamedha sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "This [cake] on one potsherd is for the Brāhmaṇa. Regarding this, it is considered: does this refer to the cake on one potsherd belonging to the Vaiśvadeva section, or to that belonging to the Vāruṇapraghāsika section? What is the prima facie view?
We say that this refers to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
What is the reason?

Because its specific rules have been prescribed: "Having adorned [the sacrificer] and having filled [the vessels], he should sacrifice in a low voice (upāṃśu)," "The back [of the altar] should be made manifest," and so forth.
However, the Vāruṇapraghāsika [rite] is devoid of specific ritual rules (adharmaka).
It is only where rules have been prescribed that it is appropriate to say, "This should be done in the same manner as that.
Therefore, the Vaiśvadevika [rite] is what is being referred to.
[Objection: But surely, because of the joint recitation with the offering to Indra and Agni, the single potsherd cake (*ekakapāla*) should also belong specifically to the Vāruṇapraghāsa sacrifice.

[Reply: No; it is not necessary that the joint recitation must occur only between two offerings belonging to the same *parvan* (section of the sacrifice), for joint recitation is not incompatible even when they belong to different *parvans*.
Therefore, the reference is to the one belonging to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
The application of the word "Sāman" should be according to the usage of the learned, by means of its denotative term.
This is heard [in the scriptures]: "He sings the Rathantara on the two following verses," "He sings the Rathantara on the Kavatī verses," and so forth; these are recorded in the Samhitā.
In this regard, there arises the inquiry: what is it that is extended by way of analogy (atidiśyate) here?
Is it not the case that whatever is expressed by the words "Rathantara" and so forth is what is extended?
"Certainly;
however, it is not known what exactly is expressed by these words.
Is it not already established that the designation 'Sāman' applies to the songs?"
In that case, an objection will be raised against what has already been established;
yet that very [objection] shall be the final determination.
If that itself is the final determination, for what purpose is the objection?
It is for the sake of firmness, like the driving in of a pillar.
In this regard, what is the conclusion?

It is stated: the term *sāman* is used by experts as a designation for that song (*gīti*) performed upon a *ṛc* verse that possesses *hiṅkāra*, *praṇava*, *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*, and which involves modifications through *stobha*, accent (*svara*), and repetition (*abhyāsa*).
Therefore, there is doubt.
Furthermore, because of the difference in names;
for there is a difference in names, such as "Rathantara," "Bṛhat," and so forth.
Because the activity of conditioning is unitary, it would be purposeless;
for in that case, a single [moment] alone would suffice,
just as in the case of a melody.
Now, as for the names of the *ṛc*s: since they are distinct from them, it is logical that their designations should be separate.

Furthermore, if the *rathantara* were the singing and the *bṛhat* were also the singing, then the application of distinct designations such as "this is the *rathantara*" and "this is the *bṛhat*" would not be possible.
But it is appropriate [to consider them] as having the name *ṛc*.
Furthermore, because of the distinctness of the modification (*vikāra*);
for with each *sāman*, there is a distinct modification.
Furthermore, a distinction in modification is observed in each individual *sāman*; this would be untenable if the singing were a single entity,
for it is only when there is a difference in the formative processes (*saṃskāra*) that a distinction in modification is seen.
For example, the state of being rice-grains results from threshing, and powder results from grinding;
however, for a single thing, there is neither the state of being rice-grains nor the state of being powder. These are merely names for various stages.
Therefore, due to the distinction between the *ṛcs*, the diversity of their modifications is logical; thus, they are called by the name "Ṛk.
To this, he recites the subsequent [sūtra]: "The application [of the name] to the *Sāman* should be according to the designation, as is traditionally taught."
The application of the word for the *sāman* should proceed according to what has been taught;
that which has been taught by the instructors to their disciples. And what, moreover, has been taught?
The *ṛc* distinguished by its *stoma* and other attributes is the *sāman*; it would thus proceed [as such]. What is the reason? Because "Rathantara" and so forth are its names.
But because words enjoin a purpose, there would be no application to another purpose; for the connection [of the word] is indeed with the action, due to its distinct nature.
Or, if there were a purpose for the action in its own right, then [the details] would be taught as being subordinate members (aṅga) of that action.
Or, if they were functioning for their own sake, the *abhivatīs* would be taught as being subordinate (*aṅga*) to the *kavatīs*.

But how can subordination to the *kavatīs* be taught in the phrase "he sings in the *kavatīs*"? It can be taught, just as in the case of: "With whatever rite one desires to prosper, there one should offer the *jayā* oblations."
But what is the purpose of the *abhivatīs* effecting the displacement of the *kavatīs*?
It is said: an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*) must be postulated. Why?

[This refers] to the action, because an action is heard [in the text]: "One sings the Rathantara on the Kavatī verses. Just as there is a purpose for the Prayāja offerings and so forth, [one might argue there is one] for the action.
It is replied: this very point is the flaw in this position, namely, that a purpose for the action must be postulated.
Therefore, this position as well is untenable.
If it is argued that it is merely sound, [we reply: no.
Because it is not produced.
This doctrine is worse than the former one.
Why?
Because it is innate.
For the relationship between a name and its object is innate;
whatever word is established by an innate relationship with a particular object,
it is incapable of conveying anything other than that.
For indeed, a horse cannot be denoted by the word "cow," and if it were so,
the treatise would be rendered meaningless.

And this being the case, the rule of extension (*atideśa-śāstra*) would be purposeless, because its object would be impossible to achieve. Therefore, it is not logical that there should be an application of the word [to the *gāna*] either.
However, the author of the *Vṛtti* thought that the science of chanting (*gāna-śāstra*), known as the *Aukthikya*, would otherwise be rendered useless.
His intention is this: when a way [to explain] exists, it is not right to assume that such great effort on the part of the learned is fruitless.
[If you say: "It is for the sake of the accent (svara)."
It is not the case that there is no connection with the Vedic revelation because of the absence of an object.
This is not so; there is no extension of the accent.
Why?
Because of the absence of meaning, that is, because the referent is absent.
Because the *abhivatī* verses do not exist within the *kavatī* verses, [one might object]:
"But surely that [quality] which is non-existent is brought into being through extension (*atideśa*). It is replied: even to bring it into being is impossible.
For it is not possible to bring about the sound that manifests the syllables within the *kavatī* verses;
if it were brought about, they would no longer be *kavatī*s.
And if it is not brought about, it has not come into being.
In the scriptural injunction "He sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses," there would be no connection with other words [of the verse];
therefore, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of the accent.
Rather, the accent should belong to the original productions (*utpatti*), because it is inseparable from the measure and the phonemes.
The word "tu" (but) serves to introduce an alternative position.
If the application of the *abhivatī* melody to the *kavatī* verses is not tenable, let it be a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in the injunction: "He sings the *rathantara* on the *kavatī* verses.
How so?

To this it is said: regarding the sentence "He sings the Rathantara on the Kavatī verses," there are two possible modes of expression. One is: "That which is the Rathantara, he sings it on the Kavatī verses"; the other is: "That which is the Rathantara, he sings it on the Kavatī verses. (The first mode is: "On the Kavatīs, that which is the Rathantara, that he sings. [Correction: The intended distinction is: One is: "On the Kavatīs, that which is the Rathantara, that he sings"; the other is: "The Rathantara, that which it is, he sings on the Kavatīs."
Of those two, that which is the second— namely, "he sings the Rathantara upon the Kavatī verses"—
is impossible if the Sāman consists of musical pitch (svara), as it has already been stated;
for it is not possible to superimpose the pitch of the Abhivatīs onto the Kavatīs.
But the former [interpretation] is possible:
"He sings the Rathantara which is in the Kavatī verses.
This is also because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga).
And an indicative mark (liṅga) is seen in this matter:
"The Rathantara [sāman] is in the two later [verses].
What is that indicative mark?
Thus he said: "I do not see the *rathantara* in the two following [verses]," and Viśvāmitra performed austerities; likewise, Vasiṣṭha said, "I do not see the *bṛhat* in the two following [verses].
Effort is made for the perception of that which exists but is not seen, just as one makes a lamp when saying, "I do not see the jar," but not when saying, "I do not see the horn of a hare."
Therefore, the Rathantara and the Bṛhat exist in the two later [verses];
these are restatements (anuvāda) of them.
However, since no modification is heard in the case of the later verses, they remain according to what is heard in the scripture.
And there would be an inconsistency regarding words.
Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency regarding the application of the terms *sāman*, such as *rathantara* and others, in the injunctions:
"The *rathantara* [is sung] on the two following verses," and "The *bṛhat* [is sung] on the two following verses.
How so?
