To this it is replied: these terms "Rathantara" or "Bṛhat" are applied to a specific collection of notes (svara) when that collection of notes constitutes a *sāman* and is established in a fixed sequence;
they become inappropriate when applied to a single part or when the sequence is altered.
Therefore, this [objection] is not tenable.
The word *sāman* refers to the tone (*svara*), and this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that.
To this, he replies: "In this way, you have refuted all possible positions;
what follows from that? Is it simply non-occurrence?"

It is said: let there be a prescription (*pradeśa*) for the *ṛc* itself. But was it not stated that it is not possible to prescribe one *ṛc* in place of another *ṛc*? Certainly; in that case, it will be a designation by way of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*).

It is said, "One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses. However, it is not possible to sing the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses [in their literal sense]. Therefore, there is an indication of location (*deśalakṣaṇā*), meaning "the location of the *kavatī* verses."
For example, as in "he stands in the fire" or "he stands in the well";
or it may be a characteristic of the ritual element (*dharma-lakṣaṇā*),
whereby the properties of the *rathantara* are extended by the word *rathantara* to the *kavatī* verses.
For example: "While the Rathantara is being chanted, one should meditate upon the earth with the mind," and so forth;
or, when the teacher has gone abroad, the service due to the teacher is extended to the teacher’s wife by the injunction, "The teacher’s wife is your teacher.

However, this should be a word denoting an action (*karmaśabda*), as its meaning is the performance of the act, because it adopts the conventional sense; for the modification is not distinct from others.
Furthermore, because it is understood according to its conventional usage:
this word "he sings" (gāyati) is well-established in the sense of the act of singing.
What, then, is that? It is a particular kind of vocal utterance.
"One who sings" means one who performs singing; and the words "rathantara" and so forth are used in the sense of grasping that [singing]. This is the meaning:
because of its being uttered by that [word], and because of the force of the accusative case.
For example, one says "he sings the *āsāritaka*" or "he sings the *vardhamānaka*.
But surely there is also utterance by means of the word itself, as in "he sings a *gāthā*" or "he sings a *ṛc*"?

True; however, having modified the word so that it means "he embellishes the *ṛc* with singing," it does not connect with the literal sense of the expression "he performs singing" [as applied] to the *ṛc*.
Therefore, it denotes singing.
For this reason as well, it denotes singing.
Why?
For modification is not distinct from other things;
and here a modification of the substance of sound is observed:
the lengthening of short syllables and the shortening of long ones.
The opening of what was closed and the closing of what was open—
that is no different from other conditioned activities (saṃskārakarma),
just as rice grains become rice-powder by threshing, or rice-flour is produced from rice-grains by grinding.
Therefore, the refinement of sounds known as "singing" (gāna) is expressed by words such as *rathantara* and so forth;
this is an injunction regarding that [refinement], such as "one sings the *rathantara* on the two [verses] beginning with *uttare*" and so on.
Furthermore, it is observed to be non-substantial (*adravya*).
Now, it was indeed argued that if they were merely preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarman*), their performance at a time when they are not [actually] employed would be purposeless. To this we reply:

their performance is for the sake of grasping the action, because they take on various forms with respect to diverse purposes; for their purpose is non-worldly (*alaukika*) due to being prescribed [by scripture].
Its purpose at the time of ritual action is for the sake of grasping [the text], in order to learn and practice it.

Regarding "in various meanings" (*nānārtheṣu*), this means in meanings that have become manifold—that is, distinct—because they possess diverse forms due to differences in their substrata; thus, that singing becomes of various forms.
Therefore, it must be learned and practiced verse by verse for the sake of achieving fluency in performance.
It is like a chariot-racer on the ground; for example, a chariot-racer practices by drawing a chariot on the ground.
That practice brings ease to him at the time of actual performance.
For the meaning of these names, such as *rathantara* and so forth, is not established through worldly convention, unlike [the meanings of] words such as *vahanti* (carrying).
Why?
Because of the injunction; for this is enjoined through the relationship between pupil and teacher, stating that "the Rathantara is of such a form."
The worldly [usage] is not understood;
therefore, this objection—that it is because of the application [of the term] at a time when there is no action—is not valid.
Furthermore, as for what was said, "because of the distinctness of the designation":
To this it is replied: there would be specific designations for those [atoms] due to the distinctness of their modifications.
And those which are prescribed in a systematic manner as being equal to the others.
That which is both a source (*yoni*) and praiseworthy (*śasya*) is "praiseworthy as a source" (*yoniśasya*).
Discussions concerning what is praiseworthy as a source are treated as equivalent to other discussions concerning what is not praiseworthy as a source, as in the following:
"He recites the *yāmī* verses; he recites the verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa*; he recites the source of the *rathantara*; he recites the source of the *bṛhat*."
What is the similarity there?
It is the designation by means of the word *śaṃsati*.
Here, although these two words, *stauti* and *śaṃsati*, share the same purpose of praising, they have distinct domains of application.

The word *stauti* (he praises) is used for mantra-texts that are chanted (*pragīta*), while the word *śaṃsati* (he recites) is used for those that are not chanted (*apragīta*), as in "he recites the *praüga*" and "he recites the *niṣkevalya*.
[Conversely,] we have "they praise with the *ājya* hymns" and "they praise with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns.
Therefore, because it is enjoined by the word *śaṃsati*, it shows that the unchanted *ṛc* is the source (*yoni*) of the *rathantara*.

And if the *rathantara* is the melody (*gīti*), then its source (*yoni*) is the unchanted *ṛc*; otherwise, this designation—"the source of the *rathantara*"—would not be logical. Therefore, the name "Sāman" applies to the melodies.
And even in what is not a womb, that which is non-womblike is seen.
If it is argued that there is no dissimilarity when there is identity of meaning;
Regarding what was said— that its function is for the purpose of apprehension—
it is there objected:
"If there is identity of referent, there can be no dissimilarity."
The chanting of the *bṛhat* is a different matter from the chanting of the *rathantara*.

Therefore, when the chanting of the *rathantara* has been mastered, the chanting of the *bṛhat* remains unmastered; thus, it is appropriate that the *bṛhat* be practiced outside of the ritual time for the sake of training once the *rathantara* has been grasped.
However, the chanting of the *rathantara* has but a single purpose.
Once one has mastered the application [of the *sāman*] in its primary form (*yoni*), one need not train further in the subsequent forms;
for in those cases, an application at a time other than the performance of the ritual action would not be appropriate as a constituent part of the rite (*saṃskārakarma*).
Therefore, when the proposition that "the word *sāman* does not denote a constituent part" has been established, he challenges it with a Sūtra.
It might be so because [the property] is not established in other objects, as in the case of cooking.
And there is the consistency of words.
And in this way, there is consistency between the word *sāman* and the word *ṛc*:
in the injunction "he sings the Rathantara upon the *kavatī* verses," the word *kavatī* will denote the *ṛc* itself, and the word *Rathantara* will denote the *sāman*.
Otherwise, there would have to be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a location within the word *kavatī*.
Or rather, in the word *rathantara*, there is a definition by characteristic (*dharmalakṣaṇā*).
Therefore, the word *sāman* refers to the chant (*gīti*).
It has been stated that when the [name] denotes an action, upon hearing it elsewhere, there would be the extension of its properties (*dharmapradeśa*).
Or rather, it applies even to the *apūrva*, because of its participation [in the result].
The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of "viparyāsa" (reversal).
The meaning of "api vā" is:

"Alternatively, both of these actions may be original (apūrva); the *juhoti* sacrifice of the Kauṇḍapāyinas' session is not preceded by the obligatory [New and Full Moon sacrifices], and the name is common to both."
Why?
Because it shares in the designation; this *juhoti* also shares in the name of that [sacrifice].

Just as there is the simultaneous utterance [of the word *agnihotram*] in the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra," so it is here as well. Since the simultaneous utterance is equal in both cases, there is no specific reason why this name belongs to that one alone and not to this one; therefore, the name is common to both, and there is no partial application of the ritual rules (*dharmapradeśa*).
This is not tenable.
Why?
Because the name is innate.
For the relationship between a name and its referent is innate.
Whatever name is well-established for a particular object through an innate relationship, it should always be understood as referring to that very object and not to anything else.
If such a fixed rule did not exist, there would be no confidence in the meaning of words.
It has been stated that it is illogical for a word to have multiple meanings.
And when it does not denote both meanings, then it first expresses the obligatory sense;
since the application of the word is also appropriate in the other case for the purpose of prescribing similarity to that [obligatory sense], there is no reason for it to denote the other meaning.
Therefore, there would be an extension of the injunction;
because of the direct connection with the quality, there would be the denotation of the action, whereas in its absence, it would remain unestablished.

In the obligatory *agnihotra*, there is a direct connection with subsidiary elements (*guṇasaṃyoga*); there are duties (*dharma*) prescribed directly: "one should milk in this manner," "one cooks in this manner," "one draws out four [ladles]," "the fuel-stick for the *agnihotra* is made of *khadira* wood," and "one offers the oblation in this manner. Thus, because of this direct connection with subsidiary elements, that name of the obligatory rite being employed here would denote the actions such as milking and so forth; the meaning is that it serves as an indicator of the ritual duties (*dharmapradeśaka*).
Furthermore, for this act of offering (*juhoti*), there are no specific ritual properties (*dharma*).
In the absence of that—that is, in the absence of those properties—it would be unestablished; it would not be understood for what purpose the word "Agnihotra" is employed here.
Or rather, [it would be unestablished] in this way.
The connection with a quality is directly perceived, as is the regular connection with a substance and a deity:
"He offers with curd," "He offers with milk," and "He offers in the evening to Agni and Prajāpati.
From this direct connection with a quality, there must be a designation of the action.
The name of the action is thus: "The oblation known as the *agnihotra* is of such a form.
Otherwise, there would be no form for that other [action] called *juhoti*; in its absence, it would be unestablished and not known—what kind of thing that *agnihotra* is.
[Objection: "But surely the month will be its form.
[Reply: No; the month is a constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*), whereas that [month] is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*).
Moreover, the Agnihotra is enjoined in reference to the month; the Agnihotra is not defined by the month.
Therefore, this is the name of that which is fixed; in other cases, there is an extension (atideśa) of it accordingly.
Is this the general rule—that every ritual name, when heard elsewhere, is a receiver of ritual properties (dharmas)?
Indeed, such is the position reached.
This being the case, the following is undertaken:
"Or rather, this scriptural statement may be for the purpose of a subordinate quality (guṇa) within the performance of the sacrificial session (satra)."
In the *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, it is heard: "The Vaiśvānara Jyotiṣṭoma becomes the opening day (*prāyaṇīyam ahar*).
However, in the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), there is a first day named the opening day, called the "opening *atirātra*.
Their distinctness is established by that very same principle: that in a different context, there is a difference in purpose.
In this regard, although this term *prāyaṇīya* is heard elsewhere as well, it does not serve to enjoin ritual details;
rather, this scriptural mention is for the purpose of [indicating] a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).
How so?

It has been stated that the name of phenomena is apprehended through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); and when the primary meaning (śrutyartha) is absent, the indicated meaning must be accepted. But here, the primary meaning itself is possible.
This word has the quality as its meaning;
by means of the quality, that is, through connection with the action,
it is employed in that object by direct Vedic statement itself.
It is called *prāyaṇīya* because by means of it they go forth (*prayanti*), or because by means of it the sacrificial session (*satra*) proceeds.
And the remainder of the sentence expresses this very meaning: "He places light itself in front.
The sense is that by which the *jyotis* becomes the *prāyaṇīya*, by that light is placed in front; thus, "he places light itself in front."
Therefore, this is not an extension (atideśa).

In the Viśvajit sacrifice where all the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed, the *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma exist because it is preceded by that [sacrifice], and the word *pṛṣṭha* is indeed present there.
Or rather, [the rule applies] from the six-day period, for in that case there are specific injunctions.
This is not a restatement; what then? It is an injunction.

A restatement (anuvāda) that does not produce a specific activity would be purposeless. Furthermore, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is no plurality of *pṛṣṭha* chants for which this could be a restatement;
however, such plurality exists in the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*).
For there are indeed injunctions such as, "The Rathantara becomes the Pṛṣṭha-stotra of the Pṛṣṭhas," and so forth.
Therefore, this is a rule that extends [the application] of the elements belonging to the six-day sacrifice (ṣāḍaha).
And this is also because of an indicative mark (liṅga).
And this indicative mark (liṅga) demonstrates this meaning:

"In the Pavamāna [stotra] one performs the Rathantara; in the Ārbhava, the Bṛhat; in the middle, the others; the Vairūpa is the Sāman of the Hotṛ; the Vairāja of the Maitrāvaruṇa; the Raivata of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the Śākvara of the Acchāvāka. This sentence, which concerns their specific placement, shows that the Pṛṣṭha-stotras belong to the six-day sacrifice (ṣāḍaha). The Jyotiṣṭoma, however, has the status of being already established.
Because of the presence of the indicative mark (*liṅga*),
it is understood that "one [hymn] there is the *pṛṣṭha* hymn for Mahendra.
Furthermore, the status of being a *pṛṣṭha* is known to belong to those [hymns] belonging to the six-day rite (*ṣāḍaha*).
How so?
For in that context it is said, "it is an injunction";
in their doctrine, the Vedic meaning of the word *pṛṣṭha* is thus accepted.
Otherwise, it would be figurative (lākṣaṇika).
Therefore, it is a reference to the elements belonging to the six-day rite (ṣāḍahika).
If it is argued that this is an injunction for both:
If you think that this is the injunction for the *pṛṣṭha* chants belonging to the six-day period,
that is not correct.
What is the reason?
In this way, the word "pṛṣṭha" is accepted as having a dual function: it both prescribes the *pṛṣṭhas* and establishes their universality (*sarvatva*). Let it be so; what is the fault?
He says: "It is impossible.
If the word *pṛṣṭha* enjoins the *pṛṣṭhas*, it cannot be qualified by the word *sarva*. But if it restates them, then it can be so qualified.
But the *pṛṣṭha* chants are not prescribed;
in their absence, for what would this "completeness" (*sarvatva*) be enjoined?
Furthermore, the performance of both [the *pṛṣṭhas* and the *stotras*] together is impossible.

Now, if it were the case that *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are obtained here as optional alternatives and only their simultaneous performance (*sāmastya*) is enjoined by the statement "it is *sarvapṛṣṭha*," meaning both *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are used and not just one,
then this fault would not arise.
Therefore, both [the teacher and the student] have the qualification;
it is not the case that [the student alone does], because the word "all" would otherwise be rendered meaningless.
Likewise, the avabhṛtha bath follows from the Soma sacrifice.
In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, it is heard in the scripture: "They go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the scrapings of the vessel for Varuṇa and with the husks.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the husks-and-scrapings mixture prescribed for the pouring out of water in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, or is there an extension of the ritual details from the Soma sacrifice's avabhṛtha?
What is the correct position?
This is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapūrṇamāsika*).
In this way, the cognition of what is proximate is upheld;
for that [proximate sacrifice] has been brought forward by the extended application (*codaka*).
[Objection: But surely that is not the *avabhṛtha* [concluding bath].
[Response: It is said: the word *avabhṛtha* does exist there;
for it is said, "This indeed is the *avabhṛtha* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

This being the case, it is said: just as there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants from the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) to the *avabhṛtha* following the Soma sacrifice, so too here there is an extension of ritual properties (*dharma*) from the *saumika-avabhṛtha*. Why? Because [the *avabhṛtha*] is similar to the Soma sacrifice.
The principle has been stated: it was said that when a verbal root is heard elsewhere, there should be an extension of the injunction;
if it is argued that this applies to the base form (*prakṛti*).

Now, as for what was said—that there might be an injunction regarding a subordinate element (guṇavidhi) in the *avabhṛtha* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices—the sūtra ending with the introductory phrase "What is the refutation of that? states: "It is not so, because it is figurative."
"Let this also be the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
"This is not correct; for it is illogical that a single term should have multiple meanings."
How, then, is the application of words [to them] possible?
Through similarity. What is this similarity?
The connection with water is this:
it is a figurative expression of praise for the sprinkling of water, saying "this is like the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath)," just as one speaks of a son in reference to a mango tree.
Therefore, there is no *avabhṛtha* in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
Therefore, there is no injunction of a subordinate quality here;
this is also because of the observation of an indicative mark.
And this indicative mark (liṅga) demonstrates this meaning. What is the indicative mark?
It says as follows: "He does not offer the āyurdā oblation, he does not sing the Sāman, nor does he mutter the mantra for departing."
By stating the prohibition of the ritual details (*dharma*) pertaining to the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice, [the text] indicates that those details are applicable [here].
Therefore, there is an extension of the ritual details from the Soma-related *avabhṛtha*.

When there is a specific mention of a substance, it should consist of that substance because of its connection with the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*); however, in the absence of such a mention, it should consist of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), because that is the original material (*prakṛti*).
The *avabhṛtha* of the *Vāruṇapraghāsas* is rightly considered a recipient of the ritual characteristics (*dharma*) from the *avabhṛtha* of the Soma sacrifice.

In this regard, the following is deliberated: is this [rite] one whose substance is the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), or is its substance the husks and scrapings? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
"It has the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) as its substance.
Why? Because the sacrificial cake is obtained by means of its name.
But is it not the case that the removal of the husks is directly heard in the scripture?
True, it is directly heard; however, it cannot be enjoined here.
Rather, the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is what is enjoined here, as in the statement, "they go to the *avabhṛtha*."
If, however, the removal of the husks were enjoined as something separate, then there would be a syntactical split (vākya-bheda) [between the injunctions]:
"They go to the final bath (avabhṛtha)" and "that [they do] by means of the removal of the husks.
What, then, is the purpose of the mention of the removal of the husks at this point?
"It would be purposeless because there is no connection.
This being the position reached, we reply: "In the case of a substitution of a substance, it is that very substance [that is used].
Regarding this substitution of a substance, [the text says]: "They go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the husks and the scrapings."
It would have that as its substance—namely, the substance for removing the husks.
Why?

Because of the connection with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); the removal of the husks is directly heard in the scripture, whereas the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is inferential, being obtained through extended application (*atideśa*).

In the *Ātithya* sacrifice, it is heard: "There is a cake on nine potsherds for Viṣṇu. Likewise, in the *Rājasūya*, regarding the first *Trisaṃyukta* [rite], it is said: "There is a cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu.

In this regard, there is an inquiry: Is this word *vaiṣṇava*—found in the injunction "the cake on three potsherds for Viṣṇu" in the *Trisaṃyukta*—a receiver (*grāhaka*) of the ritual details (*dharma*) of the *Ātithya*, or not?
What is correct?
That it is the "grasper.
Why?

It has been stated that a word observed in an action characterized by prescribed properties (vihitadharma) is understood as denoting [the same action] when heard in another context where those properties are not prescribed; it was also stated that this constitutes the expression of the action itself.

In that regard, this [word *ātithya*] was observed in the *ātithya* rite, which possesses prescribed properties; now, however, it is seen in the *triṣaṃyukta* rite, which does not possess those prescribed properties.
Therefore, [the opponent argues] that it is the apprehender of the qualities.
This being the case, we reply:
but it would not be a prescription of qualities, because of their equality.
This is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*).
It enjoins the connection with Viṣṇu as the deity as a subordinate element of the *ātithyeṣṭi*.
This [injunction] is not capable of assuming the ritual properties (*dharma*).
Why?
Because they are equal; for this [offering] is the same in the case of hospitality as it is when associated with the three [times].
Just as it prescribes Viṣṇu as the deity there, so it does here as well.

Furthermore, because the literal meaning of the Vedic text is impossible [in the other case], an agent who grasps the ritual properties (dharmas) is postulated through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā);
however, in this case, the injunction of a deity is possible precisely in its direct, literal sense.
Therefore, this is not a grasper;
and the same applies to cases such as fire produced by friction and so forth.
In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, it is heard: "They lead forward two fires; therefore he goes with two.

However, there is a leading forward of the fire in the Soma sacrifice which possesses ritual characteristics (dharmavat), whereas in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it lacks such characteristics (adharmaka).
In this regard, there is a doubt.
Is this carrying forward of the fire (praṇayana) related to the Soma sacrifice, or is it related to the New and Full Moon sacrifices?
On this point, the author begins with the sūtra itself:
"But the carrying forward is related to the Soma sacrifice; the other is indeed not to be mentioned."
And the prohibition of the *uttaravedi* is likewise.

"One does not prepare the *uttaravedi* for the *vaiśvadeva*, nor for the *sunāsīrīya*"; for a prohibition presupposes a prior application. And in the *saumika* (Soma) ritual, the *praṇayana* involves the *uttaravedi*, whereas it does not in the *dārśapaurṇamāsika* (New and Full Moon) ritual;
or rather, it is the archetypal (*prākṛta*) form, because [the names] do not denote [a specific modification].
This performance is either ordinary or belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa;
why?
Because it lacks a specific name.
The word "praṇayana" is not the name of the *praṇayana* belonging to the Soma sacrifice;
the meaning is that this is not its designator.
If this were its designator, then it would express that [Soma-ritual *praṇayana*] here.
This, however, is the name of the ritual act; it is the designator of the ritual act, namely, the leading forward [of the fire].
That which is a designator is capable here of expressing the leading forward of the fire toward the east, and that indeed exists here.
Therefore, it denotes that [meaning];
thus, the proximate expectancy is not sublated.
Now, as for what was said—that it will be like the word "tīrtha"—[that is addressed as follows].
To this we reply: the word *tīrtha* also denotes merely a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) itself.

However, having stated "he went on a pilgrimage" (*tīrthayātrām gataḥ*), certain specific sacred fords are enumerated; therefore, it is understood that the term refers to a meaning qualified by those [specific sites].
But where it is used alone, there it expresses merely a "ford" (tīrtha), as in:
"he bathes at a ford," or "for he becomes a ford for his equals.
Furthermore, when the direct meaning (śruti) is possible, a figurative meaning (lakṣaṇā) should not be accepted.
And in this case, the literal meaning of the Vedic text is possible;
therefore, it should not be understood as having a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇārtha*).
The scriptural statement is intended either for the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*), for the purpose of a subordinate quality (*guṇārtha*), or as a commendatory passage (*arthavāda*).
The carrying forward of the fires occurs for the first and the last [pressings], because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*.
It is heard in the scripture: "They lead forward two fires.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
which two?
Since no specific rule has been established, it is stated: the leading forward [of the fires] occurs in the first and last [sacrifices].
Why?
Because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*.
In this context, the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) is prohibited by the statements, "They do not prepare the *uttaravedi* for the Vaiśvadeva," and "Not for the Sunāsīrīya.
Since the placement of the fire upon the *uttaravedi* is prescribed for this specific carrying forward (*praṇayana*),
therefore, wherever there is a *praṇayana*, there the *uttaravedi* would otherwise be obtained [by default].
And since a prohibition occurs only when there is a possibility [of performance], and that [possibility] exists in the first and the last [days],
therefore the carrying forth [of the fire] takes place on those two days;
or rather, it takes place on the middle two days because of the explanatory passage (arthavāda) concerning the purpose of going.

Now, as for what was said— that it is because of the prohibition of the *uttaravedi*— to that we reply: the prohibition of the *auttaravedika* rite is not a general, unattached injunction (*anārabhyavāda*).

Without reference to any specific section (*parva*), the northern altar (*uttaravedi*) is prescribed for the four-monthly sacrifices (*cāturmāsya*) with the injunction: "They throw [the fire] upon it here. This prohibition is a restriction of that general rule (*anārabhyavidhi*).
But is it not the case that since this is obtained through the subsidiary injunctions (*guṇavākya*) of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, this statement—"here"—should refer to those alone?

This is not so; because of the context, it refers only to the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. If this were a statement regarding the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, then in that prohibition, one would have mentioned all three seasonal festivals. Or, if it were argued: "Let it be a statement regarding two of the festivals."
To this we reply: there is no *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for two *parvan*s, nor for the *Cāturmāsya*s as a whole, nor for the *Varuṇapraghāsa*s.
If there were a *prakaraṇa* for the *Varuṇapraghāsa*s, then the mention of two *parvan*s would be purposeless in the context of the prohibition.
Therefore, this is indeed a statement regarding the *Cāturmāsya*s themselves.
But even so, this is already known from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that the two middle [fires] are carried forward;
for what purpose is there a repeated hearing of the carrying forward (*praṇayana*) which has already been established?
No specific purpose has been stated in this regard.
Since there is no other purpose, this [statement] serves solely for the sake of exclusion (parisaṅkhyā),
and the faults in that regard have already been stated;
therefore, this hearing [of the text] is indeed for the sake of a specific quality (guṇa).
[Objection: But surely there is no merit [in this].
[Response: It is said that a merit is indeed heard; namely, the placing of the fire upon the *uttaravedi*.
Therefore, the repetition of the scriptural statement is for that purpose.
The *svarasāman*, the one-pot-sherd cake, and the curdled milk (*āmikṣā*) [are to be performed] because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*).

Likewise, regarding the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, after prescribing the one-potsherd offering to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivya*), the text says: "In that he performs the complete oblation (*sarvahuta*), that is one point of criticism; in that each oblation turns back [from the fire], that is the second. In this sentence, which is primarily intended as an injunction regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*), it shows that the two characteristics of the *vaiśvadeva*—namely, the complete oblation and the non-turning back—are understood to apply. Similarly, regarding the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for Mitra and Varuṇa, the statement "they do not proceed with the whey (*vājina*)" indicates the application of those characteristics by prohibiting the whey-oblation and the *vaiśvadeva* ritual procedure.
From these indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is known that they are the respective apprehenders of their own properties (*dharma*).
This was stated considering the act of performance (*pratipattikarman*) to be equal to the *vājinejyā* and the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
[The opponent] says: "An indicative mark has been pointed out; but from what [source] does its application (*prāpti*) derive?"

It is said: there is an attainment through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), but the adoption of that indication is due to an indicative mark (liṅga) or because of the commonality of the injunction (codanā).
[The application occurs] due to the commonality of being *svarasāman*, the commonality of being a single-pot offering (*ekakapāla*), or the commonality of being *āmikṣā*.
Its application is established by the rule: "That which has an indicative mark [is applied] because of its connection with the purpose.
It is like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) arising from a ritual act.
In this case, when the substance is heard first, the action is understood to be implied within that substance.
How so?

Like the sacrificial post (*yūpa*); just as the word *yūpa* is based on actions such as the selection (*joṣaṇa*) and so forth, and wherever it is heard, those actions such as the selection are understood to be implied there, so it is here as well.
Or rather, form [is not perceived] because it has become entirely non-existent.
In the case of a worldly object, it would be secular, because it serves all purposes.

Regarding the *ājyadoha* chants of the Garga-trirātra sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "They praise while placing the fire nearby. In this regard, there is a doubt: should a common (laukika) fire be placed nearby, or a Vedic (vaidika) one? What is the prima facie view?
"He is Vaidika.
Why?
Because he was produced for the purpose of all ritual actions.
"Whatever actions I shall perform, and for which I am authorized"—on this basis, it might be argued that a Vedic [fire] should be deposited.
This being the position reached, it is said: "In case of doubt, the worldly [fire] should be used, because it serves all purposes.
Regarding this point of doubt—whether it be the worldly or the Vedic fire—the worldly one should be used.
Now, as for what was said— that the Vedic [mantra] arose for the purpose of all ritual acts, and therefore it should be applied here—
we reply: no, the Vedic [mantra] is not [to be used], because of the specific indication of its purpose.
The Vedic substance, fire, is not produced by the scripture;
rather, its function is specified by the scripture itself, beginning with the injunction, "One offers in the Āhavanīya.
If that [fire] were assumed to serve all purposes, this specification would be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, a worldly fire should be placed nearby;
and these [fires], while performing their respective functions, will serve all purposes.
Thus, both [principles]—the universal utility and the specific injunction—are not contradictory.
Now, why are the *dhaiṣṇā* fires not placed in proximity?
To this it is replied: because their origin is similar to that of the others.
It would be a conditioned phenomenon, because it is a word.
In the context of the Ekādaśinī sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The upaśaya becomes a sacrificial post.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
should this substance of the upaśaya undergo consecration—should the preparatory rites such as *joṣaṇa* (selection) and so forth be performed upon it—or not?
What is appropriate?
It should be consecrated;
here, the preparatory rites such as *joṣaṇā* and so forth must be performed.
Why?
Because it is that word;
this word "yūpa" (sacrificial post) is based on consecration (*saṃskāra*).
This [self] does not arise when the formative forces (saṃskāras) are non-existent;
therefore, they must be produced.
Or rather, it is by way of figurative usage (bhakti), because the qualities are designated as being the remnants of the sacrifice (yajñaśeṣa).
Or rather, they should not be performed. Why?
Because they are not remnants of a sacrifice.
These preparatory rites (saṃskāra) are performed upon this wooden post;
through this door, they will be connected with the sacrifice (yajati).
When the sacrifice is performed with an animal tied to a post thus consecrated, it brings about the transcendental result (apūrva).
Furthermore, no animal is sacrificed upon this sacrificial bed; therefore, the consecrations performed there would be purposeless.
[Objection: But surely, by the force of the scriptural statement, they will serve an invisible (transcendental) purpose.
[Reply: It is said in response: there is no such statement here that "the sacrificial post (yūpa) must be made."
This is a statement regarding the present tense.
It is heard in the context of the fire-ritual: "They worship with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns.
In this regard, it is considered: should the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *pṛṣṭhas* be performed, or not?
What, then, are these?

The general properties (*sāmānyadharma*) are the *hiṅkāra* and so forth; the specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*) are such as "when the *rathantara* is being chanted, one should meditate on the earth with the mind," and "in the *bṛhat*, the ocean," and so on.
What, first, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)?
To this he replies: first, this must be examined by us—whether this word *pṛṣṭha* denotes an action (*karman*) or a substance (*dravya*).

But is it not already established that the word *pṛṣṭha* is a name for an action, in the rule: "In a case where there is an instruction regarding a quality, the connection is with the primary [action]"?

This has already been stated in those very injunctions: "There are seventeen *pṛṣṭha* chants; the *vairūpa* is a *pṛṣṭha*, the *vairāja* is a *pṛṣṭha*. Now, regarding the statement "they worship with the *pṛṣṭhas*," this is being considered:
what, then, is appropriate here?
To this he replies:
the word "aftermath" (pṛṣṭha) may refer to the action, because it is taught as being of such a nature.
Or rather, because of the instruction regarding the designation and because of the contradiction, the word "pṛṣṭha" should apply to substances.
He said: This is not correct;

for the sense of "attending upon" (upasthāna) is established by the direct Vedic statement (śruti) through the verb *upatiṣṭhate*, while the sense of "reciting" (abhidhāna) is established by the indicative mark (liṅga) of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Nor should the direct Vedic statement (śruti) be sublated by the indicative mark (liṅga). It is replied: here the direct statement is not sublated at all;
it remains in its own primary sense, for it expresses proximity.

To express that, [the text] uses the verb *tiṣṭhati*—meaning "one should stand near the fire"—in order to bring about the act of recitation (*abhidhāna*), as indicated by the middle voice (*ātmanepada*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
[The opponent] says: even so, the mantra is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the recitation, not of the act of standing (*upatiṣṭhati*).
In that case, there would be no connection at all between the act of worship (upasthāna) and the mantra;
likewise, the co-utterance [of the mantra] in the injunction "they worship with the *pṛṣṭha* hymns" would be purposeless.
It is replied: by bringing about the denotation [of the deity], the mantra becomes the instrument (karaṇa) of the worship.
Since it accomplishes its purpose for him—
indeed, nothing is performed without a purpose—
the term *pṛṣṭha* applies only to the mantras.
If [the objection applies] to mantras, there is no acquisition (prāpti) of dharmas;
for mantras do not possess dharmas, as they are themselves devoid of dharma.
The performance of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) follows the same principle as the sacrifice (*yajati*).

Without reference to anything else, it is heard [in scripture]: "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya. In this regard, the following point has been established: that this is an injunction for a sacrifice (*yāga*), because [the root] *yajati* involves a connection with a substance, a fruit, and an enjoyer, and thus these are connected to the ritual action (*karman*).

Likewise, this has also been stated: "In the relationship between the action and the fruit, the action is subordinate (*guṇataḥ*) and the fruit is primary (*pradhānataḥ*); because there is a connection toward each respective object, the connection indeed arises from the action; therefore, it must be an instruction regarding the action."

This has also been stated in the passage beginning with "The injunction (*codanā*) is the commencement [of action]," where it is said that the sacrifice (*yajati*) accomplishes the *apūrva*, and from that *apūrva* the fruit arises at a later time.

This being the case, regarding the injunction "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya," it is understood thus: "Having produced the *apūrva* by means of the Sūrya-sacrifice, one desiring spiritual luster should accomplish spiritual luster."
He said: "If it exists in the world, then it would certainly be known.
But if it does not exist at all, how can it be known?
It is replied: "Certainly it exists—both worldly and Vedic."
The worldly [procedure] occurs in rites such as the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, while the Vedic [procedure] occurs in rites such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.

If these injunctions presuppose that [procedure] and depend upon it—[meaning] that one should accomplish the *apūrva* by means of the *saurya* sacrifice according to the procedure as it is already known—then it is logical that there is no separate injunction for the procedure;
and indeed, no [such procedure] is enjoined.
Therefore, because there is no injunction regarding the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the sacrifice (*yajati*) possesses the same status as before, meaning it has an unenjoined procedure;
that [procedure] would be worldly (*laukika*), because its application is based on what is perceived.
Now this is considered: is the procedure (itikartavyatā) unrestricted—whether worldly or Vedic—or is it only worldly, or rather Vedic?
Since there is no specific indication here, and an absence of restriction would thus follow, it is said:
that [procedure] should be worldly.
Indeed, that method for what is to be done would be worldly.
Why?
Because it proceeds from what is perceived.

For its operation is observed in various instances, such as in the *pārvaṇasthālīpāka*, the *aṣṭakācaru*, and the *āgrahāyaṇīya* rite; thus, wherever an *apūrva* is to be accomplished by means of a sacrifice, its operation is observed there.
Therefore, from this positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is understood that this [ritual procedure] is the means for the sacrifice to accomplish the *apūrva*.
And this [procedure] is indeed a sacrifice.
Therefore, for this [scripture] as well, that very same means [of knowledge] applies;
however, its distinctness from that [perception] arises from verbal testimony.
He asks: Is this the general rule—that in all cases there is worldly customary practice?
Indeed, that is how it appears to be obtained.
That being the case, we reply: "But because of a specific scriptural statement, it is different from that."

Where there is an explicit Vedic statement, there the worldly [practice] should not apply; by the force of the statement, it must be the Vedic one alone, as in the case of the Upasads and the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice.
Or rather, it should be restricted by the indicative mark (liṅga), because that mark is subordinate to it.
Or rather, the procedure (itikartavyatā) would be regulated by the indicative mark (liṅga).
Which [procedure]?
That which has the indicative mark; and the Vedic [procedure] has the indicative mark.
Therefore, it is Vedic. What, then, is the indicative mark?
Regarding the *saurya* oblation, it is heard in the scripture concerning the rice-pap: "He offers a *kṛṣṇala* at each *prayāja*."

Likewise, in the rites for Indra and Bṛhaspati, one cuts half of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and does not cut the other half; one spreads half on the altar (*vedi*) and does not spread the other half.
Similarly, in the Pitṛyajña, one chooses a Hotṛ priest who is not an *ārṣeya*.
By these indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is known that this is a Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
How so?
Because they are its qualities.
For these, such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, are indeed the qualities (*guṇa*) of the Vedic *apūrva*.
And if its procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has been set in motion, then these [subsidiary acts] exist within these rites;
thus, statements such as "At each *prayāja* offering, one offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain" become appropriate.
Therefore, the Vedic procedure should be restricted [to these].
Or rather, because it is preceded by what is improper, there may be statements that are merely constant restatements (nityānuvāda).
But surely, being a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), it would be purposeless.
What can be done with that which has no meaning?
The statement "at each *prayāja* he offers a *kṛṣṇala*" will serve as a rule for the *prayājas*.
But how, in this case, can both the *prayāja* offerings and the *kṛṣṇala* oblation be enjoined?
For in that way the sentence would be split. If that is so, then he will not mention the *prayājas*.
He will prescribe the oblation of *kṛṣṇala* beans at the *prayāja* offerings.
Since the oblation of *kṛṣṇala* beans cannot be performed when the *prayāja* offerings are absent, he will perform the *prayāja* offerings by implication.
Therefore, there is no restriction based on the Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*).
According to the reasoning already stated, this constitutes worldly duty;
furthermore, because of their mutual contradiction, the qualities should be conceived according to their actual purpose.
To this he replies: "Now, why do both procedures not operate simultaneously?
What would happen in that case?
In this way, the equal requirement for the ritual acts would not be sublated by either one."
It is said: if, in simultaneous activity, an action were performed by one [cognition] independently [of the other], the activity of the second would be contradicted.
Therefore, because their mutual activity is contradictory, there must be a conceptualization according to the actual state of affairs;
the meaning is that the activity would belong to only one of them.
How is it that there is a conceptualization of phenomena according to their actual state within a single process?
Those phenomena which have arisen during the engagement in certain activities occur here as well in those very same [activities].
Otherwise, the phenomena of the second [process] would be inconsistent with the actual state relative to the previous phenomena, because those activities would have already been accomplished.
Thus, there is a conceptualization of reality based on a single activity;
therefore, by the phrase "there should be a conceptualization of reality," it is implied that there is a single activity.
Regarding this single activity, by the very logic already stated, it is what constitutes worldly activity.

But it should be restricted because of its being a share; for qualities are denotative, and due to their connection, they are like the denotation itself, just as [the word] "dhenu" [is connected] with "kiśora."
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the previous position.
It is not the case that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is worldly;
what then?
The Vedic [text] should be restricted.
Why?
Because of its participation.
The Vedic [procedure] is also a participant in the performance;
for it too is the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) for the *apūrva*.
And since both possess equal status as participants, the Vedic procedure alone should be adopted.
Because they are the designators of the qualities.
These qualities—the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—when observed in the *saurya* and other rites, become the designators of this matter;
that is to say, they function as indicators of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) belonging to the Vedic archetype.
Why?
Because of their connection;
for these are connected to that [action] by way of being its procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Therefore, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), they cause that [name] to indicate [the ritual];
this is like the case of a designation (*abhidhāna*).

Just as the designation "Agnihotra" in the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana is the designator of a ritual action, and it brings along those properties (*dharma*) associated with that ritual—since this designation would not be applicable here if those properties were absent—it is understood that those properties exist there.

Likewise here too, it would not be logical for the mention of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth to be non-existent in the Vedic [text]; therefore, their existence there will also be understood from this [mention].
But surely, in the absence of a logical principle (*nyāya*), a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*) is no cause [for inference].
True, that is so; however, the logical principle has already been stated [in the sūtra]: "because of the sharing [of the name]."
As for the claim that "worldly practice proceeds from what is perceived," we reply:
even if it were a practice proceeding from what is perceived, nevertheless, it would be restricted by the Vedic injunction alone.
How so?

Just as a cow [is identified] by its calf—for example, "the cow whose calf is black"—even though the word *dhenu* (cow) is observed to be applied to a cow-calf, nevertheless, because it shares the commonality of being a designation, it also applies to a horse-cow; thus, by the mark of the calf, it is understood to refer to a horse-cow. Likewise here, even though the application is based on worldly observation, nevertheless, because it shares the commonality of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it is to be understood as referring to the Vedic [rite] by that mark.
Or, due to the equality of their origins, existence may occur according to one's respective capacity.
Alternatively, there is no restriction by means of gender.
Why?
Because the origins [of the words] are equal.

The originations (*utpatti*) of the ritual acts (*dharma*), such as the *prayāja*s and so forth, are equal for all of them insofar as they constitute subsidiaries (*aṅga*) to the *āgneya* and other principal rites, not as subsidiaries to one another. What follows from this? If the *anuyāja*s and so forth were the subsidiaries of the *prayāja*s and so forth, then wherever the principal rite is located, there its subsidiaries would also be; thus, by the observation of the *prayāja*s, the *anuyāja*s and so forth would be inferred. However, when these are equal in their status as principals, then by the observation of the *prayāja*s, one may at will infer either further *prayāja*s or the specific properties (*dharma*) of the *prayāja*s.
But the after-offerings (anuyāja) and so forth are not [included].
Therefore, the indicative mark (liṅga) is not determinative.
As for the statement "like the name," [that is not a valid objection].

To this we reply: that is appropriate in that case; for it has been stated there that a word denoting another, when applied to something else, extends [the properties] of those [other things]. Moreover, that is a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

"One should offer like the Agnihotra"—this, moreover, is a restatement (anuvāda). Therefore, there is no application here even of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; how much less, then, of the *anuyāja* offerings and so forth?
Therefore, the comparison "like the name" is inappropriate;
consequently, the ritual application (bhāva) should occur according to its respective scope.
Those ritual elements (dharma) which are prescribed as belonging to the scope of a particular *apūrva* should belong to that alone.

If that is the case, then let the primary injunction and origination of the rite occur through this verb "one should offer" (*nirvapet*) in the passage "one should offer the *caru* to Sūrya," and let there be the mention of the subsidiary elements.
How so?
Because a primary act being enjoined cannot be fit for any purpose if it is not accompanied by its subsidiaries.
And by means of that, there will be a determination of the specific details of the subsidiaries obtained from these indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Regarding this, it is said:
"The statement of origin and the statement of subsidiary detail are contradictory in one and the same [context]."
Or rather, the end of the injunction should proceed according to the model sacrifice, for there is an indicative mark [showing this].
Or rather, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) would apply to injunctions such as that for the *saurya* sacrifice, not worldly practices. But what is this so-called "ritual procedure"?
The end of the injunction is the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*).
Now, what is an injunction (*vidhi*)?
It is that sentence which, having been perceived, causes a person to engage in some purpose or to desist from something;
for by it, a purpose is enjoined.
Just as in common worldly usage, in the sentence "Devadatta, drive the white cow hither," the portion beginning with "drive hither" (abhyāja) and so forth is the beginning,
while the other part is the end;
likewise in the Veda, in the injunction "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," the portion beginning with the injunction is the beginning.
The concluding injunction (*vidhyanta*) also includes the entire *Pauroḍāśika* Brāhmaṇa section, excluding the primary injunction itself.
This opening injunction, when joined with that [concluding portion], impels a person toward the accomplishment of a specific transcendental result (*apūrva*).
Therefore, that [concluding portion] constitutes its end.
Likewise, "one should sacrifice with Soma" is the beginning of the injunction (*vidhyādi*);
the *Brāhmaṇa* text pertaining to the Soma sacrifice is the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*).
This is what is called the "end of the injunction."
And in these [rites] such as the Saurya and others, there is the beginning of the injunction (vidhyādi), but there is no end of the injunction (vidhyanta).
Therefore, that end of the injunction should be supplied even for these.
How so?

A statement that is incomplete may be completed either by supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or by assuming a transposition (*vyavahitakalpanā*). Between these two, assuming a transposition is superior;
for in the case of supplying an ellipsis, something not actually heard must be postulated.
In the other case, there is a connection with what has been heard [in the preceding context].

Therefore, a remote portion of the Brāhmaṇa is postulated as completing this [sentence], just as in the cases: "He sacrifices the Kapiñjala birds for the spring" and "He sacrifices the Kalaviṅka birds for the summer."
By that means, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained.
If that Brāhmaṇa passage is imagined to be within this [text], it does not exist there;
thus, it results in the fallacy of "the peacock's dance" (*mayūranṛtya*).
It is as follows: when a peacock dances, one part is revealed while another is concealed;
likewise here too, this is concealed and that is revealed.
This is not a fault.
In that case, its existence is perceived directly;
here, however, it is inferential.
And what is inferential does not subvert what is perceived directly.
In that case, it would not follow here, because it contradicts direct perception.
It might be so if there were a contradiction;
however, there is no contradiction.

In that case as well, it will apply here too; this has already been stated: "Or rather, the end of the injunction (*vidhyanta*) should proceed according to the model (*prakṛti*) when there is a scriptural injunction. It is asked: what does "according to the model" mean? He replies: the eighth [book] will establish the rule regarding the model.
"This is its archetype"—to this it is said:
"Or rather, the end of the injunction should proceed like that of the archetype.
Whichever is the archetype of that ritual action—for instance, if the Āgneya is its archetype, then [the details] proceed from the Āgneya itself.
"Whose [sacrifice] is the *agnīṣomīya*, for him [the procedure] is from the *agnīṣomīya*"; thus it is in all cases.
Now, why is a worldly (*laukika*) ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) not postulated? It is said: because there is no worldly injunction (*vidhi*), there is no ritual procedure at all.
"How can that be a mere mental construction?
He replies: "Let the worldly *itikartavyatā* (procedure) be obtained; what is the use of postulating a Vedic injunction (*vidhyanta*)?
It is said in response: "For in this case, the *itikartavyatā* is indeed Vedic, not worldly."
Why?
Because in that way, the observation of the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—such as the *prayāja* offerings—is rendered meaningful.
Since the indicative mark is the cause [of application], in the absence of such a mark, the rule would be worldly (*laukika*).
If the Vedic means is adopted because of an indicative mark (liṅga), then in the absence of such a mark, the worldly (laukika) means should be used.
In a ritual action where there is no indicative mark whatsoever, the worldly procedure should apply;
for example: "One whose kinsmen have died should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni."

Because the indicative mark (liṅga) is as before and because of the commonality of the injunctive word (codanā-śabda), it may be determined even by a single [instance], just as by the "pot-full" (sthālī-pulāka) method.
To this it is replied: this might be so if the Vedic means were based on inference;
however, it is not based on inference.
What, then, is its basis?

It is caused by the concluding injunction (*vidhyanta*). The concluding injunction, moreover, is preceded by logical reasoning (*nyāya*), and that reasoning is the same for all modified (*vaikṛta*) rites as well as those possessing indicative marks (*liṅgavat*).
Why? Because...
Because of the commonality of the word "injunction" (*codanā*). In the injunction of ritual action, the verbal form is the same;
in all cases there is the beginning of the injunction, but not the end of the injunction.
And the connection with the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) heard elsewhere is equal by virtue of its dependence [on the same principle].

Thus, this indicative mark (liṅga), when observed even in a single instance, makes known the possession of the ritual property (dharmavattā) for all those cases that share the same underlying logic (nyāya).

Just as one knows the ripeness of other grains in a pot by crushing a single sprout among them that have been cooked equally, because the cause for the ripeness of this one and of the others is the same.

Therefore, in all cases, the Vedic procedure (*itikartavyatā*) applies. Now, as for what was said—that the worldly procedure is based on observed activity—we reply: this is taught by way of general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
And that which is a *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only if it is non-deviant; however, this [inference] is deviant,
for we observe that sacrifices such as the *gaṇayāga* do not have such a procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
Therefore, "because it proceeds from what is seen" is not a valid reason.

In a multi-day sacrifice (*ahargaṇa*), that which belongs to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāhika*) [serves as the model] because it is its archetype; whereas that which belongs to the one-day rite (*aikāhika*) would bear that name due to the addition of specific elements, just like the one-day rite itself.

Having prescribed the sacrificial session (*sattra*) with the injunction, "Those desiring offspring should undertake the Gavāmayana," it is further recorded: "Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyuḥ. It will be stated that in the Gavāmayana, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is that of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), according to the principle that "for groups [of sacrifices], the twelve-day sacrifice [applies].
In that case, the duties of the twelve-day sacrifice are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*).
However, for the one-day sacrifices (*ekāha*) as well, there are their own specific duties according to their respective names.

Those elements pertaining to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) which are not in conflict with those pertaining to the one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*) are performed according to their established application.
Regarding those that are in conflict, there is doubt:
should the rule of the twelve-day sacrifice be followed, or that of the one-day sacrifice?
What is established?
In that regard, the introduction is provided by the Sūtra itself:
"That which belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice [is applied] to the group of days, because it is its archetype."
Because the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) has the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) as its archetype (*prakṛti*), [the details] are obtained through the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) alone.
There is another interpretation of the rule *adhikāgamāt tadākhyaṃ syād ekāhavat*:
those certain properties (*dharma*) which are mentioned in the twelve-day sacrifice that are additional to those of the one-day sacrifices.
"The Abhiplava occurs on each successive day; the Gorivīta occurs on each successive day.
Due to the addition of these extra [days], it would be designated by that name.
This [period] is the twelfth-day rite (dvādaśāha), known as Jyotis or Āyus.
How so?
Like the term "Ekāha.

Just as that very word "Jyotis" and the others are used for that same Ekāha sacrifice when specific additional (vaiśeṣika) characteristics have been introduced, so too here it will be used figuratively due to the commonality of the introduction of additional elements.
Just as, because the *pṛṣṭha* stotras of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) are present, the one-day rite (*ekāha*) Viśvajit is called a "six-day rite," as it is said,
"They call that one-day rite a six-day rite," so it is here as well.
If it is secondary, it does not bring about [the acquisition];
therefore, there is no acquisition of dharma from a name.
And this is also because of the indicative mark (liṅga).
Nor is it the case that additional [elements] are not expressed by the word, because the word denotes the ritual action (*kratu*).
Nor is the twelve-day rite to be performed;
what then?
The one-day rite.
What is the reason?

By means of the *codaka* (general transfer rule), that which belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) would apply; by means of the name (*nāmadheya*), that which belongs to the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) applies;
and the name is more powerful than the *codaka*.
Why?
Because it is perceptible.
The name is perceptible, whereas the injunction is inferential.
[Objection: But is not the *vidhyanta* (the concluding ritual procedure) also directly perceived? [Reply:

True, the *vidhyanta* is directly perceived in the archetype (*prakṛti*), but in the ectype (*vikṛti*) it is inferential; however, the name is directly perceived even in the ectype, and direct perception is stronger than inference; therefore, the duty belongs to the one-day sacrifice. [The opponent argues:
The indicative mark (*liṅga*) must be a property of the collective, because of the presumption (*arthāpatti*) that it serves that purpose, just like the substance.
Now, regarding the indicative mark (liṅga) that was taught—the observation of the twelve-fold attendance (upasattva)—its refutation is stated:
"The indicative mark would be a property of the aggregate;
this indicative mark would be a property of the aggregate."
The twelve-day rite is a collection of days;
it is enjoined for the sake of a fruit:
"Those desiring prosperity should undertake the twelve-day rite."
The Gavāmayana is also a distinct collection of days;
it is prescribed for that very same purpose, namely the accomplishment of the result.

By virtue of its taking on that function, it adopts the ritual details (*dharma*) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), and not by means of the *codaka* (transfer rule), just as in the case of the sacrificial materials.

Just as the properties (dharmas) heard in connection with a substance such as rice are obtained for its substitutes which take over its function, so it is not by means of the extended injunction (codaka);
nor is it so because the properties belong to the purpose, since the composite whole is merely a subordinate factor (guṇa).
Through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), there would be the acquisition of properties (dharma) in substances.
As for what was said, "like a substance" (*dravyavat*):
this is appropriate in the case of substances.

For in that case, wild rice (*nīvāra*) which has undergone the functional transformation (*kāryāpatti*) of rice acquires the properties of that [rice] by virtue of having undergone that functional transformation.
In this case, however, the reason stated—that there is no property of aggregation in the twelvefold [senses]—is not a valid example, like the case of a substance. He asks:
"How then is this a demonstration of a logical mark (*liṅga*)?"
To this it is replied:
there is the observation of a sign (liṅga) for that which is determined by activity.
In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, the first day is the twelve-day period's first day, which is the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra;
its characteristic feature is the performance of twelve Upasad rites.
By adopting that [feature], there is favor shown to the primary element.
In the case of adopting six *upasads* for the secondary [fires] such as the *jyotis* and others, there is no purpose whatsoever in bypassing the favor due to the primary [fire] at its appointed time;
therefore, twelve *upasads* are performed for the sake of favoring that [primary fire].
Thus, this observation is established by the primary application (*pravṛtti*), not by extension through the *codaka* rule.
For the injunction is weaker than the name;
and it will be stated [later]: "In a conflict between contradictory properties, there should be conformity with the majority;
or rather, the primary one [prevails] because of the original injunction, as in common worldly usage."
Now, as for the second indicative mark mentioned— the observation of the *vihāra* (re-arrangement) in the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice—
it is said in response: the observation of the *vihāra* is for the sake of a specific [context], because the *anārabhyavāda* (unattached injunctions) pertain to the archetype (*prakṛti*).
The performance of the eleven-day sacrifice (*ekādaśinī*) has been prescribed without specific reference to a particular day. The animals should originate from that [set] as their starting point.

Accordingly, they should be sacrificed one after another day by day: on the first day, they should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni; on the second, the ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī; on the third, the brown animal dedicated to Soma; and finally, the animal dedicated to Varuṇa.

Now, however, in the case of the *paryāyas*, they should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni on the first day, a ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī on the second, a brown animal dedicated to Soma on the third, and one dedicated to Varuṇa at the end.
Since those injunctions not based on a specific context (*anārabhyavāda*) serve the purpose of the archetype (*prakṛti*), they enter into the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Because there is no plurality of days in that [Jyotiṣṭoma], it is impossible [for them to apply there]; therefore, they reach the next archetype, the Dvādaśāha.
Furthermore, even in that case, the claim that [the term] "in the turnings of the Jyotis and others" is not tenable leads to the conclusion that the third *prakṛti* has entered into the Gavāmayana;
thus, this is the view of one who has arrived at such a position.
